What general structure do all standard amino acids share?
column3: amino group, carboxyl group, H, R group on α-carbon
column4: Every amino acid has a central α-carbon bonded to an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen, and a variable side chain (R group). This tetrahedral arrangement makes the α-carbon a chiral center in all amino acids except glycine.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How many standard amino acids are used to build proteins in humans?
column4: The 20 standard (proteinogenic) amino acids are encoded by the genetic code. Each has a unique R group that determines its chemical properties and role in protein structure.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acid lacks a chiral α-carbon?
column4: Glycine's R group is simply a hydrogen atom, making both substituents on the α-carbon identical (-H). This eliminates chirality and means glycine does not rotate plane-polarized light.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the general formula for an α-amino acid?
column4: The α-amino acid backbone places the amino group on the α-carbon (adjacent to the carboxyl). The R group varies by amino acid and determines side-chain properties.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acid has its amino group incorporated into a ring, making it an imino acid?
column4: Proline's R group cyclizes back onto the nitrogen, forming a pyrrolidine ring. This secondary amine (imino group) restricts backbone rotation and disrupts alpha-helices, often found at turns.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the pKa range of the α-amino group of most amino acids?
column4: The α-amino group (–NH3+) has a pKa around 9–10, meaning it is protonated (positively charged) at physiological pH (~7.4). At pH above the pKa it loses a proton and becomes –NH2.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: To which stereochemical configuration do almost all naturally occurring amino acids belong?
column4: Using Fischer projection convention, L-amino acids have the amino group on the left. In CIP (R/S) notation most L-amino acids are S, except cysteine which is R due to sulfur's high priority.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::absolute-configuration-at-the-position MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which reference compound defines the L/D nomenclature for amino acids?
column4: Amino acids are assigned L or D by analogy to L-glyceraldehyde. L-amino acids have the same relative configuration at the α-carbon as L-glyceraldehyde, placing –NH2 on the left in a Fischer projection.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::absolute-configuration-at-the-position MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: In R/S nomenclature, which L-amino acid is an exception and has the R configuration?
column4: All other L-amino acids are S at the α-carbon. Cysteine is R because its sulfur-containing side chain has higher CIP priority than the carboxyl group, reversing the ranking relative to other amino acids.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::absolute-configuration-at-the-position MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of stereoisomers are L- and D-amino acids?
column4: L- and D-amino acids are non-superimposable mirror images of each other — enantiomers. They have identical physical properties except for the direction they rotate plane-polarized light.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::absolute-configuration-at-the-position MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the predominant ionic form of an amino acid at its isoelectric point (pI)?
column4: At the pI, the amino acid carries both a positive charge (–NH3+) and a negative charge (–COO–), resulting in zero net charge. This is the zwitterionic form and represents the most stable state in solution.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is a zwitterion?
column3: Molecule with both positive and negative charges, net charge zero
column4: A zwitterion (dipolar ion) simultaneously bears a cationic site (protonated amino group) and an anionic site (deprotonated carboxyl), making it electrically neutral overall but internally charged.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How is the isoelectric point (pI) of a simple (non-ionizable side chain) amino acid calculated?
column4: For amino acids without ionizable side chains, pI is the average of the two α-carbon pKa values (carboxyl ~2 and amino ~9–10). For those with ionizable side chains, the two pKa values flanking the zwitterion are averaged.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: At physiological pH (7.4), what charge does the α-carboxyl group of a free amino acid carry?
column4: The α-carboxyl group has a pKa of ~2. Since physiological pH (7.4) is far above this pKa, the group is fully deprotonated and negatively charged at pH 7.4.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which direction do amino acids migrate in an electric field when the pH equals their pI?
column4: At the pI, the amino acid has zero net charge, so it experiences no net electrostatic force in an electric field. This principle underlies isoelectric focusing in gel electrophoresis.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Name the nine essential amino acids that humans cannot synthesize.
column3: His, Ile, Leu, Lys, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp, Val
column4: Mnemonic: 'PVT TIM HaLL' — Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Arg (conditionally), Leu, Lys. The nine unconditionally essential are listed above. They must be obtained from the diet.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::classifications MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acid is classified as conditionally essential in premature infants and individuals under metabolic stress?
column4: Arginine can be synthesized by adults via the urea cycle but may be insufficient during rapid growth or illness. It is therefore conditionally essential.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::classifications MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What structural feature classifies an amino acid as aromatic?
column3: Aromatic ring in the side chain
column4: Phe, Tyr, and Trp are the aromatic amino acids. Their conjugated ring systems absorb UV light (~280 nm for Tyr/Trp), which is used to estimate protein concentration spectrophotometrically.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::classifications MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acids are classified as branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)?
column4: BCAAs have aliphatic branched side chains and are metabolized primarily in muscle rather than the liver. They are important in muscle protein synthesis and energy metabolism.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::classifications MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Classify each: Asp, Glu, Asn, Gln — which are acidic and which are amide derivatives?
column3: Asp and Glu are acidic; Asn and Gln are amide derivatives
column4: Aspartate (Asp) and glutamate (Glu) carry ionizable carboxyl side chains (acidic). Asparagine (Asn) and glutamine (Gln) are their amide forms — the side-chain carboxyl is replaced by –CONH2, which is uncharged and polar.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::classifications MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which two amino acids have side chains that are acidic at physiological pH?
column4: Both carry a carboxyl group in their side chain with pKa ~3.7 (Asp) and ~4.1 (Glu). At pH 7.4 these groups are fully deprotonated, giving the side chains a –1 charge.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::acidic-or-basic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which three amino acids have basic side chains?
column4: Lys (pKa ~10.5), Arg (pKa ~12.5), and His (pKa ~6.0) carry nitrogen-containing side chains. At physiological pH, Lys and Arg are fully protonated (+1); His is mostly neutral (~10% protonated).
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::acidic-or-basic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the approximate pKa of histidine's imidazole side chain?
column4: The pKa of ~6 means histidine can toggle between protonated (+1) and neutral forms near physiological pH, making it ideal as an active-site acid/base catalyst in enzymes.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::acidic-or-basic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which basic amino acid has the highest pKa side chain, making it the most basic standard amino acid?
column4: Arginine's guanidinium group (–NH–C(=NH)–NH2) is stabilized by resonance delocalization over three nitrogen atoms, giving it an extremely high pKa and keeping it positively charged under virtually all physiological conditions.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::acidic-or-basic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Why is histidine uniquely suited as an enzyme active-site residue compared to Lys and Arg?
column3: Its pKa (~6) allows proton transfer near physiological pH
column4: Because histidine's pKa is near 7, small pH changes or the local protein environment can shift it between protonated and deprotonated forms, enabling it to act as a proton shuttle in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases).
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::acidic-or-basic MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acids are classified as hydrophobic?
column3: Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Pro, Phe, Trp, Met (and Gly)
column4: Hydrophobic amino acids have nonpolar, aliphatic or aromatic side chains. They tend to cluster in the interior of globular proteins, away from the aqueous environment, stabilizing the tertiary structure via the hydrophobic effect.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrophobic-or-hydrophilic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acids are polar and uncharged (hydrophilic but not ionized) at physiological pH?
column3: Ser, Thr, Cys, Tyr, Asn, Gln
column4: These residues contain –OH, –SH, or –CONH2 groups capable of hydrogen bonding but lacking net charge at pH 7.4. They are typically found on protein surfaces or in active sites where H-bonding is needed.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrophobic-or-hydrophilic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Why is tyrosine considered amphipathic among the aromatic amino acids?
column3: It has a polar hydroxyl group on an aromatic ring
column4: Tyrosine combines a hydrophobic benzene ring with a hydrophilic –OH group. The –OH can hydrogen bond (polar) while the ring contributes hydrophobic stacking interactions. Its pKa is ~10, so it is mainly uncharged at pH 7.4.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrophobic-or-hydrophilic MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acid's side chain can be phosphorylated on a hydroxyl group to regulate protein activity?
column4: Ser, Thr, and Tyr all carry –OH groups that kinases can phosphorylate, adding a negatively charged phosphate group. This post-translational modification is a major mechanism of signal transduction regulation.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrophobic-or-hydrophilic MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What bond forms between two cysteine residues in a disulfide bridge?
column4: Oxidation of two thiol (–SH) groups produces a disulfide bond (–S–S–), forming cystine. This intramolecular or intermolecular covalent cross-link stabilizes tertiary and quaternary protein structure.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::sulfur-linkage-for-cysteine-and-cystine MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is cystine?
column3: Two cysteines linked by a disulfide bond
column4: Cystine is the oxidized dimer of cysteine. The disulfide bond is reversible — reducing agents (e.g., β-mercaptoethanol, DTT) break it back to two free thiols, which is exploited in protein denaturation experiments.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::sulfur-linkage-for-cysteine-and-cystine MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What reaction type converts two cysteine –SH groups into a disulfide bond?
column4: Each thiol loses one hydrogen (is oxidized), forming the –S–S– bond. The reverse process (reduction) requires reducing agents that donate electrons/hydrogen to break the disulfide.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::sulfur-linkage-for-cysteine-and-cystine MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: In which cellular compartment are disulfide bonds typically stable and functional?
column4: The ER lumen and extracellular environment are oxidizing. The cytoplasm is reducing (due to glutathione), so disulfide bonds in cytosolic proteins are uncommon and unstable under normal conditions.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::sulfur-linkage-for-cysteine-and-cystine MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which other sulfur-containing amino acid is standard, and how does its side chain differ from cysteine?
column3: Methionine; has a thioether (–S–CH3), not a free thiol
column4: Methionine's sulfur is in a thioether linkage (C–S–C), which cannot form disulfide bonds. Methionine is also the universal start codon amino acid (AUG) in eukaryotes.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::sulfur-linkage-for-cysteine-and-cystine MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of bond is a peptide bond?
column3: Amide bond (C–N) between carboxyl and amino groups
column4: A peptide bond forms by condensation: the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, releasing water. The resulting C–N bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What small molecule is released during peptide bond formation?
column4: Peptide bond formation is a dehydration (condensation) reaction. One water molecule is lost per peptide bond formed, which is why protein synthesis requires energy input to drive this thermodynamically unfavorable reaction.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the consequence of partial double-bond character in a peptide bond?
column3: The peptide bond is planar and cannot rotate freely
column4: Resonance delocalization gives the C–N bond ~40% double-bond character. This restricts rotation and forces the six atoms of the peptide unit (Cα-CO-NH-Cα) into a rigid plane, constraining backbone conformation.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What are the two backbone dihedral angles that CAN rotate in a polypeptide chain?
column4: Phi (φ) is the N–Cα bond rotation; psi (ψ) is the Cα–C(O) bond rotation. The ω angle (across the peptide bond) is fixed at ~180° (trans). Allowed φ/ψ combinations are mapped in a Ramachandran plot.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the predominant configuration (cis or trans) of peptide bonds, and why?
column3: Trans; minimizes steric clash between R groups
column4: In the trans configuration, adjacent R groups are on opposite sides of the peptide bond, reducing steric strain. Cis is rare (~0.1%) except before proline (~10% cis due to proline's cyclic structure).
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: By convention, from which end is a polypeptide sequence written and read?
column4: Polypeptide sequences are always written left (N-terminus) to right (C-terminus), mirroring the direction of ribosomal synthesis (N→C). The N-terminus has a free –NH2 and the C-terminus has a free –COOH.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of reaction is protein hydrolysis?
column3: Hydrolysis (addition of water to break amide bond)
column4: Water is added across the peptide bond: the carbonyl carbon bonds to –OH and the nitrogen bonds to –H, regenerating two separate amino acids. This is the reverse of condensation.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What reagent completely hydrolyzes all peptide bonds in a protein to free amino acids in the laboratory?
column4: Acid hydrolysis with 6 M HCl is the standard method for amino acid analysis. It destroys Trp and partially degrades Ser/Thr, but liberates all other amino acids for quantitation by amino acid analyzers.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acid is completely destroyed during standard acid hydrolysis (6 M HCl) of proteins?
column4: Tryptophan's indole ring is acid-labile and is oxidized/degraded under the harsh acidic conditions (6 M HCl, 110°C). Tryptophan content must be determined separately using basic hydrolysis or spectroscopy.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which enzymes catalyze hydrolysis of peptide bonds in the digestive system?
column4: Proteases are serine, cysteine, or aspartyl proteases that cleave peptide bonds. Pepsin acts in the stomach (acidic pH); trypsin and chymotrypsin act in the small intestine (neutral-basic pH) from pancreatic secretion.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: After which amino acids does trypsin cleave peptide bonds?
column4: Trypsin is specific for peptide bonds on the C-terminal side of Lys and Arg. This specificity arises from an Asp residue in its binding pocket that forms an ionic interaction with the positively charged side chains.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: After which amino acids does chymotrypsin cleave peptide bonds?
column4: Chymotrypsin's hydrophobic binding pocket accommodates bulky aromatic side chains. It cleaves on the C-terminal side of these residues. This specificity is used in peptide mapping and protein sequencing.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Is peptide bond hydrolysis thermodynamically favorable or unfavorable under physiological conditions?
column4: Hydrolysis of amide bonds is exergonic (ΔG < 0) under physiological conditions. However, it proceeds very slowly without a catalyst due to a high kinetic barrier, which is why proteases are required for rapid digestion.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the α-carbon in an amino acid?
column3: Carbon directly bonded to the carboxyl group and amino group
column4: The α-carbon is the central chiral carbon of an amino acid, bearing the amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, and R group. The 'α' designation reflects its position immediately adjacent (alpha) to the carboxyl group.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What distinguishes an α-amino acid from a β-amino acid?
column3: Amino group on α-carbon vs. β-carbon
column4: In α-amino acids (all 20 standard), the amino group is on the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl. In β-amino acids (non-standard), the amino group is one carbon farther. β-alanine is a metabolically relevant β-amino acid (found in carnosine).
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the relationship between an amino acid's pI and its charge at physiological pH (7.4)?
column3: If pI < 7.4 → negative charge; if pI > 7.4 → positive charge
column4: At pH above its pI an amino acid has donated protons and carries net negative charge; at pH below its pI it retains extra protons and carries net positive charge. This governs electrophoretic migration and protein solubility.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acids have a pI above 7 (basic pI)?
column4: Basic amino acids have positively charged side chains that must be deprotonated before the molecule reaches net zero charge, pushing the pI above 7. Arg has the highest pI (~10.8), followed by Lys (~9.7) and His (~7.6).
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which amino acids have pI values below 7 (acidic pI)?
column4: Acidic amino acids have extra carboxyl side chains that must be protonated before net zero charge is achieved, lowering the pI below 7. Asp pI ≈ 2.8; Glu pI ≈ 3.2.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::amino-acids-as-dipolar-ions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the hydrophobic effect in the context of protein folding?
column3: Nonpolar side chains cluster away from water to minimize entropy loss
column4: Water forms ordered cages around nonpolar groups (unfavorable entropy). Protein folding buries hydrophobic residues in the interior, releasing these ordered water molecules and increasing overall entropy — a primary driving force for folding.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrophobic-or-hydrophilic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What two amino acids are classified as polar but are also considered hydrophobic at high concentrations due to their aromatic rings?
column4: Phe is entirely nonpolar/hydrophobic. Trp has a polar indole NH but is still largely hydrophobic due to its large aromatic ring. Both are found in protein interiors. (Note: Tyr has a –OH making it more amphipathic.)
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrophobic-or-hydrophilic MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the name for the product of two cysteine residues joined by a disulfide bond when considered as a single amino acid unit?
column4: Cystine is the oxidized dimeric form consisting of two cysteines linked by –S–S–. In laboratory amino acid analysis it can appear as a distinct peak, and nutritional texts sometimes list it separately from cysteine.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::sulfur-linkage-for-cysteine-and-cystine MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What reducing agent is commonly used in the lab to break disulfide bonds?
column4: BME and DTT donate electrons/hydrogens to reduce –S–S– back to two –SH groups. They are added to SDS-PAGE sample buffer when fully denatured, reduced proteins are needed (e.g., molecular weight determination).
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::sulfur-linkage-for-cysteine-and-cystine MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the peptide bond's bond length compared to a pure C–N single bond?
column3: Shorter than a C–N single bond; longer than a C=N double bond
column4: Resonance gives the peptide C–N bond ~40% double-bond character, shortening it to ~1.33 Å (between a C–N single bond at 1.45 Å and a C=N double bond at 1.27 Å). This partial double bond restricts rotation.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which end of a polypeptide chain retains a free amino group?
column4: The N-terminal amino acid has its α-amino group uninvolved in a peptide bond, leaving it free (–NH2 or –NH3+ depending on pH). Protein sequencing (Edman degradation) and many post-translational modifications target the N-terminus.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the difference between a dipeptide and a polypeptide?
column3: Dipeptide: 2 amino acids; polypeptide: many amino acids (typically >10)
column4: Oligopeptides have 2–10 residues; polypeptides generally have more than 10. The term 'protein' typically refers to one or more polypeptide chains folded into a functional three-dimensional structure.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::peptide-linkage-polypeptides-and-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Partial acid hydrolysis of a protein yields what products?
column3: Mixture of peptide fragments and some free amino acids
column4: Under milder or shorter acid hydrolysis conditions, not all peptide bonds are cleaved. This generates peptide fragments of varying lengths. Complete hydrolysis (prolonged treatment) is needed to fully convert a protein to individual amino acids.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does base (alkaline) hydrolysis differ from acid hydrolysis of proteins?
column3: Base preserves Trp but destroys Cys, Ser, Thr (via elimination)
column4: Alkaline hydrolysis (NaOH) does not degrade tryptophan, allowing its quantitation. However, it causes β-elimination in serine, threonine, and cysteine and racemization of amino acids, limiting its analytical use.
column8: concept::BB::1A::amino_acids MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::amino-acids::hydrolysis MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What are the four levels of protein structure?
column4: Each level describes a progressively more complex arrangement: amino acid sequence, local folding, overall 3D shape, and multi-subunit assembly.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::structure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which type of bond is the backbone of all levels of protein structure?
column4: Peptide bonds link amino acids via a condensation reaction between the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the next; they have partial double-bond character and are planar.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::structure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the general formula for an amino acid?
column4: All 20 standard amino acids share this backbone; the R group (side chain) determines identity and chemical properties.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::structure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What property of the peptide bond restricts rotation and maintains planarity?
column4: Electron delocalization between the carbonyl carbon and amide nitrogen gives the peptide bond ~40% double-bond character, locking the six atoms in a plane.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::structure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which two dihedral angles describe rotation in the protein backbone?
column4: Phi is the N–Cα bond rotation; psi is the Cα–C bond rotation. Omega (ω) is fixed near 180° due to peptide bond planarity.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::structure MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the directionality convention for writing a polypeptide sequence?
column4: By convention, the free amino (N) terminus is written at the left and the free carboxyl (C) terminus at the right.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::structure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What defines the primary structure of a protein?
column4: Primary structure is the covalent backbone: the specific order of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, encoded directly by the gene.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::1-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of bond links amino acids in primary structure?
column4: Peptide bonds form by condensation (loss of water) between the α-carboxyl of one amino acid and the α-amino group of the next.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::1-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does a single amino acid change cause sickle-cell disease?
column3: Glutamate → valine at position 6 of β-globin
column4: This primary structure change makes HbS hydrophobic at that position, causing polymerization under low O2 — a classic MCAT example of primary structure affecting function.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::1-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What information is sufficient to determine a protein's higher-order structure, according to Anfinsen's dogma?
column4: Anfinsen's experiment with ribonuclease showed that sequence alone encodes folding information; higher-order structure is thermodynamically driven by the primary sequence.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::1-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which end of a growing polypeptide is elongated during translation?
column4: Ribosomes add incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs to the C-terminal end; the N-terminus is synthesized first.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::1-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is secondary structure in proteins?
column3: Local regular folding stabilized by hydrogen bonds
column4: Secondary structure refers to repeating patterns (α-helix, β-sheet) arising from H-bonds between backbone amide NH and carbonyl C=O groups.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::2-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What bonds stabilize secondary structure?
column3: Hydrogen bonds (backbone NH to backbone C=O)
column4: Unlike tertiary interactions, secondary structure H-bonds involve only backbone atoms, not side chains.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::2-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How many amino acids are in one complete turn of an α-helix?
column4: The α-helix rises 1.5 Å per residue with a pitch of 5.4 Å per turn. Side chains project outward.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::2-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: In an α-helix, residue i hydrogen-bonds to which residue?
column4: Each backbone NH donates an H-bond to the C=O of the residue four positions earlier in the sequence, creating a right-handed helix.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::2-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What are the two main types of β-sheet arrangements?
column4: Parallel β-sheets have strands running in the same N→C direction; antiparallel strands run in opposite directions. Antiparallel H-bonds are more linear and thus stronger.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::2-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which secondary structure element is often found at the turns connecting β-strands?
column4: β-turns allow the polypeptide chain to reverse direction; they are commonly stabilized by an H-bond between residues i and i+3.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::2-structure-of-proteins MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is tertiary structure?
column3: Overall 3D shape of a single polypeptide chain
column4: Tertiary structure results from interactions among side chains (R groups), including hydrophobic, ionic, H-bond, and disulfide interactions.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::3-structure-of-proteins-role-of-proline-cystine-hydrophobic-bonding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Why does proline disrupt α-helices?
column3: Its N is in a rigid ring; no backbone NH for H-bonding
column4: Proline's pyrrolidine ring fixes the φ angle and eliminates the amide H, preventing the H-bonds needed for helix formation — it acts as a 'helix breaker.'
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::3-structure-of-proteins-role-of-proline-cystine-hydrophobic-bonding MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What bond constitutes a 'cystine' residue in protein tertiary structure?
column3: Disulfide bond (–S–S–) between two cysteine side chains
column4: Cystine is the oxidized dimer of cysteine; disulfide bonds are covalent and provide structural rigidity, especially in extracellular proteins.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::3-structure-of-proteins-role-of-proline-cystine-hydrophobic-bonding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the primary driving force for tertiary structure formation in globular proteins?
column3: Hydrophobic effect (burial of nonpolar side chains)
column4: Nonpolar residues cluster in the interior away from water; this is entropically driven by the release of ordered water molecules.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::3-structure-of-proteins-role-of-proline-cystine-hydrophobic-bonding MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which reagent breaks disulfide bonds during protein denaturation studies?
column4: These reducing agents convert disulfide bonds back to free thiols (-SH), helping unfold proteins like in Anfinsen's ribonuclease experiment.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::3-structure-of-proteins-role-of-proline-cystine-hydrophobic-bonding MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: In what cellular compartment are disulfide bonds typically formed?
column4: The ER is oxidizing; cytoplasm is reducing. Secreted and membrane proteins form disulfide bonds in the ER with help from protein disulfide isomerase (PDI).
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::3-structure-of-proteins-role-of-proline-cystine-hydrophobic-bonding MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is quaternary protein structure?
column3: Assembly of two or more polypeptide subunits
column4: Quaternary structure describes how individual polypeptide chains (subunits) associate non-covalently (and sometimes via disulfides) into a functional complex.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::4-structure-of-proteins-bio-bc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is a homodimer vs. a heterodimer?
column3: Homodimer: two identical subunits; heterodimer: two different subunits
column4: Hemoglobin (α2β2) is a heterotetramer; many transcription factors bind DNA as homodimers or heterodimers.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::4-structure-of-proteins-bio-bc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the quaternary structure of hemoglobin?
column3: Two α and two β subunits (α2β2 tetramer)
column4: Hemoglobin's quaternary structure enables cooperative oxygen binding and the Bohr effect — features absent in the monomeric myoglobin.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::4-structure-of-proteins-bio-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What forces hold quaternary subunits together?
column4: Most quaternary contacts are noncovalent; some complexes (e.g., IgG antibody) also use interchain disulfide bonds.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::4-structure-of-proteins-bio-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is an allosteric protein, and why does quaternary structure matter for allostery?
column3: Protein whose activity changes upon ligand binding at a non-active site; requires multiple subunits for cooperativity
column4: Allostery requires conformational communication between subunits — only possible with quaternary structure. Hemoglobin is the classic MCAT example.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::4-structure-of-proteins-bio-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is conformational stability of a protein?
column3: Resistance of native fold to unfolding
column4: Stability reflects the net free energy difference (ΔG) between folded and unfolded states; most proteins are only marginally stable (~5–20 kcal/mol).
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::conformational-stability MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which interactions contribute most to the thermodynamic stability of the folded state?
column4: Hydrophobic burial provides the main enthalpic/entropic driving force; H-bonds and van der Waals interactions also contribute, while conformational entropy opposes folding.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::conformational-stability MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is a molten globule?
column3: Partially folded intermediate with secondary structure but disordered tertiary structure
column4: Molten globules are on the folding pathway; they retain secondary structure and compactness but lack the rigid side-chain packing of the native state.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::conformational-stability MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does temperature affect protein conformational stability?
column3: High temperature increases thermal motion, disrupting noncovalent bonds and denaturing the protein
column4: Thermophilic organisms have proteins with extra disulfide bonds and hydrophobic contacts to remain stable at high temperatures.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::conformational-stability MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is protein denaturation?
column3: Loss of native 3D structure without breaking peptide bonds
column4: Denaturation disrupts noncovalent interactions (and disulfide bonds if reducing agent present), unfolding the protein. Primary structure is preserved.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::denaturing-and-folding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Name four agents that can denature proteins.
column4: Heat disrupts all noncovalent bonds; extreme pH alters ionization; urea/guanidinium disrupt H-bonds; SDS coats protein in negative charge and unfolds it.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::denaturing-and-folding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the role of molecular chaperones in protein folding?
column4: Chaperones (e.g., Hsp70, GroEL) bind exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or stressed proteins, providing a protected environment for proper folding.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::denaturing-and-folding MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Is denaturation always irreversible?
column3: No; some proteins refold spontaneously (e.g., ribonuclease)
column4: Anfinsen showed ribonuclease refolds correctly after removal of urea and β-mercaptoethanol, demonstrating sequence-encoded folding information.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::denaturing-and-folding MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of protein disease results from misfolding and aggregation into β-sheet-rich fibrils?
column4: Alzheimer's (Aβ peptide), Parkinson's (α-synuclein), and prion diseases all involve pathological β-sheet aggregation — a hard MCAT concept.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::denaturing-and-folding MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the hydrophobic effect?
column3: Tendency of nonpolar groups to cluster away from water
column4: Driven by entropy gain: water molecules around nonpolar solutes form ordered cages (decreased entropy); burying hydrophobic groups releases this ordered water, increasing overall entropy.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::hydrophobic-interactions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Are hydrophobic interactions enthalpic or entropic in nature?
column3: Primarily entropic (driven by entropy increase of water)
column4: Burying nonpolar groups releases ordered water molecules, increasing solvent entropy (ΔS > 0). The enthalpy term is small or slightly unfavorable.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::hydrophobic-interactions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Where are hydrophobic amino acid side chains typically found in a globular protein?
column4: Nonpolar residues (Val, Leu, Ile, Phe, Met) pack in the hydrophobic core; charged/polar residues face the aqueous exterior.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::hydrophobic-interactions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How do hydrophobic interactions contribute to membrane bilayer stability?
column3: Fatty acid tails cluster in bilayer interior to avoid water
column4: The same hydrophobic effect that drives protein folding drives phospholipid self-assembly into bilayers — a cross-concept MCAT link.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::hydrophobic-interactions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the solvation layer (hydration shell) around a protein?
column3: Ordered water molecules surrounding the protein surface
column4: Polar and charged surface residues attract water into a structured layer. This solvation shell stabilizes the protein in solution.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::solvation-layer-entropy-bc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does the solvation layer relate to entropy during protein folding?
column3: Burial of hydrophobic surface releases ordered water, increasing entropy
column4: When nonpolar groups are exposed, surrounding water forms a low-entropy clathrate-like cage. Folding buries these groups, releasing water and increasing ΔS of the system.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::solvation-layer-entropy-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the hydrophobic collapse model of protein folding?
column3: Nonpolar residues rapidly collapse to form a compact core first
column4: The chain first collapses around the hydrophobic core (driven by the solvation entropy gain), then secondary/tertiary contacts refine — a key model in biochemical folding kinetics.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::solvation-layer-entropy-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does salt affect the solvation layer and protein solubility (salting-out effect)?
column3: High salt competes for water, stripping the solvation layer and precipitating protein
column4: Salting-out (e.g., ammonium sulfate precipitation) removes water from the protein surface, reducing solubility — used in protein purification.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::solvation-layer-entropy-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What does gel filtration (size-exclusion) chromatography separate proteins by?
column4: Larger proteins elute first because they cannot enter the pores of the resin beads; smaller proteins enter and are retarded.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::separation-techniques MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What does ion-exchange chromatography separate proteins by?
column4: Proteins bind to oppositely charged resin and are eluted by increasing salt or changing pH. Cation-exchange resins bind positively charged proteins.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::separation-techniques MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What does affinity chromatography exploit to purify a protein?
column4: The column resin carries a specific ligand; only the target protein binds and is then eluted with competing ligand or altered conditions — high selectivity.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::separation-techniques MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: In SDS-PAGE, what does SDS do to proteins?
column3: Denatures and coats them with uniform negative charge
column4: SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate) unfolds proteins and binds ~1.4 g SDS/g protein, giving all proteins a uniform charge-to-mass ratio so they migrate by size only.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::separation-techniques MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What technique separates proteins by both size and charge in two dimensions?
column4: First dimension: isoelectric focusing separates by pI. Second dimension: SDS-PAGE separates by molecular weight. Used in proteomics.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::separation-techniques MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the isoelectric point (pI) of a protein?
column3: pH at which the protein has zero net charge
column4: At the pI, the number of positive charges equals negative charges. The protein has minimum solubility and does not migrate in an electric field at this pH.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::isoelectric-point MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How is the pI of a simple amino acid calculated?
column3: Average of the two pKa values flanking the neutral (zwitterion) form
column4: For a neutral amino acid: pI = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2. For acidic amino acids, use the two lower pKas; for basic, use the two higher pKas.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::isoelectric-point MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: At a pH above the pI, what is the net charge of a protein?
column4: Above the pI, excess base deprotonates groups; the protein carries net negative charge. At pH below pI, the protein is net positive.
column8: concept::BB::1A::protein_structure MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1A::protein-structure::isoelectric-point MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the approximate pI of a protein enriched in lysine and arginine residues?
column4: Lys (pKa ~10.5) and Arg (pKa ~12.5) are positively charged at physiological pH; proteins rich in them require high pH to reach neutrality.

column1: Which amino acid has the highest pKa side chain among the 20 standard amino acids?
column4: The guanidinium group of Arg is almost always protonated at physiological pH, making it a stronger base than Lys (pKa ~10.5) or His (pKa ~6).

column1: What is electrophoresis?
column3: Migration of charged molecules in an electric field
column4: Proteins (or nucleic acids) move toward the electrode of opposite charge; speed depends on charge, size, and shape.

column1: In native PAGE (without SDS), what properties determine a protein's migration rate?
column4: Without SDS, proteins retain their native conformation and charge; migration reflects all three properties simultaneously.

column1: Which direction do negatively charged proteins migrate in gel electrophoresis?
column4: Negatively charged molecules are attracted to the positive pole. In standard SDS-PAGE setups, proteins migrate from the negative (cathode, top) to positive (anode, bottom).

column1: What is isoelectric focusing (IEF)?
column3: Electrophoresis in a pH gradient; proteins migrate to their pI
column4: A stable pH gradient is established in the gel; each protein stops migrating when it reaches the pH equal to its pI (net charge = 0).

column1: What molecular weight marker is used to calibrate SDS-PAGE gels?
column4: Known-size proteins run alongside samples; their migration distance creates a standard curve for estimating unknown protein molecular weights.

column1: What term describes a protein's ability to associate noncovalently with a ligand at a specific site?
column4: Protein binding is a reversible, noncovalent interaction at a defined binding site; specificity arises from complementary shape and chemical properties between protein and ligand.

column1: What quantity measures the affinity of a protein for its ligand (lower value = tighter binding)?
column4: Kd = [protein][ligand]/[complex]; a lower Kd indicates higher affinity because less free ligand is needed to half-saturate the binding sites.

column1: Which type of noncovalent interaction is most often the primary driver of protein-ligand binding specificity?
column4: Shape complementarity ensures selectivity; hydrogen bonds, electrostatic interactions, van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic effects all contribute to binding energy.

column1: What protein is the classic model for cooperative ligand binding in biochemistry?
column4: Hemoglobin's four subunits show cooperative O2 binding; binding at one subunit increases O2 affinity at others, producing a sigmoidal saturation curve.

column1: What term describes the phenomenon where binding of one ligand increases binding affinity for subsequent ligands?
column4: Positive cooperativity is demonstrated by hemoglobin; it produces a sigmoidal O2-saturation curve rather than the hyperbolic curve seen in myoglobin.

column1: What shape is the oxygen-saturation curve of myoglobin (a noncooperative O2-binding protein)?
column4: Myoglobin has a single binding site; its saturation follows simple Michaelis-Menten-like kinetics, giving a hyperbolic curve. Cooperative proteins (hemoglobin) give a sigmoidal curve.

column1: What allosteric effector decreases hemoglobin's O2 affinity by stabilizing the T (deoxy) state?
column4: 2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T state, shifting the O2-saturation curve rightward and facilitating O2 release in tissues.

column1: What structural change distinguishes the T (tense) state from the R (relaxed) state of hemoglobin?
column3: T state has lower O2 affinity; R state has higher O2 affinity
column4: The T state is stabilized by salt bridges between subunits. O2 binding breaks these bridges, converting hemoglobin to the R state with higher affinity for additional O2.

column1: What effect does a decrease in pH have on hemoglobin's O2 affinity (Bohr effect)?
column4: Increased H+ (lower pH) protonates histidine residues, stabilizing the T state and promoting O2 release — important in metabolically active tissues that produce CO2 and lactic acid.

column1: Which two features distinguish a competitive inhibitor's binding from a noncompetitive inhibitor's binding in terms of site?
column3: Competitive binds active site; noncompetitive binds allosteric site
column4: Competitive inhibitors can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration; noncompetitive inhibitors lower Vmax regardless of substrate concentration because they bind a separate site.

column1: What class of proteins constitutes the primary molecular recognition elements of the humoral immune response?
column4: Antibodies are glycoproteins secreted by plasma cells (differentiated B cells); they bind antigens with high specificity via their variable regions.

column1: What is the basic structural unit of an antibody?
column3: Two heavy chains + two light chains (Y-shaped tetramer)
column4: The four chains are held together by disulfide bonds; each chain has a constant (C) region and a variable (V) region. The variable regions form the antigen-binding site (Fab).

column1: What region of an antibody directly contacts and binds antigen?
column4: CDRs are hypervariable loops within the V regions of both heavy and light chains; their sequence diversity generates the enormous antibody repertoire.

column1: Name the five classes (isotypes) of human immunoglobulins.
column4: Isotype is determined by the heavy-chain constant region. IgG is most abundant in serum; IgA is in secretions; IgM is pentameric and the first produced; IgE mediates allergy.

column1: Which immunoglobulin isotype is the predominant antibody in secondary (anamnestic) immune responses?
column4: IgG is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin, crosses the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus, and is the main antibody produced in secondary immune responses.

column1: What is the function of the Fc region of an antibody?
column3: Mediates effector functions (complement activation, phagocyte binding, ADCC)
column4: The Fc region interacts with Fc receptors on immune cells and with complement component C1q, linking antigen recognition to destruction mechanisms.

column1: Which immunoglobulin isotype is a pentamer and the first antibody produced during a primary immune response?
column4: IgM's pentameric structure gives it 10 antigen-binding sites (high avidity) and makes it very efficient at activating complement, important early in infection before IgG rises.

column1: What cell type is responsible for producing antibodies?
column4: Naive B cells differentiate into plasma cells after activation by antigen (with T-cell help for T-dependent antigens); plasma cells are essentially antibody factories.

column1: What protein on cytotoxic T cells recognizes peptide antigens presented by MHC class I molecules?
column4: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognize endogenous (intracellular) peptides on MHC I present on all nucleated cells; CD4+ helper T cells recognize MHC II on antigen-presenting cells.

column1: Which complement pathway is activated directly by antibody-antigen complexes?
column4: IgM or IgG bound to antigen recruits C1q, initiating the classical complement cascade; the lectin pathway is triggered by mannose-binding lectin; the alternative pathway is antibody-independent.

column1: What term describes the increased binding strength that results from multiple simultaneous interactions between a multivalent antibody and a multivalent antigen?
column4: Avidity is distinct from affinity (strength of a single binding interaction); pentameric IgM has lower affinity per site than IgG but much higher avidity due to 10 binding sites.

column1: What is the primary nonenzymatic function of motor proteins such as myosin and kinesin?
column3: Convert chemical energy (ATP) into mechanical movement
column4: Motor proteins are ATPases that undergo conformational changes upon ATP hydrolysis, enabling directional movement along cytoskeletal filaments without acting as catalysts in metabolism.

column1: Along which cytoskeletal filament does myosin II move during muscle contraction?
column4: Myosin II is a conventional two-headed myosin; its heads walk toward the barbed (+) end of actin filaments, sliding them past thick (myosin) filaments to shorten the sarcomere.

column1: Along which cytoskeletal structure do kinesin and dynein move?
column4: Kinesin generally moves toward the plus end (anterograde, toward cell periphery); dynein moves toward the minus end (retrograde, toward the cell body/nucleus).

column1: Which motor protein moves cargo from the cell body toward the axon terminal (anterograde transport)?
column4: Kinesin walks toward the plus end of microtubules; in neurons the plus end is at the axon terminal, so kinesin carries vesicles and organelles away from the soma.

column1: Which motor protein is responsible for retrograde axonal transport (from axon terminal toward the cell body)?
column4: Dynein moves toward the minus end of microtubules; in axons this means movement back to the cell body — used for recycling organelles and as a route for certain pathogens/toxins.

column1: What molecule provides the energy for motor protein movement, and which step in the cross-bridge cycle releases the motor from the filament?
column3: ATP; ATP binding releases myosin from actin
column4: In muscle, myosin is in rigor (tightly bound to actin) after the power stroke. ATP binding to myosin causes its release from actin — this is why rigor mortis occurs when ATP is depleted.

column1: What is the role of tropomyosin in regulating myosin-actin interaction in skeletal muscle?
column3: Blocks myosin binding sites on actin at rest
column4: Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin in the absence of Ca2+. Ca2+ binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin to expose the sites and allow cross-bridge formation.

column1: Which protein in the troponin complex directly binds Ca2+ to initiate skeletal muscle contraction?
column4: The troponin complex has three subunits: TnC (Ca2+ binding), TnI (inhibitory, holds tropomyosin in blocking position), and TnT (binds tropomyosin). Ca2+ binding to TnC releases inhibition.

column1: What structural feature allows dynein to generate force along microtubules, distinguishing it from kinesin?
column3: Dynein has a large AAA+ ring domain with a stalk that contacts microtubules
column4: Dynein's motor domain is a hexameric ring of AAA+ ATPases; ATP hydrolysis in AAA1 drives the power stroke via conformational changes transmitted through the stalk — distinct from kinesin's simpler two-headed mechanism.

column1: What is the primary role of an enzyme in a biological reaction?
column4: Enzymes are biological catalysts — they increase reaction rates without being consumed or permanently altered. Almost all enzymes are proteins.

column1: Are enzymes consumed during the reactions they catalyze?
column4: Enzymes are regenerated after each catalytic cycle and can catalyze many reaction cycles, making them true catalysts.

column1: What type of macromolecule are most enzymes?
column4: Most enzymes are globular proteins, though a small class of catalytic RNAs called ribozymes also exists. The MCAT focuses on protein enzymes.

column1: Do enzymes alter the equilibrium constant (Keq) of a reaction?
column4: Enzymes speed up the rate of reaching equilibrium but do not change the thermodynamic equilibrium position (Keq or ΔG°) of the reaction.

column1: What term describes the maximum rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction when substrate is saturating?
column4: Vmax is reached when all enzyme active sites are occupied; adding more substrate cannot increase the rate further at fixed enzyme concentration.

column1: Which enzyme class catalyzes the transfer of phosphate groups?
column4: Kinases are a subset of transferases that specifically transfer phosphoryl groups, e.g., hexokinase transfers a phosphate from ATP to glucose.

column1: Which enzyme class catalyzes oxidation-reduction reactions?
column4: Oxidoreductases include dehydrogenases, oxidases, and reductases; they transfer electrons (often as H) between donors and acceptors.

column1: Which enzyme class catalyzes hydrolysis reactions?
column4: Hydrolases cleave covalent bonds using water, e.g., proteases, lipases, nucleases, and phosphatases.

column1: Which enzyme class catalyzes the addition or removal of groups to form double bonds, without hydrolysis or oxidation?
column4: Lyases break C-C, C-O, or C-N bonds non-hydrolytically; when running in reverse they are called synthases (e.g., pyruvate decarboxylase).

column1: Which enzyme class catalyzes isomerization reactions?
column4: Isomerases rearrange atoms within a molecule without adding or removing atoms, e.g., phosphoglucose isomerase in glycolysis.

column1: Which enzyme class uses ATP hydrolysis to form new bonds?
column4: Ligases (synthetases) couple bond formation to ATP hydrolysis, e.g., DNA ligase and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.

column1: Which enzyme class is also known as 'synthases' when running in the synthetic direction?
column4: Lyases that catalyze condensation reactions (the reverse of cleavage) are often called synthases, e.g., citrate synthase.

column1: What does an enzyme do to the activation energy (Ea) of a reaction?
column4: By stabilizing the transition state, enzymes reduce Ea so that more substrate molecules have sufficient energy to react, increasing reaction rate.

column1: Does lowering activation energy change the overall ΔG of the reaction?
column4: Activation energy pertains to the kinetic barrier, not the thermodynamic favorability; ΔG (and Keq) is unchanged by enzyme catalysis.

column1: How do enzymes stabilize the transition state to lower activation energy?
column3: Preferential binding of the transition state
column4: Active site residues form optimal non-covalent interactions with the transition state structure, lowering its energy relative to the substrate ground state.

column1: What is a transition state in an enzymatic reaction?
column3: Highest-energy unstable intermediate on the reaction coordinate
column4: The transition state is not an isolatable species; enzymes lower its energy, which is why competitive inhibitors that mimic it bind tightly.

column1: What is the term for the specific molecule that binds to an enzyme's active site?
column4: The substrate is the reactant that the enzyme acts upon; it binds to the active site to form the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex.

column1: What property describes an enzyme's ability to bind and act on only certain substrates?
column4: Specificity arises from the complementary shape, charge, and chemical properties of the active site relative to the substrate.

column1: Which type of enzyme specificity requires an exact structural match, accepting only one substrate?
column4: Urease, which hydrolyzes only urea, is the classic example of absolute specificity; most enzymes have broader group or linkage specificity.

column1: What is 'stereospecificity' in enzyme function?
column3: Ability to distinguish between stereoisomers (e.g., L vs D)
column4: Most enzymes act on only one enantiomer; for example, amino acid oxidases are specific for either L- or D-amino acids.

column1: What is the Michaelis constant (Km) a measure of?
column4: A low Km means high affinity (enzyme reaches half-Vmax at low [S]); Km approximates the dissociation constant of the ES complex when k2 << k-1.

column1: In the lock-and-key model, what does the 'lock' represent?
column4: The lock-and-key model (Fischer, 1894) proposes that the active site is rigid and perfectly complementary to the substrate in shape.

column1: Where on an enzyme does the substrate bind?
column4: The active site is a specific pocket or cleft on the enzyme surface, formed by amino acid residues that contact and chemically transform the substrate.

column1: Which amino acid residues typically participate in catalysis at the active site?
column3: Catalytic residues (e.g., Ser, His, Asp, Cys, Lys)
column4: These residues donate/accept protons or form covalent intermediates; the serine protease catalytic triad (Ser-His-Asp) is a classic MCAT example.

column1: What name is given to the non-catalytic region of an enzyme that undergoes conformational change to affect the active site?
column4: Allosteric sites are distinct from the active site; effector binding there causes conformational changes that regulate enzyme activity.

column1: What does the lock-and-key model assume about the active site shape before substrate binding?
column3: Active site is pre-formed and rigid (complementary to substrate)
column4: This contrasts with the induced-fit model; the lock-and-key model explains tight substrate specificity but does not account for conformational changes.

column1: Who proposed the induced-fit model of enzyme-substrate binding?
column4: Koshland proposed that substrate binding induces a conformational change in the enzyme that optimally positions catalytic residues around the substrate.

column1: What occurs to the enzyme's active site when the substrate binds in the induced-fit model?
column3: Active site changes shape to fit the substrate
column4: The conformational change brings catalytic residues into the correct orientation and excludes water where needed, enabling catalysis.

column1: How does the induced-fit model differ from the lock-and-key model?
column3: Active site is flexible (not rigid); shape adjusts upon substrate binding
column4: Induced-fit better explains broad specificity, allosteric regulation, and observed enzyme conformational changes detected by X-ray crystallography.

column1: Which model of enzyme-substrate binding is better supported by experimental evidence?
column4: Structural studies show enzymes undergo measurable conformational changes upon substrate binding, consistent with induced-fit rather than lock-and-key.

column1: In the induced-fit model, why do non-substrates generally fail to trigger catalysis even if they enter the active site?
column3: They cannot induce the correct conformational change
column4: The enzyme's conformational rearrangement is substrate-specific; an incorrect molecule may bind weakly but not align catalytic residues for catalysis.

column1: What is the general catalytic mechanism in which an enzyme active-site residue forms a temporary covalent bond with the substrate?
column4: Example: serine proteases form an acyl-enzyme intermediate via the active-site serine, then hydrolyze it to release product and regenerate the enzyme.

column1: What catalytic mechanism involves transfer of a proton between enzyme residues and the substrate?
column4: General acid-base catalysis uses histidine (ideal pKa ~6) and other residues to donate or accept protons, stabilizing the transition state.

column1: What is the catalytic triad of serine proteases?
column4: Asp positions His, which activates Ser as a nucleophile; Ser attacks the peptide bond, forming a covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate.

column1: What mechanism uses metal ions in the active site to stabilize transition states or orient substrates?
column4: Zinc in carbonic anhydrase and carboxypeptidase stabilizes negative charges in transition states; magnesium coordinates phosphates in kinases.

column1: What are cofactors in enzyme function?
column3: Non-protein chemical components required for enzyme activity
column4: Cofactors can be inorganic ions (e.g., Mg2+, Zn2+, Fe2+) or organic molecules (coenzymes); without them, the apoenzyme is inactive.

column1: What is an apoenzyme?
column3: The protein portion of an enzyme without its cofactor
column4: An apoenzyme is catalytically inactive; only when it associates with its cofactor does it become a holoenzyme (active enzyme).

column1: What is a holoenzyme?
column4: Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor. The cofactor may be tightly bound (prosthetic group) or loosely bound (coenzyme).

column1: Which inorganic cofactor is commonly required by kinases and ATP-using enzymes?
column4: Mg2+ chelates the phosphate groups of ATP, stabilizing the ATP structure and facilitating phosphoryl transfer.

column1: What is a prosthetic group?
column3: A cofactor that is tightly (covalently or very firmly) bound to the enzyme
column4: Heme in hemoglobin/cytochromes and FAD in succinate dehydrogenase are prosthetic groups; they remain bound throughout the catalytic cycle.

column1: What are coenzymes?
column3: Organic, non-protein cofactors that assist enzymes
column4: Coenzymes carry chemical groups between reactions (e.g., NAD+ carries electrons, CoA carries acyl groups); most are derived from vitamins.

column1: What coenzyme carries electrons (as hydride) in oxidation-reduction reactions and is derived from niacin (vitamin B3)?
column4: NAD+ is reduced to NADH by accepting a hydride ion; it is the primary electron carrier in catabolic pathways such as glycolysis and the TCA cycle.

column1: What coenzyme is reduced to FADH2 and is derived from riboflavin (vitamin B2)?
column4: FAD is a tightly bound prosthetic group in succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II); FADH2 donates electrons to the electron transport chain.

column1: What coenzyme transfers acyl groups and is derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)?
column4: CoA forms thioester bonds with acyl groups (e.g., acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA), activating them for transfer in metabolic reactions.

column1: What coenzyme is the primary phosphate-group donor in cells and acts as a coenzyme for kinases?
column4: ATP donates its terminal phosphate to substrates in phosphorylation reactions; it is regenerated by oxidative phosphorylation and substrate-level phosphorylation.

column1: What coenzyme derived from vitamin B12 (cobalamin) assists in methyl group and hydrogen transfers?
column4: B12 coenzymes are required by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase; deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological damage.

column1: Which water-soluble vitamin is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+?
column4: Niacin (nicotinic acid / nicotinamide) is incorporated into NAD+ and NADP+; deficiency causes pellagra (4 Ds: diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, death).

column1: Which water-soluble vitamin is the precursor of FAD and FMN?
column4: Riboflavin is phosphorylated to FMN and then combined with AMP to form FAD; both are electron-carrier coenzymes in oxidative metabolism.

column1: Which water-soluble vitamin is the precursor of coenzyme A?
column4: Pantothenic acid is an essential component of CoA; deficiency is rare but would impair all CoA-dependent reactions including the TCA cycle.

column1: Which water-soluble vitamin acts as a coenzyme in transamination and amino acid metabolism reactions?
column4: B6 is converted to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), which forms a Schiff base with amino acid substrates; required by aminotransferases and decarboxylases.
