column4: Kinases use ATP as the phosphate donor. Serine/threonine kinases and tyrosine kinases are major drug targets (e.g., imatinib targets BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase).

column1: What is glycosylation as a post-translational modification?
column3: addition of carbohydrate (sugar) chains to proteins
column4: N-linked glycosylation occurs in the ER (on Asn); O-linked glycosylation occurs in the Golgi (on Ser/Thr). Glycosylation affects protein folding, stability, and cell recognition.

column1: What is ubiquitination and what does it signal?
column3: attachment of ubiquitin chains; signals protein for proteasomal degradation
column4: Polyubiquitin chains (linked via Lys48) mark proteins for degradation by the 26S proteasome. Ubiquitin is added by a cascade of E1, E2, E3 enzymes.

column1: What post-translational modification targets proteins to lysosomes in eukaryotes?
column4: Lysosomal enzymes are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi, which is recognized by M6P receptors that direct transport to lysosomes.

column1: What is proteolytic cleavage as a post-translational modification?
column3: removal of signal peptide or activation of a zymogen by peptide cleavage
column4: Examples include cleavage of the signal peptide after ER entry and activation of insulin (proinsulin -> insulin) or digestive enzyme zymogens (trypsinogen -> trypsin).

column1: What is acetylation as a post-translational modification and where does it commonly occur?
column3: addition of acetyl group; commonly at N-terminus or histone Lys residues
column4: N-terminal acetylation can affect protein stability. Histone acetylation by HATs neutralizes positive charge, loosens chromatin, and generally activates transcription.

column1: What post-translational modification anchors proteins to the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane via a lipid?
column4: Myristoylation adds a 14-carbon fatty acid to an N-terminal Gly; palmitoylation adds a 16-carbon fatty acid to Cys. Both tether peripheral membrane proteins.

column1: What is the role of chaperone proteins in the context of translation?
column3: assist correct folding of nascent polypeptides; prevent misfolding/aggregation
column4: Hsp70 (e.g., BiP in ER) binds hydrophobic regions of unfolded proteins and uses ATP hydrolysis to facilitate correct folding. They do not specify the final structure.

column1: What signal sequence directs a newly synthesized protein to the ER?
column4: The signal recognition particle (SRP) recognizes the signal peptide and halts translation until the ribosome docks at the ER membrane (co-translational translocation).

column1: What are histones?
column3: Positively charged proteins that package DNA
column4: Histones are rich in lysine and arginine, giving them a positive charge that allows them to bind the negatively charged DNA backbone. They form the core of the nucleosome.

column1: Which five histone proteins form the nucleosome?
column4: H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 form the octamer core (two of each); H1 is the linker histone that seals DNA around the nucleosome.

column1: How many histone proteins make up the nucleosome core octamer?
column3: Eight (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4)
column4: The histone octamer is the protein spool around which ~147 bp of DNA wraps roughly 1.65 times.

column1: What amino acids make histones positively charged?
column4: These basic amino acids carry positive charges at physiological pH, enabling ionic interaction with the negatively charged phosphate backbone of DNA.

column1: Which histone modification is most associated with transcriptional activation?
column4: Histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups to lysine, neutralizing the positive charge and loosening DNA-histone contact, making DNA more accessible for transcription.

column1: What is the role of histone H1?
column3: Linker histone; compacts nucleosomes into higher-order chromatin
column4: H1 binds the linker DNA between nucleosome cores and helps fold the 10-nm nucleosome fiber into the 30-nm chromatin fiber.

column1: What effect does histone methylation generally have on chromatin?
column3: Can activate or repress transcription depending on the site
column4: Methylation of H3K4 is associated with activation; H3K9 and H3K27 methylation are associated with repression/heterochromatin formation. Context is key.

column1: What non-histone chromosomal proteins help organize higher-order chromatin structure in eukaryotes?
column3: Scaffold proteins (e.g., topoisomerase II, SMC proteins/condensins)
column4: These proteins form the proteinaceous scaffold of metaphase chromosomes after histones are stripped away, maintaining chromosome shape and enabling sister chromatid cohesion.

column1: What is single-copy DNA?
column3: DNA sequences present once (or very few times) per haploid genome
column4: Most protein-coding genes are single-copy sequences. They make up roughly 40-70% of the human genome depending on classification.

column1: What is repetitive DNA?
column3: DNA sequences present in many tandem or dispersed copies
column4: Repetitive DNA includes satellite DNA, SINEs, and LINEs. Much of it is non-coding and some is associated with centromeres and telomeres.

column1: What are SINEs and LINEs?
column3: Short and long interspersed nuclear elements; transposable element-derived repeats
column4: SINEs (e.g., Alu) are ~300 bp; LINEs (e.g., L1) are ~6 kb. Both are retrotransposons and make up a large fraction of the human genome.

column1: What type of DNA is found at centromeres and constitutes highly repetitive satellite DNA?
column3: Tandemly repeated satellite DNA (e.g., alpha-satellite in humans)
column4: Alpha-satellite repeats of ~171 bp are tandemly arrayed at centromeres and are recognized by centromere-specific proteins like CENP-A.

column1: Approximately what percentage of the human genome is composed of repetitive sequences?
column4: Nearly half the human genome consists of transposable elements and other repeats, far outnumbering the ~1.5% that codes for proteins.

column1: What is the C-value paradox?
column3: Genome size does not correlate with organismal complexity
column4: Some amphibians have much larger genomes than humans. The paradox is largely explained by variation in repetitive/non-coding DNA content, not gene number.

column1: What distinguishes moderately repetitive DNA from highly repetitive (satellite) DNA?
column3: Moderately repetitive: 10–100,000 copies; highly repetitive: >100,000 tandem copies
column4: rRNA genes, tRNA genes, and histone genes are moderately repetitive. Highly repetitive satellite DNA rarely codes for proteins.

column1: What is DNA supercoiling?
column3: Over- or under-winding of the double helix around its own axis
column4: Positive supercoiling occurs ahead of a replication or transcription fork (overwinding); negative supercoiling occurs behind it (underwinding), and is the predominant form in cells.

column1: Which enzyme relieves positive supercoiling ahead of the replication fork?
column4: Gyrase (a type II topoisomerase) cuts both strands, passes a duplex through, and religates, introducing negative supercoils that counteract positive overwinding.

column1: What is the difference between a Type I and Type II topoisomerase?
column3: Type I cuts one strand; Type II cuts both strands
column4: Type I topoisomerases change the linking number by 1 per reaction; Type II change it by 2 per reaction and require ATP.

column1: What is the linking number of a DNA molecule?
column3: Total number of times one strand winds around the other (Tw + Wr)
column4: Linking number (Lk) = twist (Tw) + writhe (Wr). Topoisomerases change Lk; the linking number is conserved unless a strand is cut.

column1: What type of supercoiling predominates in bacterial chromosomes?
column4: Negative supercoils facilitate strand separation for replication and transcription by partially unwinding the duplex, making these processes more efficient.

column1: Which topoisomerase relaxes both positive and negative supercoils but cannot decatenate chromosomes?
column4: Topoisomerase I nicks one strand and allows controlled rotation, changing Lk by ±1. It cannot separate interlinked (catenated) chromosomes after replication.

column1: What antibiotic targets bacterial gyrase (type II topoisomerase) and is used as an MCAT-relevant example?
column4: Fluoroquinolones trap the gyrase-DNA cleavage complex, blocking DNA replication and transcription. This is a classic example of targeting a prokaryote-specific enzyme.

column1: What is heterochromatin?
column4: Heterochromatin stains darkly with basic dyes, is replicated late in S phase, and is associated with gene silencing (e.g., Barr body, centromeric regions).

column1: What is euchromatin?
column4: Euchromatin stains lightly with basic dyes and contains most actively transcribed genes. It is more accessible to RNA polymerase and transcription factors.

column1: What is constitutive heterochromatin?
column3: Permanently condensed chromatin, same in all cell types (e.g., centromeres, telomeres)
column4: Constitutive heterochromatin is always condensed regardless of cell type or developmental stage, unlike facultative heterochromatin which can be activated.

column1: What is facultative heterochromatin?
column3: Chromatin that can switch between condensed and active states depending on cell type or developmental stage
column4: The inactive X chromosome (Barr body) is the classic example: genes are silenced in one X but not the other, depending on cell lineage.

column1: What is the Barr body?
column3: Condensed inactive X chromosome visible in female somatic cells
column4: In XX females, one X is inactivated and forms the Barr body; the number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes minus one. It is an example of facultative heterochromatin.

column1: Which histone modification marks heterochromatin and is associated with gene silencing?
column4: H3K9me3 is recognized by HP1 (heterochromatin protein 1), which spreads chromatin compaction and is a hallmark of silent heterochromatin domains.

column1: How does DNA methylation at CpG sites relate to heterochromatin?
column3: CpG methylation correlates with gene silencing and heterochromatin formation
column4: Methylated cytosines (5-methylcytosine) at CpG dinucleotides recruit methyl-binding proteins that promote chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression.

column1: What are telomeres?
column3: Repetitive DNA sequences capping the ends of linear chromosomes
column4: Telomeres protect chromosome ends from degradation and end-to-end fusions. In humans the repeat is TTAGGG, extending thousands of times.

column1: What enzyme synthesizes telomeric repeats?
column4: Telomerase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase) that uses its own RNA template to add TTAGGG repeats, counteracting shortening from the end-replication problem.

column1: What is the end-replication problem?
column3: Inability of DNA polymerase to fully replicate the 5' end of linear chromosomes, causing progressive telomere shortening
column4: After RNA primer removal at the lagging strand's 5' end, there is no upstream primer to fill the gap, so each cell division shortens telomeres. Telomerase compensates in stem/germ cells.

column1: What is the centromere?
column3: Chromosomal region where the kinetochore assembles for spindle attachment during cell division
column4: The centromere is defined by the presence of CENP-A (a histone H3 variant) rather than strictly by sequence. It is the constriction point visible at metaphase.

column1: What histone variant marks the centromere?
column4: CENP-A replaces histone H3 in centromeric nucleosomes and is essential for kinetochore assembly. Its epigenetic deposition, not just DNA sequence, specifies centromere identity.

column1: What is the kinetochore?
column3: Protein complex assembled at the centromere that attaches chromosomes to spindle microtubules
column4: The kinetochore mediates chromosome movement during mitosis and meiosis. Errors in kinetochore-spindle attachment lead to aneuploidy.

column1: In which cells is telomerase highly active?
column3: Germ cells, stem cells, and most cancer cells
column4: Somatic cells have low telomerase activity and shorten telomeres with each division. Cancer cells reactivate telomerase to achieve replicative immortality.

column1: What structure do G-rich telomere overhangs form to protect chromosome ends?
column3: T-loop (with G-quadruplex at the single-stranded tail)
column4: The 3' single-stranded overhang invades the double-stranded telomere repeat region to form a T-loop, hiding the end from DNA damage sensors.

column1: What is the shelterin complex?
column3: Protein complex that protects telomeres from DNA damage response activation
column4: Shelterin (containing TRF1, TRF2, POT1, and others) caps telomere ends, prevents ATM/ATR signaling, and regulates telomerase access.

column1: What is a neocentromere?
column3: A centromere that forms at an ectopic chromosomal locus, not the normal centromeric region
column4: Neocentromeres demonstrate that centromere identity is epigenetically defined by CENP-A deposition rather than solely by DNA sequence.

column1: What term describes a cluster of co-regulated prokaryotic genes transcribed as a single mRNA?
column4: An operon includes a promoter, operator, and structural genes all transcribed together, allowing coordinated regulation of related metabolic functions.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: Who proposed the operon model of gene regulation in bacteria?
column4: François Jacob and Jacques Monod described the lac operon in E. coli in 1961, earning the Nobel Prize for this foundational model of gene regulation.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is the operator in a prokaryotic operon?
column3: DNA sequence where repressor binds to block transcription
column4: The operator is located between the promoter and structural genes; repressor binding physically blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What molecule acts as the inducer for the lac operon?
column4: Allolactose (a lactose isomer) binds the lac repressor, causing it to release the operator and allowing transcription of the lactose-metabolizing genes.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What are the three structural genes of the lac operon?
column4: lacZ encodes beta-galactosidase, lacY encodes lactose permease, and lacA encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase — all needed for lactose catabolism.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: In the Jacob-Monod model, where is the repressor gene located relative to the operon it regulates?
column3: Upstream of the operon (can be distant)
column4: The regulator gene (i) in the lac operon is typically upstream but can be elsewhere on the chromosome; the repressor protein it encodes diffuses to the operator.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What distinguishes the promoter from the operator in a prokaryotic operon?
column3: Promoter binds RNA polymerase; operator binds repressor
column4: These are two distinct DNA sequences. The promoter is the RNA polymerase binding site initiating transcription; the operator is the regulatory binding site for the repressor protein.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What type of mutation in the lac operator constitutes an operator-constitutive (Oc) mutation?
column3: Mutation preventing repressor from binding the operator
column4: An Oc mutation causes constitutive (always-on) transcription because the repressor can no longer bind and block RNA polymerase, making regulation impossible.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: Is the lac repressor cis-acting or trans-acting?
column4: The repressor is a diffusible protein that can act on any lac operator in the cell, making it trans-acting; operators are cis-acting DNA elements that only affect genes on the same DNA molecule.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What type of regulation does the lac operon primarily use in the absence of glucose AND presence of lactose?
column4: The lac operon is derepressed (negative control) by allolactose and activated (positive control) by CAP-cAMP when glucose is absent, requiring both conditions for maximal transcription.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is gene repression in bacteria?
column3: Repressor protein blocks transcription by binding the operator
column4: In negative gene regulation, a repressor protein binds the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing structural genes until the repressor is removed.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: In the lac operon, when is the lac repressor active (bound to operator)?
column4: Without lactose, no allolactose is produced, so the repressor remains in its active conformation and binds the operator, preventing transcription of lac genes.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What type of molecule is the lac repressor?
column4: The lac repressor changes conformation upon allolactose binding, shifting from operator-binding (active) to non-binding (inactive) form — a classic allosteric mechanism.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is the trp operon regulated by?
column4: The trp operon encodes tryptophan biosynthesis enzymes; when tryptophan is abundant, it binds the trp aporepressor, activating it to bind the operator and shut off gene expression.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is the difference between an inducer and a corepressor in bacterial gene regulation?
column3: Inducer inactivates repressor; corepressor activates aporepressor
column4: An inducer (e.g., allolactose) prevents repressor binding, turning genes ON. A corepressor (e.g., tryptophan) activates the aporepressor to bind the operator, turning genes OFF.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: Which operon is the classic example of repressible gene regulation in bacteria?
column4: The trp operon is repressed when tryptophan levels are high (end-product repression), making it the canonical example of a repressible/anabolic operon in prokaryotes.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is attenuation in the trp operon?
column3: Premature transcription termination based on tryptophan availability
column4: Attenuation uses the ribosome's translation rate on a leader peptide encoding Trp residues to signal tryptophan availability; high Trp causes a terminator hairpin to form in the nascent mRNA, aborting transcription.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: Which operon encodes anabolic enzymes and which encodes catabolic enzymes: trp or lac?
column4: Anabolic operons (trp) are repressed by the end product; catabolic operons (lac) are induced by the substrate. This logic ensures enzymes are made only when needed.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is a constitutive mutant of the lac repressor gene (i- mutation)?
column3: Nonfunctional repressor; lac genes always transcribed
column4: An i- mutation inactivates the repressor protein. Because no functional repressor can bind the operator, lac structural genes are transcribed constitutively regardless of lactose.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is positive control of gene expression in bacteria?
column3: An activator protein stimulates transcription when bound to DNA
column4: Unlike repressor-based negative control, positive control involves a regulatory protein that must bind near the promoter to enhance RNA polymerase binding and increase transcription.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What protein mediates positive control of the lac operon?
column3: CAP (catabolite activator protein, also called CRP)
column4: CAP bound to cAMP binds the CAP site upstream of the lac promoter, recruiting RNA polymerase and dramatically increasing transcription when glucose is absent.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What molecule must bind CAP for it to activate the lac operon?
column4: CAP alone cannot bind DNA effectively; cAMP binding induces a conformational change that enables the CAP-cAMP complex to bind the CAP site and activate transcription.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What happens to intracellular cAMP levels when glucose is plentiful in E. coli?
column4: Glucose inhibits adenylyl cyclase activity, reducing cAMP production. Low cAMP means CAP cannot activate the lac operon — the basis of catabolite repression.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What is catabolite repression?
column3: Glucose suppresses transcription of catabolic operons for alternative sugars
column4: When glucose is present, cAMP falls, CAP is inactive, and operons like lac are not fully activated — the cell preferentially uses glucose over alternative carbon sources.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: Under what dual conditions is the lac operon maximally transcribed?
column4: Lactose presence removes repressor (derepression); glucose absence raises cAMP, activating CAP. Both conditions together give maximum lac operon expression.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What enzyme synthesizes cAMP from ATP in E. coli?
column4: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP + PPi. Its activity is inhibited by glucose transport, linking glucose availability to cAMP-mediated positive control of the lac operon.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: When glucose is absent but lactose is also absent, what is the transcription state of the lac operon?
column3: Low transcription (repressor bound, CAP active but no derepression)
column4: CAP-cAMP is active (high cAMP), but the lac repressor also blocks the operator. Without allolactose to remove the repressor, transcription remains minimal despite positive control.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: Is CAP-cAMP binding to its site cis-acting or trans-acting?
column4: The CAP protein is trans-acting (diffusible), but the CAP binding site on DNA is a cis-regulatory element. Understanding this distinction is important for operon mutation analysis questions.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Prokaryotes

column1: What term describes a DNA sequence that increases transcription when bound by activator proteins, regardless of orientation or distance?
column4: Enhancers are cis-regulatory elements that can act over tens of thousands of base pairs and in either orientation; they loop to contact promoters via mediator complexes.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What term describes the minimal DNA sequence required for RNA polymerase II binding and transcription initiation in eukaryotes?
column4: The core promoter typically includes the TATA box (~30 bp upstream of the transcription start site) and initiator elements recognized by general transcription factors.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What type of cis-regulatory element silences gene transcription when bound by repressor proteins?
column4: Silencers are analogous to enhancers but recruit repressor complexes that reduce RNA polymerase II activity or promote chromatin compaction.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which general transcription factor recruits RNA polymerase II to the promoter by recognizing the TATA box?
column4: TATA-binding protein (TBP), a subunit of TFIID, binds the TATA box and bends DNA, nucleating assembly of the pre-initiation complex.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the function of a mediator complex in eukaryotic transcription?
column3: Bridges activators to RNA polymerase II
column4: Mediator is a large multiprotein complex that transmits signals from enhancer-bound activators to the RNA pol II pre-initiation complex at the core promoter.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which consensus sequence located approximately 25-30 bp upstream of the transcription start site is recognized by TFIID in many eukaryotic genes?
column4: Not all eukaryotic promoters contain a TATA box; TATA-less promoters use alternative elements like the initiator (Inr) or downstream promoter element (DPE).
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What structural feature allows transcription factors to bind DNA in a sequence-specific manner?
column4: Common DNA-binding domains include zinc fingers, helix-turn-helix, leucine zippers, and helix-loop-helix motifs, each recognizing specific DNA sequences.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What type of transcription factor domain is required for activating transcription once the protein is bound to DNA?
column4: Activation domains interact with mediator or coactivators to stimulate assembly of the pre-initiation complex; they are distinct from the DNA-binding domain.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which zinc finger transcription factor motif coordinates a zinc ion using two cysteines and two histidines?
column4: The C2H2 zinc finger is the most common DNA-binding motif in eukaryotes; each finger contacts about 3 bp of DNA in the major groove.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What structural feature do leucine zipper transcription factors use to dimerize?
column4: Leucine residues spaced every 7 amino acids form a coiled-coil interaction between two alpha helices, allowing homo- or heterodimerization that alters DNA-binding specificity.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which type of transcription factor domain represses transcription by recruiting histone deacetylases?
column4: Repression domains recruit corepressors such as HDACs, which remove acetyl groups from histones, promoting chromatin compaction and transcriptional silencing.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What distinguishes a general transcription factor from a specific (regulatory) transcription factor?
column3: General: required for all pol II genes; specific: gene-selective
column4: General TFs (TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIID, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH) are needed at every RNA pol II promoter, while regulatory TFs bind enhancers/silencers to modulate specific genes.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What process increases the copy number of a specific gene beyond the normal diploid level?
column4: Gene amplification is seen in cancer (e.g., HER2/ERBB2 amplification in breast cancer) and normal development (e.g., rRNA gene amplification in oocytes).
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What evolutionary mechanism produces paralogous genes within a genome?
column4: After duplication, one copy may retain the original function while the other acquires new functions (neofunctionalization) or both share the ancestral function (subfunctionalization).
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What are the two visible cytogenetic manifestations of gene amplification in cancer cells?
column3: Double minutes and homogeneously staining regions (HSRs)
column4: Double minutes are extrachromosomal circular DNA; HSRs are expanded chromosomal segments — both reflect massively amplified gene copies.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which protein family, produced from a multigene family arising by gene duplication, carries oxygen in red blood cells and muscles respectively?
column4: The globin gene family arose through ancient gene duplications; hemoglobin is a tetramer while myoglobin is a monomer, illustrating functional divergence after duplication.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the term for a duplicated gene copy that has accumulated mutations rendering it nonfunctional?
column4: Pseudogenes lack functional promoters or contain frameshifts/stop codons; they are evolutionary relics of gene duplication and can still be transcribed into noncoding RNA in some cases.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which chemotherapy-resistant mechanism involves amplification of the DHFR gene in cancer cells treated with methotrexate?
column3: DHFR gene amplification (overproduction of dihydrofolate reductase)
column4: Methotrexate inhibits DHFR; cancer cells can amplify the DHFR gene hundreds of times, producing excess enzyme that overcomes drug inhibition — a classic example of drug resistance via amplification.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What are the non-coding intervening sequences in a pre-mRNA called?
column4: Introns are removed during RNA splicing; they are retained in the pre-mRNA (hnRNA) but absent from the mature mRNA that reaches the ribosome.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What are the coding sequences of a pre-mRNA that are retained in the mature mRNA called?
column4: Exons are 'expressed' sequences; after splicing, exons are joined together to form the open reading frame (plus 5' and 3' UTRs) of the mature mRNA.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What ribonucleoprotein complex catalyzes the removal of introns from pre-mRNA?
column4: The spliceosome is assembled from five snRNPs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) and additional proteins; it carries out two transesterification reactions to excise the intron lariat and join exons.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What consensus dinucleotide sequences mark the 5' and 3' splice sites of most introns?
column3: GU at 5' end, AG at 3' end
column4: The GU-AG rule (GT-AG in DNA) identifies nearly all spliceosomal introns; mutations at these sites cause aberrant splicing and are implicated in many genetic diseases.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What post-transcriptional process allows a single gene to produce multiple protein isoforms?
column4: By including or excluding different exons, alternative splicing greatly expands proteome diversity; estimates suggest >90% of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What intronic sequence element is required for lariat formation during splicing, defined by an adenosine residue?
column4: The 2'-OH of the branch point adenosine attacks the 5' splice site in the first transesterification, forming a lariat intermediate; mutations here disrupt splicing.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the term for a gene that, when mutated to a gain-of-function state, promotes cancer?
column4: Oncogenes arise from proto-oncogenes by mutation, amplification, translocation, or viral insertion; they drive uncontrolled cell proliferation (e.g., RAS, MYC, HER2).
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the term for a gene that normally restrains cell division and whose loss-of-function promotes cancer?
column4: Examples include TP53, RB1, BRCA1/2, and APC; typically both alleles must be inactivated (two-hit hypothesis) for tumor suppressor loss to drive cancer.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which tumor suppressor protein is called the 'guardian of the genome' and triggers apoptosis or cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage?
column4: p53 is the most commonly mutated gene in human cancers; it transactivates genes like p21 (CDK inhibitor) and BAX (pro-apoptotic) in response to genotoxic stress.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which proto-oncogene encodes a GTPase that, when mutated to be constitutively active, drives many cancers?
column4: RAS mutations (commonly G12D/V) prevent GTP hydrolysis, locking RAS in the 'on' state and continuously activating MAPK and PI3K proliferation pathways.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is Knudson's two-hit hypothesis as applied to tumor suppressor genes?
column3: Both alleles must be inactivated for tumor suppression to be lost
column4: One allele may be inactivated by germline mutation (hereditary cancer syndromes) and the other by somatic mutation; retinoblastoma (RB1) was the founding example.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which chromosomal translocation fuses BCR to ABL1, creating a constitutively active tyrosine kinase oncogene in chronic myelogenous leukemia?
column4: The BCR-ABL1 fusion protein has unregulated tyrosine kinase activity; imatinib (Gleevec) was developed specifically to inhibit it, a landmark in targeted cancer therapy.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the term for loosely packed, transcriptionally active chromatin?
column4: Euchromatin is gene-rich and acetylated at histone tails, keeping nucleosomes loosely organized and accessible to transcription machinery.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the term for densely packed, transcriptionally silent chromatin?
column4: Heterochromatin is enriched at centromeres and telomeres; it is characterized by histone H3K9 methylation and HP1 binding, keeping genes tightly compacted and silent.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What histone modification generally correlates with active gene transcription?
column4: Acetylation of lysine residues by HATs neutralizes positive charge on histones, loosening DNA-histone interactions and facilitating transcription factor access.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What enzyme removes acetyl groups from histones, promoting chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression?
column4: HDACs are recruited by corepressor complexes; HDAC inhibitors (e.g., vorinostat) are used clinically in some cancers to reactivate silenced tumor suppressor genes.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which histone methylation mark on H3 lysine 27 is associated with polycomb-mediated gene repression?
column4: H3K27me3 is written by PRC2 (containing EZH2) and read by PRC1; this system maintains developmental gene silencing and is dysregulated in many cancers.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the process by which chromatin remodeling complexes use ATP hydrolysis to reposition or eject nucleosomes?
column4: Complexes such as SWI/SNF (BAF), ISWI, and NuRD slide, eject, or restructure nucleosomes to expose or occlude regulatory DNA elements, controlling gene accessibility.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What chemical modification of cytosine residues in DNA is associated with gene silencing?
column4: In mammals, DNA methyltransferases add a methyl group to the 5' position of cytosine, predominantly at CpG dinucleotides, correlating with transcriptional repression.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: At which dinucleotide sequence does DNA methylation most commonly occur in mammals?
column4: CpG islands — stretches of high CpG density near gene promoters — are typically unmethylated in active genes; aberrant hypermethylation silences tumor suppressor genes in cancer.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which enzyme family is responsible for adding methyl groups to DNA in mammals?
column4: DNMT3A and DNMT3B establish de novo methylation; DNMT1 is the 'maintenance' methyltransferase that copies methylation patterns to daughter strands after replication.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the distinction between DNMT1 and DNMT3A/3B in terms of their function?
column3: DNMT1: maintenance methylation; DNMT3A/3B: de novo methylation
column4: DNMT1 preferentially methylates hemimethylated DNA after replication to preserve epigenetic patterns; DNMT3A/3B methylate previously unmethylated CpGs during development.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What term describes the genome-wide loss of DNA methylation observed in many cancer cells?
column4: Cancer-associated hypomethylation activates proto-oncogenes and transposable elements, contributing to genomic instability, while localized CpG island hypermethylation silences tumor suppressors.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which enzymatic pathway converts 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine as the first step in active DNA demethylation?
column4: TET1/2/3 dioxygenases oxidize 5mC to 5hmC (and further to 5fC and 5caC), which are then removed by base excision repair, completing active demethylation.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What class of small noncoding RNA, ~22 nucleotides long, silences gene expression post-transcriptionally by binding complementary mRNA?
column4: miRNAs are processed from hairpin precursors by Drosha and Dicer, then loaded into RISC; imperfect complementarity leads to translational repression or mRNA destabilization.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the name of the multiprotein complex that miRNAs guide to target mRNAs to silence them?
column4: RISC contains an Argonaute protein (AGO2) as the catalytic slicer; when complementarity is perfect, target mRNA is cleaved; imperfect complementarity causes translational repression.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What class of noncoding RNA, >200 nt, regulates gene expression in cis or trans and does not encode protein?
column4: lncRNAs such as XIST (X-inactivation), HOTAIR, and MALAT1 regulate gene expression through chromatin remodeling, splicing, and transcription factor sequestration.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: Which lncRNA coats the inactive X chromosome and recruits PRC2 to silence it in female mammals?
column4: XIST is transcribed from the inactive X, spreads in cis, and recruits polycomb complexes that deposit H3K27me3, leading to chromosome-wide silencing (lyonization).
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What class of small noncoding RNA protects the germline genome from transposable element activation by guiding Piwi-protein complexes?
column4: piRNAs are ~26-31 nt, produced independently of Dicer, and silence transposons in gonads via Piwi-protein RISC; mutations cause transposon derepression and infertility.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is the difference between siRNA and miRNA in terms of their origin and target complementarity?
column3: siRNA: exogenous/perfect complementarity; miRNA: endogenous/imperfect complementarity
column4: siRNAs derive from long dsRNA (exogenous or viral) and perfectly match their targets for cleavage; miRNAs are encoded in the genome and typically cause translational repression via imperfect pairing.
column5: Control of Gene Expression in Eukaryotes

column1: What is gene cloning?
column3: Producing identical copies of a DNA fragment in host cells
column4: Gene cloning inserts a target DNA fragment into a vector, which is then introduced into host cells (usually bacteria) that replicate, copying the insert along with their own DNA.

column1: What type of vector is most commonly used to clone small DNA fragments in bacteria?
column4: Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that replicate independently in bacteria; they carry selectable marker genes (e.g., antibiotic resistance) to identify transformed cells.

column1: What feature of a cloning vector allows selection of bacteria that took up the plasmid?
column4: Only bacteria containing the plasmid can grow on antibiotic-containing media, making selectable markers essential for identifying successful transformants.

column1: Which bacteriophage vector is used to clone large DNA inserts (up to ~23 kb)?
column4: Lambda phage can package large inserts into its protein coat; it is used when fragments are too large for typical plasmid vectors.

column1: What is a cosmid vector?
column3: Plasmid containing lambda cos sites; clones ~40–50 kb inserts
column4: Cosmids combine plasmid replication with lambda packaging signals, allowing larger inserts than either alone; useful for genomic library construction.

column1: What is the role of a multiple cloning site (MCS) in a cloning vector?
column3: Region with many unique restriction sites for inserting foreign DNA
column4: The MCS (polylinker) provides flexibility, allowing researchers to cut with different restriction enzymes to directionally insert target DNA.

column1: What do restriction enzymes recognize and cut?
column4: Type II restriction endonucleases cut double-stranded DNA at or near their palindromic recognition sequences, producing defined fragments used in cloning.

column1: What type of ends does EcoRI produce when it cuts DNA?
column4: EcoRI cuts between G and AATTC on each strand, leaving 4-nucleotide 5' overhangs that can anneal with complementary sticky ends to facilitate ligation.

column1: Which restriction enzyme cuts DNA to produce blunt ends?
column4: SmaI cuts CCCGGG straight through the middle, leaving no overhangs; blunt-end ligations are less efficient but can join any two blunt fragments.

column1: What enzyme joins two DNA fragments after restriction cutting?
column4: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds between compatible (sticky or blunt) ends, sealing nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone to create recombinant DNA.

column1: Why must insert and vector be cut with the same restriction enzyme for directional cloning?
column3: To produce compatible sticky ends that can anneal and ligate
column4: Using the same enzyme ensures that overhangs on the insert match those on the vector, promoting efficient and oriented ligation.

column1: What is the recognition sequence of EcoRI?
column4: EcoRI is one of the most commonly used restriction enzymes on the MCAT; its palindromic sequence is cut between G and A on each strand.

column1: What is a genomic library?
column3: Collection of clones containing all DNA sequences of an organism's genome
column4: A genomic library is made by cutting total genomic DNA with restriction enzymes, inserting fragments into vectors, and transforming host cells so every genomic region is represented.

column1: What is a cDNA library?
column3: Collection of clones made from mRNA of a specific tissue/condition
column4: cDNA libraries represent only expressed genes (no introns), making them useful for studying gene expression in a particular cell type or developmental stage.

column1: How does a cDNA library differ from a genomic library?
column3: cDNA lacks introns; genomic library includes all DNA including introns
column4: Because cDNA is reverse-transcribed from mRNA, it contains only exon sequences; genomic libraries contain regulatory regions and introns as well.

column1: Which vector is typically used to construct a genomic library for very large inserts (100–300 kb)?
column3: BAC (bacterial artificial chromosome) or YAC (yeast artificial chromosome)
column4: BACs and YACs can carry far larger inserts than plasmids or lambda phage, making them essential for mapping and sequencing complex genomes.

column1: What enzyme is essential for generating cDNA from mRNA?
column4: Reverse transcriptase (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) synthesizes a complementary DNA strand using mRNA as a template, a key step in retrovirus replication and cDNA cloning.

column1: What is the first product formed when reverse transcriptase acts on mRNA?
column4: Reverse transcriptase extends a primer (often oligo-dT) along the mRNA template, producing a complementary single-stranded DNA while the mRNA remains base-paired.

column1: How is the RNA strand removed from the RNA–DNA hybrid during cDNA synthesis?
column3: RNase H degrades the RNA strand
column4: RNase H specifically degrades RNA in RNA–DNA hybrids; the remaining single-stranded DNA is then used as a template for DNA polymerase to synthesize the second strand.

column1: Why is a poly-A tail on mRNA useful for cDNA synthesis?
column3: It allows oligo-dT primers to anneal as a starting point for reverse transcriptase
column4: Eukaryotic mRNAs have 3' poly-A tails; oligo-dT primers hybridize to them, providing a 3'-OH for reverse transcriptase to initiate cDNA synthesis.

column1: What key feature is absent from cDNA compared to the original genomic DNA of a eukaryotic gene?
column4: cDNA is derived from processed mRNA after splicing, so introns are removed; this is advantageous when expressing human genes in bacterial hosts that cannot splice.

column1: What is nucleic acid hybridization?
column3: Annealing of complementary single-stranded nucleic acid sequences
column4: Hybridization exploits base-pairing; a labeled probe hybridizes to its complementary target sequence in a sample, allowing detection of specific genes or transcripts.

column1: What is a nucleic acid probe?
column3: Labeled single-stranded DNA or RNA that detects a complementary target sequence
column4: Probes are labeled with radioactivity or fluorescence; after hybridization, bound probe signals reveal the location or abundance of the target nucleic acid.

column1: In hybridization experiments, what conditions favor stable duplex formation?
column3: High GC content, lower temperature, and higher salt concentration
column4: G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds; lower temperature and higher ionic strength reduce electrostatic repulsion between strands, stabilizing duplexes.

column1: What is fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) used for?
column3: Locating specific DNA sequences on chromosomes using fluorescent probes
column4: FISH probes hybridize to denatured chromosomal DNA on a slide; fluorescent signals pinpoint gene location, chromosome abnormalities, or copy number changes.

column1: What is a molecular beacon in hybridization technology?
column3: Hairpin probe that fluoresces only when bound to its target
column4: In the absence of target, the hairpin holds the fluorophore and quencher together; target binding opens the hairpin, separating them and producing fluorescence.

column1: What must be done to DNA or RNA before hybridization with a probe?
column4: Hybridization requires single-stranded targets; heat or alkali denatures double-stranded nucleic acids so the probe can access and anneal to complementary sequences.

column1: What is required for expressing a cloned eukaryotic gene in bacteria?
column3: A strong bacterial promoter and the coding sequence without introns (cDNA)
column4: Bacteria lack spliceosomes, so eukaryotic pre-mRNA cannot be processed; cDNA provides intron-free coding sequence, and a bacterial promoter drives transcription.

column1: What is an expression vector?
column3: A cloning vector engineered to drive transcription and translation of an insert
column4: Expression vectors include a strong promoter, ribosome binding site, and often a His-tag or other fusion sequence to facilitate purification of the expressed protein.

column1: What is an affinity tag and why is it added to an expression vector?
column3: Peptide sequence (e.g., His-tag) fused to protein for easy purification
column4: His-tags (6xHis) bind nickel columns; after expression, tagged protein is selectively eluted, simplifying purification from cell lysate.

column1: What is an inducible promoter and why is it used in expression vectors?
column3: Promoter activated by a specific signal (e.g., IPTG for lac promoter) to control gene expression timing
column4: Inducible promoters prevent constitutive expression of proteins that may be toxic to host cells; IPTG mimics allolactose and derepresses the lac operon.

column1: Why might a eukaryotic protein expressed in bacteria lack biological activity?
column3: Bacteria cannot glycosylate or properly fold complex eukaryotic proteins
column4: Post-translational modifications like glycosylation, disulfide bond formation, and specific chaperone-assisted folding may be required for activity but are absent in E. coli.

column1: What is the purpose of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR)?
column3: To amplify a specific DNA sequence exponentially in vitro
column4: PCR uses thermostable DNA polymerase, specific primers, and repeated thermal cycling to create millions of copies of a target sequence from minimal starting DNA.

column1: What are the three steps of each PCR cycle?
column4: Denaturation (~95°C) separates strands; annealing (~55–65°C) allows primers to bind; extension (~72°C) allows Taq polymerase to synthesize new strands.

column1: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
column3: It is thermostable and remains active at high denaturation temperatures
column4: Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus, is not denatured at 95°C, allowing repeated cycles without adding fresh enzyme after each denaturation step.

column1: What is reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) used for?
column3: Amplifying mRNA sequences by first converting mRNA to cDNA
column4: RT-PCR detects gene expression; mRNA is converted to cDNA by reverse transcriptase, then the cDNA is amplified by standard PCR to detect or quantify transcripts.

column1: After n PCR cycles, how many copies of the target sequence are theoretically produced from one original molecule?
column4: Each cycle doubles the number of target copies (exponential amplification); after 30 cycles, ~10^9 copies can be generated from a single starting molecule.

column1: What is quantitative PCR (qPCR) and what does it measure?
column3: Real-time PCR measuring fluorescence to quantify initial DNA/mRNA amount
column4: qPCR uses fluorescent dyes or probes; the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a threshold (Ct) is inversely related to the starting quantity of target nucleic acid.

column1: In gel electrophoresis, which direction do DNA fragments migrate?
column4: DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate backbone; it migrates toward the positive pole through the gel matrix under an electric field.

column1: In agarose gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragments migrate farthest from the well?
column4: Smaller DNA fragments pass more easily through the gel pores, traveling farther in a given time; molecular weight ladders are used as size standards.

column1: What is Southern blotting used to detect?
column3: Specific DNA sequences in a sample
column4: DNA fragments separated by gel electrophoresis are transferred to a membrane and probed with a labeled DNA probe that hybridizes to complementary sequences.

column1: What is the order of steps in Southern blotting?
column3: Gel electrophoresis → denaturation → transfer to membrane → hybridization with probe → detection
column4: DNA is first separated by size, denatured to single strands, transferred (blotted) to a nylon membrane, then probed to identify a specific sequence.

column1: What is the difference between Southern, Northern, and Western blotting?
column4: All three use gel separation and membrane transfer, but the molecule detected differs; the probe in Southern/Northern is a nucleic acid, while Western uses an antibody.

column1: What is the Sanger (chain termination) method of DNA sequencing based on?
column3: Incorporation of dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) that terminate chain elongation
column4: ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group; when incorporated, DNA polymerase cannot extend further, generating a set of fragments whose sizes reveal the sequence.

column1: What makes dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) terminate DNA synthesis?
column3: They lack a 3'-OH group, preventing phosphodiester bond formation
column4: Normal dNTPs have a 3'-OH that accepts the next nucleotide; ddNTPs have a 3'-H instead, blocking chain elongation after incorporation.

column1: In modern automated Sanger sequencing, how are the four ddNTPs distinguished?
column3: Each is labeled with a different fluorescent dye
column4: All four ddNTPs are used in one reaction; capillary electrophoresis separates fragments by size, and a laser detector reads the color of each terminal ddNTP to determine sequence.

column1: What is next-generation sequencing (NGS) also called?
column4: NGS sequences millions of short DNA fragments simultaneously, dramatically reducing cost and time compared to Sanger sequencing; used in whole-genome sequencing.

column1: What is pyrosequencing?
column3: Sequencing by synthesis detecting pyrophosphate release as light
column4: Each nucleotide incorporation releases pyrophosphate, which drives luciferase-based luminescence; the light signal identifies which base was incorporated at each position.

column1: What technique measures global mRNA levels across the entire transcriptome simultaneously?
column4: Microarrays hybridize fluorescently labeled cDNA to thousands of probes on a chip; RNA-seq uses NGS to quantify transcripts; both reveal genome-wide expression profiles.

column1: What is Northern blotting used for?
column3: Detecting and quantifying specific mRNA in a sample
column4: RNA separated on a gel is transferred to a membrane and probed with a labeled complementary DNA or RNA probe; band size and intensity indicate transcript size and abundance.

column1: What does RT-qPCR measure in gene expression analysis?
column4: mRNA is converted to cDNA by reverse transcriptase, then quantified by real-time PCR; a housekeeping gene normalizes for differences in total RNA input.

column1: What is a DNA microarray used for?
column3: Simultaneously measuring expression levels of thousands of genes
column4: Labeled cDNA from a sample hybridizes to gene-specific probes on the array; fluorescence intensity at each spot reflects the expression level of that gene.

column1: What does single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) uniquely reveal?
column3: Gene expression in individual cells, showing cell-to-cell heterogeneity
column4: Traditional RNA-seq averages expression across many cells; scRNA-seq isolates and sequences RNA from each cell separately, uncovering distinct cell populations.

column1: What is a knockout organism used for in genetics research?
column3: Determining the function of a specific gene by eliminating its expression
column4: Targeted gene disruption in model organisms (e.g., knockout mice) reveals the phenotypic consequences of losing a gene's function, inferring its normal role.

column1: What is RNA interference (RNAi) used for?
column3: Silencing gene expression using small interfering RNA (siRNA)
column4: Double-stranded siRNA is processed by Dicer; the antisense strand guides RISC to complementary mRNA, causing its degradation and reducing protein production.

column1: What is the CRISPR-Cas9 system used for in gene function studies?
column3: Precise gene editing — disrupting, correcting, or tagging specific genes
column4: Guide RNA directs Cas9 endonuclease to a specific genomic locus; double-strand breaks are repaired by NHEJ (causing mutations) or HDR (precise edits).

column1: What is a dominant negative mutation and how does it help determine gene function?
column3: Mutant protein that blocks the function of the wild-type protein in the same cell
column4: Expressing a dominant negative variant in cells inhibits wild-type function without removing the gene, revealing its role through the resulting phenotype.

column1: What is a reporter gene assay used to determine?
column3: Whether a specific promoter or regulatory element is active
column4: A reporter gene (e.g., luciferase or GFP) is fused downstream of a regulatory element; reporter activity indicates when and where that element drives transcription.

column1: What are embryonic stem cells (ESCs)?
column3: Pluripotent cells derived from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst
column4: ESCs can differentiate into virtually any cell type; they are used in research to study development and in generating knockout mice via homologous recombination.

column1: What does 'pluripotent' mean in the context of stem cells?
column3: Ability to differentiate into any of the three germ layers (but not placenta)
column4: Pluripotent cells can become ectoderm, mesoderm, or endoderm derivatives; totipotent cells (e.g., zygote) can also form extraembryonic tissues like the placenta.

column1: What are induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)?
column3: Adult somatic cells reprogrammed to a pluripotent state by transcription factors
column4: Yamanaka factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) reprogram differentiated cells into iPSCs, avoiding ethical issues of ESC use and enabling patient-specific cell therapy.

column1: What is the difference between pluripotent and multipotent stem cells?
column3: Pluripotent: any cell type; multipotent: limited lineage (e.g., blood cell types only)
column4: Adult stem cells (e.g., hematopoietic stem cells) are multipotent; they generate only cells of their own tissue lineage, unlike pluripotent ESCs or iPSCs.

column1: What are the four Yamanaka transcription factors used to produce iPSCs?
column4: Shinya Yamanaka's 2006 discovery that these four factors reprogram adult cells to pluripotency won the Nobel Prize; it opened avenues for regenerative medicine.

column1: What is PCR-based DNA fingerprinting (short tandem repeat analysis) used for forensically?
column3: Identifying individuals from biological samples using unique STR profiles
column4: STRs (short tandem repeats) vary in copy number between individuals; PCR amplifies specific STR loci and the fragment pattern is compared to identify suspects or victims.

column1: What is human gene therapy?
column3: Introducing functional genes into patient cells to treat genetic disease
column4: Gene therapy can replace defective genes (e.g., in SCID or cystic fibrosis) using viral vectors or CRISPR; challenges include delivery, immune response, and off-target effects.

column1: How is recombinant human insulin produced?
column3: By expressing the human insulin gene in bacteria (E. coli) or yeast
column4: The human insulin gene (cDNA) is inserted into an expression vector and transformed into bacteria; the resulting recombinant protein is purified and used therapeutically.

column1: What is bioremediation?
column3: Using microorganisms to degrade environmental pollutants
column4: Genetically engineered bacteria can break down oil spills, heavy metals, or toxic chemicals; this is an environmental application of recombinant DNA technology.

column1: What is Bt crops and how are they created?
column3: Transgenic plants expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxin genes to resist insects
column4: The Bt toxin gene is inserted into the crop plant genome; expressed protein kills specific pest insects when ingested, reducing pesticide use.

column1: What is preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD)?
column3: Genetic testing of embryos before implantation via IVF to screen for disease alleles
column4: A cell is biopsied from an embryo; PCR or array analysis checks for known mutations; only unaffected embryos are implanted, preventing inherited diseases.

column1: What is the main ethical concern with germline gene therapy?
column3: Heritable changes affect future generations without their consent
column4: Somatic gene therapy changes only the patient; germline edits are passed to offspring, raising concerns about unintended consequences and eugenics.

column1: What is the principal biosafety concern with recombinant organisms released into the environment?
column3: Horizontal gene transfer of engineered genes to wild populations
column4: Transgenes could spread to related wild species or bacteria, potentially disrupting ecosystems or creating herbicide-resistant weeds (gene flow risk).

column1: What regulatory principle requires that GMO risks be assessed before release?
column4: The precautionary principle holds that if an action raises threats of harm, protective measures should be taken even without full scientific certainty of risk.

column1: What ethical issue arises from gene patenting in biotechnology?
column3: Private ownership of genetic sequences may restrict research access and benefit distribution
column4: Patents on DNA sequences or GMOs can limit academic research, raise drug prices, and concentrate agricultural control in large corporations.

column1: What is the distinction between somatic and germline gene therapy in terms of heritability?
column3: Somatic changes are not heritable; germline changes are passed to offspring
column4: Somatic gene therapy corrects cells in one individual only; germline therapy alters the embryo's genome, affecting all cells of the resulting organism and all descendants.

column1: What scientist performed the 1928 experiment showing a 'transforming principle' could convert non-virulent bacteria to virulent bacteria?
column4: Griffith injected mice with heat-killed virulent (smooth) Streptococcus pneumoniae plus live avirulent (rough) bacteria and observed lethal infection, demonstrating that some heritable factor was transferred between strains.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: What two strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae did Griffith use in his transformation experiment?
column4: The smooth strain has a polysaccharide capsule making it virulent; the rough strain lacks the capsule and is avirulent. Transformation turned rough cells into smooth cells.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: Which scientists (1944) identified DNA — not protein or RNA — as Griffith's transforming principle?
column4: They showed that DNase destroyed transforming activity while proteases and RNase did not, directly implicating DNA as the genetic material.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: In the Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment, which enzyme destroyed transforming activity, proving DNA was the transforming principle?
column4: Treatment with DNase eliminated the ability to transform rough bacteria into smooth bacteria, whereas protease and RNase had no effect, pointing exclusively to DNA.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: What experiment used radioactive isotopes to prove that DNA, not protein, is injected into host cells by bacteriophage?
column4: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase labeled phage DNA with 32P and phage protein with 35S, then showed only 32P entered bacteria, establishing DNA as the genetic material.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, which radioactive isotope labeled phage DNA?
column4: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur, so 32P specifically tracked DNA. After infection, 32P was found inside bacteria while 35S (protein label) remained in the supernatant.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, which radioactive isotope labeled phage protein coat?
column4: Proteins contain sulfur (in cysteine and methionine) but DNA does not, so 35S specifically tracked protein. The 35S stayed outside the bacteria after infection.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: What tool did Hershey and Chase use to separate phage coats from infected bacteria after blending?
column4: They agitated mixtures in a blender to detach phage coats, then centrifuged to pellet bacteria. The 32P-labeled DNA was in the pellet; 35S-labeled protein was in the supernatant.
column5: Evidence That DNA Is Genetic Material

column1: What is a phenotype?
column3: Observable physical/biochemical traits of an organism
column4: Phenotype results from the interaction of genotype with the environment. It includes morphology, physiology, and behavior.

column1: What is a genotype?
column3: Allelic composition of an organism's genome
column4: Genotype refers specifically to the genetic makeup, often written as pairs of allele symbols (e.g., Aa, BB).

column1: Two organisms with identical phenotypes must have identical genotypes — true or false?
column4: Dominant alleles can mask recessive ones; both AA and Aa produce the same dominant phenotype.

column1: What term describes the situation where the same genotype produces different phenotypes in different environments?
column4: Environmental factors such as temperature, nutrition, and stress can alter gene expression without changing the genotype.

column1: Which component of the central dogma most directly links genotype to phenotype?
column4: DNA is transcribed to mRNA, then translated to protein; protein function underlies most observable traits.

column1: What is a gene?
column3: DNA segment encoding a functional product (protein or RNA)
column4: Genes are the fundamental units of heredity; they may encode proteins or functional RNAs such as rRNA or tRNA.

column1: Which molecule is the physical carrier of genes in eukaryotes?
column4: In eukaryotes, genes reside on linear chromosomes packaged with histone proteins in the nucleus.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::gene MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the relationship between a gene and a polypeptide according to classical genetics?
column4: The one-gene–one-enzyme hypothesis (Beadle and Tatum) was later refined to one-gene–one-polypeptide as many proteins are multimeric.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::gene MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Can one gene produce multiple protein products? Name the mechanism.
column4: Differential inclusion of exons generates distinct mRNAs from a single pre-mRNA, expanding the proteome beyond the gene count.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::gene MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What distinguishes a structural gene from a regulatory gene?
column3: Structural: encodes protein; regulatory: controls expression of other genes
column4: Regulatory genes encode transcription factors or produce regulatory RNAs that modulate when/how much structural genes are expressed.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::gene MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a locus?
column3: Specific chromosomal location of a gene
column4: Every gene occupies a fixed position (locus) on a particular chromosome; homologous chromosomes carry alleles at the same locus.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::locus MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Alleles of the same gene occupy ________ loci on homologous chromosomes.
column4: Because homologs are paired, each carries one allele at the corresponding position during meiosis and fertilization.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::locus MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a linked locus?
column3: A locus on the same chromosome as another locus of interest
column4: Genes at linked loci tend to be inherited together; the closer the loci, the lower the recombination frequency.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::locus MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does the chromosomal location of a locus affect its inheritance pattern?
column3: Sex-linked loci follow X-linked or Y-linked inheritance patterns
column4: Loci on the X chromosome show sex-linked inheritance with different frequencies in males (hemizygous) vs. females.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::locus MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes loci on different chromosomes that always assort independently?
column4: Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment applies to genes on different (non-homologous) chromosomes or loci very far apart on the same chromosome.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::locus MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is an allele?
column3: One of two or more alternative forms of a gene at a given locus
column4: Alleles arise by mutation and differ in DNA sequence; they can produce different phenotypic effects.

column1: In a diploid organism, how many alleles does each individual carry at a single autosomal locus?
column4: One allele is inherited from each parent; the pair may be identical (homozygous) or different (heterozygous).

column1: What is meant by 'multiple alleles' at a locus?
column3: Three or more allelic variants exist in the population (though each individual carries only two)
column4: ABO blood type is the classic example: I^A, I^B, and i are three alleles at one locus.

column1: Name the three alleles responsible for ABO blood type.
column4: I^A and I^B are codominant and both dominant over i (recessive). Multiple alleles increase phenotypic diversity in the population.

column1: If a locus has 4 alleles in a population, how many possible diploid genotype combinations exist?
column4: Formula: n(n+1)/2 where n = number of alleles. For n=4: 4(5)/2 = 10.

column1: What does homozygous mean?
column3: Both alleles at a locus are identical
column4: Homozygous dominant (AA) or homozygous recessive (aa); homozygotes breed true for that trait.

column1: What does heterozygous mean?
column3: The two alleles at a locus differ
column4: A heterozygote (Aa) carries one dominant and one recessive allele; phenotype depends on dominance relationship.

column1: What is the genotypic ratio of offspring from a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Aa x Aa)?
column4: The 1:2:1 genotypic ratio contrasts with the 3:1 phenotypic ratio under complete dominance.

column1: Which mating increases homozygosity in a population fastest?
column4: With each generation of selfing, heterozygosity is halved; after n generations, heterozygosity = (1/2)^n of the original.

column1: Why does inbreeding increase the risk of autosomal recessive disease expression?
column3: Inbreeding increases homozygosity, exposing recessive alleles
column4: Related individuals are more likely to carry identical recessive alleles by descent (autozygosity), raising the probability of aa offspring.

column1: What is the wild-type allele?
column3: The most common (normal) allele in a natural population
column4: Wild-type is conventionally designated '+'; mutant alleles deviate from it. Wild-type often (but not always) encodes a functional protein.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::wild-type MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: In genetic notation, how is the wild-type allele commonly symbolized?
column4: This notation is especially common in Drosophila and microbial genetics to distinguish wild-type from mutant alleles.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::wild-type MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Is the wild-type allele always dominant?
column3: No — wild-type can be recessive, dominant, or codominant
column4: For example, the recessive loss-of-function allele may be the wild-type if most individuals carry it; dominance is not defined by frequency.
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::wild-type MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does it mean for a mutation to be 'loss-of-function' relative to wild-type?
column3: Mutant allele produces reduced or absent protein function vs. wild-type
column4: Loss-of-function mutations are usually recessive because one functional wild-type copy often suffices (haploinsufficiency is the exception).
column8: concept::BB::1C::mendelian_concepts MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1C::mendelian-concepts::wild-type MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Define recessiveness in Mendelian genetics.
column3: An allele whose phenotype is masked in the presence of a dominant allele
column4: A recessive allele (a) is only expressed phenotypically when homozygous (aa), because the dominant allele (A) compensates.

column1: What is the carrier genotype for an autosomal recessive trait?
column3: Heterozygous (Aa) — unaffected but carries recessive allele
column4: Carriers have the dominant phenotype but can pass the recessive allele to offspring, potentially producing affected aa children.

column1: What probability of affected offspring results from two carrier (Aa x Aa) parents?
column4: Punnett square gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; only the aa offspring express the recessive trait.

column1: Why are X-linked recessive traits more common in males than females?
column3: Males are hemizygous (X^a Y); one recessive allele is sufficient for expression
column4: Females need two copies of the recessive allele (X^a X^a) to be affected; males have no second X to mask it.

column1: What molecular mechanism most often underlies autosomal recessive inheritance?
column3: Loss-of-function mutation; heterozygote produces enough protein from one allele
column4: 50% of normal protein usually suffices (dosage tolerance); haploinsufficiency — where 50% is not enough — causes dominant inheritance.

column1: What is complete dominance?
column3: One allele fully masks the phenotypic effect of the other allele
column4: The heterozygote (Aa) is phenotypically indistinguishable from the dominant homozygote (AA). Classic Mendelian dominance.

column1: In complete dominance, what is the phenotypic ratio of offspring from Aa x Aa?
column4: AA and Aa are phenotypically identical; only aa shows the recessive phenotype, giving the 3:1 ratio Mendel observed.

column1: What is the phenotypic ratio expected from a dihybrid cross (AaBb x AaBb) with complete dominance at both loci?
column4: Independent assortment of two unlinked loci produces four phenotypic classes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio when both show complete dominance.

column1: How does complete dominance differ from incomplete dominance at the molecular level?
column3: Complete: one allele produces sufficient product; incomplete: half-dose is insufficient
column4: When one functional copy yields full protein activity, the trait appears fully dominant. Haploinsufficiency leads to an intermediate phenotype.

column1: What is codominance?
column3: Both alleles are independently expressed in the heterozygote
column4: Neither allele is masked; both contribute distinct products visible in the phenotype. Classic example: ABO blood type AB genotype.

column1: In an individual with blood type AB, which alleles are codominant?
column4: Both A and B antigens are present on red blood cells of AB individuals; I^A and I^B are codominant, both dominant over i.

column1: How does codominance differ from incomplete dominance?
column3: Codominance: both allele products present; incomplete dominance: blended intermediate phenotype
column4: In codominance you can distinguish both parental phenotypes in the heterozygote; in incomplete dominance a novel intermediate appears.

column1: What phenotypic ratio results from crossing two codominant heterozygotes (I^A I^B x I^A I^B)?
column3: 1 I^A I^A : 2 I^A I^B : 1 I^B I^B
column4: Phenotypically: 1 type A : 2 type AB : 1 type B — a 1:2:1 ratio reflecting distinct expression of each genotype.

column1: Which inheritance pattern best explains the presence of both sickle and normal hemoglobin in a sickle-cell trait (AS) individual?
column4: HbA and HbS are both produced; the individual has both normal and sickle-shaped red blood cells under low oxygen conditions.

column1: What is incomplete dominance?
column3: Heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype between both homozygotes
column4: The blending results from neither allele fully compensating for the other; e.g., red x white snapdragons yield pink heterozygotes.

column1: What phenotypic ratio is expected from crossing two pink snapdragons (R'R x R'R) if color shows incomplete dominance?
column4: With incomplete dominance, the genotypic ratio 1:2:1 equals the phenotypic ratio because each genotype produces a distinct phenotype.

column1: Define penetrance in genetics.
column3: Proportion of individuals with a genotype who display the expected phenotype
column4: A gene is fully penetrant if 100% of carriers show the trait; reduced penetrance means some carriers show no phenotype despite having the allele.

column1: Define expressivity in genetics.
column3: Degree to which a phenotype is expressed among individuals who do show it
column4: Variable expressivity means individuals with the same genotype show different severity; e.g., neurofibromatosis has variable expression.

column1: What is genetic leakage?
column3: Rare expression of a recessive phenotype in a dominant-genotype individual
column4: Leakage occurs when a dominant allele incompletely suppresses the recessive allele's effect, producing a weak version of the recessive phenotype.

column1: A gene shows 60% penetrance. What does this mean?
column3: Only 60% of individuals carrying the allele express the associated phenotype
column4: Modifying genes, epigenetics, and environment can prevent phenotypic expression even when a causative allele is present.

column1: What distinguishes penetrance from expressivity?
column3: Penetrance: whether phenotype appears; expressivity: how strongly it appears
column4: Penetrance is an all-or-none measure across individuals; expressivity measures the range of phenotypic severity among those who do express the trait.

column1: What is hybridization in genetics?
column3: Crossing of genetically distinct individuals to produce hybrid offspring
column4: Hybridization can occur within a species (intraspecific) or between species (interspecific); it is the basis of Mendel's experimental crosses.

column1: What is hybrid viability?
column3: The ability of hybrid offspring to survive to reproductive age
column4: Not all interspecific crosses yield viable offspring; developmental incompatibilities between genomes can cause lethality.

column1: What is a lethal allele combination in the context of hybrid viability?
column3: Genotype that causes embryonic/early death (e.g., AY AY in yellow agouti mice)
column4: Homozygous yellow (AY AY) mice die in utero; thus crosses between yellow mice yield 2 yellow : 1 agouti instead of the expected 3:1 ratio.

column1: What term describes the reproductive isolation that results when interspecific hybrids are sterile?
column4: Mule (horse x donkey) is a classic example: viable but sterile due to mismatched chromosome numbers preventing normal meiosis.

column1: What is hybrid vigor (heterosis)?
column3: Enhanced fitness/performance of hybrid offspring relative to both parental lines
column4: Heterosis is attributed to increased heterozygosity, which masks deleterious recessive alleles and may enhance gene expression. Used widely in agriculture.

column1: Which post-zygotic barrier specifically describes hybrid offspring that develop but cannot reproduce?
column4: Distinct from hybrid inviability (hybrids die) and hybrid breakdown (F2 or later hybrids have reduced fitness).

column1: What is a gene pool?
column3: Total collection of alleles in a interbreeding population at a given time
