column1: Name the five cofactors required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
column4: A common mnemonic is 'The Lazy Crook Found Napping' (TPP, Lipoamide, CoA, FAD, NAD+). Each cofactor is derived from a B vitamin.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::acetyl-coa-production-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What B vitamin is the precursor to the TPP cofactor used by pyruvate dehydrogenase?
column4: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is derived from thiamine (B1). Thiamine deficiency impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase and leads to lactic acidosis.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::acetyl-coa-production-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which reaction produces acetyl-CoA from fatty acid beta-oxidation?
column4: The final step of each beta-oxidation cycle cleaves a 2-carbon acetyl-CoA unit from the acyl-CoA chain via thiolase, releasing acetyl-CoA directly.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::acetyl-coa-production-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the net equation for the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA?
column3: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → Acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH
column4: This irreversible oxidative decarboxylation loses one carbon as CO2 and produces one NADH per pyruvate, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::acetyl-coa-production-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which kinase inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase by phosphorylating it, and what activates that kinase?
column3: PDH kinase; activated by high acetyl-CoA, NADH, and ATP
column4: When energy and acetyl-CoA are abundant, PDH kinase phosphorylates (inactivates) PDC, slowing pyruvate conversion — a product-inhibition regulatory mechanism.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::acetyl-coa-production-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the first step of the citric acid cycle?
column3: Condensation of acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate
column4: Citrate synthase catalyzes this step, producing the 6-carbon molecule citrate and releasing free CoA.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name the enzyme that catalyzes the first step of the citric acid cycle.
column4: Citrate synthase converts acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate → citrate + CoA. It is strongly inhibited by its product, ATP, and NADH.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which step of the TCA cycle produces GTP (or ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation?
column4: Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples the hydrolysis of the thioester bond in succinyl-CoA to GTP synthesis in the TCA cycle.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many NADH molecules are produced per turn of the citric acid cycle?
column4: NADH is produced at the isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase steps of each cycle turn.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which enzyme converts isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate in the TCA cycle?
column4: This oxidative decarboxylation produces the first NADH and first CO2 of the cycle and is a key regulatory step.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the product of the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase reaction?
column4: This step is mechanistically analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase — both are oxidative decarboxylations requiring the same five cofactors.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which TCA cycle step produces FADH2?
column4: Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II of the ETC) oxidizes succinate to fumarate, reducing FAD to FADH2. It is the only TCA enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What molecule is regenerated at the end of each citric acid cycle turn?
column4: Malate dehydrogenase converts malate to oxaloacetate (producing NADH), regenerating the 4-carbon acceptor for the next acetyl-CoA.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many CO2 molecules are released per turn of the TCA cycle?
column4: CO2 is released at the isocitrate dehydrogenase step and the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase step. These carbons come from oxaloacetate, not the incoming acetyl group.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which TCA cycle enzyme is structurally and mechanistically analogous to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
column4: Both complexes catalyze oxidative decarboxylation and require the same five cofactors: TPP, lipoamide, CoA, FAD, and NAD+.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What stereospecific form of malate is produced in the TCA cycle by fumarase?
column4: Fumarase hydrates fumarate specifically to L-malate (not D-malate), illustrating the stereospecificity of enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name the eight enzymes of the citric acid cycle in order.
column3: Citrate synthase, aconitase, isocitrate DH, alpha-KG DH, succinyl-CoA synthetase, succinate DH, fumarase, malate DH
column4: A common mnemonic: 'Citrate Is Krebs' Starting Substrate For Making Oxaloacetate' (CS, Aconitase, IDH, aKGDH, SCS, SDH, Fumarase, MDH).
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::reactions-of-the-cycle-substrates-and-products MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which enzyme of the TCA cycle is the primary allosteric regulatory enzyme?
column4: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and Ca2+ and inhibited by ATP and NADH, making it the main pace-setter of the cycle.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What effect does a high NADH/NAD+ ratio have on the citric acid cycle?
column4: NADH inhibits isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and citrate synthase, slowing the cycle when the cell's reducing power is high.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which allosteric activator stimulates isocitrate dehydrogenase?
column4: ADP signals low energy, activating isocitrate dehydrogenase to run the TCA cycle faster and generate more NADH for ATP production.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does citrate inhibit the TCA cycle?
column4: Accumulation of citrate (e.g., when the cycle outpaces downstream steps) feeds back to inhibit citrate synthase, preventing further condensation of acetyl-CoA.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the effect of Ca2+ on TCA cycle enzymes?
column3: Activates isocitrate DH, alpha-KG DH, and PDH phosphatase
column4: Ca2+ signals muscle contraction and energy demand; it activates multiple TCA enzymes (and PDH phosphatase, which activates PDC) to boost ATP production.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which TCA cycle enzyme is inhibited by succinyl-CoA?
column4: Succinyl-CoA is a product of alpha-KG dehydrogenase; it acts as a product inhibitor along with NADH to prevent overproduction.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name three inhibitors of citrate synthase.
column4: These product/energy-status inhibitors collectively slow the first step of the TCA cycle when intermediates and reducing equivalents are already abundant.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Why can the citric acid cycle only run in the presence of oxygen, even though it does not directly use O2?
column3: NAD+ and FAD must be regenerated by the ETC, which requires O2
column4: The TCA cycle consumes NAD+ and FAD; these are regenerated only by the electron transport chain, which requires O2 as the terminal electron acceptor.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::regulation-of-the-cycle MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many ATP equivalents are produced per glucose molecule via complete aerobic respiration?
column4: The actual yield (30-32 ATP) accounts for the P/O ratio and proton leak; the older theoretical maximum of 36-38 ATP overestimates actual mitochondrial efficiency.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many NADH are produced per glucose molecule across glycolysis, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and the TCA cycle?
column4: Glycolysis yields 2 NADH, pyruvate dehydrogenase yields 2 NADH, and the TCA cycle yields 6 NADH (3 per turn x 2 turns), totaling 10 NADH per glucose.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many FADH2 are produced per glucose in aerobic respiration?
column4: Each turn of the TCA cycle produces 1 FADH2 (at succinate dehydrogenase); with 2 turns per glucose, the total is 2 FADH2.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many ATP are produced per NADH via oxidative phosphorylation (P/O ratio)?
column4: The contemporary P/O ratio for NADH is ~2.5 (not 3), reflecting the actual stoichiometry of proton pumping and ATP synthase rotation.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many ATP are produced per FADH2 via oxidative phosphorylation?
column4: FADH2 enters the ETC at Complex II (bypassing Complex I), so it pumps fewer protons and yields ~1.5 ATP vs ~2.5 ATP for NADH.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many net ATP are produced by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose in aerobic respiration?
column3: 4 ATP (2 from glycolysis + 2 GTP from TCA)
column4: Glycolysis produces 2 net ATP; the TCA cycle produces 2 GTP (one per turn, 2 turns), all by substrate-level phosphorylation, totaling 4 ATP equivalents.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Where in the cell does the citric acid cycle occur?
column4: All TCA cycle enzymes are in the mitochondrial matrix except succinate dehydrogenase, which is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many CO2 molecules are released per glucose in complete aerobic respiration?
column4: Pyruvate dehydrogenase releases 2 CO2 (one per pyruvate), and the TCA cycle releases 4 CO2 (two per turn x 2 turns), totaling 6 CO2 per glucose.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the ATP yield difference between cytoplasmic NADH (from glycolysis) and mitochondrial NADH?
column3: Cytoplasmic NADH yields ~1.5-2 ATP less than mitochondrial NADH
column4: NADH produced in the cytoplasm must use the malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle to enter the mitochondria, reducing its effective ATP yield.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which shuttle system for cytoplasmic NADH preserves the full ~2.5 ATP yield, and which reduces it to ~1.5 ATP?
column3: Malate-aspartate shuttle (2.5 ATP); glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (1.5 ATP)
column4: The malate-aspartate shuttle transfers electrons to mitochondrial NADH; the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle transfers them to FADH2, losing one proton-pumping complex.
column8: concept::BB::1D::citric_acid_cycle MCAT::section::BB MCAT::1D::citric-acid-cycle::net-molecular-and-energetic-results-of-respiration-processes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What type of bond links fatty acids to glycerol in a triacylglycerol?
column4: The carboxyl group of each fatty acid reacts with a hydroxyl group of glycerol via esterification, releasing water. Three ester bonds are formed per triacylglycerol.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the general formula for a saturated fatty acid carbon chain?
column4: Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, so the chain holds the maximum number of hydrogens. Palmitic acid (C16) and stearic acid (C18) are classic MCAT examples.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What functional group is present at the head of every free fatty acid?
column4: The carboxyl end is polar/hydrophilic; the long hydrocarbon tail is nonpolar/hydrophobic. This amphipathic character determines membrane and micelle behavior.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: How many carbons are in palmitic acid?
column4: Palmitate (C16:0) is the most abundant saturated fatty acid in humans and a key product of de novo fatty acid synthesis in the liver.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What distinguishes a cis double bond from a trans double bond in a fatty acid?
column3: Cis: H atoms same side; trans: H atoms opposite sides
column4: Cis bonds create a kink in the chain, reducing packing and lowering melting point. Trans fatty acids pack more like saturated fats and raise LDL cholesterol.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which carbon of a fatty acid is the alpha carbon?
column4: The alpha carbon is C-2, beta is C-3. Beta-oxidation involves sequential removal of two-carbon acetyl units starting at the beta carbon.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Where does fat digestion primarily begin in the GI tract?
column4: Although lingual and gastric lipases act first, the majority of triglyceride hydrolysis occurs via pancreatic lipase in the duodenum, aided by bile salts.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What enzyme is responsible for most dietary fat digestion?
column4: Pancreatic lipase cleaves ester bonds at the sn-1 and sn-3 positions of triacylglycerols, producing two free fatty acids and a 2-monoacylglycerol.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the role of bile salts in fat digestion?
column4: Bile salts are amphipathic molecules that break large fat globules into smaller droplets (micelles), allowing pancreatic lipase greater access.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which lipoprotein carries absorbed dietary fats from intestinal cells to the lymph?
column4: Enterocytes reassemble triacylglycerols and package them into chylomicrons, which enter the lymphatic system via lacteals before reaching the bloodstream.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which enzyme hydrolyzes triacylglycerols in adipose tissue during lipolysis?
column4: HSL is activated by glucagon and epinephrine (via cAMP/PKA) and inhibited by insulin. It mobilizes stored fat by releasing free fatty acids into the blood.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: How are long-chain free fatty acids transported in the blood?
column4: Long-chain fatty acids are insoluble in plasma and must be chaperoned by serum albumin. Short/medium-chain fatty acids can travel unbound to the portal vein.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What cellular compartment is the site of beta-oxidation?
column4: Fatty acids must be activated to acyl-CoA in the cytoplasm, transported into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle, then oxidized in the matrix.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the activation step before a fatty acid can undergo beta-oxidation?
column4: Fatty acid + CoA + ATP → fatty acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi. This occurs in the cytoplasm and costs 2 ATP equivalents (ATP → AMP).
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which shuttle system carries long-chain acyl-CoA into the mitochondrial matrix?
column3: Carnitine shuttle (carnitine acyltransferase I and II)
column4: CAT I on the outer membrane transfers the acyl group to carnitine; CAT II on the inner membrane restores acyl-CoA inside. Malonyl-CoA inhibits CAT I.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: How many ATP are produced per cycle of beta-oxidation (counting FADH2 and NADH only)?
column4: Each cycle yields 1 FADH2 (~1.5 ATP) and 1 NADH (~2.5 ATP) plus 1 acetyl-CoA. The acetyl-CoA then enters the TCA cycle for additional ATP.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: How many cycles of beta-oxidation does palmitate (C16) undergo?
column4: Each cycle removes 2 carbons. A C16 fatty acid generates 8 acetyl-CoA units requiring 7 cleavage cycles (n/2 - 1 cycles for an n-carbon chain).
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What extra step is required for beta-oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids?
column4: The final 3-carbon propionyl-CoA is converted to succinyl-CoA by propionyl-CoA carboxylase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12-dependent), entering the TCA cycle.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is a saturated fatty acid?
column3: Fatty acid with no carbon-carbon double bonds
column4: All carbons in the chain are saturated with hydrogen atoms. Examples include palmitic acid (16:0) and stearic acid (18:0). Solid at room temperature.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What physical state are saturated fats in at room temperature?
column4: Saturated fatty acids pack tightly together due to their straight chains, resulting in high melting points and solid consistency (e.g., butter, lard, coconut oil).
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: How do saturated fats affect LDL cholesterol levels?
column4: High dietary saturated fat intake is associated with elevated LDL ('bad') cholesterol, increasing cardiovascular disease risk.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which saturated fatty acid has 18 carbons?
column4: Stearic acid is common in animal fats and cocoa butter. The shorthand 18:0 means 18 carbons and 0 double bonds.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Why do saturated fatty acids have higher melting points than unsaturated ones of similar chain length?
column3: Straight chains allow tighter packing (more van der Waals forces)
column4: Without kinks from double bonds, saturated chains align closely, maximizing intermolecular contacts and requiring more energy to separate (higher melting point).
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is an unsaturated fatty acid?
column3: Fatty acid with one or more carbon-carbon double bonds
column4: Monounsaturated have one double bond (e.g., oleic acid, 18:1); polyunsaturated have two or more (e.g., linoleic acid, 18:2). Usually liquid at room temperature.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the geometric configuration of most naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids?
column4: Natural fatty acids predominantly have cis double bonds, which introduce kinks in the chain and reduce melting point. Trans fats are mostly industrial (partially hydrogenated oils).
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What additional enzymatic step is needed during beta-oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids?
column4: Cis double bonds must be converted to trans by an enoyl-CoA isomerase to continue beta-oxidation. Polyunsaturated fatty acids also need a 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which two fatty acids are considered essential (must be obtained from diet)?
column4: Humans lack the desaturases to introduce double bonds beyond C-9, so these polyunsaturated fatty acids must be consumed in food.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: How does the presence of double bonds in unsaturated fats affect membrane fluidity?
column4: Cis double bonds prevent tight packing of phospholipid tails, keeping membranes fluid at lower temperatures — critical for membrane function.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Where are ketone bodies produced?
column4: Ketogenesis occurs in liver mitochondria when acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation exceeds the TCA cycle's capacity — typically during fasting or uncontrolled diabetes.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Name the three ketone bodies.
column4: Acetoacetate is the primary ketone body; beta-hydroxybutyrate is its reduced form and the most abundant in blood; acetone is produced spontaneously and exhaled.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the key intermediate in ketogenesis from which all ketone bodies are derived?
column4: HMG-CoA synthase condenses two acetyl-CoA molecules with acetoacetyl-CoA. HMG-CoA lyase then cleaves it to acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which tissues can use ketone bodies as fuel but CANNOT produce them?
column4: The liver lacks succinyl-CoA transferase (thiophorase) needed to activate ketone bodies for oxidation, so it produces but cannot use them as fuel.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What enzyme is absent in the liver that prevents it from oxidizing ketone bodies?
column4: This enzyme transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA to acetoacetate, activating it for catabolism. Its absence in hepatocytes means the liver exports ketone bodies for other tissues.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the first committed step of de novo fatty acid synthesis?
column4: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) adds CO2 to acetyl-CoA using biotin as cofactor. Malonyl-CoA is the two-carbon donor in subsequent elongation steps.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: In which cellular compartment does de novo fatty acid synthesis occur?
column4: Fatty acid synthase (FAS) is a cytosolic enzyme complex. Acetyl-CoA must be exported from mitochondria as citrate, then cleaved back by ATP-citrate lyase.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the major product of fatty acid synthase in humans?
column4: FAS adds two carbons per cycle and typically stops at C16, releasing palmitate. Longer or unsaturated fatty acids require further elongases and desaturases.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which molecule inhibits carnitine acyltransferase I during active fatty acid synthesis?
column4: Malonyl-CoA allosterically inhibits CAT I, preventing newly synthesized fatty acids from re-entering the mitochondria for beta-oxidation — a key regulatory switch.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What cofactor carries the growing fatty acid chain on the fatty acid synthase complex?
column4: ACP contains a phosphopantetheine arm (derived from pantothenate/vitamin B5) that tethers intermediates during each round of chain elongation.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is nontemplate synthesis in the context of lipid biosynthesis?
column3: Enzymatic assembly without a nucleic acid template
column4: Unlike proteins (translated from mRNA) or nucleic acids, lipids are synthesized by enzyme-catalyzed reactions using small-molecule precursors — no template is required.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What are the two main precursors for de novo lipid biosynthesis in the cytosol?
column4: Acetyl-CoA provides the carbon backbone; NADPH provides reducing equivalents. The pentose phosphate pathway is a key source of NADPH for fatty acid synthesis.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: How is acetyl-CoA transported from the mitochondria to the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis?
column3: As citrate via the citrate shuttle
column4: Oxaloacetate + acetyl-CoA → citrate in mitochondria. Citrate crosses to cytosol where ATP-citrate lyase regenerates oxaloacetate + acetyl-CoA.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: Which pathway is the primary source of NADPH for fatty acid synthesis?
column4: The oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway generates 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate oxidized, supplying reductive power for anabolic reactions.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the role of elongases and desaturases in lipid biosynthesis?
column3: Elongases lengthen; desaturases add double bonds to fatty acid chains
column4: After FAS produces palmitate, ER-associated elongases add 2-carbon units and desaturases (e.g., delta-9 desaturase) introduce cis double bonds to create diverse fatty acids.
column5: Metabolism of Fatty Acids and Proteins

column1: What is the primary site of amino acid catabolism in the body?
column4: The liver is the main organ responsible for amino acid degradation, transamination, and urea synthesis. Skeletal muscle also catabolizes branched-chain amino acids.

column1: What reaction removes the amino group from an amino acid to produce a keto acid?
column4: Transamination transfers the amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing glutamate and the corresponding keto acid. This is catalyzed by aminotransferases (transaminases) requiring PLP (vitamin B6).

column1: What vitamin serves as the cofactor for all aminotransferase (transaminase) enzymes?
column4: PLP is derived from vitamin B6 and acts as an amino group shuttle during transamination. Deficiency impairs amino acid catabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

column1: What is the name of the cycle that converts toxic ammonia into urea for excretion?
column4: The urea cycle (ornithine cycle) occurs mainly in liver hepatocytes. It converts 2 NH3 + CO2 into urea, which is excreted by the kidneys.

column1: Which enzyme releases free ammonia from glutamate during amino acid catabolism?
column4: Glutamate dehydrogenase in the mitochondrial matrix oxidatively deaminates glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate + NH4+. It can use either NAD+ or NADP+.

column1: What are the two nitrogen-containing substrates that directly enter the urea cycle?
column4: One nitrogen comes from ammonia via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (mitochondria), and the second comes from aspartate in the cytoplasm. Both are incorporated into urea.

column1: Which amino acids are classified as purely ketogenic (yield only acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate)?
column4: Leucine and lysine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids; they cannot be converted to glucose. All others are either purely glucogenic or both glucogenic and ketogenic.

column1: What is the fate of the carbon skeletons of glucogenic amino acids?
column4: Glucogenic amino acids are catabolized to pyruvate, oxaloacetate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, or fumarate — all gluconeogenic precursors.

column1: Which enzyme catalyzes the first committed step of the urea cycle, forming carbamoyl phosphate?
column4: CPS I is located in the mitochondrial matrix and uses NH4+, CO2, and 2 ATP. It is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate, which signals amino acid excess.

column1: What allosteric activator is required for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I activity?
column4: N-acetylglutamate is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate when amino acid levels are high, signaling the urea cycle to upregulate. Without it, CPS I is inactive.

column1: In which cellular compartment does the first step of the urea cycle occur?
column4: Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis and its condensation with ornithine to form citrulline both occur in the mitochondria. The remaining urea cycle steps occur in the cytoplasm.

column1: What is the term for amino acids that can be both glucogenic and ketogenic?
column4: Several amino acids — including isoleucine, threonine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan — yield both gluconeogenic and ketogenic intermediates upon catabolism.

column1: What neurotoxic compound accumulates in liver failure when the urea cycle is impaired?
column4: Hyperammonemia causes cerebral edema, asterixis, and encephalopathy. Ammonia depletes alpha-ketoglutarate (TCA intermediate) and elevates glutamine in astrocytes.

column1: What is the net ATP cost of one complete turn of the urea cycle?
column4: CPS I uses 2 ATP, and argininosuccinate synthetase uses 1 ATP (converted to AMP + PPi, consuming 2 high-energy bonds), totaling 4 high-energy bonds equivalent per urea produced.

column1: Which enzyme links the urea cycle to the TCA cycle by converting fumarate to malate?
column4: Argininosuccinate lyase releases fumarate in the urea cycle; fumarate enters the TCA cycle and is converted to malate by fumarase, linking the two cycles (the 'urea-TCA bicycle').

column1: What is the final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
column4: O2 is reduced to water at Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). Without O2, the ETC halts and ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation stops.

column1: Which two electron carriers feed electrons into the electron transport chain from the matrix?
column4: NADH donates electrons to Complex I; FADH2 donates electrons to Complex II. Both are oxidized as electrons flow down the chain.

column1: Where in the cell does oxidative phosphorylation occur?
column4: The ETC complexes and ATP synthase are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is impermeable to protons, enabling the proton gradient.

column1: What are the two main products of oxidative phosphorylation?
column4: ATP is synthesized by ATP synthase using the proton gradient; water is formed when O2 accepts electrons and protons at Complex IV.

column1: How many major protein complexes make up the electron transport chain?
column4: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), II (succinate dehydrogenase), III (cytochrome bc1), and IV (cytochrome c oxidase) are the four ETC complexes.

column1: Which complex of the ETC does NOT pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
column4: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) transfers electrons from FADH2 to ubiquinone but does not translocate protons, so FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH.

column1: What small mobile electron carrier shuttles electrons between Complex I/II and Complex III?
column4: Ubiquinone (CoQ) is lipid-soluble and diffuses within the inner membrane, picking up electrons from Complexes I and II and delivering them to Complex III.

column1: What small protein shuttles electrons between Complex III and Complex IV?
column4: Cytochrome c is a peripheral membrane protein on the intermembrane space side; it carries one electron at a time via its heme iron center.

column1: In which direction do electrons flow through the ETC relative to reduction potential?
column3: From lower to higher reduction potential
column4: Electrons move spontaneously toward more positive standard reduction potentials, releasing free energy that drives proton pumping.

column1: Which ETC complex catalyzes the reduction of O2 to H2O?
column4: Complex IV accepts electrons from cytochrome c and uses them to reduce O2 to H2O, also pumping protons across the membrane.

column1: How many protons does Complex I pump per pair of electrons transferred?
column4: Complex I translocates 4 H+ from the matrix to the intermembrane space per NADH oxidized, contributing to the proton motive force.

column1: What is the total number of protons pumped across the inner membrane per NADH oxidized by the full ETC (Complexes I, III, and IV)?
column4: Complex I pumps 4, Complex III pumps 4, and Complex IV pumps 2, for a total of ~10 H+ per NADH. This drives synthesis of approximately 2.5 ATP.

column1: What is the oxidized form of NAD+?
column4: NAD+ accepts a hydride ion (H-) to become NADH. On the MCAT, knowing that NAD+ is the electron acceptor and NADH is the electron donor is essential.

column1: Which coenzyme primarily carries electrons in anabolic (biosynthetic) reactions?
column4: NADPH is the primary reductant in anabolic reactions such as fatty acid synthesis and the pentose phosphate pathway, while NADH is used mainly in catabolism for ATP production.

column1: What is the primary role of NADH in oxidative phosphorylation?
column4: NADH is oxidized by Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), transferring its two electrons to ubiquinone and releasing energy that pumps protons.

column1: In which metabolic pathway is NADPH primarily generated?
column4: The oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway produces 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate oxidized. NADPH is also produced by isocitrate dehydrogenase (NADP+-linked) in some organisms.

column1: What structural feature distinguishes NADPH from NADH?
column3: A phosphate group on the 2' ribose of adenosine
column4: The extra phosphate on NADPH allows different enzymes to discriminate between the two coenzymes, directing NADH toward catabolism and NADPH toward anabolism.

column1: Which ETC complex is a flavoprotein that oxidizes FADH2?
column4: Complex II contains an FAD prosthetic group that is reduced by succinate to FADH2, then reoxidized as electrons pass to ubiquinone.

column1: How many electrons can FAD accept at one time?
column4: FAD is reduced to FADH2 by accepting 2e- and 2H+. This distinguishes flavoproteins from cytochromes, which carry only one electron at a time.

column1: From which vitamin is FAD derived?
column4: Riboflavin (B2) is the precursor to both FAD and FMN. Deficiency impairs electron transport and fatty acid oxidation.

column1: What metal center do cytochromes contain to carry electrons?
column4: Cytochromes carry electrons via reversible Fe2+/Fe3+ interconversion in their heme prosthetic group. Each cytochrome transfers one electron at a time.

column1: How many electrons does a single cytochrome molecule carry at one time?
column4: The iron center cycles between Fe2+ (reduced) and Fe3+ (oxidized), allowing only one electron transfer per cycle — unlike NADH or FADH2, which carry two.

column1: Which ETC complex contains cytochromes b and c1?
column4: Complex III uses the Q cycle involving cytochromes b and c1 to transfer electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c while pumping protons.

column1: What is the role of cytochrome a3 in Complex IV?
column3: Directly binds and reduces O2 to H2O
column4: Cytochrome a3 (together with a nearby copper center, CuB) is the site where O2 binds and is reduced to water at the end of the ETC.

column1: Which enzyme synthesizes ATP using the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
column4: ATP synthase couples proton flow from the intermembrane space back into the matrix to drive phosphorylation of ADP to ATP via a rotating mechanism.

column1: What is chemiosmotic coupling?
column3: Using a proton gradient to drive ATP synthesis
column4: Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis proposes that the free energy stored in the electrochemical proton gradient (proton motive force) is used by ATP synthase to phosphorylate ADP.

column1: What are the two main subunit domains of mitochondrial ATP synthase?
column4: F0 contains the proton channel (c-ring); F1 contains the catalytic beta subunits where ATP is synthesized. Proton flow through F0 rotates the c-ring, driving conformational changes in F1.

column1: Approximately how many protons must flow through ATP synthase to synthesize one ATP?
column4: The c-ring of human ATP synthase has ~8 c-subunits per full rotation, and each rotation synthesizes 3 ATP from 3 ADP+Pi, giving roughly 8/3 ≈ 2.7 H+ per ATP (often rounded to ~3).

column1: Which drug inhibits ATP synthase directly by blocking the F0 proton channel?
column4: Oligomycin binds the c-ring of F0, blocking proton flow and halting ATP synthesis. It is used experimentally to measure ATP synthase-dependent oxygen consumption.

column1: What two components contribute to the proton motive force?
column4: PMF = electrical potential difference (Delta-psi) + proton concentration gradient (Delta-pH). Both components drive H+ back into the matrix through ATP synthase.

column1: In which direction is the proton gradient oriented across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
column3: Higher [H+] in the intermembrane space than in the matrix
column4: ETC complexes pump H+ from matrix to intermembrane space, making the intermembrane space more acidic (lower pH) and positively charged relative to the matrix.

column1: What happens to the proton motive force when an uncoupler is added?
column4: Uncouplers like DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) allow H+ to re-enter the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, releasing energy as heat instead of ATP.

column1: How does the antibiotic gramicidin act on the inner mitochondrial membrane?
column3: Forms nonspecific ion channels, dissipating the proton gradient
column4: Gramicidin creates pores that allow protons (and other ions) to leak across the membrane, collapsing the PMF and uncoupling electron transport from ATP synthesis.

column1: What is the approximate net ATP yield per glucose molecule in eukaryotic aerobic respiration?
column4: Modern estimates (based on H+/ATP ratios) give ~30–32 ATP per glucose, replacing the older textbook value of 36–38. MCAT often accepts either but favors the updated value.

column1: How many ATP are produced per NADH entering the ETC (P/O ratio)?
column4: With ~10 H+ pumped per NADH and ~4 H+ per ATP (including transport costs), the P/O ratio for NADH is ~2.5; for FADH2 it is ~1.5.

column1: What is the net CO2 yield per glucose in complete aerobic oxidation?
column4: Pyruvate decarboxylation yields 2 CO2 and the TCA cycle yields 4 CO2 (2 per turn × 2 turns), for a total of 6 CO2 per glucose.

column1: How many NADH are produced per glucose by glycolysis, pyruvate decarboxylation, and the TCA cycle combined?
column4: Glycolysis: 2 NADH; pyruvate decarboxylation: 2 NADH; TCA (per glucose): 6 NADH. Total = 10 NADH. These feed the ETC to drive most ATP production.

column1: What is the net ATP yield from substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose in aerobic respiration?
column4: Glycolysis produces 2 ATP (net) and the TCA cycle produces 2 GTP (equivalent to 2 ATP) per glucose via substrate-level phosphorylation.

column1: What is the primary mechanism by which ADP concentration regulates oxidative phosphorylation?
column3: High ADP stimulates the ETC and ATP synthase
column4: When ADP is abundant (low energy charge), ATP synthase runs faster, increasing O2 consumption. Low ADP (high ATP) slows respiration — this is respiratory control.

column1: What term describes the control of O2 consumption by ADP availability?
column4: The rate of oxidative phosphorylation is tightly coupled to ATP demand. Excess ATP inhibits complex IV and ATP synthase, reducing O2 uptake.

column1: How does the NADH/NAD+ ratio regulate oxidative phosphorylation?
column3: High NADH/NAD+ increases substrate supply, stimulating ETC
column4: Elevated NADH provides more electrons to Complex I, accelerating the ETC. Conversely, a low NADH/NAD+ ratio (abundant NAD+) slows ETC flux.

column1: Which small molecule acts as a competitive inhibitor of cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV)?
column4: CO binds with high affinity to the Fe2+ of cytochrome a3 in Complex IV, blocking O2 binding and halting electron transfer — causing cellular asphyxiation.

column1: Which ion, when inhibiting Complex IV, causes a similar effect to CO poisoning?
column4: Cyanide also binds cytochrome a3 at Complex IV, blocking O2 reduction. Both CN- and CO cause cytotoxic hypoxia despite normal O2 delivery.

column1: What are the two mitochondrial membranes called?
column3: Outer mitochondrial membrane and inner mitochondrial membrane
column4: The outer membrane is permeable to small molecules via porins; the inner membrane is highly impermeable and is the site of the ETC and ATP synthase.

column1: What is the name of the space between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes?
column4: The intermembrane space accumulates H+ pumped by the ETC, establishing the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase. It has a composition similar to the cytosol for small ions.

column1: Which protein, released from mitochondria, initiates the intrinsic apoptosis pathway?
column4: Upon apoptotic stress, cytochrome c is released from the intermembrane space into the cytosol, where it assembles the apoptosome with Apaf-1 and activates caspase-9.

column1: What is the role of Bcl-2 family proteins in mitochondrial apoptosis?
column4: Pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 members (Bax, Bak) promote MOMP and cytochrome c release; anti-apoptotic members (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) inhibit this. Their ratio determines cell fate.

column1: What are reactive oxygen species (ROS) and where are they primarily generated in the cell?
column3: Partially reduced O2 derivatives; primarily at the ETC (Complexes I and III)
column4: Electrons that leak from the ETC react with O2 to form superoxide (O2-•). ROS can damage DNA, proteins, and lipids — relevant to aging and disease.

column1: Which enzyme converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide in the mitochondrial matrix?
column4: MnSOD catalyzes 2 O2-• + 2H+ → H2O2 + O2. H2O2 is then detoxified by catalase or glutathione peroxidase. MnSOD is a key antioxidant defense in mitochondria.

column1: What is mitochondrial membrane potential (Delta-psi) and why is it important?
column3: Electrical potential (~-180 mV, matrix negative) across inner membrane; drives ATP synthesis and mitochondrial import
column4: The charge difference (matrix negative) arises from proton pumping. It contributes to PMF and is essential for importing nuclear-encoded proteins into the mitochondria via the TIM/TOM complexes.

column1: Which ETC complex contains an FMN prosthetic group in addition to iron-sulfur clusters?
column4: Complex I uses FMN to accept electrons from NADH, then passes them through a series of Fe-S clusters to ubiquinone. FMN is derived from riboflavin (B2).

column1: What is the Q cycle and at which ETC complex does it occur?
column3: Mechanism of electron bifurcation and proton pumping; occurs at Complex III
column4: In the Q cycle, ubiquinol donates electrons: one to cytochrome c (via cytochrome c1) and one back to ubiquinone via cytochrome b, effectively doubling proton pumping efficiency at Complex III.

column1: What class of hormones are derived from cholesterol?
column4: Steroid hormones (e.g., glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex hormones) are synthesized from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex and gonads; they are lipid-soluble and act via intracellular receptors.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the general mechanism of action of peptide hormones?
column3: Bind cell-surface receptors; activate second messengers
column4: Peptide hormones are hydrophilic and cannot cross the plasma membrane; they bind membrane receptors and signal through second messengers such as cAMP or IP3/DAG.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which second messenger is produced when glucagon binds its receptor?
column4: Glucagon activates adenylyl cyclase via Gs protein, producing cAMP, which activates PKA — a classic example of a GPCR-mediated hormonal response.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Steroid hormones travel in the blood bound to what type of carrier?
column4: Because steroids are lipophilic, they bind carrier proteins (e.g., albumin, cortisol-binding globulin) for transport; only the free fraction is biologically active.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What type of receptor do steroid hormones typically use to alter gene expression?
column4: Steroid-receptor complexes translocate to the nucleus and act as transcription factors, modulating mRNA synthesis — a slower but more prolonged response than peptide hormones.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Thyroid hormones (T3/T4) act via which type of receptor?
column4: Despite being derived from tyrosine (an amino acid), thyroid hormones are lipophilic and use nuclear receptors, making them functionally similar to steroid hormones.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Epinephrine is derived from which amino acid?
column4: Catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) are synthesized from tyrosine via DOPA. They act on adrenergic cell-surface receptors using second messengers.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which hormone class acts most rapidly: peptide, steroid, or thyroid?
column4: Peptide hormones act in seconds-to-minutes via pre-formed second messenger cascades; steroid and thyroid hormones require new protein synthesis and act over hours to days.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the primary fuel used by the brain under normal (fed) conditions?
column4: The brain is obligate glucose consumer under normal conditions, consuming ~120 g/day. It lacks significant glycogen stores and cannot oxidize fatty acids due to the blood-brain barrier.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which organ is the primary site of gluconeogenesis during fasting?
column4: The liver accounts for ~90% of gluconeogenesis; the kidney contributes the remainder, especially during prolonged fasting or acidosis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the primary fuel used by red blood cells?
column4: RBCs lack mitochondria and cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation; they rely entirely on anaerobic glycolysis and produce lactate.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which tissue is the major site of fatty acid synthesis (de novo lipogenesis)?
column4: The liver is the dominant site of de novo fatty acid synthesis; adipose tissue also performs lipogenesis but to a lesser extent. Excess carbohydrates are converted to fat here.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What fuel do cardiac muscle cells preferentially oxidize?
column4: The heart is highly aerobic and preferentially oxidizes fatty acids for ATP (~60-70%); it can also use ketone bodies, glucose, and lactate depending on availability.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What alternative fuel does the brain use during prolonged starvation?
column4: After several days of fasting, the brain adapts to use ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) produced by the liver from fatty acid oxidation, sparing muscle protein.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What metabolic process do skeletal muscles use during intense exercise?
column4: During intense exercise, muscle oxygen demand exceeds supply; pyruvate is converted to lactate by LDH, regenerating NAD+ for continued glycolysis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the Cori cycle?
column3: Lactate from muscle → glucose in liver
column4: Lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in muscle is transported to the liver, converted back to glucose by gluconeogenesis, and returned to muscle — an energy transfer cycle.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Adipose tissue releases fatty acids into circulation in what form?
column4: Hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes hydrolyzes stored triglycerides; released free fatty acids bind albumin for transport to peripheral tissues.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which enzyme in adipose tissue is activated by insulin to promote fat storage?
column4: Insulin activates LPL on capillary endothelium of adipose tissue, hydrolyzing circulating triglycerides (in VLDL/chylomicrons) so fatty acids can be taken up and stored.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the primary metabolic effect of insulin on blood glucose?
column4: Insulin promotes glucose uptake (GLUT4 translocation in muscle/fat), glycogen synthesis, glycolysis, and lipogenesis while inhibiting gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which hormone is the primary counter-regulatory hormone to insulin?
column4: Glucagon is released from pancreatic alpha cells when blood glucose is low; it raises blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which enzyme does glucagon activate to stimulate glycogen breakdown in the liver?
column4: Glucagon → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase (and inhibits glycogen synthase), driving hepatic glycogenolysis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the effect of insulin on GLUT4 transporters in muscle and adipose?
column3: Promotes GLUT4 translocation to plasma membrane
column4: Insulin signaling via PI3K/Akt causes GLUT4-containing vesicles to fuse with the plasma membrane, dramatically increasing glucose uptake into muscle and fat cells.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis by inducing expression of which key enzyme?
column4: Cortisol (a glucocorticoid) upregulates PEPCK and other gluconeogenic enzymes via nuclear receptor-mediated transcription, raising blood glucose during stress.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which hormone activates hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) in adipose tissue?
column4: HSL is activated by PKA-mediated phosphorylation in response to cAMP; glucagon and epinephrine raise cAMP in adipocytes, promoting lipolysis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What effect does insulin have on hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)?
column4: Insulin activates phosphodiesterase (lowers cAMP) and activates phosphatases that dephosphorylate/inactivate HSL, thus inhibiting triglyceride breakdown in adipose tissue.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Epinephrine stimulates glycogenolysis in muscle through which enzyme?
column4: Epinephrine binds beta-adrenergic receptors on muscle, raises cAMP, activates PKA, which phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase — mobilizing glucose-1-phosphate for glycolysis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which enzyme is activated by insulin to promote glycogen synthesis?
column4: Insulin activates protein phosphatase-1 (PP1), which dephosphorylates and activates glycogen synthase, promoting glycogen storage in liver and muscle.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the role of AMPK in fuel metabolism?
column3: Energy sensor; activates catabolism, inhibits anabolism
column4: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) is activated when AMP/ATP ratio is high; it stimulates fatty acid oxidation and glucose uptake while inhibiting fatty acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which hormone inhibits insulin secretion from beta cells and glucagon secretion from alpha cells?
column4: Somatostatin, released from pancreatic delta cells and the hypothalamus, inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion, dampening the overall endocrine pancreatic response.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the fasting blood glucose threshold for a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
column4: A fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or above on two separate occasions is diagnostic for diabetes mellitus (ADA criteria). Impaired fasting glucose = 100-125 mg/dL.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Define obesity in terms of BMI.
column4: Body mass index = weight(kg)/height(m)². Overweight = 25-29.9; Obese = 30-39.9; Morbidly obese = ≥40. BMI is a screening tool, not a direct measure of body fat.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What hormone, produced by adipose tissue, signals satiety to the hypothalamus?
column4: Leptin is released by adipocytes in proportion to fat stores; it acts on the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure. Leptin deficiency or resistance causes obesity.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What hormone produced by the stomach stimulates hunger?
column4: Ghrelin (the 'hunger hormone') is secreted by gastric fundus cells before meals; levels rise with fasting and fall after eating. It acts on the hypothalamus to increase appetite.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: In leptin resistance (common in obesity), what happens to circulating leptin levels?
column4: Obese individuals typically have high leptin levels due to abundant adipose tissue, but the hypothalamus becomes resistant to leptin's satiety signal — analogous to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which hypothalamic nucleus is the primary center for appetite regulation?
column4: The arcuate nucleus contains NPY/AgRP neurons (orexigenic) and POMC/CART neurons (anorexigenic); leptin suppresses NPY/AgRP and stimulates POMC, reducing hunger.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What metabolic condition is closely linked to central (visceral) obesity?
column4: Visceral adipose tissue releases inflammatory cytokines and free fatty acids that promote insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and hyperglycemia — collectively metabolic syndrome.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the set-point theory of body weight regulation?
column3: Body weight is defended around a physiologically set point
column4: The set-point theory proposes that the hypothalamus regulates body weight around a 'set point' via hormonal and neural feedback; deviations trigger compensatory changes in appetite and metabolic rate.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which peptide hormone released from the gut after eating promotes satiety?
column4: GLP-1 is an incretin released by L-cells of the small intestine in response to nutrients; it enhances insulin secretion, inhibits glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and suppresses appetite.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is adiponectin's effect on insulin sensitivity?
column4: Adiponectin, secreted by adipose tissue, activates AMPK and promotes fatty acid oxidation; its levels are paradoxically LOW in obese individuals, contributing to insulin resistance.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which neurotransmitter pathway mediates the reward aspect of feeding behavior?
column4: High-calorie foods activate dopaminergic reward circuits; chronic overstimulation may downregulate dopamine receptors, resembling addiction and contributing to compulsive overeating.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the primary glucose transporter expressed in the brain?
column4: GLUT1 is constitutively expressed at the blood-brain barrier and on glial cells; GLUT3 is the neuronal glucose transporter. Neither requires insulin, ensuring constant glucose supply to the brain.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the glucose transporter used by liver cells?
column4: GLUT2 has a high Km for glucose, allowing the liver to sense and respond proportionally to blood glucose concentrations. It is also found in pancreatic beta cells and small intestine.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: During fasting, which molecule does the liver export to supply peripheral tissues?
column4: In the fasted state, the liver performs gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis (exporting glucose) and beta-oxidation with ketogenesis (exporting ketone bodies) to fuel brain and other tissues.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which organ cannot perform gluconeogenesis and why?
column4: Muscle can produce glucose-6-phosphate via glycogenolysis but lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot release free glucose into the blood — glucose-6-phosphate is trapped for internal use.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What pancreatic cell type secretes insulin?
column3: Beta cells (B cells) of the islets of Langerhans
column4: Beta cells are the most abundant islet cell type (~65-80%). They secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose, amino acids, and incretins.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What pancreatic cell type secretes glucagon?
column3: Alpha cells (A cells) of the islets of Langerhans
column4: Alpha cells (~15-20% of islet cells) release glucagon in response to low blood glucose, amino acids, and sympathetic stimulation.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the incretin effect?
column3: Oral glucose causes greater insulin release than IV glucose
column4: Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) released from gut cells after oral nutrient ingestion potentiate pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion; this amplifies insulin response beyond what blood glucose alone triggers.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which key enzyme is activated by glucagon/PKA to inhibit glycolysis in the liver?
column4: PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2, activating its phosphatase activity and reducing fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels, which inhibits PFK-1 and slows glycolysis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the primary anabolic effect of insulin on protein metabolism?
column3: Stimulates protein synthesis; inhibits protein degradation
column4: Insulin activates mTOR (via PI3K/Akt), promoting ribosomal protein synthesis. It also inhibits the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, reducing muscle protein breakdown.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Name the three ketone bodies produced during fatty acid catabolism.
column4: Ketone bodies are produced in the liver from acetyl-CoA. Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are energy substrates; acetone is volatile and exhaled, causing fruity breath in ketoacidosis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What enzyme commits acetyl-CoA to ketogenesis in the liver?
column4: In the liver mitochondria, 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (via HMG-CoA synthase) → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA. This is distinct from cytosolic HMG-CoA synthase used in cholesterol synthesis.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What type of BMI is classified as 'overweight'?
column4: WHO classification: underweight <18.5, normal 18.5-24.9, overweight 25-29.9, obese ≥30. Overweight BMI significantly increases risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: Which adipokine is decreased in obesity and promotes fatty acid oxidation?
column4: Adiponectin activates AMPK in muscle and liver, stimulating fat oxidation and improving insulin sensitivity. Obesity is associated with low adiponectin, worsening metabolic dysfunction.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the primary hormone that regulates long-term energy balance vs. short-term hunger?
column4: Leptin reflects chronic fat stores and regulates long-term energy homeostasis; ghrelin fluctuates meal-to-meal and signals acute hunger. Both act on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus.
column5: Hormonal Regulation and Integration of Metabolism

column1: What is the primary general function of the plasma membrane?
column3: Selective barrier controlling what enters/exits the cell
column4: The plasma membrane maintains cellular homeostasis by regulating passage of ions, molecules, and information between the intracellular and extracellular environments.

column1: What does the plasma membrane define by acting as a barrier?
column3: The boundary of the cell (intracellular vs extracellular)
column4: By confining cytoplasm and organelles, the plasma membrane establishes the cell as a discrete, regulated compartment distinct from its surroundings.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::general-function-in-cell-containment MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What term describes the plasma membrane's ability to allow some substances through while blocking others?
column4: Selective permeability allows small nonpolar molecules to cross freely while restricting ions and large polar molecules, enabling the cell to maintain concentration gradients.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::general-function-in-cell-containment MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which property of the plasma membrane allows it to facilitate cell signaling?
column3: Membrane receptors that transduce extracellular signals
column4: Receptor proteins embedded in or on the membrane bind ligands and trigger intracellular cascades, linking environmental signals to cellular responses.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::general-function-in-cell-containment MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name two general classes of macromolecules that constitute the plasma membrane.
column4: The plasma membrane is primarily a phospholipid bilayer with embedded and associated proteins; carbohydrates are also present as glycolipids and glycoproteins on the extracellular face.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::general-function-in-cell-containment MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are the three main lipid types found in eukaryotic plasma membranes?
column4: Phospholipids form the bilayer backbone; cholesterol modulates fluidity; glycolipids contribute to the glycocalyx and cell recognition on the outer leaflet.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::composition-of-membranes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which face of the plasma membrane is enriched with carbohydrate chains?
column4: Glycolipids and glycoproteins project their sugar moieties outward, forming the glycocalyx, which is involved in cell-cell recognition and adhesion.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::composition-of-membranes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the approximate protein-to-lipid ratio (by mass) of a typical plasma membrane?
column4: The ratio varies greatly by membrane function; highly active membranes (e.g., inner mitochondrial membrane) are protein-rich, while myelin sheaths are lipid-rich.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::composition-of-membranes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What type of proteins are embedded within the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer?
column4: Integral proteins often span the entire bilayer (transmembrane proteins) and are tightly associated with the hydrophobic fatty acid tails, requiring detergents for extraction.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::composition-of-membranes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What type of proteins associate with the membrane surface but do not penetrate the hydrophobic core?
column4: Peripheral proteins bind to integral proteins or lipid head groups via noncovalent interactions and can be removed with mild treatments such as high salt or pH changes.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::composition-of-membranes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the general structure of a phospholipid?
column3: Glycerol backbone + 2 fatty acid tails + phosphate head group
column4: The phosphate-containing head is hydrophilic; the two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic. This amphipathic nature drives spontaneous bilayer formation in water.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::lipid-components-bio-bc-oc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which property of lipids allows them to spontaneously form bilayers in aqueous environments?
column4: Hydrophobic tails cluster away from water while hydrophilic heads interact with it, minimizing free energy and producing a stable bilayer without covalent bonding.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::lipid-components-bio-bc-oc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does the degree of unsaturation in fatty acid tails affect membrane fluidity?
column4: Cis double bonds introduce kinks that prevent tight fatty acid packing, keeping the membrane more fluid, especially at lower temperatures.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::lipid-components-bio-bc-oc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does fatty acid chain length affect membrane fluidity?
column3: Longer chains decrease fluidity (more van der Waals interactions)
column4: Longer saturated fatty acids pack more tightly and have stronger hydrophobic interactions, raising the melting temperature of the membrane.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::lipid-components-bio-bc-oc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which lipid component of the plasma membrane acts as a fluidity buffer across temperature ranges?
column4: At high temperatures cholesterol restrains phospholipid movement (decreasing fluidity); at low temperatures it prevents tight packing (increasing fluidity), maintaining a functional intermediate state.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::lipid-components-bio-bc-oc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the chemical nature of the head group that defines a phospholipid?
column3: Phosphate group esterified to an alcohol
column4: Common alcohols include choline, ethanolamine, serine, and inositol. The identity of the alcohol determines the specific phospholipid class (e.g., phosphatidylcholine).
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name the most abundant phospholipid in the outer leaflet of animal cell plasma membranes.
column4: Phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) is the predominant outer-leaflet phospholipid; phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine are concentrated in the inner leaflet.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the linkage between fatty acids and glycerol in a phospholipid?
column4: Fatty acids are attached at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions of glycerol via ester bonds; the sn-2 position often carries the unsaturated fatty acid.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the name of the positively charged nitrogen-containing head group in phosphatidylcholine?
column4: Choline is a quaternary ammonium compound; its positive charge paired with the negative phosphate creates a zwitterionic (overall neutral) head group.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which phospholipid, when exposed on the outer leaflet, signals apoptosis (programmed cell death)?
column4: Normally confined to the inner leaflet, phosphatidylserine flips to the outer leaflet in apoptotic cells, acting as an 'eat-me' signal recognized by macrophages.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the basic four-ring carbon skeleton common to all steroids?
column4: All steroids — including cholesterol, cortisol, and sex hormones — share this fused three cyclohexane + one cyclopentane ring backbone; functional groups determine activity.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::steroids MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What role does cholesterol play in the plasma membrane?
column4: Cholesterol's rigid ring structure inserts between phospholipids, reducing permeability to small water-soluble molecules and buffering fluidity changes with temperature.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::steroids MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Is cholesterol found in prokaryotic plasma membranes?
column4: Bacterial membranes generally lack cholesterol; some bacteria use hopanoids as functional analogs. This difference is a target for certain antifungal drugs that disrupt ergosterol (fungal sterol).
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::steroids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: At which position does cholesterol insert its hydroxyl group relative to the bilayer?
column3: At the hydrophilic interface (phospholipid head group region)
column4: The hydroxyl group at C-3 hydrogen-bonds with phospholipid head groups while the hydrophobic ring and tail extend into the fatty acid tail region.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::steroids MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the chemical composition of a wax?
column3: Long-chain fatty acid esterified to a long-chain alcohol
column4: Waxes are highly nonpolar and water-repellent due to long saturated hydrocarbon chains on both the acid and alcohol. They serve primarily as waterproofing/protective barriers.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::waxes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What biological function do waxes primarily serve?
column4: Examples include plant cuticle waxes (cutin), ear wax (cerumen), and the coating on bird feathers, all providing hydrophobic barriers against water loss and pathogens.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::waxes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How do waxes differ structurally from triglycerides?
column3: Waxes have ONE fatty acid + one long-chain alcohol; triglycerides have THREE fatty acids + glycerol
column4: Triglycerides use glycerol as the backbone with three ester bonds; waxes use a long-chain monohydric alcohol, making them more solid and less biodegradable.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::waxes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are integral membrane proteins that span the entire bilayer called?
column4: Transmembrane proteins often contain alpha-helical or beta-barrel segments rich in hydrophobic amino acids that anchor them in the lipid core; they can function as channels, receptors, or transporters.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::protein-components MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What secondary structure is most commonly used by transmembrane domains to cross the hydrophobic bilayer?
column4: The alpha helix satisfies all backbone hydrogen bonds internally, presenting only hydrophobic side chains outward, which is thermodynamically favorable in the membrane core.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::protein-components MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name the two broad functional categories of membrane proteins.
column4: Additional categories include enzymes, cell-adhesion molecules, and structural anchor proteins, but transport and signaling are the most MCAT-relevant functional groupings.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::protein-components MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is a glycoprotein?
column3: A protein with covalently attached carbohydrate chains
column4: Glycoproteins are found on the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane; their sugar chains participate in cell recognition, immune function, and protection from proteolysis.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::protein-components MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which amino acids in a transmembrane helix are typically hydrophobic?
column4: A stretch of ~20 consecutive hydrophobic amino acids is sufficient to span the 30 Å hydrophobic core of the bilayer as an alpha helix.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::protein-components MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Who proposed the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
