column4: The model describes the membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer in which proteins are embedded and can move laterally, like tiles in a mosaic floating on a sea.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::fluid-mosaic-model MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What does 'fluid' refer to in the fluid mosaic model?
column3: Lateral mobility of lipids and proteins within each leaflet
column4: Membrane components diffuse laterally (2D) rapidly but rarely flip-flop (transverse movement) between leaflets, maintaining membrane asymmetry.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::fluid-mosaic-model MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What does 'mosaic' refer to in the fluid mosaic model?
column3: The patchy distribution of proteins embedded in the lipid bilayer
column4: Proteins of various sizes and functions are interspersed throughout the bilayer, giving the membrane a mosaic-like appearance when viewed from above.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::fluid-mosaic-model MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is lipid asymmetry in the plasma membrane?
column3: Different lipid compositions in the inner vs. outer leaflet
column4: For example, phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine favor the inner leaflet; phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin favor the outer leaflet.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::fluid-mosaic-model MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What experimental technique demonstrated lateral diffusion of membrane proteins (FRAP)?
column4: FRAP bleaches fluorescently labeled membrane proteins in a small region; recovery of fluorescence as unbleached proteins diffuse in confirms lateral membrane fluidity.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::fluid-mosaic-model MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is flip-flop (transverse diffusion) of a lipid?
column3: Movement of a lipid from one leaflet to the other (rare, slow)
column4: Flip-flop requires the hydrophilic head group to pass through the hydrophobic core, making it energetically costly and very slow unless catalyzed by flippases/scramblases.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-dynamics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What enzyme catalyzes ATP-dependent lipid flip-flop from outer to inner leaflet?
column4: Flippases maintain membrane asymmetry by actively moving specific phospholipids (e.g., phosphatidylserine) to the cytoplasmic leaflet, requiring ATP hydrolysis.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-dynamics MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does temperature affect membrane fluidity?
column3: Higher temperature increases fluidity; lower temperature decreases fluidity
column4: Thermal energy disrupts ordered fatty acid packing; organisms adapt by altering fatty acid saturation (homeoviscous adaptation) to maintain appropriate fluidity.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-dynamics MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are lipid rafts?
column3: Microdomains enriched in cholesterol and sphingolipids within the bilayer
column4: Lipid rafts are more ordered and less fluid than surrounding membrane; they concentrate certain signaling proteins and receptors, facilitating efficient signal transduction.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-dynamics MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is lateral diffusion of membrane proteins?
column3: Movement of proteins within the same leaflet of the bilayer
column4: Lateral diffusion is rapid (microseconds) and accounts for most protein movement; it is constrained by the cytoskeleton 'fence' and protein-protein interactions.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-dynamics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which types of molecules can cross the plasma membrane by simple diffusion?
column3: Small nonpolar molecules and gases (O2, CO2, N2, fatty acids)
column4: These molecules dissolve in the lipid bilayer and diffuse down their concentration gradient without requiring a protein; water crosses slowly by simple diffusion but mainly via aquaporins.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::solute-transport-across-membranes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What determines the direction of net solute movement across a membrane?
column4: Net movement always occurs from high to low electrochemical potential; for charged solutes, both concentration gradient and electrical gradient (membrane potential) must be considered.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::solute-transport-across-membranes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the electrochemical gradient?
column3: Combined effect of concentration gradient + electrical potential on ion movement
column4: For ions, the net driving force is the sum of the chemical (concentration) gradient and the electrical (voltage) gradient across the membrane.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::solute-transport-across-membranes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which molecules have difficulty crossing the lipid bilayer unaided?
column3: Ions, large polar molecules, and charged species
column4: Their hydrophilicity makes it energetically costly to enter the hydrophobic core; they require protein channels or carriers to cross the membrane.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::solute-transport-across-membranes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Is simple diffusion of solutes across membranes energetically favorable?
column3: Yes, if moving down its concentration gradient (exergonic, spontaneous)
column4: Diffusion down a gradient decreases free energy (delta G < 0) and requires no external energy input; it is driven entirely by the thermodynamic tendency toward equilibrium.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::thermodynamic-considerations MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the sign of delta G for a solute moving down its concentration gradient?
column4: A negative delta G indicates a spontaneous process; moving a solute from high to low concentration releases free energy and does not require ATP.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::thermodynamic-considerations MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the Gibbs free energy equation for transporting an uncharged solute across a membrane?
column4: If [C_in] < [C_out], ln is negative, so delta G < 0 (spontaneous). For charged solutes, the electrical term (zF delta psi) is added.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::thermodynamic-considerations MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: For active transport, what is the sign of delta G for the transport step itself?
column3: Positive (delta G > 0) — unfavorable, requires energy input
column4: Active transport moves solutes against their electrochemical gradient; coupling to ATP hydrolysis (delta G < 0) makes the overall process thermodynamically favorable.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::thermodynamic-considerations MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is osmosis?
column3: Net diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from low to high solute concentration
column4: Water moves toward the side with higher osmolarity (lower water potential) until osmotic equilibrium is reached or an opposing pressure develops.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::osmosis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What term describes a solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell's cytoplasm?
column4: Cells placed in a hypertonic solution lose water by osmosis (crenation in RBCs), causing the cell to shrink.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::osmosis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What happens to an animal cell placed in a hypotonic solution?
column4: Water enters the cell by osmosis because intracellular osmolarity is higher; without a rigid cell wall, animal cells can burst (unlike plant cells that develop turgor pressure).
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::osmosis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is osmotic pressure?
column3: Pressure required to stop net osmotic flow of water across a membrane
column4: Osmotic pressure is proportional to solute concentration (van't Hoff equation: pi = iMRT); it opposes further water movement into the high-solute compartment.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::osmosis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In which direction does osmosis occur relative to solute concentration?
column3: Water moves toward higher solute concentration (lower water potential)
column4: This is equivalent to saying water moves from hypotonic to hypertonic regions — always 'uphill' in terms of solute concentration.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::osmosis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the van't Hoff equation for osmotic pressure?
column4: pi = osmotic pressure, i = van't Hoff factor (number of particles), M = molarity, R = gas constant, T = temperature (Kelvin). Only solute particle number matters, not identity.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::colligative-properties-osmotic-pressure-gc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are colligative properties?
column3: Properties that depend on the NUMBER of solute particles, not their identity
column4: Osmotic pressure, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, and vapor pressure lowering are all colligative. Adding more particles has a greater effect regardless of solute type.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::colligative-properties-osmotic-pressure-gc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does a 1 M NaCl solution compare in osmotic pressure to a 1 M glucose solution?
column3: NaCl has roughly twice the osmotic pressure (i≈2 vs i=1)
column4: NaCl dissociates into Na+ and Cl- (i≈2), doubling the particle count; glucose does not dissociate (i=1), so NaCl exerts approximately twice the osmotic pressure.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::colligative-properties-osmotic-pressure-gc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the van't Hoff factor (i) for a non-electrolyte solute like glucose?
column4: Non-electrolytes do not dissociate in solution, so each formula unit contributes one particle; i = 1 for glucose, sucrose, urea, and similar solutes.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::colligative-properties-osmotic-pressure-gc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which colligative property directly relates to membrane transport across a semipermeable membrane?
column4: Osmotic pressure is the only colligative property that involves membrane-mediated water movement; the others (BP elevation, FP depression, vapor pressure lowering) operate in bulk solution.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::colligative-properties-osmotic-pressure-gc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is passive transport?
column3: Movement of solutes across the membrane without energy input, down the electrochemical gradient
column4: Passive transport includes simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion; both are thermodynamically spontaneous and do not require ATP.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::passive-transport MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What distinguishes facilitated diffusion from simple diffusion?
column3: Facilitated diffusion requires a protein (channel or carrier); simple diffusion does not
column4: Both move solutes down their gradient, but facilitated diffusion is faster, saturable, and specific to the solute because it uses a protein mediator.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::passive-transport MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What kinetic feature indicates that facilitated diffusion uses a protein carrier?
column3: Saturability — rate plateaus at high solute concentration (Km and Vmax)
column4: Like enzyme kinetics, carrier-mediated transport can become saturated when all protein binding sites are occupied, unlike simple diffusion which increases linearly with concentration.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::passive-transport MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Give an example of a molecule that uses facilitated diffusion in erythrocytes.
column4: Red blood cells lack insulin-stimulated glucose uptake; GLUT1 constitutively facilitates glucose entry down its gradient, supplying fuel for glycolysis.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::passive-transport MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Can facilitated diffusion move a solute against its concentration gradient?
column4: Facilitated diffusion speeds up equilibration but cannot achieve net uphill transport; active transport is required to move solutes against their electrochemical gradient.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::passive-transport MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is active transport?
column3: Movement of solutes against their electrochemical gradient using energy (ATP or co-transport)
column4: Active transport maintains concentration gradients vital for cell function (e.g., low intracellular Na+, high intracellular K+); it is energetically unfavorable and requires energy coupling.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::active-transport MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are the two main forms of active transport?
column3: Primary (directly uses ATP) and secondary (uses ion gradient established by primary transport)
column4: The Na+/K+-ATPase is primary active transport; the Na+/glucose symporter is secondary active transport, driven by the Na+ gradient created by the pump.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::active-transport MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is a symporter?
column3: A cotransporter that moves two substances in the SAME direction
column4: Example: Na+/glucose symporter in intestinal epithelium moves Na+ and glucose together into the cell, using the Na+ gradient as the energy source.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::active-transport MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is an antiporter?
column3: A cotransporter that moves two substances in OPPOSITE directions
column4: Example: Na+/Ca2+ exchanger moves 3 Na+ in and 1 Ca2+ out, using the Na+ gradient to drive Ca2+ out against its concentration gradient.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::active-transport MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Is secondary active transport considered active or passive?
column3: Active — it moves solutes against their gradient (even though it doesn't directly hydrolyze ATP)
column4: The energy ultimately comes from ATP hydrolysis by the primary pump that created the ion gradient; thus secondary active transport is energetically dependent on active processes.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::active-transport MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the primary action of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump?
column3: Pumps 3 Na+ OUT and 2 K+ IN per ATP hydrolyzed
column4: This electrogenic pump maintains the low intracellular Na+ and high intracellular K+ gradients essential for membrane potential, cell volume regulation, and secondary active transport.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::sodium-potassium-pump MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many Na+ and K+ ions does the Na+/K+-ATPase move per cycle?
column4: The unequal exchange (3 out vs 2 in) makes the pump electrogenic — it moves net positive charge out, contributing to the negative resting membrane potential.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::sodium-potassium-pump MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Why is the Na+/K+-ATPase called electrogenic?
column3: It moves net positive charge across the membrane (3+ out, 2+ in)
column4: Each cycle exports one net positive charge, slightly hyperpolarizing the membrane (making inside more negative). This contributes to the resting membrane potential.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::sodium-potassium-pump MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What class of enzyme is the Na+/K+-ATPase?
column4: P-type ATPases form a covalent phosphorylated intermediate during the transport cycle; other examples include Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) and H+/K+-ATPase.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::sodium-potassium-pump MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which drug inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase and is used in heart failure treatment?
column4: By inhibiting the pump, intracellular Na+ rises, reducing Na+/Ca2+ exchanger activity, so intracellular Ca2+ increases — strengthening cardiac muscle contraction.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::sodium-potassium-pump MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are ion channels?
column3: Transmembrane protein pores that allow rapid ion flow down electrochemical gradients
column4: Ion channels are passive — they do not use ATP. They can be gated (opened/closed by voltage, ligand, or mechanical force) or non-gated (always open, 'leak' channels).
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-channels MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the difference between a gated and a non-gated ion channel?
column3: Gated channels open/close in response to a stimulus; non-gated (leak) channels are always open
column4: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open with depolarization; ligand-gated channels (e.g., nAChR) open when a neurotransmitter binds; leak K+ channels maintain resting potential.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-channels MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is an aquaporin?
column3: A protein channel specific for rapid water transport across membranes
column4: Aquaporins (AQPs) dramatically accelerate water flux; AQP2 in kidney collecting ducts is regulated by ADH (vasopressin) to control water reabsorption.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-channels MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What feature of ion channels allows ion selectivity?
column3: The selectivity filter — narrow region with specific geometry and charge
column4: For K+ channels, the selectivity filter coordinates K+ via backbone carbonyl oxygens, mimicking the hydration shell. Na+ is too small to be properly coordinated and is excluded.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-channels MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the resting membrane potential of a typical neuron?
column4: The resting potential arises primarily from K+ leak channels allowing K+ to diffuse out and from the Na+/K+-ATPase pumping Na+ out, leaving a net negative charge inside.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-potential MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which ion is most responsible for establishing the resting membrane potential?
column4: At rest, membranes are most permeable to K+ via leak channels. K+ diffuses out down its concentration gradient, leaving negative charges behind, creating the negative interior.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-potential MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the Nernst equation used for?
column3: Calculating the equilibrium potential for a single ion
column4: E_ion = (RT/zF) ln([ion]_out/[ion]_in). At this potential, the electrical gradient exactly balances the concentration gradient for that ion, so there is no net ion flow.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-potential MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What does 'depolarization' mean in the context of membrane potential?
column3: The membrane potential becomes less negative (moves toward 0 or positive)
column4: During an action potential, depolarization occurs as voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ rushes in, and the inside becomes transiently positive (~+30 mV).
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-potential MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the Goldman equation used for?
column3: Calculating membrane potential considering multiple ions simultaneously
column4: Unlike the Nernst equation (single ion), the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation incorporates the permeabilities and concentrations of Na+, K+, and Cl- to give the actual resting potential.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-potential MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are the two main types of membrane receptors by mechanism?
column3: Ligand-gated ion channels (ionotropic) and G-protein coupled receptors (metabotropic)
column4: Ionotropic receptors directly open ion channels upon ligand binding (fast); metabotropic receptors activate second messenger cascades via G proteins (slower, amplified).
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-receptors MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)?
column3: A transmembrane receptor that phosphorylates tyrosine residues upon ligand binding
column4: Insulin receptor and growth factor receptors are RTKs; ligand binding causes receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, activating downstream signaling cascades.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-receptors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What second messenger does Gs-protein coupled receptor activation typically produce?
column4: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase → ATP → cAMP → PKA activation. cAMP is a key second messenger for hormones like glucagon, epinephrine, and PTH.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-receptors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What happens to a receptor after ligand binding that reduces cell sensitivity over time?
column4: Chronic stimulation leads to receptor phosphorylation, arrestin binding, and endocytosis, reducing cell-surface receptor number and blunting the response to the ligand.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::membrane-receptors MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is exocytosis?
column3: Secretory vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane, releasing contents outside the cell
column4: Exocytosis is used for secretion of hormones, neurotransmitters, and digestive enzymes; it requires SNARE protein interactions and is often Ca2+-triggered.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::exocytosis-and-endocytosis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is endocytosis?
column3: The cell engulfs extracellular material by membrane invagination, forming an intracellular vesicle
column4: Endocytosis subtypes include phagocytosis (large particles), pinocytosis (fluid/small molecules), and receptor-mediated endocytosis (specific ligands via coated pits).
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::exocytosis-and-endocytosis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is receptor-mediated endocytosis?
column3: Selective uptake of specific ligands via clathrin-coated pits after receptor binding
column4: Example: LDL-cholesterol uptake. LDL binds its receptor, the complex clusters in clathrin-coated pits, which invaginate to form clathrin-coated vesicles.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::exocytosis-and-endocytosis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is phagocytosis?
column3: Engulfment of large particles (bacteria, debris) forming a phagosome
column4: Phagocytosis is performed by macrophages and neutrophils as part of innate immunity; the phagosome fuses with lysosomes to degrade the ingested material.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::exocytosis-and-endocytosis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What coat protein mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis via coated pits?
column4: Clathrin triskelions self-assemble into a lattice that curves the membrane inward; dynamin GTPase pinches off the vesicle. Clathrin is then recycled after vesicle formation.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::exocytosis-and-endocytosis MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are intercellular junctions?
column3: Specialized protein complexes connecting adjacent cells or cells to the extracellular matrix
column4: Junctions mediate adhesion, communication, and barrier formation; the major types in animals are tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::intercellular-junctions-bio MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which intercellular junctions are found exclusively in animals (not plants)?
column3: Tight junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions
column4: Plant cells communicate via plasmodesmata (analogous to gap junctions) and lack tight junctions and desmosomes; animal junctions reflect the absence of a rigid cell wall.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::intercellular-junctions-bio MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What general cytoskeletal element anchors most cell-cell junctions?
column3: Actin filaments (tight junctions, adherens junctions) or intermediate filaments (desmosomes)
column4: Tight junctions and adherens junctions link to actin; desmosomes and hemidesmosomes link to intermediate filaments (keratin in epithelial cells), providing mechanical strength.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::intercellular-junctions-bio MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the primary function of gap junctions?
column3: Direct cell-to-cell communication via passage of small molecules and ions
column4: Gap junctions are hydrophilic channels connecting the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, allowing passage of molecules < ~1 kDa (ions, cAMP, glucose). They coordinate tissue responses.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::gap-junctions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What protein subunits form gap junctions?
column3: Connexins (6 per connexon hemichannel; 2 connexons form one gap junction)
column4: Six connexin proteins oligomerize into a connexon; two connexons from adjacent cells dock to form the complete intercellular channel with a 1.5 nm pore.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::gap-junctions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In cardiac muscle, what is the role of gap junctions?
column3: Synchronize electrical signals so cardiac muscle contracts as a functional syncytium
column4: Action potentials spread rapidly through gap junctions between cardiomyocytes, ensuring coordinated contraction of the heart; this is why cardiac muscle is called a functional syncytium.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::gap-junctions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Can gap junctions be regulated?
column3: Yes — they close in response to high intracellular Ca2+ or low pH
column4: Closing gap junctions isolates damaged cells (which have high Ca2+ and low pH) from healthy neighbors, preventing the spread of injury signals.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::gap-junctions MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the primary function of tight junctions?
column3: Seal the space between epithelial cells, creating a paracellular diffusion barrier
column4: Tight junctions prevent ions and molecules from passing between cells (paracellular pathway), forcing transport to occur transcellularly through regulated channels and carriers.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::tight-junctions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In which tissue are tight junctions especially critical for maintaining distinct luminal and basolateral environments?
column3: Intestinal epithelium (and other polarized epithelia like kidney tubules)
column4: Tight junctions maintain polarity by keeping apical transporters (e.g., SGLT1) separate from basolateral transporters (GLUT2), enabling directional nutrient absorption.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::tight-junctions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What proteins form the sealing strands of tight junctions?
column4: Claudins are the primary structural proteins; occludins and junctional adhesion molecules (JAMs) also contribute. Claudin composition determines paracellular permeability selectivity.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::tight-junctions MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Do tight junctions anchor to actin or intermediate filaments?
column4: The cytoplasmic plaque of tight junctions connects to the actin cytoskeleton via scaffolding proteins like ZO-1, ZO-2, and ZO-3, enabling mechanical coupling to the cell cortex.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::tight-junctions MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the primary function of desmosomes?
column3: Mechanical adhesion — anchor adjacent cells together to resist shearing forces
column4: Desmosomes are especially abundant in tissues subject to mechanical stress, such as skin (epidermis) and cardiac muscle, where they prevent cell-cell separation.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::desmosomes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What cytoskeletal filaments are anchored by desmosomes?
column3: Intermediate filaments (e.g., keratin in epithelium, desmin in cardiac muscle)
column4: Unlike tight junctions (actin), desmosomes connect to intermediate filaments, distributing mechanical tension across the tissue and providing tensile strength.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::desmosomes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What transmembrane proteins mediate cell-cell adhesion in desmosomes?
column4: These calcium-dependent cadherins form trans-interactions between adjacent cells; the intracellular tail connects via desmoplakin and plakophilin to intermediate filaments.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::desmosomes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In which disease does autoimmune attack of desmogleins lead to skin blistering?
column4: Autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 (and desmoglein-1) disrupt desmosome integrity in the epidermis, causing keratinocytes to separate (acantholysis) and forming potentially life-threatening blisters.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::desmosomes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How do hemidesmosomes differ from desmosomes?
column3: Hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the BASEMENT MEMBRANE (extracellular matrix), not to adjacent cells
column4: Hemidesmosomes use integrins (not cadherins) to link the intermediate filament network to laminin in the basal lamina, anchoring epithelial sheets to underlying connective tissue.
column8: concept::BB::2A::plasma_membrane MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2A::plasma-membrane::desmosomes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the defining nuclear feature that distinguishes eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic cells?
column4: Eukaryotes sequester their DNA within a double-membrane nucleus; prokaryotes have no nuclear membrane and their DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What type of cell division is characteristic of eukaryotic somatic cells?
column4: Eukaryotic somatic cells divide by mitosis, producing genetically identical daughter cells; prokaryotes use binary fission instead.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which of these is found in eukaryotes but NOT prokaryotes: ribosomes, mitochondria, plasma membrane, or DNA?
column4: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles exclusive to eukaryotes; ribosomes, plasma membranes, and DNA are present in both domains.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Name three membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotic cells but absent in prokaryotes.
column4: Membrane-bound compartmentalization is the hallmark of eukaryotes; any three of nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, or peroxisomes are acceptable.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What cytoskeletal structure, present in eukaryotes, is required to form the mitotic spindle during cell division?
column4: Microtubules (made of tubulin) polymerize into the spindle apparatus that segregates chromosomes during mitosis; prokaryotes lack true tubulin-based spindles.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the primary function of the nucleus in a eukaryotic cell?
column3: Storage and protection of genetic information (DNA)
column4: The nucleus houses the cell's chromosomal DNA and is the site of transcription; the nuclear envelope physically separates DNA from the cytoplasm.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the name of the region inside the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is synthesized?
column4: The nucleolus is a non-membrane-bound subcompartment of the nucleus; it is the site of rRNA transcription and ribosome subunit assembly.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the term for the complex of DNA and histone proteins found in the eukaryotic nucleus?
column4: Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes during mitosis; it exists as euchromatin (active) or heterochromatin (inactive) during interphase.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which transport process moves large molecules and RNA out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm?
column4: Nuclear pores contain protein complexes that selectively allow passage of mRNA, ribosomal subunits, and proteins; large cargo requires energy and nuclear localization signals.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated within the nucleus?
column4: S phase is part of interphase; faithful duplication of chromosomal DNA in the nucleus ensures each daughter cell receives a complete genome after mitosis.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are the two primary functions of compartmentalization in eukaryotic cells?
column4: Compartmentalization allows, for example, DNA replication in the nucleus while translation occurs in the cytoplasm, preventing interference and increasing efficiency.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Where is genetic information (DNA) stored in a eukaryotic cell?
column4: The nucleus is the primary storage site; mitochondria and chloroplasts also contain small circular DNA molecules, but the vast majority of genetic information is nuclear.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which organelle demonstrates that compartmentalization allows organelle-specific pH maintenance?
column4: Lysosomes maintain an acidic interior (~pH 4.5-5) optimal for their hydrolytic enzymes, isolated from the neutral cytoplasm by their membrane.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Mitochondria and chloroplasts retain their own DNA. What does this suggest about their evolutionary origin?
column4: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that ancestral eukaryotes engulfed aerobic bacteria (mitochondria) and cyanobacteria (chloroplasts), which became permanent organelles.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Where is the nucleolus located?
column4: The nucleolus is a dense, non-membrane-bound structure within the nucleus, typically associated with nucleolar organizer regions of specific chromosomes.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the primary function of the nucleolus?
column3: Synthesis of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and assembly of ribosome subunits
column4: The nucleolus transcribes rRNA genes and packages rRNA with ribosomal proteins into large and small subunit precursors before export to the cytoplasm.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What happens to the nucleolus during mitosis?
column4: During mitosis the chromosomes condense and transcription ceases; the nucleolus disassembles and reforms after cell division when transcription resumes.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: A cell that produces large quantities of protein would be expected to have how many/what size nucleoli compared to a less active cell?
column4: Cells with high biosynthetic demands require more ribosomes; an enlarged nucleolus reflects increased rRNA production. Rapidly dividing cancer cells often show prominent nucleoli.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which RNA polymerase transcribes rRNA in the nucleolus?
column4: In eukaryotes, RNA Pol I synthesizes the large 45S rRNA precursor (cleaved into 28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus; Pol II makes mRNA and Pol III makes tRNA/5S rRNA.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: How many membranes surround the nucleus?
column4: The nuclear envelope consists of an outer membrane (continuous with the rough ER) and an inner membrane; the space between them is the perinuclear space.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What structure spans the nuclear envelope to allow transport between nucleus and cytoplasm?
column4: Nuclear pore complexes (~120 MDa protein assemblies) permit passive diffusion of small molecules and active transport of larger macromolecules like mRNA and proteins.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: With which cytoplasmic organelle is the outer nuclear membrane continuous?
column4: The outer nuclear membrane is studded with ribosomes and is structurally continuous with the rough ER membrane, forming a connected endomembrane network.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What signal sequence directs a protein to be imported through nuclear pores into the nucleus?
column4: NLS sequences (rich in basic amino acids like Lys and Arg) are recognized by importin proteins that facilitate active, energy-dependent transport through nuclear pores.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What happens to the nuclear envelope during open mitosis (as in most animal cells)?
column4: Phosphorylation of lamins by CDK1 causes the nuclear lamina to depolymerize, allowing the nuclear envelope to fragment so spindle microtubules can access chromosomes.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the primary function of mitochondria?
column4: Mitochondria are the site of the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and the electron transport chain, producing the majority of cellular ATP.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: How many membranes do mitochondria have?
column4: Mitochondria possess an outer membrane and a folded inner membrane (cristae); the space between them is the intermembrane space and the interior is the matrix.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What evidence supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria?
column3: Own circular DNA, double membrane, 70S ribosomes, binary fission
column4: Mitochondria resemble alpha-proteobacteria: circular DNA, prokaryotic-sized ribosomes, and reproduction by fission rather than de novo synthesis all support endosymbiosis.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: In what cellular process do mitochondria play a key role besides ATP synthesis?
column4: Mitochondria release cytochrome c into the cytoplasm to activate caspases; they integrate pro- and anti-apoptotic signals from the Bcl-2 protein family.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the mitochondrial matrix?
column3: Aqueous interior enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane
column4: The matrix contains enzymes for the citric acid cycle, mitochondrial DNA, ribosomes, and substrates; it is the site of pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Where does the majority of cellular ATP synthesis occur?
column4: The proton gradient established by the electron transport chain across the inner membrane drives ATP synthase (Complex V) to phosphorylate ADP to ATP via chemiosmosis.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What metabolic pathway, occurring in the cytoplasm, feeds pyruvate into mitochondria for ATP production?
column4: Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytosol; pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix via specific transporters to be oxidized via pyruvate dehydrogenase and the TCA cycle.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: In which mitochondrial compartment does the citric acid (Krebs) cycle occur?
column4: TCA cycle enzymes reside in the matrix; the cycle generates NADH and FADH2 that donate electrons to the electron transport chain embedded in the inner membrane.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Approximately how many ATP molecules are produced per glucose molecule via complete aerobic respiration?
column4: Modern estimates yield ~30-32 ATP (older textbooks cite 36-38); the variability reflects proton leak and varying P/O ratios across different cell types.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the role of the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane in ATP synthesis?
column4: NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the ETC, which pumps H+ into the intermembrane space; H+ flows back through ATP synthase, providing energy to phosphorylate ADP.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are the two membranes of the mitochondrion called?
column3: Outer mitochondrial membrane and inner mitochondrial membrane
column4: The outer membrane is permeable to small molecules via porins; the inner membrane is highly impermeable and forms the cristae, which increase surface area for the ETC.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are cristae?
column3: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane
column4: Cristae dramatically increase the surface area of the inner membrane, accommodating more ETC complexes and ATP synthase molecules to maximize ATP output.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which mitochondrial membrane is permeable to most small molecules and ions?
column4: The outer membrane contains porins (VDAC channels) that allow free passage of molecules up to ~5 kDa; the inner membrane is selectively impermeable to maintain the proton gradient.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Where exactly are the proteins of the electron transport chain located in mitochondria?
column4: Complexes I-IV and ATP synthase (Complex V) are embedded in the inner membrane; this location is essential for establishing the proton gradient across this membrane.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the intermembrane space of mitochondria, and why is its composition important?
column3: Space between outer and inner membranes; high [H+] drives ATP synthesis
column4: Protons pumped by the ETC accumulate in the intermembrane space, creating the electrochemical gradient (proton-motive force) that powers ATP synthase when they flow back into the matrix.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Can mitochondria reproduce independently within a cell?
column4: Mitochondria self-replicate by dividing in a process similar to bacterial binary fission; the number of mitochondria in a cell can increase in response to high-energy demands.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What genetic material do mitochondria contain that allows them to self-replicate?
column4: Mitochondria carry their own circular, double-stranded DNA encoding 13 proteins, 22 tRNAs, and 2 rRNAs; most mitochondrial proteins are still encoded by nuclear DNA.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: From which parent is mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) almost exclusively inherited?
column4: The egg contributes the vast majority of cytoplasm and organelles; sperm mitochondria are typically degraded after fertilization, making mtDNA maternally inherited in most species.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Why can't mitochondria be synthesized de novo (from scratch) in a cell?
column3: They require a pre-existing mitochondrial membrane/template to replicate
column4: Mitochondria can only arise from pre-existing mitochondria by growth and division; their complex double-membrane structure and own genome require a template for duplication.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What protein, analogous to a bacterial cell-division protein, is required for mitochondrial fission?
column4: DRP1 is a GTPase that forms a ring around mitochondria to constrict and sever them during fission; mutations in DRP1 are linked to mitochondrial disease.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are lysosomes?
column4: Lysosomes are single-membrane organelles that maintain an acidic lumen (~pH 4.5-5) optimal for ~50 acid hydrolases that degrade proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the approximate pH inside a lysosome?
column4: H+-ATPase pumps protons into the lysosomal lumen; this acidic environment activates lysosomal hydrolases and is maintained separately from the neutral cytoplasm.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What process delivers worn-out cytoplasmic organelles to lysosomes for degradation?
column4: During autophagy, a double-membrane autophagosome engulfs cytoplasmic contents and fuses with a lysosome; the contents are then degraded and recycled by lysosomal hydrolases.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Lysosomes fuse with phagosomes to destroy engulfed pathogens. What is this combined structure called?
column4: Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils) engulf pathogens into phagosomes; fusion with lysosomes delivers hydrolytic enzymes and reactive oxygen species to destroy the pathogen.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What class of genetic disease results from a deficiency of a specific lysosomal hydrolase?
column4: Examples include Tay-Sachs (absent hexosaminidase A), Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency), and Fabry disease; substrate accumulates in lysosomes causing cell damage.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are the two main components of the endoplasmic reticulum?
column4: The ER is a continuous membrane network; the rough ER is studded with ribosomes and involved in protein synthesis, while the smooth ER lacks ribosomes and handles lipid metabolism and detoxification.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum?
column3: Interior space enclosed by the ER membrane
column4: The ER lumen is topologically equivalent to the extracellular space; proteins destined for secretion or membrane insertion are threaded into or through the ER lumen during translation.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which organelle is the ER membrane continuous with?
column4: The ER forms a connected network with the outer nuclear membrane; this continuity allows direct communication between the nuclear envelope and the ER lumen.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What cellular process is monitored in the ER lumen to ensure proper protein folding?
column3: Unfolded protein response (UPR) / ER quality control
column4: Misfolded proteins in the ER lumen are detected by chaperones (BiP/GRP78); the UPR signals the nucleus to upregulate folding machinery or trigger apoptosis if stress is unresolvable.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What distinguishes rough ER from smooth ER in appearance under electron microscopy?
column3: Rough ER has ribosomes on its cytoplasmic surface; smooth ER does not
column4: The ribosomes attached to rough ER give it a granular (rough) appearance; smooth ER appears tubular and lacks ribosomes because it does not synthesize secretory or membrane proteins.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is a major function of the smooth ER in liver hepatocytes?
column3: Detoxification of drugs and toxins (cytochrome P450 enzymes)
column4: Smooth ER in hepatocytes is abundant and houses cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidases that hydroxylate lipid-soluble toxins and drugs, making them more water-soluble for excretion.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: In muscle cells, the smooth ER is called what, and what is its function?
column3: Sarcoplasmic reticulum; stores and releases Ca2+ for muscle contraction
column4: The sarcoplasmic reticulum sequesters Ca2+ at rest; action potential triggers Ca2+ release, which binds troponin to initiate actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which component of the ER is primarily responsible for lipid (phospholipid) synthesis?
column4: Enzymes embedded in the smooth ER membrane synthesize most cellular phospholipids and cholesterol; newly made lipids can be flipped to the other leaflet by flippases.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the function of ribosomes on the rough ER?
column3: Synthesize proteins destined for secretion, membranes, or lysosomes
column4: Ribosomes dock on the rough ER when translating proteins with a signal sequence; the nascent polypeptide is threaded into the ER lumen or embedded in the membrane co-translationally.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What short amino acid sequence targets a ribosome to the rough ER during translation?
column4: The N-terminal signal peptide (hydrophobic core ~8-12 aa) is recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP), which docks the ribosome on the rough ER translocon.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What protein complex threads the nascent polypeptide through the rough ER membrane during cotranslational translocation?
column4: The Sec61 translocon is a protein-conducting channel in the ER membrane; it opens laterally to release transmembrane segments into the lipid bilayer or allows soluble proteins to enter the lumen.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Where are free ribosomes (not on the rough ER) located, and what type of proteins do they synthesize?
column4: Free ribosomes synthesize proteins that remain in the cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, or peroxisomes; ribosomes themselves are not inherently different — targeting depends on the mRNA/protein signal.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What post-translational modification begins in the rough ER lumen as proteins are translocated?
column4: An oligosaccharyltransferase adds a pre-assembled 14-sugar oligosaccharide (Glc3Man9GlcNAc2) to asparagine residues (N-X-S/T sequon) co-translationally in the rough ER lumen.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: How many membranes does the endoplasmic reticulum have?
column4: The ER is bounded by a single lipid bilayer (unlike mitochondria or the nucleus); the membrane encloses the ER lumen and is continuous with the outer nuclear envelope.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Which organelles have a double (two) membrane structure?
column4: A double membrane is a key feature of the nucleus (nuclear envelope), mitochondria, and chloroplasts; most other organelles (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, peroxisomes) are single-membrane.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Why is the distinction between single- and double-membrane organelles significant for the MCAT?
column3: Double-membrane organelles have endosymbiotic/nuclear origins; single-membrane organelles bud from the endomembrane system
column4: Mitochondria and chloroplasts derived from engulfed prokaryotes retain two membranes; the nucleus, Golgi, ER, and lysosomes are part of the endomembrane system with single membranes.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: The inner membrane of the mitochondrion is evolutionarily homologous to what bacterial structure?
column4: During endosymbiosis, the engulfed bacterium's plasma membrane became the inner mitochondrial membrane; the outer membrane derived from the host's phagosomal membrane.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the role of the smooth ER in membrane biosynthesis?
column3: Site of phospholipid and cholesterol synthesis
column4: Smooth ER enzymes (e.g., glycerophosphate acyltransferase) assemble phospholipids from fatty acids and glycerol; new membrane lipids are distributed throughout the endomembrane system via vesicular transport.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: After synthesis in the smooth ER, how are new membrane lipids distributed to other organelles?
column3: Vesicular transport and lipid transfer proteins
column4: ER-derived vesicles bud and fuse with the Golgi and plasma membrane; lipid transfer proteins (CERT, OSBP) also shuttle specific lipids (ceramide, cholesterol) between organelles non-vesicularly.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What enzyme flips newly synthesized phospholipids from the cytoplasmic to the luminal leaflet of the ER membrane?
column4: Phospholipids are initially inserted into the cytoplasmic leaflet; ATP-dependent flippases and ATP-independent scramblases equilibrate lipid distribution between leaflets in the ER.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Where is the first step of N-linked glycosylation (addition of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide) completed?
column4: Dolichol phosphate carries the 14-sugar oligosaccharide precursor; oligosaccharyltransferase transfers it to nascent polypeptides in the ER lumen — the foundation of N-linked glycosylation and membrane glycoprotein biosynthesis.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What type of proteins are synthesized on the rough ER and destined for secretion from the cell?
column4: Proteins containing an N-terminal signal peptide are cotranslationally inserted into the ER lumen; they travel through the Golgi and are exported via secretory vesicles via the constitutive or regulated secretory pathway.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Name the sequential organelles a secretory protein passes through from synthesis to exocytosis.
column3: Rough ER → Golgi (cis→medial→trans) → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
column4: This is the classic secretory pathway; the Golgi sorts, modifies, and packages proteins into vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane for exocytosis.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the default destination for a protein that travels through the secretory pathway and lacks a retention/retrieval signal?
column4: In the absence of specific retention signals (e.g., KDEL for ER, HDEL for ER in yeast), proteins are carried by default vesicular flow to the plasma membrane and secreted.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What signal sequence retains soluble proteins (e.g., chaperones) in the ER lumen?
column4: KDEL is recognized by KDEL receptors in the Golgi cis face; escaped ER-resident proteins are retrieved and returned to the ER in COPI vesicles (retrograde transport).
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What class of vesicle transports secretory proteins from the ER to the Golgi (anterograde)?
column4: COPII coat proteins mediate ER-to-Golgi anterograde transport; COPI vesicles handle Golgi-to-ER retrograde transport; clathrin vesicles mediate Golgi-to-endosome/lysosome transport.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What is the overall function of the Golgi apparatus?
column3: Modify, sort, and package proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery to organelles
column4: The Golgi receives cargo from the ER, performs glycosylation and other modifications, and sorts proteins into vesicles destined for lysosomes, the plasma membrane, or secretion.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are the three functional regions of the Golgi apparatus, in order from ER to secretory side?
column3: Cis, medial, trans (cis-Golgi network → trans-Golgi network)
column4: Cargo enters the Golgi at the cis face (nearest the ER), is processed through medial cisternae, and exits at the trans face; the trans-Golgi network is the main sorting station.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What carbohydrate modifications occur in the Golgi after the initial N-linked glycosylation in the ER?
column3: Trimming of mannose residues and addition of complex oligosaccharides (N-glycan processing)
column4: In the Golgi, high-mannose N-glycans are trimmed by mannosidases and rebuilt into complex or hybrid types by glycosyltransferases; O-linked glycosylation also occurs in the Golgi.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag on proteins directs them from the Golgi to lysosomes?
column4: Lysosomal hydrolases are tagged with M6P in the Golgi; M6P receptors in the trans-Golgi network bind them and package them into vesicles targeted to late endosomes/lysosomes.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What would happen to lysosomal enzymes if the Golgi's mannose-6-phosphate tagging system failed?
column3: Lysosomal enzymes would be secreted extracellularly instead of reaching lysosomes
column4: This is the basis of I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), where failure to add M6P tags causes lysosomal hydrolases to be secreted, leaving lysosomes unable to degrade substrates.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are peroxisomes?
column3: Single-membrane organelles that contain oxidative enzymes and catalase
column4: Peroxisomes use molecular oxygen to oxidize substrates (e.g., fatty acids, amino acids), generating H2O2; catalase within the peroxisome immediately degrades H2O2 to water and oxygen.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What enzyme in peroxisomes neutralizes hydrogen peroxide?
column4: Catalase converts 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2; its high concentration in peroxisomes prevents H2O2 from escaping and damaging the cell.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What metabolic process for fatty acid oxidation occurs in peroxisomes (especially for very long-chain fatty acids)?
column4: Peroxisomes initiate beta-oxidation of VLCFA (>C22) that mitochondria cannot handle; the products (shorter acyl chains) are then transferred to mitochondria for complete oxidation.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What genetic disease is caused by defective peroxisome biogenesis, leading to accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids?
column4: Zellweger syndrome results from mutations in PEX genes (peroxins); without functional peroxisomes, VLCFA and other peroxisomal substrates accumulate, causing severe neurological damage.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: Unlike mitochondria, peroxisomes do NOT have their own DNA. How do new peroxisomes form?
column3: By growth and division of existing peroxisomes, or from the ER
column4: Peroxisomal membrane proteins are imported post-translationally from the cytoplasm; peroxisomes can also bud from the ER. Their matrix proteins carry a PTS1 or PTS2 targeting signal.
column5: Membrane-Bound Organelles and Defining Characteristics of Eukaryotic Cells

column1: What are the three main components of the cytoskeleton?
column4: These three polymer networks provide structural support, enable movement, and organize organelles within eukaryotic cells.

column1: Which cytoskeletal element is primarily responsible for maintaining cell shape against mechanical stress?
column4: Intermediate filaments are the most stable cytoskeletal component and resist deformation, giving cells mechanical resilience.

column1: What cytoskeletal structure forms the basis of cell motility via crawling (e.g., lamellipodia)?
column4: Actin polymerization at the leading edge pushes the plasma membrane forward, driving cell migration.

column1: Which cytoskeletal element is used as a track for motor protein-driven organelle transport?
column4: Kinesin and dynein motor proteins walk along microtubule tracks to move vesicles, organelles, and chromosomes.

column1: What term describes the dynamic process by which cytoskeletal filaments add and lose monomers at their ends?
column4: Treadmilling occurs in both actin and microtubules; net polymerization at the plus end and depolymerization at the minus end allow net movement without net change in length.

column1: Which cytoskeletal filament exhibits 'dynamic instability,' rapidly switching between growth and shrinkage?
column4: Dynamic instability allows microtubules to rapidly explore cellular space and is driven by GTP hydrolysis in tubulin dimers.

column1: What protein monomer polymerizes to form microfilaments?
column4: Globular actin (G-actin) monomers polymerize into filamentous actin (F-actin) double helices, forming microfilaments.

column1: What is the diameter of microfilaments?
column4: Microfilaments are the thinnest cytoskeletal element at ~7 nm; microtubules are ~25 nm and intermediate filaments ~10 nm.

column1: What structure composed of microfilaments constricts the cell during cytokinesis?
column4: The actin-myosin contractile ring assembles at the equator of a dividing cell and pinches the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.

column1: Which motor protein works with actin microfilaments to generate contraction?
column4: Myosin II uses ATP hydrolysis to walk along actin filaments; this interaction drives muscle contraction and cytokinesis.

column1: What nucleotide do actin monomers bind to stabilize microfilament polymerization?
column4: ATP-actin adds preferentially to the plus (barbed) end; after incorporation, ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP, destabilizing that region.

column1: Which end of an actin filament is the preferred site of monomer addition (the 'fast-growing' end)?
column4: The plus end grows faster; the minus (pointed) end depolymerizes more readily, enabling treadmilling.

column1: What proteins make up microtubules?
column4: Alpha and beta tubulin form dimers that polymerize head-to-tail into protofilaments; 13 protofilaments form one microtubule.

column1: What is the approximate diameter of a microtubule?
column4: Microtubules are hollow cylinders ~25 nm in diameter, making them the largest cytoskeletal element by diameter.

column1: Which nucleotide is hydrolyzed during microtubule polymerization?
column4: GTP-tubulin adds to the plus end; GTP hydrolysis to GDP destabilizes the lattice, promoting depolymerization (dynamic instability).

column1: In which direction does kinesin typically move along a microtubule?
column4: Conventional kinesin walks toward the plus end, transporting cargo away from the nucleus toward the plasma membrane.

column1: In which direction does cytoplasmic dynein move along a microtubule?
column4: Dynein moves toward the minus end, transporting cargo toward the centrosome/nucleus (retrograde transport).

column1: What mitotic structure is composed entirely of microtubules and separates chromosomes during cell division?
column4: The mitotic spindle's kinetochore, polar, and aster microtubules capture and pull sister chromatids to opposite poles.

column1: Which drug stabilizes microtubules by preventing depolymerization and is used in cancer therapy?
column4: Taxol locks microtubules in the polymerized state, blocking mitosis by preventing spindle disassembly after chromosome separation.

column1: Which drug depolymerizes microtubules by binding free tubulin dimers, and is also used in cancer treatment?
column4: Colchicine binds tubulin dimers and prevents their addition to microtubule ends, blocking mitosis; vinca alkaloids have a similar mechanism.

column1: What are intermediate filaments primarily composed of in most non-epithelial cells?
column4: Vimentin is a common intermediate filament protein in mesenchymal cells; other types include desmin (muscle), neurofilaments (neurons), and keratins (epithelial).

column1: What intermediate filament protein is found in epithelial cells?
column4: Keratin intermediate filaments connect desmosomes and hemidesmosomes, providing mechanical strength to epithelial sheets.

column1: What is the approximate diameter of intermediate filaments?
column4: At ~10 nm, intermediate filaments are intermediate in size between actin microfilaments (7 nm) and microtubules (25 nm).

column1: Unlike actin and tubulin, intermediate filament proteins do not require what for polymerization?
column4: Intermediate filaments polymerize spontaneously without nucleotide hydrolysis, making them more stable and less dynamic than microfilaments or microtubules.

column1: What intermediate filament forms the nuclear lamina, supporting the nuclear envelope?
column4: Lamins A, B, and C form a meshwork just inside the inner nuclear membrane, giving the nucleus structural rigidity.

column1: Which cell junction anchors intermediate filaments between adjacent epithelial cells?
column4: Desmosomes link keratin intermediate filaments of neighboring cells through cadherins (desmogleins/desmocollins), distributing mechanical stress.

column1: What is the '9+2' arrangement found in motile cilia and flagella?
column3: 9 outer doublet microtubules + 2 central single microtubules
column4: The axoneme of motile cilia/flagella contains 9 peripheral doublets surrounding a central pair, connected by radial spokes and nexin links.

column1: What motor protein drives the bending of cilia and flagella?
column4: Axonemal dynein arms connect adjacent microtubule doublets; their ATP-dependent walking generates the sliding force that bends the axoneme.

column1: How does a flagellum propel a cell compared to a cilium?
column3: Flagella have a whip-like undulating motion; cilia beat in coordinated strokes
column4: Eukaryotic flagella (e.g., sperm) generate wave-like propulsion; cilia beat in a power stroke/recovery stroke pattern and can move substances over cell surfaces.

column1: What disease results from defective dynein arms in cilia, causing immotile cilia?
column4: Loss of functional axonemal dynein immobilizes cilia; hallmarks include chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus.

column1: What is the structural arrangement of microtubules in non-motile (primary) cilia?
column4: Primary cilia lack the central microtubule pair and dynein arms; they function as sensory antennae rather than motility organelles.

column1: What is the basal body, and from what organelle is it derived?
column3: Anchor for cilia/flagella; derived from centrioles
column4: The basal body is a modified centriole (triplet microtubules) that nucleates the axoneme of a cilium or flagellum at the plasma membrane.

column1: What is the primary protein component of centrioles?
column4: Each centriole consists of nine triplet microtubule sets (A, B, C tubules) arranged in a cylinder; no central pair (9+0 triplet pattern).

column1: What is the name of the structure that contains the centrioles and organizes the mitotic spindle?
column4: The centrosome (two centrioles plus pericentriolar material) is the main MTOC in animal cells, nucleating microtubules for the mitotic spindle.

column1: What protein in the pericentriolar material nucleates microtubule polymerization?
column4: Gamma-tubulin ring complexes (gamma-TuRCs) serve as templates for new microtubule nucleation, establishing the minus end at the centrosome.

column1: How many centrioles are present in a typical animal cell before S phase?
column4: The single centrosome contains two centrioles (mother and daughter); duplication occurs during S phase to yield two centrosomes before mitosis.

column1: What is the arrangement of microtubule triplets in a centriole?
column4: Centrioles have 9 sets of fused triplet microtubules (A, B, C) arranged in a ring, distinct from the 9+2 axoneme of motile cilia.

column1: Do plant cells have centrioles?
column4: Most plant cells organize their mitotic spindle without centrioles, using diffuse MTOCs; they do not have centrosomes but can still form functional spindles.

column1: What term describes the region from which microtubules grow within the cell?
column4: MTOCs (including centrosomes in animal cells) establish microtubule polarity by anchoring minus ends and allowing plus ends to grow outward.

column1: What is the primary function of epithelial tissue?
column3: Covers body surfaces; lines cavities; secretion
column4: Epithelial tissue serves as a barrier, controls substance movement, and forms glands. It lines the skin, GI tract, respiratory tract, and other surfaces.

column1: Which junctions tightly seal adjacent epithelial cells to prevent paracellular transport?
column4: Tight junctions fuse the outer leaflets of adjacent plasma membranes, creating a seal that controls which molecules can pass between cells.

column1: Name the three shapes of epithelial cells.
column4: Shape classification is based on cross-sectional cell morphology. Squamous cells are flat, cuboidal are cube-like, and columnar are taller than wide.

column1: What term describes epithelial tissue that is only one cell layer thick?
column4: Simple epithelium has a single cell layer where all cells contact the basement membrane. It contrasts with stratified epithelium, which has multiple layers.

column1: What is pseudostratified epithelium?
column3: Single-layered epithelium that appears multilayered due to staggered nuclei
