column4: All cells contact the basement membrane, but nuclei are at different heights, giving a false appearance of stratification. It lines the trachea and bronchi.

column1: Which epithelial cell junction anchors cells to the basement membrane via intermediate filaments?
column4: Hemidesmosomes use integrins to connect keratin intermediate filaments inside the cell to laminin in the basement membrane, providing mechanical stability.

column1: What type of epithelium lines most of the urinary bladder and can stretch?
column4: Transitional epithelium has the unique ability to accommodate large changes in volume; cells flatten when the bladder is distended.

column1: Which cell junction allows passage of ions and small molecules directly between adjacent cells?
column4: Gap junctions are composed of connexin proteins forming connexons (hemichannels). They are critical for electrical coupling in cardiac muscle and smooth muscle.

column1: What anchoring structure underlies all epithelial tissue and is secreted by the epithelial cells themselves?
column4: The basement membrane contains collagen IV, laminin, and proteoglycans. It provides structural support and acts as a selective barrier.

column1: Which type of epithelial secretion releases entire cells filled with product (e.g., sebaceous glands)?
column4: In holocrine secretion the entire cell lyses to release its secretory product. Merocrine secretion uses exocytosis; apocrine secretion sheds the apical portion.

column1: What distinguishes merocrine from apocrine secretion in epithelial glands?
column3: Merocrine uses exocytosis; apocrine sheds apical cytoplasm
column4: Most glands (e.g., pancreatic acini, eccrine sweat glands) are merocrine. Apocrine glands (e.g., mammary, axillary sweat glands) lose a small amount of cytoplasm with each secretion.

column1: What are the four main types of connective tissue cells (not fibers)?
column4: Fibroblasts synthesize ECM; adipocytes store fat; mast cells release histamine; macrophages phagocytose debris and pathogens. Plasma cells and leukocytes are also present.

column1: Which connective tissue cell is the primary producer of collagen and other extracellular matrix proteins?
column4: Fibroblasts secrete collagen, elastin, and ground substance (proteoglycans). Activated fibroblasts become myofibroblasts during wound healing.

column1: What cell type stores energy as triglycerides and is the main cell of adipose tissue?
column4: White adipocytes have a single large lipid droplet and thin rim of cytoplasm. Brown adipocytes have multiple droplets and many mitochondria for thermogenesis.

column1: Which connective tissue cell releases histamine and heparin during allergic reactions?
column4: Mast cells contain granules packed with histamine and heparin. They are activated by IgE-antigen crosslinking and play a central role in immediate hypersensitivity (Type I).

column1: What is the most abundant protein in the human body and the major structural protein of connective tissue?
column4: Collagen's triple-helix structure (Gly-X-Y repeat) gives tensile strength. Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline/lysine; deficiency causes scurvy.

column1: Which connective tissue fiber is responsible for the elastic recoil of skin, lungs, and blood vessels?
column4: Elastin is cross-linked by desmosine bonds, allowing stretch and recoil. Marfan syndrome involves fibrillin-1 mutations that disrupt elastin fiber microfibrils.

column1: What is the activated, phagocytic form of monocytes found in connective tissue?
column4: Monocytes circulate in blood and differentiate into tissue macrophages. They phagocytose pathogens, present antigens, and release cytokines, coordinating immune responses.

column1: Which connective tissue type has a gel-like ground substance rich in hyaluronic acid and is found in embryos and the umbilical cord?
column4: Wharton's jelly is a specialized loose connective tissue. It is a common source of mesenchymal stem cells and illustrates how ground substance composition varies by tissue type.

column1: What vitamin is required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine during collagen synthesis, and what disease results from its deficiency?
column4: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases require vitamin C as a cofactor. Without hydroxylation, collagen triple helices are unstable, causing fragile vessels, poor wound healing, and bleeding gums.

column1: Who first described cells using a microscope and coined the term 'cell'?
column4: Hooke observed cork tissue and named the compartments 'cells' because they resembled monks' rooms. His work was published in Micrographia.

column1: Which scientist first described living cells (animalcules) in pond water?
column4: Leeuwenhoek used improved single-lens microscopes in the 1670s to observe bacteria and protozoa, the first observations of free-living microorganisms.

column1: Who proposed that all plants are composed of cells?
column4: Schleiden, a botanist, concluded that the cell is the basic unit of plant structure, contributing to the formulation of cell theory.

column1: Who extended cell theory to animals, stating all animals are composed of cells?
column4: Schwann collaborated with Schleiden and unified the observation that both plants and animals are composed of cells, forming the core of classical cell theory.

column1: Which scientist added the principle that all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula e cellula)?
column4: Virchow's principle refuted spontaneous generation for cellular origin and established the continuity of life through cell division.

column1: What Latin phrase summarizes Virchow's contribution to cell theory?
column4: Meaning 'every cell from a cell,' this phrase encapsulates the principle of biotic succession and cell reproduction by division.

column1: Whose experiments in the 1850s–1860s disproved spontaneous generation, supporting Virchow's cell principle?
column4: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments showed that microorganisms come from pre-existing microorganisms, reinforcing that cells only arise from cells.

column1: Which three scientists are most directly credited with establishing classical cell theory in the 19th century?
column4: Schleiden (plants), Schwann (animals), and Virchow (cells from cells) together defined the three tenets of classical cell theory.

column1: What technological advancement enabled the formulation of cell theory in the 17th–19th centuries?
column4: Progressive refinements in lens grinding and microscope design allowed scientists to consistently observe cellular structure across diverse organisms.

column1: Which tenet of cell theory was added in the modern era to address heredity?
column3: DNA is passed from cell to cell during division
column4: Modern cell theory extends classical tenets to include that genetic information (DNA) is transmitted from parent to daughter cells, uniting cell theory with molecular biology.

column1: What are the three tenets of classical cell theory?
column3: All living things are cells; cell is basic unit; cells from pre-existing cells
column4: These three principles, established by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow, define classical cell theory and remain foundational in biology.

column1: How did cell theory change the understanding of the basic unit of life?
column3: Established the cell as the basic structural and functional unit
column4: Before cell theory, organisms were studied as whole entities; recognizing the cell as the fundamental unit redirected biology toward reductionist, mechanistic analysis.
column8: concept::BB::2B::cell_theory MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2B::cell-theory::impact-on-biology MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How did cell theory contribute to the germ theory of disease?
column4: By establishing that all life is cellular, cell theory supported the idea that pathogens are living cells, leading Pasteur and Koch to develop germ theory.
column8: concept::BB::2B::cell_theory MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2B::cell-theory::impact-on-biology MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the significance of Virchow's 'cells from cells' principle for cancer biology?
column3: Cancer cells arise by uncontrolled division of pre-existing cells
column4: Virchow himself applied his principle to cancer, recognizing tumors as abnormal cellular proliferation — a foundation for modern oncology.

column1: How did cell theory unify the study of plant and animal biology?
column3: Both kingdoms share the cell as their common structural unit
column4: Before cell theory, plants and animals were studied separately; recognizing shared cellular composition created a unified framework for all eukaryotic biology.
column8: concept::BB::2B::cell_theory MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2B::cell-theory::impact-on-biology MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which fundamental process in cell biology is a direct consequence of the 'cells from cells' tenet?
column4: The principle that cells only arise from pre-existing cells means reproduction at the cellular level must occur through division processes such as mitosis and meiosis.
column8: concept::BB::2B::cell_theory MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2B::cell-theory::impact-on-biology MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Why are viruses considered an exception to classical cell theory?
column3: Viruses are not cells and cannot self-replicate independently
column4: Viruses lack cellular structure and require a host cell to reproduce, making them non-cellular entities that do not fit the 'all life is cellular' tenet.
column8: concept::BB::2B::cell_theory MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2B::cell-theory::impact-on-biology MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does cell theory relate to the concept of multicellularity?
column3: Multicellular organisms are cooperative assemblies of individual cells
column4: Cell theory implies that complex organisms arise from the coordinated activity of discrete cellular units, each capable of fundamental life processes.
column8: concept::BB::2B::cell_theory MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2B::cell-theory::impact-on-biology MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two prokaryotic domains recognized in the three-domain system?
column4: The three-domain system (Woese) divides life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. Both Bacteria and Archaea lack a true nucleus, distinguishing them from Eukarya.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which domain of life contains organisms that are prokaryotic yet more closely related to eukaryotes than to bacteria?
column4: Phylogenetic analyses based on rRNA sequences show Archaea share more molecular features with Eukarya (e.g., similar RNA polymerase, initiator tRNA) than with Bacteria, despite both being prokaryotes.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What ribosomal RNA molecule is most commonly used to classify and differentiate prokaryotic domains?
column4: Carl Woese used 16S rRNA sequences to establish the three-domain system. 16S rRNA is highly conserved yet contains variable regions useful for phylogenetic comparison.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: In the three-domain system, which domain(s) are prokaryotic?
column4: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Both Bacteria and Archaea fit this description; Eukarya are eukaryotic.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which scientist developed the three-domain classification system based on rRNA sequences?
column4: In the 1970s–1980s, Carl Woese (with George Fox) used 16S rRNA comparisons to show that Archaea are a distinct domain, separate from Bacteria and Eukarya.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: In what extreme environments are Archaea most commonly found?
column3: Extreme environments (hot springs, salt lakes, anaerobic habitats)
column4: Many Archaea are extremophiles: thermophiles live in hot springs, halophiles in high-salt environments, and methanogens in anaerobic conditions. This is a classic MCAT association.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which group of Archaea produces methane as a metabolic byproduct?
column4: Methanogens are strictly anaerobic Archaea that reduce CO2 with H2 to produce CH4. They inhabit swamps, wetlands, and animal intestines (including human gut).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Do Archaea have peptidoglycan in their cell walls?
column4: Unlike Bacteria, Archaea lack peptidoglycan. Their cell walls may contain pseudopeptidoglycan, S-layers, or glycoproteins. This difference makes Archaea naturally resistant to antibiotics targeting peptidoglycan synthesis (e.g., penicillin).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What type of RNA polymerase do Archaea possess, and how does it compare to bacteria?
column3: Multiple-subunit RNA polymerase similar to eukaryotes
column4: Archaea have a complex RNA polymerase resembling eukaryotic RNA Pol II, rather than the single bacterial RNA polymerase. This is a key molecular feature linking Archaea to Eukarya.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the initiator tRNA used in Archaea for translation initiation?
column4: Unlike Bacteria (which use formyl-methionine, fMet), Archaea use regular Met-tRNA like eukaryotes. This is one of several eukaryote-like features of Archaea.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the defining structural feature that distinguishes bacteria from eukaryotes at the cellular level?
column4: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA is located in a nucleoid region not enclosed by a nuclear envelope. This is the fundamental distinction from eukaryotic cells.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the name of the non-membrane-bound region in bacteria where the chromosome is located?
column4: The nucleoid is an irregularly shaped region in the bacterial cytoplasm containing the circular chromosome. It is not enclosed by a membrane, unlike the eukaryotic nucleus.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What type of genetic elements, in addition to the chromosome, do many bacteria carry that confer antibiotic resistance?
column4: Plasmids are small, circular, extrachromosomal DNA molecules that replicate independently. They often carry genes for antibiotic resistance and can be transferred between bacteria via conjugation.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the sedimentation coefficient of bacterial ribosomes?
column4: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, composed of a 50S large subunit and a 30S small subunit. This differs from eukaryotic 80S ribosomes and is the basis for selective antibiotic targeting.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which type of DNA topology is found in the bacterial chromosome?
column4: The bacterial chromosome is typically a single, circular, covalently closed dsDNA molecule. It is negatively supercoiled and compacted by nucleoid-associated proteins (not histones).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What shape describes cocci bacteria?
column4: Cocci (singular: coccus) are round or spherical bacteria. Examples include Staphylococcus and Streptococcus. The arrangement of cocci (clusters vs. chains) helps identify genera.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What shape describes bacilli bacteria?
column4: Bacilli (singular: bacillus) are cylindrical/rod-shaped bacteria. Examples include Escherichia coli and Bacillus anthracis. Do not confuse the genus Bacillus with the shape descriptor bacillus.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What shape describes spirilli bacteria?
column4: Spirilli (singular: spirillum) are rigid spiral-shaped bacteria. Related spirochetes (e.g., Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi) are flexible spirals and are sometimes considered separately.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What term describes a chain of cocci?
column4: Streptococcus bacteria divide in one plane and remain attached, forming chains. The prefix 'strepto-' means twisted chain, distinguishing them from clusters (staphylococci).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What term describes a grape-like cluster arrangement of cocci?
column4: Staphylococci divide in multiple planes, producing irregular grape-like clusters. Staphylococcus aureus is the classic example and is an important MCAT pathogen.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What term describes a pair of cocci?
column4: Diplococci are cocci that remain in pairs after division. Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Streptococcus pneumoniae are classic diplococcal pathogens tested on the MCAT.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the characteristic shape of Bacillus anthracis?
column4: B. anthracis, the causative agent of anthrax, is a large, Gram-positive, endospore-forming rod. Its shape classifies it as a bacillus.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What shape are the bacteria Escherichia coli?
column4: E. coli is a Gram-negative rod-shaped (bacillus) bacterium. It is the most commonly used model organism in microbiology and molecular biology.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is a coccobacillus?
column3: An intermediate rod-coccus shape (short, oval rod)
column4: Coccobacilli are so short and wide they appear intermediate between cocci and bacilli. Haemophilus influenzae is a classic coccobacillus example.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What unique structure do some bacilli form to survive harsh environmental conditions?
column4: Certain rod-shaped bacteria (e.g., Bacillus, Clostridium) produce dormant endospores extremely resistant to heat, desiccation, and chemicals. Endospores are not reproductive structures — they are survival structures.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which Gram stain result do most bacilli such as E. coli and Salmonella share?
column4: Many clinically important rod-shaped bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella, Pseudomonas) are Gram-negative due to their thin peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane. Notable Gram-positive rods include Bacillus and Clostridium.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What disease is caused by the spiral-shaped bacterium Treponema pallidum?
column4: Treponema pallidum is a spirochete (flexible spiral bacterium) that causes syphilis. Spirochetes have axial filaments (endoflagella) that allow corkscrew motility.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What type of motility apparatus is unique to spirochetes?
column4: Spirochetes move via axial filaments located in the periplasmic space, creating a corkscrew motion. This differs from the external flagella of most other bacteria.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which spiral-shaped bacterium causes Lyme disease?
column4: B. burgdorferi is a spirochete transmitted by Ixodes (deer) ticks. It causes Lyme disease characterized by erythema migrans rash, arthritis, and neurological symptoms.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What distinguishes a spirochete from a spirillum in terms of cell wall rigidity?
column3: Spirochetes are flexible; spirilla are rigid
column4: Spirilla (e.g., Spirillum minus) have rigid cell walls and external flagella. Spirochetes (e.g., Treponema) have flexible bodies and periplasmic flagella (axial filaments).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What Gram stain result is typically seen with spirochetes like Treponema pallidum?
column4: Treponema pallidum is so thin it does not stain well with Gram stain and is typically visualized by darkfield microscopy. It is technically Gram-negative but usually classified by other methods.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What shape are Streptococcus pyogenes bacteria?
column4: Streptococcus pyogenes is a Gram-positive coccus arranged in chains. It causes strep throat, rheumatic fever, and scarlet fever.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What arrangement of cocci characterizes Staphylococcus aureus?
column4: S. aureus divides in multiple planes, producing clusters. It is a Gram-positive coccus associated with skin infections, pneumonia, and toxin-mediated diseases (TSST, food poisoning).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What Gram stain result do Neisseria gonorrhoeae (diplococci) produce?
column4: Neisseria gonorrhoeae are Gram-negative diplococci (kidney-bean shaped pairs). Most cocci are Gram-positive, making Neisseria an important exception to know for the MCAT.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What arrangement describes Streptococcus pneumoniae?
column4: S. pneumoniae appears as pairs of lancet-shaped cocci (diplococci). It is encapsulated, Gram-positive, and causes pneumonia, meningitis, and otitis media.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which cocci are classified as Gram-positive: Staphylococci, Streptococci, or Neisseria?
column4: Neisseria are the classic Gram-negative cocci (a high-yield exception). Staphylococci and Streptococci are both Gram-positive cocci and are the most common Gram-positive bacteria on the MCAT.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is absent in prokaryotic cells that is present in eukaryotic cells to enclose the genetic material?
column4: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; their DNA resides in the nucleoid. The absence of a nuclear envelope means transcription and translation can be coupled in bacteria.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What process do prokaryotes use to divide instead of mitosis?
column4: Prokaryotes replicate by binary fission, a simpler process than mitosis. The chromosome replicates, the cell elongates, and a septum forms to divide the cell into two identical daughters.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What prokaryotic structure is functionally analogous to the mitotic spindle but is used in binary fission?
column4: FtsZ, a tubulin homolog, polymerizes into a Z-ring at the division plane and constricts to divide the cell. It is the prokaryotic functional analog of the eukaryotic spindle apparatus.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What key consequence of lacking a nuclear membrane allows bacteria to couple transcription and translation?
column3: mRNA can be translated while still being transcribed
column4: Because there is no nuclear envelope separating the chromosome from the cytoplasm, ribosomes attach to mRNA as it is being synthesized. This co-translational process does not occur in eukaryotes.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Do prokaryotes undergo meiosis?
column4: Prokaryotes are haploid and reproduce asexually by binary fission. They do not undergo meiosis. Genetic diversity arises via transformation, transduction, and conjugation — not sexual reproduction.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which membrane-bound organelle found in eukaryotes is absent in prokaryotes and produces ATP via oxidative phosphorylation?
column4: Prokaryotes lack mitochondria; aerobic respiration occurs at the plasma membrane and associated mesosome-like invaginations. The electron transport chain is embedded in the bacterial plasma membrane.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which membrane-bound organelle responsible for photosynthesis in plant cells is absent in prokaryotes?
column4: Photosynthetic prokaryotes (e.g., cyanobacteria) carry out photosynthesis using internal membrane stacks (thylakoids), but these are not membrane-bound organelles enclosed in a double membrane as in eukaryotes.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Do prokaryotes have an endoplasmic reticulum?
column4: Prokaryotes lack the endomembrane system (ER, Golgi, lysosomes). Protein secretion occurs via direct translocation through the plasma membrane using the Sec pathway, not via ER-Golgi vesicle trafficking.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the one type of organelle that prokaryotes DO possess?
column4: Ribosomes are the only organelles found in prokaryotes. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S), which distinguishes them from eukaryotic 80S ribosomes and allows selective antibiotic targeting.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What do prokaryotes have instead of a cytoskeleton of actin and tubulin for maintaining cell shape?
column4: The rigid cell wall (peptidoglycan in bacteria) maintains shape instead of an extensive cytoskeleton. Bacteria do have cytoskeletal homologs (MreB ~ actin; FtsZ ~ tubulin), but not the same elaborate cytoskeleton as eukaryotes.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the primary structural polymer that makes up the bacterial cell wall?
column4: Peptidoglycan is a mesh-like polymer of NAM (N-acetylmuramic acid) and NAG (N-acetylglucosamine) cross-linked by short peptides. It provides structural rigidity and protects bacteria from osmotic lysis.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What color does a Gram-positive bacterium appear after Gram staining?
column4: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains the crystal violet-iodine complex even after alcohol decolorization, staining purple. Gram-negative bacteria are counterstained pink with safranin.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What additional outer membrane structure is found in Gram-negative bacteria but not Gram-positive bacteria?
column4: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer sandwiched between the inner plasma membrane and an outer membrane containing LPS. LPS (endotoxin) triggers strong immune responses.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which class of antibiotics inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins and blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking?
column4: Beta-lactams irreversibly inhibit transpeptidases (PBPs) that cross-link peptidoglycan strands. They are ineffective against Mycoplasma (no cell wall) and Archaea (no peptidoglycan).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What enzyme does lysozyme target in the bacterial cell wall?
column3: Cleaves glycosidic bonds between NAM and NAG in peptidoglycan
column4: Lysozyme (found in tears, saliva, mucus) is a natural antibacterial enzyme that hydrolyzes the beta-1,4 glycosidic bond between NAM and NAG in peptidoglycan, weakening and lysing the cell wall.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What term describes a bacterium that has had its cell wall completely removed?
column4: Protoplasts (from Gram-positive bacteria) and spheroplasts (from Gram-negative bacteria, which retain some outer membrane) are osmotically fragile cells without a complete cell wall.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the primary function of bacterial flagella?
column4: Bacterial flagella are whip-like appendages that rotate to propel the bacterium through liquid. The direction of rotation determines forward movement (counterclockwise) or tumbling (clockwise).
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What protein is the primary structural component of bacterial flagella?
column4: Flagellin subunits polymerize to form the hollow flagellar filament. The flagellin gene (fliC) is important in immunology as flagellin is recognized by TLR5 on innate immune cells.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What drives the rotation of bacterial flagella?
column3: Proton motive force (H+ gradient across the plasma membrane)
column4: The bacterial flagellar motor is powered by proton (H+) flow down the electrochemical gradient — NOT by ATP hydrolysis. This is a key distinction from eukaryotic cilia/flagella, which are powered by dynein using ATP.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What direction does the flagellum rotate during smooth swimming (runs) in E. coli?
column4: Counterclockwise rotation bundles the flagella together for smooth forward motion (run). Clockwise rotation unbundles flagella, causing random tumbling to reorient the bacterium.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What term describes the directed movement of bacteria toward a chemical attractant?
column4: Bacteria sense chemical gradients via membrane receptors and adjust their run-to-tumble ratio accordingly. More runs toward attractants (or away from repellents) result in net directed movement.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What are the three main structural components of the bacterial flagellum from base to tip?
column4: The basal body anchors the motor in the cell membrane; the hook is a curved universal joint; the filament is the long helical propeller made of flagellin. Understanding this structure is useful for MCAT mechanics questions.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: How does the energy source for bacterial flagellar rotation differ from eukaryotic ciliary/flagellar motion?
column3: Bacteria use proton motive force; eukaryotes use ATP (dynein)
column4: Bacterial flagella are powered by H+ flow (proton motive force). Eukaryotic cilia and flagella have a 9+2 microtubule axoneme and are powered by dynein ATPase. This is a classic MCAT comparison.
column5: Classification and Structure of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the primary mode of reproduction in prokaryotes?
column4: Binary fission is asexual reproduction where a prokaryote duplicates its chromosome and divides into two identical daughter cells. It is not mitosis — no spindle apparatus is used.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What type of DNA replication initiates binary fission in bacteria?
column4: Replication begins at a single origin of replication (oriC) and proceeds bidirectionally until the chromosome is fully duplicated, enabling cell division.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which protein forms the contractile ring during bacterial cytokinesis?
column4: FtsZ is a tubulin homolog that polymerizes into a Z-ring at the cell midpoint, constricting the membrane to complete binary fission.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Approximately how long is the generation time of E. coli under optimal conditions?
column4: E. coli can divide every 20 minutes under ideal conditions, making it a classic model for exponential bacterial growth studies.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Binary fission is analogous to which process in eukaryotes?
column4: Both result in two genetically identical daughter cells, but binary fission lacks a nuclear envelope and spindle apparatus; chromosome segregation occurs via attachment to the cell membrane.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Does binary fission contribute to genetic variation in offspring?
column4: Binary fission is asexual; genetic diversity in bacteria arises from mutation and horizontal gene transfer (transformation, transduction, conjugation), not from reproduction itself.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What term describes the transfer of genetic material between bacteria via a sex pilus?
column4: Conjugation allows a donor cell to transfer plasmid DNA (often carrying antibiotic resistance genes) to a recipient cell through a conjugation bridge, enabling rapid spread of resistance.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which genetic element most commonly carries antibiotic resistance genes in bacteria?
column4: R (resistance) plasmids are extrachromosomal circular DNA that can replicate independently and be transferred between bacteria, rapidly disseminating antibiotic resistance.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is transformation in the context of bacterial genetic adaptability?
column3: Uptake of free DNA from the environment
column4: Competent bacteria can take up naked DNA from their surroundings. If that DNA carries resistance genes, the bacterium becomes resistant — a key mechanism of horizontal gene transfer.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What process transfers bacterial genes via a bacteriophage vector?
column4: In transduction, a phage accidentally packages bacterial DNA and injects it into a new host, transferring genes including antibiotic resistance markers.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What are transposons (transposable elements) and their relevance to antibiotic resistance?
column3: Mobile DNA segments that can jump between chromosomes/plasmids
column4: Transposons can carry resistance genes and insert them into new genomic locations or spread them to plasmids, accelerating resistance gene dissemination.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which bacterial enzyme is targeted by fluoroquinolone antibiotics?
column4: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase, blocking DNA replication. Resistance often arises from point mutations in the gyrase gene, illustrating rapid bacterial adaptability.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What mathematical relationship describes bacterial population growth during the exponential phase?
column4: During exponential (log) phase, each division doubles the population. The growth curve is J-shaped when plotted on a linear scale and linear on a log scale.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Name the four phases of a bacterial growth curve in order.
column4: Lag: adaptation; Log: rapid doubling; Stationary: growth = death (nutrients limited); Death: population declines as cells die faster than they divide.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What limits bacterial growth and ends the exponential phase?
column4: Exponential growth is unsustainable; as nutrients run out or toxic byproducts accumulate, growth rate slows and the population enters stationary phase.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: During which growth phase is a bacterial culture most metabolically active and sensitive to antibiotics?
column4: Antibiotics targeting cell wall synthesis (e.g., penicillin) or ribosomes are most effective during log phase when cells are actively dividing and synthesizing macromolecules.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is generation time in bacterial growth?
column3: Time for a population to double
column4: Also called doubling time, it is the interval between successive binary fissions. Shorter generation times mean faster exponential growth.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: If a bacterium has a generation time of 30 minutes, how many bacteria arise from one cell after 3 hours?
column4: 3 hours = 6 generations; 2⁶ = 64. This illustrates the power of exponential growth even over short time periods.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What distinguishes obligate anaerobes from aerotolerant anaerobes?
column3: Obligate anaerobes are killed by O₂; aerotolerant are not
column4: Obligate anaerobes (e.g., Clostridium) lack superoxide dismutase and catalase, so reactive oxygen species are lethal. Aerotolerant anaerobes survive in O₂ but don't use it.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which enzyme allows aerobic bacteria to detoxify hydrogen peroxide?
column4: Catalase converts H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂, protecting cells from oxidative damage. The catalase test (bubble formation with H₂O₂) is a key clinical microbiology test.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What metabolic end-products are characteristic of obligate anaerobic fermentation?
column4: Obligate anaerobes rely on fermentation, producing organic acids (butyrate, acetate) and gases. Clostridium species are classic examples linked to gas gangrene and tetanus.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Define obligate aerobe.
column4: Obligate aerobes (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis) use O₂ as the terminal electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation and cannot survive without it.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Define facultative anaerobe.
column3: Can grow with or without O₂, preferring O₂
column4: Facultative anaerobes (e.g., E. coli, Staphylococcus aureus) perform aerobic respiration when O₂ is available but switch to fermentation anaerobically. They are the most metabolically flexible.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which oxygen class describes an organism that requires low (but not zero) O₂ concentrations?
column4: Microaerophiles (e.g., Helicobacter pylori, Campylobacter) are damaged by normal atmospheric O₂ (~21%) and require reduced O₂ (~5%) for optimal growth.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is a parasitic relationship between a bacterium and its host?
column4: Pathogenic bacteria (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis) derive nutrients from the host while causing disease. This is a classic parasitic interaction.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Define mutualism in the context of bacterial–host relationships.
column4: Example: E. coli in the large intestine synthesizes vitamin K and B vitamins for the host while receiving nutrients and shelter. This is mutualistic symbiosis.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What type of symbiosis describes Rhizobium bacteria living in legume root nodules?
column4: Rhizobium fixes atmospheric N₂ into ammonia (usable by the plant) while receiving carbon compounds from the plant — a textbook mutualistic nitrogen-fixing symbiosis.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is commensalism in bacterial ecology?
column4: Many skin bacteria (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis under normal conditions) benefit from the host environment without causing harm or providing clear benefit.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What term describes bacteria that only cause disease in immunocompromised hosts?
column4: Opportunistic pathogens (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) are commensal or environmental organisms that become parasitic when host defenses are weakened.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: How do endosymbiotic bacteria differ from free-living parasites?
column3: Endosymbionts live inside host cells and may be essential to the host
column4: Endosymbiosis (e.g., mitochondria from alpha-proteobacteria) involves intracellular residency that is often obligate and mutually beneficial, unlike extracellular parasitism.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is chemotaxis in bacteria?
column3: Directed movement toward attractants or away from repellents
column4: Bacteria use chemotaxis to swim toward favorable chemicals (e.g., glucose) or away from toxins, mediated by a two-component signaling system involving chemoreceptors.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which organelle propels bacteria during chemotaxis?
column4: The bacterial flagellum rotates like a propeller. Counterclockwise rotation causes smooth swimming (runs); clockwise rotation causes tumbling, reorienting the cell.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is a 'run' versus a 'tumble' in bacterial chemotaxis?
column3: Run = straight swimming; tumble = random reorientation
column4: Bacteria bias their run-tumble ratio based on chemical gradients: more runs toward attractants, more tumbles (then new run direction) away from repellents.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: Which proteins sense chemical gradients in bacterial chemotaxis?
column4: MCPs are transmembrane receptors that detect attractants/repellents and relay signals through CheA/CheY two-component system to control flagellar rotation.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What signal transduction system mediates bacterial chemotaxis?
column3: Two-component system (CheA histidine kinase / CheY response regulator)
column4: CheA autophosphorylates when MCPs detect repellents and transfers phosphate to CheY; phospho-CheY binds the flagellar motor switch, causing clockwise rotation (tumbling).
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is the role of methylation in bacterial chemotaxis adaptation?
column3: Allows bacteria to adapt to constant stimuli and detect changes
column4: CheR methylates MCPs to restore baseline signaling; CheB demethylates them. This adaptation lets bacteria respond to relative changes in concentration rather than absolute levels.
column5: Growth and Physiology of Prokaryotic Cells

column1: What is a plasmid?
column3: Small, circular, extrachromosomal DNA molecule in bacteria
column4: Plasmids replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome and often carry genes conferring selective advantages such as antibiotic resistance.

column1: What term describes DNA that exists outside the main bacterial chromosome?
column4: Plasmids are the primary example of extragenomic DNA in prokaryotes; mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA are analogous structures in eukaryotes.

column1: What type of genes are most commonly carried on plasmids?
column4: R-plasmids (resistance plasmids) carry genes encoding enzymes that inactivate antibiotics, a major clinical concern for drug-resistant infections.

column1: Are plasmids essential for bacterial survival under normal conditions?
column3: No — they are non-essential accessory elements
column4: Bacteria can survive without plasmids under standard lab conditions; plasmids provide advantages only in specific selective environments (e.g., antibiotic exposure).

column1: What is an episome?
column3: A plasmid capable of integrating into the host chromosome
column4: When integrated, an episome replicates with the chromosome; the F factor of E. coli is the classic episome example (forming Hfr strains).

column1: What structural feature allows plasmids to replicate independently?
column4: The origin of replication allows the host's replication machinery to copy the plasmid autonomously, separate from chromosomal replication.

column1: What is a virulence plasmid?
column3: A plasmid carrying genes that increase pathogenicity
column4: Examples include plasmids encoding toxins (e.g., heat-labile toxin in enterotoxigenic E. coli) or adhesion factors; distinct from R-plasmids.

column1: What distinguishes a high-copy-number plasmid from a low-copy-number plasmid?
column3: Number of copies per cell (high: ~100; low: 1-5)
column4: High-copy plasmids are controlled by simple mechanisms and produce many copies; low-copy plasmids have strict replication controls and are often larger (e.g., F factor: 1-2 copies/cell).

column1: What is bacterial transformation?
column3: Uptake and incorporation of naked exogenous DNA by a bacterium
column4: Transformation is one of three main mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer in prokaryotes; it does not require cell-to-cell contact.

column1: What state must a bacterium be in to take up exogenous DNA during transformation?
column4: Competence is a physiological state (natural or artificially induced) in which bacteria express surface proteins that bind and import extracellular DNA.

column1: Who first demonstrated bacterial transformation?
column4: Griffith's experiment with smooth and rough Streptococcus pneumoniae showed that a 'transforming principle' (later identified as DNA by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty) could change bacterial phenotype.

column1: What experiment proved the 'transforming principle' in transformation is DNA?
column4: They treated cell extracts with DNase, RNase, or protease; only DNase destroyed transforming activity, proving DNA carries genetic information.

column1: What happens to exogenous DNA after it enters a bacterium during transformation?
column3: It is integrated into the chromosome by homologous recombination
column4: The incoming single-stranded DNA fragment pairs with the homologous region of the host chromosome and is incorporated, replacing the original sequence.

column1: Which bacteria are naturally competent for transformation?
column3: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Bacillus subtilis, Haemophilus influenzae (among others)
column4: Natural competence is species-specific and often induced by specific environmental signals; many lab strains (e.g., E. coli) require artificial competence induction.

column1: How is artificial competence induced in E. coli for laboratory transformation?
column3: CaCl2 treatment followed by heat shock
column4: Calcium ions destabilize the membrane; heat shock (42°C, 90 sec) drives DNA uptake. Electroporation is an alternative high-efficiency method.

column1: What is the fate of transforming DNA that has no homology to the host chromosome?
column3: It is degraded (unless it is a self-replicating plasmid)
column4: Without homologous recombination sites, linear foreign DNA is typically destroyed by host nucleases; circular plasmids can persist autonomously.

column1: What is bacterial conjugation?
column3: Direct DNA transfer between bacteria via physical cell contact
column4: Conjugation requires a pilus (sex pilus) formed by the donor cell; it is the most efficient means of horizontal gene transfer among bacteria.

column1: What plasmid encodes the machinery required for conjugation in E. coli?
column4: The F plasmid carries tra (transfer) genes encoding the pilus and mating-pair stabilization proteins required for conjugation.

column1: What is an F+ cell?
column3: A bacterium containing the F plasmid (donor)
column4: F+ cells can form sex pili and transfer a copy of the F plasmid to F- (recipient) cells, converting them to F+.

column1: What is an Hfr cell?
column3: A bacterium with the F factor integrated into the chromosome
column4: Hfr (high frequency recombination) cells transfer chromosomal genes at high frequency during conjugation; recipients rarely become Hfr because transfer of the complete chromosome is rare.

column1: Which strand of DNA is transferred during bacterial conjugation?
column3: One strand of the donor's DNA (rolling-circle replication)
column4: The F plasmid or chromosome is nicked at oriT; one strand is transferred to the recipient while the donor simultaneously resynthesizes the complementary strand.

column1: Why do Hfr x F- matings rarely produce F- recipients that become Hfr?
column3: The tra genes are at the end of the chromosome and are seldom transferred completely
column4: Transfer begins at oriT within the integrated F factor; the entire chromosome must transfer for the recipient to acquire the tra genes needed to become Hfr — this rarely completes in time.

column1: What is an F' (F-prime) plasmid?
column3: An F plasmid carrying bacterial chromosomal genes acquired during excision
column4: Imprecise excision of an integrated F factor can pick up adjacent chromosomal genes; F' cells can transfer these genes to F- cells, creating partial diploids (merozygotes).

column1: What is sexduction (F-duction)?
column3: Gene transfer via an F' plasmid carrying chromosomal genes
column4: Sexduction allows complementation analysis; the recipient becomes a partial diploid (merodiploid) harboring two copies of the transferred chromosomal region.

column1: How does conjugation differ from transformation in terms of cell contact?
column3: Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact; transformation does not
column4: Conjugation uses a sex pilus to establish physical contact; transformation involves uptake of free DNA from the environment with no donor cell required.

column1: What is a transposon?
column3: A mobile DNA segment that can move (transpose) to new genomic locations
column4: Transposons ('jumping genes') encode transposase, the enzyme that catalyzes their excision and insertion; they are present in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

column1: What enzyme is encoded by transposons and is essential for their movement?
column4: Transposase recognizes the inverted terminal repeats flanking the transposon and catalyzes the cut-and-paste (or replicative) transposition reaction.

column1: What structural sequences flank most transposons?
column4: Inverted terminal repeats are recognized by transposase; after insertion, short direct repeats of host DNA flank the transposon due to staggered cuts at the target site.

column1: What are the two main mechanisms of transposition?
column4: Cut-and-paste removes the transposon from the donor site and inserts it elsewhere; replicative transposition copies the transposon so both donor and target sites retain a copy.

column1: What is an insertion sequence (IS element)?
column3: The simplest transposon, encoding only transposase and flanked by IRs
column4: IS elements are the smallest bacterial transposons (~700-2500 bp); complex transposons (Tn elements) additionally carry genes such as antibiotic resistance genes.

column1: How can transposon insertion cause a mutation?
column3: By disrupting a gene at the insertion site
column4: Random insertion of a transposon into a coding sequence or promoter inactivates gene function; this is exploited in transposon mutagenesis screens.

column1: What eukaryotic transposons use an RNA intermediate?
column4: Retrotransposons are transcribed to RNA, reverse-transcribed to DNA by reverse transcriptase, then inserted into the genome — analogous to retroviral replication.

column1: What are target-site duplications (TSDs) and what creates them?
column3: Short direct repeats of host DNA flanking a transposon, created by staggered cuts
column4: Transposase makes staggered cuts at the insertion site; after gap-filling by DNA polymerase, short direct repeats of host sequence appear on both sides of the newly inserted transposon.

column1: What scientist discovered transposons ('jumping genes')?
column4: McClintock discovered transposons in maize (corn) in the 1940s-50s; she received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1983 for this discovery.

column1: What are the two essential macromolecular components found in ALL viruses?
column4: Every virus has a genome (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat called a capsid. These two components are the minimum requirement for a functional virus.

column1: What is the protein coat surrounding a viral genome called?
column4: The capsid is made of protein subunits called capsomeres and protects the viral nucleic acid. Its shape (helical, icosahedral, or complex) is characteristic for each virus type.

column1: What is a viral envelope derived from?
column4: Enveloped viruses acquire a lipid bilayer from the host cell during budding. The envelope contains viral glycoproteins embedded in the host-derived membrane.

column1: What term describes the complex of viral nucleic acid plus its surrounding capsid?
column4: The nucleocapsid is the core structure of every virion. In enveloped viruses, the nucleocapsid is further surrounded by the lipid envelope.

column1: Which type of virus — enveloped or nonenveloped — is generally MORE resistant to drying, detergents, and harsh environments?
column4: Nonenveloped viruses lack a lipid envelope, so detergents and desiccation cannot disrupt them as easily. Enveloped viruses are inactivated by soap because it dissolves their lipid coat.

column1: What are the protein subunits that assemble to form a viral capsid called?
column4: Capsomeres self-assemble around the viral genome. Their arrangement determines capsid geometry — icosahedral (20 triangular faces) or helical.

column1: An enveloped virus loses its envelope. What most likely happens to its infectivity?
column4: The envelope contains viral attachment glycoproteins needed to bind host receptors. Without the envelope, the virus typically cannot enter host cells.

column1: Do viruses have mitochondria?
column4: Viruses are acellular and completely lack membrane-bound organelles, including mitochondria, ribosomes, and a nucleus. They rely entirely on host cell machinery for energy and biosynthesis.

column1: Do viruses contain ribosomes?
column4: Because viruses lack ribosomes, they cannot independently synthesize proteins. They hijack the host cell's ribosomes to translate their mRNA into viral proteins.

column1: Because viruses lack their own ribosomes, what must they use for protein synthesis?
column4: This obligate dependence on host ribosomes (and energy metabolism) is why viruses are considered obligate intracellular parasites. They cannot replicate outside a host cell.

column1: Viruses are described as obligate intracellular parasites. What structural deficiency most directly explains this?
column3: Lack of organelles (no ribosomes, no ATP-generating machinery)
column4: Without organelles for energy production and protein synthesis, viruses cannot carry out independent metabolism and must co-opt host cell machinery to replicate.

column1: Do viruses have a nucleus or nucleoid region?
column3: No — neither a nucleus nor a nucleoid
column4: Unlike eukaryotes (membrane-bound nucleus) and prokaryotes (nucleoid), viruses simply have a genome packed inside a protein capsid with no surrounding membrane compartment.

column1: What is the name of the protein tail fibers on a T4 bacteriophage used for?
column4: Tail fibers are part of the phage's base plate complex and bind specifically to surface receptors on the bacterial host, determining host range.

column1: What shape is the head (capsid) of the T4 bacteriophage?
column4: The T4 phage has a prolate (elongated) icosahedral head that houses the double-stranded DNA genome. The head connects to a helical tail.

column1: Name the three main structural regions of a typical T4 bacteriophage.
column4: The head stores the genome; the tail (with sheath and core) acts as an injection device; the tail fibers mediate host attachment. This complex 'syringe-like' structure is unique to bacteriophages.

column1: What happens to the bacteriophage tail sheath during DNA injection into a bacterium?
column3: It contracts, driving the tail core through the bacterial cell wall
column4: The tail sheath is a contractile protein spring. Contraction forces the hollow tail core (tube) through the bacterial membrane, injecting phage DNA while the capsid remains outside.

column1: In bacteriophage structure, what component stays outside the bacterial cell during infection?
column3: The phage capsid (head) and tail proteins
column4: Only the nucleic acid is injected; the protein coat remains external. This was confirmed by the Hershey-Chase experiment using radioactive labels on DNA and protein.

column1: What enzyme do some bacteriophages carry in their tail to help degrade the bacterial cell wall during infection?
column4: Phage lysozyme locally digests the peptidoglycan layer, allowing the tail core to penetrate and deliver DNA. The same enzyme is also used during lysis at the end of the lytic cycle.

column1: Can a bacteriophage infect a eukaryotic cell?
column4: Bacteriophages are specific to bacteria because their tail fibers recognize bacterial surface receptors. They cannot attach to or infect eukaryotic cells.

column1: Can a virus genome be composed of RNA?
column4: Viruses are unique in that their genome can be either DNA or RNA — never both. Examples of RNA viruses include HIV (retrovirus), influenza, and poliovirus.

column1: What is a retrovirus's genome composed of?
column4: Retroviruses (e.g., HIV) carry two copies of positive-sense ssRNA. After infection, reverse transcriptase converts the RNA genome into dsDNA for integration into the host genome.

column1: Which enzyme unique to retroviruses converts their RNA genome into DNA?
column4: Reverse transcriptase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase encoded by the virus and packaged in the virion. It is a key drug target in HIV therapy (e.g., nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors).

column1: Positive-sense ssRNA viral genomes can be directly translated by host ribosomes. True or false?
column4: Positive-sense RNA has the same sequence as mRNA, so host ribosomes can translate it immediately. Negative-sense RNA must first be converted to positive-sense by viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

column1: What distinguishes a negative-sense RNA virus genome from a positive-sense RNA genome?
column3: Negative-sense is complementary to mRNA; cannot be directly translated
column4: Negative-sense (antisense) RNA must be transcribed into positive-sense mRNA by a viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (packaged in the virion) before translation can occur. Influenza is a classic example.

column1: T4 bacteriophage carries what type of nucleic acid as its genome?
column4: Most bacteriophages, including T-even phages (T2, T4), have dsDNA genomes. Some phages (e.g., M13) have ssDNA, and some (e.g., Qbeta) have ssRNA.

column1: Can a single virus contain both a DNA and an RNA genome simultaneously?
column3: No — viruses have either DNA or RNA, never both
column4: This is a fundamental rule of virology. Viruses are classified as DNA viruses or RNA viruses based on their genome type; no known virus carries both nucleic acid types.

column1: Compared to bacteria, how large are most viruses?
column3: Much smaller — typically 10–100x smaller than bacteria
column4: Most viruses range from ~20–300 nm in diameter; bacteria are typically 1–10 micrometers. This size difference explains why viruses pass through filters that trap bacteria.

column1: What is the approximate size range for most viruses?
column4: The smallest viruses (e.g., parvoviruses) are ~20 nm; the largest (e.g., Mimivirus) can exceed 700 nm. For MCAT, remember viruses are submicroscopic and not visible by light microscopy.

column1: Can typical viruses be seen with a light (optical) microscope?
column4: Viruses are below the resolution limit (~200 nm) of light microscopy. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is the standard method for visualizing individual virions.

column1: How does the size of a virus compare to a eukaryotic cell?
column3: Viruses are roughly 1,000–10,000 times smaller than a eukaryotic cell
column4: A typical eukaryotic cell is 10–100 micrometers; a typical virus is 20–300 nm. This scale difference emphasizes that viruses are not cells but molecular machines.

column1: What is the approximate size of a typical bacterium (e.g., E. coli)?
column4: Bacteria are much larger than viruses but smaller than most eukaryotic cells. E. coli is about 2 micrometers long — visible with a light microscope but not the naked eye.

column1: Because of their small size, viruses can pass through what type of filter that normally traps bacteria?
column4: The discovery that filtered fluids could still cause disease (e.g., tobacco mosaic disease) led to the original definition of viruses as 'filterable agents.' This was evidence that they were smaller than bacteria.

column1: Rank from smallest to largest: virus, bacterium, eukaryotic cell.
column4: Virus: ~20–300 nm; Bacterium: ~1,000–10,000 nm (1–10 µm); Eukaryotic cell: ~10,000–100,000 nm (10–100 µm). Remembering this order is a common MCAT comparison question.

column1: What term describes obligate intracellular parasites that require a host cell to replicate?
column4: Viruses lack ribosomes and metabolic machinery, so they must hijack host cell systems to produce new viral particles. This is the defining feature distinguishing viruses from cellular life.

column1: Which macromolecule do viruses lack that makes independent protein synthesis impossible?
column4: Without ribosomes, viruses cannot translate their own mRNA into protein. This is why all viruses are obligate intracellular parasites.

column1: What is the protein coat surrounding a virus's nucleic acid called?
column4: The capsid is made of repeating protein subunits called capsomeres. Together with the enclosed nucleic acid it forms the nucleocapsid.

column1: What term describes the complete, mature viral particle capable of infecting a host?
column4: A virion is the extracellular form of a virus — the infectious unit consisting of nucleic acid, capsid, and (in enveloped viruses) a lipid envelope.

column1: What are the two categories of nucleic acid a virus may carry as its genome?
column4: Each virus contains either DNA or RNA, never both. This distinguishes viral classes and dictates replication strategy inside the host.

column1: What structural feature distinguishes enveloped viruses from naked (non-enveloped) viruses?
column4: Enveloped viruses acquire a lipid membrane from the host cell during budding. This envelope is studded with viral glycoproteins used for host attachment.

column1: Why are viruses not considered living organisms under most definitions?
column3: They lack metabolism and cannot self-replicate outside a host
column4: Viruses do not carry out independent metabolism, grow, or replicate without host machinery. They are acellular and depend entirely on a living host cell.

column1: What is the first step of the bacteriophage lytic cycle?
column4: The phage tail fibers recognize and bind specific receptor molecules on the bacterial cell surface. Host-range specificity is determined at this step.

column1: Name the two replication strategies available to temperate bacteriophages.
column4: In the lytic cycle the phage replicates and lyses the cell immediately. In the lysogenic cycle the phage DNA integrates as a prophage and replicates with the host genome.

column1: In the lytic cycle, what event immediately precedes release of new phage particles?
column4: Phage-encoded enzymes (lysins) degrade the bacterial cell wall, causing the cell to burst and release hundreds of new phage particles.

column1: What term describes the phage DNA integrated into the host bacterial chromosome?
column4: As a prophage, viral DNA is replicated passively along with the host genome during every bacterial cell division. Induction converts the prophage back to lytic replication.

column1: During which phase of the lytic cycle are no complete viral particles detectable inside the host cell?
column4: The eclipse period follows injection of viral nucleic acid. Components are being made but not yet assembled, so no intact virions can be isolated.

column1: What is the key difference between the lytic and lysogenic cycles regarding host cell fate?
column3: Lytic: host cell is destroyed; lysogenic: host cell survives
column4: In the lytic cycle the host is lysed to release progeny. In the lysogenic cycle the host lives on, carrying the prophage until induction occurs.

column1: What induces a prophage to switch from lysogenic to lytic replication?
column3: Environmental stress (e.g., UV radiation, DNA damage)
column4: DNA-damaging agents activate the SOS response, which cleaves the phage repressor protein, allowing the prophage to excise and enter the lytic cycle.

column1: Which molecule on the host cell surface does a bacteriophage recognize during attachment?
column3: Specific receptor protein on the bacterial cell wall/membrane
column4: Phage tail fibers bind to specific surface receptors (e.g., lipopolysaccharide, pili, or outer-membrane proteins). This interaction defines host range.

column1: How does bacteriophage T4 deliver its DNA into the host without the capsid entering?
column3: It injects DNA through the tail into the bacterium
column4: The phage tail contracts, driving the tail tube through the cell wall and membrane. Only the nucleic acid enters; the capsid remains outside.

column1: What process do enveloped animal viruses commonly use to enter host cells?
column4: Enveloped viruses fuse their lipid envelope with the host membrane, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. Alternatively, the virion may be endocytosed and the envelope fuses with the endosomal membrane.

column1: What is the term for the viral surface proteins that recognize and bind host cell receptors?
column4: These glycoproteins determine cell and tissue tropism. For HIV, gp120 binds CD4; for influenza, hemagglutinin binds sialic acid residues.

column1: How do non-enveloped animal viruses typically enter the host cell?
column4: The naked virion is engulfed by the cell; acidification of the endosome triggers conformational changes that disrupt the membrane, releasing viral nucleic acid.

column1: What term describes the viral glycoprotein on HIV that binds the CD4 receptor?
column4: gp120 on HIV's surface binds CD4 on helper T cells and macrophages. A co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) is also required for fusion, mediated by gp41.

column1: After entering the host cell, which cellular organelle do DNA viruses typically use for replication?
column4: Most DNA viruses replicate their genomes in the nucleus, exploiting host DNA polymerases and nuclear import machinery. Poxviruses are a notable exception (cytoplasmic replication).

column1: Where do RNA viruses typically replicate their genomes?
column4: RNA viruses generally replicate in the cytoplasm using viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). Retroviruses and influenza are exceptions requiring nuclear steps.

column1: What host machinery do viruses use to translate viral proteins?
column4: Viruses commandeer the host's translational apparatus entirely. Viral mRNAs are translated by the same 80S ribosomes used for host proteins.

column1: What enzyme do RNA viruses encode to replicate an RNA genome from an RNA template?
column4: RdRp is not present in uninfected host cells, so viruses must supply it. It copies the viral RNA genome for replication and produces mRNA for translation.

column1: How does a positive-sense (+) ssRNA virus genome differ from a negative-sense (-) ssRNA virus in terms of immediate function?
column3: Positive-sense RNA can be directly translated; negative-sense cannot
column4: (+) ssRNA acts directly as mRNA. (-) ssRNA must first be transcribed into a complementary (+) strand by the virion-packaged RdRp before translation.

column1: Why must retroviruses package reverse transcriptase inside the virion?
column3: To convert their RNA genome to DNA before host-cell transcription machinery can be used
column4: Reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy of the RNA genome in the cytoplasm. Without pre-packaged enzyme, there is no host enzyme to perform this step.

column1: What is the process called by which new virions assemble from synthesized viral components?
column4: Capsid proteins spontaneously aggregate around the viral nucleic acid due to complementary molecular interactions. No additional energy input beyond synthesis is required.

column1: What are the two main mechanisms by which viruses are released from host cells?
column4: Non-enveloped viruses typically lyse the cell. Enveloped viruses bud through the host membrane, acquiring their lipid envelope as they exit — the host cell may survive initially.

column1: Which type of virus acquires its envelope during the budding process?
column4: As the nucleocapsid pushes through the host plasma membrane, it wraps in a lipid bilayer containing viral glycoproteins inserted by the virus, forming the envelope.

column1: What enzyme does influenza use to release newly formed virions from the host cell surface?
column4: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid linkages that would tether budding virions to the host cell surface, allowing efficient release and spread. It is the target of oseltamivir (Tamiflu).

column1: Why do non-enveloped viruses typically lyse the host cell upon release?
column3: They have no mechanism to bud; accumulated particles rupture the cell
column4: Without an envelope to merge with the plasma membrane, non-enveloped virions accumulate until the cell's structural integrity fails, causing lysis and mass release.

column1: What is the difference between a virion budding from the apical vs. basolateral surface of epithelial cells, and why does it matter?
column3: Apical: released into lumen (respiratory spread); basolateral: spreads to deeper tissues
column4: Directional budding determines viral tropism and spread pattern. Influenza buds apically, aiding airborne transmission. HIV buds basolaterally, facilitating systemic spread.

column1: What is transduction in bacteriology?
column3: Transfer of bacterial DNA from one bacterium to another via a bacteriophage
column4: A phage accidentally packages host bacterial DNA and injects it into the next bacterium it infects. This is a form of horizontal gene transfer.

column1: What is the difference between generalized and specialized transduction?
column3: Generalized: any host gene transferred; specialized: only genes adjacent to prophage insertion site
column4: In generalized transduction, the phage accidentally packages random fragments of bacterial DNA during lytic replication. In specialized transduction, imprecise excision of the prophage carries flanking bacterial genes.

column1: Which type of phage replication is required for specialized transduction to occur?
column4: Specialized transduction requires a prophage that integrates at a specific chromosomal site; imprecise excision brings adjacent bacterial genes along with the phage genome.

column1: What bacteriophage is the classic model for specialized transduction, and which genes does it transfer?
column3: Lambda phage; gal (galactose) or bio (biotin) genes
column4: Lambda integrates between gal and bio loci. Imprecise excision can capture either flanking gene, producing a transducing phage that carries gal or bio sequences.

column1: How does transduction differ from transformation as a mechanism of horizontal gene transfer?
column3: Transduction uses a phage vector; transformation involves uptake of naked DNA
column4: In transduction a phage delivers DNA; in transformation a competent bacterium directly takes up free DNA from the environment. Both result in new gene acquisition.

column1: What type of nucleic acid does HIV carry as its genome?
column4: HIV is a retrovirus with a diploid RNA genome — two identical positive-sense ssRNA strands. Each virion packages two copies of the genome.

column1: What enzyme do retroviruses use to convert their RNA genome into DNA?
column4: Reverse transcriptase (an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) first makes a DNA:RNA hybrid, then degrades the RNA (via RNase H activity), then synthesizes the complementary DNA strand to produce dsDNA.

column1: What is the integrated DNA form of the retroviral genome called?
column4: Once the double-stranded DNA copy of the retroviral genome is integrated into the host chromosome by integrase, it is called a provirus. It is replicated with the host DNA permanently.

column1: Which enzyme integrates retroviral dsDNA into the host chromosome?
column4: Integrase catalyzes the insertion of viral dsDNA into the host genome at a quasi-random site. The provirus then persists as a stable element in the host cell's DNA.

column1: What is the correct order of enzymatic steps in the retroviral life cycle after host cell entry?
column3: Reverse transcriptase → integrase → host RNA polymerase
column4: Reverse transcriptase makes dsDNA from RNA genome; integrase inserts dsDNA into host chromosome; host RNA pol II transcribes the provirus into new viral RNA genomes and mRNAs.

column1: Which host cell receptor does HIV primarily use for entry, and which coreceptor is required?
column4: gp120 binds CD4; conformational change exposes the coreceptor binding site. CCR5 is used by macrophage-tropic strains; CXCR4 by T-cell-tropic strains. gp41 then mediates membrane fusion.

column1: Why is reverse transcriptase a major target for HIV antiretroviral drugs?
column3: It has no host equivalent and is essential for HIV replication
column4: Human cells have no RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, so drugs targeting reverse transcriptase (NRTIs, NNRTIs) selectively inhibit viral replication with limited host toxicity.

column1: Why does HIV have an unusually high mutation rate compared to DNA viruses?
column3: Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading (3'→5' exonuclease) activity
column4: Without proofreading, reverse transcriptase introduces ~1 error per genome per replication cycle. This high mutation rate enables rapid immune escape and drug resistance.

column1: What are prions?
column4: Prions are abnormally folded isoforms (PrP^Sc) of a normal host protein (PrP^C). They propagate by inducing normal protein to misfold, causing fatal neurodegenerative disease.

column1: What diseases are caused by prions in humans?
column3: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), kuru, fatal familial insomnia, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker
column4: All human prion diseases are fatal spongiform encephalopathies. Variant CJD is linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease).

column1: What are viroids?
column3: Small, circular, naked ssRNA molecules that infect plants
column4: Viroids have no protein coat and no encoded proteins. They replicate using host RNA polymerase and cause disease in plants (e.g., potato spindle tuber viroid) by unknown mechanisms.

column1: How do prions replicate without encoding any nucleic acid?
column3: PrP^Sc templates misfolding of normal host PrP^C protein
column4: The abnormally folded prion protein converts native PrP^C into PrP^Sc by direct contact (conformational templating), exponentially increasing the misfolded form without nucleic acid involvement.

column1: What property makes prions resistant to standard sterilization methods?
column3: Heat, UV, and chemical agents that destroy nucleic acid do not inactivate prions
column4: Prions are extraordinarily resistant because they contain no nucleic acid to denature and the misfolded protein is very stable. Autoclaving at higher temperatures and sodium hydroxide are required.

column1: How do viroids differ from viruses in terms of structure?
column3: Viroids have no capsid and no protein; viruses have at least a protein capsid
column4: Viroids are naked RNA molecules. They are smaller than any known virus and encode no proteins, yet replicate autonomously in plant hosts using plant enzymes.

column1: What is the normal cellular isoform of the prion protein, and where is it found?
column3: PrP^C; expressed on the surface of neurons (and other cells)
column4: PrP^C is a GPI-anchored cell-surface glycoprotein with unclear normal function. Conversion to the beta-sheet-rich PrP^Sc form is the key event in prion disease.

column1: During which mitotic phase do chromosomes first condense and become visible?
column4: In prophase, chromatin fibers condense into distinct chromosomes. The mitotic spindle also begins to form as centrosomes migrate toward opposite poles.

column1: During which mitotic phase do chromosomes align along the cell's equatorial plate?
column4: In metaphase, chromosomes align at the metaphase plate (cell equator), attached to spindle fibers via kinetochores. This ensures each daughter cell receives one copy of each chromosome.

column1: During which mitotic phase do sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles?
column4: Cohesin proteins are cleaved by separase in anaphase, allowing sister chromatids to be pulled apart by shortening kinetochore microtubules toward opposite poles.

column1: During which mitotic phase does the nuclear envelope re-form around each set of chromosomes?
column4: In telophase, nuclear envelopes reassemble around each daughter nucleus and chromosomes begin to decondense. Cytokinesis typically begins during or shortly after telophase.

column1: During which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?
column4: S (synthesis) phase is part of interphase, not mitosis. Interphase consists of G1, S, and G2; the cell spends most of its life in interphase.

column1: Which sub-phase of prophase is characterized by disappearance of the nucleolus and breakdown of the nuclear envelope?
column4: Prometaphase (sometimes considered a distinct stage between prophase and metaphase) is when the nuclear envelope fully breaks down, allowing spindle fibers to attach to kinetochores.

column1: What is the mitotic spindle primarily composed of?
column4: The mitotic spindle is made of microtubules (polymers of alpha- and beta-tubulin). Kinetochore microtubules attach to chromosomes; polar microtubules push poles apart.
column8: concept::BB::2C::mitosis MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2C::mitosis::mitotic-structures MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the cleavage furrow, and in which type of cell does it form during cytokinesis?
column4: In animal cells, a contractile ring of actin and myosin pinches the cell in two. Plant cells instead form a cell plate from Golgi-derived vesicles.
column8: concept::BB::2C::mitosis MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2C::mitosis::mitotic-structures MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structure forms at the site where the cell plate will develop in dividing plant cells?
column4: The phragmoplast is an array of microtubules and actin filaments that guides vesicles to the midzone to build the new cell wall between daughter cells.
column8: concept::BB::2C::mitosis MCAT::section::BB MCAT::2C::mitosis::mitotic-structures MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are asters in the context of cell division?
column3: Radial arrays of microtubules around each centrosome
column4: Asters anchor the spindle apparatus to the cell cortex and help position the spindle. They are prominent in animal cells but absent in most plant cells.

column1: How many centrioles does a typical animal cell contain before S phase?
column4: Each centrosome contains a pair of centrioles. Before mitosis, the centrosome duplicates in S phase, giving two centrosomes (four centrioles total) to form the bipolar spindle.

column1: What is the orientation of the two centrioles within a centrosome?
column4: The two centrioles in a centrosome are arranged at right angles. This geometry is also seen in the basal body of cilia and flagella, as centrioles can nucleate these structures.

column1: Which type of spindle microtubule does NOT attach to chromosomes but instead overlaps with microtubules from the opposite pole?
column4: Polar microtubules extend from each pole past the equator and interact with those from the other pole, pushing the poles apart via motor proteins like kinesin-5 (Eg5).

column1: Do plant cells have centrioles?
