column4: Papain cleaves at the hinge above the disulfide bond, yielding two monovalent Fab fragments and one Fc; pepsin cleaves below the hinge, yielding one F(ab')₂ fragment.

column1: How many antigen-binding sites does an IgG molecule have?
column4: IgG is a monomer with two Fab arms, making it bivalent; IgM is a pentamer with 10 potential binding sites.

column1: What is the role of the hinge region in an antibody?
column3: Provides flexibility between the two Fab arms
column4: The hinge allows the two antigen-binding arms to move independently to engage antigens at varying distances, enhancing binding avidity.

column1: What is the immunological basis of autoimmune disease?
column3: Loss of self-tolerance; immune attack on self-antigens
column4: When central or peripheral tolerance mechanisms fail, self-reactive lymphocytes escape deletion/anergy and attack host tissues.

column1: Name two organ-specific autoimmune diseases.
column4: In type 1 DM, CTLs destroy beta cells; in Hashimoto's, autoantibodies and T cells attack thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin.

column1: Name two systemic (non-organ-specific) autoimmune diseases.
column3: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis
column4: SLE involves anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies forming immune complexes; RA involves anti-citrullinated protein antibodies targeting joint synovium.

column1: What autoantibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
column4: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies are highly specific for SLE and are used diagnostically; anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) are sensitive but not specific.

column1: What mechanism allows the immune system to distinguish self from non-self during central tolerance?
column3: Clonal deletion (apoptosis) of self-reactive lymphocytes in primary lymphoid organs
column4: T cells binding self-antigen too strongly in the thymus and B cells reacting to self in bone marrow are eliminated; surviving cells make up the mature repertoire.

column1: What is the MHC (major histocompatibility complex) and its key function?
column3: A set of cell-surface proteins that present peptide antigens to T cells
column4: MHC molecules display self and foreign peptides so T cells can survey cellular contents and mount appropriate immune responses.

column1: What is the human name for MHC molecules?
column4: HLA-A, -B, -C are class I; HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR are class II; HLA mismatching between donor and recipient drives transplant rejection.

column1: Which cells express MHC class I molecules?
column4: MHC I presents endogenous peptides; every nucleated cell can be surveilled by CD8+ CTLs, allowing detection of intracellular infections or mutations.

column1: Which cells express MHC class II molecules?
column3: Professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells)
column4: MHC II expression is normally restricted to APCs; IFN-γ can induce MHC II on other cell types in inflammatory contexts.

column1: How many polypeptide chains make up MHC class I?
column4: The MHC I alpha chain is encoded within the MHC; β2m is encoded on chromosome 15 (not within MHC) and is required for stable surface expression.

column1: How many polypeptide chains make up MHC class II?
column3: One alpha chain + one beta chain (both encoded in MHC)
column4: MHC II is a non-covalent heterodimer of α and β chains; the peptide-binding groove is formed by contributions from both chains.

column1: What length of peptide is typically presented by MHC class I?
column4: MHC I has a closed peptide-binding groove that accommodates short peptides (8-10 aa); MHC II binds longer peptides (13-25 aa) in an open-ended groove.

column1: What is the first step of mechanical digestion in humans?
column4: Teeth mechanically break food into smaller pieces, increasing surface area for enzymatic digestion. This is the primary function of ingestion at the oral level.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::ingestion MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of digestion begins in the mouth?
column4: Mastication provides mechanical breakdown while salivary amylase initiates chemical (enzymatic) digestion of starch. Both occur simultaneously during ingestion.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::ingestion MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cranial nerves stimulate salivation?
column4: These parasympathetic fibers innervate the salivary glands. Salivary secretion is a reflex response to food in the mouth or even the sight/smell of food.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::ingestion MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What enzyme is present in saliva that begins starch digestion?
column4: Salivary amylase cleaves alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds in starch, producing maltose and dextrins. It is inactivated by the low pH of the stomach.

column1: What glycoprotein in saliva provides lubrication for swallowing?
column4: Mucin is a heavily glycosylated protein that forms mucus, coating food to ease its passage through the esophagus. It also protects oral mucosa.

column1: What is the function of lingual lipase found in saliva?
column3: Initiates fat digestion in the mouth and stomach
column4: Lingual lipase begins hydrolysis of triglycerides; it remains active in the acidic stomach environment, unlike salivary amylase. It is a minor contributor to overall fat digestion.

column1: What is the primary function of the esophagus?
column3: Transport food from pharynx to stomach
column4: The esophagus is a muscular tube that moves a food bolus via peristalsis. It has no significant digestive or absorptive function.

column1: What sphincter prevents reflux of stomach acid into the esophagus?
column4: The lower esophageal sphincter remains tonically closed and relaxes to allow food entry into the stomach. Its dysfunction leads to GERD.

column1: What type of muscle makes up the upper, middle, and lower thirds of the esophagus respectively?
column4: The upper third is skeletal (voluntary), the middle is mixed, and the lower third is smooth (involuntary). This transition is tested in the context of swallowing control.

column1: What is the normal pH range of the stomach?
column4: The highly acidic environment is created by HCl secreted by parietal cells. This pH is essential for pepsin activity and killing ingested microorganisms.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::stomach MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cells of the gastric mucosa secrete HCl?
column4: Parietal cells also secrete intrinsic factor, which is required for vitamin B12 absorption. HCl converts pepsinogen to active pepsin.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::stomach MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cells secrete pepsinogen in the stomach?
column4: Pepsinogen is the inactive zymogen form of pepsin. It is activated by the low pH of gastric juice or by existing pepsin (autocatalytic activation).
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::stomach MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the main role of the stomach in digestion?
column3: Mechanical churning and protein digestion initiation
column4: The stomach's muscular contractions mix food with gastric juice to form chyme, while pepsin begins protein hydrolysis. Limited absorption occurs here (e.g., alcohol, aspirin).

column1: What is the semi-liquid mixture formed in the stomach called?
column4: Chyme is the acidic, partially digested food mass that exits the stomach through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum. Its composition regulates gastric emptying rate.

column1: Which sphincter regulates the passage of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum?
column4: The pyloric sphincter opens to release small amounts of chyme into the duodenum. Fat-rich chyme slows gastric emptying via CCK-mediated feedback.

column1: What protects the stomach lining from self-digestion by pepsin and HCl?
column3: Thick mucus layer secreted by mucous neck cells
column4: The bicarbonate-rich mucus creates a pH gradient at the stomach wall, keeping the epithelium near neutral. Breakdown of this barrier causes peptic ulcers.

column1: Which cells secrete the mucus that protects the stomach from self-digestion?
column3: Mucous neck cells (goblet cells of stomach)
column4: These cells line the gastric pits and secrete alkaline mucus. Prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion, which is why NSAIDs can cause gastric ulcers.

column1: What bacterium is associated with disruption of the gastric mucus barrier and peptic ulcer disease?
column4: H. pylori produces urease, which neutralizes local acid and allows colonization of the mucosa. It damages the protective mucus layer, predisposing to ulcers.

column1: What enzyme produced by the stomach digests proteins?
column4: Pepsin is a protease active at low pH (optimum ~2). It is secreted as the inactive zymogen pepsinogen and cleaves peptide bonds, especially next to aromatic amino acids.

column1: At what pH is pepsin maximally active?
column4: Pepsin is a protease optimally active in the acidic gastric environment. Above pH 5, pepsin is irreversibly denatured, explaining why its activity ceases in the duodenum.

column1: What are the four main regions of the stomach from proximal to distal?
column4: The fundus and body are the main storage regions; the antrum (part of pylorus) is where mixing and grinding occur. The cardia surrounds the gastroesophageal junction.

column1: What are the three layers of smooth muscle in the stomach wall?
column4: The stomach has an extra oblique layer (not found elsewhere in the GI tract) that aids in churning and mixing food into chyme. The small intestine has only two muscle layers.

column1: What is the largest internal organ in the body?
column4: The liver weighs approximately 1.5 kg in adults. It performs over 500 functions including bile production, detoxification, and metabolic regulation.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::liver MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Via which vessel does nutrient-rich blood from the intestines reach the liver?
column4: The portal vein delivers absorbed nutrients directly to the liver for processing before entering systemic circulation. This portal circulation is key to first-pass metabolism.

column1: What vessel carries oxygenated blood to the liver?
column4: The liver has a dual blood supply: the hepatic portal vein (nutrient-rich, deoxygenated) and the hepatic artery (oxygenated). Blood exits via the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.

column1: Where does bile flow after leaving the liver?
column3: Into the common bile duct, then the duodenum (or stored in the gallbladder)
column4: Bile produced in hepatocytes flows through bile canaliculi → bile ducts → common hepatic duct → common bile duct → duodenum (or stored in gallbladder via cystic duct).

column1: What cells of the liver produce bile?
column4: Hepatocytes are the main functional cells of the liver. They synthesize bile salts from cholesterol, package them into bile, and secrete bile into bile canaliculi.

column1: What are the two main organic components of bile?
column4: Bile salts (derived from cholesterol) emulsify fats; bilirubin is a waste product of heme breakdown. Bile also contains cholesterol, phospholipids, and electrolytes.

column1: From what molecule are bile salts synthesized in the liver?
column4: Hepatocytes convert cholesterol to primary bile acids (cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid), which are conjugated with glycine or taurine to form bile salts. This is a major route of cholesterol elimination.

column1: What is the liver's primary role in blood glucose regulation?
column3: Glycogenesis (storing glucose as glycogen) and glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis (releasing glucose)
column4: After a meal the liver stores glucose as glycogen (insulin-driven); during fasting it breaks down glycogen or synthesizes new glucose via gluconeogenesis to maintain blood glucose levels.

column1: What process does the liver use to convert ammonia to a less toxic form?
column4: Hepatocytes run the urea cycle to detoxify ammonia (from amino acid catabolism) into urea, which is excreted by the kidneys. Liver failure causes hyperammonemia and encephalopathy.

column1: What cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver primarily perform?
column3: Oxidative metabolism/detoxification of drugs and xenobiotics
column4: CYP450 enzymes hydroxylate nonpolar compounds to make them more water-soluble for excretion. This is first-pass metabolism; enzyme induction or inhibition alters drug levels.

column1: Where is bile stored between meals?
column4: The gallbladder concentrates and stores bile (up to 5-fold concentration) until a fatty meal triggers CCK release, causing gallbladder contraction and bile release into the duodenum.

column1: Which hormone triggers gallbladder contraction to release bile?
column4: CCK is released by I-cells in the duodenal mucosa in response to fats and proteins. It contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to release bile.

column1: What is the main function of bile in digestion?
column4: Bile salts are amphipathic; they surround fat droplets and break them into smaller micelles, greatly increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase to act on triglycerides.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::function MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is enterohepatic circulation of bile salts?
column3: Reabsorption of bile salts in the ileum and return to the liver via portal blood
column4: About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and recycled to the liver. This efficient recycling conserves bile salts; ileal disease (e.g., Crohn's) disrupts this cycle.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::function MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the exocrine function of the pancreas?
column3: Secretion of digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum
column4: Acinar cells produce digestive enzymes; ductal cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid. Together they form pancreatic juice that neutralizes chyme and digests macronutrients.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::pancreas MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the endocrine function of the pancreas?
column3: Secretion of insulin and glucagon from islets of Langerhans
column4: Beta cells secrete insulin (lowers blood glucose); alpha cells secrete glucagon (raises blood glucose). The endocrine pancreas regulates glucose homeostasis.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::pancreas MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Name four digestive enzymes produced by the pancreas.
column3: Trypsin, chymotrypsin, pancreatic lipase, pancreatic amylase
column4: The pancreas also produces elastase, carboxypeptidases, phospholipase A2, and nucleases. Proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens to prevent autodigestion.

column1: What activates trypsinogen to trypsin in the duodenum?
column3: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) secreted by duodenal brush border cells
column4: Enteropeptidase cleaves the activation peptide from trypsinogen. Active trypsin then autocatalytically activates more trypsinogen and activates other pancreatic zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, etc.).

column1: What prevents premature activation of pancreatic proteases within the pancreas?
column3: Secretion as inactive zymogens and presence of trypsin inhibitor
column4: The pancreas secretes trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, and proelastase (inactive forms). A trypsin inhibitor also provides a safety mechanism; failure of these leads to acute pancreatitis.

column1: Via which duct do pancreatic enzymes reach the duodenum?
column3: Pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung), joining the common bile duct at the ampulla of Vater
column4: Both bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), controlled by the sphincter of Oddi. Blockage at this point affects both secretions.

column1: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?
column4: CCK released from duodenal I-cells (in response to fats and proteins) stimulates pancreatic acinar cells. Secretin stimulates the bicarbonate-rich fluid from ductal cells.

column1: What is the primary site of nutrient absorption in the GI tract?
column4: The small intestine absorbs most carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals. Its enormous surface area (due to villi and microvilli) maximizes absorption efficiency.

column1: What are the three anatomical divisions of the small intestine in order?
column4: The duodenum receives chyme from the stomach and digestive secretions from the liver and pancreas. The jejunum is the primary absorptive region; the ileum absorbs bile salts and vitamin B12.

column1: Which segment of the small intestine specifically absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts?
column4: Vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex is absorbed by specific receptors in the terminal ileum. Bile salts are also reclaimed here for enterohepatic recirculation.

column1: What are microvilli on intestinal epithelial cells collectively called?
column4: Microvilli dramatically increase the apical surface area of enterocytes. Brush border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases) are located here for final digestion steps.

column1: How are fatty acids and monoglycerides absorbed across the intestinal epithelium?
column3: Simple diffusion (as micelles, then reassembled into chylomicrons)
column4: Fat-digestion products form micelles with bile salts, diffuse across the apical membrane, are re-esterified into triglycerides in the ER, packaged into chylomicrons, and enter lacteals (lymphatics).

column1: Via which transport system do chylomicrons leave intestinal cells?
column4: Chylomicrons are too large for blood capillaries; they enter lacteals and travel through the lymphatic system (thoracic duct) before reaching the bloodstream. This bypasses the portal circulation.

column1: What are villi in the small intestine?
column3: Finger-like projections of the mucosa that increase absorptive surface area
column4: Each villus contains a central lacteal and a capillary network. Nutrients absorbed by enterocytes enter either the blood capillaries or the lacteal depending on their size and solubility.

column1: What is the purpose of the lacteal within a villus?
column3: Absorb dietary fats (as chylomicrons) into the lymphatic system
column4: The lacteal is a blind-ended lymphatic capillary in the core of each villus. Chylomicrons packaged in enterocytes are secreted by exocytosis into the lacteal.

column1: What are the circular folds (plicae circulares) in the small intestine?
column3: Permanent mucosal and submucosal folds that increase surface area ~3-fold
column4: Unlike rugae (stomach folds), plicae circulares are permanent and do not flatten with distension. They slow chyme passage, aiding absorption. Villi and microvilli provide additional amplification.

column1: Which enzyme on the brush border digests lactose?
column4: Lactase cleaves lactose into glucose and galactose. Lactase deficiency (common in adults worldwide) leads to lactose intolerance: bloating, diarrhea, and gas due to bacterial fermentation.

column1: Where does the final digestion of disaccharides and dipeptides occur?
column3: Brush border of the small intestine
column4: Brush border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase, aminopeptidases, dipeptidases) complete hydrolysis at the surface of enterocytes immediately before absorption.

column1: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion to neutralize stomach acid in the duodenum?
column4: Secretin is released by S-cells in the duodenal mucosa in response to acid (low pH chyme). It acts on pancreatic ductal cells to increase bicarbonate secretion, raising duodenal pH.

column1: What is the approximate pH of pancreatic juice?
column4: Pancreatic juice contains a high concentration of bicarbonate (HCO3-), making it strongly alkaline. This neutralizes acidic chyme and creates the optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity (~7-8).

column1: Which duodenal cells release secretin?
column3: S-cells (in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa)
column4: S-cells sense low pH in the duodenum and release secretin into the bloodstream. Secretin classically inhibits gastric acid secretion as well as stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate release.

column1: What is the primary function of the large intestine?
column3: Absorption of water and electrolytes; formation and storage of feces
column4: The large intestine absorbs most remaining water from indigestible material, concentrating it into feces. It has no significant digestive enzyme secretion.

column1: What are the four main regions of the large intestine?
column4: The colon is further divided into ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid segments. The cecum connects to the ileum at the ileocecal valve and contains the appendix.

column1: How much water does the large intestine absorb per day?
column4: About 1.5 L of the ~2 L of fluid entering the large intestine daily is reabsorbed. Failure of this absorption (e.g., in diarrhea) leads to significant fluid loss.

column1: What is the mechanism of water absorption in the large intestine?
column4: Na+ is actively transported out of the lumen; water follows osmotically through aquaporins. Aldosterone increases Na+ absorption in the colon, thereby increasing water reabsorption.

column1: What vitamins do colonic bacteria produce that are absorbed by the host?
column3: Vitamin K and some B vitamins (biotin, B12)
column4: Gut microbiota synthesize vitamin K2 (menaquinone), which is important for blood clotting and bone metabolism. Antibiotic use can deplete these bacteria and reduce vitamin K availability.

column1: What is the approximate number of bacteria in the human colon?
column3: ~10^11 bacteria per mL of colon contents (trillions total)
column4: The gut microbiome contains more cells than human body cells. These bacteria ferment undigested carbohydrates, produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and support immune function.

column1: What are short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced by colonic bacteria?
column4: SCFAs are produced by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber. Butyrate is the primary energy source for colonocytes. SCFAs also regulate gene expression and immune responses.

column1: What is the function of the rectum?
column3: Temporary storage of feces prior to defecation
column4: Feces accumulate in the rectum; distension triggers the defecation reflex. The internal anal sphincter (smooth, involuntary) and external anal sphincter (skeletal, voluntary) control defecation.

column1: Which sphincter of the anus is under voluntary control?
column4: The external anal sphincter is composed of skeletal muscle and is under somatic (voluntary) control via the pudendal nerve. The internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle) is involuntary.

column1: What is peristalsis?
column3: Wave-like smooth muscle contractions that propel food through the GI tract
column4: Peristalsis involves circular muscle contraction behind the bolus (pushing) and relaxation ahead (receiving). It is coordinated by the enteric nervous system and occurs throughout the GI tract.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::peristalsis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of GI motility mixes chyme with digestive juices without propelling it forward?
column4: Segmentation involves rhythmic contractions of circular smooth muscle that divide and remix chyme in the same region, maximizing contact with the mucosa for absorption. It is distinct from peristalsis.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::peristalsis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is mass peristalsis in the large intestine?
column3: Strong propulsive contractions that move contents from the colon to the rectum
column4: Mass peristalsis occurs 1-3 times daily, often triggered by the gastrocolic reflex after eating. It moves large amounts of fecal material toward the rectum.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::peristalsis MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which hormone stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastric motility?
column4: Gastrin is released by G-cells in the gastric antrum in response to protein, stomach distension, and vagal stimulation. It acts on parietal cells to stimulate HCl secretion.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::hormones MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which hormone inhibits gastric emptying and stimulates bile and pancreatic enzyme release?
column4: CCK is released by duodenal I-cells when fat and protein enter the duodenum. It delays gastric emptying, contracts the gallbladder, and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::hormones MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which hormone is released in response to acid in the duodenum and inhibits gastric acid secretion?
column4: Secretin released by S-cells counteracts excess acid: it inhibits gastrin and gastric acid secretion while stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate. It is the first hormone ever discovered (Bayliss & Starling, 1902).
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::hormones MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What GI hormone is released after eating and promotes satiety by acting on the hypothalamus?
column4: CCK acts on the hypothalamus to signal satiety and reduce food intake. Leptin and GLP-1 also contribute to satiety, but CCK is the classic MCAT-tested hormone from the gut.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::hormones MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which GI hormone, produced by the stomach, stimulates appetite?
column4: Ghrelin ('hunger hormone') rises before meals and falls after eating. It acts on the hypothalamus to increase appetite. It is the only known orexigenic gut hormone.
column8: concept::BB::3B::digestive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::digestive-system::hormones MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the target cells of gastrin?
column3: Parietal cells of the stomach (stimulates HCl) and chief cells (stimulates pepsinogen)
column4: Gastrin binds CCK-B receptors on parietal cells to stimulate HCl secretion and on chief cells to stimulate pepsinogen release, synergizing with acetylcholine and histamine.

column1: On which cells does secretin act to produce its major GI effects?
column3: Pancreatic ductal cells (bicarbonate secretion) and stomach parietal cells (inhibition)
column4: Secretin stimulates pancreatic ductal cells to secrete HCO3- and inhibits parietal cells to reduce HCl. It thus protects the duodenum from excess acid.

column1: What cells are the primary target of CCK for enzyme secretion?
column4: CCK binds CCK-A receptors on acinar cells, triggering release of digestive enzyme-rich pancreatic juice. CCK also acts on the gallbladder smooth muscle and the sphincter of Oddi.

column1: What is the enteric nervous system (ENS)?
column3: The intrinsic nervous system of the GI tract ('gut brain'), consisting of myenteric and submucosal plexuses
column4: The ENS can function autonomously from the CNS. It contains over 100 million neurons and controls GI motility, secretion, and blood flow.

column1: What are the two main plexuses of the enteric nervous system?
column4: The myenteric plexus lies between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers and controls GI motility. The submucosal plexus regulates secretion and local blood flow.

column1: What is the function of the myenteric plexus?
column4: The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus coordinates contraction and relaxation of longitudinal and circular smooth muscle layers to drive peristalsis and segmentation throughout the gut.

column1: What neurotransmitter in the ENS stimulates smooth muscle contraction on the oral side of a bolus during peristalsis?
column4: The law of intestine (peristaltic reflex): ACh and substance P are released on the oral (ascending) side to contract muscle; VIP and NO are released on the anal side to relax muscle (receptive relaxation).

column1: What effect does parasympathetic stimulation (vagus nerve) have on GI motility and secretion?
column3: Increases motility and secretion ('rest and digest')
column4: Parasympathetic input via the vagus nerve (CN X) enhances GI activity. Sympathetic stimulation inhibits GI activity. The ENS mediates local reflexes even without CNS input.

column1: What is the gastrocolic reflex?
column3: Distension of the stomach triggers increased colonic motility
column4: The gastrocolic reflex is mediated by the ENS and hormones (especially gastrin and CCK). It explains the urge to defecate after eating and is a classic example of ENS-coordinated gut reflexes.

column1: What is the endocrine control mechanism by which a fatty meal inhibits further gastric emptying?
column3: Release of CCK from duodenal I-cells inhibits gastric motility (enterogastric reflex)
column4: Fat in the duodenum triggers CCK release and neural signals (enterogastric reflex) that slow gastric emptying, allowing the duodenum time to digest and absorb fat before receiving more chyme.

column1: Which hormonal axis regulates the migrating motor complex (MMC) between meals?
column4: Motilin is secreted by Mo-cells in the small intestine during fasting and initiates the MMC (housekeeping waves) that sweep residual contents toward the colon. It is suppressed after eating.

column1: What is the role of glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) in GI endocrine control?
column3: Stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells in response to glucose and fat
column4: GIP (formerly 'gastric inhibitory peptide') is an incretin hormone released by K-cells in the duodenum/jejunum. It potentiates insulin release; it is a target of GLP-1 receptor agonist drug class mechanisms.

column1: What is the primary organ of the excretory system responsible for filtering blood?
column4: The kidneys filter approximately 180 L of blood plasma per day, producing about 1.5 L of urine. They are the central organs of the excretory system.

column1: Which organ produces erythropoietin (EPO) to stimulate red blood cell production?
column4: The kidneys sense low oxygen levels and secrete EPO, which acts on bone marrow to increase RBC production, linking excretory and hematopoietic systems.

column1: Which hormone, activated by the kidneys, is the final active form of vitamin D?
column4: The kidneys convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol via 1-alpha-hydroxylase, regulating calcium and phosphate homeostasis.

column1: What enzyme do the kidneys secrete to initiate the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system?
column4: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, ultimately leading to aldosterone release and increased sodium/water retention, raising blood pressure.

column1: Name two non-nitrogenous waste products the kidneys excrete to maintain homeostasis.
column3: Excess water and excess ions (e.g., Na+, K+, H+)
column4: The kidneys regulate water balance, electrolyte concentrations, and pH by selectively excreting or retaining water and ions.

column1: What is the term for the pressure that drives fluid out of the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's space?
column4: This pressure (~55 mmHg) is the main force favoring filtration; it is opposed by capsular hydrostatic pressure (~15 mmHg) and oncotic pressure (~30 mmHg).

column1: Which RAAS hormone directly causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release?
column4: Angiotensin II is the primary effector of the RAAS, raising systemic vascular resistance and promoting Na+/water retention to increase blood pressure.

column1: What is the net filtration pressure (NFP) formula at the glomerulus?
column3: NFP = glomerular hydrostatic pressure - (capsular pressure + oncotic pressure)
column4: Normal values: 55 - (15 + 30) = 10 mmHg net filtration pressure driving ultrafiltrate into Bowman's capsule.

column1: Which arteriole constriction raises glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by increasing glomerular pressure?
column4: Constricting the efferent arteriole traps blood in the glomerulus, raising hydrostatic pressure and GFR. Afferent constriction does the opposite.

column1: What baroreceptor-independent mechanism do the kidneys use to autoregulate GFR when blood pressure rises?
column4: The macula densa detects increased NaCl delivery and signals afferent arteriole constriction; the myogenic reflex also directly constricts afferent arterioles in response to stretch.

column1: What term describes regulation of body fluid osmolarity and volume by the kidneys?
column4: Osmoregulation involves balancing water intake/loss and solute concentrations to maintain a stable internal environment.

column1: Which hormone increases water permeability of the collecting duct?
column4: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels into collecting duct cells, allowing water reabsorption and producing concentrated urine.

column1: Where is ADH synthesized and where is it released?
column3: Synthesized in hypothalamus; released from posterior pituitary
column4: ADH is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and stored/released from the posterior pituitary.

column1: Which hormone promotes Na+ reabsorption in the distal tubule and collecting duct to increase blood volume?
column4: Aldosterone (a mineralocorticoid from the adrenal cortex) upregulates Na+/K+-ATPase and ENaC channels, retaining Na+ and water while excreting K+.

column1: What is the osmolarity of normal human blood plasma?
column4: The kidneys defend this narrow range; significant deviations trigger ADH release, thirst, or aldosterone secretion.

column1: What is the main buffer system used by the kidneys to regulate blood pH?
column4: The kidneys reabsorb or excrete HCO3- and secrete H+ to adjust pH; slow but powerful compared to respiratory buffering.

column1: In metabolic acidosis, what compensatory action do the kidneys take?
column3: Increase H+ secretion and increase HCO3- reabsorption
column4: The kidneys generate new bicarbonate and excrete excess acid (as NH4+ or titratable acid), slowly correcting metabolic acidosis over hours to days.

column1: Where in the nephron is most bicarbonate reabsorbed?
column4: The proximal tubule reabsorbs the majority of filtered HCO3- via carbonic anhydrase-mediated H+ secretion.

column1: What form do the kidneys use to excrete excess acid in the urine?
column4: Glutamine is metabolized in tubular cells to form NH4+; phosphate buffers also accept secreted H+ to form H2PO4-, both allowing acid excretion without lowering urine pH to dangerous levels.

column1: A patient with chronic kidney disease has high blood pH and low HCO3-. What is the primary acid-base disorder?
column4: Wait — low HCO3- with high pH is contradictory. Normal metabolic alkalosis has HIGH HCO3-. CKD more typically causes metabolic acidosis (low pH, low HCO3-) due to impaired H+ excretion.

column1: What enzyme in renal tubular cells catalyzes CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3?
column4: Carbonic anhydrase is critical for acid secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption in both the proximal tubule and intercalated cells of the collecting duct.

column1: What is the primary nitrogenous waste excreted in human urine?
column4: Urea is produced in the liver via the urea cycle from ammonia (derived from amino acid catabolism) and is highly soluble, making it safe to excrete in urine.

column1: What nitrogenous waste is produced from purine catabolism and excreted in human urine?
column4: Purines (adenine, guanine) are degraded to uric acid in humans. Accumulation causes gout; uric acid is less soluble than urea.

column1: In which organ is urea synthesized from ammonia?
column4: The urea cycle occurs in hepatocytes; urea is then transported in the blood to the kidneys for filtration and excretion.

column1: What nitrogenous compound is the primary waste in aquatic fish (teleosts)?
column4: Fish excrete ammonia directly across gills because water dilutes it rapidly. Humans convert ammonia to less toxic urea for excretion.

column1: What nitrogenous waste is most characteristic of birds and reptiles, excreted as a paste?
column4: Uric acid's low water solubility allows excretion with minimal water loss — an adaptation to arid environments and shelled eggs.

column1: What are the two main regions of the kidney?
column4: The cortex contains glomeruli and convoluted tubules; the medulla contains loops of Henle and collecting ducts arranged in renal pyramids.

column1: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
column4: Each human kidney contains ~1 million nephrons; each nephron filters blood and processes filtrate to produce urine.

column1: What structure connects the renal pelvis to the bladder?
column4: Two ureters, one per kidney, transport urine via peristalsis to the urinary bladder for storage.

column1: What is the renal hilum?
column3: The medial indentation where the renal artery, vein, nerves, and ureter enter/exit the kidney
column4: The hilum is the gateway for all vascular and urine-conducting structures of the kidney.

column1: What percentage of cardiac output do the kidneys receive at rest?
column4: Despite being <1% of body weight, the kidneys receive a disproportionately large blood supply to enable continuous filtration of plasma.

column1: Which kidney structures are located exclusively in the cortex?
column3: Glomeruli and Bowman's capsules (renal corpuscles); proximal and distal convoluted tubules
column4: The renal cortex is the filtering zone; all renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules reside here, while the medulla contains loops and collecting ducts.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::cortex MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What specialized cells in the cortex form the macula densa?
column3: Specialized cells of the distal tubule (thick ascending limb)
column4: The macula densa monitors NaCl concentration in tubular fluid and signals the juxtaglomerular apparatus to regulate renin release and GFR.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::cortex MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)?
column3: The junction of the afferent arteriole and distal tubule containing JG cells (renin-secreting) and macula densa
column4: The JGA is the regulatory hub for GFR and blood pressure; JG cells are granular cells that store and release renin in response to low blood pressure or low NaCl.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::cortex MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which layer of the kidney contains the renal pyramids?
column4: Renal pyramids are cone-shaped structures whose apices (renal papillae) drain into minor calyces; they contain loops of Henle and collecting ducts.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::medulla MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the osmolarity gradient maintained within the renal medulla (cortex to papilla)?
column4: This gradient, established by the countercurrent multiplier, allows concentrated urine formation; the deep medulla is hypertonic due to NaCl and urea accumulation.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::medulla MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which two solutes primarily establish the hypertonic medullary interstitium?
column3: NaCl (from thick ascending limb) and urea (from collecting duct)
column4: Active NaCl transport in the thick ascending limb and urea recycling from the collecting duct create and maintain the medullary osmotic gradient.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::medulla MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Name the five main segments of the nephron in order.
column3: Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct
column4: Blood is filtered at the glomerulus/Bowman's capsule; filtrate is processed sequentially through each segment before entering the collecting duct.

column1: What are the two types of nephrons based on loop of Henle length?
column4: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops that penetrate deep into the medulla and are responsible for producing concentrated urine.

column1: What is the vasa recta?
column3: The capillary network surrounding juxtamedullary nephron loops of Henle
column4: The vasa recta run parallel to the loop of Henle and serve as a countercurrent exchanger, preserving the medullary osmotic gradient while removing reabsorbed water and solutes.

column1: What type of epithelium lines the proximal tubule?
column3: Simple cuboidal epithelium with brush border (microvilli)
column4: The microvilli greatly increase surface area, facilitating the massive reabsorption (about 67% of filtered load) that occurs in the proximal tubule.

column1: What is the difference between cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons regarding location of glomeruli?
column3: Cortical: glomeruli in outer cortex; juxtamedullary: glomeruli near cortex-medulla junction
column4: Juxtamedullary nephrons have longer loops critical for urine concentration; their glomeruli sit close to the medulla.

column1: What two cell layers make up the filtration barrier of the glomerulus?
column3: Fenestrated endothelium of capillaries and podocytes (with filtration slits), separated by a basement membrane
column4: All three layers act as size and charge filters. The basement membrane (negatively charged) repels negatively charged proteins like albumin.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::glomerulus MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the normal GFR in a healthy adult?
column4: GFR is the volume of plasma filtered per minute; it is estimated clinically by creatinine clearance or the CKD-EPI equation.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::glomerulus MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the normal molecular weight cutoff for glomerular filtration?
column4: Molecules smaller than ~70 kDa freely filter; albumin (~69 kDa) is mostly excluded by charge repulsion and size, keeping proteins in the blood.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::glomerulus MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What specialized glomerular cells form foot processes (pedicels) around capillaries?
column4: Podocytes are visceral epithelial cells; their interdigitating foot processes create filtration slits covered by nephrin-containing slit diaphragms that prevent protein loss.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::glomerulus MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the contractile cells within the glomerulus that regulate capillary surface area?
column4: Mesangial cells provide structural support, phagocytose debris, and can contract to reduce filtration surface area in response to angiotensin II.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::glomerulus MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the space between the glomerular capillaries and Bowman's capsule called?
column4: Filtrate from the glomerulus enters Bowman's space and then flows into the proximal tubule.

column1: What are the two layers of Bowman's capsule?
column3: Parietal (outer) layer and visceral (inner, podocyte) layer
column4: The parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium; the visceral layer is the podocytes that wrap glomerular capillaries.

column1: What is the combined structure of the glomerulus + Bowman's capsule called?
column4: The renal corpuscle is the filtration unit; it is found only in the cortex.

column1: What percentage of filtered water is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
column4: The proximal tubule reabsorbs the bulk of filtered water, sodium, glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate by isosmotic reabsorption.

column1: By what transport mechanism is glucose reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
column4: SGLT2 (apical) cotransports glucose with Na+ down Na+'s electrochemical gradient; GLUT2 (basolateral) moves glucose into the interstitium by facilitated diffusion.

column1: What is the renal threshold for glucose (plasma glucose level at which glucose appears in urine)?
column4: Above this concentration, SGLT2 transporters become saturated (transport maximum reached) and glucose spills into urine — glucosuria, as seen in uncontrolled diabetes.

column1: What is the primary driving force for reabsorption in the proximal tubule?
column4: The basolateral pump maintains a low intracellular Na+ concentration, creating the gradient that drives Na+-coupled cotransport of glucose, amino acids, and other solutes across the apical membrane.

column1: Which secretion pathway in the proximal tubule handles most organic anions and cations (drugs, toxins)?
column3: Organic anion transporter (OAT) and organic cation transporter (OCT) systems
column4: These transporters actively secrete compounds like penicillin, creatinine (partly), and uric acid into the tubular lumen, important for drug pharmacokinetics.

column1: Name the two limbs of the loop of Henle.
column4: The descending limb is permeable to water but not salt; the ascending limb actively transports NaCl but is impermeable to water — this asymmetry drives urine concentration.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::loop-of-henle MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which limb of the loop of Henle actively transports NaCl into the medullary interstitium?
column4: The NKCC2 cotransporter in the thick ascending limb moves Na+, K+, and 2Cl- into cells, with Na+/K+-ATPase pumping Na+ into the interstitium — the key step of countercurrent multiplication.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::loop-of-henle MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the permeability profile of the descending limb of the loop of Henle?
column3: Permeable to water; impermeable to solutes (NaCl)
column4: As filtrate descends into the hypertonic medulla, water leaves by osmosis, concentrating the tubular fluid.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::loop-of-henle MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What diuretic class blocks the NKCC2 transporter in the thick ascending limb?
column4: By blocking NKCC2, loop diuretics prevent NaCl reabsorption in the ascending limb, abolishing the medullary gradient and producing profuse dilute urine.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::loop-of-henle MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the osmolarity of filtrate at the bottom of the loop of Henle (hairpin turn) in a maximally concentrating kidney?
column4: This matches the deepest medullary interstitium; the countercurrent multiplier has concentrated the tubular fluid by progressive water loss and NaCl accumulation.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::loop-of-henle MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the primary function of the distal tubule?
column3: Fine-tuning of Na+, K+, Ca2+, and H+ reabsorption/secretion under hormonal control
column4: The distal tubule responds to aldosterone (Na+/K+ exchange) and PTH (Ca2+ reabsorption), performing regulated adjustments to ion balance.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::distal-tubule MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which diuretic class blocks the NCC (Na+-Cl-) cotransporter in the distal tubule?
column4: Thiazides (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) inhibit NCC, reducing Na+ reabsorption in the distal tubule; they also increase Ca2+ reabsorption as a side effect.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::distal-tubule MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What ion does PTH cause the distal tubule to reabsorb?
column4: PTH activates apical TRPV5 channels and basolateral NCX/PMCA pumps in the distal tubule to increase Ca2+ reabsorption, raising plasma Ca2+.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::distal-tubule MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What happens to K+ secretion in the distal tubule when aldosterone is elevated?
column3: K+ secretion increases (more K+ lost in urine)
column4: Aldosterone upregulates ROMK channels and Na+/K+-ATPase, increasing K+ secretion as Na+ is reabsorbed — explaining why hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemia.
column8: concept::BB::3B::excretory_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::excretory-system::distal-tubule MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two main cell types in the collecting duct?
column4: Principal cells respond to ADH and aldosterone; intercalated cells (alpha and beta subtypes) regulate acid-base by secreting H+ or HCO3-.

column1: What aquaporin channels does ADH insert into the collecting duct apical membrane?
column4: ADH binds V2 receptors on principal cells, triggering cAMP-mediated insertion of AQP2 vesicles into the apical membrane, increasing water permeability.

column1: Which segment of the nephron is the final site of urine concentration?
column4: As concentrated collecting duct fluid passes through the hypertonic medullary interstitium in the presence of ADH, water is osmotically reabsorbed, concentrating the urine.

column1: What is the role of urea recycling in the collecting duct?
column3: Urea exits the inner medullary collecting duct to contribute to medullary hypertonicity
column4: The inner medullary collecting duct is permeable to urea (via UT-A1/3 channels, upregulated by ADH); urea recycling contributes ~50% of the deep medullary osmotic gradient.

column1: What is the term for the process by which blood is filtered at the glomerulus?
column4: Glomerular filtration is a passive process driven by hydrostatic pressure; it produces ~180 L/day of protein-free ultrafiltrate.

column1: What substance is used clinically to measure GFR because it is freely filtered and neither secreted nor reabsorbed?
column3: Inulin (clinical gold standard); creatinine is used clinically as an approximation
column4: Inulin clearance equals GFR exactly; creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR because creatinine is also secreted by the proximal tubule.

column1: What is the filtration fraction (FF)?
column3: FF = GFR / renal plasma flow (RPF); normally ~20%
column4: FF = 125 mL/min GFR / 625 mL/min RPF ≈ 0.20; about 20% of plasma entering the kidney is filtered at the glomerulus.

column1: What is the formula for renal clearance?
column4: C = clearance (mL/min), U = urine concentration, V = urine flow rate (mL/min), P = plasma concentration. If C > GFR, the substance is secreted; if C < GFR, it is reabsorbed.

column1: Which substance has a clearance equal to zero under normal conditions because it is completely reabsorbed?
column4: Under normal plasma glucose levels, glucose is 100% reabsorbed by SGLT transporters; clearance is 0 because none appears in urine.

column1: Where is approximately 67% of filtered sodium reabsorbed?
column4: The proximal tubule performs bulk reabsorption of Na+, Cl-, water, glucose, amino acids, and HCO3- isosmotically.

column1: Which solutes are completely reabsorbed under normal physiological conditions?
column4: All filtered glucose and amino acids are reclaimed in the proximal tubule; their appearance in urine (glucosuria, aminoaciduria) signals disease or tubular overload.

column1: What is meant by tubular secretion in the nephron?
column3: Active transport of substances from peritubular capillaries into the tubular lumen
column4: Secretion allows the kidney to excrete substances that may be protein-bound (not filtered) or present in excess, such as H+, K+, and drugs like penicillin.

column1: Where is PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) used as a marker for and why?
column3: Renal plasma flow (RPF); it is nearly 100% secreted in one pass
column4: PAH is both filtered and completely secreted by the proximal tubule; its clearance approximates effective RPF, which when divided by FF gives GFR.

column1: In the thick ascending limb, which cotransporter reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl- simultaneously?
column4: NKCC2 is the target of loop diuretics; it drives NaCl reabsorption without water, creating the dilute tubular fluid that exits the ascending limb.

column1: What is the maximum urine osmolarity achievable by the human kidney?
column4: This maximum concentration depends on the depth of the medullary gradient established by the countercurrent multiplier and urea recycling.

column1: What is the minimum urine osmolarity the human kidney can produce?
column4: In the absence of ADH (e.g., diabetes insipidus), the collecting duct is water-impermeable; dilute tubular fluid from the ascending limb is excreted unchanged.

column1: What hormone must be present for the kidney to produce maximally concentrated urine?
column4: ADH increases collecting duct water permeability via AQP2; without ADH, water cannot be reabsorbed in the collecting duct regardless of the medullary gradient.

column1: What condition results from ADH deficiency and causes the production of large volumes of dilute urine?
column4: Central DI: ADH not produced/released; nephrogenic DI: collecting duct insensitive to ADH. Both produce polyuria with dilute urine and polydipsia.

column1: What is the role of urea in concentrating urine?
column3: Urea accumulates in the inner medullary interstitium, raising osmolarity to pull water from the collecting duct
column4: High-protein diets enhance the medullary urea gradient; urea recycling from the collecting duct is essential for maximal urine concentration.

column1: What is the countercurrent multiplier?
column3: The mechanism by which the loop of Henle establishes a hyperosmotic medullary gradient
column4: The descending limb loses water; the ascending limb pumps NaCl without losing water — this multiplies osmolarity progressively from cortex to papilla.

column1: What is the countercurrent exchanger and where is it found?
column3: The vasa recta; capillaries that run parallel to the loop of Henle
column4: The vasa recta remove reabsorbed water and solutes from the medulla without dissipating the gradient, because blood flows in opposite directions in descending and ascending vessels.

column1: Why is the ascending limb of the loop of Henle impermeable to water?
column3: Lack of aquaporin channels in the ascending limb membrane
column4: This impermeability is essential for the countercurrent mechanism: NaCl is pumped out without water following, creating a hyperosmotic interstitium and a dilute tubular fluid.

column1: What is the osmolarity of fluid leaving the ascending limb of the loop of Henle (entering the distal tubule)?
column4: Active NaCl removal without water reabsorption dilutes the tubular fluid as it ascends, earning the ascending limb the name 'diluting segment.'

column1: How does a longer loop of Henle affect urine concentration ability?
column3: Longer loops create a deeper and steeper medullary gradient, enabling more concentrated urine
column4: Juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops penetrate deeper into the hypertonic medulla, amplifying the countercurrent effect and allowing greater water reabsorption.

column1: What is the order of structures through which urine travels from kidney to outside the body?
column3: Collecting duct → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra
column4: This pathway is the lower urinary tract; each structure has a distinct role in transporting or storing urine.

column1: What type of muscle makes up the walls of the ureter?
column4: Ureteral peristalsis propels urine from the kidney to the bladder; smooth muscle contraction occurs in waves every 10-15 seconds.

column1: What type of epithelium lines the ureter and bladder?
column4: Transitional epithelium can stretch without tearing — ideal for organs that fill and empty; it is also relatively impermeable to urine solutes.

column1: What smooth muscle layer surrounds the bladder?
column4: The detrusor is composed of three layers of smooth muscle that contract during micturition under parasympathetic (pelvic nerve) control.

column1: What is the normal bladder capacity and at what volume does the urge to void typically begin?
column3: Capacity ~400-600 mL; urge begins at ~150-300 mL
column4: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall initiate the micturition reflex when the bladder reaches ~150-300 mL; the reflex can be voluntarily suppressed up to full capacity.

column1: Which segment of the nephron reabsorbs amino acids from the filtrate?
column4: All essential amino acids are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule via Na+-coupled cotransporters; aminoaciduria occurs in Fanconi syndrome or other proximal tubule defects.

column1: What drives water reabsorption from the peritubular capillaries after proximal tubule reabsorption?
column3: High oncotic pressure and low hydrostatic pressure of peritubular capillaries
column4: After filtration at the glomerulus, peritubular capillary protein concentration rises (high oncotic pressure), drawing reabsorbed water from the interstitium into the capillaries.

column1: Which ion's reabsorption in the proximal tubule drives the isosmotic reabsorption of water?
column4: Active Na+ reabsorption creates an osmotic gradient that drives water reabsorption paracellularly and transcellularly, maintaining isosmolarity of the proximal tubule reabsorbate.

column1: Which ion is secreted (not reabsorbed) in the proximal tubule to buffer secreted H+?
column3: HPO4^2- (dibasic phosphate) accepts H+ to become H2PO4- (titratable acid)
column4: Phosphate buffering in the tubular lumen allows excretion of H+ as titratable acid without further lowering tubular pH, aiding acid excretion.

column1: What is the internal urethral sphincter composed of and what controls it?
column3: Smooth muscle; controlled involuntarily by the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic)
column4: The internal sphincter is kept closed by sympathetic tone (alpha-1 receptors) during bladder filling; it relaxes during micturition under parasympathetic activation.

column1: What is the external urethral sphincter composed of and what controls it?
column3: Skeletal muscle; controlled voluntarily by the somatic nervous system (pudendal nerve)
column4: The external sphincter provides voluntary control of urination; it is under conscious control from the cortex via the pudendal nerve.

column1: What occurs to the detrusor muscle and internal urethral sphincter during the micturition reflex?
column3: Detrusor contracts; internal urethral sphincter relaxes
column4: Parasympathetic (pelvic nerve) stimulation causes detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation simultaneously, allowing urine to flow into the urethra.

column1: Which nervous system division maintains the internal urethral sphincter closed during urine storage?
column3: Sympathetic nervous system (hypogastric nerve, alpha-1 adrenergic)
column4: During bladder filling, sympathetic activity contracts the internal sphincter and relaxes the detrusor (beta-3 receptors), allowing storage without leakage.

column1: What type of spinal cord injury can result in loss of voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter?
column3: Upper motor neuron lesion above the sacral micturition center (S2-S4)
column4: Lesions above S2-S4 disrupt voluntary inhibition from the cortex, causing spastic bladder with loss of voluntary sphincter control; lower motor neuron lesions at S2-S4 cause flaccid bladder.

column1: What is the primary function of the seminal vesicles?
column4: Seminal vesicles contribute ~60% of semen volume; fructose serves as the primary energy source for sperm motility.

column1: What structure connects the testes to the urethra and stores mature sperm?
column4: Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis; the vas deferens transports them to the urethra during ejaculation.

column1: What is the function of the fallopian tubes in females?
column3: Transport oocyte from ovary to uterus; site of fertilization
column4: Fertilization typically occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube; cilia and peristalsis move the egg/zygote toward the uterus.

column1: What gland secretes a slightly alkaline fluid that neutralizes urethral acidity and lubricates the urethra prior to ejaculation?
column4: The alkaline secretion protects sperm from the acidic environment of the urethra; these glands are analogous to Bartholin's glands in females.

column1: What is the function of the prostate gland?
column3: Secretes slightly alkaline fluid to activate and nourish sperm
column4: Prostatic fluid contains zinc, citrate, and enzymes; it constitutes ~30% of semen volume and helps liquefy the coagulated semen after ejaculation.

column1: Which layer of the uterus is shed during menstruation?
column4: The stratum functionalis of the endometrium proliferates and is shed each cycle; the stratum basalis remains and regenerates the functional layer.

column1: What type of cells in the testes produce testosterone?
column4: Leydig cells are located in the interstitium between seminiferous tubules and are the primary source of androgens in males.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::gonads MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What cells in the testes support spermatogenesis and secrete inhibin?
column4: Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier, nourish developing sperm, and secrete inhibin, which negatively feeds back on FSH release.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::gonads MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the primary steroid hormone produced by the ovarian follicle before ovulation?
column4: Granulosa cells of the growing follicle produce estradiol; rising estradiol triggers the LH surge that causes ovulation.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::gonads MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What ovarian cell type produces progesterone after ovulation?
column4: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrium for potential implantation.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::gonads MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cells in the ovary produce androgens that are converted to estrogen by granulosa cells?
column4: The two-cell, two-gonadotropin model: LH stimulates theca cells to make androgens; FSH stimulates granulosa cells to aromatize them into estrogens.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::gonads MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What happens to the corpus luteum if fertilization does not occur?
column4: Without hCG from an embryo to maintain it, the corpus luteum regresses after ~14 days, progesterone falls, and menstruation begins.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::gonads MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the male external genitalia?
column4: The scrotum houses the testes at a temperature ~2-3°C below core body temperature, which is required for normal spermatogenesis.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::genitalia MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the role of the scrotum in male fertility?
column3: Maintains testes at temperature below core body (~34°C)
column4: Spermatogenesis requires a cooler environment; the cremaster muscle and pampiniform plexus regulate testicular temperature.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::genitalia MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structure in the female is the anatomical homologue of the glans penis?
column4: Both structures develop from the same embryonic genital tubercle; the clitoris is richly innervated and serves a sensory role in sexual response.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::genitalia MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two pairs of skin folds that constitute the female external genitalia?
column4: The labia majora are homologous to the scrotum; the labia minora are inner folds surrounding the vestibule containing the urethral and vaginal openings.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::genitalia MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which glands in females are homologous to the male bulbourethral glands and provide lubrication during arousal?
column4: Located on either side of the vaginal opening, Bartholin's glands secrete mucus to lubricate the vestibule; they are analogous to Cowper's glands in males.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::genitalia MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the gubernaculum and what role does it play in males?
column3: Ligament that guides testicular descent into scrotum
column4: During fetal development, androgens cause shortening of the gubernaculum, pulling the testes from the abdomen into the scrotum; failure results in cryptorchidism.
column8: concept::BB::3B::reproductive_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::reproductive-system::genitalia MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What embryonic structure gives rise to the male internal genitalia (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles)?
column4: Testosterone from fetal Leydig cells stabilizes the Wolffian ducts; without testosterone, they regress (as in females).

column1: What embryonic structure gives rise to the female internal genitalia (fallopian tubes, uterus, upper vagina)?
column4: In males, anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) from Sertoli cells causes regression of the Mullerian ducts; in females (no AMH), they develop into female structures.

column1: Which hormone secreted by fetal Sertoli cells causes regression of the Mullerian ducts in males?
column4: AMH (also called Mullerian-inhibiting substance, MIS) is secreted early in male fetal development, ensuring Mullerian structures do not persist.

column1: What chromosomal gene triggers differentiation of the indifferent gonad into a testis?
column4: SRY (sex-determining region Y) encodes the testis-determining factor; its presence drives Sertoli cell differentiation and subsequent male development.

column1: In the absence of testosterone and AMH, what default sex does the embryo develop into?
column4: Female development is the default; ovaries and Mullerian structures develop passively without the hormonal signals required for male differentiation.

column1: What enzyme converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in target tissues?
column4: DHT is required for differentiation of external male genitalia (penis, scrotum, prostate); deficiency of 5-alpha reductase causes 46,XY individuals to appear phenotypically female at birth.

column1: Which pituitary hormone stimulates testosterone production in males?
column4: LH acts on Leydig cells via cAMP to stimulate cholesterol conversion to testosterone; testosterone negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary.

column1: Which pituitary hormone stimulates spermatogenesis in males?
column4: FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support sperm maturation; Sertoli cells produce inhibin, which selectively inhibits FSH secretion (not LH).

column1: What hypothalamic hormone triggers release of FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary?
column4: GnRH is released in a pulsatile fashion; continuous (non-pulsatile) GnRH exposure paradoxically suppresses FSH/LH, a principle used in pharmacologic castration.

column1: What hormone does the corpus luteum secrete to maintain the endometrium during early pregnancy?
column4: Progesterone inhibits uterine contractions and maintains the endometrial lining; if fertilization occurs, hCG from the embryo sustains the corpus luteum.

column1: Which hormone from the early embryo prevents regression of the corpus luteum?
column4: hCG mimics LH and sustains corpus luteum progesterone production until the placenta takes over; elevated hCG is the basis of pregnancy tests.

column1: Which hormone selectively inhibits FSH secretion in both males and females?
column4: Inhibin is secreted by Sertoli cells (males) and granulosa cells (females); it provides negative feedback specifically on FSH without affecting LH.

column1: What is the first hormone to rise at puberty in both sexes?
column4: Increased pulsatile GnRH from the hypothalamus initiates puberty by stimulating FSH and LH release, which then act on the gonads.

column1: What hormone drives the pubertal growth spurt and closure of epiphyseal plates?
column4: Estrogen (from ovaries in females; aromatized from testosterone in males) is the primary driver of epiphyseal fusion; males who lack estrogen action have delayed plate closure and tall stature.

column1: What is adrenarche?
column3: Adrenal androgen secretion preceding puberty (DHEA/DHEAS rise)
column4: Adrenarche typically occurs around ages 6-8; adrenal androgens drive pubic/axillary hair development (pubarche) before gonadal activation.

column1: What is the Tanner stage system used to classify?
column4: Tanner stages 1-5 describe breast development and pubic hair in females, and genital/pubic hair development in males; used clinically to assess pubertal progress.

column1: What event marks the beginning of puberty in females?
column4: Thelarche is typically the first sign of puberty in females (~ages 8-13), driven by rising estrogen from the ovaries.

column1: Which androgen is primarily responsible for development of male secondary sex characteristics at puberty?
column4: Testosterone drives muscle growth, voice deepening, and spermatogenesis; DHT (from 5-alpha reductase) mediates facial hair, prostate growth, and scalp hair recession.

column1: What are the three phases of the female menstrual cycle?
column4: The follicular phase (days 1-14 on average) involves follicle maturation; ovulation occurs at mid-cycle; the luteal phase (days 15-28) follows ovulation.

column1: On what day of a typical 28-day menstrual cycle does ovulation occur?
column4: Ovulation is triggered by the LH surge, which peaks ~36 hours before follicle rupture; this is the point of peak fertility.

column1: What triggers ovulation in the female menstrual cycle?
column4: Rising estradiol from the dominant follicle creates a positive feedback loop, causing a massive LH surge from the anterior pituitary that triggers ovulation ~36-48 hours later.

column1: What event initiates menstruation?
column3: Fall in progesterone (and estrogen) after corpus luteum regression
column4: When the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone and estrogen drop, causing vasoconstriction of spiral arteries, endometrial ischemia, and shedding.

column1: During which phase of the menstrual cycle does estrogen peak, triggering the LH surge?
column4: Sustained high estradiol (>200 pg/mL for >50 hours) switches estrogen's feedback from negative to positive, causing the pre-ovulatory LH surge.

column1: What change in cervical mucus occurs at ovulation that facilitates sperm transport?
column4: Estrogen thins the mucus at ovulation; after ovulation, progesterone makes it thick and viscous again, inhibiting sperm penetration.

column1: What is the approximate lifespan of the corpus luteum in the absence of pregnancy?
column4: Without hCG stimulation, the corpus luteum undergoes luteolysis at around day 26-28, causing progesterone levels to fall and triggering menstruation.

column1: What hormone does the placenta produce to maintain pregnancy after the first trimester?
column4: By weeks 8-10, the placenta takes over progesterone production from the corpus luteum (the luteal-placental shift), sustaining the pregnancy.

column1: What hormone stimulates uterine contractions during labor?
column4: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drives uterine contractions in a positive feedback loop during labor; synthetic oxytocin (Pitocin) is used to induce labor.

column1: What hormone is detected in urine to confirm pregnancy?
column4: hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast shortly after implantation; home pregnancy tests use antibodies that detect urinary hCG.

column1: What hormone is essential for milk production (lactogenesis) after delivery?
column4: High estrogen/progesterone during pregnancy inhibit prolactin's milk-producing action; delivery removes this inhibition, allowing lactation to begin.

column1: What is the milk let-down reflex mediated by?
column4: Infant suckling stimulates hypothalamic oxytocin release, causing myoepithelial cells in the breast to contract and eject milk; this is a neuroendocrine reflex.

column1: Why do lactating women often experience amenorrhea?
column3: High prolactin suppresses GnRH, inhibiting ovulation
column4: Prolactin inhibits GnRH pulsatility, reducing FSH/LH release; this lactational amenorrhea provides partial (not complete) contraception.

column1: What softens the cervix and relaxes pelvic ligaments in preparation for labor?
column4: Relaxin (produced by the corpus luteum and placenta) remodels collagen in the cervix and symphysis pubis, allowing the birth canal to widen.

column1: What branch of the autonomic nervous system mediates penile erection?
column4: The mnemonic: 'Point and Shoot' — parasympathetic = erection (point); sympathetic = ejaculation (shoot). Parasympathetic causes vasodilation via NO release.

column1: What branch of the autonomic nervous system controls ejaculation?
column4: Sympathetic (hypogastric nerve) controls emission and ejaculation via smooth muscle contraction of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate.

column1: What neurotransmitter mediates vasodilation of penile vasculature during erection?
column4: Parasympathetic neurons release ACh and stimulate NO synthesis in endothelium; NO activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP, relaxing smooth muscle, increasing blood flow.

column1: How does sildenafil (Viagra) produce erection?
column4: PDE5 degrades cGMP in penile smooth muscle; sildenafil inhibits PDE5, prolonging cGMP-mediated smooth muscle relaxation and maintaining erection.

column1: What spinal cord level mediates the parasympathetic innervation of the reproductive organs?
column4: Pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from sacral spinal levels S2-S4 and innervate the bladder, rectum, and reproductive organs; damage at this level causes sexual dysfunction.

column1: What hypothalamic nucleus integrates reproductive hormonal signals with autonomic control of sexual function?
column4: The MPOA of the hypothalamus receives hormonal inputs (androgens, estrogen) and coordinates both neuroendocrine (GnRH) and autonomic outputs governing sexual behavior and function.

column1: What is the primary function of skeletal muscle?
column4: Skeletal muscle attaches to bones via tendons and generates force to produce body movement; it is under voluntary (somatic) control.

column1: Which muscle type is responsible for generating body heat through thermogenesis?
column4: Skeletal muscles produce heat as a byproduct of contraction; shivering is a coordinated rapid contraction-relaxation cycle that generates heat without useful movement.

column1: Which muscle type maintains posture and stabilizes joints?
column4: Postural muscles are skeletal muscles that maintain tone continuously to stabilize the skeleton against gravity.

column1: What role does smooth muscle play in the digestive system?
column4: Smooth muscle in the GI tract wall contracts rhythmically (peristalsis) to move food and waste along the tract.

column1: What is the function of cardiac muscle specifically?
column4: Cardiac muscle generates the contractile force of each heartbeat, propelling blood into the pulmonary and systemic circulations.

column1: Name the three general functions of the muscle system.
column4: These three broad functions encompass locomotion, joint stabilization, and thermogenesis — all accomplished by the three muscle types acting together.

column1: What structure connects skeletal muscle to bone?
column4: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue that transmit the contractile force of muscle to bone, enabling movement at joints.
