column1: What is the origin of a skeletal muscle?
column4: The origin is typically on the stationary bone; contraction moves the insertion toward the origin, producing joint movement.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::support-mobility MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the insertion of a skeletal muscle?
column4: The insertion is pulled toward the origin during contraction; distinguishing origin from insertion is important for understanding movement direction.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::support-mobility MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of lever system do most skeletal muscles operate in the human body?
column4: In third-class levers, effort is applied between the fulcrum and load (e.g., biceps brachii); they sacrifice mechanical advantage for speed and range of motion.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::support-mobility MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which muscle property allows a resting muscle to resist passive stretch?
column4: Muscle tone is maintained by a small number of motor units firing asynchronously; it stabilizes posture without full contraction.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::support-mobility MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How do skeletal muscles assist venous return of blood to the heart?
column3: Skeletal muscle pump (compresses veins during contraction)
column4: Contracting limb muscles compress deep veins; one-way venous valves ensure blood moves toward the heart, aiding circulation especially in the legs.

column1: What prevents blood from flowing backward in veins during the skeletal muscle pump?
column4: Semilunar valves in veins ensure unidirectional flow toward the heart whenever surrounding muscles squeeze the vessel.

column1: Which condition results partly from failure of the skeletal muscle pump in leg veins?
column4: Incompetent venous valves allow backflow and pooling; prolonged standing without muscular movement exacerbates venous insufficiency.

column1: What is the respiratory pump and how does it assist venous return?
column3: Thoracic pressure changes during breathing draw blood toward heart
column4: Inhalation decreases intrathoracic pressure, expanding the vena cava and right atrium, increasing venous return — complementing the skeletal muscle pump.

column1: What is shivering?
column3: Involuntary rapid skeletal muscle contractions to generate heat
column4: Shivering is triggered by the hypothalamus when core temperature drops; the rapid ATP hydrolysis during futile contractions releases heat.

column1: Which brain region initiates the shivering reflex?
column4: The posterior hypothalamus integrates cold signals from peripheral thermoreceptors and activates somatic motor pathways to drive shivering.

column1: What metabolic process powers heat generation during shivering?
column4: Muscles hydrolyze ATP during cross-bridge cycling; ~75% of the energy is lost as heat, which is the thermogenic goal of shivering.

column1: How does vasoconstriction complement shivering during cold exposure?
column3: Reduces heat loss at skin surface
column4: Sympathetic vasoconstriction shunts blood away from the periphery, conserving core heat while shivering simultaneously generates heat.

column1: What is non-shivering thermogenesis and in which tissue does it occur?
column3: Heat from brown adipose tissue (BAT) uncoupling
column4: BAT contains uncoupling protein-1 (thermogenin), which dissipates the proton gradient as heat rather than synthesizing ATP — important in neonates.

column1: Which muscle type has striations and is multinucleated?
column4: Skeletal muscle fibers are formed by fusion of myoblasts, creating long multinucleated syncytia; the regular sarcomere arrangement produces visible striations.

column1: Which muscle type is uninucleate, non-striated, and involuntary?
column4: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, have a single central nucleus, lack organized sarcomeres (hence non-striated), and are controlled by the ANS.

column1: What is the distinguishing structural feature of cardiac muscle cells?
column4: Intercalated discs connect cardiac myocytes end-to-end; gap junctions allow ionic coupling so the heart acts as a functional syncytium.

column1: How many nuclei does a typical cardiac muscle cell have?
column4: Unlike skeletal muscle (multinucleate) and smooth muscle (uninucleate), cardiac cells commonly have one nucleus but can have two.

column1: Which muscle type contains dense bodies instead of Z-discs?
column4: Smooth muscle actin filaments anchor to dense bodies (cytoplasmic) and dense plaques (membrane), functionally analogous to Z-discs in striated muscle.

column1: Which muscle types are striated?
column4: Both skeletal and cardiac muscle have organized sarcomeres (A, I, H bands, M and Z lines) that produce a striated appearance under light microscopy.

column1: What is a sarcomere?
column3: Functional contractile unit of striated muscle (Z-line to Z-line)
column4: The sarcomere contains overlapping thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments; its shortening produces muscle contraction.

column1: What proteins make up the thin filament of a sarcomere?
column4: Globular actin (G-actin) polymerizes into F-actin; tropomyosin covers myosin-binding sites at rest, and the troponin complex (T, I, C) regulates this blockade.

column1: Which band of the sarcomere contains only thin filaments (actin)?
column4: The I band spans the region between adjacent A bands and contains only actin; it appears light under EM and shortens during contraction.

column1: Which band of the sarcomere does NOT shorten during contraction?
column4: The A band equals the length of the thick (myosin) filament and remains constant; the I band and H zone shorten as filaments slide past each other.

column1: What zone disappears when a muscle is maximally contracted?
column4: The H zone (myosin only, no actin overlap) disappears when thin filaments fully overlap the thick filaments at maximal contraction.

column1: What is the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction?
column3: Actin and myosin filaments slide past each other without shortening
column4: Myosin heads pull actin filaments toward the M line, shortening the sarcomere; filament lengths themselves do not change.

column1: What is the T-tubule system?
column3: Invaginations of sarcolemma that conduct action potentials into the fiber interior
column4: T-tubules (transverse tubules) allow the action potential to reach deep into the muscle fiber rapidly, ensuring synchronous activation of all sarcomeres.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::t-tubule-system MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: At what structure does the T-tubule contact the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
column4: In skeletal muscle, each T-tubule is flanked by two SR terminal cisternae, forming a triad; this juxtaposition allows rapid Ca²⁺ release signaling.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::t-tubule-system MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which receptor on the T-tubule senses the action potential in skeletal muscle?
column4: DHPR is a voltage-gated L-type Ca²⁺ channel that acts as a voltage sensor; in skeletal muscle it mechanically gates the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the SR.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::t-tubule-system MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the role of the dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR) in cardiac muscle versus skeletal muscle?
column3: Cardiac: requires Ca²⁺ influx; skeletal: mechanical coupling only
column4: In cardiac muscle, DHPR conducts Ca²⁺ influx that triggers RyR2 (calcium-induced calcium release); in skeletal muscle, DHPR mechanically gates RyR1 without requiring Ca²⁺ influx.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::t-tubule-system MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the contractile apparatus of muscle?
column3: Thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments that generate force
column4: The contractile apparatus refers collectively to myosin II (thick filaments) and the actin-troponin-tropomyosin (thin filaments) that interact to produce contraction.

column1: What is the power stroke in muscle contraction?
column3: Myosin head pivots, pulling actin toward M-line after Pi release
column4: After ATP hydrolysis, the myosin head (ADP+Pi bound) attaches to actin; Pi release triggers the power stroke, then ADP is released. New ATP binding allows detachment.

column1: What happens to the myosin head when ATP binds after the power stroke?
column4: ATP binding reduces myosin's affinity for actin, causing cross-bridge detachment — this is why rigor mortis (no ATP) causes permanent actomyosin linkage.

column1: What is rigor mortis and why does it occur?
column3: Post-mortem muscle stiffness due to absence of ATP
column4: Without ATP, myosin cannot detach from actin; all cross-bridges lock, stiffening muscles. It resolves as proteins degrade hours later.

column1: Which subunit of the troponin complex binds calcium?
column4: TnC binds Ca²⁺ (similar to calmodulin); this conformational change moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding site on actin, enabling contraction.

column1: What is the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)?
column3: Specialized smooth ER that stores and releases Ca²⁺ in muscle
column4: The SR surrounds each myofibril and releases Ca²⁺ upon nerve stimulation; Ca²⁺ reuptake by SERCA pumps terminates contraction.

column1: Which pump returns Ca²⁺ to the sarcoplasmic reticulum after contraction?
column4: SERCA actively transports Ca²⁺ back into the SR lumen at the cost of ATP, lowering cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ and allowing tropomyosin to re-block actin.

column1: Which receptor on the SR releases Ca²⁺ in skeletal muscle?
column4: RyR1 is mechanically gated by DHPR in skeletal muscle; it forms a large ion channel that floods the cytoplasm with Ca²⁺ during excitation.

column1: What is the role of calsequestrin in the SR?
column3: Ca²⁺ storage protein inside SR lumen
column4: Calsequestrin binds large amounts of Ca²⁺ with low affinity and high capacity, allowing the SR to store Ca²⁺ without raising free luminal concentrations excessively.

column1: What is a Type I (slow-twitch) muscle fiber primarily adapted for?
column4: Type I fibers have high mitochondrial density, myoglobin content (red color), and oxidative capacity; they are fatigue-resistant and used for sustained activity.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::fiber-type MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fiber primarily adapted for?
column4: Type II fibers have low mitochondrial density, rely on glycolysis, contract rapidly, and fatigue quickly; they are recruited for sprinting and heavy lifting.

column4: Myoglobin is an oxygen-binding protein in muscle (analogous to hemoglobin in blood); it stores O₂ and facilitates its diffusion to mitochondria.

column1: Which muscle type has the fastest contractile velocity?
column4: Fast-twitch skeletal fibers have the highest myosin ATPase activity, enabling rapid cross-bridge cycling and the fastest shortening velocity.

column1: Which muscle type has the slowest contractile velocity?
column4: Smooth muscle myosin has low ATPase activity and lacks organized sarcomeres, making it the slowest-contracting type — but it can sustain prolonged contraction with little energy.

column1: How does contractile velocity of cardiac muscle compare to skeletal and smooth?
column3: Intermediate — faster than smooth, slower than fast skeletal
column4: Cardiac muscle has organized sarcomeres and moderate myosin ATPase activity; its contractile speed is between slow smooth and fast skeletal muscle.

column1: What property allows smooth muscle to maintain tension with low energy at long lengths?
column4: In the latch state, dephosphorylated myosin cross-bridges detach slowly, allowing sustained force (tonic contraction) with minimal ATP consumption — important in vascular walls.

column1: What triggers contraction in cardiac muscle?
column3: Action potential → Ca²⁺ influx via L-type channels → CICR
column4: Depolarization opens L-type (DHPR) Ca²⁺ channels; small Ca²⁺ influx triggers RyR2 on SR (calcium-induced calcium release, CICR), amplifying Ca²⁺ to activate contraction.

column1: What is calcium-induced calcium release (CICR)?
column3: Small Ca²⁺ influx triggers much larger Ca²⁺ release from SR
column4: In cardiac muscle, L-type channel Ca²⁺ influx activates RyR2, releasing SR Ca²⁺ stores; this amplification ensures sufficient Ca²⁺ for cardiac troponin C to enable contraction.

column1: How does the Frank-Starling law relate to cardiac muscle contraction?
column3: Greater stretch → stronger contraction (up to a point)
column4: Increased end-diastolic volume stretches cardiomyocytes, increasing actin-myosin overlap and Ca²⁺ sensitivity; this intrinsic mechanism matches cardiac output to venous return.

column1: Which ion determines the plateau phase of the cardiac action potential?
column4: Phase 2 (plateau) of the ventricular action potential results from Ca²⁺ influx through L-type channels, which also initiates CICR and contraction.

column1: How does sympathetic stimulation increase cardiac contractility?
column3: Norepinephrine → β₁ → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates Ca²⁺ channels and phospholamban
column4: PKA increases L-type channel open probability (more Ca²⁺ influx) and phosphorylates phospholamban (disinhibits SERCA), accelerating relaxation and allowing faster heart rate.

column1: What is oxygen debt (EPOC)?
column3: Excess post-exercise O₂ consumption to restore resting state
column4: After intense exercise, elevated O₂ consumption replenishes ATP and phosphocreatine, oxidizes lactate, and restores body temperature and hormone levels.

column1: What is the primary cause of muscle fatigue during intense exercise?
column3: Accumulation of metabolic byproducts (Pi, H⁺, ADP)
column4: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) and H⁺ from ATP hydrolysis and lactic acid production impair cross-bridge cycling and SR Ca²⁺ release; lactate itself is not the direct cause of fatigue.

column1: What is phosphocreatine and what is its role in muscle?
column3: High-energy phosphate buffer that rapidly regenerates ATP
column4: Creatine kinase transfers phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP, regenerating ATP within seconds; this sustains maximal effort for ~10 seconds before glycolysis must take over.

column1: What metabolic pathway produces lactate during intense exercise?
column4: When O₂ supply is insufficient, pyruvate is reduced to lactate by LDH, regenerating NAD⁺ for continued glycolysis; lactate is then exported and oxidized or converted to glucose in the liver (Cori cycle).

column1: What is central fatigue versus peripheral fatigue?
column3: Central: reduced neural drive; peripheral: impaired muscle function
column4: Central fatigue involves decreased motor neuron firing from the brain/spinal cord; peripheral fatigue is at the muscle itself (impaired cross-bridge cycling, ion imbalance).

column1: What type of neuron innervates skeletal muscle?
column4: Alpha motor neurons are large-diameter, myelinated neurons whose cell bodies are in the ventral horn of the spinal cord; each innervates multiple skeletal muscle fibers.

column1: What is a motor unit?
column3: One alpha motor neuron and all muscle fibers it innervates
column4: All fibers in a motor unit are the same fiber type and contract together when the neuron fires; fine motor control uses small motor units with few fibers.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::nervous-control MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the size principle of motor unit recruitment?
column3: Smallest (slow) motor units recruited first, largest (fast) last
column4: Henneman's size principle: small, low-threshold motor units (Type I) are recruited first; large, high-threshold units (Type IIb) are added for greater force demands.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::nervous-control MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is summation in muscle physiology?
column3: Successive twitches add to produce greater force
column4: If a second action potential arrives before the first twitch fully relaxes, Ca²⁺ remains elevated and force is greater — leading to unfused tetanus, then fused tetanus at high frequencies.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::nervous-control MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is tetanus in muscle physiology?
column3: Sustained maximal contraction from high-frequency stimulation
column4: At high stimulation frequencies, Ca²⁺ remains continuously elevated, maintaining full cross-bridge cycling; fused tetanus is the maximal sustained force a muscle can produce.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::nervous-control MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a motor neuron?
column3: Efferent neuron that transmits signals from CNS to muscle
column4: Motor neurons relay commands from the spinal cord or brainstem to effector muscles; alpha motor neurons control extrafusal muscle fibers for force generation.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::motor-neurons MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the difference between upper and lower motor neurons?
column3: Upper: CNS (cortex/brainstem); lower: spinal cord to muscle
column4: Upper motor neurons (corticospinal tract) synapse on lower motor neurons in the spinal cord; lower motor neurons directly innervate skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::motor-neurons MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a gamma motor neuron?
column3: Motor neuron that innervates intrafusal (spindle) muscle fibers
column4: Gamma motor neurons maintain tension on muscle spindles during contraction, keeping the stretch reflex sensitive regardless of muscle length changes.
column8: concept::BB::3B::muscle_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::muscle-system::motor-neurons MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction?
column4: ACh is released from motor neuron terminals into the synaptic cleft and binds nicotinic ACh receptors on the motor end plate, triggering depolarization.

column1: What type of receptor does acetylcholine bind at the motor end plate?
column4: nAChRs are ligand-gated ion channels; ACh binding opens the channel, allowing Na⁺ influx and K⁺ efflux, producing an end-plate potential (EPP).

column1: What enzyme degrades acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft?
column4: AChE rapidly hydrolyzes ACh to acetate and choline, terminating the signal; organophosphate nerve agents and some pesticides inhibit AChE, causing prolonged muscle stimulation.

column1: What disease involves autoimmune destruction of nicotinic ACh receptors at the NMJ?
column4: Antibodies against nAChRs reduce end-plate potential amplitude; patients experience fatigable muscle weakness, especially of extraocular muscles.

column1: What toxin blocks ACh release from motor neuron terminals?
column4: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins required for synaptic vesicle fusion, preventing ACh release and causing flaccid paralysis.

column1: How does curare cause paralysis?
column3: Competitive antagonist of nAChR at motor end plate
column4: Curare (d-tubocurarine) blocks nicotinic receptors without activating them, preventing ACh from depolarizing the end plate and causing flaccid paralysis.

column1: Which division of the ANS increases heart rate?
column4: Sympathetic fibers release norepinephrine (NE) onto SA node β₁ receptors, increasing cAMP, accelerating If and ICaL channels to speed depolarization (positive chronotropy).

column1: Which neurotransmitter does the parasympathetic nervous system release at cardiac and smooth muscle targets?
column4: Parasympathetic postganglionic fibers are cholinergic; ACh acts on muscarinic receptors (M2 in heart, M3 in smooth muscle) to slow heart rate and constrict airways/GI.

column1: Which receptor type mediates parasympathetic effects on the heart?
column4: M2 activation in the SA node opens GIRK channels (IKACh), hyperpolarizing the node and slowing spontaneous depolarization (negative chronotropy and dromotropy).

column1: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on bronchial smooth muscle?
column4: NE/epinephrine activate β₂ receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, raising cAMP and reducing Ca²⁺ sensitivity, causing relaxation and airway widening.

column1: Which neurotransmitter receptor mediates sympathetic vasoconstriction in most peripheral arteries?
column4: NE binds α₁ receptors on vascular smooth muscle, activating Gq→PLC→IP₃→SR Ca²⁺ release, causing contraction and increased peripheral resistance.

column1: Which muscles are classified as voluntary?
column4: Voluntary muscles are under conscious control via the somatic nervous system; they can be moved at will, unlike smooth and cardiac muscle.

column1: Which muscle types are involuntary?
column4: Smooth and cardiac muscles are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and intrinsic pacemakers; they function without conscious thought.

column1: Can cardiac muscle be directly controlled voluntarily?
column4: The SA node generates spontaneous action potentials; the ANS modulates rate and force but does not initiate or stop cardiac contraction voluntarily.

column1: What makes smooth muscle involuntary at a cellular level?
column3: Controlled by ANS and local hormones, lacks somatic innervation
column4: Smooth muscle lacks NMJs with somatic motor neurons; instead, diffuse autonomic varicosities release neurotransmitters, and smooth muscle also responds to hormones and local signals.

column1: Which involuntary muscle type can generate action potentials spontaneously (autorhythmicity)?
column4: Cardiac pacemaker cells and some smooth muscle (e.g., GI interstitial cells of Cajal) depolarize spontaneously, driving rhythmic contraction without neural input.

column1: Which muscle type is characterized by striated banding patterns AND voluntary control?
column4: Skeletal muscle is striated (organized sarcomeres) and under voluntary (somatic) nervous control, distinguishing it from cardiac (striated, involuntary) and smooth (non-striated, involuntary).

column1: Which muscle type is non-striated and involuntary?
column4: Smooth muscle lacks the organized sarcomere structure of striated muscle, so it appears non-striated under microscopy and is controlled by the autonomic nervous system.

column1: Which structural feature is unique to cardiac muscle cells but absent in skeletal muscle cells?
column4: Intercalated discs connect cardiac myocytes, allowing electrical coupling via gap junctions so the heart acts as a functional syncytium. Skeletal muscle fibers are electrically independent.

column1: What term describes the branched, single-nucleus cells of cardiac muscle?
column4: Unlike skeletal muscle fibers which are multinucleated syncytia, cardiac muscle cells are branched and typically have one (occasionally two) centrally located nucleus.

column1: Which type of muscle has multiple peripheral nuclei per fiber?
column4: Skeletal muscle fibers are large multinucleated syncytia formed by myoblast fusion; nuclei are pushed to the periphery. Cardiac and smooth muscle cells are uninucleate with centrally located nuclei.

column1: Smooth muscle cells use which type of structure instead of sarcomeres to generate force?
column4: Smooth muscle lacks sarcomeres; instead actin filaments anchor to dense bodies (analogous to Z-lines) scattered through the cytoplasm and on the cell membrane.

column1: Which property distinguishes cardiac muscle contraction from skeletal muscle contraction regarding refractory period?
column3: Cardiac has a prolonged absolute refractory period
column4: The long absolute refractory period of cardiac muscle prevents tetanus, ensuring the heart can refill with blood between contractions — a critical functional difference from skeletal muscle.

column1: Why do red (slow-twitch) muscle fibers contain abundant mitochondria?
column3: To generate ATP via oxidative phosphorylation
column4: Red/slow-twitch (Type I) fibers rely on aerobic respiration for sustained, fatigue-resistant contractions; the high mitochondrial density supports continuous ATP production from fatty acids and glucose.

column1: What pigment gives red muscle fibers their red color and aids oxygen delivery to mitochondria?
column4: Myoglobin is an oxygen-binding protein in muscle (analogous to hemoglobin in blood) that stores O2 and facilitates its diffusion to mitochondria in red muscle fibers.

column1: Which muscle fiber type relies primarily on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP?
column4: White/fast-twitch fibers have fewer mitochondria and less myoglobin; they generate ATP rapidly via glycolysis but fatigue quickly due to lactate accumulation.

column1: Which metabolic substrate do red muscle fibers preferentially oxidize for sustained activity?
column4: Slow-twitch red fibers are specialized for aerobic metabolism and preferentially use fatty acid beta-oxidation, which yields more ATP per molecule than glucose, supporting endurance activity.

column1: The high mitochondrial density in red muscle cells primarily increases the rate of which metabolic process?
column4: Mitochondria are the site of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase; more mitochondria = greater capacity for oxidative phosphorylation and thus sustained aerobic ATP production.

column1: Which fiber type is most fatigue-resistant: Type I, Type IIa, or Type IIb?
column4: Type I fibers have the most mitochondria, highest oxidative capacity, and rely on aerobic metabolism — all features that confer fatigue resistance. Type IIb (fast glycolytic) fatigue fastest.

column1: What is the name of the thicker filament in the sarcomere?
column4: Myosin II is the motor protein that forms thick filaments; its globular heads bind actin and hydrolyze ATP to generate force during the cross-bridge cycle.

column1: What is the thinner filament in the sarcomere composed of?
column4: Thin filaments are composed of polymerized G-actin monomers forming a double-helical F-actin strand, plus associated regulatory proteins troponin and tropomyosin.

column1: According to the sliding filament model, what happens to the lengths of actin and myosin filaments during muscle contraction?
column4: The sliding filament model states that thick and thin filaments slide past each other; the filaments themselves do not shorten — rather the sarcomere shortens because filaments overlap more.

column1: What energy source drives the myosin head's power stroke during cross-bridge cycling?
column4: Myosin head binds ATP → hydrolyzes to ADP + Pi → conformational change (cocked state) → binds actin → releases Pi triggering the power stroke → ADP released → new ATP binds to release myosin from actin.

column1: What state is the myosin head in immediately after ATP hydrolysis but before the power stroke?
column4: After ATP hydrolysis to ADP+Pi, the myosin head is in a high-energy conformation (cocked) and can bind actin; release of Pi then triggers the power stroke that moves the thin filament.

column1: What happens to myosin heads in the absence of ATP (e.g., rigor mortis)?
column3: They remain rigidly bound to actin
column4: ATP binding is required to detach myosin from actin. Without ATP (as in rigor mortis after death), myosin heads stay locked onto actin, causing muscle stiffness.

column1: What does the 'I' band of a sarcomere contain?
column4: The I (isotropic) band appears light under polarized light and contains only thin actin filaments — no myosin. It spans from the Z-line to the edge of the A-band.

column1: What does the 'A' band of a sarcomere contain?
column4: The A (anisotropic) band spans the full length of the thick myosin filament, including regions of overlap with thin actin filaments. It appears dark under polarized light.

column1: What structure defines the boundary between adjacent sarcomeres?
column4: Z-lines are protein discs to which thin actin filaments from adjacent sarcomeres anchor. One sarcomere = Z-line to Z-line.

column1: What is the 'H' zone of a sarcomere?
column3: Central region of A band with thick filaments only (no actin overlap)
column4: The H zone (from German 'Helles' = bright) is the lighter central region of the A band where myosin thick filaments exist without overlapping actin thin filaments.

column1: What is located at the center of the H zone?
column4: The M-line (Mittelscheibe) is a protein scaffold at the midpoint of the sarcomere that anchors and aligns myosin thick filaments.

column1: During muscle contraction, which sarcomere region DOES NOT change width?
column4: The A band width equals the length of the myosin thick filament, which does not change. The I band and H zone narrow as filaments slide and overlap more during contraction.

column1: During maximal muscle contraction, what happens to the H zone?
column4: When the sarcomere is maximally shortened, actin filaments from both sides fully overlap the myosin, eliminating the H zone. The I band also narrows to near zero.

column1: What protein complex sits on the actin thin filament and contains three subunits?
column4: Troponin is a heterotrimeric regulatory protein (TnT, TnI, TnC) bound at intervals along the thin filament. It works with tropomyosin to regulate myosin-binding site exposure on actin.

column1: What is the function of tropomyosin at rest?
column4: At rest (low Ca2+), tropomyosin lies over the myosin-binding sites on actin, sterically preventing cross-bridge formation and keeping muscle relaxed.

column1: Which troponin subunit binds calcium ions?
column4: TnC is the calcium-sensing subunit of the troponin complex; it binds Ca2+ with high affinity, triggering a conformational change in the entire troponin-tropomyosin complex that exposes actin's myosin-binding sites.

column1: Which troponin subunit anchors the troponin complex to tropomyosin?
column4: TnT (T for tropomyosin-binding) attaches the troponin complex to tropomyosin along the thin filament, positioning TnC and TnI correctly for regulation.

column1: Which troponin subunit inhibits myosin ATPase activity in the absence of calcium?
column4: TnI (I for inhibitory) interacts with actin to hold tropomyosin in its blocking position. Calcium binding to TnC reduces TnI-actin interaction, allowing tropomyosin to shift and expose binding sites.

column1: Why does smooth muscle lack troponin?
column3: Smooth muscle uses calmodulin-myosin light chain kinase instead
column4: Smooth muscle regulation is myosin-based: Ca2+ binds calmodulin → activates MLCK → phosphorylates myosin light chains → contraction. Troponin-tropomyosin regulation is specific to striated (skeletal and cardiac) muscle.

column1: What ion triggers skeletal muscle contraction?
column4: An action potential releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytoplasm; Ca2+ binds troponin C, initiating the conformational changes that expose myosin-binding sites on actin.

column1: Where is calcium stored in skeletal muscle cells prior to contraction?
column4: The SR is the muscle cell's specialized endoplasmic reticulum; it sequesters Ca2+ at rest and releases it rapidly upon membrane depolarization to trigger contraction.

column1: What structure transmits the action potential from the sarcolemma deep into the muscle fiber to reach the SR?
column4: T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that run perpendicular to the muscle fiber, ensuring the electrical signal rapidly reaches the SR throughout the fiber's interior.

column1: What protein on the SR membrane senses depolarization and triggers Ca2+ release?
column4: In skeletal muscle, the voltage-sensor DHPR (dihydropyridine receptor) on the T-tubule physically couples to RyR1 on the SR, causing it to open and release Ca2+ — no Ca2+ influx from outside needed.

column1: How is cytoplasmic Ca2+ returned to the SR after muscle contraction?
column4: SERCA (sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) actively pumps Ca2+ back into the SR using ATP, lowering cytoplasmic [Ca2+] and allowing troponin-I to re-inhibit myosin binding, causing relaxation.

column1: In cardiac muscle, what additional Ca2+ source (beyond SR) contributes to contraction?
column3: Extracellular Ca2+ via L-type Ca2+ channels
column4: Cardiac muscle uses Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR): extracellular Ca2+ enters through L-type (DHPR) channels on the T-tubule and triggers ryanodine receptors (RyR2) to release far more Ca2+ from the SR.

column1: What is the minimum cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration required to initiate cross-bridge cycling in skeletal muscle?
column4: At rest, cytoplasmic [Ca2+] is ~10^-7 M (100 nM). Contraction initiates when SR release raises it to ~10^-6 M (1 µM), sufficient to saturate TnC and expose actin-binding sites.

column1: Name five major functions of the skeletal system.
column3: Support, protection, movement, mineral storage, blood cell production
column4: The skeleton provides structural support, protects organs, acts as levers for muscle movement, stores calcium/phosphate, and houses red bone marrow for hematopoiesis.

column1: Which organ system is primarily responsible for hematopoiesis in adults?
column4: Red bone marrow in flat bones (sternum, ribs, pelvis, skull) is the primary site of hematopoiesis in adult humans.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::functions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the term for blood cell production that occurs within bone marrow?
column4: Hematopoiesis occurs in red bone marrow and produces erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets from hematopoietic stem cells.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::functions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which function of the skeletal system involves acting as levers to amplify muscle force?
column4: Bones act as rigid levers, with joints as fulcrums, so muscle contractions produce movement of the body or limbs.

column1: Besides calcium, which other major mineral is stored in bone?
column4: Bone stores ~85% of the body's phosphate as part of hydroxyapatite crystals alongside calcium, making it important for phosphate homeostasis.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::functions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What percentage of total body calcium is stored in the skeleton?
column4: Nearly all body calcium resides in bone as hydroxyapatite; only ~1% circulates in blood and soft tissues, yet this small fraction is critical for nerve/muscle function.

column1: What property of bone allows it to resist compressive forces and bear body weight?
column4: The mineral component of bone (hydroxyapatite) provides hardness and resistance to compression, while collagen provides tensile strength and flexibility.

column1: Which component of bone provides tensile strength and flexibility, preventing brittleness?
column4: Collagen fibers form an organic framework that is then mineralized; without collagen, bone becomes brittle. This is demonstrated in osteogenesis imperfecta.

column1: What is the mineral compound that gives bone its hardness?
column4: Hydroxyapatite crystals deposit on collagen fibers during mineralization, providing bone with compressive strength and rigidity.

column1: What disease results from inadequate bone mineralization in adults, causing soft, weak bones?
column4: Osteomalacia (rickets in children) occurs with vitamin D deficiency, impairing calcium absorption and hydroxyapatite deposition, reducing structural rigidity.

column1: What architectural feature of long bone shafts maximizes strength while minimizing mass?
column3: Hollow cylindrical shape (diaphysis with medullary cavity)
column4: A hollow cylinder resists bending forces more efficiently per unit mass than a solid rod, reducing skeletal weight while maintaining structural support.

column1: What hormone signals osteoclasts to release calcium from bone into the blood?
column4: PTH is released when blood calcium falls; it activates osteoclasts to resorb bone, releasing Ca²⁺ and phosphate into circulation to restore calcium levels.

column1: What hormone promotes calcium deposition into bone and lowers blood calcium?
column4: Calcitonin, secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, inhibits osteoclast activity and promotes osteoblast activity, reducing blood calcium.

column1: Which vitamin is essential for intestinal calcium absorption, indirectly supporting bone calcium stores?
column4: Calcitriol (active vitamin D) upregulates calcium-binding proteins in intestinal epithelial cells, increasing Ca²⁺ absorption and availability for bone mineralization.

column1: What is the process by which osteoclasts break down bone matrix to release calcium?
column4: Osteoclasts secrete hydrochloric acid and proteases into a sealed resorption pit, dissolving hydroxyapatite and digesting collagen to release Ca²⁺ and PO4³⁻.

column1: Which bones are the last resort calcium reservoir mobilized during prolonged hypocalcemia?
column4: Trabecular bone is resorbed first due to its high surface area; cortical bone of long-bone shafts is mobilized last, compromising structural integrity significantly.

column1: Which vital organ does the skull protect?
column4: The skull (cranium) forms a rigid bony case around the brain, protecting it from mechanical trauma; the vertebral column similarly protects the spinal cord.

column1: What bony structure protects the heart and lungs?
column4: The rib cage, formed by 12 pairs of ribs, the sternum, and thoracic vertebrae, encases and protects the heart, lungs, and great vessels.

column1: Which structure of the vertebral column directly protects the spinal cord?
column4: Each vertebra has a vertebral foramen; together they form the spinal canal through which the spinal cord passes, shielding it from physical damage.

column1: Which flat bones protect the pelvic organs?
column4: The bony pelvis surrounds and protects the bladder, reproductive organs, and rectum; it also transmits body weight from the spine to the lower limbs.

column1: What are the four main categories of bone classified by shape?
column4: Long bones (femur) are longer than wide; short bones (carpals) are cube-shaped; flat bones (skull) are thin and plate-like; irregular bones (vertebrae) have complex shapes.

column1: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
column4: The adult skeleton has 206 bones; infants have ~270-300 because many bones (e.g., cranial bones, sacrum) fuse during development.

column1: What are the two main divisions of the adult human skeleton?
column4: The axial skeleton (80 bones) includes skull, vertebral column, and rib cage. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) includes limbs and girdles.

column1: Which bones make up the axial skeleton?
column4: The axial skeleton forms the central axis of the body; it protects the brain, spinal cord, and thoracic organs and provides attachment for limb muscles.

column1: How many vertebrae are in each region of the adult vertebral column?
column4: Mnemonic for meal times: Breakfast 7am, Lunch 12pm, Dinner 5pm — matches cervical, thoracic, lumbar vertebra counts.

column1: What term describes sesamoid bones, and what is the largest example?
column4: Sesamoid bones develop within tendons to protect them from compressive stress and improve mechanical advantage; the patella is the largest sesamoid bone.

column1: What type of bone contains a large medullary cavity and serves primarily for movement?
column4: Long bones (humerus, femur, tibia) have a diaphysis, epiphyses, and medullary cavity; they act as levers and also contain yellow marrow (fat) in adults.

column1: Which bone type is found in the wrist and ankle and is roughly cube-shaped?
column4: Short bones provide stability and limited gliding motion; they are composed mostly of spongy bone with a thin cortical shell.

column1: What specialized feature of flat bones makes them important for hematopoiesis?
column3: Large areas of red bone marrow (spongy bone between two cortical plates)
column4: Flat bones (sternum, ilium, ribs, skull) contain abundant red marrow sandwiched between compact bone plates (inner and outer tables), supporting hematopoiesis.

column1: What name is given to the growth plate in long bones where longitudinal growth occurs?
column4: The epiphyseal plate consists of hyaline cartilage; chondrocytes proliferate and are replaced by bone, extending the diaphysis until the plate ossifies at puberty's end.

column1: What is the difference between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone?
column3: Epiphysis = expanded ends; diaphysis = elongated shaft
column4: The epiphyses contain spongy bone and articular cartilage for joint surfaces; the diaphysis is the hollow cylindrical shaft of compact bone enclosing the medullary cavity.

column1: What type of joint allows the greatest range of motion?
column4: Synovial joints have a fluid-filled joint cavity, articular cartilage, and a fibrous capsule; examples include the shoulder (ball-and-socket) and knee (hinge).

column1: What is the function of synovial fluid in a joint?
column3: Lubrication and nutrient delivery to articular cartilage
column4: Synovial fluid is secreted by the synovial membrane; it reduces friction between articular cartilage surfaces and supplies nutrients to avascular cartilage.

column1: What are the three structural classifications of joints?
column4: Fibrous joints (sutures) are immovable; cartilaginous joints (intervertebral discs) allow slight movement; synovial joints allow free movement.

column1: What type of cartilage covers the articular surfaces of bones in synovial joints?
column4: Hyaline cartilage provides a smooth, low-friction surface that cushions joint surfaces; it is avascular and relies on synovial fluid for nutrition.

column1: What is the term for immovable fibrous joints found between skull bones?
column4: Sutures are synarthroses — immovable fibrous joints where bone edges interlock and are bound by dense fibrous connective tissue; they allow no significant motion.

column1: What structure within the knee joint acts as a fibrocartilaginous shock absorber?
column4: The menisci deepen the knee joint, distribute compressive loads, and stabilize the joint; they are frequently torn in athletic injuries.

column1: Which type of synovial joint allows rotation only, as in C1-C2 articulation?
column4: Pivot joints allow uniaxial rotation; the atlantoaxial joint (C1 rotating on C2's dens/odontoid process) allows the 'no' head shake motion.

column1: What is the key difference between an endoskeleton and an exoskeleton?
column3: Endoskeleton is internal; exoskeleton is external
column4: Vertebrates have endoskeletons made of bone/cartilage inside the body. Arthropods have exoskeletons (chitin) outside, providing protection but requiring molting for growth.

column1: Which biological polymer forms the exoskeleton of arthropods?
column4: Chitin is a polysaccharide (N-acetylglucosamine polymer) that is lightweight yet tough; it is secreted by epidermal cells and molted (ecdysis) as the animal grows.

column1: What is the major disadvantage of an exoskeleton compared to an endoskeleton?
column3: Must be shed (molted) for growth; limits maximum body size
column4: Molting (ecdysis) leaves arthropods vulnerable; exoskeletons also cannot scale efficiently, limiting maximum size due to weight-to-strength constraints.

column1: Name one invertebrate with an endoskeleton.
column4: Echinoderms have an internal calcareous endoskeleton (ossicles) derived from mesoderm; this contrasts with the chitin exoskeleton of arthropods.

column1: What is the growth advantage of an endoskeleton over an exoskeleton?
column4: Endoskeletons grow with the organism via appositional and endochondral mechanisms, avoiding the vulnerable molting stage required by exoskeletal animals.

column1: What are the two macroscopic types of bone tissue?
column4: Compact bone forms the dense outer shell of bones; spongy bone is the lattice-like interior filled with red or yellow marrow, found mainly in epiphyses and flat bones.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the basic structural unit of compact bone?
column4: Each osteon is a concentric cylinder of lamellae surrounding a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves; osteons run parallel to the bone's long axis.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the central canal of an osteon called?
column4: The Haversian canal runs longitudinally and contains blood vessels and nerves; it is connected to the periosteum by transverse Volkmann's canals.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the small cavities within bone matrix where osteocytes reside?
column4: Lacunae are spaces in the mineralized matrix housing osteocytes; fine channels called canaliculi connect lacunae to each other and to Haversian canals for nutrient exchange.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the tiny channels connecting lacunae to Haversian canals in bone?
column4: Canaliculi contain cytoplasmic extensions of osteocytes; they allow exchange of nutrients, wastes, and signaling molecules between osteocytes and the blood supply.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What fibrous membrane covers the outer surface of bone and contains osteoprogenitor cells?
column4: The periosteum is a dense connective tissue sheath; its inner layer contains osteoblasts and osteoprogenitor cells essential for appositional growth and fracture repair.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What membrane lines the medullary cavity and inner trabecular surfaces of bone?
column4: The endosteum is a thin connective tissue layer containing osteoblasts and osteoclasts; it is active in bone remodeling and lines all internal bone surfaces.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the transverse canals in compact bone that connect Haversian canals to the periosteum?
column4: Volkmann's canals run perpendicular to Haversian canals, carrying blood vessels and nerves from the periosteum into the osteons, ensuring vascular supply throughout bone.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skeletal_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skeletal-system::bone-structure MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two main components of the bone matrix (osteoid)?
column4: Type I collagen provides tensile strength and flexibility; hydroxyapatite [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2] provides compressive strength and rigidity. Together they make bone tough but not brittle.

column1: What is the term for unmineralized bone matrix secreted by osteoblasts?
column4: Osteoid is the organic pre-bone matrix (mainly collagen); it becomes mineralized when hydroxyapatite crystals deposit on collagen fibrils, forming mature bone.

column1: What ratio of organic to inorganic material approximately describes mature bone matrix?
column4: Bone is roughly 35% organic (collagen, glycoproteins) and 65% inorganic (hydroxyapatite); this combination optimizes both flexibility and hardness.

column1: Which non-collagen protein in bone matrix binds calcium and regulates mineralization?
column4: Osteocalcin is a vitamin K-dependent protein secreted by osteoblasts; it binds calcium and hydroxyapatite and is used as a serum marker of bone formation.

column1: What disease results from defective collagen in bone, causing extremely fragile bones?
column4: Osteogenesis imperfecta is caused by mutations in COL1A1/COL1A2 (type I collagen); without a proper collagen scaffold, hydroxyapatite cannot deposit properly and bones fracture easily.

column1: What are the three main cell types found in bone?
column4: Osteoblasts synthesize bone matrix; osteocytes are mature bone cells maintaining matrix; osteoclasts resorb bone. Together they regulate bone remodeling.

column1: What is the function of osteoblasts?
column3: Synthesize and secrete bone matrix (osteoid); promote mineralization
column4: Osteoblasts are mononuclear cells derived from mesenchymal stem cells; they produce type I collagen and regulatory proteins, then become trapped as osteocytes.

column1: From which precursor cell type do osteoclasts originate?
column4: Osteoclasts are multinucleated giant cells derived from fusion of monocyte precursors; this distinguishes them from osteoblasts and osteocytes, which are of mesenchymal origin.

column1: What is the ruffled border of an osteoclast, and what is its function?
column3: Infolded plasma membrane; secretes acid and enzymes to resorb bone
column4: The ruffled border vastly increases osteoclast surface area; it pumps H⁺ (via carbonic anhydrase and H⁺-ATPase) and lysosomal enzymes (cathepsin K) into the resorption pit.

column1: What is the fate of an osteoblast once it becomes surrounded by bone matrix?
column4: Trapped osteoblasts differentiate into osteocytes — the most abundant bone cell — which maintain the matrix and act as mechanosensors via their canalicular network.

column1: What signaling molecule produced by osteoblasts stimulates osteoclast differentiation?
column4: RANKL on osteoblast surfaces binds RANK on osteoclast precursors, promoting osteoclastogenesis. Osteoprotegerin (OPG), a decoy receptor, blocks this interaction, inhibiting resorption.

column1: What type of cartilage is most abundant in the body and forms the articular surfaces of joints?
column4: Hyaline cartilage contains type II collagen and proteoglycans; it is found at joint surfaces, costal cartilages, tracheal rings, and in embryonic skeletons (replaced by bone via endochondral ossification).

column1: What type of cartilage forms the intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis?
column4: Fibrocartilage has abundant type I collagen and few chondrocytes; it is the strongest cartilage type, designed to resist compression and shear in high-stress areas.

column1: What type of cartilage is found in the external ear and epiglottis, providing flexibility?
column4: Elastic cartilage contains elastic fibers (elastin) in addition to type II collagen; it resists deformation and springs back to shape after bending.

column1: Why is cartilage typically avascular, and how does it receive nutrients?
column3: Lacks blood vessels; nutrients diffuse through the matrix from surrounding perichondrium
column4: Avascular cartilage relies on diffusion through its gel-like proteoglycan matrix; damage heals poorly because chondrocytes cannot migrate and no blood-borne repair cells arrive.

column1: What cells are responsible for producing and maintaining cartilage matrix?
column4: Chondrocytes occupy small spaces called lacunae within the cartilage matrix; they synthesize type II collagen and proteoglycans (aggrecan) to maintain the extracellular matrix.

column1: Which cartilage type is used as a template during endochondral ossification of long bones?
column4: In endochondral ossification, a hyaline cartilage model is gradually replaced by bone; chondrocytes hypertrophy, calcify, and die, allowing osteoblasts to deposit bone matrix.

column1: What is the function of ligaments in the skeletal system?
column3: Connect bone to bone; stabilize joints
column4: Ligaments are dense regular connective tissue (mainly type I collagen) that limit excessive joint motion and provide passive joint stability without active muscle contraction.

column1: What is the function of tendons?
column3: Connect muscle to bone; transmit contractile force
column4: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue that transfer force from contracting muscle to bone, enabling skeletal movement; they have high tensile strength with little stretch.

column1: Which collagen type predominates in both tendons and ligaments?
column4: Type I collagen fibers are packed in parallel arrays in tendons (very ordered) and slightly less ordered in ligaments, conferring high tensile strength in the direction of loading.

column1: What type of cells produce and maintain the collagen matrix in tendons and ligaments?
column4: Fibroblasts/tenocytes are aligned between collagen fiber bundles and maintain the extracellular matrix; tendons and ligaments are relatively hypovascular, limiting healing capacity.

column1: What is the key structural difference between tendons and ligaments?
column3: Tendons: highly ordered parallel fibers; ligaments: slightly less ordered, allow more multi-directional load
column4: Tendons transmit force primarily in one direction (unidirectional loading) so fibers are highly parallel; ligaments resist forces in multiple directions, requiring a less regular arrangement.

column1: Which hormone from the parathyroid gland is the primary regulator of blood calcium via bone resorption?
column4: PTH raises blood [Ca²⁺] by stimulating osteoclast activity (bone resorption), increasing renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, and activating vitamin D to boost intestinal absorption.

column1: Which gland secretes calcitonin, and what is its effect on bone?
column3: Thyroid (parafollicular C cells); inhibits osteoclasts, lowers blood calcium
column4: Calcitonin is released when blood calcium is high; it inhibits osteoclast activity and promotes osteoblast function, depositing calcium into bone and reducing serum Ca²⁺.

column1: How does estrogen influence bone density?
column3: Inhibits osteoclast activity; promotes bone conservation
column4: Estrogen suppresses RANKL expression and osteoclast differentiation; estrogen loss at menopause accelerates bone resorption, leading to osteoporosis in postmenopausal women.

column1: What is the effect of growth hormone on the skeletal system?
column3: Stimulates longitudinal bone growth via IGF-1
column4: Growth hormone (GH) acts on the liver to produce IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1), which stimulates chondrocyte proliferation at epiphyseal plates, promoting endochondral ossification.

column1: How does active vitamin D (calcitriol) support bone mineralization?
column3: Increases intestinal Ca²⁺ and phosphate absorption
column4: Calcitriol upregulates calbindin in enterocytes, promoting Ca²⁺ uptake; it also stimulates renal reabsorption of phosphate, ensuring adequate mineral supply for hydroxyapatite formation.

column1: What is the effect of chronic glucocorticoid excess on bone?
column4: Glucocorticoids inhibit osteoblast activity, decrease intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption, and increase renal Ca²⁺ excretion, leading to bone loss — a major side effect of chronic steroid therapy.

column1: Which enzyme in osteoclasts generates H⁺ ions used to dissolve hydroxyapatite during bone resorption?
column4: Carbonic anhydrase II converts CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; the H⁺ is pumped into the resorption pit by H⁺-ATPase, acidifying it to dissolve mineral.

column1: What are the three main layers of the skin from superficial to deep?
column4: The epidermis is the outermost avascular layer, the dermis contains connective tissue and appendages, and the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) is the deepest fatty layer.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skin_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skin-system::structure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which layer of the skin is avascular (lacks blood vessels)?
column4: The epidermis receives nutrients by diffusion from the dermis. Its avascular nature means wounds limited to the epidermis do not bleed.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skin_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skin-system::structure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of tissue makes up the dermis?
column4: The dermis consists mainly of collagen and elastin fibers arranged irregularly, providing strength and elasticity to skin.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skin_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skin-system::structure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which layer of skin contains hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands?
column4: These appendages originate in the dermis and may extend into the hypodermis, allowing them to be vascularized and innervated.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skin_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skin-system::structure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the hypodermis primarily composed of?
column3: Adipose tissue and loose connective tissue
column4: The hypodermis anchors the skin to underlying muscle and bone and stores energy as fat; it is not considered a true skin layer by all sources but is functionally integral.
column8: concept::BB::3B::skin_system MCAT::section::BB MCAT::3B::skin-system::structure MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the five layers of the epidermis from deep to superficial?
column4: Mnemonic: 'Baby Sharks Get Lost Constantly.' The stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin (palms, soles).

column1: Which epidermal layer contains stem cells that continuously divide to replenish the epidermis?
column4: Mitotically active keratinocytes in the stratum basale push daughter cells superficially as they differentiate and eventually die.

column1: What is the predominant cell type of the epidermis?
column4: Keratinocytes produce keratin, a fibrous structural protein that contributes to the skin's protective barrier and water-impermeability.

column1: Which epidermal cell type functions in immune surveillance and antigen presentation?
column4: Langerhans cells are dendritic cells residing in the stratum spinosum; they capture antigens and migrate to lymph nodes to activate T cells.

column1: Which cell type in the stratum basale produces melanin?
column4: Melanocytes transfer melanin granules to surrounding keratinocytes via dendritic processes; melanin absorbs UV radiation protecting DNA.

column1: In which epidermal layer do keratinocytes first show keratohyalin granules indicating terminal differentiation?
column4: Keratohyalin granules contain profilaggrin and loricrin; as cells move into the stratum corneum they die and are filled with keratin.

column1: What mechanoreceptor cell found in the stratum basale detects light touch?
column4: Merkel cells synapse with sensory nerve endings to convey fine-touch and pressure information; they are among the few non-keratinocyte cells in the basal layer.

column1: What structural feature of the stratum corneum makes the skin relatively impermeable to water?
column3: Cornified (dead) keratinocytes embedded in lipid lamellae
column4: Lamellar bodies in the stratum granulosum secrete lipids (ceramides, cholesterol, fatty acids) forming a 'brick-and-mortar' barrier that resists water movement.

column1: What protein fills cells of the stratum corneum to create a water-resistant barrier?
column4: Cross-linked keratin fibers pack the cytoplasm of cornified cells; combined with intercellular lipids, this minimizes transepidermal water loss (TEWL).

column1: What term describes water loss through the skin that is not sweating?
column4: TEWL is the passive diffusion of water through the epidermal barrier; it increases dramatically when the stratum corneum is damaged (e.g., burns, eczema).

column1: Which lipids secreted by lamellar bodies are most critical for epidermal water-barrier function?
column4: Ceramides are the most abundant lipid in the stratum corneum intercellular space; deficiency (as in atopic dermatitis) disrupts the barrier and increases TEWL.

column1: Why can some small, lipid-soluble drugs be administered transdermally?
column3: They can diffuse through the lipid-rich stratum corneum
column4: Lipid-soluble (nonpolar) molecules can penetrate the skin's lipid lamellae; this route bypasses first-pass metabolism (e.g., nitroglycerin patch).

column1: How does the skin contribute to osmoregulation?
column3: By regulating water and electrolyte loss through sweating
column4: Sweat glands can adjust sweat output; in heat, copious sweat is produced. Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption from sweat ducts, conserving electrolytes.

column1: Which hormone acts on sweat gland ducts to reabsorb sodium and help maintain plasma osmolarity?
column4: Like in the kidney, aldosterone stimulates Na+/K+ ATPase in sweat duct cells, reducing NaCl content of final sweat and conserving blood volume.

column1: How does the skin participate in calcium homeostasis?
column3: Via UV-driven synthesis of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
column4: UV-B converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin to previtamin D3, which isomerizes to vitamin D3; activated vitamin D3 increases intestinal Ca2+ absorption.

column1: What precursor molecule in the skin is converted to vitamin D by UV light?
column4: 7-dehydrocholesterol is photolyzed in the stratum spinosum/basale to previtamin D3, which then undergoes thermal isomerization to vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol).

column1: What is the primary mechanism by which the skin dissipates body heat when core temperature rises?
column4: Eccrine sweat glands secrete hypotonic fluid; evaporation of water from the skin surface carries away heat, cooling the body.

column1: Which division of the autonomic nervous system stimulates eccrine sweat glands?
column4: Unlike most sympathetic effectors that use norepinephrine, eccrine sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic postganglionic fibers that release acetylcholine.

column1: How does vasodilation of dermal capillaries aid thermoregulation?
column3: Increases heat loss by radiation and convection from skin surface
column4: When core temperature rises, sympathetic vasodilator signals reduce arteriolar tone in the dermis, shunting warm blood to the skin surface for heat dissipation.

column1: What is the role of piloerection in thermoregulation in humans vs. other mammals?
column3: Minimal in humans; in furry mammals it traps air for insulation
column4: Arrector pili muscle contraction raises hair follicles ('goosebumps'), which has negligible insulating effect in humans due to sparse body hair.

column1: What is the term for blood vessel shunts in the skin that bypass capillaries to rapidly reduce or increase heat loss?
column4: AVAs are direct connections between arterioles and venules in the dermis; when open, they allow large blood flow near the skin surface for heat dissipation; when closed, they conserve heat.

column1: What muscle is associated with each hair follicle and causes piloerection?
column4: The arrector pili is a small band of smooth muscle; contraction (triggered by sympathetic norepinephrine) pulls the follicle upright, producing goosebumps.

column1: What neurotransmitter causes contraction of the arrector pili muscle?
column4: Arrector pili are innervated by sympathetic adrenergic fibers; contraction occurs with cold or emotional stress (fight-or-flight).

column1: What part of the hair follicle contains stem cells that allow hair to regenerate?
column4: The bulge is a reservoir of epithelial stem cells in the outer root sheath near the arrector pili attachment; these cells cycle to regenerate the hair matrix.

column1: What type of gland is associated with hair follicles and secretes sebum?
column4: Sebaceous glands are holocrine glands; the entire cell disintegrates to release sebum, which lubricates the hair shaft and skin surface and has mild antimicrobial properties.

column1: What is the primary role of the subcutaneous fat layer (hypodermis) in thermoregulation?
column3: Thermal insulation — reduces heat loss to the environment
column4: Adipose tissue has low thermal conductivity, slowing heat loss from the body core; thicker fat layers (as in cold-climate animals) provide better insulation.

column1: What additional function does the fat layer of the hypodermis serve besides insulation?
column4: Triglycerides stored in adipocytes are a long-term fuel reserve; the fat also absorbs mechanical shocks protecting underlying structures.

column1: Which adipokine secreted by subcutaneous adipose tissue regulates appetite and energy balance?
column4: Leptin signals satiety to the hypothalamus; subcutaneous and visceral fat both secrete leptin, with levels proportional to fat mass.

column1: How does subcutaneous fat distribution differ between males and females on the MCAT?
column3: Females have more subcutaneous fat (gynoid); males more visceral (android)
column4: This sexually dimorphic distribution is mediated by sex hormones; gynoid fat is metabolically less harmful than visceral (android) fat.

column1: In which layer of the skin are eccrine sweat glands located?
column3: Dermis (body of gland in dermis; duct opens at skin surface)
column4: The secretory coil of eccrine glands sits deep in the reticular dermis or at the dermis-hypodermis junction; the duct spirals through the epidermis to the pore.

column1: What type of sweat gland is most numerous and responsible for thermoregulatory sweating?
column4: Eccrine glands are found all over the body (most dense on palms, soles, forehead); they produce hypotonic, watery sweat for evaporative cooling.

column1: What type of sweat gland is found primarily in the axillae and groin and becomes active at puberty?
column4: Apocrine glands secrete a protein-rich fluid into hair follicles; bacterial decomposition of this secretion produces body odor. They are regulated by emotional stimuli.

column1: What is the ionic composition of eccrine sweat relative to plasma?
column3: Hypotonic — lower NaCl concentration than plasma
column4: The secretory coil produces an isotonic primary secretion; the duct reabsorbs Na+ and Cl- (aided by aldosterone) making final sweat hypotonic.

column1: Which segment of the eccrine sweat duct reabsorbs sodium under aldosterone influence?
column4: Analogous to the renal distal tubule, the eccrine duct's principal cells express Na+ channels and Na+/K+ ATPase upregulated by aldosterone.

column1: Which type of secretion mechanism characterizes eccrine sweat glands?
column4: Eccrine glands release secretion by exocytosis without losing cellular material, unlike apocrine (budding) or holocrine (cell disintegration) secretion.

column1: What happens to dermal capillaries during vasodilation to increase heat loss?
column3: They dilate, increasing blood flow to the skin surface
column4: Sympathetic withdrawal (or active vasodilator signals) causes arteriolar smooth muscle to relax, increasing cutaneous blood flow and heat radiation.

column1: What happens to skin capillaries in response to cold to conserve body heat?
column3: Vasoconstriction — reduced blood flow to the skin
column4: Sympathetic adrenergic signals cause arteriolar smooth muscle contraction, diverting blood away from the skin surface to minimize heat loss.

column1: Which neurotransmitter mediates vasoconstriction of dermal capillaries?
column4: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine, activating alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle to cause contraction and vasoconstriction.

column1: What vasodilator substance released during inflammation causes redness and warmth of the skin?
column4: Histamine from mast cells acts on H1 receptors to dilate arterioles and increase capillary permeability, producing the classic signs of inflammation: rubor, calor.

column1: In Raynaud's phenomenon, what causes episodic vasospasm of skin vessels?
column3: Exaggerated sympathetic vasoconstriction triggered by cold or stress
column4: Excessive alpha-adrenergic response causes digital arteries to spasm, leading to color changes: white (ischemia) → blue (cyanosis) → red (reperfusion).

column1: What is the primary physical barrier function of the skin?
column3: Prevents entry of pathogens and loss of body fluids
column4: Intact skin with its keratinized epidermis and low pH surface (acid mantle) forms the first line of defense against microorganisms and dehydration.

column1: What is the acid mantle of the skin and why is it protective?
column3: Slightly acidic surface pH (~4.5–5.5) that inhibits bacterial growth
column4: Sebum and sweat combine to lower skin surface pH; most pathogens grow poorly in acidic environments, providing non-specific antimicrobial protection.

column1: Which skin protein provides mechanical strength against shear forces?
column4: The dense keratin network within corneocytes and the protein envelope of the stratum corneum resists mechanical abrasion and penetration.

column1: What role do melanocytes play in physical protection of the skin?
column3: Produce melanin to absorb UV radiation and protect DNA
column4: Melanin acts as a natural sunscreen; UV-B induces melanin production (tanning response), reducing DNA damage and risk of carcinogenesis in deeper layers.

column1: What is the function of nails in physical protection?
column3: Protect distal phalanges and enhance fine touch/manipulation
column4: Nails are hard keratin plates over the dorsal nail bed; they shield the fingertip, enable pinching of small objects, and can scratch pathogens from skin.

column1: What are calluses and what causes them to form?
column3: Thickened stratum corneum from repeated mechanical friction
column4: Chronic pressure triggers keratinocyte hyperproliferation; the resulting callus is a localized, painless thickening that protects against further abrasion.

column1: Which part of the nail is responsible for its growth?
column4: The nail matrix contains actively dividing keratinocytes that push forward to form the nail plate; the visible pale lunula marks the distal matrix.

column1: What type of keratin is found in nails vs. soft keratin in skin?
column3: Hard (alpha-) keratin with more disulfide bonds in nails
column4: Nail keratin has a higher cysteine content, forming more disulfide cross-links that make it rigid compared to the softer keratin of skin and hair cortex.

column1: What is the function of body hair in protection from the environment?
column3: Reduces UV exposure, traps debris, and senses touch via follicle nerve endings
column4: Facial and body hair provides modest UV shielding; follicle-associated mechanoreceptors (hair follicle receptors) detect movement before contact, aiding threat detection.

column1: How does intact skin protect against bacterial infection?
column3: Physical barrier + acid mantle + antimicrobial peptides + normal flora
column4: Defensins and cathelicidins secreted by keratinocytes kill microbes; commensal bacteria outcompete pathogens for nutrients and attachment sites.

column1: Which antimicrobial peptides are produced by keratinocytes?
column4: These peptides disrupt microbial membranes. Cathelicidins are deficient in atopic dermatitis, contributing to recurrent skin infections.

column1: How does the stratum corneum's constant shedding (desquamation) contribute to protection?
column3: Removes surface microorganisms before they colonize deeper layers
column4: Keratinocytes shed continuously via protease-mediated breakdown of corneodesmosomes, physically removing adherent bacteria and fungi from the skin surface.

column1: Why is the skin a poor entry route for most water-soluble pathogens?
column3: Lipid-rich stratum corneum blocks hydrophilic molecules and organisms
column4: Bacteria and most viruses cannot penetrate intact keratinized skin; breaks in the barrier (cuts, burns, insect bites) are required for most pathogens to enter.

column1: What is the role of Langerhans cells in skin protection against pathogens?
column3: Innate immune surveillance; capture antigens and activate adaptive immunity
column4: Langerhans cells are skin-resident dendritic cells; after encountering antigens, they migrate to draining lymph nodes and present antigen to naive T cells.

column1: Which hormone stimulates increased sweating to dissipate heat?
column3: Acetylcholine (sympathetic cholinergic signal, not a classic hormone)
column4: Thermoregulatory sweating is controlled by sympathetic cholinergic nerves; epinephrine from the adrenal medulla also stimulates eccrine glands during stress.

column1: Which hormone promotes sodium reabsorption from sweat gland ducts, reducing sweat NaCl concentration?
column4: Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) increases Na+ channel expression in sweat duct cells, analogous to its action in the renal distal tubule.

column1: Which catecholamine causes cutaneous vasoconstriction by activating alpha-1 adrenergic receptors?
column4: Sympathetic adrenergic tone maintains baseline vasoconstriction in skin; cold stress or hemorrhage increases norepinephrine release, maximizing vasoconstriction to conserve heat/blood pressure.

column1: How does epinephrine differ from norepinephrine in its effect on skin blood vessels?
column3: Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction at alpha-1 and vasodilation at beta-2; net effect is vasoconstriction in skin
column4: Skin arterioles have predominantly alpha-1 receptors; at physiological concentrations, epinephrine's alpha-1 effect dominates, causing cutaneous vasoconstriction during fight-or-flight.

column1: Which prostaglandins contribute to vasodilation and increased skin blood flow during inflammation?
column4: Prostaglandins E2 and I2 relax vascular smooth muscle and sensitize nociceptors; NSAIDs block their synthesis via COX inhibition, reducing inflammatory vasodilation.

column1: What hormone excess causes hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating) in hyperthyroidism?
column4: Thyroid hormones increase basal metabolic rate and heat production; the body compensates with increased sweating. Hyperhidrosis is a classic symptom of hyperthyroidism.

column1: What are the SI base units for length, mass, and time?
column4: These three SI base units (m, kg, s) underpin nearly all mechanics quantities tested on the MCAT.

column1: What is the SI unit of force?
column4: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². Force = mass × acceleration, so its unit is derived from kg, m, and s.

column1: What is the SI unit of energy?
column4: 1 J = 1 kg·m²/s² = 1 N·m. Both work and energy are measured in joules.

column1: What is the dimension of pressure in SI base units?
column4: Pressure = Force/Area = (kg·m/s²)/m² = kg/(m·s²). The SI unit pascal equals this.

column1: What is the dimension of velocity in SI base units?
column4: Velocity = displacement/time; its dimension is length per time, i.e., m/s.

column1: What is the SI unit of power?
column4: 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 kg·m²/s³. Power is rate of energy transfer.

column1: How many centimeters are in one meter?
column4: The prefix 'centi-' denotes 10⁻². This conversion is fundamental for unit analysis on the MCAT.

column1: What prefix denotes 10⁻³ in SI?
column4: Examples: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m; 1 mL = 10⁻³ L. Distinguishing milli- (10⁻³) from micro- (10⁻⁶) is a common source of error.

column1: Which SI prefix corresponds to 10⁻⁶?
column4: Example: 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m. Used frequently in biology contexts (cell sizes, drug doses).

column1: What is dimensional analysis used for in physics problems?
column4: If the units on both sides of an equation do not match, the equation is incorrect. Dimensional analysis is a powerful error-checking tool.

column1: What distinguishes a vector from a scalar quantity?
column3: Vectors have magnitude AND direction; scalars have magnitude only
column4: Examples of vectors: displacement, velocity, force. Examples of scalars: speed, distance, mass, temperature.

column1: Is speed a vector or scalar quantity?
column4: Speed is the magnitude of velocity; it has no directional information. Velocity is the corresponding vector.

column1: How do you find the x-component of a vector A at angle θ above the horizontal?
column4: The x-component uses cosine of the angle from the horizontal; y-component uses sine. Remember: CAH-SOH-TOA.

column1: How do you find the y-component of a vector A at angle θ above the horizontal?
column4: Sine gives the component opposite the angle (vertical here). Cosine gives the adjacent component (horizontal).

column1: What is the magnitude of a 2D vector with components Aₓ and Aᵧ?
column4: This follows directly from the Pythagorean theorem applied to the right triangle formed by the components.

column1: What angle does a vector make with the x-axis if Aₓ = 3 and Aᵧ = 3?
column4: θ = arctan(Aᵧ/Aₓ) = arctan(1) = 45°. Equal components always yield a 45° angle.

column1: What is a unit vector?
column4: Unit vectors indicate direction only. They are often used to express the direction of a larger vector (e.g., î, ĵ, k̂ along x, y, z axes).

column1: If a vector points at 180° from the positive x-axis, what are its x and y components relative to its magnitude A?
column4: cos 180° = −1 and sin 180° = 0, so the vector points entirely in the negative x-direction.

column1: What is the commutative property of vector addition?
column4: The order of adding vectors does not affect the resultant. Graphically this is seen with the parallelogram or tip-to-tail method.

column1: Describe the tip-to-tail (head-to-tail) method of vector addition.
column3: Place the tail of B at the tip of A; resultant goes from tail of A to tip of B
column4: This graphical method works for any number of vectors. The resultant closes the polygon formed by successive vectors.

column1: How do you subtract vector B from vector A using vector addition?
column4: Reversing B's direction (negating it) and then adding gives the difference. −B has the same magnitude as B but opposite direction.

column1: When adding vectors analytically, how do you find the x-component of the resultant?
column4: R_x = A_x + B_x + … This component-wise addition is the standard algebraic method for vector addition.
