column1: What is the resultant magnitude when two equal vectors of magnitude F are added at 90° to each other?
column4: |R| = √(F² + F²) = F√2 ≈ 1.41F. A common MCAT scenario (e.g., two equal perpendicular forces).

column1: What is the maximum possible magnitude of the sum of two vectors each of magnitude 5?
column4: Maximum resultant occurs when both vectors point in the same direction: |R|_max = |A| + |B|.

column1: What is the minimum possible magnitude of the sum of two vectors each of magnitude 5?
column4: Minimum resultant occurs when vectors are antiparallel (opposite directions): |R|_min = ||A| − |B|| = 0 for equal magnitudes.

column1: What is the resultant direction when two perpendicular vectors of magnitudes 3 and 4 are added?
column4: This is the classic 3-4-5 right triangle. The angle is arctan(opposite/adjacent).

column1: What is the associative property of vector addition?
column4: Grouping does not matter in vector addition. This allows solving multi-vector problems in any convenient order.

column1: Define average speed.
column3: Total distance traveled divided by total time
column4: Average speed = d_total / t_total. Unlike average velocity, it uses path length (scalar), not displacement.

column1: Define average velocity.
column3: Total displacement divided by total time elapsed
column4: v_avg = Δx / Δt. It is a vector; direction matches net displacement. Can differ greatly from average speed.

column1: Define instantaneous velocity.
column3: Velocity at a specific instant; limit of Δx/Δt as Δt → 0
column4: Mathematically it is the derivative dx/dt. On a position-time graph, it equals the slope of the tangent line at that point.

column1: A runner completes a 400 m lap in 50 s. What is the average velocity?
column4: Starting and ending at the same point means net displacement = 0, so average velocity = 0 even though average speed = 8 m/s.

column1: On a position-time graph, what does the slope represent?
column4: Slope = Δx/Δt = velocity. A steeper slope means higher speed; a negative slope means motion in the negative direction.

column1: On a position-time graph, what does a horizontal line (zero slope) indicate?
column4: No change in position over time means zero velocity. This is an easy question but frequently appears in data interpretation.

column1: Can an object have nonzero speed but zero average velocity? Give an example.
column3: Yes — circular motion or round trip back to start
column4: If displacement is zero but distance is nonzero, average speed > 0 while average velocity = 0.

column1: What is the SI unit of velocity?
column4: Velocity is displacement per unit time; its SI unit is meters per second. This is both a vector and its unit is m/s.

column1: How does instantaneous speed relate to instantaneous velocity?
column3: Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity
column4: Speed is always ≥ 0; velocity can be negative. This mirrors the scalar vs. vector distinction.

column1: Define acceleration.
column3: Rate of change of velocity with respect to time
column4: a = Δv / Δt. Acceleration is a vector; its direction matches the direction of the velocity change, not necessarily the direction of motion.

column1: What are the SI units of acceleration?
column4: Acceleration = change in velocity / time = (m/s)/s = m/s². Recognizing this unit quickly is important for dimensional analysis.

column1: On a velocity-time graph, what does the slope represent?
column4: Slope = Δv/Δt = acceleration. A positive slope means speeding up (in positive direction); negative slope means slowing down or reversing.

column1: What is the approximate value of gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface?
column4: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² directed downward. The MCAT often permits using g = 10 m/s² for easier arithmetic.

column1: Can an object have zero velocity but nonzero acceleration?
column4: At the top of a vertical throw, velocity = 0 but acceleration = g downward. This is a classic MCAT conceptual question.

column1: Can an object accelerate while moving at constant speed?
column3: Yes — if direction changes (e.g., uniform circular motion)
column4: Acceleration requires changing velocity (magnitude or direction). Speed unchanged but direction changing still constitutes acceleration.

column1: What is the kinematic equation relating final velocity to initial velocity, acceleration, and time?
column4: This is one of the four standard kinematics equations. It applies when acceleration is constant.

column1: What is the kinematic equation for displacement using initial velocity, acceleration, and time?
column4: Derived by integrating v = v₀ + at. The ½at² term accounts for the acceleration contribution to displacement.

column1: What kinematic equation relates velocity, initial velocity, acceleration, and displacement without time?
column4: Useful when time is unknown. Derived by combining v = v₀ + at and x = v₀t + ½at².

column1: What does a negative acceleration (deceleration) mean when an object moves in the positive direction?
column4: When acceleration opposes the direction of motion, the object decelerates. 'Deceleration' simply means acceleration opposite to velocity direction.

column1: On a velocity-time graph, what does the area under the curve represent?
column4: Area = ∫v dt = displacement. For constant acceleration this gives a trapezoid or triangle whose area equals net displacement.

column1: What does Newton's First Law state about an object at rest?
column3: Remains at rest unless acted upon by net force
column4: An object at rest stays at rest if the net external force on it is zero. This is the principle of inertia for stationary objects.

column1: What does Newton's First Law state about an object in motion?
column3: Continues at constant velocity unless net force acts
column4: An object moving at constant velocity (including direction) will continue so indefinitely in the absence of a net external force — the hallmark of inertia.

column1: What property of matter is described by Newton's First Law?
column4: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes to its state of motion. It is quantified by mass.

column1: Which quantity measures the inertia of an object?
column4: The greater an object's mass, the greater its inertia and the more force is required to change its velocity. Inertia has no separate unit — it scales directly with mass (kg).

column1: A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly. Which law explains this?
column4: The passenger's body tends to continue moving forward at the original speed when the bus decelerates — a classic demonstration of inertia.

column1: What condition must be true for Newton's First Law to apply exactly?
column4: Newton's First Law holds only in inertial reference frames. In non-inertial frames, pseudo-forces appear that complicate the analysis.

column1: State the mathematical form of Newton's Second Law.
column4: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. Both F and a are vectors; acceleration is in the same direction as net force.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::newton-s-second-law-f-ma MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If the net force on an object doubles while mass stays constant, what happens to acceleration?
column4: From F = ma, acceleration is directly proportional to net force at constant mass. Doubling F doubles a.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::newton-s-second-law-f-ma MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If mass doubles while net force stays constant, what happens to acceleration?
column4: a = F/m; acceleration is inversely proportional to mass at constant net force. Doubling m halves a.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::newton-s-second-law-f-ma MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the net force on a 5 kg object accelerating at 3 m/s²?
column4: F = ma = 5 kg × 3 m/s² = 15 N. Straightforward application of Newton's Second Law.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::newton-s-second-law-f-ma MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In Newton's Second Law, what does 'F' represent?
column4: Only the vector sum of all forces acting on the object — not any individual force — produces the acceleration. This is a common source of error on the MCAT.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::newton-s-second-law-f-ma MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the weight (gravitational force) of a 70 kg person on Earth (g = 10 m/s²)?
column4: W = mg = 70 kg × 10 m/s² = 700 N. Weight is a force, measured in newtons, distinct from mass (kg).
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::newton-s-second-law-f-ma MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which form of Newton's Second Law applies when mass is constant versus when mass changes?
column3: F = ma (constant mass); F = dp/dt (changing mass)
column4: The more general form is F = dp/dt (rate of change of momentum). F = ma is derived assuming constant mass, valid for most MCAT scenarios.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::newton-s-second-law-f-ma MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State Newton's Third Law in words.
column3: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
column4: When object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal in magnitude, opposite in direction force on object A. The two forces act on different objects.

column1: Newton's Third Law force pairs always act on how many objects?
column4: Action and reaction forces never act on the same object, so they cannot cancel each other. Each force of the pair acts on a different body.

column1: A swimmer pushes backward on the water. In which direction does the water push the swimmer?
column4: Newton's Third Law: the water exerts a reaction force on the swimmer equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the swimmer's push — propelling the swimmer forward.

column1: Are Newton's Third Law force pairs equal in magnitude even when the objects have very different masses?
column4: A car hits a bug: the force the car exerts on the bug equals the force the bug exerts on the car. The accelerations differ because the masses differ (a = F/m).

column1: Why don't Newton's Third Law force pairs cancel to give zero net force?
column4: Cancellation of forces (Newton's First or Second Law) requires forces on the same object. Third Law pairs are on separate bodies, so each body has its own net force analysis.

column1: What are the four characteristics shared by every Newton's Third Law pair?
column3: Equal magnitude, opposite direction, same type, different objects
column4: Third Law pairs are the same type of interaction (both normal, both gravitational, etc.), equal in size, opposite in direction, and each acts on a different body.

column1: Define static friction.
column3: Friction preventing relative motion between surfaces at rest
column4: Static friction is a reactive force that adjusts up to a maximum value (f_s ≤ μ_s N) to keep two surfaces from sliding. It acts before any sliding occurs.

column1: Define kinetic friction.
column3: Friction acting between surfaces already sliding
column4: Kinetic friction opposes the direction of sliding motion and has a constant magnitude f_k = μ_k N, independent of sliding speed for most MCAT purposes.

column1: What is the formula for the maximum static friction force?
column4: μ_s is the coefficient of static friction and N is the normal force. The actual static friction can be anywhere from zero up to this maximum.

column1: Which is typically larger: the coefficient of static friction or kinetic friction for the same surfaces?
column4: It takes more force to start an object sliding than to keep it sliding — so μ_s > μ_k for nearly all surface pairs. This is a commonly tested distinction.

column1: On what does kinetic friction force depend?
column3: Coefficient of kinetic friction and normal force
column4: f_k = μ_k N. Notably, kinetic friction does NOT depend on the area of contact or the speed of sliding (in the standard MCAT model).

column1: A block rests on a horizontal surface with a horizontal applied force less than f_s(max). What is the net force on the block?
column4: Static friction exactly matches the applied force (up to its maximum), so the block stays at rest with zero net force — an application of Newton's First Law.

column1: How does friction force change when a block on a flat surface is tilted to increase the normal force?
column4: Both f_s(max) and f_k are proportional to N. Increasing the normal force (e.g., pressing harder) increases the maximum available friction force by the same factor.

column1: On an inclined plane at angle θ, what is the normal force on a block of mass m?
column4: The normal force balances the component of gravity perpendicular to the incline. This is distinct from mg, which is the total gravitational force.

column1: Define the center of mass of a system.
column3: Weighted average position of all mass in the system
column4: r_cm = Σ(m_i r_i) / Σm_i. It is the single point where the net external force can be considered to act for translational motion.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Where is the center of mass of a uniform, symmetric object?
column4: For a uniform sphere, cylinder, or rectangular block, symmetry ensures equal mass on all sides of the geometric center, placing the center of mass there.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What happens to the center of mass of a system when no external forces act?
column3: It remains stationary (or moves at constant velocity)
column4: By Newton's First Law applied to the system, the center of mass velocity is unchanged if net external force is zero — even if internal forces cause parts to move.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How is the center of mass of a two-body system (masses m1 and m2 at positions x1 and x2) calculated?
column4: The center of mass is closer to the heavier mass. For equal masses, x_cm = (x1 + x2)/2, the midpoint.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A 60 kg person stands 1 m from a 30 kg child on a seesaw. Where is the center of mass from the person?
column4: x_cm = (60×0 + 30×1)/(60+30) = 30/90 = 0.33 m. The center of mass lies closer to the heavier person.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Can the center of mass of an object lie outside its physical boundaries?
column4: A donut or boomerang has its center of mass in the empty space at its center. This is possible whenever mass is distributed non-uniformly or in a non-convex shape.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: For a system of two people on a frictionless ice rink who push apart, what is true of their center of mass?
column4: No external horizontal force acts on the system, so the center of mass cannot accelerate. The two individuals move in opposite directions such that m1v1 = –m2v2.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does the center of mass relate to torque and rotational equilibrium on the MCAT?
column3: Weight acts at the center of mass; torque = weight × lever arm from pivot
column4: For static equilibrium problems, gravity acts as a single downward force at the center of mass. Balancing torques about a pivot uses this position to find the lever arm.
column8: concept::CP::4A::force MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::force::center-of-mass MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the condition for translational equilibrium of a point object?
column4: When the vector sum of all forces acting on an object is zero, the object is in translational equilibrium and has no linear acceleration.

column1: What does it mean for a point object to be in static equilibrium?
column3: Object is at rest with net force = 0
column4: Static equilibrium requires both zero net force (no translation) and, for extended objects, zero net torque (no rotation).

column1: When resolving forces on a point object, what two components are each force broken into?
column4: Using trigonometry, Fx = F cosθ and Fy = F sinθ, where θ is measured from the horizontal. The net of each component set must equal zero for equilibrium.

column1: What formula gives the x-component of a force F at angle θ from the horizontal?
column4: The cosine function projects the force onto the horizontal axis. For equilibrium, ΣFx = 0 must hold simultaneously with ΣFy = 0.

column1: If three concurrent forces keep a point object in equilibrium, what geometric relationship do their vectors form when drawn tip-to-tail?
column4: For any number of forces in equilibrium, their vectors arranged tip-to-tail form a closed polygon, meaning the resultant is zero.

column1: A point object is suspended by two ropes making angles θ₁ and θ₂ with the horizontal. Which equilibrium equations are used to find the tensions?
column4: T₁cosθ₁ = T₂cosθ₂ (horizontal) and T₁sinθ₁ + T₂sinθ₂ = mg (vertical), yielding two equations for two unknowns.

column1: As the angle a supporting rope makes with the horizontal decreases toward zero, what happens to the tension in that rope?
column4: T = W/(sinθ); as θ→0, sinθ→0, so T→∞. Ropes oriented nearly horizontally must carry enormous tension to support any vertical load.

column1: What is the resultant of two equal forces acting on a point object at 120° to each other?
column3: A force equal in magnitude to either force
column4: Using the parallelogram law with 120° between vectors of equal magnitude F, the resultant = F. This arises because the triangle formed is equilateral.

column1: When a point object is on a frictionless inclined plane, which two forces act on it?
column4: On a frictionless surface, only the perpendicular normal force and gravity act. For the object to be in equilibrium a third force (e.g., tension) must also be present to balance the net of the other two.

column1: Define torque.
column3: Force times perpendicular lever arm (τ = r × F)
column4: Torque measures the rotational effect of a force. Only the component of force perpendicular to the position vector (or equivalently, the perpendicular distance from the pivot) produces torque.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the SI unit of torque?
column4: Although N·m is dimensionally equivalent to joules, torque is not energy and the units are kept distinct to avoid confusion.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Define lever arm (moment arm).
column3: Perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action of force
column4: The lever arm is the shortest distance between the axis of rotation and the line along which the force acts. τ = F × lever arm.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the condition for rotational equilibrium?
column4: For an object to be in complete static equilibrium, both ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 must be satisfied about any chosen pivot point.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In a first-class lever, where is the fulcrum relative to the effort and load?
column3: Between the effort and the load
column4: A seesaw is a classic first-class lever. The mechanical advantage depends on the ratio of the effort arm to the load arm.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the mechanical advantage of a lever?
column3: MA = load arm length / effort arm length (or effort / load force)
column4: A longer effort arm relative to the load arm multiplies the applied force (MA > 1), while a shorter effort arm reduces force but increases speed/distance.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: When calculating torque, if the force is applied at angle θ to the lever arm, what is the torque?
column4: Only the perpendicular component of force (F sinθ) produces torque. A force applied parallel to the lever arm (θ = 0°) produces zero torque.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Can the pivot point for applying Στ = 0 be chosen freely in a static equilibrium problem?
column3: Yes, any point can serve as the pivot
column4: In static equilibrium the net torque is zero about every point. Choosing the pivot at an unknown force's location eliminates that force from the torque equation, simplifying calculation.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In a second-class lever, where is the load relative to the effort and fulcrum?
column3: Between the fulcrum and the effort
column4: Second-class levers (e.g., wheelbarrow) always have MA > 1. The load is between the pivot and the applied effort force.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What distinguishes a third-class lever from first and second class?
column3: Effort is between the fulcrum and the load
column4: Third-class levers (e.g., forearm bicep curl) have MA < 1 — they sacrifice force for speed and range of motion. The effort arm is always shorter than the load arm.
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If a uniform horizontal beam of mass M and length L is supported at one end and by a wire at angle θ at the other end, what is the tension T in the wire?
column4: Taking torques about the supported end: T sinθ · L = Mg · L/2, so T = Mg/(2sinθ). Gravity acts at the center of mass (L/2 for uniform beam).
column8: concept::CP::4A::equilibrium MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::equilibrium::torques-lever-arms MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the formula for work done by a constant force?
column4: W is work in joules, F is the magnitude of the force, d is the displacement, and θ is the angle between the force vector and the displacement vector.

column1: What is the SI unit of work?
column4: One joule equals one newton times one meter (N·m). Work and energy share the same unit.

column1: What value of θ (angle between force and displacement) gives maximum positive work?
column4: When force is parallel to displacement, cosθ = 1, so work is maximized. At 90°, cosθ = 0 and no work is done.

column1: What is the work done by a force perpendicular to displacement?
column4: cos 90° = 0, so W = Fd cos90° = 0. A centripetal force, for example, does no work because it is always perpendicular to velocity.

column1: When is work done by a force negative?
column4: cosθ is negative for angles in the second quadrant, so work is negative when force and displacement have components in opposite directions (e.g., friction opposing motion).

column1: A 10 N force is applied at 60° to horizontal to move a box 5 m horizontally. What is the work done?
column4: W = (10)(5)cos60° = 50 × 0.5 = 25 J. Only the component of force along the displacement does work.

column1: What is the work done by gravity when a 2 kg object falls 3 m vertically?
column4: W = mgh = (2)(9.8)(3) = 58.8 J. Gravity does positive work when the object moves in the direction of gravitational force (downward).

column1: If a force of 50 N acts on an object but the object does not move, how much work is done?
column4: W = Fd cosθ; if displacement d = 0, then W = 0 regardless of the force applied. Isometric muscle contractions produce force but do no mechanical work.

column1: Define mechanical advantage (MA).
column3: Output force divided by input force
column4: MA = F_out / F_in. A MA > 1 means the machine multiplies force; a MA < 1 means the machine multiplies speed/distance instead.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the ideal mechanical advantage (IMA) of a lever in terms of arm lengths?
column4: The longer the effort arm relative to the resistance arm, the greater the force multiplication. A crowbar is a classic first-class lever example.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the trade-off when a simple machine provides a mechanical advantage greater than 1?
column3: Greater input distance (or smaller output distance)
column4: Work in = Work out (ideal machine). If output force is multiplied, output displacement is reduced proportionally: F_in × d_in = F_out × d_out.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the mechanical advantage of an inclined plane of length L and height h?
column4: The slope reduces the required force to move an object to height h, but the object must travel the full length L of the ramp.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does the number of rope segments supporting the load relate to mechanical advantage in a pulley system?
column3: MA equals the number of supporting rope segments
column4: Each rope segment bears an equal share of the load. A single movable pulley has 2 supporting segments, giving MA = 2.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why does friction reduce the actual mechanical advantage below the ideal mechanical advantage?
column3: Friction converts some input work to heat
column4: Actual MA = F_out / F_in < IMA because extra input force must overcome friction. Efficiency = Actual MA / IMA × 100%.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A pulley system has 4 supporting rope segments. What minimum force is needed to lift a 200 N load (frictionless)?
column4: MA = 4, so F_in = F_out / MA = 200 / 4 = 50 N. The input rope must be pulled 4× the distance the load rises.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A first-class lever has an effort arm of 3 m and a resistance arm of 1 m. What is its IMA?
column4: IMA = effort arm / resistance arm = 3/1 = 3. The fulcrum is between the effort and load in a first-class lever.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::mechanical-advantage MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State the Work-Kinetic Energy Theorem.
column3: Net work equals change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE)
column4: W_net = KE_final − KE_initial = ½mv² − ½mv₀². This theorem relates the net work done on an object to its change in motion.

column1: What is the formula for kinetic energy?
column4: Kinetic energy depends on mass (kg) and speed squared (m²/s²), giving units of joules. It is always non-negative.

column1: If the net work done on an object is zero, what happens to its speed?
column4: By the Work-Kinetic Energy Theorem, W_net = ΔKE = 0 means KE is unchanged, so speed does not change (though direction may).

column1: A 4 kg object accelerates from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. What is the net work done on it?
column4: W_net = ½(4)(5²) − ½(4)(3²) = 50 − 18 = 32 J. The Work-Kinetic Energy Theorem gives this directly without needing force or distance separately.

column1: How does the Work-Kinetic Energy Theorem differ from conservation of energy?
column3: W-KE applies net work to KE only; conservation includes all energy forms
column4: The Work-KE Theorem relates net work to ΔKE alone. Conservation of energy accounts for KE, PE, heat, and other forms — it is broader.

column1: A car brakes to a stop. Using the Work-Kinetic Energy Theorem, what can be said about work done by friction?
column3: Friction does negative work equal to initial KE
column4: W_friction = ΔKE = 0 − ½mv² = −½mv². Friction does negative work (opposes displacement), removing kinetic energy from the car.

column1: If an object's speed doubles, by what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
column4: KE ∝ v², so doubling speed quadruples KE. This is a commonly tested relationship on the MCAT.

column1: A 2 kg object is pushed by a net force of 6 N over 9 m. What is its final speed if it starts from rest?
column4: W_net = Fd = 6×9 = 54 J. ΔKE = 54 J = ½(2)v², so v² = 54, v ≈ 7.35 m/s. Demonstrates W-KE Theorem application.

column1: Define a conservative force.
column3: A force whose work is path-independent (depends only on start and end points)
column4: For conservative forces, work done along any path between two points is equal. Equivalently, work around any closed path is zero.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Name two examples of conservative forces.
column4: Gravity and ideal spring forces are conservative — they store and release energy as potential energy. Friction is a classic non-conservative force.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What quantity is associated with conservative forces that is not associated with non-conservative forces?
column4: Conservative forces can be associated with a potential energy function (e.g., gravitational PE = mgh, elastic PE = ½kx²). Non-conservative forces like friction cannot.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Is friction a conservative or non-conservative force?
column4: Friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy; work done by friction depends on path length, not just endpoints. More path = more work lost.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the relationship between conservative force and potential energy mathematically?
column3: F = −dU/dx (force is negative gradient of PE)
column4: In one dimension, the conservative force equals the negative derivative of potential energy with respect to position. This means force points in the direction of decreasing PE.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How is total mechanical energy conserved when only conservative forces act?
column4: If no non-conservative forces do work, E_total = KE + PE remains constant throughout the motion. This is the principle of conservation of mechanical energy.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What happens to mechanical energy when a non-conservative force like friction acts?
column4: W_non-conservative = ΔE_mechanical = ΔKE + ΔPE. Friction removes mechanical energy from the system, converting it to internal (thermal) energy.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: For a conservative force, what is the net work done over a complete closed-loop path?
column4: This is the defining property of conservative forces. Any work done going out is exactly recovered coming back, making the net round-trip work equal to zero.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Is the normal force conservative or non-conservative?
column4: The normal force is always perpendicular to displacement, so it does zero work (W = Fd cos90° = 0). It cannot be classified as conservative or non-conservative in the usual sense.
column8: concept::CP::4A::work MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4A::work::conservative-forces MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the formula for kinetic energy of a point object?
column4: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and the square of velocity; doubling speed quadruples KE while doubling mass only doubles KE.

column1: What are the SI units of kinetic energy?
column4: 1 J = 1 kg·m²/s². Since KE = ½mv², units are kg·(m/s)² = kg·m²/s² = J.

column1: If an object's speed doubles, by what factor does its kinetic energy change?
column4: KE ∝ v², so doubling v multiplies KE by 2² = 4. This quadratic relationship is a common MCAT trap.

column1: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
column4: KE = ½(2)(3²) = ½(2)(9) = 9 J. Always square the velocity before multiplying.

column1: Can kinetic energy ever be negative?
column4: KE = ½mv² involves v², which is always non-negative, and mass is always positive, so KE ≥ 0.

column1: What is the relationship between net work done on an object and its kinetic energy?
column3: Net work = change in KE (Work-Energy Theorem)
column4: W_net = ΔKE = KE_final − KE_initial. This is the work-energy theorem and is critical for solving force/motion problems without kinematics.

column1: An object's mass is halved and its speed is doubled. How does its KE change?
column4: New KE = ½(m/2)(2v)² = ½(m/2)(4v²) = mv² = 2·(½mv²). So KE increases by a factor of 2.

column1: What is potential energy?
column3: Stored energy due to position or configuration
column4: Potential energy is not associated with motion but with an object's state or arrangement relative to a reference point or force field.

column1: Name the two types of potential energy most commonly tested on the MCAT.
column4: Gravitational PE = mgh; elastic PE = ½kx². Both are forms of stored energy that can be converted to kinetic energy.

column1: Which type of potential energy is relevant when a muscle stretches a tendon?
column4: Tendons and springs store elastic PE when deformed; this energy can be released to do mechanical work (e.g., during running).

column1: What reference point is typically used for gravitational potential energy in MCAT problems?
column3: An arbitrary chosen reference point (often the ground or lowest point)
column4: Only changes in PE matter physically; the absolute value depends on the chosen reference. Setting the reference at the lowest point simplifies calculations.

column1: In which direction does an object spontaneously move relative to a potential energy gradient?
column4: Objects naturally move to minimize potential energy (e.g., falling downward in a gravitational field), analogous to electrons moving toward lower electric potential energy.

column1: What does it mean for a force to be 'conservative' in the context of potential energy?
column3: Work done is path-independent; PE can be defined
column4: Gravity and spring forces are conservative — only the starting and ending positions matter, not the path taken. Friction is non-conservative.

column1: What is the formula for gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface?
column4: m = mass (kg), g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (often approximated as 10 m/s² on the MCAT), h = height above reference point (m).

column1: What value of g is used in MCAT calculations for gravitational PE?
column4: The MCAT commonly rounds g to 10 m/s² for easier arithmetic. Always check if the passage specifies a value.

column1: A 5 kg object is lifted 4 m above the ground. What is its gravitational PE? (use g = 10 m/s²)
column4: PE = mgh = 5 × 10 × 4 = 200 J. This energy would equal the KE gained if the object were dropped from that height.

column1: What assumption is made when using PE = mgh vs. a more general gravitational formula?
column3: g is constant (object is near Earth's surface)
column4: PE = mgh applies only locally where g ≈ constant. For large distances from Earth, the general formula PE = −GMm/r must be used.

column1: If an object is dropped from height h, what is its speed just before impact? (use conservation of energy)
column4: mgh = ½mv² → v² = 2gh → v = √(2gh). Mass cancels, so speed is independent of mass — a key MCAT insight.

column1: How does gravitational PE change when an object moves horizontally at constant height?
column4: PE = mgh depends only on vertical height h. Horizontal displacement with no change in h means no change in gravitational PE.

column1: What is the formula for elastic (spring) potential energy?
column4: k is the spring constant (N/m) and x is the displacement from the equilibrium (natural) length. The energy is always positive.

column1: What are the units of the spring constant k?
column4: From Hooke's Law F = kx, k = F/x = N/m. A stiffer spring has a larger k value.

column1: If the compression of a spring is doubled, by what factor does the stored elastic PE change?
column4: PE = ½kx², so PE ∝ x². Doubling x multiplies PE by 2² = 4. Same quadratic relationship as kinetic energy and velocity.

column1: What is the elastic PE stored in a spring with k = 200 N/m compressed by 0.1 m?
column4: PE = ½(200)(0.1²) = ½(200)(0.01) = 1 J. Always square x before multiplying.

column1: At what displacement from equilibrium is the elastic PE of a spring at maximum?
column4: At maximum displacement (amplitude A), all energy is elastic PE and KE = 0. At the equilibrium position, PE = 0 and KE is maximum.

column1: A spring with k = 400 N/m has a mass attached. At x = 0.05 m from equilibrium, what is the elastic PE?
column4: PE = ½(400)(0.05²) = ½(400)(0.0025) = 0.5 J. This PE converts to KE as the mass passes through equilibrium.

column1: What is the relationship between elastic PE and the restoring force at a given displacement?
column4: Since F = kx, substituting gives PE = ½(F/x)x² = ½Fx. Knowing force and displacement, PE can be found without knowing k directly.

column1: State the law of conservation of energy.
column3: Total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant in a closed system with no non-conservative forces
column4: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. In the absence of friction or air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved.

column1: What is the formula for total mechanical energy E?
column4: In a conservative system, KE + PE = constant. As an object falls, PE decreases while KE increases by the same amount.

column1: When is mechanical energy NOT conserved?
column3: When non-conservative forces (e.g., friction, air resistance) do work
column4: Non-conservative forces convert mechanical energy to thermal or other forms. Total energy is still conserved, but mechanical energy decreases.

column1: A ball is thrown upward. At the highest point, what is true about its KE and PE?
column4: At the peak, velocity = 0 so KE = 0. All initial KE has been converted to gravitational PE. The total mechanical energy remains constant.

column1: A roller coaster car starts from rest at height h. What is its speed at height h/2? (ignore friction)
column4: Energy conservation: mgh = ½mv² + mg(h/2) → ½mv² = mgh/2 → v² = gh → v = √(gh).

column1: How does friction affect the conservation of mechanical energy in a system?
column3: Converts mechanical energy to thermal energy; decreases total mechanical energy
column4: Work done by friction is negative (W_friction < 0), so E_final = E_initial + W_friction < E_initial. Thermal energy generated equals the mechanical energy lost.

column1: A pendulum swings from angle θ. At what point is its speed maximum?
column4: At the bottom of the swing, all PE has been converted to KE (minimum height = minimum PE = maximum KE). Speed is maximum there.

column1: If a 3 kg ball falls from rest at 5 m and loses 20 J to air resistance, what is its KE just before landing? (g = 10 m/s²)
column4: Initial PE = mgh = 3×10×5 = 150 J. KE = 150 − 20 = 130 J. When non-conservative forces act, subtract their work from available energy.

column1: What is the definition of power?
column3: Rate of doing work (or rate of energy transfer)
column4: Power = Work/time = Energy transferred/time. It tells us how quickly energy is used or delivered, not just how much total work is done.

column1: What are the SI units of power?
column4: 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 kg·m²/s³. Named after James Watt; also expressed as horsepower in non-SI systems (1 hp ≈ 746 W).

column1: What is the formula for power in terms of force and velocity?
column4: Since P = W/t and W = Fd, P = Fd/t = F(d/t) = Fv. This form is useful when force and speed are given rather than work and time.

column1: A 600 W motor lifts a 30 kg load. What is the maximum speed at which it can lift the load? (g = 10 m/s²)
column4: P = Fv → v = P/F = 600/(30×10) = 600/300 = 2 m/s. The motor power limits the speed against gravity.

column1: A person does 500 J of work in 10 seconds. What is their power output?
column4: P = W/t = 500/10 = 50 W. This is roughly the resting metabolic power output of a human organ system.

column1: How does power relate to the time needed to complete a task requiring a fixed amount of work?
column3: Higher power → less time (P = W/t → t = W/P)
column4: For a fixed amount of work W, doubling the power halves the time required. Power and time are inversely related for constant work.

column1: What is the unit equivalence: 1 Watt = ?
column4: Knowing this equivalence helps with unit analysis in MCAT calculations involving power, energy, and time.

column1: An engine delivers a constant force of 200 N to a vehicle moving at 15 m/s. What is the engine's power output?
column4: P = Fv = 200 × 15 = 3000 W = 3 kW. This formula applies whenever force and velocity are parallel and both constant.

column1: What is the amplitude of a wave?
column4: Amplitude determines the energy carried by a wave; energy is proportional to amplitude squared.

column1: What is the frequency of a periodic wave?
column3: Number of complete cycles per second (Hz)
column4: Frequency f = 1/T, where T is the period. The SI unit is hertz (Hz = s⁻¹).

column1: What is the period of a simple pendulum of length L (small angle)?
column4: Period depends only on length and gravitational acceleration, not mass or amplitude (for small angles).

column1: What is the period of a mass-spring system with mass m and spring constant k?
column4: Period increases with greater mass and decreases with stiffer springs; it is independent of amplitude (for ideal springs obeying Hooke's law).

column1: How does energy in simple harmonic motion depend on amplitude?
column4: Total mechanical energy E = ½kA² for a spring; doubling amplitude quadruples energy.

column1: What is phase in the context of periodic motion?
column3: The position of a wave within its cycle, expressed in degrees or radians
column4: Two waves in phase have a phase difference of 0 (or 2π); waves 180° (π radians) out of phase interfere destructively.

column1: What phase difference produces complete constructive interference?
column4: Constructive interference occurs when crests align with crests; path difference equals nλ (n = 0, 1, 2, …).

column1: What phase difference produces complete destructive interference?
column4: Destructive interference occurs when crest meets trough; path difference equals (n + ½)λ.

column1: At which point in simple harmonic motion is velocity maximum?
column4: All potential energy converts to kinetic energy at equilibrium; v_max = Aω where ω = 2πf.

column1: What is angular frequency (ω) in terms of frequency f?
column4: Angular frequency has units of rad/s. For a spring: ω = √(k/m); for a pendulum: ω = √(g/L).

column1: In a transverse wave, how does particle displacement orient relative to wave propagation?
column3: Perpendicular to the direction of propagation
column4: Examples include light (electromagnetic waves) and waves on a string; the medium oscillates at 90° to energy travel.

column1: In a longitudinal wave, how does particle displacement orient relative to wave propagation?
column3: Parallel to the direction of propagation
column4: Sound is the key MCAT example; particles compress and rarefy along the same axis the wave travels.

column1: What is the wavelength of a wave?
column3: Distance between two successive identical points (e.g., crest to crest)
column4: Wavelength λ is related to speed and frequency by v = fλ.

column1: What equation relates wave speed, frequency, and wavelength?
column4: Wave speed is a property of the medium; frequency is set by the source. Changing medium changes λ while f stays constant.

column1: Is sound a transverse or longitudinal wave?
column4: Sound travels as pressure variations (compressions and rarefactions) parallel to wave travel; it cannot propagate in a vacuum.

column1: How does wave speed in a medium change when frequency is doubled (medium unchanged)?
column3: Wave speed does not change; wavelength halves
column4: Speed depends on medium properties, not source frequency. Since v = fλ and v is constant, λ = v/f decreases.

column1: In which medium does sound travel fastest: air, water, or steel?
column4: Wave speed in solids > liquids > gases because solids have the highest bulk/elastic modulus relative to density.

column1: What happens to the wavelength of light when it enters a denser medium (frequency unchanged)?
column4: Speed decreases in a denser medium (v = c/n), and since f is constant, λ must decrease proportionally.

column1: What is the approximate speed of sound in air at room temperature?
column4: Speed of sound in air increases with temperature (~0.6 m/s per °C increase); memorize ~340 m/s as the MCAT reference value.

column1: Can transverse waves propagate through liquids and gases?
column3: No — only through solids (and electromagnetic fields)
column4: Transverse mechanical waves require a restoring shear force, which fluids cannot sustain; only longitudinal waves travel through fluids.

column1: What is the SI unit of density?
column4: Density ρ = mass/volume. In CGS, g/cm³ is also common; water's density is 1000 kg/m³ = 1 g/cm³.

column1: Define specific gravity.
column3: ratio of substance density to water density
column4: Specific gravity is dimensionless: SG = ρ_substance / ρ_water. SG > 1 means the object sinks in water.

column1: What is the density of water at 4°C in SI units?
column4: Water reaches maximum density at 4°C; this value is the reference for specific gravity calculations.

column1: If a substance has a specific gravity of 0.8, does it float or sink in water?
column4: SG < 1 means less dense than water, so the object floats. SG > 1 means it sinks.

column1: How does temperature affect the density of most liquids?
column4: Most liquids expand when heated, increasing volume while mass stays constant, so ρ decreases. Water is an exception between 0–4°C.

column1: A substance has a specific gravity of 13.6. What substance is this?
column4: Mercury's density ≈ 13,600 kg/m³, giving SG = 13.6. This is a high-yield value for manometer problems.

column1: State Archimedes' Principle.
column3: buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid
column4: F_b = ρ_fluid × V_displaced × g. The fluid displaced need not equal the object's full volume if it floats partially submerged.

column1: What determines whether an object floats or sinks?
column3: comparison of object density to fluid density
column4: If ρ_object < ρ_fluid the object floats; if ρ_object > ρ_fluid it sinks; equal densities give neutral buoyancy.

column1: What fraction of an iceberg is submerged in seawater (ρ_ice ≈ 917, ρ_seawater ≈ 1025 kg/m³)?
column4: Fraction submerged = ρ_ice / ρ_seawater ≈ 917/1025 ≈ 0.89. This illustrates Archimedes' equilibrium condition.

column1: How does the buoyant force on a fully submerged object change as it is pushed deeper?
column4: Buoyant force depends on volume of fluid displaced, not depth, so F_b is constant for a fully submerged incompressible object.

column1: A steel ball sinks; a hollow steel sphere of identical mass floats. Why?
column3: hollow sphere displaces more fluid, larger buoyant force
column4: The hollow sphere has greater total volume, displacing more fluid. If average density (mass/total volume) < ρ_fluid, it floats.

column1: Define hydrostatic pressure.
column3: pressure exerted by a fluid at rest due to gravity
column4: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth because the weight of the fluid column above presses down. It acts equally in all directions.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::hydrostatic-pressure MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the gauge pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool 3 m deep? (ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
column4: P_gauge = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 3 = 30,000 Pa. Gauge pressure excludes atmospheric pressure.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::hydrostatic-pressure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In a fluid at rest, how does pressure vary with horizontal position at the same depth?
column4: Hydrostatic pressure depends only on depth (vertical height), not horizontal position or container shape.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::hydrostatic-pressure MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the approximate atmospheric pressure at sea level in Pascals?
column4: Standard atmosphere = 101,325 Pa = 760 mmHg = 1 atm. Used as the baseline for absolute vs. gauge pressure.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::hydrostatic-pressure MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State Pascal's Law.
column3: pressure applied to a confined fluid transmits equally in all directions
column4: Pascal's Law is the basis of hydraulic systems: a small force over a small area can generate a large force over a large area (F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂).
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::pascal-s-law MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In a hydraulic lift, piston 1 has area 0.01 m² and piston 2 has area 0.1 m². If 100 N is applied to piston 1, what force acts on piston 2?
column4: Pascal's Law: P₁ = P₂ → F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ → F₂ = 100 × (0.1/0.01) = 1000 N.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::pascal-s-law MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Does a hydraulic machine create energy?
column3: no — work in equals work out (ignoring friction)
column4: W = F × d. Larger force on piston 2 comes at the cost of smaller displacement. Energy is conserved.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::pascal-s-law MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What medical device relies on Pascal's Law to measure blood pressure?
column4: The cuff transmits pressure through an enclosed air column to occlude the brachial artery; gauge reading equals transmitted pressure.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::pascal-s-law MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Give the formula for hydrostatic pressure as a function of depth.
column4: P = hydrostatic pressure, ρ = fluid density, g = gravitational acceleration, h = depth below surface. Absolute pressure = P_atm + ρgh.

column1: How does pressure change when depth doubles in the same fluid?
column4: Since P_gauge = ρgh, doubling h doubles gauge pressure. Absolute pressure increases by ρgh but not by a factor of 2.

column1: Two columns of different fluids are connected at the bottom. What is equal at the connection point?
column4: Pressure at the same horizontal level in connected fluid is equal: ρ₁gh₁ = ρ₂gh₂, which allows manometer calculations.

column1: A mercury manometer reads 120 mmHg. Convert to Pascals. (ρ_Hg = 13,600 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²)
column4: P = ρgh = 13,600 × 9.8 × 0.120 ≈ 15,974 Pa ≈ 16 kPa. Memorize that 1 mmHg ≈ 133 Pa.

column1: At what depth in water (ρ=1000 kg/m³, g=10 m/s²) does gauge pressure equal 1 atm (≈100,000 Pa)?
column4: h = P/(ρg) = 100,000 / (1000 × 10) = 10 m. Each 10 m of water adds ~1 atm of pressure.

column1: Define viscosity in the context of fluid mechanics.
column3: resistance of a fluid to flow (internal friction)
column4: Higher viscosity means more resistance; blood is more viscous than water. Units: Pa·s (Pascal-seconds) or poise.

column1: State Poiseuille's Law relating flow rate to vessel radius.
column3: Q ∝ r⁴ (flow rate proportional to radius to the 4th power)
column4: Q = πr⁴ΔP / (8ηL). Doubling vessel radius increases flow 16-fold. This is why small changes in arteriole radius dramatically affect blood flow.

column1: In Poiseuille's Law, how does flow rate change if vessel length doubles (all else constant)?
column4: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL); Q ∝ 1/L. Longer vessels have more resistance.

column1: What is the unit of dynamic viscosity?
column4: Dynamic (absolute) viscosity η has SI units Pa·s. An older unit is the poise (1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s). Water ≈ 0.001 Pa·s at 20°C.

column1: How does temperature affect the viscosity of most liquids?
column4: Increased thermal energy disrupts intermolecular attractions, reducing resistance to flow. Contrast gases, whose viscosity increases with temperature.

column1: In Poiseuille flow, what is the velocity profile across a cylindrical tube?
column3: parabolic — fastest at center, zero at walls
column4: The no-slip condition means fluid velocity = 0 at the wall. Velocity increases parabolically toward the center.

column1: State the continuity equation for an incompressible fluid.
column4: The product of cross-sectional area and velocity is constant along a streamline. When area decreases, velocity must increase.

column1: What physical principle underlies the continuity equation?
column3: conservation of mass (or conservation of volume for incompressible fluids)
column4: For an incompressible fluid, the volume flowing past any cross-section per unit time must be equal everywhere in a closed system.

column1: Blood flows through an artery of radius 0.5 cm at 20 cm/s. What is the velocity in a capillary of radius 0.0005 cm (using continuity)?
column3: 0.002 cm/s (using A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ for a single capillary)
column4: A₁ = π(0.5)² = 0.785 cm²; A₂ = π(0.0005)² ≈ 7.85×10⁻⁷ cm²; v₂ = (0.785×20)/7.85×10⁻⁷ — but the body has millions of capillaries in parallel, dramatically reducing velocity.

column1: Why is blood velocity slowest in capillaries despite them being narrow?
column3: enormous total cross-sectional area of capillary bed
column4: Continuity: v = Q/A_total. Millions of capillaries in parallel give huge total A, so v is very low — allowing time for gas exchange.

column1: If a pipe narrows from area 0.04 m² to 0.01 m², by what factor does velocity increase?
column4: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ → v₂/v₁ = A₁/A₂ = 0.04/0.01 = 4.

column1: Define turbulent flow in a fluid.
column3: chaotic, irregular flow with eddies and vortices
column4: Turbulence occurs at high velocities, low viscosity, or large vessel diameter. It increases resistance and energy loss compared to laminar flow.

column1: What dimensionless number predicts the onset of turbulence?
column4: Re = ρvL/η. Turbulence typically occurs when Re > 2000–4000 in pipes. Low Re → laminar; high Re → turbulent.

column1: What is the formula for the Reynolds number?
column4: ρ = fluid density, v = flow velocity, D = pipe diameter, η = dynamic viscosity. Each variable makes physical sense: denser, faster, wider flow → more turbulence.

column1: Which factors increase the likelihood of turbulent flow in a blood vessel?
column3: high velocity, large diameter, low viscosity, high density
column4: All increase the Reynolds number. Anemia (low viscosity/density) and stenosis followed by sudden dilation (high velocity) can cause audible turbulence (bruits).

column1: At what approximate Reynolds number does fully turbulent flow typically develop in a smooth cylindrical pipe?
column4: The transition zone is Re 2000–4000; above 4000 flow is consistently turbulent. Below 2000 flow is laminar.

column1: Define surface tension.
column3: inward cohesive force at a liquid surface resisting expansion
column4: Surface tension (γ) arises because surface molecules have fewer neighbors, creating a net inward force. Units: N/m or J/m².
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::surface-tension MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which intermolecular force primarily accounts for the high surface tension of water?
column4: Strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules create large cohesive forces, giving water one of the highest surface tensions of common liquids (~0.072 N/m at 25°C).
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::surface-tension MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does a surfactant (like pulmonary surfactant) affect surface tension?
column4: Surfactants are amphipathic molecules that disrupt cohesive forces at the surface. Pulmonary surfactant prevents alveolar collapse by reducing surface tension.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::surface-tension MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is capillary action and what causes it?
column3: rise of liquid in a narrow tube due to adhesion exceeding cohesion
column4: Adhesion of water to glass pulls the liquid up; surface tension supports the weight of the column. Narrower tubes show greater rise.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::surface-tension MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the Laplace pressure equation for a spherical bubble with two surfaces (e.g., soap bubble)?
column4: Two surfaces (inner and outer) each contribute γ/r, giving ΔP = 4γ/r. For a single surface (droplet or alveolus): ΔP = 2γ/r.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::surface-tension MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why do smaller alveoli tend to collapse into larger ones without surfactant?
column3: smaller radius → higher Laplace pressure → air flows to larger alveolus
column4: ΔP = 2γ/r; smaller r → larger ΔP. Without surfactant equalizing tension, small alveoli empty into large ones (atelectasis).
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::surface-tension MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State Bernoulli's equation.
column3: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline
column4: Valid for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow along a streamline. Each term has units of pressure (Pa). It expresses conservation of energy per unit volume.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::bernoulli-s-equation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: According to Bernoulli's equation, what happens to pressure when fluid velocity increases (at constant height)?
column4: If ½ρv² increases and ρgh is constant, P must decrease to keep the sum constant. Fast flow → low pressure (Venturi effect).
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::bernoulli-s-equation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What four assumptions underlie Bernoulli's equation?
column3: steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow along a streamline
column4: Real fluids violate viscosity and compressibility assumptions, so Bernoulli is an approximation. It is inapplicable to turbulent flow.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::bernoulli-s-equation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A fluid flows horizontally through a constriction. Using Bernoulli, what happens to static pressure in the narrow region?
column4: Continuity increases velocity in the narrow region; Bernoulli then requires pressure to drop (constant height, so ρgh unchanged).
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::bernoulli-s-equation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Derive the relationship between pressure and height for a static fluid using Bernoulli's equation.
column3: P + ρgh = constant → P increases with depth
column4: For a static fluid v = 0 everywhere, so Bernoulli reduces to P + ρgh = constant, recovering the hydrostatic equation P = ρgh + P_surface.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::bernoulli-s-equation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In Bernoulli's equation, what does the term ½ρv² represent?
column4: ½ρv² is the kinetic energy per unit volume of the fluid. P is static pressure; ρgh is gravitational potential energy per unit volume.
column8: concept::CP::4B::fluids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::fluids::bernoulli-s-equation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the Venturi effect?
column3: fluid velocity increases and pressure decreases in a constriction
column4: Combining continuity (A decreases → v increases) with Bernoulli (v increases → P decreases) explains the Venturi effect, used in atomizers, carburetors, and medical nebulizers.

column1: What does a pitot tube measure?
column3: fluid (or airspeed) velocity using stagnation pressure
column4: A pitot tube has a forward-facing opening where flow stops (stagnation point); the pressure difference between stagnation and static pressure gives velocity via Bernoulli: v = √(2ΔP/ρ).

column1: What is the stagnation pressure at the entrance of a pitot tube?
column4: At the stagnation point v = 0, so all kinetic energy converts to pressure: P_stagnation = P_static + ½ρv². This total pressure is also called Pitot pressure.

column1: Name a clinical or physiological example of the Venturi effect.
column3: bronchial narrowing increasing air velocity and reducing pressure (dynamic airway collapse) / Venturi masks for O₂ delivery
column4: Venturi masks use a constriction to entrain room air at a fixed ratio, delivering precise FiO₂. Dynamic airway collapse in asthma also results from Venturi-effect pressure drops.

column1: Using Bernoulli, derive the formula for fluid velocity from a pitot tube reading.
column4: At stagnation: P_total = P_static + ½ρv² → ΔP = ½ρv² → v = √(2ΔP/ρ). Pitot tubes on aircraft measure airspeed this way.

column1: In a Venturi meter, two pressure taps are placed at wide and narrow sections. How is flow rate calculated?
column3: using Q = A₂√(2ΔP / ρ(1−(A₂/A₁)²)) from Bernoulli + continuity
column4: Combining A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (continuity) with Bernoulli's equation yields Q as a function of the measured pressure difference ΔP and the areas.

column1: What is the normal systolic blood pressure in a healthy adult?
column4: Systolic pressure reflects peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction. The standard normal range is 90–120 mmHg systolic.

column1: What is the normal diastolic blood pressure in a healthy adult?
column4: Diastolic pressure is the minimum arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation. Normal is below 80 mmHg.

column1: Which vessel type contains the highest blood pressure in the systemic circulation?
column4: Pressure is highest in the aorta immediately after it leaves the left ventricle and progressively drops through arterioles, capillaries, and veins.

column1: What is pulse pressure?
column4: Pulse pressure = systolic BP − diastolic BP (normal ~40 mmHg). It reflects stroke volume and arterial compliance.

column1: What is mean arterial pressure (MAP)?
column4: MAP ≈ DBP + (1/3)(PP) because the heart spends more time in diastole. It represents the average driving pressure for tissue perfusion.

column1: Which vessels offer the greatest resistance to blood flow?
column4: Arterioles are the primary resistance vessels; their smooth muscle tone controls systemic vascular resistance and regulates blood flow to capillary beds.

column1: In which vessels does the steepest pressure drop occur?
column4: Because arterioles have the highest resistance, the largest pressure gradient (drop) across any single vessel segment occurs there.

column1: What percentage of total blood volume is contained in the venous system at rest?
column4: Veins act as capacitance (reservoir) vessels; their high compliance allows them to hold most circulating blood volume at low pressure.

column1: What is the approximate pressure of blood in the venae cavae entering the right atrium?
column4: Venous pressure drops to nearly zero by the time blood reaches the great veins, driving the pressure gradient that returns blood to the heart.

column1: What structural feature of veins allows them to act as capacitance vessels?
column4: Veins have thinner walls with less smooth muscle and elastin than arteries, giving them greater compliance and the ability to hold large volumes at low pressure.

column1: Which vessels have the largest total cross-sectional area in the circulation?
column4: The enormous number of capillaries gives the greatest combined cross-sectional area, slowing blood velocity to facilitate exchange of gases and nutrients.

column1: According to Poiseuille's law, how does vessel radius affect flow rate?
column3: Flow is proportional to radius to the fourth power
column4: Q = (πr⁴ΔP)/(8ηL). A twofold increase in radius increases flow 16-fold, making radius the most powerful determinant of vascular resistance.

column1: What is vascular resistance proportional to, according to Poiseuille's law?
column3: Inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power
column4: R = 8ηL/(πr⁴). Small changes in arteriolar radius produce dramatic changes in resistance and therefore flow — the basis of vasomotor regulation.

column1: What is the relationship between blood flow velocity and cross-sectional area?
column3: Velocity is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area
column4: By continuity (Q = Av), as total cross-sectional area increases (e.g., capillaries), velocity must decrease proportionally if flow rate is constant.

column1: Where is blood flow velocity lowest in the systemic circulation?
column4: Capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area, so by the continuity equation flow velocity is slowest there, maximizing time for gas and nutrient exchange.

column1: What property of arteries allows them to dampen pulsatile flow?
column4: Large elastic arteries (aorta, pulmonary trunk) stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, converting pulsatile output into smoother continuous flow — the Windkessel effect.

column1: What mechanisms assist venous return against gravity in the limbs?
column3: Skeletal muscle pump and venous valves
column4: Muscle contraction squeezes veins; one-way valves prevent backflow, propelling blood toward the heart. Respiratory pressure changes (thoracic pump) also assist.

column1: What happens to total peripheral resistance (TPR) when arterioles dilate?
column4: Arteriolar dilation reduces resistance, increasing blood flow to that capillary bed and, if widespread, lowering systemic blood pressure.

column1: What is the formula relating mean arterial pressure, cardiac output, and total peripheral resistance?
column4: Analogous to Ohm's law (V = IR). Any increase in cardiac output or peripheral resistance raises MAP; arteriolar dilation lowers TPR and MAP.

column1: Which vessel type lacks smooth muscle and only has an endothelial layer plus basement membrane?
column4: The thin single-cell wall of capillaries is essential for diffusion of O2, CO2, nutrients, and wastes between blood and interstitial fluid.

column1: What are the three layers (tunics) of artery walls, from innermost to outermost?
column3: Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica adventitia
column4: The media is thickest in arteries (smooth muscle + elastin) conferring pressure resistance; veins have a thinner media and relatively thicker adventitia.

column1: What is the Windkessel effect?
column3: Elastic artery recoil smoothing pulsatile flow
column4: During diastole, the elastic recoil of large arteries maintains pressure and flow continuity, preventing pressure from dropping to zero between heartbeats.

column1: In which part of the circulation is blood pressure lowest?
column4: Blood pressure decreases progressively from the aorta through arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins, reaching its nadir at the right atrium.

column1: What is the driving force for blood flow through a vessel?
column4: Blood flows from regions of higher pressure to lower pressure. The pressure difference between two points (ΔP) drives flow, opposed by vascular resistance.

column1: How does increased blood viscosity affect vascular resistance?
column4: R = 8ηL/(πr⁴); viscosity (η) is directly proportional to resistance. Conditions like polycythemia increase viscosity and raise TPR and blood pressure.

column1: What is the SI unit of absolute temperature?
column4: The Kelvin scale is the SI absolute temperature scale; 0 K is absolute zero, the lowest theoretically possible temperature where molecular motion ceases.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::absolute-temperature-k-kelvin-scale MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is absolute zero in degrees Celsius?
column4: Absolute zero (0 K) corresponds to -273.15°C; at this point, all classical thermal motion stops and ideal gas volume theoretically reaches zero.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::absolute-temperature-k-kelvin-scale MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What formula converts Celsius to Kelvin?
column4: On the MCAT, use K = °C + 273 (the 0.15 is omitted for simplicity). All gas law calculations require temperature in Kelvin, never Celsius.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::absolute-temperature-k-kelvin-scale MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why must gas law calculations use Kelvin rather than Celsius?
column3: Kelvin is proportional to average kinetic energy; Celsius is not
column4: Celsius has an arbitrary zero (freezing point of water), so ratios of Celsius temperatures are physically meaningless. Kelvin starts at true zero energy, making it proportional to KE.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::absolute-temperature-k-kelvin-scale MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which temperature scale has a direct proportional relationship between temperature and average molecular kinetic energy?
column4: KE_avg = (3/2)k_B T only when T is in Kelvin. Doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles the average kinetic energy of gas molecules.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::absolute-temperature-k-kelvin-scale MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the temperature in Kelvin at which a gas theoretically exerts zero pressure?
column4: By Charles' and Gay-Lussac's laws, both volume and pressure of an ideal gas approach zero as T approaches 0 K (at constant n).
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::absolute-temperature-k-kelvin-scale MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What does a simple mercury barometer measure?
column4: A mercury barometer balances atmospheric pressure against the weight of a mercury column; standard atmosphere supports 760 mm Hg (torr).
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::pressure-simple-mercury-barometer MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is standard atmospheric pressure expressed in mm Hg?
column4: 1 atm = 760 mm Hg = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa. The mm Hg unit is also called a torr, named after Evangelista Torricelli.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::pressure-simple-mercury-barometer MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In a mercury barometer, what occupies the space above the mercury column?
column4: The closed top of the barometer tube is evacuated; the mercury rises until the pressure exerted by the mercury column equals atmospheric pressure.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::pressure-simple-mercury-barometer MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does altitude affect the height of a mercury column in a barometer?
column3: Higher altitude → shorter mercury column (lower pressure)
column4: Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because less air mass is above. At high altitude, the mercury column is shorter because less pressure supports it.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::pressure-simple-mercury-barometer MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why is mercury preferred over water in a barometer?
column3: Mercury's high density makes the column a manageable height (~76 cm vs ~10 m for water)
column4: A water barometer would need a ~10.3 m tall column. Mercury's density (~13.6× water) keeps the column at a convenient 76 cm.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::pressure-simple-mercury-barometer MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (0°C and 1 atm)?
column4: At standard temperature and pressure (STP: 0°C, 1 atm), one mole of any ideal gas occupies exactly 22.4 L. This is a key MCAT memorization fact.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::molar-volume-at-0-c-and-1-atm-22-4-l-mol MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: At what conditions does one mole of ideal gas occupy 22.4 L?
column4: STP is defined as 0°C and 1 atm. Under these conditions, PV = nRT gives V/n = RT/P = (0.0821 L·atm/mol·K)(273 K)/(1 atm) ≈ 22.4 L/mol.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::molar-volume-at-0-c-and-1-atm-22-4-l-mol MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the approximate molar volume of an ideal gas at standard conditions of 25°C and 1 atm (SATP)?
column4: At SATP (25°C, 1 atm) the molar volume is ~24.5 L/mol, higher than 22.4 L/mol at 0°C because temperature is higher. The MCAT most commonly uses 22.4 L at STP.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::molar-volume-at-0-c-and-1-atm-22-4-l-mol MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Using molar volume, how many liters does 0.5 mol of ideal gas occupy at STP?
column4: At STP, V = n × 22.4 L/mol = 0.5 mol × 22.4 L/mol = 11.2 L. Molar volume is a handy shortcut when T and P are at STP.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::molar-volume-at-0-c-and-1-atm-22-4-l-mol MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Does the molar volume of 22.4 L/mol depend on the identity of the gas?
column3: No — it is the same for all ideal gases at STP
column4: Because ideal gases obey PV = nRT with no intermolecular forces, only n, T, and P determine volume, not the molecular identity. This is Avogadro's principle.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::molar-volume-at-0-c-and-1-atm-22-4-l-mol MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What two assumptions define an ideal gas?
column3: Point-mass molecules with no intermolecular forces
column4: Ideal gas molecules have (1) negligible volume compared to container and (2) no attractive or repulsive forces between molecules. Collisions are perfectly elastic.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::definition MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Under what conditions do real gases behave most like ideal gases?
column4: At high T, molecules move fast enough that intermolecular attractions are negligible. At low P, molecules are far apart and their finite volume is insignificant.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::definition MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which type of real gas deviates most from ideal behavior?
column3: Gases with strong intermolecular forces and/or large molecular size
column4: Polar gases (e.g., NH3, H2O vapor) and large molecules deviate most because their real intermolecular forces and finite volume are largest relative to ideal assumptions.
