column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::definition MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What does the compressibility factor Z equal for an ideal gas?
column4: Z = PV/nRT. For an ideal gas Z = 1 always. Z > 1 indicates repulsive dominance (high P); Z < 1 indicates attractive dominance (moderate P).
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::definition MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: At very high pressures, does a real gas have a larger or smaller volume than an ideal gas?
column4: At extreme pressures, finite molecular volume dominates; real gas molecules cannot be compressed to zero volume, so V_real > V_ideal and Z > 1.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::definition MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the Ideal Gas Law equation?
column4: P = pressure (atm), V = volume (L), n = moles, R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), T = temperature (K). All gas law problems on the MCAT stem from this equation.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas-law-pv-nrt MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the value of the ideal gas constant R in L·atm/(mol·K)?
column4: R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) is the most useful form for MCAT gas calculations. It can also be expressed as 8.314 J/(mol·K) for thermodynamic calculations.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas-law-pv-nrt MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Using PV = nRT, what happens to pressure if the number of moles of gas in a fixed-volume container is doubled at constant temperature?
column4: At constant V and T, P = nRT/V, so P is directly proportional to n. Doubling n doubles P. This principle underlies Dalton's law of partial pressures.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas-law-pv-nrt MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A gas at 2 atm, 10 L, 300 K is compressed to 5 L at 600 K. What is the new pressure?
column4: Use P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2: (2)(10)/300 = P2(5)/600 → P2 = (2×10×600)/(300×5) = 8 atm. This combined gas law is derived from PV = nRT at constant n.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas-law-pv-nrt MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the value of R in J/(mol·K)?
column4: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is used in thermodynamic contexts (e.g., ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q). On the MCAT, 8.314 ≈ 8 J/(mol·K) is a useful approximation.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas-law-pv-nrt MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State Boyle's Law in words.
column3: At constant T and n, pressure and volume are inversely proportional
column4: Boyle's Law: P1V1 = P2V2 (constant T, n). As pressure increases, volume decreases proportionally — gas molecules are pushed closer together.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::boyle-s-law-pv-constant MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the mathematical expression for Boyle's Law?
column4: At constant temperature and moles, PV = nRT = constant, so P1V1 = P2V2. Tripling pressure reduces volume to one-third.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::boyle-s-law-pv-constant MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A gas occupies 4 L at 3 atm. What volume does it occupy at 6 atm (constant T)?
column4: Boyle's Law: P1V1 = P2V2 → (3)(4) = (6)V2 → V2 = 2 L. Doubling the pressure halves the volume.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::boyle-s-law-pv-constant MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: On a P vs. V graph for a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant temperature, what shape is the curve?
column4: Because P = nRT/V (a constant divided by V), P vs. V is a hyperbola. Each isotherm on a P-V diagram is a hyperbola at a different temperature.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::boyle-s-law-pv-constant MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does Boyle's Law relate to the concept of isothermal compression?
column3: Isothermal compression: T constant, so PV = constant (Boyle's Law applies)
column4: During isothermal compression there is no temperature change, so PV remains constant and Boyle's Law precisely describes the P-V relationship.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::boyle-s-law-pv-constant MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State Charles' Law in words.
column3: At constant P and n, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature
column4: Charles' Law: V/T = constant. When temperature doubles (in Kelvin), volume doubles. Gas expands when heated because molecules move faster and push outward.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::charles-law-v-t-constant MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the mathematical expression for Charles' Law?
column4: At constant pressure and moles, V = nR/P × T, so V is proportional to T. Temperature must be in Kelvin.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::charles-law-v-t-constant MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A gas occupies 3 L at 300 K. What volume does it occupy at 600 K at constant pressure?
column4: Charles' Law: V1/T1 = V2/T2 → 3/300 = V2/600 → V2 = 6 L. Doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles the volume.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::charles-law-v-t-constant MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If a balloon is cooled from 400 K to 200 K at constant pressure, by what factor does its volume change?
column4: V ∝ T (Charles' Law). Halving the absolute temperature (400→200 K) halves the volume. This is why balloons shrink in cold air.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::charles-law-v-t-constant MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Charles' Law predicts that a gas will have zero volume at what temperature?
column4: Extrapolating V/T = constant to V = 0 gives T = 0 K. Real gases liquefy or solidify before reaching 0 K, but the extrapolation defined the Kelvin scale.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::charles-law-v-t-constant MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State Avogadro's Law in words.
column3: At constant T and P, volume is directly proportional to moles of gas
column4: Avogadro's Law: V/n = constant. Equal volumes of different ideal gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules — the basis of molar volume.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::avogadro-s-law-v-n-constant MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the mathematical expression for Avogadro's Law?
column4: At constant T and P, V = nRT/P so V ∝ n. If moles double, volume doubles. This is why 22.4 L holds for any gas at STP.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::avogadro-s-law-v-n-constant MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If 1 mol of N2 occupies 22.4 L at STP, what volume does 3 mol of CO2 occupy at the same conditions?
column4: By Avogadro's Law, volume is proportional to moles: 3 mol × 22.4 L/mol = 67.2 L. The identity of the gas (N2 vs CO2) is irrelevant for ideal behavior.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::avogadro-s-law-v-n-constant MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Avogadro's Law implies that equal volumes of ideal gases at same T and P contain equal numbers of what?
column4: This is Avogadro's hypothesis: V/n = constant, so same V, T, P → same n → same number of molecules (Avogadro's number × moles).
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::avogadro-s-law-v-n-constant MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: A 10 L container holds 2 mol of gas at constant T and P. If 1 more mole is added, what is the new volume?
column4: Avogadro's Law: V2 = V1 × (n2/n1) = 10 L × (3/2) = 15 L. Volume and moles are directly proportional at fixed T and P.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::avogadro-s-law-v-n-constant MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What does the Kinetic Molecular Theory (KMT) state about the size of gas molecules?
column3: Molecules are point masses; their volume is negligible compared to the container
column4: KMT Assumption 1: gas molecules are infinitely small points. This allows the ideal gas model to assume all space is free for translational motion.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: According to KMT, what is the average kinetic energy of gas molecules proportional to?
column4: KE_avg = (3/2)k_BT. At higher temperatures, molecules move faster on average. This proportionality (in Kelvin) is a cornerstone of KMT.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: According to KMT, what type of collisions do ideal gas molecules undergo?
column4: In elastic collisions, kinetic energy is conserved (no energy lost to heat or vibration). This assumption maintains constant average KE at constant temperature.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What does KMT state about intermolecular forces in an ideal gas?
column3: No attractive or repulsive forces between molecules
column4: Between collisions, ideal gas molecules travel in straight lines with no forces acting on them. This is why they expand to fill any container.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does KMT explain gas pressure?
column3: Pressure = force per area from molecular collisions with container walls
column4: Molecules strike the container walls and exert a force. More collisions (higher n or T) or harder collisions (higher T) → higher pressure. P = F/A at the macroscopic level.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which gas molecules have the highest average speed at a given temperature: light or heavy molecules?
column3: Lighter molecules (lower molar mass) move faster
column4: From KE_avg = (1/2)mv² = (3/2)k_BT, v_rms = √(3RT/M). Lower molar mass M → higher speed at the same T. H2 moves fastest, heavy gases slowest.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the formula for root-mean-square (rms) speed of gas molecules?
column4: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T in Kelvin, M = molar mass in kg/mol. v_rms captures the speed associated with average kinetic energy.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: According to Graham's Law (derived from KMT), how does the rate of effusion of a gas depend on its molar mass?
column4: Graham's Law: rate1/rate2 = √(M2/M1). Lighter gases effuse faster. A gas with 4× the molar mass effuses at half the rate.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What type of energy distribution among gas molecules does KMT predict, displayed as a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve?
column3: A broad distribution; most molecules near the peak speed, with a tail toward high speeds
column4: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is right-skewed. Most probable speed < average speed < rms speed. Higher T flattens and shifts the curve rightward.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::kinetic-molecular-theory-of-gases MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the heat capacity of an ideal monatomic gas at constant volume (Cv)?
column4: A monatomic ideal gas has only 3 translational degrees of freedom, each contributing (1/2)R to Cv. So Cv = (3/2)R ≈ 12.5 J/(mol·K).
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::heat-capacity-at-constant-volume-and-at MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the heat capacity of an ideal monatomic gas at constant pressure (Cp)?
column4: Cp = Cv + R = (3/2)R + R = (5/2)R. The extra R accounts for the work done by the gas expanding against constant pressure (w = PΔV = nRΔT).
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::heat-capacity-at-constant-volume-and-at MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the ratio Cp/Cv (gamma, γ) for an ideal monatomic gas?
column4: γ = Cp/Cv = (5/2)R / (3/2)R = 5/3. This ratio appears in adiabatic processes. For diatomic gases γ = 7/5 = 1.4.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::heat-capacity-at-constant-volume-and-at MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why is Cp always greater than Cv for any ideal gas?
column3: At constant P, gas does PdV work against surroundings; extra energy is needed beyond raising T
column4: At constant V, all heat input goes to raising internal energy. At constant P, some heat is used for expansion work, requiring more heat for the same ΔT. Cp = Cv + R.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::heat-capacity-at-constant-volume-and-at MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is Cv for an ideal diatomic gas at moderate temperatures (translational + rotational modes only)?
column4: A diatomic gas has 3 translational + 2 rotational degrees of freedom = 5 modes, each (1/2)R. At high T, vibrational modes activate and Cv increases further.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::heat-capacity-at-constant-volume-and-at MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: By how much does Cp exceed Cv for any ideal gas, regardless of its complexity?
column4: This is a universal relation for ideal gases derived from PV = nRT. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). The difference is always exactly R for ideal gases, regardless of molecular structure.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::heat-capacity-at-constant-volume-and-at MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the ideal gas assumption regarding intermolecular forces?
column3: No intermolecular forces (neither attractive nor repulsive)
column4: This key assumption, combined with negligible molecular volume, allows derivation of PV = nRT. Real gases violate this at high P or low T.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which law is expressed as PV = nRT?
column4: PV = nRT combines Boyle's, Charles', and Avogadro's Laws into one equation. P in atm, V in L, n in mol, T in K, R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K).
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the combined (general) gas law derived from Boyle's and Charles' Laws?
column4: Combining PV = const (Boyle) and V/T = const (Charles) gives P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2. Use when n is constant but all three of P, V, T may change.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: For an ideal gas in a rigid container, how does pressure change with temperature?
column3: Pressure is directly proportional to temperature (Gay-Lussac's Law: P/T = constant)
column4: Gay-Lussac's Law: P1/T1 = P2/T2 at constant V and n, derived from PV = nRT. Heating a closed, rigid container raises pressure proportionally.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which of these gases deviates least from ideal behavior at room temperature and 1 atm: He, NH3, or CO2?
column4: Helium is a noble gas: smallest size (negligible volume), no permanent dipole, weakest London dispersion forces. These features make He closest to ideal.
column8: concept::CP::4B::gas_phase MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::gas-phase::ideal-gas MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is Boltzmann's constant (k_B)?
column4: Boltzmann's constant relates the average kinetic energy of gas particles to absolute temperature. It is the gas constant R divided by Avogadro's number (k_B = R/N_A).

column1: What is the relationship between Boltzmann's constant (k_B) and the universal gas constant (R)?
column4: Dividing R (8.314 J/mol·K) by Avogadro's number (6.022 × 10²³) gives k_B. This converts the per-mole gas constant to a per-molecule quantity.

column1: What physical quantity does Boltzmann's constant connect temperature to?
column4: The average translational kinetic energy of a monatomic ideal gas molecule is (3/2)k_B T. k_B bridges macroscopic temperature and microscopic energy.

column1: What is the average translational kinetic energy of an ideal gas molecule expressed using Boltzmann's constant?
column4: This applies to monatomic ideal gases. T must be in Kelvin. The factor 3/2 arises from three translational degrees of freedom (each contributing (1/2)k_B T by equipartition).

column1: What are the SI units of Boltzmann's constant?
column4: Since k_B links energy (joules) to temperature (kelvin), its units are J·K⁻¹. Knowing these units helps verify equations dimensionally on the MCAT.

column1: How does Boltzmann's constant relate to the Ideal Gas Law at the molecular level?
column3: PV = Nk_BT, where N = number of molecules
column4: The macroscopic form PV = nRT uses moles; the microscopic form PV = Nk_BT uses individual molecules. Replacing N with nN_A and k_B with R/N_A recovers the familiar form.

column1: Under what two conditions do real gases deviate MOST from ideal gas behavior?
column4: High pressure forces molecules close together so intermolecular attractions matter; low temperature slows molecules so they cannot overcome those attractions. Both violate ideal gas assumptions.

column1: Which two assumptions of the Ideal Gas Law break down for real gases?
column3: Zero molecular volume; no intermolecular forces
column4: Real molecules occupy finite volume and experience attractions (London dispersion, dipole-dipole, H-bonding). These deviations grow at high pressure and low temperature.

column1: How do intermolecular attractions cause real gas pressure to be LOWER than ideal gas pressure?
column3: Attractions slow molecules before hitting the wall
column4: As a molecule approaches the container wall, neighboring molecules pull it back, reducing impact force. Therefore P_real < P_ideal when attractions dominate (low T, moderate P).

column1: How does the finite volume of real gas molecules cause measured pressure to be HIGHER than ideal predictions at very high pressure?
column4: At very high pressures, the actual space available to molecules is less than V. Molecules are compressed into a smaller free volume, raising collision frequency and thus pressure above ideal.

column1: Which real gas behaves most like an ideal gas: H₂, N₂, NH₃, or H₂O?
column4: H₂ has negligible intermolecular forces (only weak London dispersion) and a very small molecular size, making it closest to ideal across a wide range of conditions.

column1: At very high pressures, is the compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT greater or less than 1 for most real gases?
column4: At very high P, excluded volume dominates; the gas occupies more volume than ideal, so Z > 1. At moderate P, attractions dominate and Z < 1.

column1: What does the Van der Waals 'a' constant correct for in the real gas equation?
column4: The 'a' term subtracts from pressure: P_corrected = (observed P) + a(n/V)². Larger 'a' means stronger intermolecular attractions (e.g., polar or H-bonding gases have higher 'a').

column1: What does the Van der Waals 'b' constant correct for?
column4: 'b' is subtracted from the molar volume: (V – nb). It accounts for the physical space occupied by the molecules themselves, preventing infinite compression.

column1: Write the Van der Waals equation for n moles of a real gas.
column4: The pressure term adds back attractive interactions (which lower P); the volume term removes excluded volume. Setting a=0 and b=0 recovers the Ideal Gas Law.

column1: For which gas would you expect a larger Van der Waals 'a' constant: He or H₂O?
column4: H₂O has strong hydrogen bonding and dipole-dipole attractions, so 'a' is much larger (~0.55 for He vs ~5.54 L²·atm/mol² for H₂O).

column1: For which gas would you expect a larger Van der Waals 'b' constant: H₂ or Cl₂?
column4: 'b' reflects molecular size. Cl₂ is a larger molecule than H₂, so it excludes more volume per mole (b_Cl₂ ≈ 0.0562 L/mol vs b_H₂ ≈ 0.0266 L/mol).

column1: If a = 0 and b = 0 in the Van der Waals equation, what does the equation reduce to?
column4: Setting both correction constants to zero removes the real-gas corrections, recovering ideal behavior. This confirms the Ideal Gas Law is a limiting case of Van der Waals.

column1: What is the mole fraction (χ) of a component in a gas mixture?
column3: Moles of component / total moles of mixture
column4: χ_A = n_A / n_total. Mole fractions are dimensionless and always sum to 1.0 for all components. They are used to calculate partial pressures via Dalton's Law.

column1: Define partial pressure of a gas in a mixture.
column3: Pressure that gas would exert alone in the same volume
column4: Partial pressure P_A = χ_A × P_total. Each gas in a mixture acts independently (ideal behavior), and the sum of all partial pressures equals total pressure.

column1: If oxygen makes up 21% of dry air at 760 mmHg, what is the partial pressure of O₂?
column4: P_O₂ = 0.21 × 760 ≈ 160 mmHg. This is a key MCAT value — at sea level, P_O₂ in alveoli is slightly lower (~104 mmHg) due to water vapor and CO₂.

column1: A gas mixture contains 0.4 mol N₂ and 0.6 mol O₂ at a total pressure of 5 atm. What is the mole fraction of N₂?
column4: χ_N₂ = 0.4 / (0.4 + 0.6) = 0.4. Then P_N₂ = 0.4 × 5 atm = 2 atm. Mole fractions always reflect proportions of moles, not mass.

column1: How does the partial pressure of a gas relate to its mole fraction and total pressure?
column4: This is the defining relationship for partial pressure. It follows from combining Dalton's Law with the definition of mole fraction for ideal gas mixtures.

column1: If 2 mol CO₂ and 3 mol N₂ are in a 10 L container at 300 K, what is the partial pressure of CO₂? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K)
State Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures.
column3: P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + … (sum of partial pressures)
column4: Each gas in a mixture contributes independently to total pressure. This law assumes ideal gas behavior (no intermolecular interactions between different gases).

column1: According to Dalton's Law, how is the partial pressure of a gas related to its mole fraction in a mixture?
column4: Dalton's Law combined with mole fraction definition gives this relationship. It allows calculation of any component's pressure from composition data alone.

column1: Why does water vapor reduce the partial pressure of O₂ in alveolar air compared to atmospheric air?
column3: Water vapor occupies a portion of total pressure
column4: Alveolar air is saturated with water vapor (P_H₂O ≈ 47 mmHg at 37°C). By Dalton's Law, P_O₂ (alveolar) = 0.21 × (760 – 47) ≈ 150 mmHg, lower than 160 mmHg in dry air.

column1: A diver breathes a gas mixture with P_O₂ = 0.21 atm and P_N₂ = 0.79 atm. What is the total pressure?
column4: By Dalton's Law, P_total = 0.21 + 0.79 = 1.00 atm. At depth, total pressure increases, so partial pressures of each gas increase proportionally — relevant to nitrogen narcosis and O₂ toxicity.

column1: How does Dalton's Law apply to collecting gas over water in a laboratory?
column4: When gas is collected over water, water vapor mixes with the collected gas. Subtracting the vapor pressure of water (temperature-dependent) from total pressure gives the dry gas pressure.

column1: Two gases, A (χ = 0.30) and B (χ = 0.70), are in a sealed container. If P_A = 90 mmHg, what is P_total?
column4: P_total = P_A / χ_A = 90 / 0.30 = 300 mmHg. Then P_B = 0.70 × 300 = 210 mmHg. Check: 90 + 210 = 300 mmHg. ✓ Dalton's Law confirmed.

column1: What qualitative effect do strong intermolecular forces have on a gas's deviation from ideal behavior?
column3: Greater negative deviation (lower P than ideal)
column4: Strong attractions (e.g., H-bonding in HF or H₂O vapor) pull molecules together, reducing the force of wall collisions. Real pressure falls below ideal pressure (Z < 1).
column8: concept::CP::4B::constant_pressure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::constant-pressure::qualitative MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Qualitatively, why do large molecules deviate more from ideal behavior than small molecules?
column3: Larger excluded volume and stronger London dispersion forces
column4: Bigger molecules have more electrons → stronger London forces (more attraction) and physically occupy more space (more excluded volume), both increasing deviation from ideal.
column8: concept::CP::4B::constant_pressure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::constant-pressure::qualitative MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: At low pressures, how does real gas behavior compare to ideal gas behavior?
column4: At low pressure, molecules are far apart, so intermolecular forces and excluded volume effects are negligible. PV ≈ nRT is a good approximation under these conditions.
column8: concept::CP::4B::constant_pressure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::constant-pressure::qualitative MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Qualitatively, which factor dominates real gas deviation at MODERATE pressures: molecular volume or intermolecular attractions?
column4: At moderate pressures molecules are close enough to attract each other but not so compressed that excluded volume matters. This leads to Z < 1 (pressure lower than ideal).
column8: concept::CP::4B::constant_pressure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::constant-pressure::qualitative MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which qualitative graph shape describes the compressibility factor Z vs. pressure for most real gases at room temperature?
column3: Dips below 1 at moderate P, then rises above 1 at high P
column4: Initially attractions lower Z below 1; at very high P, excluded volume pushes Z above 1. H₂ and He are exceptions — they show Z > 1 even at low P (very weak attractions).
column8: concept::CP::4B::constant_pressure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::constant-pressure::qualitative MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why do H₂ and He show Z > 1 at all measurable pressures while most other gases show Z < 1 at moderate pressures?
column3: H₂ and He have negligible intermolecular attractions
column4: With virtually no attractive forces, excluded volume effects dominate even at low-moderate pressures, making PV > nRT (Z > 1) for these gases across the board.
column8: concept::CP::4B::constant_pressure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4B::constant-pressure::qualitative MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
column4: One coulomb is the charge of approximately 6.24 × 10^18 protons. The elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C.

column1: What is the charge of one proton?
column4: The elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C; protons carry +e and electrons carry -e. This value is frequently tested on the MCAT.

column1: In a conductor, where do excess charges reside at electrostatic equilibrium?
column4: Free electrons in a conductor redistribute until the internal electric field is zero; all excess charge moves to the surface.

column1: What is the electric field inside a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium?
column4: Any net internal field would accelerate free electrons until they redistribute and cancel it, so E_internal = 0 at equilibrium.

column1: State the law of conservation of electric charge.
column3: Total charge of an isolated system is constant
column4: Charge can be transferred but not created or destroyed; the net charge before equals net charge after any interaction.

column1: What happens to charge distribution on a conductor when a charged object is brought nearby but does not touch it?
column4: Free electrons in the conductor redistribute: the near side acquires opposite charge to the external object, the far side acquires like charge.

column1: Which property distinguishes a conductor from an insulator in terms of charge mobility?
column4: Metals have a sea of delocalized electrons that can move freely; insulators have tightly bound electrons that cannot move.

column1: Define an insulator in terms of electrical conductivity.
column3: Material with no free charge carriers
column4: Insulators (e.g., rubber, glass, plastic) hold electrons tightly; charge placed on an insulator stays localized rather than spreading.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::insulators MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Where does excess charge remain on an insulator?
column3: At the location it was placed
column4: Unlike conductors, insulators cannot redistribute charge because electrons are not free to move through the material.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::insulators MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Name two common examples of electrical insulators.
column4: These materials are used to coat wires and make handles for electrical tools because they prevent charge flow.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::insulators MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does charge transfer by friction (triboelectric effect) work between two insulators?
column3: Surface electrons transfer from one material to the other
column4: The material with higher electron affinity gains electrons and becomes negative; the other becomes positive.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::insulators MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why is the electric field NOT necessarily zero inside an insulator?
column3: Insulators lack free charges to cancel the field
column4: Without mobile charges, an internal field cannot be neutralized by redistribution, so E inside an insulator can be non-zero.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::insulators MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is Coulomb's Law?
column4: The electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::coulomb-s-law MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the value of Coulomb's constant k?
column4: Often approximated as 9 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2 on the MCAT. Related to permittivity of free space: k = 1/(4πε₀).
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::coulomb-s-law MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If the distance between two charges is doubled, by what factor does the Coulomb force change?
column4: F ∝ 1/r^2; doubling r gives F ∝ 1/(2r)^2 = 1/(4r^2), so force becomes one-fourth as large.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::coulomb-s-law MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the direction of the Coulomb force between two like charges?
column4: Like charges (both positive or both negative) repel; unlike charges attract. The force is along the line joining the two charges.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::coulomb-s-law MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does Coulomb's Law compare structurally to Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation?
column4: Key difference: gravity is always attractive; Coulomb force can be attractive or repulsive, and electrostatic forces are generally much stronger.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::coulomb-s-law MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In Coulomb's Law, what does it mean if the computed force is negative?
column4: When q1 and q2 have opposite signs, their product is negative, indicating attraction toward each other.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::coulomb-s-law MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Define electric field E.
column3: Force per unit positive test charge: E = F/q
column4: E = F/q0, where q0 is a small positive test charge. Units are N/C or V/m (equivalent).

column1: What are the SI units of electric field?
column4: Both units are equivalent; V/m is often more convenient when discussing potentials and potential differences.

column1: What is the electric field due to a point charge q at distance r?
column4: Direction is radially outward for positive q and inward for negative q. Derived by combining Coulomb's Law with E = F/q.

column1: What is the direction of the electric field produced by a positive point charge?
column4: A positive test charge placed near a positive source charge is pushed away; field lines point away from positive charges.

column1: What is the electric field inside a parallel-plate capacitor?
column4: Between the plates, the field is approximately uniform (ignoring fringe effects) and equals the voltage divided by the plate separation.

column1: If a positive charge is placed in an electric field, in which direction does it accelerate?
column3: In the direction of the electric field
column4: F = qE; for positive q, force and field are in the same direction. Negative charges accelerate opposite to E.

column1: What do electric field lines represent?
column3: Direction of force on a positive test charge
column4: Field lines show the direction a positive charge would be pushed; the density of lines indicates field strength.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::field-lines MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What does the density (spacing) of electric field lines indicate?
column4: Closely spaced lines indicate a strong field; widely spaced lines indicate a weak field.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::field-lines MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Where do electric field lines begin and end?
column3: Begin on positive charges, end on negative charges
column4: Field lines never cross each other and always originate from positive sources and terminate on negative sinks (or at infinity for isolated charges).
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::field-lines MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Can two electric field lines ever cross?
column4: If lines crossed, a test charge at that point would experience two directions of force simultaneously, which is impossible. The field at any point is unique.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::field-lines MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the relationship between field lines and equipotential surfaces?
column3: Field lines are perpendicular to equipotential surfaces
column4: No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential; the force (and field) must therefore be perpendicular to that surface.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::field-lines MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How do field lines appear around an isolated positive point charge?
column4: By symmetry, field lines point away from a positive charge in all directions, like spokes of a wheel in 3D.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::field-lines MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What pattern do field lines form between two equal and opposite charges (electric dipole)?
column3: Curved lines from positive to negative charge
column4: Lines originate on the positive charge and curve around to terminate on the negative charge, with highest density directly between the two.
column8: concept::CP::4C::electrostatics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::electrostatics::field-lines MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the electric field inside a uniformly charged spherical shell?
column4: By shell theorem (Gauss's Law), a uniformly charged spherical shell produces no net field inside it; all contributions cancel by symmetry.

column1: Outside a uniformly charged sphere, how does the electric field behave?
column4: By Gauss's Law, the external field of a uniformly charged sphere is identical to that of a point charge Q at the center.

column1: What is the electric field due to an infinite line of charge with linear charge density λ?
column4: Derived via Gauss's Law using a cylindrical Gaussian surface; field decreases as 1/r (not 1/r^2 like a point charge).

column1: What is the electric field due to an infinite plane of surface charge density σ?
column3: E = σ/(2ε₀), uniform and perpendicular to plane
column4: Derived via Gauss's Law using a pillbox surface; notably, this field is constant (independent of distance from the plane).

column1: How does the electric field vary with distance from an infinite line charge vs. a point charge?
column4: The different geometry (cylindrical vs. spherical) changes the surface area factor in Gauss's Law, leading to different distance dependencies.

column1: What principle allows electric fields from multiple charges to be added together?
column4: Electric fields are vectors; the total field at a point is the vector sum of the fields due to each individual charge.

column1: Define electric potential (voltage) at a point in space.
column3: Electric potential energy per unit charge: V = U/q
column4: V = U/q0; units are joules per coulomb = volts (V). It is a scalar quantity, unlike electric field (vector).

column1: What is the electric potential due to a point charge q at distance r?
column4: Note V ∝ 1/r (not 1/r^2 like E). Potential is positive near positive charges and negative near negative charges.

column1: What is the relationship between electric field and electric potential?
column3: E = -dV/dr (E is negative gradient of V)
column4: The electric field points in the direction of decreasing potential (downhill in voltage). For uniform field: E = -ΔV/Δd.

column1: What is the electrostatic potential energy of two point charges q1 and q2 separated by distance r?
column4: Positive U means the pair repels (like charges); negative U means they attract (unlike charges). This is the work needed to assemble the pair from infinity.

column1: How much work is done moving a charge q through a potential difference ΔV?
column4: Work done by the electric field equals qΔV (positive work when charge moves in the direction the field would push it, i.e., downhill in potential for positive q).

column1: What is the electric potential at the surface of a charged conductor relative to its interior?
column4: Because E = 0 inside the conductor, no work is done moving a charge inside it, so V is constant everywhere in and on the conductor.

column1: What is the SI unit of electric potential?
column4: 1 V = 1 J/C. Potential difference (voltage) drives current in circuits and determines energy of charges in fields.

column1: How does electric potential due to a point charge differ in sign for positive vs. negative source charges?
column3: Positive charge gives positive V; negative charge gives negative V
column4: V = kq/r: if q > 0, V > 0 everywhere; if q < 0, V < 0 everywhere (assuming V = 0 at infinity).

column1: At what location is the electric potential defined to be zero by convention for point charges?
column4: V = kq/r → 0 as r → ∞. This reference point makes potential a well-defined quantity for isolated charge distributions.

column1: What is the formula for electric current?
column4: Current is the rate of charge flow. ΔQ is charge in coulombs, Δt is time in seconds, giving current in amperes (A).

column1: What is the SI unit of electric current?
column4: 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second. Named after André-Marie Ampère.

column1: By convention, conventional current flows in which direction relative to electron flow?
column4: Conventional current flows from positive to negative; electrons (negative charge) physically flow from negative to positive.

column1: What is the charge of one electron in coulombs?
column4: This fundamental constant is used to convert between number of electrons and total charge: Q = ne.

column1: If 3 coulombs of charge pass a point in 6 seconds, what is the current?
column4: I = ΔQ/Δt = 3/6 = 0.5 A. Direct application of the current definition.

column1: What does direct current (DC) mean in terms of charge flow?
column3: Charge flows in one constant direction
column4: In DC circuits, conventional current always flows from high to low potential. Batteries produce DC; contrast with AC where direction alternates.

column1: What is electromotive force (EMF)?
column3: Energy per unit charge supplied by a source
column4: EMF (ε) is measured in volts. It is not a true force but the work done per coulomb by a battery or generator driving current around a circuit.

column1: What is the SI unit of voltage (potential difference)?
column4: 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb. Voltage represents the potential energy difference per unit charge between two points.

column1: How does terminal voltage of a battery differ from its EMF when current flows?
column3: Terminal voltage = EMF − I·r (r = internal resistance)
column4: Internal resistance causes a voltage drop inside the battery, so the terminal voltage is less than EMF during discharge.

column1: What does voltage (potential difference) between two points physically represent?
column3: Work per unit charge to move charge between points
column4: V = W/Q. A higher voltage means more energy is available per coulomb to drive current through a circuit element.

column1: If a battery has EMF = 9 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, what is terminal voltage when 2 A flows?
column4: V_terminal = EMF − I·r = 9 − (2)(1) = 7 V. Internal resistance always reduces usable terminal voltage under load.

column1: What is electrical resistance?
column4: Resistance (R) is measured in ohms (Ω). It converts electrical energy to heat (in ohmic resistors) and limits current magnitude.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::resistance MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the SI unit of resistance?
column4: 1 Ω = 1 V/A. Named after Georg Ohm.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::resistance MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does resistance change when temperature increases in a metallic conductor?
column4: Higher temperature increases lattice vibrations, causing more electron scattering and greater resistance. R ∝ T for metals.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::resistance MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What two geometric factors increase the resistance of a wire?
column4: R = ρL/A. Doubling length doubles R; halving area doubles R. Narrower, longer wires resist more.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::resistance MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What distinguishes an ohmic resistor from a non-ohmic device?
column3: Ohmic: constant R regardless of voltage; non-ohmic: R varies
column4: Ohmic resistors obey V = IR linearly. Diodes and transistors are non-ohmic — their resistance changes with applied voltage.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::resistance MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: State Ohm's Law.
column3: V = IR (voltage equals current times resistance)
column4: Ohm's Law relates voltage, current, and resistance for ohmic conductors. Rearrangements: I = V/R and R = V/I.

column1: In Ohm's Law, if voltage doubles and resistance stays constant, what happens to current?
column4: I = V/R. Current is directly proportional to voltage for a fixed resistance.

column1: What is the power dissipated by a resistor in terms of current and resistance?
column4: Derived from P = IV and V = IR: P = I(IR) = I²R. Also expressible as P = V²/R. Units are watts (W).

column1: A 10 Ω resistor carries 2 A. What power does it dissipate?
column4: P = I²R = (2)²(10) = 40 W. This power is released as heat in the resistor.

column1: What is the voltage across a 5 Ω resistor when 3 A flows through it?
column4: V = IR = (3)(5) = 15 V. Direct application of Ohm's Law.

column1: What is the formula for total resistance of resistors in series?
column4: Series resistors simply add. Current is the same through each; voltage divides among them.

column1: In a series circuit, how does current compare across each resistor?
column3: Current is the same through all resistors
column4: There is only one path for current in series. I is identical at every point in the loop.

column1: In a series circuit, how is voltage distributed among resistors?
column4: V_i = I·R_i. The larger the resistance, the greater its share of the total voltage (voltage divider principle).

column1: If a series circuit has resistors 4 Ω and 6 Ω connected to 20 V, what current flows?
column4: R_total = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω; I = V/R = 20/10 = 2 A. Same current through both resistors.

column1: Why does adding more resistors in series always increase total resistance?
column3: Each added resistor provides additional opposition; no extra paths
column4: Series configuration forces all current through every resistor, so each additional resistor adds to the total opposition.

column1: What is the formula for total resistance of resistors in parallel?
column4: Parallel paths provide additional routes for current, reducing total resistance below any individual resistor.

column1: In a parallel circuit, how does voltage compare across each branch?
column3: Voltage is the same across all parallel branches
column4: All parallel resistors share the same two nodes, so each experiences the full source voltage.

column1: In a parallel circuit, how does current divide among branches?
column3: Current divides inversely proportional to resistance
column4: I_i = V/R_i. Lower-resistance branches carry more current (more current takes the easier path).

column1: What is the equivalent resistance of two identical 8 Ω resistors in parallel?
column4: 1/R = 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8; R = 4 Ω. Two identical resistors in parallel always give half the individual resistance.

column1: Why is total resistance in a parallel circuit always less than the smallest individual resistor?
column3: Additional paths reduce total opposition to current
column4: Each added parallel branch provides another route for current, lowering effective resistance below any single branch.

column1: What is the formula for resistivity?
column4: ρ (rho) is the intrinsic material property (Ω·m). R = ρL/A shows resistance increases with length and decreases with area.

column1: What are the SI units of resistivity?
column4: Resistivity is a material constant — e.g., copper ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, much lower than insulator values.

column1: If a wire's length doubles and its cross-sectional area halves, by what factor does resistance change?
column4: R = ρL/A. Doubling L doubles R; halving A doubles R again. Overall: R × 2 × 2 = 4R.

column1: How does resistivity differ from resistance?
column3: Resistivity is an intrinsic material property; resistance depends on geometry too
column4: ρ depends only on material and temperature. R = ρL/A incorporates shape (L and A). Same material, different shapes → same ρ but different R.

column1: Which has lower resistivity: copper or rubber?
column4: Copper is an excellent conductor (ρ ≈ 10⁻⁸ Ω·m); rubber is an insulator (ρ ≈ 10¹³ Ω·m). Lower resistivity = better conductor.

column1: What is capacitance?
column3: Ability of a capacitor to store charge per unit voltage
column4: C = Q/V. Higher capacitance means more charge stored for the same voltage. Units are farads (F).
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::capacitance MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the SI unit of capacitance?
column4: 1 F = 1 C/V. Practical capacitors are typically in microfarads (μF) or picofarads (pF) as 1 F is very large.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::capacitance MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the formula relating charge, capacitance, and voltage?
column4: Rearranges to C = Q/V and V = Q/C. A larger capacitance stores more charge at the same voltage.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::capacitance MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does capacitance change if charge stored doubles but voltage also doubles?
column4: C = Q/V. If both Q and V double, the ratio is unchanged. Capacitance is a geometric/material property, not dependent on Q or V individually.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::capacitance MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What does it mean for a capacitor to be fully charged?
column3: No current flows; voltage across capacitor equals source voltage
column4: At steady state in a DC circuit, a capacitor acts as an open circuit — no further charge transfer occurs once V_cap = V_source.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::capacitance MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the formula for capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor?
column4: C increases with larger plate area (A) and decreases with greater plate separation (d). ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m is permittivity of free space.

column1: In a parallel plate capacitor, what type of electric field exists between the plates?
column4: Ideal parallel plates produce a uniform field E = V/d between them, directed from positive to negative plate.

column1: How does increasing plate separation affect capacitance in a parallel plate capacitor?
column4: C = ε₀A/d. Larger d means smaller C. Physically, charges are farther apart and attract less strongly.

column1: What is the electric field between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor with separation d and voltage V?
column4: This uniform field formula applies between ideal parallel plates. Units: V/m or N/C.

column1: If plate area of a parallel plate capacitor is doubled and separation is halved, how does capacitance change?
column4: C = ε₀A/d. Doubling A doubles C; halving d doubles C again. Net effect: 4× original capacitance.

column1: What is the formula for energy stored in a capacitor?
column4: Also expressible as U = Q²/2C = ½QV. Energy is stored in the electric field between the plates.

column1: In what form is the energy in a charged capacitor stored?
column4: The energy density of the electric field (u = ½ε₀E²) accounts for the energy stored when a capacitor is charged.

column1: A capacitor with C = 4 μF is charged to 10 V. What energy does it store?
How does energy stored in a capacitor change if voltage doubles (capacitance fixed)?
column4: U = ½CV². Since V appears squared, doubling V increases U by 2² = 4. Energy is very sensitive to voltage.

column1: Which expression for capacitor energy uses charge (Q) instead of voltage?
column4: Derived from U = ½CV² and Q = CV: substitute V = Q/C → U = ½C(Q/C)² = Q²/2C. Useful when Q is known.

column1: What is the formula for total capacitance of capacitors in series?
column4: Series capacitors reduce total capacitance (like parallel resistors). Voltage divides; charge on each is the same.

column1: In capacitors in series, what quantity is the same across all capacitors?
column4: The same charge accumulates on each capacitor in series because there is only one path for charge to flow.

column1: In capacitors in series, how is voltage distributed?
column3: Voltage divides inversely proportional to capacitance
column4: V_i = Q/C_i. Smaller capacitors have larger voltage drops — opposite pattern to resistors in series.

column1: What is the equivalent capacitance of two 6 μF capacitors in series?
column4: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6; C = 3 μF. Two identical capacitors in series give half the individual capacitance.

column1: Why does total capacitance decrease when capacitors are added in series?
column3: Effective plate separation increases, reducing C
column4: Series capacitors act like one capacitor with greater separation (d_total = d₁ + d₂). Since C = ε₀A/d, larger d means lower C.

column1: What is the formula for total capacitance of capacitors in parallel?
column4: Parallel capacitors simply add (like series resistors). Total effective plate area increases, raising capacitance.

column1: In capacitors in parallel, what quantity is the same across all capacitors?
column4: All parallel capacitors share the same two nodes, so they experience the same potential difference.

column1: In capacitors in parallel, how does charge distribute among capacitors?
column4: Q_i = C_i·V. Larger capacitors store more charge since they share the same voltage.

column1: What is the equivalent capacitance of 3 μF and 9 μF capacitors in parallel?
column4: C_total = 3 + 9 = 12 μF. Parallel capacitances add directly.

column1: Why does total capacitance increase when capacitors are added in parallel?
column3: Effective plate area increases, raising total charge storage
column4: Parallel capacitors act like one capacitor with a larger combined area. Since C = ε₀A/d, more area → more capacitance.

column1: What is a dielectric?
column3: Insulating material placed between capacitor plates
column4: Dielectrics increase capacitance by reducing the effective electric field between the plates via polarization of the material.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::dielectrics MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the dielectric constant (κ)?
column3: Factor by which capacitance increases when dielectric is inserted
column4: C = κ·C₀ where C₀ is capacitance without dielectric. κ ≥ 1; for vacuum/air κ = 1.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::dielectrics MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What happens to capacitance when a dielectric is inserted between the plates?
column3: Capacitance increases by factor κ (dielectric constant)
column4: C = κε₀A/d. The dielectric reduces effective E-field (polarization partially cancels applied field), allowing more charge to be stored.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::dielectrics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If a capacitor is connected to a battery and a dielectric is inserted, what happens to charge stored?
column4: Voltage is held constant by the battery; since C increases by κ and Q = CV, charge increases proportionally.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::dielectrics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: If a capacitor is isolated (disconnected) and a dielectric is inserted, what happens to voltage?
column4: Q is fixed (isolated); since C increases by κ and V = Q/C, voltage decreases by factor κ. Energy also decreases (given to polarizing material).
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::dielectrics MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is electrical conductivity?
column3: Measure of a material's ability to conduct electric current
column4: Conductivity (σ) = 1/ρ (reciprocal of resistivity). Units: siemens per meter (S/m). High σ = good conductor.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::conductivity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the relationship between conductivity and resistivity?
column4: They are reciprocals. High conductivity (good conductor) corresponds to low resistivity. Copper: high σ; glass: low σ.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::conductivity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the unit of electrical conductivity?
column4: 1 S = 1/Ω (siemens = reciprocal ohm). Conductivity is also sometimes expressed as (Ω·m)⁻¹.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::conductivity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does conductivity of a semiconductor compare to that of a metal?
column3: Semiconductor conductivity is much lower than metal
column4: Metals: σ ≈ 10⁶–10⁸ S/m; semiconductors: σ ≈ 10⁻⁴–10⁴ S/m. Semiconductors are intermediate between conductors and insulators.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::conductivity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does increasing temperature affect the conductivity of a metallic conductor?
column4: More lattice vibrations at higher T scatter electrons more, increasing ρ and decreasing σ = 1/ρ. Opposite is true for semiconductors.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::conductivity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What type of particles carry charge in metallic conductors?
column4: Metals have a 'sea' of delocalized conduction electrons that move in response to an electric field. Positive metal ions remain fixed in the lattice.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::metallic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why do metals have high electrical conductivity?
column3: Large number of free (delocalized) conduction electrons
column4: Metallic bonding releases outer electrons to roam freely throughout the lattice, making electron flow (current) easy.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::metallic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does resistivity of a metal change with temperature?
column4: Higher T → more phonon (lattice vibration) scattering of electrons → higher ρ. This is opposite the behavior of semiconductors.

column1: What is a superconductor, and below what condition does it occur?
column3: Zero resistance material; occurs below critical temperature (T_c)
column4: At T < T_c, resistance drops to exactly zero. Electrons form Cooper pairs that move without scattering. Not tested deeply on MCAT but concept is fair game.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::metallic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why do metals become better conductors at lower temperatures?
column3: Fewer lattice vibrations reduce electron scattering
column4: At low T, reduced thermal motion means fewer collisions for conduction electrons, lowering resistivity and increasing conductivity.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::metallic MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What carries charge in an electrolytic conductor?
column4: In electrolyte solutions, dissolved salts dissociate into positive and negative ions, both of which migrate and carry current.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::electrolytic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Name two common examples of electrolytic conductors.
column4: Any ionic solution conducts electricity. Biological fluids (blood, cytoplasm) are also electrolytic conductors relevant to the MCAT.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::electrolytic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does conductivity of an electrolytic solution change as ion concentration increases?
column4: More ions → more charge carriers → greater current for the same voltage → higher conductivity. Dilute solutions conduct less than concentrated ones.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::electrolytic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does temperature affect conductivity of electrolytic conductors?
column4: Higher T increases ion mobility (less viscous solvent, faster ion movement), increasing conductivity. Opposite to metallic conductors.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::electrolytic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What distinguishes electrolytic conduction from metallic conduction at the atomic level?
column4: In metals, only electrons carry current. In electrolytes, both cations (to cathode) and anions (to anode) carry current.

column1: What does an ammeter measure, and how is it connected in a circuit?
column4: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance so it does not disturb current. It must be in series to measure the current flowing through a branch.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::meters MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What does a voltmeter measure, and how is it connected in a circuit?
column4: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance so no current flows through it. It is placed across (in parallel with) the element being measured.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::meters MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why must an ideal ammeter have zero (or very low) resistance?
column3: To avoid changing the current it is measuring
column4: If an ammeter had significant resistance, adding it in series would increase total circuit resistance and reduce current, giving an inaccurate reading.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::meters MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why must an ideal voltmeter have infinite (or very high) resistance?
column3: To avoid drawing current that would alter circuit voltage
column4: A low-resistance voltmeter in parallel would create a short-circuit path, drawing current and lowering the voltage across the measured element.

column1: What is a galvanometer used for?
column4: A galvanometer is the basic movement in both ammeters and voltmeters. A shunt resistor (in parallel) converts it to an ammeter; a series resistor converts it to a voltmeter.
column8: concept::CP::4C::circuit_elements MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4C::circuit-elements::meters MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How is a galvanometer converted into a voltmeter?
column3: Add a large resistor in series with the galvanometer
column4: The large series resistor limits current so the galvanometer deflects in proportion to the applied voltage without drawing significant current.

column1: What is the SI unit of magnetic field strength (B)?
column4: 1 Tesla = 1 kg/(A·s²). The tesla is a large unit; Earth's magnetic field is about 50 µT, while MRI machines operate at 1–3 T.

column1: What symbol is used to denote the magnetic field vector?
column4: B is the magnetic flux density (magnetic field). It is a vector quantity with both magnitude and direction, distinct from H (magnetic field intensity).

column1: What is the direction of the magnetic field produced by a long straight current-carrying wire?
column4: Curl the right hand around the wire with the thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current; the fingers curl in the direction of B.

column1: What smaller unit of magnetic field is equivalent to 10⁻⁴ Tesla?
column4: The Gauss (G) is the CGS unit of magnetic field. Earth's surface field (~0.5 G) is often expressed in Gauss; 1 T = 10,000 G.

column1: What is the relationship between magnetic flux Φ, field B, and area A for a uniform field perpendicular to a surface?
column4: Magnetic flux is the total field passing through a surface. Units are Webers (Wb); 1 Wb = 1 T·m². When B is not perpendicular, Φ = BA cosθ.

column1: What physical quantity does the magnetic field B represent in terms of force per unit moving charge?
column3: Force per unit charge per unit velocity (F = qvB)
column4: B is defined such that the magnetic force on a charge q moving at velocity v is F = qv × B. B has units of N/(C·m/s) = T.

column1: What distinguishes magnetic field lines from electric field lines regarding their origin and termination?
column3: Magnetic field lines form closed loops; they have no beginning or end (no magnetic monopoles)
column4: Because isolated magnetic monopoles have never been observed, ∇·B = 0 (Gauss's law for magnetism), so all B field lines close on themselves.

column1: What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I? (give the formula)
column4: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A is the permeability of free space. Field decreases as 1/r from a long wire.

column1: What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on a charge q moving at speed v perpendicular to field B?
column4: When v and B are perpendicular, sinθ = 1, giving maximum force. If v is parallel to B, the force is zero.

column1: In what direction does the magnetic force act relative to the velocity of a moving charge?
column3: Perpendicular to both v and B
column4: Because F = qv × B (cross product), the force is always perpendicular to velocity, meaning the magnetic force does NO work on the particle.

column1: What type of path does a charged particle follow when moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field?
column4: The magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration. Since the force is always perpendicular to v, speed is constant and the path is a perfect circle.

column1: What is the formula for the radius of circular motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field?
column4: Setting centripetal force equal to magnetic force: mv²/r = qvB → r = mv/(qB). A heavier or faster particle curves less; stronger B or larger charge curves more.

column1: What path does a charged particle follow when its velocity has components both parallel and perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field?
column4: The parallel component is unaffected (no force), while the perpendicular component produces circular motion, combining into a helix along the field direction.

column1: How much work does the magnetic force do on a moving charged particle?
column4: Because F is always perpendicular to v, F·v = 0 at every instant. The magnetic force changes direction but never changes the kinetic energy or speed of the particle.

column1: What is the cyclotron frequency (cyclotron angular frequency) of a charged particle in a magnetic field?
column4: From r = mv/(qB) and ω = v/r, ω = qB/m. The cyclotron frequency is independent of the particle's speed — the basis of the cyclotron particle accelerator.

column1: In what direction does a positive charge moving to the right (+x) in a magnetic field pointing out of the page (+z) experience a magnetic force?
column4: F = q(v × B). v = +x̂, B = +ẑ; x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ. For a positive charge, F is in the −y direction (downward). Negative charges curve the opposite way.

column1: What is the period of circular motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field?
column4: T = 2πr/v = 2π(mv/qB)/v = 2πm/(qB). Like cyclotron frequency, the period is independent of particle speed — only depends on mass, charge, and B.

column1: What type of cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction?
column4: An electrolytic cell requires an external power source (voltage) to force a non-spontaneous redox reaction to occur, the opposite of a galvanic cell.

column1: In an electrolytic cell, which electrode is connected to the positive terminal of the external power source?
column4: The external source pulls electrons away from the anode, making it positive; oxidation occurs there. In galvanic cells the anode is also the oxidation electrode but is negative.

column1: What is the key difference between an electrolytic cell and a galvanic cell in terms of spontaneity?
column4: Galvanic cells generate electricity from spontaneous redox reactions; electrolytic cells consume electricity to drive non-spontaneous reactions.

column1: In an electrolytic cell, which sign does the anode carry?
column4: Unlike a galvanic cell where the anode is negative, in an electrolytic cell the external source forces the anode positive, attracting anions from the solution.

column1: What is the minimum voltage required to drive electrolysis called?
column4: This is the voltage at which the applied EMF just overcomes the back-EMF of the cell and electrolysis begins; it equals the standard cell potential of the reverse reaction.

column1: What process occurs at the electrodes of an electrolytic cell to decompose a substance using electric current?
column4: Electrolysis drives redox reactions at electrodes — reduction at the cathode and oxidation at the anode — using an external electrical energy source.

column1: What is produced at the cathode during electrolysis of molten NaCl?
column4: Na+ ions are reduced at the cathode: Na+ + e- → Na. At the anode, Cl- is oxidized to Cl2 gas.

column1: During electrolysis of aqueous NaCl, what gas is preferentially produced at the cathode?
column4: Water is more easily reduced than Na+ in aqueous solution, so 2H2O + 2e- → H2 + 2OH- occurs at the cathode instead of Na deposition.

column1: During electrolysis of water, which gas is produced at the anode?
column4: Water is oxidized at the anode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e-. Hydrogen is produced at the cathode in a 2:1 volume ratio (H2:O2).

column1: In electroplating, which electrode is the object being plated?
column4: The object to be plated is made the cathode so that metal cations from the solution are reduced and deposited onto its surface.

column1: What is the ratio of H2 to O2 gas volumes produced during electrolysis of water?
column4: The half-reactions require 4 electrons to produce 1 mol O2 but only 2 electrons per mol H2, so twice as many moles (and volume) of H2 are produced.

column1: At which electrode does oxidation always occur in any electrochemical cell?
column4: Mnemonic: 'AN OX' — ANode = OXidation. This is true for both galvanic and electrolytic cells regardless of the sign of the electrode.

column1: At which electrode does reduction always occur in any electrochemical cell?
column4: Mnemonic: 'RED CAT' — REDuction at CAThode. Cations are attracted to the cathode and gain electrons.

column1: In a galvanic cell, which electrode has a negative charge?
column4: In a galvanic cell the anode releases electrons into the external circuit, making it the negative terminal (electron source). This is opposite to the electrolytic cell.

column1: In an electrolytic cell, which electrode is negative?
column4: The external power source pumps electrons into the cathode, giving it a negative charge and enabling reduction of cations at its surface.

column1: Which electrode in a galvanic cell is labeled the positive terminal?
column4: In a galvanic cell the cathode attracts electrons from the external circuit; it is the positive terminal and site of reduction.

column1: Define electrolyte as it relates to electrochemical cells.
column3: Substance that dissociates into ions in solution
column4: Electrolytes allow ionic conduction within the cell. Strong electrolytes (e.g., KCl, HCl) fully dissociate; weak electrolytes partially dissociate.

column1: What role does the electrolyte play in a galvanic cell?
column3: Conducts ions between half-cells (maintains charge balance)
column4: Without ionic conduction through the electrolyte (or salt bridge), charge would build up and stop the flow of electrons through the external circuit.

column1: What is the purpose of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
column3: Maintains electrical neutrality in both half-cells
column4: The salt bridge allows ions to migrate between the two half-cells to balance charge without mixing the solutions; without it, current flow ceases.

column1: Which of the following is a strong electrolyte: acetic acid, glucose, or KNO3?
column4: KNO3 is an ionic compound that fully dissociates in water. Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte; glucose is a non-electrolyte.

column1: State Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis.
column3: Mass deposited is proportional to charge passed
column4: m = (M × Q) / (n × F), where M = molar mass, Q = charge (coulombs), n = moles of electrons, F = Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol).

column1: What is the value of Faraday's constant?
column4: One Faraday is the charge of one mole of electrons. On the MCAT, 96,500 C/mol is commonly used for calculations.

column1: How many coulombs of charge are required to deposit 1 mole of a divalent metal (n=2) by electrolysis?
column4: Each mole of a 2+ ion requires 2 moles of electrons; using Q = n × F gives 2 × 96,500 C.

column1: If a current of 2 A flows for 965 seconds, how many moles of electrons are transferred?
In Faraday's electrolysis formula m = MQ/(nF), what does 'n' represent?
column3: Moles of electrons per mole of substance (charge number)
column4: n is the number of electrons transferred per formula unit in the half-reaction (e.g., n=2 for Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu).

column1: What is the relationship between current (I), charge (Q), and time (t)?
column4: Charge in coulombs equals current in amperes multiplied by time in seconds. This is the starting point for all Faraday's Law MCAT calculations.

column1: In which direction do electrons flow through the external circuit of a galvanic cell?
column4: Electrons are produced at the anode (oxidation) and consumed at the cathode (reduction); current (conventional) flows opposite — cathode to anode.

column1: What process occurs at the anode of a galvanic cell?
column4: The anode electrode is oxidized: atoms give up electrons which travel through the external circuit to the cathode.

column1: At which electrode of an electrolytic cell does reduction occur?
column4: In both galvanic and electrolytic cells, reduction always occurs at the cathode regardless of the cell type.

column1: In conventional current notation, in which direction does current flow in the external circuit of a galvanic cell?
column3: From cathode to anode (positive to negative)
column4: Conventional current flows opposite to electron flow. Electrons go from anode to cathode; conventional current flows from cathode (positive) to anode (negative).

column1: Which species is oxidized and which is reduced in the reaction Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu?
column4: Zn loses electrons (0 → +2, oxidized); Cu2+ gains electrons (+2 → 0, reduced). Zn is the reducing agent; Cu2+ is the oxidizing agent.

column1: What type of cell spontaneously converts chemical energy to electrical energy?
column4: Galvanic/voltaic cells harness spontaneous redox reactions (negative ΔG) to produce an electric current. They are the basis of batteries.
