column1: What is the sign of ΔG for the reaction driving a galvanic cell?
column4: Spontaneous reactions have ΔG < 0. The relationship ΔG = -nFE_cell confirms that a positive cell potential corresponds to a negative ΔG.

column1: In a galvanic cell, which compartment contains the anode?
column3: The compartment where the reducing agent (more active metal) is oxidized
column4: The more easily oxidized metal serves as the anode. Example: in Zn-Cu cell, Zn is the anode because it is more easily oxidized than Cu.

column1: What is the equation relating cell potential to Gibbs free energy?
column4: n = moles of electrons transferred, F = Faraday's constant, E_cell = standard cell potential. A positive E gives negative ΔG (spontaneous).

column1: What is the standard cell potential of the Daniell cell (Zn | ZnSO4 || CuSO4 | Cu)?
column4: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = +0.34 V (Cu2+/Cu) - (-0.76 V) (Zn2+/Zn) = +1.10 V. A classic galvanic cell example.

column1: Define a half-reaction in electrochemistry.
column3: A reaction showing either oxidation or reduction alone
column4: Every redox reaction can be split into two half-reactions: one oxidation (anode) and one reduction (cathode). Electrons appear explicitly in each.

column1: How do you balance electrons when combining two half-reactions to obtain the overall cell reaction?
column3: Multiply half-reactions so electrons cancel (equal numbers)
column4: Scale each half-reaction by the smallest integer that makes the electrons transferred equal, then add them so electrons cancel out.

column1: In the half-reaction MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- → Mn2+ + 4H2O, what is the oxidizing agent?
column4: MnO4- is reduced (Mn goes from +7 to +2), so it is the oxidizing agent. The 8H+ are needed to balance the half-reaction in acidic solution.

column1: When balancing a half-reaction in acidic solution, what species are used to balance oxygen atoms?
column4: Add H2O to balance O, then H+ to balance H, then electrons to balance charge. In basic solution, add OH- after balancing with H2O/H+.

column1: What is the standard reduction potential (E°) of the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)?
column4: The SHE (H+ / H2, 1 M, 1 atm, 25°C) is the reference electrode against which all other standard reduction potentials are measured.

column1: How is the standard cell potential (E°cell) calculated from reduction potentials?
column4: Both values are looked up as standard reduction potentials. Subtracting (not flipping the sign of the anode) avoids double-counting the sign change.

column1: What does a positive standard cell potential (E°cell > 0) indicate?
column3: The reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions
column4: Positive E°cell → negative ΔG° → spontaneous. Also indicates the equilibrium constant K > 1 via ΔG° = -RT ln K = -nFE°.

column1: What is the standard reduction potential of Zn2+/Zn?
column4: Zn is easily oxidized (low reduction potential). In a galvanic cell, Zn serves as the anode relative to many metal electrodes.

column1: What is the standard reduction potential of Cu2+/Cu?
column4: Cu2+ is relatively easily reduced. Combined with Zn (E° = -0.76 V), the Daniell cell gives E°cell = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V.

column1: A half-reaction has a very negative standard reduction potential. Is this species a good oxidizing or reducing agent?
column4: Low (very negative) E° means the species is easily oxidized; it tends to give up electrons, making it a strong reducing agent.

column1: In a galvanic cell, in which direction do electrons flow through the external circuit?
column4: The anode is the source of electrons (negative terminal); they flow through the wire to the cathode (positive terminal) where they reduce species.

column1: In which direction do cations migrate through the salt bridge of a galvanic cell?
column4: As cations are consumed (reduced) at the cathode, cations from the salt bridge migrate in to maintain electrical neutrality in the cathode compartment.

column1: In which direction do anions migrate through the salt bridge of a galvanic cell?
column4: Oxidation at the anode generates cations in solution; anions from the salt bridge migrate in to balance the increasing positive charge.

column1: What happens to the cell potential of a galvanic cell if the direction of the spontaneous reaction is reversed?
column3: Cell potential becomes negative (equal magnitude, opposite sign)
column4: Reversing the reaction is equivalent to forcing the non-spontaneous direction, as in an electrolytic cell; E changes sign.

column1: What is a concentration cell?
column3: A galvanic cell with identical electrodes but different ion concentrations
column4: The potential arises solely from the concentration difference between the two half-cells. The reaction drives toward equalizing concentrations.

column1: What is the cell potential of a concentration cell when concentrations in both half-cells are equal?
column4: When concentrations are equal, Q = 1 and ln Q = 0, so by the Nernst equation E = E° - (RT/nF) ln Q = 0 - 0 = 0.

column1: Which equation is used to calculate the cell potential of a concentration cell at non-standard conditions?
column3: Nernst equation: E = E° - (RT/nF) ln Q
column4: For a concentration cell E° = 0, so E = -(RT/nF) ln Q = -(0.0592/n) log Q at 25°C. Potential is positive when Q < 1.

column1: What is the standard EMF of a concentration cell (identical electrodes, same metal)?
column4: Because both half-reactions are identical (same metal/ion), they cancel and E° = 0. Any actual potential comes only from the Nernst term.

column1: What is the fundamental function of a battery?
column3: Stores chemical energy and converts it to electrical energy
column4: Batteries are galvanic cells (or series of cells) in which spontaneous redox reactions are harnessed to do electrical work.

column1: What distinguishes a primary battery from a secondary battery?
column4: Primary batteries (e.g., alkaline AA) are used until reactants are depleted. Secondary batteries (e.g., lead-acid, NiCd) can be recharged by reversing the reaction.

column1: What are the two electrodes and the electrolyte in a common alkaline battery?
column3: Anode: Zn; Cathode: MnO2; Electrolyte: KOH
column4: In an alkaline cell, Zn is oxidized at the anode and MnO2 is reduced at the cathode in a basic (KOH) electrolyte solution.

column1: What is the approximate cell voltage of a single alkaline (Zn-MnO2) cell?
column4: Most standard single-cell alkaline batteries produce approximately 1.5 V. Multiple cells in series multiply the voltage.

column1: Which term describes the maximum work a battery can do per unit charge?
column4: EMF (in volts) equals the maximum energy per coulomb the cell can deliver; it equals the open-circuit cell potential under ideal conditions.

column1: Define electromotive force (EMF) in an electrochemical context.
column3: The potential difference that drives current; energy per unit charge
column4: EMF (measured in volts = J/C) is the maximum voltage a cell can produce; it equals E°cell under standard conditions and accounts for all redox driving force.

column1: What is the unit of electromotive force?
column4: 1 V = 1 J/C. EMF is the energy provided per coulomb of charge and is measured in volts, the same unit as potential difference.

column1: How does internal resistance affect the terminal voltage of a battery?
column3: Terminal voltage = EMF - I × r (lower than EMF)
column4: When current flows, voltage drops across the internal resistance r; the actual terminal voltage is less than the open-circuit EMF. Higher current → larger drop.

column1: What is the relationship between EMF, Gibbs free energy, and moles of electrons?
column4: n = moles of electrons, F = 96,500 C/mol, E° = standard cell potential. A cell with E° = +1 V transferring 1 mol e- releases 96.5 kJ.

column1: What is the Nernst equation used for?
column3: Calculating cell potential at non-standard conditions
column4: E = E° - (RT/nF) ln Q; at 25°C this simplifies to E = E° - (0.0592/n) log Q. It relates Q (reaction quotient) to actual cell potential.

column1: What are the two electrodes in a lead-storage (lead-acid) battery?
column4: During discharge: Pb is oxidized at the anode and PbO2 is reduced at the cathode. Both electrodes are converted to PbSO4 during discharge.

column1: What is the electrolyte in a lead-acid battery?
column4: Concentrated H2SO4 provides the SO42- ions that form PbSO4 at both electrodes during discharge and is regenerated during charging.

column1: What is the approximate cell voltage of a single lead-acid cell?
column4: A car battery uses 6 lead-acid cells in series to produce ~12 V total (6 × 2 V). The high current capacity makes it suitable for starter motors.

column1: What happens to PbSO4 during recharging of a lead-acid battery?
column3: It is converted back to Pb and PbO2
column4: Charging reverses the discharge reaction: PbSO4 at the anode is oxidized back to Pb, and PbSO4 at the cathode is reduced back to PbO2.

column1: What overall product builds up at BOTH electrodes during discharge of a lead-acid battery?
column4: At the anode: Pb + SO42- → PbSO4 + 2e-. At the cathode: PbO2 + SO42- + 4H+ + 2e- → PbSO4 + 2H2O. Both produce PbSO4.

column1: What is the anode reaction during discharge of a lead-acid battery?
column4: Pb(0) is oxidized to Pb(+2), forming insoluble PbSO4 on the electrode surface. This is the oxidation (anode) half-reaction.

column1: What are the two electrodes in a nickel-cadmium (NiCd) battery?
column4: During discharge, Cd is oxidized at the anode and NiOOH is reduced to Ni(OH)2 at the cathode. The electrolyte is KOH.

column1: What is the electrolyte in a nickel-cadmium battery?
column4: NiCd batteries use an alkaline (basic) electrolyte, unlike lead-acid batteries which use an acidic electrolyte (H2SO4).

column1: What is the approximate cell voltage of a NiCd battery?
column4: NiCd cells produce about 1.2 V per cell, slightly less than alkaline (1.5 V) but they are rechargeable and maintain voltage better during discharge.

column1: What is the 'memory effect' associated with NiCd batteries?
column3: Capacity loss if repeatedly recharged before full discharge
column4: If NiCd batteries are recharged before fully depleted, they 'remember' the shorter cycle and deliver less capacity in subsequent cycles.

column1: What is produced at the cathode of a NiCd battery during discharge?
column4: NiOOH is reduced: NiOOH + H2O + e- → Ni(OH)2 + OH-. During recharging, Ni(OH)2 is oxidized back to NiOOH.

column1: Why are NiCd batteries classified as secondary (rechargeable) batteries?
column3: The discharge reactions are electrochemically reversible
column4: Applying an external voltage reverses the cell reactions, regenerating Cd and NiOOH from the discharge products Cd(OH)2 and Ni(OH)2.

column1: What is the myelin sheath?
column4: Myelin is formed by wrapping glial cell membranes around the axon multiple times, greatly increasing conduction velocity by reducing membrane capacitance.

column1: Which cells produce myelin in the peripheral nervous system?
column4: Each Schwann cell myelinates a single segment of one peripheral axon; contrast with oligodendrocytes in the CNS, which can myelinate multiple axons.

column1: Which glial cells produce myelin in the central nervous system?
column4: One oligodendrocyte can wrap multiple axon segments, while a Schwann cell wraps only one. This distinction is commonly tested on the MCAT.

column1: How does myelin insulation affect the electrical resistance of the axon membrane?
column4: High resistance prevents ion leakage across the membrane between nodes, forcing current to flow longitudinally down the axon, enabling faster propagation.

column1: How does myelination affect membrane capacitance of the axon?
column4: Myelin increases the effective thickness of the membrane 'dielectric,' reducing capacitance (C = εA/d). Lower capacitance means less charge must be deposited to change voltage, speeding conduction.

column1: What is the net effect of myelination on action potential conduction velocity?
column4: By insulating the axon, myelin allows the action potential to jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction) rather than propagating continuously, dramatically speeding transmission.

column1: What autoimmune disease destroys CNS myelin, slowing or blocking nerve conduction?
column4: In MS, immune cells attack oligodendrocytes and myelin, creating demyelinated plaques that impair saltatory conduction and cause varied neurological deficits.

column1: What is the approximate conduction velocity range for large, heavily myelinated (Aα) axons?
column4: Myelinated Aα fibers (motor and proprioception) conduct at 70–120 m/s; unmyelinated C fibers conduct at only 0.5–2 m/s, illustrating the impact of myelin on speed.

column1: What are nodes of Ranvier?
column3: Gaps in the myelin sheath exposing the axon membrane
column4: Nodes of Ranvier are short (~1 µm) unmyelinated segments spaced ~1–2 mm apart where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are densely concentrated, allowing action potential regeneration.

column1: What type of ion channels are concentrated at nodes of Ranvier?
column4: High density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels at nodes allows rapid membrane depolarization, regenerating the action potential at each node during saltatory conduction.

column1: What term describes the jumping of an action potential from node to node along a myelinated axon?
column4: From Latin saltare (to jump). The action potential is regenerated only at nodes of Ranvier, skipping the insulated internodal segments, which greatly increases speed and energy efficiency.

column1: Why is saltatory conduction more energy-efficient than continuous conduction?
column3: Fewer Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps needed to restore ion gradients
column4: Because ions cross the membrane only at nodes, less Na⁺ enters and less K⁺ leaves per impulse, so the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase must do less work to restore resting gradients.

column1: In what direction does the action potential propagate along an axon under normal physiological conditions?
column3: Unidirectional (away from soma, toward axon terminal)
column4: The refractory period of the node just depolarized prevents backward propagation; the action potential advances only to the next node in the forward direction.

column1: What prevents an action potential from propagating backward through previously activated nodes?
column4: Na⁺ channels enter an inactivated (closed, non-openable) state immediately after depolarization; they cannot be reopened until the membrane repolarizes, enforcing one-way propagation.

column1: What happens to saltatory conduction when nodes of Ranvier are blocked by a local anesthetic?
column4: Local anesthetics (e.g., lidocaine) block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels at nodes; without Na⁺ influx the action potential cannot be regenerated and conduction fails.

column1: What is the approximate spacing between adjacent nodes of Ranvier on a myelinated axon?
column4: This spacing allows the local circuit current from one node to depolarize the next node to threshold without decrement, enabling faithful saltatory conduction over long distances.

column1: How does demyelination specifically disrupt impulse propagation at nodes of Ranvier?
column3: Current leaks through bare membrane, reducing depolarization at next node
column4: Without myelin insulation, longitudinal current dissipates across the exposed internodal membrane rather than reaching the next node, slowing or blocking saltatory conduction.

column1: What type of wave is sound?
column4: Sound propagates as a longitudinal wave: compressions and rarefactions travel in the same direction as energy transfer. It requires a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::production-of-sound MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What physical mechanism produces sound waves?
column3: Vibrating object compresses and rarifies surrounding medium
column4: Any vibrating object — vocal cords, tuning fork, speaker cone — periodically displaces adjacent air molecules, generating alternating high- and low-pressure regions that propagate outward.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::production-of-sound MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the SI unit of frequency for sound?
column4: 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second. Audible human range is approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::production-of-sound MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: How does the speed of sound relate to wavelength and frequency?
column4: The wave equation v = fλ applies to all mechanical waves. For sound at a given medium and temperature, v is fixed, so frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::production-of-sound MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What property of the medium primarily determines the speed of sound?
column3: Elasticity and density of the medium
column4: Speed of sound v = sqrt(B/ρ) for fluids, where B is bulk modulus (elasticity) and ρ is density. Higher elasticity increases speed; higher density decreases it.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::production-of-sound MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In which state of matter is sound fastest: solid, liquid, or gas?
column4: Solids have much higher elastic moduli relative to density, allowing sound to propagate fastest. The order is solids > liquids > gases.

column1: Rank the speed of sound from slowest to fastest: air, water, steel.
column4: Approximate values: air ~343 m/s, water ~1480 m/s, steel ~5000 m/s. Greater intermolecular forces and elasticity in condensed phases transmit vibrations more rapidly.

column1: How does increasing temperature affect the speed of sound in air?
column4: At higher temperatures, gas molecules move faster, transmitting compressions more quickly. Approximately v ∝ sqrt(T) where T is absolute temperature in Kelvin.

column1: Why does sound travel faster in water than in air despite water being denser?
column3: Water's bulk modulus is much greater than air's
column4: Although water is ~800× denser than air, its bulk modulus is ~15,000× larger, so the net effect is faster propagation (v = sqrt(B/ρ)).

column1: How does increasing air pressure alone (at constant temperature) affect the speed of sound?
column4: Both bulk modulus and density increase proportionally with pressure, so they cancel in v = sqrt(B/ρ). Speed of sound in an ideal gas depends only on temperature.

column1: What is the formula for sound intensity level in decibels?
column4: I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² is the threshold of human hearing. Each 10 dB increase represents a 10-fold increase in intensity; each 3 dB ≈ doubling of intensity.

column1: What is the threshold of human hearing in W/m²?
column4: This reference intensity I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² corresponds to 0 dB. Normal conversation is ~60 dB (10⁻⁶ W/m²).

column1: If sound intensity increases by a factor of 100, by how many decibels does the level increase?
column4: β = 10 log(100) = 10 × 2 = 20 dB. Each factor of 10 in intensity corresponds to 10 dB; factor of 100 = 10 dB + 10 dB = 20 dB.

column1: How does sound intensity vary with distance from a point source?
column4: The inverse square law: I ∝ 1/r². Doubling distance reduces intensity to 1/4, which corresponds to a 6 dB decrease.

column1: If the intensity of sound doubles, by approximately how many decibels does the level increase?
column4: 10 log(2) ≈ 3.01 dB. This is a key MCAT approximation: doubling intensity ≈ +3 dB; halving intensity ≈ −3 dB.

column1: What is attenuation (damping) of sound?
column3: Gradual loss of sound intensity as it travels through a medium
column4: Attenuation occurs due to absorption (energy converted to heat), scattering, and spreading. Higher frequencies attenuate more rapidly in most media.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::attenuation-damping MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which sound frequencies are attenuated more quickly in tissue?
column4: Higher-frequency ultrasound has greater tissue attenuation, limiting penetration depth. Lower frequencies penetrate deeper but provide less resolution — a trade-off important in medical imaging.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::attenuation-damping MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the primary mechanism of sound attenuation in air?
column3: Absorption (viscous and thermal losses) and scattering
column4: Air molecules absorb acoustic energy converting it to heat; humidity and temperature affect this. Scattering off particles also contributes.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::attenuation-damping MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In what unit is sound attenuation commonly expressed per unit distance?
column4: Attenuation coefficient α is given in dB/cm (or dB/cm·MHz in ultrasound). Tissue attenuation is approximately 0.5 dB/cm/MHz.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::attenuation-damping MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the Doppler Effect?
column3: Apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between source and observer
column4: When source and observer approach each other, observed frequency is higher than emitted; when receding, it is lower. The wave equation for Doppler accounts for both source and observer velocity.

column1: What is the Doppler equation for observed frequency?
column4: v = speed of sound, v_o = observer speed, v_s = source speed. Upper signs (+v_o, −v_s) when moving toward each other (increasing frequency); lower signs when moving apart.

column1: If a sound source moves toward a stationary observer, how does the observed frequency compare to the emitted frequency?
column3: Observed frequency is higher than emitted frequency
column4: The source compresses the wave fronts ahead of it, decreasing the effective wavelength and increasing observed frequency. This is the classic Doppler blueshift for sound.

column1: In medical Doppler ultrasound, what is being detected?
column3: Frequency shift of sound reflected from moving blood cells
column4: Red blood cells moving toward the transducer reflect ultrasound at a higher frequency; those moving away reflect at lower frequency. The shift magnitude indicates blood flow velocity.

column1: How does the Doppler shift differ when the observer moves toward a stationary source versus when the source moves toward a stationary observer at the same speed?
column3: Observer moving produces a different (slightly smaller) frequency shift than source moving
column4: These two scenarios are NOT equivalent in classical wave mechanics (unlike light). When the observer moves, the relative velocity changes; when the source moves, the wavelength changes. The Doppler equation gives different f_obs values for the same relative speed.

column1: What is pitch?
column4: Pitch is the subjective perception corresponding to the physical quantity of frequency. Higher frequency = higher pitch. The human audible range is ~20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::pitch MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What range of frequencies can the human ear typically perceive?
column4: Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound; above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound. The range narrows with age, particularly at high frequencies.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::pitch MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which physical property of a sound wave primarily determines pitch?
column4: Pitch is the auditory correlate of frequency. Amplitude (related to intensity/loudness) and waveform (timbre) are separate perceptual dimensions.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::pitch MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is a harmonic in the context of sound and pitch?
column3: Integer multiple of the fundamental frequency
column4: The nth harmonic = n × f₁ (fundamental). Harmonics determine the timbre (quality) of a sound; the relative amplitudes of harmonics distinguish instruments playing the same pitch.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::pitch MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why does a flute sound different from a violin playing the same pitch?
column4: Both play the same fundamental frequency, but the relative amplitudes of higher harmonics differ. This mixture of harmonics is called timbre or tone quality.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::pitch MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What are the boundary conditions for a pipe open at both ends?
column4: Open ends are pressure nodes / displacement antinodes. Harmonics for open-open pipe: f_n = nv/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … (all harmonics present).

column1: What is the fundamental frequency of an open-open pipe of length L?
column4: The fundamental (first harmonic) fits half a wavelength in the pipe: L = λ/2, so λ = 2L and f₁ = v/2L. All harmonics (n = 1, 2, 3, …) are present.

column1: What are the boundary conditions for a pipe closed at one end?
column3: Node at closed end, antinode at open end
column4: The closed end is a displacement node (pressure antinode); the open end is a displacement antinode. Only odd harmonics are present: f_n = nv/(4L), n = 1, 3, 5, …

column1: What is the fundamental frequency of a pipe closed at one end with length L?
column4: L = λ/4 for the fundamental, so λ = 4L and f₁ = v/4L. Only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) resonate in a closed-end pipe.

column1: Which harmonics are present in a closed-open pipe: all or only odd?
column4: Closed-open pipes resonate at f_n = nv/(4L) for n = 1, 3, 5, … This contrasts with open-open or fixed-fixed strings, which support all integer harmonics.

column1: What are the boundary conditions for a vibrating string fixed at both ends?
column4: Fixed ends cannot vibrate, so they are displacement nodes. The string supports all harmonics: f_n = nv/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … — identical in form to an open-open pipe.

column1: How does increasing the tension in a string affect its fundamental frequency?
column4: Wave speed on a string v = sqrt(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is linear mass density. Higher tension → higher v → higher f₁ = v/(2L). Guitar tuning exploits this.

column1: What frequency range defines ultrasound?
column4: Ultrasound is sound above the upper limit of human hearing (~20 kHz). Medical imaging uses frequencies of 1–20 MHz for high resolution at limited tissue depth.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::ultrasound MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What physical principle underlies ultrasound imaging?
column3: Pulse-echo: reflection of ultrasound waves at tissue interfaces
column4: A transducer emits a short ultrasound pulse and detects returning echoes. The time delay and amplitude of echoes yield depth and acoustic impedance mismatch information.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::ultrasound MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is acoustic impedance?
column3: Z = ρv (density × speed of sound in medium)
column4: Acoustic impedance Z determines how much sound is reflected vs. transmitted at an interface. Greater mismatch in Z between tissues → greater reflection (stronger echo).
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::ultrasound MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Why is ultrasound gel used during imaging?
column3: To eliminate air gaps and reduce acoustic impedance mismatch between transducer and skin
column4: Air has very low acoustic impedance compared to tissue; the gel provides acoustic coupling so nearly all ultrasound energy enters the body rather than reflecting off skin.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::ultrasound MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Which ultrasound frequency provides better resolution but less tissue penetration?
column4: Higher frequency → shorter wavelength → better spatial resolution, but more attenuation in tissue. Lower frequency penetrates deeper but resolves less detail. Clinical choice depends on target depth.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::ultrasound MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the piezoelectric effect as used in ultrasound transducers?
column3: Mechanical deformation of a crystal generates voltage (and vice versa)
column4: Ultrasound transducers use piezoelectric crystals that vibrate when voltage is applied (emitting sound) and generate voltage when sound waves return (detecting echoes). Same crystal serves as emitter and receiver.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::ultrasound MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is a shock wave?
column3: Conical pressure wave created when an object moves faster than the speed of sound
column4: When a source exceeds sound speed (Mach > 1), it outruns its own wave fronts, piling them up into a conical shock wave (sonic boom). Mach number = v_source / v_sound.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::shock-waves MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the Mach number?
column3: Ratio of object's speed to the speed of sound (v_object / v_sound)
column4: Mach 1 = speed of sound. Subsonic < 1; supersonic > 1; hypersonic > 5. The Mach angle of the conical shock wave: sin θ = v_sound / v_object = 1/M.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::shock-waves MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the Mach angle of a shock wave?
column4: θ is the half-angle of the cone. As the Mach number increases, the cone becomes narrower (smaller θ). At Mach 1 the cone angle is 90° (flat front).
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::shock-waves MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What happens to wave fronts ahead of a supersonic source?
column3: They cannot outrun the source; wave fronts pile up into a shock wave
column4: At v_source > v_sound, the source overtakes previously emitted wave fronts. The superposition of these fronts creates a steep pressure discontinuity — the shock wave.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::shock-waves MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: In medical lithotripsy, what principle related to shock waves is used?
column3: Focused shock waves shatter kidney stones (acoustic cavitation and mechanical stress)
column4: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) focuses high-energy shock waves onto kidney stones, fragmenting them via intense pressure gradients and cavitation, avoiding surgery.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::shock-waves MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the Cherenkov radiation analogue for sound (shock waves)?
column3: Bow wave (or sonic boom / Mach cone)
column4: Just as Cherenkov radiation occurs when a charged particle exceeds the speed of light in a medium, a Mach cone (sonic boom) forms when an object exceeds the local speed of sound.
column8: concept::CP::4D::sound MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::sound::shock-waves MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What phenomenon occurs when two waves overlap and their amplitudes add together?
column4: Interference is the superposition of waves. Constructive interference increases amplitude; destructive interference reduces it. Young's double-slit experiment demonstrates this with light.

column1: In Young's double-slit experiment, what condition produces a bright (constructive) fringe?
column4: When the path difference between waves from the two slits is an integer multiple of the wavelength, the waves arrive in phase and constructively interfere, producing a bright fringe.

column1: In Young's double-slit experiment, what condition produces a dark (destructive) fringe?
column4: A half-wavelength path difference means the waves arrive exactly out of phase, canceling each other to produce a dark fringe.

column1: In Young's double-slit experiment, what happens to fringe spacing when slit separation increases?
column4: Fringe spacing y = λL/d; as slit separation d increases, spacing y decreases. Widely separated slits produce closely packed fringes.

column1: In Young's double-slit experiment, what happens to fringe spacing when wavelength increases?
column4: y = λL/d; spacing is directly proportional to wavelength. Longer wavelength (redder) light produces wider-spaced fringes.

column1: What type of interference pattern does Young's double-slit experiment produce?
column4: The alternating constructive and destructive interference creates a series of equally spaced bright (maxima) and dark (minima) bands on the screen.

column1: What is thin-film interference?
column3: Interference of light reflected from two surfaces of a thin film
column4: Light reflects from both the top and bottom surface of a thin film; the path difference (2t) determines whether constructive or destructive interference occurs.

column1: When does a reflected wave undergo a 180° phase shift at an interface?
column3: When reflecting off a medium with higher index of refraction
column4: Light going from low-n to high-n medium undergoes a half-wavelength (180°) phase inversion on reflection, similar to a wave on a string reflecting from a fixed end.

column1: For a diffraction grating, what equation gives the angles of principal maxima?
column4: d is the grating spacing, θ is the diffraction angle, m is the order (integer), and λ is the wavelength. Multiple wavelengths diffract at different angles, dispersing light into a spectrum.

column1: In single-slit diffraction, what condition locates the first dark fringe?
column3: a sin θ = λ (a = slit width)
column4: For a single slit of width a, the first minimum occurs when a sinθ = λ. Narrower slits produce wider central maxima.

column1: How does the central maximum width in single-slit diffraction change when slit width decreases?
column4: Width of the central maximum is inversely proportional to slit width. Narrower slit → more spreading (diffraction). This is why very small apertures blur images.

column1: What does X-ray diffraction measure in crystalline solids?
column3: Interplanar spacing (d) of crystal lattice planes
column4: Bragg's law (2d sinθ = nλ) relates the angle of diffracted X-rays to the spacing between crystal planes, enabling determination of crystal structure.

column1: State Bragg's Law for X-ray diffraction.
column4: d is the interplanar spacing, θ is the glancing angle of incidence, n is an integer, and λ is the X-ray wavelength. Constructive interference occurs when this condition is satisfied.

column1: Why are X-rays (not visible light) used to probe crystal structures?
column3: X-ray wavelength is comparable to atomic spacing (~0.1 nm)
column4: Crystal lattice spacings are on the order of angstroms. Visible light wavelengths (~400-700 nm) are too large to resolve these spacings; X-rays have the right wavelength.

column1: What is the diffraction phenomenon responsible for the spreading of waves around obstacles or through openings?
column4: Diffraction occurs when waves encounter an obstacle or aperture. The degree of bending is significant when the aperture size is comparable to the wavelength.

column1: What is the resolving power of an optical instrument limited by?
column4: The Rayleigh criterion (θ = 1.22λ/D) defines the minimum angular separation resolvable by a lens or mirror of diameter D. Larger apertures and shorter wavelengths improve resolution.

column1: What is linear (plane) polarization of light?
column3: Electric field oscillates in a single plane
column4: In linearly polarized light, the electric field vector vibrates in only one direction perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

column1: What device produces linearly polarized light from unpolarized light?
column4: A polaroid filter transmits only the component of the electric field aligned with its transmission axis, blocking the perpendicular component.

column1: According to Malus's Law, what is the intensity of light after passing through a polarizer at angle θ to the polarization axis?
column4: Malus's Law: transmitted intensity equals original intensity times the cosine squared of the angle between the light's polarization direction and the polarizer axis.

column1: What is circular polarization of light?
column3: Electric field vector rotates as the wave propagates
column4: In circularly polarized light, the electric field rotates at constant magnitude, tracing a helix. It can be right- or left-handed depending on rotation direction.

column1: By what methods can unpolarized light become polarized?
column3: Reflection, refraction, scattering, or use of a polarizer
column4: Brewster's angle polarization by reflection and Rayleigh scattering (sky polarization) are common MCAT examples. A polaroid filter is the direct method.

column1: What angle of incidence produces completely polarized reflected light?
column4: At Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular (90°). The reflected beam is completely polarized parallel to the surface.

column1: What is the speed of electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum?
column4: The speed of light in vacuum, c ≈ 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s, is a universal constant. In any other medium, light travels slower (v = c/n).

column1: What is the relationship between frequency, wavelength, and wave speed for electromagnetic radiation?
column4: For EM radiation in vacuum, speed c equals frequency times wavelength. As frequency increases, wavelength decreases proportionally.

column1: How does the frequency of electromagnetic radiation change when it passes from air into glass?
column4: When light enters a denser medium, its speed and wavelength decrease, but its frequency remains constant. Only the medium's refractive index changes wave speed.

column1: What happens to the wavelength of light when it enters a medium with refractive index n?
column4: In a medium, the wave slows to v = c/n, so wavelength shrinks to λ/n while frequency stays the same. This is important for thin-film interference calculations.

column1: Do electromagnetic waves require a medium to propagate?
column4: Unlike mechanical waves, EM waves are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields and require no medium, allowing them to travel through outer space.

column1: What is the constant value of the speed of light in vacuo (c)?
column4: c is the universal speed limit and is constant in vacuum regardless of the motion of the source or observer. This is a postulate of special relativity.

column1: Does the speed of light in vacuum depend on the frequency of the light?
column3: No; c is the same for all frequencies in vacuum
column4: All EM waves travel at c in vacuum, regardless of wavelength or frequency. Dispersion (different speeds) occurs only in material media, not in vacuum.

column1: How is the meter defined in terms of the speed of light?
column4: Since 1983, the meter is defined by fixing c = 299,792,458 m/s exactly. The speed of light in vacuum is therefore a defined constant, not a measured one.

column1: What happens to the speed of light as it enters a medium with refractive index n > 1?
column4: v = c/n. Glass (n ≈ 1.5) slows light to about 2 × 10⁸ m/s. This slowing is responsible for refraction.

column1: In an electromagnetic wave, in which directions do the electric and magnetic fields oscillate?
column3: Perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation
column4: E and B fields are mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the wave's direction of travel, making EM waves transverse waves.

column1: What is the relationship between the magnitudes of E and B fields in an electromagnetic wave in vacuum?
column4: In vacuum, the electric field magnitude equals c times the magnetic field magnitude. They oscillate in phase (reach maxima and minima simultaneously).

column1: Are electromagnetic waves transverse or longitudinal?
column4: Both the E and B field oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. This transverse nature allows EM waves to be polarized.

column1: What generates electromagnetic waves according to classical physics?
column4: An oscillating or accelerating charge produces changing E and B fields that propagate outward as an EM wave. This is the basis of antenna radiation and synchrotron radiation.

column1: What is the direction of propagation of an electromagnetic wave relative to E and B?
column3: Perpendicular to both E and B (given by E × B)
column4: The Poynting vector S = E × B points in the direction of energy flow (propagation). The cross product of E and B determines the wave's direction of travel.

column1: List the electromagnetic spectrum regions from lowest to highest frequency.
column3: Radio, microwave, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma
column4: Mnemonic: 'Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns.' As frequency increases, energy increases and wavelength decreases.

column1: What is the equation for the energy of a photon?
column4: h is Planck's constant (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s), f is frequency. Higher frequency photons carry more energy. This is fundamental to the photoelectric effect.

column1: What is Planck's constant?
column4: Planck's constant h relates photon energy to frequency (E = hf). It also appears in the de Broglie relation λ = h/p for matter waves.

column1: Which type of electromagnetic radiation has the highest photon energy?
column4: Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength in the EM spectrum, so E = hf is greatest. They can ionize atoms and damage DNA.

column1: What is the approximate wavelength range of X-rays?
column4: X-rays sit between UV light and gamma rays. Their wavelengths are comparable to atomic spacings, which is why they can be used for crystallographic diffraction.

column1: How does photon energy relate to wavelength?
column3: E = hc/λ; energy is inversely proportional to wavelength
column4: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency, hence higher energy (E = hf = hc/λ). Blue/violet light photons are more energetic than red light photons.

column1: What is the approximate wavelength range of the visible spectrum?
column4: Visible light is the narrow band of EM radiation detectable by the human eye. Violet has the shortest wavelength (~400 nm) and red the longest (~700 nm).

column1: Which color of visible light has the highest frequency?
column4: Violet light (~400 nm) has the shortest wavelength and thus the highest frequency and photon energy among visible colors. Red (~700 nm) has the lowest.

column1: What color of light is perceived when all wavelengths of visible light are combined?
column4: White light is the superposition of all visible wavelengths. A prism disperses white light into its component colors by refracting each wavelength a different amount.

column1: In what order does a prism disperse white light from least to most refraction?
column3: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet (ROYGBV)
column4: Refractive index increases with frequency; violet light bends the most, red the least. This creates the spectrum in the order ROYGBV from least to most deviated.

column1: What color is seen when red and green light are mixed?
column4: Additive color mixing (light): red + green = yellow; red + blue = magenta; green + blue = cyan; all three = white. This differs from subtractive (pigment) mixing.

column1: Why does an object appear red in white light?
column3: It absorbs all wavelengths except red, which it reflects
column4: Object color results from selective absorption. A red object absorbs most visible wavelengths and reflects only red wavelengths to the observer's eye.

column1: Which color of visible light has the longest wavelength?
column4: Red light has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency (and thus lowest photon energy) in the visible spectrum. It is least refracted by a prism.

column1: What complementary color pairs sum to white light?
column4: Complementary colors are opposite on the color wheel; mixing them additively produces white. Knowing these pairs helps on questions about filter and light subtraction.

column1: What is the approximate frequency of green light (λ ≈ 550 nm) in Hz?
column4: f = c/λ = (3 × 10⁸ m/s) / (550 × 10⁻⁹ m) ≈ 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. This is a useful benchmark for visible light frequency calculations.

column1: What wavelength range defines the infrared (IR) region of the electromagnetic spectrum?
column4: IR spectroscopy probes molecular vibrations. Wavenumber (cm⁻¹) is the unit most used on the MCAT; higher wavenumber = higher energy within IR.

column1: What type of molecular motion does IR spectroscopy primarily detect?
column4: IR radiation is absorbed when its frequency matches a bond's natural vibrational frequency, causing changes in bond length or angle.

column1: What property of a bond must change for a vibration to be IR-active?
column3: Dipole moment must change during vibration
column4: Symmetric stretches that produce no net dipole change (e.g., O=C=O symmetric stretch) are IR-inactive. Asymmetric or polar bond vibrations are IR-active.

column1: Which bonds generally absorb at higher wavenumbers (>3000 cm⁻¹) in an IR spectrum?
column4: Lighter atoms and stronger bonds vibrate at higher frequencies. O–H stretch appears as a broad peak ~3200–3550 cm⁻¹; N–H ~3300–3500 cm⁻¹.

column1: Where does a carbonyl (C=O) stretch appear in an IR spectrum?
column4: The exact position shifts: ketones ~1715, aldehydes ~1725, carboxylic acids ~1710, amides ~1680, esters ~1735 cm⁻¹. Conjugation lowers the frequency.

column1: What distinguishes a stretching vibration from a bending vibration in a molecule?
column3: Stretching changes bond length; bending changes bond angle
column4: Stretching absorbs at higher wavenumbers than bending for the same bond. Both types contribute to the IR fingerprint region.

column1: What are the two types of stretching vibrations for a molecule with more than two atoms?
column4: In symmetric stretching both bonds lengthen/shorten together; in asymmetric stretching one lengthens while the other shortens. These have different IR absorption frequencies.

column1: How many vibrational modes does a nonlinear molecule of N atoms have?
column4: Three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom are subtracted from 3N total. Linear molecules have 3N – 5 because they lack one rotational mode.

column1: What types of bending vibrations are named 'scissoring,' 'rocking,' 'wagging,' and 'twisting'?
column3: In-plane (scissoring, rocking) and out-of-plane (wagging, twisting) bends
column4: These are all deformation modes. Scissoring and rocking keep motion in the molecular plane; wagging and twisting involve out-of-plane displacement.

column1: What is the 'fingerprint region' of an IR spectrum?
column4: This region contains complex overlapping C–C, C–N, C–O single-bond stretches and bending vibrations unique to each molecule, allowing compound identification by comparison to reference spectra.

column1: Which IR absorption is characteristic of a primary or secondary alcohol?
column4: Hydrogen bonding broadens the O–H peak. A free (non-H-bonded) O–H gives a sharper peak near 3600 cm⁻¹.

column1: What IR absorption indicates the presence of a terminal alkyne (C≡C–H)?
column3: C≡C stretch ~2100–2260 cm⁻¹ and terminal C–H stretch ~3300 cm⁻¹
column4: Triple bonds absorb between the single- and double-bond regions. The terminal alkynyl C–H is sharp and strong near 3300 cm⁻¹, distinguishing it from O–H or N–H.

column1: What IR feature distinguishes a carboxylic acid from a ketone?
column3: Carboxylic acid has broad O–H stretch ~2500–3300 cm⁻¹ and C=O ~1710 cm⁻¹
column4: Ketones lack the broad O–H absorption. The carboxylic acid O–H is exceptionally broad due to strong hydrogen bonding in the dimer form.

column1: How does conjugation affect the position of a carbonyl C=O IR absorption?
column3: Conjugation lowers (red-shifts) the C=O stretching frequency
column4: Resonance delocalization weakens the C=O bond, reducing its force constant, so it absorbs at a lower wavenumber (~20–40 cm⁻¹ lower than unconjugated).

column1: What wavelength range defines the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum?
column4: Violet light is at the short-wavelength end (~400 nm) and red at the long-wavelength end (~700 nm). Visible spectroscopy is relevant to colored biological molecules.

column1: What is the relationship between the wavelength of light absorbed and the color a compound appears?
column3: Compound appears the complementary color to the wavelength absorbed
column4: Complementary colors are opposite on the color wheel. A molecule absorbing red (~700 nm) appears green; absorbing blue (~450 nm) appears orange.

column1: What type of electronic transitions are responsible for absorption in the visible region?
column3: π→π* and n→π* transitions in conjugated or colored systems
column4: Extensive conjugation lowers the HOMO–LUMO gap, shifting absorption into the visible range. Most simple organic molecules absorb in the UV, not the visible.

column1: What color does a solution appear if it absorbs maximally at ~420 nm (violet)?
column4: This is a classic complementary color example. Beer-Lambert law governs how absorbance relates to concentration in visible spectrophotometry.

column1: What color does beta-carotene appear, and approximately what wavelength does it absorb?
column4: Beta-carotene's 11 conjugated double bonds lower the HOMO–LUMO gap enough to absorb blue-violet light, giving the complementary orange appearance.

column1: Why does beta-carotene absorb visible light while most simple alkenes absorb only UV?
column3: Extended conjugation in carotene lowers the π→π* transition energy into the visible range
column4: Each additional conjugated double bond red-shifts the absorption maximum. Beta-carotene has 11 conjugated double bonds, shifting λ_max to ~450 nm.

column1: What structural feature is required for a molecule to appear colored to the human eye?
column3: Chromophore that absorbs light in the 400–700 nm range
column4: A chromophore is the part of the molecule responsible for color. Extended conjugation (as in carotenoids, porphyrins, and dyes) is the most common structural basis.

column1: What color would a compound appear if it absorbed all visible wavelengths equally?
column4: Selective absorption of only certain wavelengths produces color via the complementary color principle; complete absorption of all visible light gives black.

column1: How do acid-base indicators change color upon protonation or deprotonation?
column3: Protonation/deprotonation changes the conjugation or chromophore, shifting λ_max
column4: For example, phenolphthalein is colorless (lactone form, broken conjugation) in acid and pink-red (extended quinoid conjugation) in base. Structural change alters light absorption.

column1: What structural change in phenolphthalein causes its color change from colorless to pink?
column3: Ring opening forms extended conjugated quinoid system in basic conditions
column4: In acid, phenolphthalein exists as a closed lactone with limited conjugation (colorless). Base opens the lactone, creating a conjugated trianion that absorbs ~550 nm (pink).

column1: How does increasing conjugation generally affect the UV-visible absorption maximum (λ_max)?
column3: Increasing conjugation red-shifts λ_max (to longer wavelengths)
column4: More conjugated pi electrons mean a smaller HOMO–LUMO energy gap, so lower-energy (longer wavelength) photons are sufficient to promote electrons.

column1: What effect does adding an electron-donating substituent to a conjugated chromophore have on λ_max?
column4: Electron donors raise the HOMO energy, reducing the HOMO–LUMO gap. Electron-withdrawing groups can also lower the LUMO, also producing a red shift in push-pull systems.

column1: What wavelength range defines the ultraviolet (UV) region relevant to organic spectroscopy?
column4: The near-UV (200–400 nm) is used in UV-Vis spectroscopy. Vacuum UV (<200 nm) is less commonly discussed on the MCAT.

column1: What instrument is used to measure UV-visible absorption spectra?
column4: Beer-Lambert Law (A = εbc) relates absorbance (A) to molar absorptivity (ε), path length (b), and concentration (c). This is used in labs to quantify molecules like NADH.

column1: What is Beer-Lambert Law and what does each variable represent?
column3: A = εbc; A=absorbance, ε=molar absorptivity, b=path length, c=concentration
column4: The law states absorbance is directly proportional to both concentration and path length. It is widely used to quantify DNA, proteins, and cofactors like NADH (λ=340 nm).

column1: Which simple functional groups absorb in the UV region (~200–250 nm)?
column4: Isolated double bonds and carbonyls absorb in the far UV (below 220 nm); conjugation shifts absorption to longer wavelengths accessible by standard UV spectrophotometers.

column1: What wavelength does NADH absorb, making it detectable by UV spectroscopy?
column4: NAD+ does not absorb at 340 nm, so the increase in absorbance at 340 nm during enzymatic reactions directly measures NADH formation — a key biochemistry assay.

column1: What type of electronic transition involves promotion of a pi electron to an antibonding pi* orbital?
column4: This transition occurs in compounds with pi bonds (alkenes, carbonyls, aromatics). Conjugation lowers the energy gap, red-shifting absorption. Generally high molar absorptivity (ε).

column1: What type of electronic transition involves promotion of a lone pair electron to an antibonding pi* orbital?
column4: n→π* transitions occur in carbonyl, azo, and nitro compounds. They produce weaker (low ε) absorption at longer wavelengths than π→π* transitions.

column1: Which transition, n→π* or π→π*, typically has a higher molar absorptivity (ε)?
column4: π→π* transitions are symmetry-allowed with ε ~10,000–100,000 L/mol·cm. n→π* are symmetry-forbidden, giving ε ~10–100 L/mol·cm (weak absorption band).

column1: For a simple ketone, which transition appears at longer wavelength — n→π* or π→π*?
column3: n→π* appears at longer wavelength (~270–280 nm)
column4: n→π* of the carbonyl occurs ~270 nm (low intensity); π→π* of the C=O occurs ~180 nm (high intensity, not visible on standard UV). Conjugation with the carbonyl moves both to longer wavelengths.

column1: How does solvent polarity affect the n→π* transition of a carbonyl compound?
column3: More polar solvents blue-shift (hypsochromic shift) the n→π* band
column4: Polar solvents stabilize the ground-state lone pair more than the excited state, increasing the energy gap. Conversely, π→π* red-shifts with increasing solvent polarity.

column1: What is a conjugated system in organic chemistry?
column3: Alternating single and multiple bonds allowing pi electron delocalization
column4: Examples: 1,3-butadiene, benzene, beta-carotene. Delocalization lowers the HOMO–LUMO gap, shifting UV-Vis absorption to longer wavelengths.

column1: What is the minimum number of conjugated double bonds required for a molecule to absorb in the visible range?
column3: Approximately 8–10 conjugated double bonds (varies with structure)
column4: Beta-carotene (11 conjugated double bonds) absorbs at ~450 nm (visible). Lycopene (11 conjugated double bonds, different geometry) absorbs at ~470 nm (red-orange visible).

column1: What is the Woodward-Fieser rule used for?
column3: Predicting UV λ_max of conjugated dienes and enones
column4: The rules assign base values and increments for substituents, rings, and additional conjugation to estimate the π→π* absorption wavelength. Tested at a conceptual level on the MCAT.

column1: How does cis vs. trans geometry affect λ_max in a conjugated diene?
column3: Trans (s-trans conformation) absorbs at longer wavelength than cis
column4: In the s-trans conformation, the p orbitals of the diene overlap more effectively, giving better conjugation and a lower energy gap than the s-cis form.

column1: What physical phenomenon is the basis of NMR spectroscopy?
column3: Absorption of radiofrequency energy by nuclei in a magnetic field (nuclear spin resonance)
column4: Nuclei with odd mass or odd atomic number (e.g., ¹H, ¹³C) have spin and align with or against an external magnetic field; RF energy flips the spin, producing a detectable signal.

column1: Which nuclei are most commonly observed in MCAT-relevant NMR spectroscopy?
column4: ¹H NMR gives information about the hydrogen environment; ¹³C NMR reveals carbon framework. ¹H NMR is more sensitive and more commonly discussed on the MCAT.

column1: What is chemical shift (δ) in NMR spectroscopy measured in?
column4: Chemical shift normalizes the resonance frequency to the instrument field strength, allowing comparison across instruments. TMS (tetramethylsilane) is defined as 0 ppm reference.

column1: What causes a proton to be deshielded and resonate at a higher chemical shift (downfield)?
column3: Electron-withdrawing groups or environments reduce electron density around the proton
column4: Less electron density = less shielding from the external field = more downfield. Protons near electronegative atoms (O, N, halogens) or pi systems appear at higher δ.

column1: In ¹H NMR, what does the integration (area) of each peak represent?
column3: Relative number of protons giving rise to that signal
column4: Integration does not give absolute numbers — only ratios. A peak with area ratio 3:2:1 might represent 6:4:2 or 3:2:1 protons depending on the molecular formula.

column1: What are chemically equivalent protons in NMR?
column3: Protons in identical chemical environments that produce a single NMR signal
column4: Equivalent protons are interchangeable by symmetry operations. For example, the three methyl protons of CH₃Br are all equivalent and give one singlet.

column1: How many distinct ¹H NMR signals does ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) produce?
column4: The three methyl protons are equivalent (1 signal), the two methylene protons are equivalent (1 signal), and the OH proton is distinct (1 signal) — total 3 signals.

column1: What is the difference between homotopic and enantiotopic protons in NMR?
column3: Homotopic: equivalent in all solvents; enantiotopic: equivalent in achiral solvents only
column4: Homotopic protons give identical shifts always. Enantiotopic protons (like the two CH₂ protons in achiral ethanol) are equivalent in achiral media but can be distinguished by chiral shift reagents.

column1: What are diastereotopic protons?
column3: Protons on the same carbon that are NOT equivalent and give different NMR signals
column4: Diastereotopic protons arise adjacent to a stereocenter. They are non-equivalent in all environments and show different chemical shifts and different coupling to neighboring protons.

column1: What is spin-spin splitting (coupling) in ¹H NMR?
column3: Splitting of a proton's NMR signal by adjacent nonequivalent protons through bonds
column4: Neighboring protons with spin-up or spin-down states alter the effective magnetic field at the observed proton, splitting the signal into a multiplet.

column1: State the N+1 rule for ¹H NMR spin-spin splitting.
column3: A proton with N equivalent neighboring protons splits into N+1 lines
column4: This applies to first-order spectra where coupling constants are small relative to chemical shift differences. Example: CH₃ adjacent to CH₂ appears as a triplet (2+1=3 lines).

column1: What is the multiplicity of the CH₂ signal in CH₃CH₂Br by the N+1 rule?
column4: The CH₂ protons are adjacent to three equivalent CH₃ protons; N=3, so multiplicity = 3+1 = 4 (quartet).

column1: What is the coupling constant (J) in NMR, and what are typical values for vicinal (3-bond) coupling?
column3: J = frequency difference between lines in a multiplet; vicinal J ≈ 6–8 Hz
column4: J is field-independent (reported in Hz). Vicinal (H-C-C-H) coupling constants depend on dihedral angle (Karplus equation): trans H–H in alkenes ~12–18 Hz, cis ~6–12 Hz.

column1: Why do equivalent (homotopic) protons not split each other in ¹H NMR?
column3: Equivalent protons couple but produce no observable splitting (net effect cancels)
column4: Coupling between equivalent protons exists but does not cause observable peak splitting in a standard NMR spectrum. Only coupling between nonequivalent protons is observed.

column1: What pattern of peak intensities is observed for a quartet in ¹H NMR?
column4: Pascal's triangle gives multiplet intensities: doublet 1:1, triplet 1:2:1, quartet 1:3:3:1, quintet 1:4:6:4:1. This reflects binomial distribution of neighboring spin states.

column1: What is the law of reflection?
column3: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
column4: Both angles are measured from the normal to the surface at the point of incidence. This applies to plane mirrors and all smooth reflective surfaces.

column1: From what reference line are angles of incidence and reflection measured?
column4: The normal is perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of contact. Not measured from the surface itself.

column1: Where does a plane mirror form the image of an object placed 5 cm in front of it?
column4: Plane mirrors produce virtual, upright, same-size images located the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

column1: What is the magnification of an image in a plane mirror?
column4: Plane mirrors neither magnify nor minify; lateral magnification = 1. The image is laterally inverted (left-right) but not inverted top-to-bottom.

column1: Is the image formed by a plane mirror real or virtual?
column4: Light rays do not actually converge behind the mirror; the image cannot be projected onto a screen. Virtual images are always upright.

column1: Define the index of refraction (n) of a medium.
column3: n = c / v (speed of light in vacuum / speed in medium)
column4: n is always ≥ 1. A higher n means light travels more slowly in that medium. n for vacuum = 1, for air ≈ 1, for water ≈ 1.33, for glass ≈ 1.5.

column1: State Snell's law of refraction.
column3: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
column4: Relates the angles of incidence and refraction at an interface between two media of indices n₁ and n₂. Angles measured from the normal.

column1: When light passes from air (n=1) into glass (n=1.5), how does the refracted ray bend relative to the normal?
column4: Going from lower to higher n, the ray bends toward the normal; θ₂ < θ₁ per Snell's law. Mnemonic: entering a denser medium = closer to normal.

column1: Using Snell's law, if n₁=1.0, θ₁=30°, n₂=1.5, what is sin θ₂?
column4: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ → (1.0)(0.5) = 1.5 sin θ₂ → sin θ₂ = 0.5/1.5 = 1/3. θ₂ ≈ 19.5°.

column1: What happens to the wavelength of light as it enters a medium with higher refractive index?
column4: λ_medium = λ_vacuum / n. The frequency remains constant; the speed and wavelength both decrease proportionally in a denser medium.

column1: What is optical dispersion?
column3: Variation of refractive index with wavelength
column4: Different wavelengths (colors) travel at slightly different speeds in a medium, causing separation of white light into its spectrum (e.g., a prism).

column1: Which color of visible light has the highest index of refraction in glass?
column4: Shorter wavelengths are refracted more strongly. In glass: n_violet > n_red. ROY G BIV — violet bends most, red bends least.

column1: Which color of visible light has the lowest index of refraction in glass?
column4: Longer wavelengths experience less refraction. Red light bends the least through a prism, appearing at the bottom of a rainbow spectrum.

column1: What phenomenon causes a glass prism to separate white light into a rainbow?
column4: Because n varies with wavelength, each color refracts by a different angle, separating the spectrum. Violet deviates most, red least.

column1: Chromatic aberration in lenses is caused by which property of light?
column3: Dispersion (different wavelengths focus at different points)
column4: Because different colors have different indices of refraction, they are focused at slightly different distances, producing colored fringes around images.

column1: What is total internal reflection (TIR)?
column3: Complete reflection of light back into the denser medium at an interface
column4: Occurs when light in a denser medium strikes a less-dense medium at an angle ≥ the critical angle. No transmitted ray exits; all light is reflected.

column1: What are the two conditions required for total internal reflection?
column3: Light travels from higher n to lower n AND angle of incidence ≥ critical angle
column4: Both conditions must hold. TIR cannot occur when going from low n to high n because refracted ray always exists in that direction.

column1: What is the formula for the critical angle (θ_c) for total internal reflection?
column4: Derived from Snell's law with θ₂ = 90°: n₁ sin θ_c = n₂ sin 90° → sin θ_c = n₂/n₁. The critical angle decreases as n₁ increases.

column1: What is the critical angle for glass (n=1.5) to air (n=1.0)?
column4: sin θ_c = 1.0/1.5 = 0.667 → θ_c ≈ 41.8°. Any ray hitting the glass-air interface at ≥ 41.8° undergoes TIR.

column1: Which technology relies on total internal reflection to transmit data via light pulses?
column4: Light traveling down a glass fiber hits the glass-cladding interface at angles exceeding the critical angle, ensuring TIR keeps the light confined within the fiber.

column1: What type of image does a concave (converging) spherical mirror produce for an object beyond the center of curvature?
column4: Object beyond C → image between F and C, real and inverted, smaller than object. Mnemonic: beyond C, image is on the same side and diminished.

column1: What type of image does a convex (diverging) spherical mirror always produce?
column4: Convex mirrors always produce virtual images regardless of object position. They are used as security mirrors and car side mirrors for wide field of view.

column1: What is the mirror equation?
column4: Relates object distance (do), image distance (di), and focal length (f). Same form as thin-lens equation; sign conventions differ for mirrors.

column1: For a spherical mirror, what is the sign convention for a virtual image distance?
column4: In the standard mirror sign convention, real images (in front of mirror) have positive di; virtual images (behind mirror) have negative di.

column1: What is the lateral magnification formula for mirrors?
column4: A negative m means the image is inverted; |m| > 1 means enlarged. For virtual images di is negative, so m is positive (upright).

column1: Define the center of curvature (C) of a spherical mirror.
column3: Center of the sphere of which the mirror is a section
column4: The radius from C to any point on the mirror surface is the radius of curvature (R). C lies on the principal axis, twice as far from the mirror as the focal point.

column1: What is the relationship between the radius of curvature (R) and focal length (f) for a spherical mirror?
column4: The focal point is halfway between the mirror surface and the center of curvature. This follows from the paraxial approximation for small angles.

column1: Where is the center of curvature located relative to the focal point for a concave mirror?
column3: Twice as far from mirror as focal point; C = 2f from vertex
column4: Because f = R/2, the center of curvature is at distance R = 2f along the principal axis. An object at C produces a real, same-size, inverted image at C.

column1: What happens to parallel rays that strike a concave spherical mirror?
column3: They converge at the focal point F
column4: This defines the focal point for concave (converging) mirrors. Rays parallel to the principal axis reflect through F.

column1: What is the focal length of a spherical mirror with radius of curvature 20 cm?
column4: f = R/2 = 20/2 = 10 cm. Concave mirror focal length is positive; convex mirror focal length is negative in the standard convention.

column1: What is the sign of the focal length for a concave mirror?
column4: Concave (converging) mirrors have positive focal lengths. Convex (diverging) mirrors have negative focal lengths in the standard sign convention.

column1: An object is placed at the focal point of a concave mirror. Where is the image?
column4: When do = f, the mirror equation gives 1/di = 0, so di → ∞. Reflected rays are parallel and never converge.

column1: For a convex mirror, is the focal length positive or negative?
column4: Convex mirrors are diverging; their focal point is behind the mirror (virtual focus), giving f < 0 by convention. This ensures di is always negative (virtual image).

column1: Define a real image in optics.
column3: Image formed by actual convergence of light rays
column4: Real images can be projected onto a screen, are formed on the same side as outgoing light (for mirrors: same side as object; for lenses: opposite side), and are always inverted.

column1: Define a virtual image in optics.
column3: Image formed where light rays appear to diverge from (not actual convergence)
column4: Virtual images cannot be projected on a screen. For mirrors they appear behind the mirror; for lenses they appear on the same side as the object. Always upright.

column1: A converging lens produces a virtual image. Where must the object be located?
column3: Between the lens and focal point (do < f)
column4: When an object is inside the focal length of a converging lens, the lens acts like a magnifying glass, producing an upright, virtual, magnified image on the same side as the object.

column1: Which type of mirror always produces a virtual image regardless of object position?
column4: Convex mirrors have a negative focal length; the mirror equation always yields a negative di, indicating a virtual image behind the mirror.

column1: Is a real image upright or inverted relative to the object?
column4: Real images formed by single mirrors or lenses are always inverted (m is negative). Virtual images produced by single optical elements are always upright.

column1: What is a thin lens?
column3: A lens whose thickness is negligible compared to its radii of curvature
column4: The thin-lens approximation allows use of the simple formula 1/do + 1/di = 1/f, treating refraction as occurring at a single plane.
