column1: What are the two rules used to locate images with a thin converging lens ray diagram?
column3: Ray through center passes straight; ray parallel to axis refracts through focal point
column4: Third rule: ray through near focal point exits parallel to axis. Any two of the three standard rays suffice to locate the image.
column8: concept::CP::4D::geometrical_optics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::geometrical-optics::thin-lenses MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: What is the lensmaker's equation?
column4: Relates focal length to the lens material's index of refraction and the radii of curvature of its two surfaces. High-yield context: explains why lens shape and material set focal length.
column8: concept::CP::4D::geometrical_optics MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4D::geometrical-optics::thin-lenses MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY

column1: Define a converging (convex) lens.
column3: Lens thicker at center than edges; brings parallel rays to a focal point
column4: Converging lenses have positive focal lengths. They correct farsightedness (hyperopia) by converging light before it reaches the cornea/retina.

column1: Define a diverging (concave) lens.
column3: Lens thinner at center than edges; spreads parallel rays apart
column4: Diverging lenses have negative focal lengths and always produce virtual, upright, reduced images. They correct nearsightedness (myopia).

column1: What type of image does a diverging lens always produce?
column4: Because f < 0, the thin-lens equation always yields di < 0 for real objects; the image is on the same side as the object, virtual and smaller than the object.

column1: Which type of lens is used to correct myopia (nearsightedness)?
column4: In myopia the eye converges light too much, focusing in front of the retina. A diverging lens pre-diverges the light so it focuses on the retina.

column1: Which type of lens is used to correct hyperopia (farsightedness)?
column4: In hyperopia the focal point falls behind the retina. A converging lens adds extra convergence so light focuses correctly on the retina.

column1: State the thin-lens equation.
column4: do = object distance (positive for real objects), di = image distance (positive for real images on opposite side of lens from object), f = focal length.

column1: In the thin-lens equation, what is the sign of di for a real image formed by a converging lens?
column4: Real images are formed on the opposite side of the lens from the object. By convention, this is the positive side for transmitted light.

column1: In the thin-lens equation, what is the sign of f for a diverging lens?
column4: Diverging lenses have negative focal lengths by sign convention. Converging lenses have positive f. This is critical for correct application of 1/do + 1/di = 1/f.

column1: An object is 30 cm from a converging lens with f = 10 cm. Where is the image?
column4: 1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/10 − 1/30 = 3/30 − 1/30 = 2/30; di = 15 cm. Positive di → real image.

column1: What is the magnification produced by the lens when do = 30 cm and di = 15 cm?
column4: m = −di/do = −15/30 = −0.5. Negative → inverted; |m| < 1 → reduced (smaller than object).

column1: Using 1/do + 1/di = 1/f, if do = f/2 for a converging lens, what is di?
column3: di = −f (virtual image, same side as object)
column4: 1/di = 1/f − 2/f = −1/f → di = −f. Negative di → virtual image. Object inside focal point gives magnifying glass behavior.

column1: What is lens power, and what are its units?
column4: Focal length must be in meters. A converging lens of f = 0.5 m has P = +2 D. A diverging lens with f = −0.25 m has P = −4 D.

column1: What is the power (in diopters) of a lens with focal length 25 cm?
column4: f = 0.25 m; P = 1/0.25 = 4 D. Convert cm to m before computing diopters.

column1: A diverging lens has f = −50 cm. What is its power in diopters?
column4: f = −0.50 m; P = 1/(−0.50) = −2 D. Negative power indicates a diverging lens.

column1: A person's corrective lens is prescribed as −3.5 D. What type of refractive error do they have?
column4: Negative diopters indicate a diverging lens prescription, used to correct myopia. Positive diopters correct hyperopia.

column1: How is the total power calculated for two thin lenses in contact?
column4: Powers add algebraically when lenses are in contact (or combined as a system in the thin-lens approximation). Equivalently, 1/f_total = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂.

column1: Two converging lenses have focal lengths 20 cm and 30 cm. What is the combined focal length when placed in contact?
How do you find the image for two separated thin lenses?
column3: Use image of first lens as object for second lens
column4: Apply 1/do + 1/di = 1/f to lens 1; that image distance determines object distance for lens 2. Total magnification = m₁ × m₂.

column1: What is the total magnification of a two-lens system?
column4: Each lens contributes its own magnification factor (m = −di/do). The system magnification is the product of individual magnifications.

column1: What is chromatic aberration in a lens?
column3: Different wavelengths focus at different points along the axis
column4: Caused by dispersion: blue/violet light (higher n) focuses closer to the lens than red light. Results in colored fringing. Corrected with achromatic doublets.

column1: What is spherical aberration?
column3: Peripheral rays focus at different point than paraxial rays
column4: Rays passing through the edges of a spherical lens are refracted more strongly than those near the center, creating a blurred focal region rather than a sharp point.

column1: How is chromatic aberration corrected in optical instruments?
column3: Achromatic doublet (converging + diverging lens of different glass)
column4: Combining a converging and diverging lens made of glass with different dispersion properties causes the chromatic errors to cancel, bringing two wavelengths to the same focus.

column1: What is the near point of the normal human eye?
column4: The near point is the closest distance at which the eye can focus comfortably. It increases with age (presbyopia). Standard MCAT value is 25 cm.

column1: What is the far point of a normal (emmetropic) eye?
column4: A normal eye can focus on objects at infinity without accommodation. In myopia, the far point is closer than infinity; in hyperopia, it is behind the eye (virtual).

column1: What structure in the eye changes shape to accommodate near and far vision?
column4: Ciliary muscles contract to make the lens more curved (higher power) for near objects, and relax for far objects. This process is called accommodation.

column1: Where does the image form in a myopic (nearsighted) eye?
column4: The myopic eye is too long or the lens too powerful; parallel light from distant objects converges before reaching the retina, causing blurred distance vision.

column1: What is the angular magnification formula for a simple magnifier (object at near point)?
column4: 25 cm is the standard near point. A lens with f = 5 cm gives M = 5×. The shorter the focal length, the greater the magnification.

column1: In a compound microscope, which lens is positioned near the specimen?
column4: The objective lens has a short focal length and forms a real, magnified, inverted image of the specimen. The eyepiece (ocular) then magnifies that intermediate image further.

column1: What is the function of the eyepiece (ocular) in a compound microscope?
column3: Acts as a magnifier for the intermediate image formed by the objective
column4: The eyepiece is a simple magnifying glass (converging lens) that the observer looks through. Total magnification = M_objective × M_eyepiece.

column1: In a refracting telescope, what is the role of the objective lens?
column3: Collects light and forms a real image of the distant object at its focal plane
column4: The objective has a long focal length to gather light from distant sources. The eyepiece then magnifies the real image produced by the objective.

column1: What eye condition is presbyopia, and what lens corrects it?
column3: Age-related loss of accommodation; corrected by converging (reading) lenses
column4: The crystalline lens stiffens with age, reducing accommodation ability. Reading glasses (converging lenses) help by reducing the focusing demand on the ciliary muscles.

column1: What does the atomic number (Z) represent?
column3: Number of protons in the nucleus
column4: The atomic number uniquely identifies an element; it equals the number of protons and, in a neutral atom, the number of electrons.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::atomic-number-atomic-weight MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the atomic mass unit (amu) defined as?
column4: One amu ≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; this scale makes the masses of protons and neutrons both approximately 1 amu.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::atomic-number-atomic-weight MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Atomic weight of an element on the periodic table represents what type of average?
column4: Atomic weight accounts for the natural abundance of each isotope, so it is rarely a whole number.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::atomic-number-atomic-weight MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the mass number (A) of an atom?
column4: A = Z + N; mass number is always a whole number, distinguishing it from the decimal atomic weight.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::atomic-number-atomic-weight MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How does the atomic number change when an element loses an electron to form a cation?
column4: Atomic number depends only on proton count; gaining or losing electrons changes the charge but not Z.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::atomic-number-atomic-weight MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: An element has Z = 17 and A = 35. How many neutrons does it have?
column4: N = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18; this is chlorine-35, the most abundant chlorine isotope.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::atomic-number-atomic-weight MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is a proton's approximate mass in amu?
column4: Protons and neutrons both have masses close to 1 amu; electrons are ~1836 times lighter and contribute negligibly to atomic mass.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::neutrons-protons-isotopes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Define isotopes.
column3: Atoms with same Z but different N (and A)
column4: Isotopes of an element have identical chemical behavior but different nuclear properties (mass, stability, radioactivity).
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::neutrons-protons-isotopes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which subatomic particle carries no electric charge?
column4: Neutrons are electrically neutral; they reside in the nucleus alongside positively charged protons.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::neutrons-protons-isotopes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes. How do they differ?
column4: Both have Z = 6; C-12 has N = 6, C-14 has N = 8. C-14 is radioactive and used in radiocarbon dating.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::neutrons-protons-isotopes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What makes an isotope a radioisotope?
column3: Its nucleus is unstable and spontaneously decays
column4: Radioisotopes have unfavorable neutron-to-proton ratios or excess binding energy configurations that lead to radioactive decay.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::neutrons-protons-isotopes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which element has only one naturally occurring stable isotope?
column4: Fluorine-19 is the only stable isotope of fluorine; many elements (e.g., Bi, Au) also have only one stable isotope.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::neutrons-protons-isotopes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the strong nuclear force?
column4: The strong force overcomes electromagnetic repulsion between protons; it acts over ~1–3 fm and is the same between any two nucleons.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::nuclear-forces-binding-energy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Define nuclear binding energy.
column3: Energy released when nucleons assemble into a nucleus
column4: Binding energy = mass defect × c²; it represents how tightly the nucleus is held together and equals the energy needed to fully disassemble the nucleus.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::nuclear-forces-binding-energy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is mass defect?
column3: Difference between summed nucleon masses and actual nuclear mass
column4: Mass defect (Δm) is converted to binding energy via E = Δm·c²; the nucleus is lighter than the sum of its free nucleons.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::nuclear-forces-binding-energy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which nucleus has the highest binding energy per nucleon?
column4: Fe-56 sits at the peak of the binding energy per nucleon curve; fusing lighter nuclei or fissioning heavier nuclei releases energy toward this maximum.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::nuclear-forces-binding-energy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Why is nuclear fusion of light nuclei energetically favorable?
column3: Products have higher binding energy per nucleon than reactants
column4: Moving up the binding energy curve (light to Fe-56) releases energy; fusion powers stars by combining hydrogen isotopes.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::nuclear-forces-binding-energy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What neutron-to-proton ratio is generally stable for light nuclei (Z < 20)?
column4: Heavy nuclei need N/Z > 1 to offset proton repulsion; light nuclei are stable near N = Z (e.g., C-12, O-16).
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::nuclear-forces-binding-energy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Define radioactive decay.
column3: Spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus emitting particles/energy
column4: Radioactive decay converts a parent nuclide to a daughter nuclide, releasing energy to achieve a more stable nuclear configuration.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::radioactive-decay MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is a decay series (decay chain)?
column3: Sequence of decays from parent to stable daughter
column4: Heavy nuclei (e.g., U-238) undergo multiple α and β decays before reaching a stable isotope (e.g., Pb-206).
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::radioactive-decay MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What drives a nucleus to undergo radioactive decay?
column4: Nuclei with too many or too few neutrons relative to protons are unstable; decay adjusts the N/Z ratio toward stability.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::radioactive-decay MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Is radioactive decay affected by temperature, pressure, or chemical bonding?
column3: No — it is independent of physical/chemical conditions
column4: Because decay originates in the nucleus (not electron shell), external chemical and physical conditions do not alter decay rates.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::radioactive-decay MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is a positron emission (β⁺ decay) in terms of nuclear change?
column4: β⁺ decay decreases Z by 1 and is favored when N/Z is too low (too many protons relative to neutrons).
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::radioactive-decay MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What particles are emitted in alpha (α) decay?
column4: α decay decreases A by 4 and Z by 2; it is common in heavy nuclei (Z > 83) seeking to reduce nuclear size.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::decay MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How does β⁻ decay change the atomic number?
column4: In β⁻ decay a neutron converts to a proton + electron + antineutrino; the mass number A stays the same.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::decay MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which type of radioactive decay does NOT change A or Z?
column4: Gamma decay releases excess nuclear energy as a high-energy photon; the nuclide identity (Z, A) is unchanged — only the energy state changes.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::decay MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which decay type has the greatest penetrating power?
column4: γ rays require lead or thick concrete to stop; α particles are stopped by paper and β particles by a few mm of aluminum.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::decay MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which decay type has the least penetrating power?
column4: α particles are heavy and doubly charged, losing energy quickly; they are stopped by skin or a sheet of paper.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::decay MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In β⁻ decay, what is emitted along with the electron?
column4: The antineutrino carries away momentum and energy to conserve lepton number; neutrinos interact very weakly with matter.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::decay MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What nuclear change occurs in electron capture?
column3: Inner-shell electron absorbed by nucleus; proton → neutron
column4: Electron capture competes with β⁺ decay; Z decreases by 1 and A stays the same, and an X-ray is emitted as outer electrons fill the vacancy.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::decay MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Define half-life (t₁/₂) of a radioactive isotope.
column3: Time for half the nuclei to decay
column4: After one half-life, 50% of the parent remains; after two, 25%; after n half-lives, (1/2)ⁿ of the original amount remains.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::half-life-exponential-decay-semi-log-plots MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the mathematical relationship between the decay constant (λ) and half-life?
column4: A larger decay constant means faster decay and a shorter half-life; λ is the probability of decay per unit time.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::half-life-exponential-decay-semi-log-plots MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Write the equation for radioactive decay (amount remaining vs. time).
column4: This first-order exponential decay equation applies to both number of nuclei and activity; activity A = λN also decays exponentially.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::half-life-exponential-decay-semi-log-plots MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: On a semi-log plot of ln N vs. time for radioactive decay, what is the shape of the graph?
column4: Taking ln of N = N₀e^(−λt) gives ln N = ln N₀ − λt; the linearity confirms first-order kinetics.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::half-life-exponential-decay-semi-log-plots MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: After 3 half-lives, what fraction of the original radioactive sample remains?
column4: (1/2)³ = 1/8; each half-life multiplies the remaining amount by 1/2.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::half-life-exponential-decay-semi-log-plots MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is 'activity' of a radioactive sample and what are its SI units?
column3: Decays per second; SI unit is Becquerel (Bq)
column4: Activity A = λN; 1 Bq = 1 decay/s. The older unit Curie (Ci) = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::half-life-exponential-decay-semi-log-plots MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Carbon-14 has a half-life of ~5730 years. After 11,460 years, what fraction of C-14 remains?
column4: 11,460 years = 2 × 5730 years = 2 half-lives; (1/2)² = 1/4.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::half-life-exponential-decay-semi-log-plots MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the basic principle of a mass spectrometer?
column4: Ions are accelerated and deflected by magnetic/electric fields; lighter or more highly charged ions curve more, allowing separation and detection.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectrometer MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Name the four main stages of a mass spectrometer in order.
column4: Sample is ionized, ions are accelerated by an electric field, deflected by a magnetic field by m/z, and detected to produce a spectrum.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectrometer MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In a mass spectrometer, how are heavier ions deflected compared to lighter ions (same charge)?
column3: Heavier ions are deflected less (larger radius)
column4: The radius of curvature r = mv/(qB); greater mass → larger r → less deflection for the same charge and velocity.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectrometer MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What quantity does a mass spectrometer directly measure?
column4: The x-axis of a mass spectrum is m/z; for singly charged ions (z = 1), m/z equals the mass in amu.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectrometer MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which ionization method is commonly used in mass spectrometry for small volatile molecules?
column4: EI bombards the sample with high-energy electrons, producing radical cations (M⁺•); it often causes extensive fragmentation.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectrometer MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the molecular ion peak (M⁺) in mass spectrometry?
column3: Peak corresponding to the intact ionized molecule
column4: The M⁺ peak gives the molecular weight; the base peak is the tallest peak (most abundant fragment), which may or may not be M⁺.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectrometer MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What information does mass spectroscopy provide about a compound?
column3: Molecular mass and structural fragmentation pattern
column4: The molecular ion peak gives molecular weight; fragmentation peaks reveal structural features (functional groups, carbon skeleton).
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectroscopy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What does the base peak represent in a mass spectrum?
column3: Most abundant ion (tallest peak, set to 100% relative abundance)
column4: The base peak is the most stable fragment; it is not necessarily the molecular ion but is often a characteristic structural fragment.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectroscopy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How can mass spectroscopy distinguish isotopes of the same element?
column3: Isotopes appear as separate peaks differing by mass number
column4: E.g., Cl has two isotopes (³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, ~3:1 ratio); a chlorine-containing compound shows an M and M+2 peak in ~3:1 ratio.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectroscopy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What does an M+2 peak of roughly equal intensity to M indicate in mass spectroscopy?
column3: Presence of bromine (⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, ~1:1 ratio)
column4: Bromine's two isotopes are nearly equal in abundance, giving a characteristic 1:1 doublet; chlorine gives a 3:1 M:M+2 pattern.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectroscopy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In mass spectroscopy, what structural information can be inferred from the difference between the M⁺ peak and a fragment peak?
column3: Mass of the lost neutral fragment
column4: E.g., M − 15 suggests loss of CH₃; M − 29 suggests loss of CHO or C₂H₅; this aids structural elucidation.
column8: concept::CP::4E::atomic_nucleus MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::atomic-nucleus::mass-spectroscopy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the principal quantum number n?
column4: n determines the energy level and average distance of electrons from the nucleus in the hydrogen atom; higher n means higher energy.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy shell n?
column4: For n=1: 2 electrons; n=2: 8 electrons; n=3: 18 electrons. This follows from the 2(2l+1) rule summed over all subshells.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How many subshells (l values) exist in shell n?
column4: For n=3 there are three subshells: s (l=0), p (l=1), d (l=2). The azimuthal quantum number l ranges from 0 to n−1.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number l for a p subshell?
column4: l=0 → s, l=1 → p, l=2 → d, l=3 → f. Each l value defines a subshell shape.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What values can the magnetic quantum number ml take for a given l?
column4: For l=1 (p): ml = −1, 0, +1 giving three p orbitals. ml specifies orbital orientation in space.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How many orbitals are in the d subshell (l=2)?
column4: ml ranges from −2 to +2, giving 5 values. Each orbital holds 2 electrons, so d holds a maximum of 10 electrons.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the maximum number of electrons in a single orbital?
column4: The Pauli exclusion principle requires the two electrons to have opposite spin quantum numbers (ms = +½ and −½).
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In a hydrogen atom, which quantum number alone determines orbital energy?
column4: Hydrogen is a one-electron atom; energy depends only on n (En = −13.6/n² eV). In multi-electron atoms, both n and l affect energy.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the ground-state energy of hydrogen (n=1) in eV?
column4: En = −13.6/n² eV. The negative sign indicates a bound state; ionization from n=1 requires +13.6 eV.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How many total orbitals exist in shell n=3?
column4: n=3 has subshells s (1 orbital), p (3 orbitals), d (5 orbitals) → 1+3+5=9. Total electrons = 2×9 = 18.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the spin quantum number ms and its allowed values?
column4: ms describes intrinsic electron spin (up or down). Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite ms values (Pauli exclusion principle).
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: For hydrogen in the n=2 shell, how many orbitals exist and what are their designations?
column4: l=0 gives one 2s orbital; l=1 gives three 2p orbitals (ml=−1,0,+1). All four are degenerate in hydrogen.

column1: What is the minimum value of n for the d subshell to exist?
column4: The d subshell requires l=2, and l can only reach 2 when n ≥ 3. Thus the first d subshell is 3d.

column1: Which set of quantum numbers is forbidden by the Pauli exclusion principle?
column3: Two electrons with identical n, l, ml, and ms
column4: No two electrons in an atom may share all four quantum numbers. Differing ms (±½) is the minimum requirement for two electrons in the same orbital.

column1: In hydrogen, the 2s and 2p orbitals are degenerate. Why does this NOT hold for multi-electron atoms?
column3: Electron shielding/penetration differentiates energy by l
column4: In multi-electron atoms, s electrons penetrate closer to the nucleus and are less shielded, lowering their energy relative to p electrons of the same n.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the shape of an s orbital (l=0)?
column4: All s orbitals are spherically symmetric. The 1s orbital has no nodes; each successive s orbital adds one radial node.

column1: How many radial nodes does the 2s orbital have?
column4: Number of radial nodes = n − l − 1. For 2s: 2−0−1 = 1. Nodes are regions of zero electron probability density.

column1: What is the total number of nodes (angular + radial) for any orbital in shell n?
column4: Total nodes = n−1; angular nodes = l; radial nodes = n−l−1. For 3p: 2 total, 1 angular, 1 radial.
column8: concept::CP::4E::electronic_structure MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::electronic-structure::orbital-structure-of-hydrogen-atom-principal-quantum-number-n-number-of-electrons-per MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PHY MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the ground state of an atom?
column3: Lowest possible energy configuration of electrons
column4: In the ground state, electrons occupy the lowest available energy orbitals. Any addition of energy can promote electrons to higher (excited) states.

column1: What is an excited state of an atom?
column3: Higher energy electron configuration above ground state
column4: When an atom absorbs energy, one or more electrons jump to higher energy orbitals, creating an excited state. These states are unstable and electrons return to ground state by emitting photons.

column1: When an electron transitions from an excited state to the ground state, what is released?
column4: The photon's energy equals the energy difference between the two levels: E = hf. This is the basis of atomic emission spectra.

column1: What determines the energy of the photon emitted when an electron drops from n=3 to n=1?
column3: Energy difference between n=3 and n=1 levels
column4: E_photon = E_3 - E_1. For hydrogen, E_n = -13.6/n² eV. The emitted photon has energy equal exactly to this difference.

column1: Which transition produces a higher energy photon: n=3→n=1 or n=3→n=2?
column4: A larger energy gap between levels produces higher energy (shorter wavelength) photons. The n=3→n=1 gap is much larger than n=3→n=2.

column1: What are absorption line spectra?
column3: Dark lines in continuous spectrum where atoms absorb photons
column4: When white light passes through a gas, atoms absorb photons matching their quantized energy differences, producing dark lines at specific wavelengths.

column1: What are emission line spectra?
column3: Bright colored lines emitted by excited atoms
column4: When excited atoms return to lower energy states, they emit photons at specific wavelengths, producing a series of bright lines unique to each element — an atomic fingerprint.

column1: What is the relationship between the absorption and emission spectra of the same element?
column4: The same energy transitions responsible for absorption also produce emission lines. Absorbed wavelengths appear as dark lines; emitted wavelengths appear as bright lines at the same positions.

column1: Which series of hydrogen emission lines falls in the visible range?
column4: Balmer series transitions end at n=2 and produce visible light (violet to red). Lyman series (to n=1) is UV; Paschen series (to n=3) is infrared.

column1: Which hydrogen emission series lies in the ultraviolet region?
column4: Lyman series involves transitions from higher levels down to n=1, releasing high-energy UV photons. This is the highest energy hydrogen series.

column1: What does the Pauli Exclusion Principle state?
column3: No two electrons can share the same four quantum numbers
column4: Since three quantum numbers (n, l, ml) define an orbital, a fourth (ms = +1/2 or -1/2) allows at most two electrons per orbital with opposite spins.

column1: What is the maximum number of electrons in any single orbital according to the Pauli Exclusion Principle?
column4: Two electrons can occupy the same orbital only if their spin quantum numbers differ: one +1/2 (spin-up) and one -1/2 (spin-down).

column1: Using the Pauli Exclusion Principle, what is the maximum number of electrons in the n=2 shell?
column4: n=2 has s (2 electrons) and p (6 electrons) subshells: 2+6=8 total. Formula: max electrons per shell = 2n².

column1: What are the four quantum numbers that uniquely identify an electron?
column4: n=principal, l=azimuthal (subshell), ml=magnetic (orbital orientation), ms=spin (+1/2 or -1/2). No two electrons in an atom can have identical sets of all four.

column1: How many electrons can the 3d subshell hold, and why?
column4: The d subshell has l=2, giving ml values of -2,-1,0,+1,+2 — five orbitals. Each holds 2 electrons by the Pauli Exclusion Principle.

column1: What is paramagnetism?
column3: Attraction to external magnetic field due to unpaired electrons
column4: Atoms or molecules with one or more unpaired electrons are paramagnetic. Unpaired electron spins create a net magnetic moment that is attracted to external fields.

column1: What is diamagnetism?
column3: Weak repulsion from magnetic field; all electrons paired
column4: When all electrons are spin-paired, their magnetic moments cancel. Diamagnetic substances are slightly repelled by external magnetic fields.

column1: Is oxygen (O2) paramagnetic or diamagnetic?
column4: O2 has two unpaired electrons in degenerate π* antibonding orbitals (by Hund's rule). This paramagnetism is a classic MCAT example.

column1: Is zinc (Zn, [Ar] 3d10 4s2) paramagnetic or diamagnetic?
column4: Zinc has a completely filled 3d subshell and filled 4s subshell. All electrons are paired, yielding no net magnetic moment.

column1: Which ion is paramagnetic: Cu+ ([Ar] 3d10) or Cu2+ ([Ar] 3d9)?
column4: Cu+ has a fully filled 3d10 shell (diamagnetic). Cu2+ has 3d9 with one unpaired electron, making it paramagnetic.

column1: In conventional electron configuration notation, what does '2p4' mean?
column4: The number before the letter is the principal quantum number (n=2), the letter is the subshell (p), and the superscript is the number of electrons (4).

column1: What is the ground-state electron configuration of carbon (atomic number 6)?
column4: Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy: 1s (2), 2s (2), 2p (2). By Hund's rule, the two 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins.

column1: What is the abbreviated (noble gas core) electron configuration of chlorine (Z=17)?
column4: Neon (Z=10) fills 1s2 2s2 2p6. The remaining 7 electrons of Cl fill 3s2 3p5. This shorthand saves writing the inner shells.

column1: What is the electron configuration of Cu (Z=29)?
column4: Copper's actual configuration is [Ar] 3d10 4s1 rather than [Ar] 3d9 4s2, because a completely filled 3d subshell provides extra stability.

column1: Which element has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s1 instead of [Ar] 3d4 4s2?
column4: Cr adopts [Ar] 3d5 4s1 because a half-filled 3d subshell (all 5 orbitals singly occupied) is especially stable due to exchange energy.

column1: What did the Bohr model of the atom propose about electron orbits?
column3: Electrons travel in fixed circular orbits with quantized energies
column4: Bohr postulated that electrons only occupy certain allowed orbits (n=1,2,3…) and do not radiate energy while in them, explaining hydrogen's discrete spectrum.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::bohr-atom MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In the Bohr model, what happens when an electron absorbs energy?
column3: It jumps to a higher orbit (higher n)
column4: Energy absorption promotes an electron from a lower to a higher energy orbit. It later returns to a lower orbit by emitting a photon.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::bohr-atom MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the energy of the ground-state electron in hydrogen according to the Bohr model?
column4: For hydrogen, E_n = -13.6/n² eV. At n=1 (ground state), E = -13.6 eV. The negative sign indicates the electron is bound.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::bohr-atom MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: For a hydrogen-like atom, how does the Bohr energy formula change with atomic number Z?
column4: Greater nuclear charge (Z) increases the attraction, lowering each energy level. For He+ (Z=2), ground state energy = -13.6 × 4 = -54.4 eV.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::bohr-atom MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the key limitation of the Bohr model?
column3: Only accurately predicts hydrogen and hydrogen-like (one-electron) atoms
column4: Bohr's model fails for multi-electron atoms because it ignores electron-electron repulsions and the wave nature of electrons (no orbitals, only orbits).
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::bohr-atom MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What does the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle state?
column3: Cannot simultaneously know exact position and momentum of a particle
column4: Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2. The more precisely position is measured, the less precisely momentum is known, and vice versa. This is fundamental, not a measurement artifact.

column1: What is the mathematical expression for the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle?
column4: Where Δx is uncertainty in position, Δp is uncertainty in momentum, and ℏ = h/2π (reduced Planck's constant). The product of uncertainties has a minimum lower bound.

column1: How does the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle justify the concept of atomic orbitals rather than orbits?
column3: Electrons cannot have defined trajectories; probability clouds (orbitals) describe likely positions
column4: Because position and momentum cannot both be precisely known, electrons are described by probability distributions (orbitals) rather than Bohr's fixed circular paths.

column1: If the uncertainty in an electron's position is very small, what happens to the uncertainty in its momentum?
column4: By Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2, decreasing Δx forces Δp to increase proportionally. This is why confining electrons (e.g., in a nucleus) implies enormous kinetic energies.

column1: What is effective nuclear charge (Zeff)?
column3: Net nuclear charge felt by an electron after shielding
column4: Zeff = Z - σ, where Z is the actual nuclear charge and σ is the shielding constant from inner/same-shell electrons. Outer electrons experience a reduced nuclear attraction.

column1: What is electron shielding (screening)?
column3: Inner electrons reduce nuclear charge felt by outer electrons
column4: Core electrons partially cancel the nuclear pull on valence electrons, lowering their effective nuclear charge and increasing their orbital radius (energy).

column1: How does effective nuclear charge change across a period (left to right)?
column4: Going left to right, Z increases by 1 each step but shielding increases by less than 1 (added electrons are in same shell, poor shielders). Net Zeff rises, pulling electrons closer.

column1: How does effective nuclear charge relate to atomic radius trends?
column4: As Zeff increases across a period, valence electrons are held more tightly by the nucleus, shrinking the atom. This explains why atomic radius decreases across a period.

column1: Which electrons provide the most effective shielding: core (inner shell) or same-shell electrons?
column3: Core (inner shell) electrons shield more effectively
column4: Electrons in inner shells are between the nucleus and the outer electrons, blocking much of the nuclear charge. Same-shell electrons are poor shielders because they don't shield each other well.

column1: What is the photoelectric effect?
column3: Emission of electrons from metal surface when struck by light
column4: When photons with sufficient energy hit a metal surface, electrons are ejected. This demonstrated the particle nature of light (photons), as explained by Einstein.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::photoelectric-effect MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the work function (φ) in the photoelectric effect?
column3: Minimum energy needed to eject an electron from the metal surface
column4: If the photon energy (hf) is less than φ, no electrons are ejected regardless of intensity. The work function is a characteristic property of each metal.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::photoelectric-effect MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the equation for kinetic energy of ejected electrons in the photoelectric effect?
column4: KE is kinetic energy of the ejected electron, hf is photon energy (h=Planck's constant, f=frequency), and φ is the work function. Energy above threshold becomes kinetic energy.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::photoelectric-effect MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What happens to the kinetic energy of ejected electrons if light intensity is doubled but frequency stays constant?
column3: KE stays the same; more electrons are ejected
column4: Intensity determines the number of photons, not individual photon energy. KE depends only on photon frequency (energy). More photons eject more electrons, but each electron has the same KE.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::photoelectric-effect MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What property of the photoelectric effect cannot be explained by classical wave theory of light?
column3: Existence of a threshold frequency below which no electrons are ejected
column4: Classical wave theory predicts any frequency of sufficient intensity should eject electrons. The threshold frequency (requiring minimum photon energy = work function) proves light comes in quantized packets (photons).
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::photoelectric-effect MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In the photoelectric effect, what happens if photon frequency is below the threshold, even with very high intensity?
column4: Each photon interacts with one electron. If hf < φ, no single photon has enough energy to eject an electron, no matter how many photons (intensity) strike the surface.
column8: concept::CP::4E::orbital MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::orbital::photoelectric-effect MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What group number are the alkali metals on the periodic table?
column4: Alkali metals occupy Group 1; they have one valence electron and readily lose it to form +1 cations.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the common oxidation state of alkali metals in compounds?
column4: Losing their single ns1 valence electron gives alkali metals the stable electron configuration of the preceding noble gas.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which alkali metal has the highest electronegativity?
column4: Electronegativity decreases down a group; Li is at the top of Group 1 and is the most electronegative alkali metal.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: How do alkali metals react with water?
column3: Vigorously, producing H2 gas and a metal hydroxide
column4: The reaction is: 2M + 2H2O → 2MOH + H2; reactivity increases down the group (Cs reacts explosively).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which property of alkali metals decreases as you go down Group 1?
column4: Larger atomic radius and greater electron shielding make it easier to remove the outermost electron as you descend the group.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which alkali metal is the strongest reducing agent?
column4: Despite having the highest ionization energy among alkali metals, Li has the highest standard reduction potential in solution due to its very high hydration energy.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the electron configuration notation for all alkali metals' valence shell?
column4: Each alkali metal has one electron in its outermost s subshell, making it highly reactive and prone to forming +1 ions.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What group number are the alkaline earth metals?
column4: Alkaline earth metals have two valence electrons (ns2) and typically form +2 cations by losing both.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the common oxidation state of alkaline earth metals?
column4: Losing both ns2 valence electrons gives alkaline earth metals a noble-gas electron configuration and forms stable +2 cations.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which alkaline earth metal does NOT form a +2 ion under normal conditions?
column4: Be has such high charge density that it polarizes electron clouds strongly, leading to predominantly covalent character in its compounds rather than ionic +2 behavior.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: How does the reactivity of alkaline earth metals with water compare to alkali metals?
column4: Alkaline earth metals need more energy to remove two electrons; Be barely reacts with water, Mg reacts slowly, but Ca, Sr, Ba react readily.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the solubility trend for alkaline earth metal hydroxides?
column4: Be(OH)2 is insoluble, Mg(OH)2 is sparingly soluble, Ca(OH)2 slightly soluble, and Ba(OH)2 is quite soluble in water.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which alkaline earth metal sulfate is essentially insoluble in water?
column4: BaSO4 is so insoluble that it is used as a contrast agent in GI imaging without risk of absorption; in contrast, MgSO4 is highly soluble.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What group number are the halogens?
column4: Halogens have seven valence electrons (ns2np5) and need only one more electron to achieve a noble-gas configuration.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What oxidation state do halogens most commonly form when acting as oxidizing agents?
column4: Halogens gain one electron to form halide ions (F-, Cl-, Br-, I-), which is their most stable and common oxidation state.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which halogen is the strongest oxidizing agent?
column4: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity and the smallest atomic radius in the group; it has no d orbitals to expand and always takes oxidation state -1 (never positive).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the trend in boiling points of halogens going down Group 17?
column3: Boiling point increases down the group
column4: Larger molar mass leads to stronger London dispersion forces; F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid, and I2 is a solid at room temperature.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which halogen cannot have a positive oxidation state?
column4: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and has no available d orbitals; it cannot expand its octet or take a positive oxidation state.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What type of reaction do halogens undergo with hydrogen to form hydrohalic acids?
column4: H2 + X2 → 2HX; reactivity with H2 decreases down the group (F2 reacts explosively, I2 reacts only partially and slowly).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What group number are the noble gases?
column4: Noble gases have completely filled valence shells (ns2np6, except He which is 1s2) and are chemically inert under normal conditions.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the valence electron configuration of noble gases (excluding helium)?
column4: A full octet makes noble gases extremely stable and unreactive; helium is the exception with a full 1s2 configuration.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which noble gases can form compounds under extreme conditions?
column4: Heavier noble gases have larger, more polarizable electrons and can form compounds with highly electronegative elements like fluorine and oxygen (e.g., XeF2, XeF4).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What intermolecular forces hold noble gas atoms together in the liquid/solid state?
column4: Noble gases are monatomic and nonpolar; the only attraction between atoms is induced dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) forces.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Why do noble gases have very low boiling points?
column3: Very weak London dispersion forces due to small, non-polarizable electron clouds
column4: Boiling point increases down the group as atomic size and polarizability increase (He < Ne < Ar < Kr < Xe < Rn).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which noble gas has the largest atomic radius?
column4: Atomic radius increases down any group; Rn has the most electron shells and is the largest naturally occurring noble gas.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What d-block groups make up the transition metals?
column4: Transition metals are characterized by partially filled d subshells in the atom or its common ions, giving rise to characteristic colors, magnetism, and variable oxidation states.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What property distinguishes transition metals from main-group metals?
column3: Partially filled d orbitals (in atom or ion)
column4: This partially filled d subshell enables multiple oxidation states, colored compounds, and catalytic behavior not seen in s-block metals.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Why do transition metals exhibit multiple oxidation states?
column3: Small energy differences between ns and (n-1)d electrons
column4: Both the outer s electrons and the inner d electrons have similar energies and can be removed, allowing variable oxidation states (e.g., Fe2+ and Fe3+).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which two transition metals are exceptions to the expected electron configuration, having only one s electron?
column4: Cr is [Ar]3d54s1 and Cu is [Ar]3d104s1; half-filled and fully-filled d subshells provide extra stability, causing one s electron to shift into the d subshell.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Why are transition metal compounds often colored?
column3: d-d electron transitions absorb visible light
column4: Ligands split the d orbitals into energy levels; electrons absorb specific visible wavelengths when transitioning between these levels, giving the compound its color.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What makes transition metals good catalysts?
column3: Variable oxidation states and ability to form coordination complexes
column4: Transition metals can accept and donate electrons easily (changing oxidation states) and can bind reactants as ligands, lowering activation energy.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which transition metal is the most abundant in Earth's crust?
column4: Iron is the fourth most abundant element overall and the most abundant transition metal; it is central to biology (hemoglobin) and industry.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What are 'representative elements' on the periodic table?
column4: Representative elements have their highest-energy electrons in s or p orbitals; their chemical behavior is largely predictable from their group number and valence electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: How many valence electrons do Group 13 representative elements have?
column4: Group 13 (e.g., boron, aluminum) has three valence electrons and commonly forms +3 ions or three covalent bonds.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the octet rule as it applies to representative elements?
column3: Atoms gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve 8 valence electrons
column4: Representative elements are most stable with a complete valence shell of 8 electrons; exceptions include H, He (2), and some elements like Be and B (electron deficient).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which representative element group forms the most stable monatomic anions with a -2 charge?
column4: Oxygen, sulfur, selenium, and tellurium each have 6 valence electrons and gain 2 electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration, forming O2-, S2-, etc.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What trend in atomic radius is observed across a period for representative elements?
column3: Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period
column4: Increasing nuclear charge (more protons) pulls electrons closer without adding a new shell, so atoms get smaller across a period.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the dividing line between metals and nonmetals on the periodic table called?
column4: The staircase runs from boron to astatine on the right side of the p-block; elements along the line (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, At) are metalloids.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What are the two general categories of elements based on their electrical conductivity?
column4: Metals conduct heat and electricity well due to delocalized electrons; nonmetals generally do not conduct. Metalloids have intermediate properties.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Where on the periodic table are metals predominantly located?
column3: Left and center (s-block, d-block, f-block, and left p-block)
column4: The majority of elements are metals; they occupy Groups 1–2, all transition metals (3–12), and the lower-left of the p-block.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the general trend in metallic character across a period from left to right?
column4: Increasing nuclear charge and ionization energy make it harder to lose electrons, shifting character from metallic to nonmetallic across a period.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which property distinguishes metallic from nonmetallic oxides when dissolved in water?
column3: Metal oxides form basic solutions; nonmetal oxides form acidic solutions
column4: Metal oxides (e.g., Na2O, CaO) react with water to form hydroxides (bases); nonmetal oxides (e.g., CO2, SO3) form acids (carbonic acid, sulfuric acid).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What are metalloids, and name three examples?
column3: Elements with properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals; e.g., Si, Ge, As
column4: Metalloids (also called semimetals) act as semiconductors; silicon and germanium are crucial in electronics. They lie along the zigzag staircase on the periodic table.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which nonmetal is a liquid at room temperature?
column4: Bromine is the only nonmetal that is liquid at standard conditions (25°C, 1 atm); mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the general trend in ionization energy comparing metals vs. nonmetals?
column3: Nonmetals have higher ionization energies than metals
column4: Nonmetals hold their electrons more tightly due to higher effective nuclear charge; metals lose electrons easily, reflected in their low ionization energies.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is another name for Group 16 elements?
column4: The name 'chalcogen' derives from the Greek for 'ore former'; oxygen, sulfur, selenium, tellurium, and polonium comprise this group.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the most common oxidation state of oxygen in compounds?
column4: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and gains 2 to complete its octet, forming the oxide ion O2-. Exceptions include peroxides (-1) and OF2 (+2).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)?
column4: In H2O2, each oxygen has oxidation state -1; the O-O bond is a peroxide linkage, not a full 2- reduction as in H2O.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in oxygen difluoride (OF2)?
column4: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen and always takes -1; since there are two F atoms (-2 total), oxygen must be +2 in OF2.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: How do the boiling points of Group 16 hydrides compare to what periodic trends would predict for H2O?
column3: H2O has an anomalously high boiling point due to hydrogen bonding
column4: H2S, H2Se, and H2Te follow the expected trend, but H2O boils at 100°C instead of the extrapolated -80°C because of extensive hydrogen bonding.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What are the two common allotropes of oxygen?
column4: O2 is the stable, diatomic form essential for aerobic respiration; O3 (ozone) is the triatomic allotrope found in the stratosphere that absorbs UV radiation.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: Which Group 16 element can expand its octet and show oxidation states higher than +2?
column4: Unlike oxygen, sulfur has accessible 3d orbitals that allow it to expand its octet; sulfur commonly shows +4 (SO2) and +6 (SO3, H2SO4) oxidation states.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Classification of Elements Into Groups by Electronic Structure

column1: What are valence electrons?
column3: Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom
column4: Valence electrons determine chemical reactivity and bonding behavior. For main-group elements, the number of valence electrons equals the group number.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: How many valence electrons does a Group IIA element have?
column4: Group IIA (alkaline earth metals) all have 2 valence electrons in the s subshell, giving them the configuration ns².
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which subshells contain valence electrons for main-group (s- and p-block) elements?
column3: s and p subshells of the outermost shell
column4: For elements in groups IA–VIIIA, valence electrons occupy the outermost s and p orbitals. Transition metals also involve d electrons but are not typically the focus for MCAT valence discussions.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: How many valence electrons does phosphorus (Group VA) have?
column4: Phosphorus has the configuration [Ne]3s²3p³, giving 5 valence electrons. Group VA elements all have 5 valence electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why do noble gases (Group VIII/0) have full valence shells?
column3: They have 8 valence electrons (2 for He)
column4: Noble gases have a complete octet (except He with 2), making them chemically inert. This full shell configuration is the basis of the octet rule.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: For d-block (transition) metals, which electrons are considered valence electrons?
column3: Outermost s electrons and the d electrons
column4: Transition metals can use both their (n-1)d and ns electrons in bonding, which is why they can exhibit multiple oxidation states.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Define first ionization energy.
column3: Energy to remove the first valence electron from a neutral gaseous atom
column4: First ionization energy (IE1) is always endothermic (energy required). It measures how tightly the outermost electron is held by the nucleus.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of first ionization energy across a period (left to right)?
column4: As atomic number increases across a period, nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, pulling electrons closer and making them harder to remove.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of first ionization energy down a group?
column4: Electrons are added to higher principal energy levels farther from the nucleus, and increased shielding reduces effective nuclear charge, making outermost electrons easier to remove.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Define second ionization energy.
column3: Energy to remove a second electron from a singly charged cation
column4: IE2 is always greater than IE1 because removing an electron from a positive ion requires overcoming greater effective nuclear charge.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why is there a dramatic jump in ionization energy between IE2 and IE3 for a Group IIA element like Mg?
column3: Third electron must come from an inner shell (core electron)
column4: After removing 2 valence electrons, the third electron is a core electron held much more tightly by the nucleus. The large jump signals the transition from valence to core electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which element has an anomalously lower first ionization energy than expected: B or Be?
column4: Boron's outermost electron is in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and less tightly held than beryllium's 2s electron, causing the dip despite higher nuclear charge.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Define ionization energy in general.
column3: Energy required to completely remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion
column4: Ionization energy is always positive (endothermic). It is expressed in kJ/mol or eV and increases with each successive removal.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What does a high ionization energy indicate about an element?
column3: Strong attraction between nucleus and valence electrons
column4: Elements with high ionization energies (e.g., noble gases, halogens) hold their electrons tightly and tend not to form cations easily.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What units are commonly used to report ionization energy?
column4: Both units appear in MCAT contexts. 1 eV = 96.5 kJ/mol (approximately). The MCAT typically uses kJ/mol for comparative questions.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: How does effective nuclear charge (Zeff) relate to ionization energy?
column4: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge experienced by valence electrons after accounting for shielding. Greater Zeff pulls electrons closer, increasing IE.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why does ionization energy generally increase from Na to Cl across Period 3?
column3: Increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding increases Zeff
column4: Each added proton increases nuclear charge, while electrons added to the same shell provide minimal additional shielding, so valence electrons experience stronger attraction.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Predict whether Ca or Sr has a higher first ionization energy and explain why.
column4: Sr is in the same group but Period 5; its valence electrons are in the 5s shell, farther from the nucleus with more shielding, making them easier to remove.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why do half-filled p subshells (e.g., N, P) have anomalously high ionization energies?
column3: Half-filled subshells are extra stable; electrons resist removal
column4: Nitrogen's 2p³ configuration has one electron per p orbital with parallel spins (Hund's rule stability). Removing one disrupts this stable arrangement, requiring more energy.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Predict which has higher IE1: O or N, and why.
column3: N has higher IE1 than O
column4: Oxygen has a paired electron in one 2p orbital; electron-electron repulsion in that pair makes one electron easier to remove than any of nitrogen's unpaired 2p electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Define electron affinity.
column3: Energy change when a neutral gaseous atom gains one electron
column4: A negative electron affinity means energy is released (exothermic) upon gaining an electron — this is the most common case for nonmetals. More negative = greater tendency to accept electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which group of elements has the most negative (most exothermic) electron affinities?
column4: Halogens need only one electron to complete their octet, so they have a strong tendency to gain an electron; Cl has the most negative EA among all elements.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the electron affinity of noble gases approximately?
column4: Noble gases have complete octets; adding an electron would require it to enter a higher, less stable energy level. They strongly resist gaining electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why does N have a less negative electron affinity than C or O?
column3: Half-filled 2p³ is extra stable; adding electron increases repulsion
column4: Nitrogen's half-filled p subshell is particularly stable. The added electron must pair up in an already-occupied orbital, increasing electron-electron repulsion.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Define electron affinity as a thermodynamic quantity.
column3: Energy released or absorbed when an atom gains one electron (X + e⁻ → X⁻)
column4: By convention, a negative EA value (energy released) indicates stability of the anion. A more negative EA means the atom more readily accepts electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Distinguish electron affinity from electronegativity.
column3: EA: energy for actual e⁻ gain; electronegativity: relative attraction for shared e⁻ in a bond
column4: EA is a measurable thermodynamic quantity in kJ/mol; electronegativity is a dimensionless comparative scale (e.g., Pauling). Both increase toward the upper right of the periodic table.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of electron affinity across a period (left to right)?
column3: Becomes more negative (greater tendency to gain electrons)
column4: As nuclear charge increases across a period, atoms pull added electrons more strongly. Halogens have the most negative EA in each period.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of electron affinity down a group?
column3: Becomes less negative (weaker tendency to gain electrons)
column4: Down a group, added electrons enter larger, more diffuse orbitals farther from the nucleus, so the atom attracts them less strongly.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why does Cl have a more negative electron affinity than F, despite being below it in Group VIIA?
column3: F's small size causes electron-electron repulsion in compact 2p orbitals
column4: F's 2p shell is small and crowded; the added electron experiences significant repulsion, reducing the energy released. Cl's 3p shell is larger and experiences less repulsion.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Define electronegativity.
column3: Relative ability of a bonded atom to attract shared electrons toward itself
column4: Electronegativity is a dimensionless property on the Pauling scale (F = 4.0 is the highest). It governs bond polarity and determines whether a bond is ionic, polar covalent, or nonpolar.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
column4: Fluorine is the most electronegative element. Its small atomic radius and high nuclear charge give it an exceptional ability to attract bonding electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of electronegativity across a period?
column3: Increases from left to right (excluding noble gases)
column4: Increasing nuclear charge across a period draws bonding electrons closer to each atom's nucleus, increasing electronegativity.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of electronegativity down a group?
column4: Valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, reducing the nucleus's pull on shared bonding electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which scale is most commonly used for electronegativity on the MCAT?
column4: The Pauling scale assigns F = 4.0 as the highest. Other values: O ≈ 3.5, N ≈ 3.0, C ≈ 2.5, H ≈ 2.1. These are the key values to memorize.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What electronegativity difference threshold distinguishes ionic from polar covalent bonds?
column4: A difference < 0.5 is nonpolar covalent; 0.5–1.7 is polar covalent; > 1.7 is considered ionic. These are approximate guidelines, not absolute cutoffs.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What are the approximate Pauling electronegativity values for O, N, and C?
column4: These three values are essential for MCAT: O > N > C. They explain bond polarity in organic molecules and biological macromolecules (e.g., peptide bonds, nucleotides).
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row
