column1: Rank these elements from highest to lowest electronegativity: F, O, Cl, N.
column4: F (4.0) > O (3.5) > N (3.0) > Cl (3.2 — actually slightly above N). Chlorine ≈ 3.2, which is between N and O. Key MCAT fact: F > O > Cl > N.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why is hydrogen's electronegativity (≈ 2.1) important for MCAT biochemistry?
column3: Determines polarity of C–H vs. O–H and N–H bonds
column4: C–H bonds (difference ≈ 0.4) are nearly nonpolar; O–H and N–H bonds are polar, enabling hydrogen bonding. This drives water's properties and protein/nucleic acid structure.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which is more electronegative: S or O?
column3: O is more electronegative than S
column4: O (3.5) > S (2.6). Both are in Group VIA, but O is smaller with higher Zeff relative to its shell, giving it a stronger pull on bonding electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the electronegativity of metals (general range)?
column4: Metals readily give up electrons (low IE, low EN). Alkali metals have the lowest electronegativities (Li ≈ 1.0, Na ≈ 0.9), consistent with their tendency to form cations.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What determines the size (atomic radius) of an atom?
column3: Number of electron shells (principal quantum number) and effective nuclear charge
column4: Atomic radius increases with more electron shells (down a group) and decreases with higher Zeff across a period, as greater nuclear pull contracts the electron cloud.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of atomic radius across a period (left to right)?
column4: Adding protons increases nuclear charge without significantly adding shielding (same shell), so Zeff increases and pulls electrons inward, shrinking atomic radius.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the general trend of atomic radius down a group?
column4: Each new period adds a new electron shell farther from the nucleus. Increased shielding also reduces Zeff experienced by outermost electrons, further expanding size.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which is larger: Na or Mg?
column4: Both are in Period 3, but Mg has one more proton (higher Zeff) with electrons in the same shell, so the electron cloud is pulled closer in Mg.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which is larger: Na or K?
column4: K is directly below Na in Group IA. K has an additional electron shell (4s vs 3s), making it significantly larger despite having more protons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why do noble gases have anomalously large atomic radii by van der Waals measurement?
column3: Their radii are measured as van der Waals radii (non-bonded), which are larger than covalent radii
column4: Noble gases do not form covalent bonds, so their 'size' is measured differently. When compared using the same measurement type, trends hold, but absolute values are larger.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: How does the size of a cation compare to its neutral parent atom?
column3: Cation is smaller than the neutral atom
column4: Removing an electron reduces electron-electron repulsion and, if the outer shell is emptied, removes an entire shell. The remaining electrons experience greater Zeff per electron.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: How does the size of an anion compare to its neutral parent atom?
column3: Anion is larger than the neutral atom
column4: Adding an electron increases electron-electron repulsion, causing the electron cloud to expand. The same nuclear charge now holds more electrons less tightly.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which is larger: Na⁺ or Na?
column3: Na is larger (neutral atom is bigger)
column4: Na⁺ has lost its 3s electron, removing the entire third shell. Na⁺ has the electron configuration of Ne and is significantly smaller than neutral Na.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which is larger: Cl⁻ or Ar?
column4: Both are isoelectronic (18 electrons), but Ar has 18 protons vs Cl's 17. More protons in Ar pull the same electrons closer, making Ar slightly smaller than Cl⁻.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Rank these isoelectronic species from largest to smallest: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺
column4: All three have 10 electrons (neon configuration), but nuclear charges differ: Na⁺ (11p), Mg²⁺ (12p), Al³⁺ (13p). More protons → smaller radius due to greater pull on the same electrons.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Which is larger: O²⁻ or F⁻?
column4: Both are isoelectronic with 10 electrons, but F has 9 protons vs O's 8. The greater nuclear charge in F⁻ contracts the electron cloud more than in O²⁻.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: Why does forming a 2+ cation (like Mg²⁺) dramatically reduce ionic radius compared to Mg?
column3: Two electrons removed; often empties outer shell, increasing Zeff per remaining electron
column4: Mg²⁺ loses its 3s² electrons, dropping to the n=2 shell. With 12 protons holding 10 electrons (vs 12 holding 12), Zeff per electron is much higher.
column5: The Periodic Table ― Variations of Chemical Properties with Group and Row

column1: What is the molecular weight of water (H₂O)?
column4: H = 1 g/mol × 2 = 2, O = 16 g/mol; total = 18 g/mol. This is a fundamental value used in countless stoichiometry calculations.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::molecular-weight MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the molecular weight of CO₂?
column4: C = 12 + O₂ = 32; total = 44 g/mol. Memorizing common molecular weights speeds up MCAT calculations.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::molecular-weight MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How is molecular weight (molar mass) calculated from a chemical formula?
column3: Sum of atomic masses of all atoms in formula
column4: Each element's atomic mass (in g/mol) is multiplied by its subscript and summed. Units are g/mol.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::molecular-weight MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the molecular weight of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)?
column4: 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 g/mol. Glucose molecular weight appears frequently in biochemistry and stoichiometry problems.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::molecular-weight MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the molecular weight of NaCl?
column4: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5; total = 58.5 g/mol. For ionic compounds, molecular weight is called formula weight.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::molecular-weight MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the distinction between molecular weight and formula weight?
column3: Formula weight used for ionic compounds; molecular weight for covalent
column4: Ionic compounds don't exist as discrete molecules, so 'formula weight' is technically more correct, though both terms refer to the mass in g/mol.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::molecular-weight MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What does an empirical formula represent?
column3: Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound
column4: The empirical formula reduces all subscripts to their lowest whole-number ratio; e.g., glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ has empirical formula CH₂O.

column1: What does a molecular formula represent?
column3: Actual number of each atom in one molecule
column4: The molecular formula may be a multiple of the empirical formula; e.g., benzene molecular formula C₆H₆, empirical formula CH.

column1: What is the empirical formula of H₂O₂?
column4: H₂O₂ has a 1:1 ratio of H to O when reduced, giving empirical formula HO. H₂O₂ is the molecular formula.

column1: How do you determine the molecular formula from an empirical formula?
column3: Divide molar mass by empirical formula mass; multiply subscripts
column4: If empirical formula mass = 30 and molar mass = 60, the multiplier n = 2, so all subscripts are doubled to get the molecular formula.

column1: A compound has empirical formula CH₂O and molar mass 60 g/mol. What is the molecular formula?
column4: Empirical formula mass of CH₂O = 30 g/mol; 60/30 = 2; multiply each subscript by 2 → C₂H₄O₂ (acetic acid).

column1: Which formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula?
column4: Molecular formula = n × (empirical formula), where n is a positive integer. When n = 1, they are identical.

column1: What is the SI base unit of amount of substance?
column4: The mole is the SI unit for counting particles; 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ entities.

column1: What prefix denotes 10⁻³ in the metric system?
column4: 1 milliliter (mL) = 10⁻³ L; 1 millimole (mmol) = 10⁻³ mol. Commonly used in solution concentrations.

column1: What prefix denotes 10⁻⁶ in the metric system?
column4: 1 micromole (μmol) = 10⁻⁶ mol. Used in biochemical concentrations where amounts are very small.

column1: How many milliliters are in one liter?
column4: Milli = 10⁻³, so 1 L = 10³ mL. This conversion is fundamental for molarity and dilution problems.

column1: What are the SI units of pressure commonly used in chemistry?
column4: 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. On the MCAT, atm and mmHg (torr) are most commonly encountered; 1 atm = 760 mmHg.

column1: What metric prefix denotes 10⁻⁹?
column4: 1 nanometer (nm) = 10⁻⁹ m. Wavelengths of visible light are commonly expressed in nm (400–700 nm).

column1: How is percent mass (percent composition by mass) defined?
column4: Percent mass tells you what fraction of a compound's mass is contributed by each element; used to determine empirical formulas.

column1: What is the percent mass of oxygen in water (H₂O)?
column4: O mass = 16 g/mol; molar mass H₂O = 18 g/mol; 16/18 × 100 ≈ 88.9%. Oxygen dominates water's mass.

column1: What is the percent mass of carbon in CO₂?
column4: C = 12 g/mol; molar mass CO₂ = 44 g/mol; 12/44 × 100 ≈ 27.3%. The remaining ~72.7% is oxygen.

column1: How do you find an empirical formula from percent composition data?
column3: Assume 100 g sample, convert % to grams, divide by atomic mass, find simplest ratio
column4: Step 1: treat % as grams. Step 2: divide each by its atomic mass to get moles. Step 3: divide all by smallest mole value. Step 4: round to whole numbers.

column1: A compound is 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?
How many particles are in one mole of a substance?
column4: Avogadro's number (N_A) = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole of any substance contains this many formula units, molecules, or atoms.

column1: What is Avogadro's number?
column4: Named after Amedeo Avogadro. It defines the mole: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ entities.

column1: How many moles are in 44 g of CO₂?
column4: Molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g/mol; 44 g ÷ 44 g/mol = 1 mol. Mass ÷ molar mass = moles.

column1: How many molecules are in 2 mol of water?
column4: 2 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules.

column1: At STP, what volume does 1 mole of an ideal gas occupy?
column4: Standard molar volume at STP (0°C, 1 atm) = 22.4 L/mol. This allows mole-to-volume conversions for gases.

column1: How many atoms are in 1 mol of H₂?
column4: 1 mol H₂ = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules; each molecule has 2 H atoms; 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ atoms.

column1: How is density defined?
column4: SI units are kg/m³, but g/mL or g/cm³ are most common in chemistry. For water, d = 1 g/mL at 4°C.

column1: What is the density of liquid water at 4°C?
column4: Water reaches maximum density at 4°C. This value is used as a reference for specific gravity and in many solution calculations.

column1: How do you calculate the volume of a substance given its mass and density?
column4: Rearranging d = m/V gives V = m/d. Used to convert between mass and volume when density is known.

column1: Which has greater density: ice or liquid water, and why?
column3: Liquid water; ice is less dense due to hydrogen bond lattice
column4: Ice floats on water because its crystalline H-bond network is more open (less dense) than liquid water. This is an anomalous property of water.

column1: What is the relationship between density and specific gravity?
column3: Specific gravity = density of substance / density of water (dimensionless)
column4: Since density of water ≈ 1 g/mL, specific gravity numerically equals density in g/mL. It is dimensionless.

column1: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in most compounds?
column4: Oxygen is almost always -2 except in peroxides (-1) and when bonded to fluorine (+2). This is a high-yield MCAT rule.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::oxidation-number MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation number of hydrogen in most compounds?
column4: Hydrogen is +1 in most compounds except metal hydrides (e.g., NaH), where it is -1.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::oxidation-number MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation number of a free element (e.g., O₂, Fe)?
column4: Any element in its standard elemental form has an oxidation number of 0, regardless of bonding within the element.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::oxidation-number MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)?
column4: In peroxides (O–O bond present), oxygen's oxidation number is -1 rather than the typical -2. A high-yield exception.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::oxidation-number MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in H₂SO₄?
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::oxidation-number MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄?
column4: K = +1; O = -2 (×4 = -8); +1 + Mn + (-8) = 0 → Mn = +7. KMnO₄ is a strong oxidizing agent due to Mn's high oxidation state.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::oxidation-number MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in HClO₄ (perchloric acid)?
column4: H = +1; O = -2 (×4 = -8); +1 + Cl + (-8) = 0 → Cl = +7. Chlorine exhibits its highest oxidation state here.
column8: concept::CP::4E::stoichiometry MCAT::section::CP MCAT::4E::stoichiometry::oxidation-number MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Name a common oxidizing agent used in redox reactions.
column4: KMnO₄ is a strong oxidizing agent; Mn goes from +7 to +2 (in acid) or +4 (in neutral/basic). Other common oxidizers: O₂, Cr₂O₇²⁻, H₂O₂.

column1: What is an oxidizing agent?
column4: Oxidizing agents cause oxidation in other species by accepting electrons themselves — they are reduced. Memory tip: OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).

column1: What is a reducing agent?
column4: Reducing agents donate electrons to other species — they are oxidized in the process. Common examples: H₂, metals, NADH.

column1: Name two common biological reducing agents.
column4: NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons in the electron transport chain, acting as reducing agents. They are oxidized to NAD⁺ and FAD, respectively.

column1: Which is a stronger oxidizing agent: F₂ or Cl₂?
column4: F₂ has the highest reduction potential of any element (+2.87 V), making it the strongest oxidizing agent. Electronegativity trend supports this.

column1: What role does H₂O₂ play in redox reactions?
column3: Can act as either oxidizing or reducing agent
column4: H₂O₂ oxidizes some species (acting as oxidizer) and can be oxidized by stronger oxidizers (acting as reducer). This dual role arises because O is in an intermediate -1 state.

column1: What is a disproportionation reaction?
column3: One element simultaneously oxidized and reduced
column4: In disproportionation, the same element in a single species undergoes both oxidation and reduction, producing two different products. Also called auto-oxidation-reduction.

column1: Give an example of a disproportionation reaction.
column4: In H₂O₂, oxygen is -1. In H₂O, oxygen is -2 (reduced); in O₂, oxygen is 0 (oxidized). The same element undergoes both changes.

column1: In a disproportionation reaction, which species is both oxidized and reduced?
column3: The same element in a single reactant species
column4: Both half-reactions involve the same element from the same reactant, distinguishing disproportionation from ordinary redox reactions.

column1: What is the reverse of a disproportionation reaction called?
column4: In comproportionation, two different oxidation states of the same element combine to form one intermediate oxidation state product.

column1: Is the decomposition of Cl₂ in water a disproportionation?
column4: Cl₂ (0) → Cl⁻ (-1, reduced) and Cl in HClO (+1, oxidized). Same element undergoes both changes — classic disproportionation.

column1: What does a chemical equation describe?
column3: Reactants consumed and products formed in a reaction
column4: A balanced chemical equation shows the identities and relative amounts of all substances involved. Arrows indicate direction of reaction.

column1: What do the coefficients in a balanced chemical equation represent?
column3: Mole ratios of reactants and products
column4: Coefficients indicate the relative numbers of moles (or molecules) of each substance. They are the stoichiometric ratios used for calculations.

column1: What is a net ionic equation?
column3: Equation showing only species that change during the reaction
column4: Spectator ions (ions that don't participate) are omitted. Net ionic equations highlight the actual chemical change occurring.

column1: What is the difference between a complete ionic equation and a net ionic equation?
column3: Net ionic equation omits spectator ions
column4: Complete ionic equation shows all ions dissociated in solution. Net ionic equation removes spectator ions on both sides, showing only the reactive species.

column1: What does the symbol (aq) indicate in a chemical equation?
column3: Species is dissolved in aqueous solution
column4: State symbols: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = aqueous. They provide information about the phase of each substance.

column1: What convention is used to indicate a gas evolved in a chemical equation?
column4: A gas product may be indicated by ↑ after the formula or by (g). Similarly, a precipitate is indicated by ↓ or (s).

column1: What does a double arrow (⇌) indicate in a chemical equation?
column4: A double arrow shows that the reaction proceeds in both forward and reverse directions, establishing a dynamic equilibrium.

column1: What convention indicates a catalyst in a chemical equation?
column3: Written above or below the arrow
column4: Catalysts are not reactants or products; they are written above (or below) the reaction arrow to show they facilitate the reaction without being consumed.

column1: What does a single arrow (→) indicate in a chemical equation?
column3: Reaction proceeds predominantly in one direction
column4: A single arrow implies the forward reaction is strongly favored (essentially irreversible under given conditions), as opposed to equilibrium (⇌).

column1: What does the symbol Δ above a reaction arrow indicate?
column3: Heat (thermal energy) is applied to the reaction
column4: Δ above the arrow means the reaction is heated. It is a shorthand for supplying thermal energy as a reactant condition.

column1: What law must be satisfied when balancing a chemical equation?
column4: The number of atoms of each element must be equal on both sides of the equation. Mass is neither created nor destroyed.

column1: What is the first step in balancing a simple chemical equation?
column3: Write correct formulas for all reactants and products
column4: Never change a subscript to balance — only adjust coefficients. Changing subscripts would change the identity of the compound.

column1: What is the half-reaction method used for?
column4: Separate the overall reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balance each, then multiply and add so electrons cancel.

column1: In the half-reaction method in acidic solution, what species is added to balance oxygen atoms?
column4: Add H₂O molecules to balance O, then add H⁺ ions to balance H. In basic solution, add OH⁻ instead.

column1: In the half-reaction method, what is added to balance charge in each half-reaction?
column4: Electrons are added to the side with greater positive charge to balance the charge in each half-reaction before combining them.

column1: When combining half-reactions, what must be true about the electrons?
column3: Electrons gained must equal electrons lost (cancel out)
column4: Multiply each half-reaction by an integer so that the number of electrons lost in oxidation equals electrons gained in reduction. Electrons must cancel completely.

column1: What is a limiting reactant?
column3: Reactant that is completely consumed first, stopping the reaction
column4: The limiting reactant determines the maximum amount of product that can form. The other reactant(s) are in excess.

column1: How do you identify the limiting reactant?
column3: Calculate moles of product each reactant could produce; smallest amount wins
column4: Convert each reactant to moles of product using stoichiometry. The reactant that produces the least product is the limiting reactant.

column1: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, if you have 1 mol N₂ and 2 mol H₂, which is the limiting reactant?
column4: 1 mol N₂ requires 3 mol H₂; only 2 mol H₂ available. H₂ runs out first → limiting reactant. Only 2/3 mol N₂ reacts.

column1: How much excess reactant remains after a reaction if the limiting reactant is fully consumed?
column3: Initial moles of excess reactant minus moles consumed by limiting reactant
column4: Use stoichiometry to find how much excess reactant was used, then subtract from the initial amount. The difference is what remains.

column1: What is the theoretical yield?
column3: Maximum amount of product that can be produced from limiting reactant
column4: Theoretical yield is calculated assuming 100% conversion of the limiting reactant to product, with no losses.

column1: What is percent yield?
column4: Percent yield compares what was actually obtained in the lab to the maximum theoretically possible. It is always ≤ 100% in practice.

column1: Why is actual yield usually less than theoretical yield?
column3: Side reactions, incomplete reactions, product loss during purification
column4: Real reactions rarely achieve 100% efficiency; competing reactions, equilibrium limits, and mechanical losses all reduce actual yield.

column1: How do you calculate theoretical yield from a limiting reactant?
column3: Moles of limiting reactant × (mole ratio) × molar mass of product
column4: Use stoichiometric coefficients to convert moles of limiting reactant to moles of product, then multiply by product's molar mass to get grams.

column1: If a reaction has a theoretical yield of 50 g and an actual yield of 38 g, what is the percent yield?
column4: Percent yield = (38/50) × 100% = 76%. Values significantly below 100% indicate losses or competing reactions.

column1: Can percent yield ever exceed 100%, and if so, what does that indicate?
column3: No under ideal conditions; >100% indicates impure product or measurement error
column4: A percent yield above 100% is physically impossible unless the product retains impurities (e.g., water) that add mass. It always signals an experimental error.

column1: According to Brønsted-Lowry theory, what is an acid?
column4: Brønsted-Lowry acids donate H+ to a base; this definition is broader than Arrhenius (which requires H+ in water) and is the primary framework used on the MCAT.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::br-nsted-lowry-definition-of-acid-base MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: According to Brønsted-Lowry theory, what is a base?
column4: Brønsted-Lowry bases accept H+ from an acid; water can act as either acid or base, making it amphoteric.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::br-nsted-lowry-definition-of-acid-base MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which Brønsted-Lowry role does water play when it reacts with ammonia (NH3)?
column4: Water donates H+ to NH3, forming NH4+ and OH–. Water acts as an acid here because NH3 is the base accepting the proton.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::br-nsted-lowry-definition-of-acid-base MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What distinguishes a Brønsted-Lowry acid from a Lewis acid?
column3: Lewis acid accepts electron pairs; B-L acid donates protons
column4: All Brønsted-Lowry acids are Lewis acids, but not vice versa — Lewis acids include species like BF3 that accept electron pairs without involving proton transfer.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::br-nsted-lowry-definition-of-acid-base MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In the reaction HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl–, which species is the Brønsted-Lowry base?
column4: Water accepts a proton from HCl to become H3O+, making it the base. HCl is the acid.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::br-nsted-lowry-definition-of-acid-base MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What term describes a substance that can act as both a Brønsted-Lowry acid and base?
column4: Water is the classic amphoteric substance — it donates H+ to strong bases and accepts H+ from strong acids. HCO3– is another common MCAT example.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::br-nsted-lowry-definition-of-acid-base MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What process does 'ionization of water' describe?
column4: Water self-ionizes to a small extent, producing equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions. This equilibrium underlies the Kw expression.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::ionization-of-water MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the Kw expression for water?
column4: Kw is the water dissociation constant; the product of hydronium and hydroxide concentrations always equals Kw at a given temperature.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::k-its-approximate-value-k-h-oh-10-14-w-w-at-25-c-1-atm MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the numerical value of Kw at 25°C and 1 atm?
column4: This value is essential for converting between [H+] and [OH–]. If [H+] = 10⁻³, then [OH–] = 10⁻¹¹ M.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::k-its-approximate-value-k-h-oh-10-14-w-w-at-25-c-1-atm MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does Kw change as temperature increases above 25°C?
column4: Because water's autoionization absorbs heat, raising temperature shifts equilibrium toward products, increasing both [H+] and [OH–] and thus Kw.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::k-its-approximate-value-k-h-oh-10-14-w-w-at-25-c-1-atm MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In a neutral aqueous solution at 25°C, what are [H+] and [OH–]?
column4: Neutral means [H+] = [OH–]; since Kw = 10⁻¹⁴, each concentration is 10⁻⁷ M, corresponding to pH = 7.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::k-its-approximate-value-k-h-oh-10-14-w-w-at-25-c-1-atm MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: If Kw at body temperature (37°C) is ~2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴, what is the neutral pH at 37°C?
column4: Neutral pH = –log([H+]neutral) = –log(√Kw) = ½ × pKw. At 37°C, pKw ≈ 13.6, so neutral pH ≈ 6.8 — slightly below 7, yet the solution is still neutral.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::k-its-approximate-value-k-h-oh-10-14-w-w-at-25-c-1-atm MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Define pH.
column4: pH is a logarithmic scale; each unit change represents a 10-fold change in [H+]. Lower pH = more acidic.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-of-ph-ph-of-pure-water MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the pH of pure water at 25°C?
column4: Pure water at 25°C has [H+] = [OH–] = 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = –log(10⁻⁷) = 7. pH 7 is the neutral point only at 25°C.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-of-ph-ph-of-pure-water MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the relationship between pOH and pH at 25°C?
column4: Because Kw = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C, taking –log of both sides gives pH + pOH = pKw = 14.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-of-ph-ph-of-pure-water MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: A solution has [H+] = 3 × 10⁻⁴ M. Estimate its pH.
column4: pH = –log(3 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 4 – log 3 ≈ 4 – 0.48 ≈ 3.52. MCAT shortcut: pH lies between the exponent and one less.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-of-ph-ph-of-pure-water MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does pH change when [H+] decreases 100-fold?
column4: Each 10-fold decrease in [H+] raises pH by 1; a 100-fold decrease raises it by 2. This reflects the logarithmic nature of pH.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-of-ph-ph-of-pure-water MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is a conjugate acid-base pair?
column3: An acid and the base formed after it donates a proton
column4: The conjugate base of an acid differs by one H+. Example: CH3COOH/CH3COO– is a conjugate pair.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::conjugate-acids-and-bases-e-g-nh-and-nh-4-3 MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the conjugate base of NH4+?
column4: NH4+ donates H+ to become NH3. Conversely, NH3 is the conjugate base of NH4+. NH3/NH4+ is a classic MCAT buffer pair.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::conjugate-acids-and-bases-e-g-nh-and-nh-4-3 MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the conjugate acid of HCO3–?
column4: HCO3– accepts a proton to form H2CO3. HCO3– is amphoteric — it is also the conjugate base of H2CO3.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::conjugate-acids-and-bases-e-g-nh-and-nh-4-3 MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the relationship between Ka of an acid and Kb of its conjugate base?
column4: This reciprocal relationship means a stronger acid has a weaker conjugate base. Use it to calculate Kb from Ka or vice versa.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::conjugate-acids-and-bases-e-g-nh-and-nh-4-3 MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which conjugate base is stronger: Cl– or CH3COO–?
column4: Acetic acid (Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) is a weak acid, so its conjugate base acetate is relatively strong. HCl is a strong acid, so Cl– is an essentially inert conjugate base.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::conjugate-acids-and-bases-e-g-nh-and-nh-4-3 MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name four common strong acids.
column3: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3 (also H2SO4, HClO4)
column4: Strong acids dissociate 100% in water. The MCAT commonly tests HCl, H2SO4 (first proton), HNO3, and HClO4.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::strong-acids-and-bases-e-g-nitric-sulfuric MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name two common strong bases.
column4: Group I and heavy group II metal hydroxides (Ca(OH)2, Ba(OH)2) are strong bases that dissociate fully. NaOH and KOH are the most frequently tested.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::strong-acids-and-bases-e-g-nitric-sulfuric MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: H2SO4 is a diprotic acid. Which ionization step is 'strong'?
column4: The first proton dissociates completely (strong). The second (HSO4– ⇌ H+ + SO4²–) has Ka2 ≈ 0.012, which is large but not complete — treated as weak for precise calculations.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::strong-acids-and-bases-e-g-nitric-sulfuric MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the pH of a 0.01 M HCl solution?
column4: HCl is a strong acid; [H+] = 0.01 = 10⁻² M. pH = –log(10⁻²) = 2.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::strong-acids-and-bases-e-g-nitric-sulfuric MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Why does adding 100 mL of 1 M NaOH to 100 mL of 1 M HCl produce a neutral solution?
column3: Moles of H+ = moles of OH–; complete neutralization
column4: Strong acid-strong base neutralization produces water and a salt (NaCl). Neither Na+ nor Cl– hydrolyzes, so the resulting solution is pH 7.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::strong-acids-and-bases-e-g-nitric-sulfuric MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which of these is a strong acid: HF or HCl?
column4: HF is a weak acid (Ka ≈ 6.8 × 10⁻⁴) despite fluorine's high electronegativity, because the H–F bond is very strong. HCl dissociates completely.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::strong-acids-and-bases-e-g-nitric-sulfuric MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Give two examples of weak acids tested on the MCAT.
column4: Weak acids partially dissociate. Other common examples include HF, H3PO4, and benzoic acid. Ka values are much less than 1.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::weak-acids-and-bases-e-g-acetic-benzoic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Give two examples of weak bases tested on the MCAT.
column4: Weak bases partially accept protons. Amines (organic derivatives of NH3) are the most commonly tested class of weak bases on the MCAT.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::weak-acids-and-bases-e-g-acetic-benzoic MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the approximate Ka of acetic acid?
column4: Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.75) is the benchmark weak acid. Knowing this order of magnitude helps estimate pH of acetate-containing solutions.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::weak-acids-and-bases-e-g-acetic-benzoic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: For a weak acid HA, what is the expression for Ka?
column4: Ka quantifies the extent of dissociation. For weak acids, Ka << 1; approximations (x << initial concentration) simplify the ICE calculation when Ka is very small.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::weak-acids-and-bases-e-g-acetic-benzoic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: A weak acid with pKa 5 is more or less acidic than one with pKa 3?
column4: Higher pKa means lower Ka, meaning less dissociation and weaker acid. pKa 3 corresponds to Ka = 10⁻³, which is larger than Ka = 10⁻⁵.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::weak-acids-and-bases-e-g-acetic-benzoic MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which is a stronger weak acid: benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) or acetic acid (pKa 4.75)?
column4: Lower pKa → larger Ka → more dissociation → stronger acid. The electron-withdrawing resonance of the phenyl ring stabilizes the carboxylate anion of benzoic acid.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::weak-acids-and-bases-e-g-acetic-benzoic MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What approximation is valid when solving for [H+] from a weak acid?
column4: If Ka/[HA]₀ < 0.01 (i.e., percent dissociation <5%), ignore x in the denominator. Always verify by checking the % dissociation is below 5%.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::weak-acids-and-bases-e-g-acetic-benzoic MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What happens to the pH of a weak acid solution when a salt of its conjugate base is added?
column4: Adding the conjugate base (e.g., NaA to HA) shifts equilibrium left, consuming H+, raising pH. This is the basis of buffer action.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::dissociation-of-weak-acids-and-bases-with-or-without-added-salt MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the common ion effect?
column3: Added common ion suppresses dissociation of a weak electrolyte
column4: Adding CH3COO– (e.g., via NaCH3COO) to acetic acid reduces its dissociation by Le Chatelier's principle, lowering [H+] and raising pH.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::dissociation-of-weak-acids-and-bases-with-or-without-added-salt MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Adding NaCl to a weak acid solution — how does it affect pH?
column3: Essentially no effect (Cl– is not the conjugate base)
column4: Cl– is the conjugate base of a strong acid (HCl) and does not participate in the weak acid equilibrium. Only the conjugate base of that specific weak acid would cause a common ion effect.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::dissociation-of-weak-acids-and-bases-with-or-without-added-salt MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does diluting a weak acid affect its percent dissociation?
column4: Dilution lowers concentration of all species. The equilibrium shifts right to produce more ions, so a larger fraction of the acid dissociates even though [H+] decreases.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::dissociation-of-weak-acids-and-bases-with-or-without-added-salt MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Adding NH4Cl to NH3 solution — what is the effect on [OH–]?
column4: NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3; its presence is the common ion effect, shifting NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH– to the left, lowering [OH–].
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::dissociation-of-weak-acids-and-bases-with-or-without-added-salt MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is hydrolysis of a salt?
column3: Reaction of a salt's ions with water to produce acidic or basic solution
column4: Hydrolysis occurs when cations/anions of weak acids or bases react with water. Salts of strong acid + strong base do NOT hydrolyze (pH = 7).
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::hydrolysis-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: A salt formed from a strong base and a weak acid — will its aqueous solution be acidic, basic, or neutral?
column4: Example: sodium acetate (NaCH3COO). Acetate hydrolyzes: CH3COO– + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH–, producing excess OH–, making the solution basic.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::hydrolysis-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: A salt formed from a weak base and a strong acid — will its aqueous solution be acidic, basic, or neutral?
column4: Example: ammonium chloride (NH4Cl). NH4+ hydrolyzes: NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O+, producing H3O+. Cl– does not hydrolyze.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::hydrolysis-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What determines the pH of a salt of a weak acid and a weak base?
column3: Relative Ka (acid) vs. Kb (base); pH ≈ 7 + ½(pKa – pKb)
column4: If Ka > Kb (pKa < pKb), solution is acidic; if Kb > Ka, it is basic; if Ka = Kb, neutral. Both ions hydrolyze, and the larger K wins.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::hydrolysis-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which ions do NOT undergo hydrolysis?
column3: Conjugate bases of strong acids (Cl–, Br–, NO3–, SO4²–) and conjugate acids of strong bases (Na+, K+)
column4: These ions are essentially inert in water because their parent acids/bases are fully dissociated — there is no equilibrium to shift.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::hydrolysis-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula for the pH of a salt of a weak acid (e.g., NaA)?
column3: pH = 7 + ½(pKa) — or equivalently, pH = ½(pKw + pKa)
column4: Derived from Kb = Kw/Ka for A–. This formula applies when the only source of H+ is water autoionization balanced against hydrolysis. Use: pH = ½(14 + pKa).
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::calculation-of-ph-of-solutions-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Calculate the pH of 0.1 M sodium acetate (pKa of acetic acid = 4.74).
column4: pH = ½(pKw + pKa) = ½(14 + 4.74) = ½(18.74) = 9.37. The solution is basic because acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::calculation-of-ph-of-solutions-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Calculate the pH of 0.1 M NH4Cl (pKb of NH3 = 4.74, so pKa of NH4+ = 9.26).
column4: pH = ½(pKw – pKb) = ½(14 – 4.74) = ½(9.26) = 4.63; alternatively pH = ½(pKw – pKb) for the cation. Shortcut: pH = 7 – ½pKb = 7 – 2.37 = 4.63.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::calculation-of-ph-of-solutions-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What formula gives [H+] for a solution of a weak acid salt (A–) of concentration C?
column4: Since A– acts as a base, use Kb = Kw/Ka. Assuming x << C, [OH–] ≈ √(Kb·C). Then convert using Kw.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::calculation-of-ph-of-solutions-of-salts-of-weak-acids-or-bases MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Define Ka for a weak acid.
column4: Ka quantifies equilibrium of HA ⇌ H+ + A–. Larger Ka = stronger (more dissociated) weak acid.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::equilibrium-constants-k-and-k-pk-pk-a-b-a-b MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Define pKa.
column4: Lower pKa means larger Ka and stronger acid. The pKa is numerically equal to the pH at the half-equivalence point in a titration of a weak acid.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::equilibrium-constants-k-and-k-pk-pk-a-b-a-b MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the relationship between Ka and Kb for a conjugate acid-base pair?
column4: Equivalently, pKa + pKb = pKw = 14. Use this to interconvert Ka and Kb for any conjugate pair.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::equilibrium-constants-k-and-k-pk-pk-a-b-a-b MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: An acid has Ka = 10⁻⁶. What is the Kb of its conjugate base?
column4: Kb = Kw / Ka = 10⁻¹⁴ / 10⁻⁶ = 10⁻⁸. pKb = 8. Weaker acid → stronger conjugate base.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::equilibrium-constants-k-and-k-pk-pk-a-b-a-b MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which is the stronger base: A– with pKb = 3 or B– with pKb = 8?
column3: A– (lower pKb = larger Kb = stronger base)
column4: pKb = 3 → Kb = 10⁻³; pKb = 8 → Kb = 10⁻⁸. A– is 100,000× stronger as a base.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::equilibrium-constants-k-and-k-pk-pk-a-b-a-b MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: If pKa + pKb = 14, what is pKb for acetic acid's conjugate base (pKa = 4.74)?
column4: pKb = 14 – pKa = 14 – 4.74 = 9.26. This corresponds to Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, confirming acetate is a weak base.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::equilibrium-constants-k-and-k-pk-pk-a-b-a-b MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is a buffer?
column3: A solution that resists pH change upon addition of acid or base
column4: Buffers contain a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid). They work by consuming added H+ or OH– through the equilibrium.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::buffers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation?
column4: Derived from Ka = [H+][A–]/[HA]. It directly relates pH to pKa and the ratio of conjugate base to acid. Essential for buffer and titration calculations.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::buffers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: At what ratio of [A–]/[HA] does a buffer have maximum capacity?
column4: When the ratio is 1, log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa. Buffers are most effective within 1 pH unit of pKa (ratio between 0.1 and 10).
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::buffers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name the components of the bicarbonate buffer system in blood.
column4: This is the primary physiological buffer (pKa ≈ 6.1). CO2 from respiration replenishes H2CO3, and the kidneys regulate HCO3–, making it a powerful open system.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::buffers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the effective buffering range for a buffer?
column4: Within one unit of pKa, the buffer ratio stays between 0.1 and 10, maintaining meaningful capacity. Outside this range, the buffer is essentially exhausted on one side.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::buffers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What happens to the pH of a buffer when a strong base is added?
column4: OH– reacts with the weak acid component (HA + OH– → A– + H2O), shifting the [A–]/[HA] ratio upward and increasing pH, but by far less than in an unbuffered solution.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::buffers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which phosphate species make up the intracellular phosphate buffer?
column4: The pKa of 7.2 makes this pair well-suited for buffering near physiological pH (7.4). It is less important in blood plasma but significant inside cells.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-and-concepts-common-buffer-systems MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Name a common laboratory buffer with pKa near 7.4.
column4: HEPES (pKa 7.5) and PBS (phosphate-buffered saline) are widely used in biochemistry. Tris buffers near pH 8 but has significant temperature dependence.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-and-concepts-common-buffer-systems MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the pKa of the bicarbonate buffer system (H2CO3/HCO3–)?
column4: Despite pKa 6.1 being far from blood pH 7.4, the bicarbonate system is highly effective because it is an open system — lung and kidney regulation maintain a fixed HCO3–/H2CO3 ratio (~20:1).
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-and-concepts-common-buffer-systems MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What ratio of HCO3– to H2CO3 gives blood pH 7.4 (pKa = 6.1)?
column4: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3–]/[H2CO3]) = 7.4 → log(ratio) = 1.3 → ratio ≈ 20. This ratio is maintained by the lungs (CO2) and kidneys (HCO3–).
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::definition-and-concepts-common-buffer-systems MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: On a weak acid–strong base titration curve, where does the half-equivalence point occur?
column3: At half the volume of base needed to reach equivalence
column4: At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A–], so the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa. This is how pKa is read directly from a titration curve.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::influence-on-titration-curves MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the equivalence point in an acid-base titration?
column3: The point where moles of added base equal moles of acid (or vice versa)
column4: At equivalence, the original acid/base is fully neutralized. For weak acid–strong base titrations, pH > 7 at equivalence (conjugate base hydrolyzes).
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::influence-on-titration-curves MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Why is the pH > 7 at the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration?
column3: Conjugate base (A–) hydrolyzes to produce OH–
column4: A– + H2O ⇌ HA + OH– occurs at equivalence, making the solution basic. The degree of basicity depends on pKa — weaker acid → more basic equivalence point.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::influence-on-titration-curves MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: For a strong acid–strong base titration, what is the pH at the equivalence point?
column4: The resulting salt (e.g., NaCl) has neither cation nor anion that hydrolyzes, so the solution is neutral at 25°C.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::influence-on-titration-curves MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: On a titration curve, what feature indicates the buffer region?
column3: The flat plateau region near pH = pKa
column4: In the buffer region, pH changes slowly as base is added. The flattest point occurs at half-equivalence (pH = pKa). A wide, flat plateau indicates an effective buffer.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::influence-on-titration-curves MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does the shape of a diprotic acid titration curve differ from a monoprotic one?
column3: Two equivalence points and two buffer plateaus (one per proton)
column4: Each acidic proton produces its own S-shaped region, half-equivalence point, and equivalence point. The curve shows two distinct inflection points corresponding to pKa1 and pKa2.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::influence-on-titration-curves MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What indicator characteristic is needed to signal the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration?
column3: Indicator pKa ≈ pH at equivalence point (typically 8-10)
column4: Phenolphthalein (color change 8.2–10) is appropriate for weak acid–strong base. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4) is used for strong acid–strong base or strong acid–weak base.
column8: concept::CP::5A::acid_base_equilibria MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::acid-base-equilibria::influence-on-titration-curves MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the charge of the ammonium ion (NH4)?
column4: NH4+ is a common polyatomic cation formed when ammonia (NH3) accepts a proton. It appears frequently in buffer systems and biological contexts on the MCAT.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the phosphate ion?
column4: Phosphate is a triprotic anion central to ATP, DNA/RNA backbone, and phospholipids. Its 3– charge reflects full deprotonation of phosphoric acid at high pH.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the sulfate ion?
column4: Sulfate (SO4^2–) is a common anion in aqueous chemistry. Distinguishing it from sulfite (SO3^2–) is a common MCAT trap.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the charge of the carbonate ion (CO3)?
column4: Carbonate (CO3^2–) is the conjugate base of bicarbonate (HCO3–). It is important in blood buffering and renal physiology.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the nitrate ion?
column4: Nitrate (NO3–) has nitrogen in the +5 oxidation state. It differs from nitrite (NO2–), where nitrogen is in the +3 state.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the hydrogen phosphate ion?
column4: Hydrogen phosphate retains one ionizable proton compared to fully deprotonated phosphate (PO4^3–). It is relevant in the phosphate buffer system in biological fluids.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the dihydrogen phosphate ion?
column4: H2PO4– is the monobasic form of phosphate with two remaining ionizable protons. Together with HPO4^2–, it constitutes the main intracellular phosphate buffer pair.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the sulfite ion?
column4: Sulfite (SO3^2–) has one fewer oxygen than sulfate (SO4^2–). Sulfur is in the +4 oxidation state in sulfite versus +6 in sulfate.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the bicarbonate ion?
column4: Bicarbonate (HCO3–) is the primary blood buffer; it is the conjugate base of carbonic acid (H2CO3, pKa ~6.1) and conjugate acid of carbonate (CO3^2–).
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the charge of the chromate ion (CrO4)?
column4: Chromate (CrO4^2–) contains Cr in the +6 oxidation state. Like sulfate and carbonate it carries a 2– charge, a pattern useful for recall.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the oxidation state of sulfur in the sulfate ion (SO4^2–)?
column4: Each oxygen is –2 (4 × –2 = –8); with an overall charge of –2, sulfur must be +6. Knowing oxidation states helps distinguish sulfate from sulfite (S = +4).
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula and charge of the permanganate ion?
column4: Permanganate (MnO4–) contains Mn in the +7 oxidation state. It is a strong oxidizing agent commonly tested in redox chemistry.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What distinguishes the charge of the nitrite ion from the nitrate ion?
column3: Both are 1–; nitrite is NO2–, nitrate is NO3–
column4: Nitrite (NO2–) has N in the +3 state; nitrate (NO3–) has N in the +5 state. The charges are the same (1–) but the formulas and oxidation states differ — a common confusion point.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the charge of the oxalate ion (C2O4)?
column4: Oxalate (C2O4^2–) is the deprotonated form of oxalic acid; it chelates calcium and is relevant to kidney stone formation (calcium oxalate stones).
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::anion-cation-common-names-formulas-and-charges-for-familiar-ions-e-g-nh-ammonium-4-po-3-phosphate-so-2-sulfate-4-4 MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is a hydrated ion?
column3: An ion surrounded by water molecules
column4: In aqueous solution, ions attract the polar water dipoles (cations attract O; anions attract H), forming a hydration shell that stabilizes dissolved ions.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the hydronium ion?
column4: When an acid donates H+ to water, water accepts it to form H3O+. The hydronium ion is the actual carrier of 'free protons' in aqueous solution.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the formula of the hydronium ion?
column4: H3O+ results from H+ (proton) bonding to one lone pair on a water molecule. In solution, H+ and H3O+ are used interchangeably for the proton concentration.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which end of a water molecule points toward a cation in the hydration shell?
column4: Water's oxygen bears a partial negative charge (delta–), so it is attracted to positively charged cations. This is the basis of ion-dipole interactions.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What type of intermolecular force holds water molecules in a hydration shell around an ion?
column4: Ion-dipole forces are stronger than dipole-dipole or London dispersion forces, which is why ionic compounds readily dissolve in water (hydration energy overcomes lattice energy).
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does the size of an ion affect the strength of its hydration?
column3: Smaller ions are more strongly hydrated
column4: Smaller ions have higher charge density, creating stronger ion-dipole interactions with water. Li+ is more strongly hydrated than Cs+, for example, despite having a smaller radius.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What happens to the number of water molecules in the hydration shell as ionic charge increases?
column3: The hydration shell grows (more water molecules attracted)
column4: Higher charge means a stronger electric field around the ion, attracting more water dipoles. Mg2+ has a larger hydration shell than Na+ despite a smaller ionic radius.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In what reaction is the hydronium ion produced?
column3: When an acid donates H+ to water (acid-base reaction)
column4: HA + H2O → H3O+ + A–. The hydronium ion represents the acidic proton in aqueous solution and its concentration determines pH.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the relationship between [H3O+] and pH?
column4: Since H3O+ is the form of the proton in water, pH is defined from its concentration. At 25°C, neutral water has [H3O+] = 1×10^–7 M and pH = 7.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Why does dissolving NaCl in water release energy (enthalpy of hydration)?
column3: Ion-dipole interactions between ions and water release energy
column4: The hydration enthalpy released when ions are surrounded by water can offset the lattice energy required to separate the ionic crystal, driving dissolution.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which ion — Na+ or Cl– — has a larger primary hydration shell, and why?
column3: Na+ (smaller, higher charge density attracts more water tightly)
column4: Despite carrying the same magnitude charge (1), Na+ has a much smaller radius, giving it higher charge density and stronger interactions with nearby water molecules.
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the autoionization of water, and what ions does it produce?
column3: 2 H2O ⇌ H3O+ + OH–; produces hydronium and hydroxide
column4: Water can self-ionize to a small extent (Kw = 1×10^–14 at 25°C). This equilibrium underpins the definition of pH, pOH, and the neutral point (pH = 7 at 25°C).
column8: concept::CP::5A::ions_in_solutions MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::ions-in-solutions::hydration-the-hydronium-ion MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What are the units of molarity?
column3: moles of solute per liter of solution
column4: Molarity (M) = mol/L. It is the most common concentration unit on the MCAT and is temperature-dependent because volume changes with temperature.

column1: Define molality.
column3: moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
column4: Molality (m) = mol/kg solvent. Unlike molarity, molality is temperature-independent and is used in colligative property calculations.

column1: What is mole fraction?
column3: moles of component divided by total moles in mixture
column4: Mole fraction (χ) is dimensionless and ranges from 0 to 1. Sum of all mole fractions in a mixture equals 1.

column1: How is mass percent (% w/w) defined?
column4: Mass percent is temperature-independent. It is commonly used in stock reagent labels (e.g., 37% HCl by mass).

column1: How do you convert molarity to molality when solution density is given?
column3: use density to find mass of solution, subtract solute mass for solvent mass
column4: m = (M × 1000) / (1000d − M × MW_solute), where d = density in g/mL and MW = molar mass. For dilute aqueous solutions, M ≈ m.

column1: What is normality?
column3: equivalents of solute per liter of solution
column4: Normality = n × Molarity, where n is equivalents per mole (protons for acids, electrons for redox). It simplifies titration math (N₁V₁ = N₂V₂).

column1: Which concentration unit is temperature-independent: molarity or molality?
column4: Molality uses mass (kg solvent), which does not change with temperature. Molarity uses volume, which expands/contracts with temperature.

column1: For a dilute aqueous solution, which two concentration units are numerically approximately equal?
column4: Because the density of water is ~1 kg/L, 1 L of dilute aqueous solution ≈ 1 kg solvent, so M ≈ m at low concentrations.

column1: What is the solubility product constant (Ksp)?
column3: equilibrium constant for dissolution of a sparingly soluble salt
column4: For AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. Pure solids are omitted from the expression. A smaller Ksp means lower solubility.

column1: Write the Ksp expression for Ca3(PO4)2.
column4: Each ion is raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. Ca₃(PO₄)₂ → 3 Ca²⁺ + 2 PO₄³⁻, so Ksp = [Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]².

column1: What does it mean when Q > Ksp for a salt solution?
column3: the solution is supersaturated; precipitation occurs
column4: When the ion product Q exceeds Ksp, the system shifts left, precipitating salt until Q = Ksp. When Q < Ksp, more salt can dissolve.

column1: For a 1:1 salt MX with Ksp, what is the molar solubility s?
column4: MX → M⁺ + X⁻; [M⁺] = [X⁻] = s, so Ksp = s². Therefore s = √Ksp. For higher-stoichiometry salts the algebra differs.

column1: For PbI2 (Ksp = 4s³), what is the molar solubility s?
column4: PbI₂ → Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻; [Pb²⁺] = s, [I⁻] = 2s. Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³. Solving: s = ∛(Ksp/4).

column1: Can Ksp be used to compare solubilities only when salts have the same ion ratio?
column3: yes, only same stoichiometry types are directly comparable
column4: Comparing Ksp directly (e.g., 1:1 vs. 1:2 salts) is misleading. A salt with a larger Ksp may have lower molar solubility if its stoichiometry differs.

column1: What does Ksp not account for that affects real solubility?
column4: Ksp assumes ideal behavior. Real ionic strength, hydrolysis of ions (e.g., PO₄³⁻ + H₂O), and ion pairing all increase apparent solubility above the Ksp prediction.

column1: What is the common-ion effect?
column3: addition of a shared ion decreases solubility of a sparingly soluble salt
column4: By Le Chatelier's principle, adding a common ion shifts dissolution equilibrium left, reducing how much salt dissolves. Example: adding NaCl to a AgCl solution lowers [Ag⁺].

column1: Adding Na2SO4 to a BaSO4 solution will do what to BaSO4 solubility?
column4: SO₄²⁻ is the common ion. Increasing [SO₄²⁻] drives BaSO₄ ⇌ Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ to the left, decreasing [Ba²⁺] and thus solubility.

column1: How is the common-ion effect used in laboratory separations?
column3: selective precipitation by adding a common ion to precipitate one ion while leaving another in solution
column4: Example: adding Cl⁻ to a mixture of Ag⁺ and Pb²⁺ selectively precipitates AgCl (much lower Ksp) before PbCl₂, allowing separation by filtration.

column1: If AgCl is dissolved in 0.1 M NaCl, how does its molar solubility compare to pure water?
column3: much lower than in pure water
column4: With [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.1 M from NaCl, [Ag⁺] = Ksp/0.1 (very small). The common-ion effect dramatically suppresses AgCl dissolution.

column1: Does the common-ion effect change the value of Ksp?
column3: no; Ksp is constant at constant temperature
column4: Adding a common ion shifts the equilibrium position but does not alter the equilibrium constant. Ksp depends only on temperature.

column1: How does ionic strength affect solubility compared to the common-ion prediction?
column3: high ionic strength increases solubility beyond Ksp prediction (salting-in)
column4: Non-common ions increase ionic strength, decreasing activity coefficients, which effectively increases ion solubility — partially counteracting the common-ion effect in real solutions.

column1: What is a complex ion?
column3: a metal ion bonded to one or more ligands via coordinate covalent bonds
column4: Example: [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ is a complex ion where Cu²⁺ is the central metal and NH₃ molecules are ligands donating electron pairs.

column1: What is a ligand?
column3: a Lewis base that donates an electron pair to a metal ion
column4: Ligands can be neutral (H₂O, NH₃) or anionic (Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻). They form coordinate covalent bonds with the central metal ion.

column1: What is the formation constant (Kf)?
column3: equilibrium constant for formation of a complex ion from its components
column4: For M + nL ⇌ MLn, Kf = [MLn] / ([M][L]ⁿ). A large Kf means the complex is very stable. Kf is also called the stability constant.

column1: Name four common monodentate ligands.
column4: Monodentate ligands donate one electron pair. CN⁻ is one of the strongest field ligands; H₂O is the weakest common one. MCAT favors these four.

column1: What is a chelate?
column3: a complex in which a polydentate ligand forms multiple bonds with one metal ion
column4: EDTA is a hexadentate chelating agent. Chelates are more stable than analogous monodentate complexes (chelate effect) due to favorable entropy.

column1: Why are chelating agents more stable than analogous monodentate complexes?
column3: entropy gain from releasing multiple water molecules upon binding
column4: Replacing several monodentate ligands with one polydentate ligand releases many solvent molecules, increasing entropy (ΔS > 0), which stabilizes the chelate thermodynamically.

column1: What is the relationship between Kf and Kd (dissociation constant) of a complex?
column4: Kf measures complex formation; Kd measures complex dissociation. They are reciprocals. A large Kf corresponds to a small Kd (stable complex).

column1: How does complex ion formation affect the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt?
column3: it increases solubility by removing free metal ions from solution
column4: Forming a stable complex (large Kf) pulls the dissolution equilibrium to the right by consuming the metal ion product, increasing the amount of salt that dissolves.

column1: What happens to AgCl solubility when excess NH3 is added?
column3: solubility increases due to [Ag(NH3)2]+ complex formation
column4: Ag⁺ + 2NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (Kf large). This removes Ag⁺ from solution, shifting AgCl dissolution right and increasing total Ag dissolved.

column1: Write the net reaction for dissolving AgCl in excess NH3.
column4: The net equilibrium constant = Ksp × Kf. If Ksp × Kf is large, significant dissolution occurs even though Ksp alone is tiny.

column1: What is the overall equilibrium constant for dissolving a salt in a complexing agent?
column4: The salt dissolution and complex formation steps are added; equilibrium constants multiply. A large K_net indicates the salt dissolves readily in the complexing agent.

column1: Which ion forms a soluble complex with excess Cl⁻, increasing solubility?
column4: PbCl₂ is sparingly soluble, but in high [Cl⁻] it forms the soluble [PbCl₄]²⁻ complex, a classic MCAT example of complex ion re-dissolving a precipitate.

column1: Why does adding CN⁻ dissolve Zn(OH)2 precipitate?
column3: CN⁻ forms the stable [Zn(CN)4]²⁻ complex, removing Zn²⁺
column4: [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ has a very large Kf. Its formation depletes free Zn²⁺, pulling Zn(OH)₂ dissolution equilibrium to the right. Net K = Ksp × Kf.

column1: How does decreasing pH (adding acid) affect the solubility of a basic salt like Mg(OH)2?
column4: H⁺ reacts with OH⁻ released during dissolution (OH⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O), removing a product and driving the dissolution equilibrium to the right.
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which type of salts are more soluble in acidic solution?
column3: salts of weak acids (e.g., carbonates, hydroxides, sulfides, phosphates)
