column4: If the anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid, H⁺ protonates it, removing it from solution and increasing dissolution. Salts of strong acids (NaCl) are unaffected.
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Does the solubility of AgCl change significantly with pH?
column3: no; Cl⁻ is conjugate base of strong acid HCl
column4: Because HCl is a strong acid, Cl⁻ has negligible basicity and is not protonated at any relevant pH. Therefore AgCl solubility is pH-independent.
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How does increasing pH affect the solubility of a metal hydroxide like Fe(OH)3?
column4: Higher [OH⁻] shifts Fe(OH)₃ ⇌ Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ to the left via the common-ion effect, reducing [Fe³⁺] and decreasing solubility.
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Why does CaCO3 dissolve readily in stomach acid?
column3: H⁺ protonates CO3²⁻ to H2CO3/CO2 + H2O, removing the anion
column4: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂(g). Removing CO₃²⁻ drives CaCO₃ dissolution to completion. This is why antacid tablets (CaCO₃) effervesce in acid.
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is amphoteric dissolution, and give an example relevant to pH and solubility?
column3: Al(OH)3 dissolves in both acidic and basic conditions
column4: In acid: Al(OH)₃ + 3H⁺ → Al³⁺ + 3H₂O. In base: Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻. Maximum precipitation (minimum solubility) occurs at intermediate pH.
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: At what pH is metal hydroxide solubility at its minimum?
column3: at the pH where neither excess H⁺ nor excess OH⁻ drives dissolution
column4: For most metal hydroxides this is an intermediate pH value. Adding acid or base beyond this point redissolves the precipitate, a U-shaped solubility-vs-pH curve.
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How does dissolved CO2 (carbonic acid) in water affect the solubility of carbonate minerals?
column3: increases solubility by providing H⁺ that protonates CO3²⁻
column4: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. The H⁺ reacts with CO₃²⁻ from CaCO₃ dissolution, driving more mineral to dissolve — the basis of cave formation (karst).
column8: concept::CP::5A::solubility MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::solubility::solubility-and-ph MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is an acid-base indicator?
column3: Weak acid/base whose conjugate changes color
column4: Indicators change color at a specific pH range because the protonated and deprotonated forms absorb different wavelengths of light. The color change spans roughly pKa ± 1.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What color does phenolphthalein appear in acidic solution?
column4: Phenolphthalein is colorless below pH ~8.2 and turns pink/magenta above ~10. It is commonly used for strong acid–strong base titrations.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What color does litmus appear in basic solution?
column4: Litmus is red in acid and blue in base; it transitions around pH 7. It is less precise than phenolphthalein and is rarely used for equivalence point detection.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: At what pH does an indicator change color relative to its pKa?
column4: The color change range spans one pH unit on each side of the indicator's pKa. Outside this window, the indicator is effectively one pure color.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which indicator is best for a weak acid–strong base titration?
column4: Weak acid–strong base titrations have equivalence points above pH 7 (typically pH 8-10), matching phenolphthalein's transition range of ~8.2–10.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which indicator is best for a strong acid–weak base titration?
column4: Strong acid–weak base equivalence points fall below pH 7 (acidic). Methyl orange transitions in the pH 3.1–4.4 range, making it appropriate.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What determines the appropriate indicator for a titration?
column3: Indicator pKa must match equivalence point pH
column4: The indicator's color-change range (pKa ± 1) should bracket the sharp pH jump at the equivalence point to minimize titration error.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Why can a single indicator give an inaccurate result if chosen incorrectly?
column3: Color change occurs before or after equivalence point
column4: If the indicator's transition range does not overlap the steep pH jump at equivalence, the observed endpoint differs from the true equivalence point, introducing systematic error.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the endpoint of a titration?
column4: The endpoint is the observed color change, which approximates but is not identical to the true equivalence point. Proper indicator choice minimizes the discrepancy.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::indicators MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is neutralization in acid-base chemistry?
column3: Acid and base react to form salt and water
column4: The general reaction is HA + BOH → BA + H2O. Complete neutralization occurs at the equivalence point when moles of acid equal moles of base (for 1:1 stoichiometry).
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the equivalence point of a titration?
column3: Point where moles of acid equal moles of base
column4: At equivalence, stoichiometric amounts of acid and base have reacted. For polyprotic acids or polyvalent bases, equivalents (moles × n) must be equated instead.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the pH at the equivalence point of a strong acid–strong base titration?
column4: Strong acid and strong base produce a neutral salt and water. Neither ion hydrolyzes, so the resulting solution is exactly neutral at 25 °C.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What formula relates titrant and analyte at equivalence in neutralization?
column4: Moles of acid = Moles of base at equivalence. For reactions with different stoichiometric ratios, multiply by the appropriate coefficient (e.g., n1M1V1 = n2M2V2).
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the pH at the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration?
column4: At equivalence the solution contains the conjugate base of the weak acid, which hydrolyzes water to produce OH-, raising pH above 7.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the pH at the equivalence point of a strong acid–weak base titration?
column4: At equivalence the conjugate acid of the weak base is present; it donates a proton to water, producing H3O+ and lowering the pH below 7.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What species is present at the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration?
column3: Conjugate base of the weak acid
column4: All the weak acid has been converted to its conjugate base (A-). This anion then undergoes hydrolysis, making the solution basic.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the half-equivalence point in a weak acid titration?
column3: Point where pH = pKa of weak acid
column4: At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A-], so the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa. This is also where buffer capacity is maximal.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::neutralization MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What shape does the titration curve of a strong acid with a strong base have near the equivalence point?
column4: The large pH jump (e.g., pH 4 to 10) over a very small volume of added base is characteristic of strong acid–strong base titrations and allows any indicator near pH 7 to work.

column1: At what volume does the equivalence point occur in a titration curve?
column3: Volume at the inflection point (steepest slope)
column4: The equivalence point corresponds to the inflection point on the sigmoidal titration curve—where the pH vs. volume curve changes from concave to convex.

column1: What is the plateau region on a weak acid–strong base titration curve called?
column4: In the buffer region, added base converts HA to A- without large pH changes. It spans roughly pH = pKa ± 1 and corresponds to volumes between 0 and the equivalence point.

column1: How do you read the pKa of a weak acid from its titration curve?
column3: pH at the half-equivalence point (half the equivalence volume)
column4: At half-equivalence, [HA]=[A-], so pH = pKa. Identify half the equivalence volume on the x-axis and read the corresponding pH.

column1: How does a weak acid–strong base curve differ from a strong acid–strong base curve?
column3: Higher initial pH, less steep jump, equivalence point above pH 7
column4: Weak acids start at higher pH due to partial dissociation, have a visible buffer region, and reach equivalence above pH 7 rather than at 7.

column1: How many equivalence points does a diprotic acid titration curve show?
column4: A diprotic acid (e.g., H2CO3) has two distinct equivalence points, each corresponding to donation of one proton. Two plateau/buffer regions and two inflection points appear on the curve.

column1: What does a very flat (nearly horizontal) titration curve near the equivalence point indicate?
column3: Very weak acid or base (pKa near 7)
column4: When the pKa of a weak acid is close to 7, the equivalence point pH overlaps the buffer region, flattening the curve and making endpoint detection difficult.

column1: Why is the pH jump smaller for a weak acid–strong base than for a strong acid–strong base at equivalence?
column3: Buffering by conjugate base blunts the jump
column4: Near equivalence in a weak acid titration, the conjugate base resists pH change, making the steep portion less extreme compared to a strong acid system.

column1: What is the initial pH of a 0.1 M weak acid titration curve determined by?
column3: Ka and concentration of weak acid
column4: Initial pH = 0.5(pKa - log C) from the approximation [H+] = sqrt(Ka*C). It is higher than the initial pH of a strong acid at the same concentration.

column1: What is a redox titration?
column3: Titration based on electron transfer between analyte and titrant
column4: Instead of proton transfer, the reaction involves oxidation and reduction. Common examples include permanganate (KMnO4) or dichromate (K2Cr2O7) titrations of reducing agents.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::redox-titration MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What color change indicates the endpoint in a KMnO4 redox titration (self-indicating)?
column4: Permanganate (MnO4-) is deep purple; it is reduced to colorless Mn2+ in acidic solution. At the endpoint, excess MnO4- gives a persistent faint pink.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::redox-titration MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO4?
column4: In KMnO4, potassium is +1 and each oxygen is -2 (×4 = -8), so Mn must be +7. MnO4- is reduced to Mn2+ (+2) in acidic conditions, gaining 5 electrons.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::redox-titration MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In an acidic KMnO4 redox titration, what is MnO4- reduced to?
column4: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- → Mn2+ + 4H2O. Five electrons are gained per permanganate ion in acidic solution. In neutral/basic conditions, MnO2 (brown) is the product.

column1: What is the role of H2SO4 in a permanganate redox titration?
column3: Provides acidic medium for Mn2+ product formation
column4: Acid supplies H+ needed in the half-reaction MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- → Mn2+. HCl is avoided because Cl- can be oxidized by MnO4-, interfering with the titration.

column1: What is the equivalence condition in a redox titration?
column3: Moles of electrons lost = moles of electrons gained
column4: The stoichiometry is based on electron equivalents: n_ox × mol oxidizing agent = n_red × mol reducing agent, where n is electrons transferred per formula unit.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::redox-titration MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Why is HCl not used as the acid source in a permanganate titration?
column3: Cl- is oxidized by MnO4-, introducing error
column4: Chloride ions are reducing agents; MnO4- can oxidize Cl- to Cl2, consuming extra oxidant and giving a falsely high result. H2SO4 is used instead.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::redox-titration MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the oxidation state of Cr in K2Cr2O7?
column4: In K2Cr2O7, K is +1 (×2), O is -2 (×7 = -14). Solving: 2(+1) + 2(Cr) - 14 = 0 → Cr = +6. Cr2O72- is reduced to Cr3+ (+3), gaining 3 electrons per Cr.
column8: concept::CP::5A::titration MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5A::titration::redox-titration MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How many electrons does each dichromate ion (Cr2O72-) gain when reduced to Cr3+?
column4: Cr goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons per atom. With 2 Cr per Cr2O72-, each dichromate ion gains 6 electrons total in the half-reaction.

column1: What is the iodometric titration technique?
column3: I2 (or I3-) generated or consumed is titrated with thiosulfate
column4: An oxidizing analyte oxidizes I- to I2, which is then titrated with Na2S2O3 (sodium thiosulfate) using starch as the indicator (blue-black to colorless at endpoint).

column1: What does a Lewis electron dot formula represent?
column3: valence electrons around atoms in a molecule
column4: Lewis dot structures show bonding and lone-pair electrons, helping predict molecular geometry and reactivity.

column1: How many valence electrons does nitrogen have in a Lewis dot structure?
column4: Nitrogen is in Group VA, so it has 5 valence electrons; it typically forms 3 bonds and has 1 lone pair.

column1: What is the octet rule in the context of Lewis structures?
column3: atoms tend to have 8 electrons in their valence shell
column4: Most second-row elements achieve stability by surrounding themselves with 8 valence electrons (shared or unshared).

column1: Which elements commonly violate the octet rule by having an expanded valence shell?
column3: elements in period 3 and beyond (e.g., P, S, Cl)
column4: Third-period elements have accessible d orbitals allowing more than 8 electrons; examples include PCl5 and SF6.

column1: Which element is an exception to the octet rule by having only 6 electrons in its Lewis structure?
column4: Boron has only 3 valence electrons and commonly forms stable compounds with 6 electrons (electron-deficient).

column1: What is a resonance structure?
column3: one of two or more Lewis structures for the same molecule differing only in electron placement
column4: Resonance structures are drawn when a single Lewis structure cannot represent a molecule; the true structure is a hybrid of all resonance contributors.

column1: In which molecule is resonance most classically demonstrated?
column4: Benzene has two equivalent Kekulé structures with alternating single and double bonds; the real structure has equal bond lengths due to delocalization.

column1: Which resonance contributor is the most stable (major contributor)?
column3: the one with the lowest formal charges and negative charge on the most electronegative atom
column4: Structures with minimal formal charge separation and charges on appropriate atoms are weighted more heavily in the resonance hybrid.

column1: What is the relationship between resonance structures and bond length?
column3: bonds have intermediate lengths between single and double bond
column4: Delocalized electrons spread across multiple bonds, making each bond length intermediate (e.g., C–C bonds in benzene are 1.40 Å, between 1.54 Å single and 1.34 Å double).

column1: What happens to the energy of a molecule that has resonance structures compared to any single Lewis structure?
column3: actual molecule is lower in energy (more stable) than any single contributor
column4: This extra stabilization is called resonance energy (or delocalization energy); benzene is ~36 kcal/mol more stable than a localized cyclohexadiene.

column1: What is the formal charge formula?
column3: formal charge = valence electrons − lone pair electrons − (1/2) bonding electrons
column4: Formal charge tracks electron 'ownership'; it is a bookkeeping tool, not a true charge, used to evaluate Lewis structures.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::formal-charge MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the formal charge on nitrogen in NH4+?
column4: N has 5 valence e−; in NH4+ it has 0 lone pairs and 4 bonds (8 bonding e−): 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::formal-charge MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the formal charge on oxygen in water?
column4: O has 6 valence e−, 4 lone-pair e−, and 2 bonds (4 bonding e−): 6 − 4 − 2 = 0.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::formal-charge MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In a valid Lewis structure, which atom should bear the negative formal charge?
column4: Placing negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom (e.g., O > N > C) gives the most stable and realistic structure.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::formal-charge MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is a Lewis acid?
column4: Lewis acids accept a lone pair from a Lewis base to form a coordinate covalent bond; BF3 and Al3+ are classic examples.

column1: What is a Lewis base?
column4: Lewis bases donate a lone pair to a Lewis acid; NH3, H2O, and most anions are Lewis bases.

column1: How does the Lewis acid-base definition differ from the Brønsted-Lowry definition?
column3: Lewis definition includes reactions not involving proton transfer
column4: Brønsted-Lowry requires H+ transfer; the Lewis definition is broader and includes metal–ligand coordination, where no proton is exchanged.

column1: Which of the following is a Lewis acid: NH3, BF3, or OH−?
column4: BF3 is electron-deficient (6 valence electrons on B) and accepts lone pairs; NH3 and OH− are Lewis bases (electron donors).

column1: What determines the partial ionic character of a covalent bond?
column3: electronegativity difference between the two bonded atoms
column4: The greater the electronegativity difference, the more ionic character the bond has; at ΔEN ≥ 1.7, the bond is considered predominantly ionic.

column1: At what electronegativity difference does a bond transition from polar covalent to ionic?
column4: ΔEN 0–0.4 = nonpolar covalent; 0.4–1.7 = polar covalent; ≥1.7–2.0 = ionic. MCAT commonly uses ~1.7.

column1: Which bond has the greatest partial ionic character: C–H, N–H, or O–H?
column4: O is more electronegative than N, which is more electronegative than C; thus O–H has the greatest electronegativity difference and most ionic character.

column1: What is the role of electronegativity in determining charge distribution within a molecule?
column3: more electronegative atom pulls electron density toward itself, gaining partial negative charge
column4: The δ− end of a polar bond is the more electronegative atom; this unequal sharing creates a dipole with δ+ on the less electronegative atom.

column1: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
column4: The electronegativity trend increases up and to the right on the periodic table; F is at the top-right corner.

column1: In a C=O bond, which atom bears the partial negative charge?
column4: Oxygen (EN ≈ 3.44) is more electronegative than carbon (EN ≈ 2.55), so electron density is pulled toward oxygen, making it δ−.

column1: How does inductive effect relate to charge distribution in covalent bonds?
column3: electronegative substituents withdraw electron density through sigma bonds via inductive effect
column4: Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., halogens) pull electron density through sigma bonds, altering charge distribution and acidity/reactivity along the chain.

column1: What is a dipole moment?
column3: a measure of the polarity of a bond or molecule (charge × distance)
column4: Dipole moment μ = q × d; units are Debye (D). It indicates the magnitude and direction of charge separation in a polar bond or molecule.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::dipole-moment MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which molecule has a zero net dipole moment despite having polar bonds: CO2 or H2O?
column4: CO2 is linear; the two C=O dipoles are equal and opposite, canceling to zero. H2O is bent, so its dipoles do not cancel.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::dipole-moment MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What molecular geometry leads to cancellation of bond dipoles even when individual bonds are polar?
column3: symmetric geometry (e.g., linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral with identical substituents)
column4: If bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically, they vector-cancel; CCl4 (tetrahedral) and BF3 (trigonal planar) have zero net dipole.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::dipole-moment MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: In which direction does the conventional dipole moment arrow point?
column3: from positive (δ+) to negative (δ−) end (toward more electronegative atom)
column4: By IUPAC convention the arrow points from δ+ to δ−; in physics texts it sometimes points the opposite direction—know the chemistry convention for MCAT.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::dipole-moment MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is a sigma (σ) bond?
column3: a bond formed by head-on (end-to-end) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis
column4: σ bonds are the first bond formed between atoms; they allow free rotation and are present in all covalent bonds (single, double, triple).
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::and-bonds MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is a pi (π) bond?
column3: a bond formed by side-to-side (lateral) overlap of p orbitals above and below the internuclear axis
column4: π bonds are present only in double and triple bonds; they restrict rotation and are weaker than σ bonds.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::and-bonds MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How many σ and π bonds are in a C≡C triple bond?
column3: one σ bond and two π bonds
column4: Every bond between two atoms contains exactly one σ bond; additional bonds are π. A triple bond = 1σ + 2π.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::and-bonds MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Why do π bonds restrict free rotation about a double bond?
column3: rotating the bond would break the lateral p-orbital overlap of the π bond
column4: Breaking the π bond requires energy (~60–65 kcal/mol for C=C); this restricted rotation is the basis for cis-trans (geometric) isomerism.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::and-bonds MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: Which type of bond (σ or π) is stronger?
column4: σ bonds have greater orbital overlap along the internuclear axis, resulting in stronger, more stable bonds compared to π bonds.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::and-bonds MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What hybridization does a carbon with four single bonds (e.g., methane) adopt?
column4: sp3 hybridization: one s + three p orbitals mix to form four equivalent hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally (109.5°).

column1: What is the bond angle in an sp2 hybridized carbon?
column4: sp2 hybridization: one s + two p orbitals form three planar orbitals at 120°; one unhybridized p orbital forms the π bond.

column1: What is the bond angle in an sp hybridized carbon?
column4: sp hybridization: one s + one p orbital form two linear orbitals at 180°; two unhybridized p orbitals form two π bonds (as in alkynes).

column1: What hybridization does the nitrogen in ammonia (NH3) have?
column4: Nitrogen in NH3 has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair; four electron groups → sp3, giving a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

column1: How many unhybridized p orbitals remain on an sp2 hybridized atom?
column4: sp2 uses 1s + 2p = 3 hybrid orbitals; the remaining 1 p orbital is unhybridized and participates in π bonding.

column1: What is the VSEPR prediction for the shape of NH3?
column4: NH3 has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair (4 electron groups → tetrahedral e− geometry), but the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal.

column1: What is the molecular geometry of water (H2O) according to VSEPR?
column4: H2O has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs (4 electron groups → tetrahedral e− geometry), giving a bent molecular shape with ~104.5° bond angle.

column1: What is the molecular geometry of CO2?
column4: CO2 has 2 double bonds and no lone pairs on carbon; 2 electron groups → linear geometry with 180° bond angle.

column1: Why is the H–N–H bond angle in NH3 less than the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°?
column3: lone pair–bonding pair repulsion compresses the bond angle
column4: Lone pairs exert greater repulsion than bonding pairs, pushing the N–H bonds closer together; the actual angle is ~107°.

column1: What electron geometry does a molecule with 5 electron groups (e.g., PCl5) adopt?
column4: 5 electron groups arrange in a trigonal bipyramidal geometry with axial (90°) and equatorial (120°) positions.

column1: What is the structural formula of glycine, the simplest amino acid?
column4: Glycine has an amine group (NH2), a methylene (CH2), and a carboxylic acid (COOH); knowing structural formulas of simple biomolecules is MCAT-relevant.

column1: How many bonds does phosphorus form in phosphoric acid (H3PO4)?
column4: Phosphorus in H3PO4 forms 4 bonds (3 P–OH and 1 P=O), using an expanded octet; P is in the +5 oxidation state.

column1: What is the typical bonding pattern of sulfur in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)?
column3: two single bonds to C and one bond to O (with lone pairs)
column4: In DMSO (CH3)2S=O, sulfur has 2 C–S bonds, 1 S=O bond, and 1 lone pair; it uses an expanded octet (period 3 element).

column1: What is electron delocalization?
column3: spreading of electron density over multiple atoms via overlapping p orbitals
column4: Delocalized electrons are not confined to a single bond or atom; they reduce electron-electron repulsion and stabilize the molecule or ion.

column1: In the carboxylate ion (COO−), are the C–O bonds equivalent?
column3: yes, both are equivalent due to electron delocalization
column4: The negative charge is delocalized equally over both oxygens; both C–O bonds have the same intermediate bond length (~1.26 Å).

column1: Why are carboxylate ions more stable than alkoxide ions?
column3: charge is delocalized over two oxygens in carboxylate, not localized on one
column4: Resonance delocalization of the negative charge over two electronegative oxygens stabilizes the carboxylate, making carboxylic acids much stronger acids than alcohols.

column1: What is a double bond composed of?
column3: one σ bond and one π bond
column4: A double bond always has one σ (head-on overlap) and one π (side-on overlap); the σ bond is stronger and the π bond confers restricted rotation.
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::multiple-bonding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is a triple bond composed of?
column3: one σ bond and two π bonds
column4: Triple bonds (as in N2, C2H2) have the most electron density between atoms and are very strong (N≡N bond energy ≈ 945 kJ/mol).
column8: concept::CP::5B::covalent_bond MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5B::covalent-bond::multiple-bonding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How does bond order relate to bond strength and bond length?
column3: higher bond order → stronger bond and shorter bond length
column4: Triple bonds are stronger and shorter than double bonds, which are stronger and shorter than single bonds; more electron density pulls nuclei closer.

column1: Rank C–C, C=C, and C≡C bonds from shortest to longest.
column4: Bond lengths: C≡C ≈ 1.20 Å, C=C ≈ 1.34 Å, C–C ≈ 1.54 Å. More shared electron density pulls atoms together.

column1: What is the approximate bond dissociation energy of a C–H bond?
column4: C–H bonds are among the strongest single bonds in organic chemistry; knowing approximate BDEs helps compare bond stability on the MCAT.

column1: Why do π bonds restrict rigidity in molecular structure?
column3: π bond overlap is broken by rotation, enforcing a fixed geometry
column4: Rotation about a C=C double bond requires ~250 kJ/mol (to break the π bond), making the molecule rigid and enabling geometric isomerism.

column1: What structural feature makes benzene rigid and planar?
column3: delocalized π system requires all atoms to remain coplanar for orbital overlap
column4: The continuous overlap of p orbitals in the aromatic ring locks benzene into a flat hexagon; any deviation would disrupt the delocalization and destabilize the ring.

column1: How does restricted rotation about a double bond lead to geometric isomers?
column3: fixed geometry means substituents can be on same (cis/Z) or opposite (trans/E) sides
column4: Because rotation is restricted, two different arrangements of substituents about the double bond can exist as distinct, non-interconvertible isomers.

column1: What is a stereocenter (chiral center)?
column3: an atom (usually C) bonded to four different groups
column4: A tetrahedral carbon with four distinct substituents is a stereocenter; it can exist in two non-superimposable mirror-image configurations.

column1: What is the maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n stereocenters?
column4: Each stereocenter doubles the possible stereoisomers; the actual number may be less if the molecule has internal symmetry (meso compounds).

column1: What makes a molecule optically active?
column3: the molecule is chiral (non-superimposable on its mirror image)
column4: Chiral molecules rotate plane-polarized light; achiral molecules (including meso compounds) do not rotate light and are optically inactive.

column1: What are constitutional (structural) isomers?
column3: molecules with the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms
column4: Structural isomers differ in how atoms are bonded; e.g., butane (CH3CH2CH2CH3) and isobutane ((CH3)3CH) are structural isomers.

column1: Do structural isomers have the same physical and chemical properties?
column3: no, they generally differ in physical and chemical properties
column4: Different connectivity means different functional groups or carbon skeletons, leading to different boiling points, reactivity, etc.

column1: Which pair are structural isomers: ethanol/dimethyl ether or ethanol/propanol?
column4: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) and dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3) share the molecular formula C2H6O but differ in connectivity; propanol has a different formula (C3H8O).

column1: What are stereoisomers?
column3: molecules with the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement of atoms
column4: Stereoisomers include enantiomers, diastereomers, and cis-trans isomers; they share the same molecular formula and atom connectivity.

column1: What is the relationship between enantiomers?
column3: non-superimposable mirror images of each other
column4: Enantiomers differ only in the arrangement at all stereocenters; they have identical physical properties except for the direction of optical rotation.

column1: What are diastereomers?
column3: stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images of each other
column4: Diastereomers differ at one or more (but not all) stereocenters; they have different physical and chemical properties unlike enantiomers.

column1: What is a meso compound?
column3: a molecule with stereocenters but an internal plane of symmetry making it achiral
column4: Meso compounds are superimposable on their mirror images; they are optically inactive despite having chiral centers (e.g., meso-tartaric acid).

column1: What is required for cis-trans isomerism in a double bond?
column3: each carbon of the double bond must have two different substituents
column4: If either doubly-bonded carbon has two identical groups, cis-trans isomers cannot exist (no geometric isomerism possible).

column1: What are conformational isomers (conformers)?
column3: structures that differ by rotation about single bonds, interconvertible at room temperature
column4: Conformers (e.g., staggered vs. eclipsed ethane) are not distinct compounds; they interconvert rapidly and cannot be isolated separately.

column1: Which conformation of cyclohexane is most stable?
column4: Chair conformation minimizes torsional and angle strain; bulky substituents preferentially occupy equatorial positions to minimize steric strain.

column1: Which Newman projection of ethane is lowest in energy?
column4: In the staggered form, C–H bonds on adjacent carbons are 60° apart (anti or gauche), minimizing torsional strain compared to the eclipsed conformation.

column1: What is the energy difference between anti and gauche conformations of butane?
column4: In butane, anti places the two methyl groups 180° apart (lowest energy); gauche places them 60° apart with slight steric interaction.

column1: What is plane-polarized light?
column3: light with electric field oscillations restricted to a single plane
column4: Ordinary light vibrates in all planes; a polarizer transmits only one plane. Chiral molecules rotate this plane of polarization.

column1: What is specific rotation [α]?
column3: the rotation of plane-polarized light by 1 g/mL of a substance in a 1 dm path length
column4: Specific rotation [α]D = observed rotation α / (concentration × path length); it is a characteristic physical property of chiral compounds.

column1: What is a racemic mixture?
column4: A racemic mixture (racemate) has zero net optical rotation because the two enantiomers rotate light equally in opposite directions, canceling each other.

column1: What is the specific rotation of a racemic mixture?
column4: Equal amounts of (+) and (−) enantiomers cancel each other's rotation; the mixture is optically inactive despite both components being chiral.

column1: What do R and S designations describe?
column3: absolute configuration (3D arrangement) at a stereocenter
column4: R (rectus = right) and S (sinister = left) describe the actual spatial arrangement of groups at a chiral center using the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) priority rules.

column1: What does relative configuration indicate?
column3: spatial arrangement of groups relative to a reference compound, without knowing absolute 3D structure
column4: Before X-ray crystallography was used, configurations were assigned relative to glyceraldehyde (D/L system); relative configuration does not specify R or S directly.

column1: Which technique determines absolute configuration experimentally?
column4: X-ray crystallography with heavy-atom anomalous scattering can determine which enantiomer a compound is in absolute terms.

column1: What is the first step in assigning R or S configuration?
column3: assign CIP priority to the four substituents on the stereocenter (highest atomic number = highest priority)
column4: CIP rules: rank substituents by atomic number at the point of difference; then arrange lowest priority group away from viewer and read 1→2→3.

column1: If rotation from priority 1→2→3 is clockwise (with group 4 pointing away), what is the configuration?
column4: Clockwise rotation = R; counterclockwise = S. Mnemonic: R = clockwise like a steering wheel turning Right.

column1: When assigning R/S, what correction is needed if the lowest-priority group points toward you?
column3: reverse the assignment (swap R and S)
column4: The standard procedure has the lowest-priority group pointing away; if it points toward you, the observed rotation must be inverted to get the correct R or S designation.

column1: What is the E/Z naming system used for?
column3: specifying geometry about double bonds when cis/trans is ambiguous
column4: E (entgegen = opposite) and Z (zusammen = together) use CIP priorities; Z = higher priority groups on same side, E = on opposite sides.

column1: In the E/Z system, what does Z mean?
column3: higher priority groups on the same side of the double bond (zusammen = together)
column4: Z is equivalent to 'cis' when both higher-priority groups are on the same side; determined by CIP priority rules on each doubly-bonded carbon.

column1: When does E/Z designation differ from cis/trans designation?
column3: when the higher-priority group is not the same as the larger group (e.g., with substituents of different atomic number)
column4: cis/trans uses identical/similar groups for reference; E/Z uses CIP priorities. E.g., (Z)-1-bromo-1-fluoroethene: F and Br on the same side, but it could be labeled 'cis' to F if using the older system.

column1: How do you assign CIP priority at a double bond for E/Z assignment?
column3: assign priority to two groups on each doubly-bonded carbon separately using CIP rules, then compare sides
column4: Each carbon of the double bond gets its two substituents ranked independently; then compare whether higher-priority groups are on same side (Z) or opposite sides (E).

column1: What type of intermolecular force involves N-H, O-H, or F-H donors interacting with lone pairs on N, O, or F acceptors?
column4: Hydrogen bonds require a highly electronegative atom (N, O, F) bonded to H as donor, and a lone pair on N, O, or F as acceptor. They are the strongest type of dipole-dipole interaction.

column1: Which three elements can act as hydrogen bond donors when bonded to hydrogen?
column4: Only N, O, and F are electronegative enough to polarize the O-H, N-H, or F-H bond sufficiently to form a true hydrogen bond. Carbon is NOT a donor under MCAT conventions.

column1: What property of water is primarily responsible for its unusually high boiling point relative to its molecular weight?
column4: Water forms up to four hydrogen bonds per molecule (two donor, two acceptor), creating a highly associated liquid that requires more energy to vaporize than predicted by molecular weight alone.

column1: How does hydrogen bonding affect the viscosity of a liquid compared to a similar non-hydrogen-bonding liquid?
column4: Hydrogen bonds link molecules together, increasing resistance to flow (viscosity). Glycerol, with three OH groups, is far more viscous than a comparable non-polar molecule.

column1: Why does ice float on liquid water?
column3: Hydrogen bonds form a less dense crystalline lattice
column4: In ice, each water molecule forms four tetrahedral hydrogen bonds, creating an open hexagonal lattice that is less dense than liquid water where bonds are partially broken and molecules are closer together.

column1: Which molecule has a higher boiling point: HF or HCl?
column4: Despite HCl having a larger size, HF forms strong hydrogen bonds (F is the most electronegative element), dramatically raising its boiling point. HCl relies only on weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces.

column1: Can a molecule be a hydrogen bond acceptor but NOT a hydrogen bond donor? Give an example.
column3: Yes — acetone (C=O accepts, no O-H or N-H to donate)
column4: A hydrogen bond acceptor needs only a lone pair on N, O, or F. Acetone has a carbonyl oxygen with lone pairs but no N-H or O-H bond, so it accepts but cannot donate hydrogen bonds.

column1: What is the approximate energy range of a typical hydrogen bond in biological systems?
column4: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds (~80–100 kcal/mol) but stronger than van der Waals forces (~0.5–2 kcal/mol). Their cumulative effect in proteins and DNA is biologically critical.

column1: Why does DNA base pairing rely on hydrogen bonds rather than covalent bonds between complementary strands?
column3: Hydrogen bonds allow reversible, strand-specific recognition
column4: Covalent bonds would make DNA replication and transcription impossible. Hydrogen bonds provide enough stability for the double helix yet are weak enough to be broken enzymatically during replication.

column1: What is a dipole-dipole interaction?
column3: Attraction between permanent dipoles of polar molecules
column4: Polar molecules have a permanent separation of charge (dipole moment). The partial positive end of one molecule is attracted to the partial negative end of a neighboring molecule.

column1: Which type of molecules experience dipole-dipole forces?
column3: Polar molecules (those with a net dipole moment)
column4: A net dipole moment requires both polar bonds AND an asymmetric geometry. For example, CO2 has polar bonds but no net dipole (linear/symmetric), so it does NOT experience dipole-dipole forces.

column1: How does increasing temperature affect dipole-dipole interactions?
column3: Decreases their effectiveness (thermal motion overcomes alignment)
column4: At higher temperatures, molecules have more kinetic energy and rotate more rapidly, disrupting the favorable head-to-tail alignment of dipoles and reducing the net attractive force.

column1: What is a dipole-induced dipole interaction?
column3: Attraction between a permanent dipole and a temporarily induced dipole in a nonpolar neighbor
column4: A polar molecule's electric field distorts the electron cloud of an adjacent nonpolar molecule, inducing a temporary dipole. This force is weaker than dipole-dipole but stronger than London dispersion alone.

column1: How do dipole-dipole forces compare in strength to London dispersion forces for molecules of similar size?
column4: Permanent dipoles provide a consistent attractive interaction, whereas London forces arise from transient fluctuations. However, for large nonpolar molecules, London forces can exceed dipole-dipole forces in magnitude.

column1: Why does SO2 have a higher boiling point than CO2 despite similar molar masses?
column3: SO2 is polar (bent geometry) and has dipole-dipole interactions; CO2 is nonpolar (linear)
column4: CO2 is linear so its bond dipoles cancel, giving zero net dipole. SO2 is bent with a net dipole, adding dipole-dipole attractions that raise its boiling point.

column1: What is the relationship between dipole moment magnitude and the strength of dipole-dipole interactions?
column3: Larger dipole moment → stronger dipole-dipole interactions
column4: Dipole-dipole force strength scales with the product of the two dipole moments. A larger charge separation or longer dipole arm increases the moment and thus the intermolecular attraction.

column1: Which intermolecular interaction is present in a mixture of a polar solvent and a nonpolar solute?
column4: The polar solvent induces a temporary dipole in the nonpolar solute. This dipole-induced dipole interaction is responsible for some solubility of nonpolar gases in polar solvents, though it is relatively weak.

column1: What is another name for London dispersion forces?
column3: Van der Waals forces (or induced dipole-induced dipole forces)
column4: London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous fluctuations in electron distribution that create temporary dipoles, inducing dipoles in neighboring molecules. They exist in ALL molecules, polar or nonpolar.

column1: Which intermolecular force is present in ALL molecules, regardless of polarity?
column3: London dispersion forces (Van der Waals forces)
column4: Even perfectly nonpolar molecules (e.g., noble gases, N2, CH4) experience instantaneous dipole fluctuations that induce neighboring dipoles, creating transient attractive forces.

column1: What two molecular properties most strongly determine the magnitude of London dispersion forces?
column3: Molecular size (number of electrons) and surface area/shape
column4: More electrons mean a more polarizable electron cloud, creating larger instantaneous dipoles. Greater surface area increases the number of contact points between molecules, amplifying total dispersion attraction.

column1: Why does n-pentane have a higher boiling point than neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane) despite identical molecular formulas?
column3: n-Pentane has greater surface area, stronger London dispersion forces
column4: Linear n-pentane molecules can align closely along their length, maximizing electron cloud contact. Spherical neopentane has minimal surface contact, weaker dispersion forces, and thus a lower boiling point.

column1: How does polarizability relate to London dispersion force strength?
column3: Higher polarizability → stronger London dispersion forces
column4: Polarizability measures how easily an electron cloud is distorted. Larger atoms with electrons farther from the nucleus (e.g., I vs. F) are more polarizable, creating larger instantaneous dipoles and stronger dispersion.

column1: Which has a higher boiling point: CH4 or CCl4? Why?
column3: CCl4 — larger, more polarizable, stronger London dispersion forces
column4: CCl4 has many more electrons and a much larger surface area than CH4, leading to substantially stronger London dispersion forces and a boiling point of 76.7°C vs. −161.5°C for CH4.

column1: Why do noble gases (e.g., He, Ne, Ar) have progressively higher boiling points down the group?
column3: Increasing atomic size and electron count raise polarizability and London forces
column4: He has only 2 electrons and boils at −269°C; Xe has 54 electrons, is far more polarizable, and boils at −108°C. Greater polarizability means stronger instantaneous dipoles and more dispersion attraction.

column1: At what distance do London dispersion forces fall off, and what does this imply?
column3: Force falls off as 1/r^6 — extremely short-range forces
column4: London forces are only significant when molecules are very close (near contact). This explains why gases have negligible intermolecular forces but liquids/solids, where molecules are touching, are significantly affected.

column1: Which intermolecular force is SOLELY responsible for holding I2 molecules together in solid iodine?
column4: I2 is nonpolar and has no dipole moment, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds or dipole-dipole interactions. Its solid state is maintained entirely by London dispersion forces, which are strong due to iodine's large, polarizable electron cloud.

column1: What property of two solvents must differ for liquid-liquid extraction to work?
column4: Liquid-liquid extraction relies on the solute's preferential solubility in one of two immiscible solvents; the distribution is governed by the partition coefficient K.

column1: What is the partition coefficient (K) in liquid-liquid extraction?
column4: K expresses the equilibrium ratio of solute concentration in the organic phase to the aqueous phase; a high K means the compound favors the organic layer.

column1: Which layer typically sits on the bottom in a separatory funnel when water and diethyl ether are used?
column4: Diethyl ether (density ~0.71 g/mL) is less dense than water (1.00 g/mL), so the organic ether layer floats on top.

column1: How does making a compound ionic (e.g., protonating an amine) affect its extractability into the aqueous phase?
column3: Increases aqueous solubility; moves it into aqueous layer
column4: Ionic species are far more water-soluble; adding acid protonates amines (R-NH3+), driving them from organic to aqueous layer — a classic pH-based extraction.

column1: Why is multiple extraction with small volumes more efficient than a single extraction with one large volume?
column3: More equilibrations remove more solute each time
column4: Each extraction removes a fraction K/(K+1) of solute; repeated small-volume extractions multiply these fractions and recover more total solute than a single large extraction.

column1: What reagent is added to extract an acidic compound (carboxylic acid) selectively into the aqueous phase?
column4: Base deprotonates the carboxylic acid to its carboxylate anion, making it water-soluble and separating it from neutral or basic compounds remaining in the organic layer.

column1: What physical property difference between components is exploited in distillation?
column4: Components with lower boiling points vaporize preferentially and are collected as distillate, separating them from higher-boiling components remaining in the flask.

column1: What type of distillation is used when two compounds are completely immiscible in each other?
column4: Steam distillation allows a high-boiling, water-immiscible compound to be distilled at a temperature below 100°C because the total vapor pressure equals atmospheric when the two vapor pressures sum to 1 atm.

column1: What is fractional distillation used for compared to simple distillation?
column3: Separating compounds with similar (close) boiling points
column4: A fractionating column provides multiple vaporization-condensation cycles (theoretical plates), enabling resolution of mixtures whose boiling points differ by less than ~25°C.

column1: What is an azeotrope, and why is it a limitation of distillation?
column3: Constant-boiling mixture that cannot be separated further by distillation
column4: At the azeotropic composition, vapor and liquid have the same ratio, so distillation produces no enrichment; example: 95.6% ethanol/water azeotrope.

column1: What are the two phases present in all chromatography techniques?
column4: The stationary phase is fixed; the mobile phase carries the sample through it. Separation occurs because components partition differently between the two phases.

column1: Define retention time in chromatography.
column3: Time for a component to travel through the column to the detector
column4: Compounds with greater affinity for the stationary phase are retained longer and elute later, giving longer retention times that serve as identifying characteristics.

column1: What fundamental property drives separation in all chromatography methods?
column3: Differential affinity for stationary vs. mobile phase
column4: Compounds that interact more strongly with the stationary phase move more slowly; those that prefer the mobile phase elute faster, achieving separation.

column1: What is the Rf value in chromatography?
column3: Distance traveled by compound / distance traveled by solvent front
column4: Rf ranges 0–1; an Rf of 0 means the compound stays at the origin, while Rf of 1 means it moved with the solvent. Used in TLC and paper chromatography.

column1: What does a higher Rf value indicate about a compound's polarity relative to the stationary phase in normal-phase chromatography?
column3: Compound is less polar (lower affinity for polar stationary phase)
column4: In normal-phase systems, the stationary phase is polar; less-polar compounds interact less and travel farther with the (less-polar) mobile phase, giving higher Rf.

column1: What is the stationary phase in standard (normal-phase) column chromatography?
column4: Silica gel is the most common stationary phase; it is polar and adsorbs polar compounds more strongly, causing them to elute later.

column1: In normal-phase column chromatography, which solvent polarity elutes compounds fastest?
column3: Less polar solvent elutes nonpolar compounds first; increasing polarity elutes more polar compounds
column4: A nonpolar solvent like hexane moves nonpolar compounds quickly through the polar silica. Switching to a more polar solvent (e.g., ethyl acetate) then displaces polar compounds.

column1: What technique uses an increasing-polarity solvent gradient in column chromatography to elute compounds sequentially?
column4: Starting with a nonpolar solvent and gradually increasing polarity releases compounds from the polar stationary phase in order of increasing polarity.

column1: What is reversed-phase column chromatography, and which compounds elute first?
column3: Nonpolar stationary phase; polar compounds elute first
column4: Reversed-phase uses a nonpolar stationary phase (e.g., C18-silica) with a polar mobile phase; polar compounds have little affinity for the stationary phase and elute first.

column1: What are the two phases in gas-liquid chromatography (GLC)?
column3: Mobile phase: inert carrier gas; stationary phase: liquid on solid support
column4: Helium or nitrogen carries the vaporized sample through the column; components partition between the gas phase and the liquid stationary phase based on volatility and polarity.

column1: What physical property must a compound have to be analyzed by gas-liquid chromatography?
column4: GLC requires compounds to exist in the gas phase; thermally labile or very high-boiling compounds cannot be analyzed directly and may need derivatization.

column1: In GLC, what determines the order in which compounds elute?
column3: Boiling point and interaction with the stationary phase (volatility)
column4: More volatile (lower-boiling) compounds spend more time in the gas phase and elute earlier; interactions with the liquid stationary phase also affect retention.

column1: What detector is most commonly paired with GLC for quantitative analysis?
column4: The FID burns organic compounds in a hydrogen-air flame, producing ions detected as current; it is highly sensitive to carbon-containing compounds.

column1: What distinguishes HPLC from classical column chromatography?
column3: High pressure forces mobile phase through fine-particle column
column4: HPLC uses small-diameter stationary-phase particles (<10 µm) and high pressure (up to ~400 atm), giving superior resolution, speed, and sensitivity compared to gravity-fed columns.

column1: What is the most common stationary phase used in reverse-phase HPLC?
column4: C18 silica provides a nonpolar surface; compounds are eluted with aqueous-organic mobile phases, with more organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) eluting nonpolar compounds faster.

column1: What type of detector is most universally used in HPLC?
column4: Most organic compounds absorb UV light; a UV detector monitors absorbance at a set wavelength (often 254 nm) as eluate passes through the flow cell.

column1: What advantage does HPLC have over GLC for biological molecules?
column3: HPLC works in liquid phase — no vaporization needed
column4: Many biological molecules (proteins, nucleotides, sugars) are non-volatile or thermally labile and cannot be vaporized for GLC; HPLC separates them in solution.

column1: What is the stationary phase in paper chromatography?
column3: Water adsorbed on cellulose paper fibers
column4: The water bound to cellulose acts as the polar stationary phase; the mobile phase is an organic solvent that ascends the paper by capillary action.

column1: In paper chromatography, how are separated spots visualized?
column3: UV light, ninhydrin spray, or iodine vapor
column4: Amino acids are visualized with ninhydrin (turns purple/pink); colored pigments are visible directly; UV-absorbing spots appear under 254-nm UV light.

column1: In paper chromatography, which amino acids would have higher Rf values — polar or nonpolar?
column3: Nonpolar amino acids (less affinity for polar stationary phase)
column4: The stationary phase (water on cellulose) is polar; nonpolar amino acids partition more into the organic mobile phase and travel farther, giving higher Rf.

column1: What is two-dimensional paper chromatography used for?
column3: Separating complex mixtures by running two solvent systems perpendicular to each other
column4: After the first run, the paper is rotated 90° and developed with a different solvent, dramatically increasing resolution of complex mixtures like amino acid hydrolysates.

column1: What is the stationary phase in thin-layer chromatography (TLC)?
column3: Silica gel or alumina coated on glass, aluminum, or plastic plate
column4: Like normal-phase column chromatography, TLC uses a polar stationary phase; compounds adsorb onto it and are displaced by the mobile phase (solvent).

column1: What is the primary use of TLC in organic chemistry?
column4: TLC is fast and requires tiny sample amounts; chemists compare Rf values of starting material, product, and reaction mixture to track conversion.

column1: How does increasing mobile-phase polarity affect Rf values in TLC?
column4: A more polar solvent competes better for the polar stationary phase, displacing compounds and carrying them farther up the plate.

column1: What does co-spotting two compounds on a TLC plate demonstrate if they show a single spot?
column3: Tentative evidence the compounds are identical (same Rf)
column4: If two samples co-spot into one spot, they likely have the same identity; however, confirmation requires another solvent system or spectroscopic analysis since different compounds can share an Rf.

column1: What visualization method is used for TLC spots that are UV-inactive and colorless?
column3: Iodine chamber or chemical staining (e.g., KMnO4, anisaldehyde)
column4: Compounds without UV chromophores or color require derivatization; iodine reversibly stains most organics brown; KMnO4 stains oxidizable compounds yellow-brown on a purple background.

column1: Name the four major techniques used to separate and purify peptides.
column3: Gel filtration, ion-exchange chromatography, affinity chromatography, electrophoresis
column4: These methods exploit size, charge, specific binding, or charge-to-size ratio, respectively, and are often combined sequentially for high purity.

column1: What property of a peptide does gel-filtration (size-exclusion) chromatography separate by?
column4: Smaller molecules enter the pores of the stationary-phase beads and elute later; larger molecules are excluded from pores and elute first in the void volume.

column1: In gel filtration chromatography, which elutes first — a large protein or a small peptide?
column3: Large protein (excluded from pores, elutes first)
column4: Large molecules cannot enter the gel matrix pores and pass through the column quickly; small molecules enter pores, are retarded, and elute later.

column1: What property of peptides does ion-exchange chromatography exploit?
column3: Net charge (positive or negative) at a given pH
column4: Cation exchangers bind positively charged proteins; anion exchangers bind negatively charged ones. Elution is achieved by increasing salt concentration or changing pH.

column1: What is the principle of affinity chromatography for peptide purification?
column3: Specific binding between target protein and ligand attached to stationary phase
column4: The column contains an immobilized ligand (e.g., substrate analog, antibody); only the protein of interest binds and is later eluted by competing ligand or changed conditions, yielding very high purity.

column1: What does SDS-PAGE separate proteins by?
column4: SDS denatures proteins and coats them uniformly with negative charge; in the polyacrylamide gel matrix, all proteins migrate toward the anode and are separated solely by size.

column1: What does isoelectric focusing (IEF) separate proteins by?
column4: A pH gradient is established in the gel; each protein migrates until it reaches the pH equal to its pI, where it has zero net charge and stops moving.

column1: In 2D-PAGE, what two properties are used to separate proteins in the two dimensions?
column3: First dimension: pI (isoelectric focusing); second dimension: molecular weight (SDS-PAGE)
column4: 2D-PAGE provides extremely high resolution; thousands of proteins in a complex mixture can be resolved on a single gel by combining charge and size separations.

column1: What is the purpose of dialysis in peptide purification?
column3: Remove small molecules (salts, solvents) from a protein solution
column4: A semipermeable membrane allows small solutes to diffuse out while retaining macromolecules; used to exchange buffers or remove ammonium sulfate after precipitation.

column1: What reagent is used in the Bradford assay to detect protein presence during purification?
column4: Coomassie dye binds proteins and shifts absorbance from 465 nm to 595 nm; the A595 reading is proportional to protein concentration, allowing tracking of protein during purification steps.

column1: What property of a protein does SDS-PAGE primarily separate proteins by?
column4: SDS denatures proteins and coats them with uniform negative charge, so migration in the gel depends only on size, not charge or shape.

column4: SDS coats proteins in negative charge, so they migrate toward the positive pole (anode) when current is applied.

column3: Concentrate proteins into a tight band before separation

column1: In native PAGE (non-denaturing), what two properties determine protein migration rate?

column4: Proteins migrate through a pH gradient until they reach the pH equal to their pI, where net charge is zero and movement stops.

column1: What is 2D gel electrophoresis? Name the two dimensions used.
column4: First dimension separates by isoelectric point; second dimension (perpendicular) separates by molecular weight, allowing high-resolution proteome mapping.

column1: What does the Beer-Lambert Law relate in quantitative protein analysis?
column3: Absorbance to concentration and path length
column4: A = εcl; absorbance equals molar absorptivity times concentration times path length. Used with UV spectrophotometry to quantify proteins.

column4: Tryptophan and tyrosine absorb strongly at 280 nm. A280 readings are used for rapid protein concentration estimates.

column4: Coomassie dye shifts from red to blue upon protein binding; absorbance at 595 nm is proportional to protein concentration. Compared to a BSA standard curve.

column3: Relate absorbance of known concentrations to unknown sample
column4: Known concentrations of a standard (e.g., BSA) are measured to plot absorbance vs. concentration; unknown sample absorbance is interpolated from this curve.

column4: Large molecules cannot enter pores in the beads and elute first; small molecules enter pores, travel a longer path, and elute last.

column4: Large proteins are excluded from the stationary phase pores and travel only through the void volume, reaching the detector before smaller molecules.

column4: The technique is also called gel filtration or molecular sieve chromatography because the porous beads act as molecular sieves.

column4: The void volume is the total solvent volume outside the beads; molecules too large to enter pores elute in this volume.

column4: Proteins of known MW are run to generate a standard curve of elution volume vs. log(MW); the unknown protein's MW is read from this curve.

column1: What principle underlies ion-exchange chromatography?
column3: Electrostatic attraction between protein and charged resin
column4: Proteins bind to an oppositely charged stationary phase; they are eluted by increasing salt concentration or changing pH to disrupt ionic interactions.

column4: Above its pI, the protein carries net negative charge and is attracted to the positively charged anion-exchange resin.

column4: A ligand with high affinity for the target protein is covalently attached to the resin; all non-target proteins wash through, and the protein of interest is eluted specifically.

column1: What is immunoaffinity chromatography?
column3: Affinity chromatography using an antibody as the ligand
column4: An antibody specific to the target protein is immobilized on the resin; the target binds via antigen–antibody interaction and is eluted under denaturing or low-pH conditions.

column1: What is a racemic mixture?
column4: A racemic mixture (racemate) contains equal amounts of R and S enantiomers, resulting in zero net optical rotation.

column1: What instrument measures the optical rotation of a chiral compound?
column4: A polarimeter passes plane-polarized light through a sample; the angle of rotation observed indicates whether the compound is dextrorotatory (+) or levorotatory (−).

column1: Why cannot enantiomers be separated by ordinary achiral chromatography or distillation?
column3: They have identical physical properties in achiral environments
column4: Enantiomers share the same boiling point, melting point, and solubility; only their interaction with other chiral entities differs, so a chiral environment is needed for separation.

column1: What are diastereomers formed from enantiomers + a chiral resolving agent called?
column4: Reacting a racemic mixture with an enantiopure chiral reagent creates two diastereomers, which differ in physical properties and can be separated by crystallization or chromatography.

column1: What type of stationary phase is used to separate enantiomers by chiral HPLC?
column4: CSPs contain enantiopure ligands (e.g., cyclodextrins, amino acid derivatives) that interact differently with each enantiomer, allowing resolution.

column1: What is the optical rotation of a pure racemic mixture?
column4: Because equal amounts of (+) and (−) enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions, the net rotation cancels to zero.

column1: What classical method separates enantiomers by converting them to diastereomeric salts that crystallize differently?
column4: A chiral acid or base reacts with the racemic mixture to form diastereomeric salts with different solubilities; the less soluble salt crystallizes first and is filtered off.

column1: What is the specific rotation [α] used to characterize in a pure enantiomer?
column3: Optical rotation normalized for concentration and path length
column4: [α] = observed rotation / (concentration in g/mL × path length in dm). A consistent value identifies a pure enantiomer; a racemate gives [α] = 0.

column1: Which amino acids contribute most to a protein's absorbance at 280 nm?
column4: Both contain aromatic rings that absorb UV light at 280 nm; tryptophan has a higher molar absorptivity (~5500 M−1cm−1) than tyrosine (~1490 M−1cm−1).
