column1: What three components make up a nucleotide?
column3: Nitrogenous base, pentose sugar, phosphate group
column4: All three must be present to call it a nucleotide; absence of the phosphate makes it a nucleoside. This distinction is high-yield on the MCAT.

column1: What distinguishes a nucleoside from a nucleotide?
column4: A nucleoside = base + sugar only. Adding one or more phosphates yields a nucleotide (mono-, di-, or triphosphate).

column1: What sugar is found in ribonucleotides?
column4: Ribose has a hydroxyl group on its 2' carbon, distinguishing it from deoxyribose used in DNA.

column1: What sugar is found in deoxyribonucleotides?
column4: The 2'-OH of ribose is replaced by H in deoxyribose, making DNA more chemically stable than RNA.

column1: At which carbon of the sugar does the nitrogenous base attach?
column4: The base is linked to C-1' of the pentose via an N-glycosidic bond (between N-1 of pyrimidines or N-9 of purines and C-1').

column1: Name the nucleoside formed from adenine and ribose.
column4: Nucleoside naming: purine + ribose = drop '-ine,' add '-osine' (adenine→adenosine, guanine→guanosine). Pyrimidines add '-idine.'

column1: Which nucleotide is the primary energy currency of the cell?
column4: Hydrolysis of the gamma-phosphate of ATP releases ~7.3 kcal/mol under standard conditions, driving biosynthetic reactions.

column1: What type of bond connects the phosphate groups in ATP?
column4: The alpha-beta and beta-gamma linkages in ATP are high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds; hydrolysis of these is thermodynamically favorable.

column1: What linkage forms the sugar-phosphate backbone of nucleic acids?
column4: The phosphate bridges the 3'-OH of one nucleotide to the 5'-OH of the next, creating the backbone with a free 5'-phosphate at one end and a 3'-OH at the other.

column1: In which direction is a nucleic acid chain conventionally read and synthesized?
column4: DNA polymerases and RNA polymerases add nucleotides exclusively to the 3'-OH end, so synthesis proceeds 5'→3'.

column1: What charge does the sugar-phosphate backbone carry at physiological pH?
column4: The phosphate groups (pKa ~1) are fully deprotonated at pH 7.4, giving the backbone a strong negative charge that attracts positively charged histones.

column1: What is the name of the bond between successive nucleotides in DNA or RNA?
column4: One phosphate esterifies to the 3'-OH of the preceding sugar and the 5'-OH of the following sugar, forming a diester.

column1: Which enzyme cleaves phosphodiester bonds in DNA by hydrolyzing them?
column4: DNases are endonucleases or exonucleases that hydrolyze the phosphodiester backbone; restriction enzymes are sequence-specific endonucleases.

column1: Why is RNA more susceptible to hydrolysis than DNA?
column3: RNA has a 2'-OH that attacks the phosphodiester bond
column4: The 2'-OH of ribose acts as a nucleophile in a transesterification reaction, making RNA inherently less stable than DNA under alkaline conditions.

column1: What terminates the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) elongation in the ddNTP method?
column4: Without a 3'-OH, no phosphodiester bond can form; chain termination sequencing (Sanger) uses this property to determine sequence.

column1: Which two bases are purines?
column4: Purines have a fused bicyclic structure (pyrimidine ring fused to imidazole ring). Mnemonic: 'PURe As Gold' — Purines = Adenine, Guanine.

column1: Which three bases are pyrimidines?
column4: Pyrimidines have a single six-membered ring. Mnemonic: 'CUT the PY' — Cytosine, Uracil, Thymine are PyYrimidines.

column1: Which base is found in RNA but not DNA?
column4: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA. Uracil lacks the 5-methyl group of thymine, making it cheaper to synthesize but unable to signal deamination damage as readily.

column1: How many hydrogen bonds form between cytosine and guanine?
column4: G-C pairs form 3 H-bonds (vs. 2 for A-T/A-U), making G-C-rich regions more thermally stable (higher Tm).

column1: How many hydrogen bonds form between adenine and thymine?
column4: A-T pairs form 2 H-bonds. Because G-C pairs are stronger, a higher G-C content raises the melting temperature of dsDNA.

column1: Which purine pairs with thymine in DNA?
column4: Watson-Crick base pairing: A-T (2 H-bonds) and G-C (3 H-bonds). Purines always pair with pyrimidines to maintain uniform helix width.

column1: What functional group distinguishes guanine from adenine?
column4: Adenine has an amino group at C-6; guanine has a carbonyl at C-6 and an amino at C-2. These differences drive specific H-bonding with their partners.

column1: Which pyrimidine has a methyl group at C-5?
column4: The 5-methyl group distinguishes thymine from uracil. Loss of the methyl from thymine by deamination produces uracil, a mutation that DNA repair systems detect.

column1: What is the difference between B-DNA and Z-DNA in terms of helical handedness?
column3: B-DNA is right-handed; Z-DNA is left-handed
column4: B-DNA is the predominant physiological form. Z-DNA forms in GC-rich regions under certain conditions and may play a regulatory role.

column1: What are the two strands of the DNA double helix relative to each other?
column4: One strand runs 5'→3' while the complementary strand runs 3'→5'. This antiparallel arrangement is required for correct Watson-Crick base pairing.

column1: Where are the bases located in the B-form DNA double helix?
column4: Hydrophobic base stacking in the interior stabilizes the helix; the hydrophilic sugar-phosphate backbone faces the aqueous exterior.

column1: What type of RNA carries the genetic message from DNA to the ribosome?
column4: mRNA is transcribed from the template strand of DNA and translated by ribosomes. It is typically single-stranded and linear in eukaryotes.

column1: What type of RNA forms part of the ribosome?
column4: rRNA is the most abundant RNA in the cell. It provides both structural scaffolding and catalytic activity (peptidyl transferase) in the ribosome.

column1: What secondary structure does tRNA adopt?
column4: tRNA has four stem-loops arranged in a cloverleaf in 2D; in 3D it folds into an L-shape. The anticodon loop and 3'-CCA acceptor arm are at opposite ends.

column1: What sequence is always found at the 3' end of a tRNA molecule?
column4: The 3'-CCA terminus is the site of amino acid attachment (to the 3'-OH of the terminal adenosine) via an aminoacyl bond.

column1: What intramolecular RNA structure forms when a single strand folds back on itself?
column4: Complementary sequences within a single RNA strand can base-pair, forming a double-stranded stem with an unpaired loop at the tip.

column1: Which form of DNA helix is most common in cells under physiological conditions?
column4: B-DNA has ~10 base pairs per turn, a rise of 3.4 Å per bp, and a 20 Å diameter. A-form can occur in dehydrated or RNA-DNA hybrid duplexes.

column1: What stabilizes base stacking in the DNA double helix?
column3: Hydrophobic interactions (van der Waals) between stacked bases
column4: Base stacking contributes more to helix stability than hydrogen bonding; the aromatic bases stack with favorable van der Waals contact and exclude water.

column1: What is the pKa of a phosphate monoester group in nucleotides?
column4: Because the pKa is ~1, phosphate groups in nucleotides are essentially fully deprotonated at physiological pH, contributing a negative charge per phosphate.

column1: What type of reaction adds a nucleotide to a growing chain during polymerization?
column4: The 3'-OH of the growing chain attacks the alpha-phosphorus of the incoming dNTP/NTP, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) and driving the reaction forward.

column1: What drives the thermodynamic favorability of nucleotide polymerization?
column4: PPi released during polymerization is rapidly hydrolyzed to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making the net reaction highly exergonic.

column1: What type of bond links the amino acid to tRNA?
column4: The carboxyl group of the amino acid forms a high-energy ester bond with the 3'-OH (or 2'-OH) of the terminal adenosine of tRNA; aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase catalyzes this.

column1: At what position is the nitrogenous base connected to the sugar in a nucleotide?
column3: N-glycosidic bond at C-1' of the sugar
column4: Purines bond via N-9; pyrimidines bond via N-1. This N-glycosidic bond can be cleaved by glycosylases during DNA base excision repair.

column1: What is the net charge of AMP at physiological pH?
column4: AMP has one phosphate group with two ionizable protons (pKa ~1 and ~6.5). At pH 7.4, both are deprotonated, giving a charge of -2.

column1: What is the role of cAMP as a second messenger?
column4: cAMP is synthesized from ATP by adenylyl cyclase. It binds the regulatory subunits of PKA, releasing active catalytic subunits that phosphorylate target proteins.

column1: Which enzyme synthesizes cAMP from ATP?
column4: Adenylyl cyclase is activated by Gs-coupled GPCRs. It converts ATP to cAMP + PPi. cAMP is a key intracellular amplifier of hormonal signals.

column1: What nucleotide acts as a cofactor carrying electrons in redox reactions?
column4: NAD+ accepts hydride (H-) to become NADH during catabolism; NADH donates electrons to the electron transport chain. FAD/FADH2 similarly contains a riboflavin-ADP unit.

column1: What is the role of GTP in signal transduction?
column4: G-proteins are active when bound to GTP and inactive when GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP. Intrinsic GTPase activity turns off the signal.

column1: Which nucleotide is the direct phosphate donor in most kinase reactions inside the cell?
column4: Kinases catalyze phosphoryl transfer from ATP to a substrate (protein, sugar, etc.). GTP is used by some specific kinases (e.g., in the citric acid cycle by succinyl-CoA synthetase).

column1: What is the function of cGMP in phototransduction?
column3: Keeps cation channels open in photoreceptors (in the dark)
column4: In darkness, high cGMP keeps Na+/Ca2+ channels open (depolarized). Light activates phosphodiesterase, cGMP falls, channels close, and the cell hyperpolarizes.

column1: Which enzyme degrades cAMP, terminating its second messenger signal?
column4: Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cAMP to 5'-AMP. Drugs like sildenafil inhibit phosphodiesterase type 5 (cGMP-specific), prolonging vasodilation.

column1: What nucleotide-derived coenzyme is central to fatty acid synthesis?
column4: NADPH is the reductive coenzyme for anabolic reactions (fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol synthesis). Generated mainly by the pentose phosphate pathway.

column1: What functional groups are present on every amino acid at the α carbon?
column4: All 20 standard amino acids share an α-amino group and an α-carboxyl group; they differ only in the R (side-chain) group.

column1: What is the general structural formula of an α-amino acid?
column4: The α carbon is chiral (except glycine) and bears the amine, carboxyl, hydrogen, and R group. This tetrahedral arrangement gives rise to stereoisomers.

column1: Which amino acid has no chiral center?
column4: Glycine's R group is simply H, making both substituents on the α carbon identical, so it is achiral and has no enantiomers.

column1: How many standard amino acids are used to build proteins?
column4: Twenty proteinogenic amino acids are encoded by the standard genetic code; they differ in side-chain structure, charge, polarity, and size.

column1: What bond connects the α-amino group to the α-carbon in an amino acid?
column4: The α carbon forms four single (σ) bonds to the amine nitrogen, carboxyl carbon, hydrogen, and R group, making it sp3 hybridized.

column1: What is the configuration of nearly all naturally occurring amino acids at the α carbon?
column4: Biological amino acids are L-enantiomers by convention (related to L-glyceraldehyde). D-amino acids occur in some bacterial cell walls but not in human proteins.

column1: What is the R/S designation of most L-amino acids?
column4: L-cysteine is the R enantiomer because the sulfur in its side chain ranks higher than the carboxyl oxygen, reversing the priority order used in CIP rules.

column1: In the Fischer projection used to assign L/D configuration to amino acids, what is the reference molecule?
column4: L-amino acids have the same spatial arrangement of the α-amino group as the hydroxyl group in L-glyceraldehyde (on the left in a Fischer projection).

column1: In a Fischer projection of an L-amino acid, where is the amino group drawn?
column4: By convention, the backbone is vertical with the carboxyl at top; the amino group on the left indicates L configuration, mirroring L-glyceraldehyde.

column1: Which amino acid can exist in both L and D forms that are both biologically relevant?
column4: D-Alanine is incorporated into peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls, making it a target for some antibiotics; all other standard protein amino acids are L.

column1: What is a zwitterion (dipolar ion) of an amino acid?
column4: At physiological pH (~7.4), the carboxyl group is deprotonated (-COO-) and the amino group is protonated (-NH3+), yielding a net-neutral but internally charged species.

column1: At what pH does an amino acid exist predominantly as a zwitterion?
column4: The pI is the pH at which the molecule carries no net charge; the zwitterionic form dominates and the molecule does not migrate in an electric field.

column1: What net charge does a zwitterion carry?
column4: The positive charge on -NH3+ and the negative charge on -COO- cancel, giving zero net charge even though both ionizable groups are charged.

column1: Why do amino acids have higher melting points than typical organic molecules of similar mass?
column3: Zwitterionic form creates ionic crystal lattice interactions
column4: The strong electrostatic attractions between -NH3+ and -COO- groups in the solid state (like an ionic compound) require more energy to break, raising melting points.

column1: At a pH well below the pKa of the carboxyl group, what is the predominant form of an amino acid?
column4: At very low pH, both the amine and carboxyl groups are protonated, giving the amino acid a net +1 charge.

column1: Which classification distinguishes amino acids by polarity of their side chains?
column4: Side-chain polarity determines protein folding: nonpolar residues cluster in the hydrophobic core; polar/charged residues appear on the surface interacting with water.

column1: Name the four chemical categories used to classify amino acid side chains.
column3: Nonpolar, polar uncharged, acidic (negatively charged), basic (positively charged)
column4: These categories reflect ionization state at pH 7.4 and side-chain chemistry, which together govern protein structure and enzyme active sites.

column1: Which amino acids are classified as aromatic?
column4: Phe, Tyr, and Trp contain aromatic rings that absorb UV light at ~280 nm; His has an aromatic imidazole ring and is sometimes included.

column1: Which amino acid is classified as an imino acid rather than an amino acid?
column4: Proline's side chain cyclizes back onto the α-nitrogen, forming a pyrrolidine ring; its nitrogen has no free H, making it a secondary amine (imino acid).

column1: What structural feature makes proline unique among standard amino acids regarding peptide bond geometry?
column3: Its cyclic pyrrolidine ring restricts rotation, often causing cis peptide bonds
column4: Proline is a helix-breaker; its rigid ring prevents the backbone dihedral angles required for α-helices and introduces kinks in protein structure.

column1: Which two amino acids have acidic side chains?
column4: Asp and Glu contain carboxyl groups in their side chains (pKa ~3.7 and 4.3, respectively) that are deprotonated (-COO-) at physiological pH.

column1: What is the pKa of the histidine side chain (imidazole ring)?
column4: Histidine's pKa near physiological pH makes it an ideal proton shuttle in enzyme active sites; it can be protonated or deprotonated by small pH changes.

column1: Which basic amino acid has the highest pKa side chain (~12.5)?
column4: Arginine's guanidinium group is resonance-stabilized and almost always protonated at physiological pH, making Arg the strongest base among standard amino acids.

column1: At physiological pH (7.4), what charge does the aspartate side chain carry?
column4: Asp's side-chain pKa is ~3.7, well below 7.4, so the carboxyl is fully deprotonated (-COO-) at physiological pH.

column1: Which amino acids are classified as hydrophobic (nonpolar)?
column3: Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Phe, Trp, Pro, Gly
column4: These residues lack polar or ionizable groups; they are buried in the protein interior away from water. Gly and Pro are sometimes listed separately.

column1: Which polar amino acids contain hydroxyl (-OH) groups in their side chains?
column4: Ser, Thr, and Tyr have -OH groups that can form hydrogen bonds and are common phosphorylation sites in signal transduction.

column1: Which amino acid contains a thiol (-SH) group in its side chain?
column4: Cysteine's thiol can form disulfide bonds (-S-S-) with other cysteines, stabilizing protein tertiary structure. It is polar but often buried in the protein core.

column1: Which amino acids contain amide groups in their side chains?
column4: Asn and Gln are the amide derivatives of Asp and Glu; their polar amide groups (-CONH2) form hydrogen bonds, making them hydrophilic.

column1: What property of tryptophan makes it both aromatic and hydrophobic?
column4: Trp's bicyclic indole ring is predominantly nonpolar and bulky; it is typically buried in the protein core and absorbs UV light at 280 nm.

column1: What is the Strecker synthesis used to produce?
column4: Strecker synthesis converts an aldehyde to an α-amino acid via reaction with ammonia and HCN, followed by hydrolysis of the resulting α-aminonitrile. The product is a racemate.

column1: What are the three reagents used in the first step of the Strecker synthesis?
column4: The aldehyde first reacts with NH3 to form an imine, which then undergoes nucleophilic addition with HCN to give an α-aminonitrile intermediate.

column1: What intermediate is hydrolyzed in the final step of the Strecker synthesis?
column4: The nitrile group (-CN) is hydrolyzed under acidic or basic aqueous conditions to give the carboxylic acid, yielding the final α-amino acid.

column1: Why does Strecker synthesis produce a racemic mixture?
column3: HCN adds to the planar imine from both faces equally
column4: The sp2 imine intermediate has no stereocontrol; nucleophilic attack from either face gives equal amounts of R and S enantiomers.

column1: What reagent is the nitrogen source in Strecker synthesis?
column4: NH3 condenses with the aldehyde to form an imine (Schiff base), which is the electrophilic intermediate for HCN addition.

column1: What starting material does the Gabriel synthesis use to introduce the nitrogen of an amino acid?
column4: Phthalimide's NH is alkylated; after hydrolysis, the phthalate is removed, liberating a primary amine with no overalkylation — a key advantage.

column1: What is the key advantage of Gabriel synthesis over direct ammonolysis for making primary amines?
column3: Prevents over-alkylation; gives only primary amines
column4: The phthalimide nitrogen has only one N-H, so only one alkylation can occur. Direct use of NH3 gives mixtures of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and quaternary ammonium.

column1: What step follows alkylation of potassium phthalimide in the Gabriel synthesis?
column3: Acidic or basic hydrolysis to release the primary amine
column4: Hydrolysis cleaves both C=O bonds of the phthalimide ring, releasing phthalic acid and the free primary amine (or amino acid if an α-halo acid is used).

column1: What electrophile is used in Gabriel synthesis to produce an α-amino acid?
column4: An α-halo acid undergoes SN2 alkylation with phthalimide; subsequent hydrolysis liberates the free amino acid with the carboxyl group intact.

column1: What is the disulfide bond in proteins formed from?
column3: Two cysteine thiol groups (-SH) oxidized to -S-S-
column4: Oxidation of two Cys residues' thiol groups forms a covalent disulfide bridge (-S-S-); these stabilize tertiary and quaternary protein structure.

column1: What type of chemical reaction converts two cysteine thiols to a disulfide bond?
column4: Each thiol loses one hydrogen (one electron each); a mild oxidant (O2, H2O2, or disulfide exchange) drives the reaction. Reduction (e.g., by DTT) reverses it.

column1: Where are disulfide bonds most commonly found relative to a cell?
column3: In extracellular proteins (secreted proteins, membrane proteins)
column4: The reducing environment of the cytoplasm disfavors disulfide bond formation; disulfide bonds form in the oxidizing environment of the ER lumen and extracellular space.

column1: What reagent is commonly used to reduce disulfide bonds in the laboratory?
column4: These reducing agents provide excess thiol groups that exchange with the disulfide, breaking it into two free -SH groups. Used to denature proteins in SDS-PAGE.

column1: What type of bond is a peptide bond?
column3: Amide bond (C-N bond between carboxyl and amino groups)
column4: The peptide bond forms between the α-carboxyl of one amino acid and the α-amino group of the next, releasing water (condensation reaction).

column1: What is the geometry of the peptide bond?
column4: Resonance delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives the C-N bond ~40% double-bond character; rotation is restricted, keeping the bond planar.

column1: In what configuration are most peptide bonds found in native proteins?
column4: The trans configuration places R groups on opposite sides of the peptide bond, minimizing steric clashes. The cis form occurs rarely, mainly before proline residues.

column1: What is the N-terminus of a polypeptide?
column3: The end with a free α-amino group (-NH3+)
column4: By convention, polypeptides are written and read from N-terminus (left) to C-terminus (right); the N-terminus has a free amino group.

column1: What reaction forms a peptide bond?
column4: The α-COOH of one amino acid reacts with the α-NH2 of another, losing H2O to form the amide (peptide) bond.

column1: How many peptide bonds are present in a tripeptide?
column4: Each peptide bond connects adjacent amino acids; n amino acids form n-1 peptide bonds. A tripeptide has 3 amino acids and 2 peptide bonds.

column1: What reaction cleaves peptide bonds?
column4: Peptide bond hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation; it is thermodynamically favorable but kinetically slow without catalysis by acid, base, or proteases.

column1: Which enzymes catalyze protein hydrolysis in the digestive tract?
column4: These serine or aspartyl proteases cleave peptide bonds with varying specificity: trypsin after Arg/Lys, chymotrypsin after large aromatics/nonpolar residues.

column1: After what residues does trypsin cleave peptide bonds?
column3: After basic residues: Lysine (Lys) and Arginine (Arg)
column4: Trypsin's active-site Asp residue complements the positive charge of Lys/Arg side chains, directing cleavage on the C-terminal side of these residues.

column1: After what residues does chymotrypsin cleave peptide bonds?
column3: After large aromatic/nonpolar residues: Phe, Trp, Tyr
column4: Chymotrypsin's hydrophobic pocket accommodates bulky aromatic side chains, cleaving on their C-terminal side; it can also act on Leu and Met.

column1: What bond is specifically cleaved by cyanogen bromide (CNBr) in protein sequencing?
column4: CNBr converts Met to homoserine lactone, cleaving the polypeptide chain. Because Met is rare, CNBr produces a small number of large fragments useful for sequencing.

column1: What types of interactions stabilize protein structure overall?
column3: H-bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions, disulfide bonds, van der Waals forces
column4: No single force dominates; the cumulative effect of many weak interactions and the hydrophobic effect drives protein folding into the native state.

column1: What is denaturation of a protein?
column3: Loss of 3D structure without breaking primary (peptide bond) structure
column4: Heat, extremes of pH, urea, and detergents disrupt noncovalent interactions and disulfide bonds (with reducing agents), unfolding the protein without hydrolyzing peptide bonds.

column1: What driving force is most important for protein folding in aqueous solution?
column3: The hydrophobic effect (burial of nonpolar residues)
column4: Sequestering nonpolar side chains from water increases entropy of the solvent and is the dominant thermodynamic driving force for protein folding.

column1: What defines the primary structure of a protein?
column3: The linear sequence of amino acids (N- to C-terminus)
column4: Primary structure is encoded by DNA and determines all higher levels of structure. Even one amino acid substitution can cause disease (e.g., sickle cell anemia).

column1: What method is used to determine amino acid sequence (primary structure) of a protein?
column4: Edman degradation sequentially removes and identifies the N-terminal residue using phenyl isothiocyanate (PITC) without hydrolyzing the rest of the chain.

column1: What bond constitutes primary structure?
column4: Primary structure is the covalent backbone; disulfide bonds are also sometimes considered part of primary structure because they are covalent.

column1: In sickle cell disease, what single amino acid substitution occurs in hemoglobin?
column3: Val replaces Glu at position 6 of the β-globin chain
column4: Replacement of a polar, charged Glu with nonpolar Val causes HbS to polymerize under low O2, distorting red blood cells into sickle shapes.

column1: What is the most common type of secondary structure in proteins?
column4: Both are stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups. α-helices are right-handed; β-sheets are parallel or antiparallel.

column1: What stabilizes the α-helix?
column3: Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O of residue n and N-H of residue n+4
column4: Each turn of the α-helix spans 3.6 amino acids and 5.4 Å; H-bonds run parallel to the helix axis, giving the structure stability.

column1: How are hydrogen bonds oriented in antiparallel β-sheets versus parallel β-sheets?
column3: Antiparallel: H-bonds are perpendicular and straight; parallel: H-bonds are oblique
column4: Antiparallel β-sheets (adjacent strands run in opposite directions) form stronger, more linear H-bonds; parallel sheets are less stable.

column1: Which amino acid disrupts α-helices and why?
column3: Proline, because its cyclic ring prevents the N-H required for helix hydrogen bonding
column4: Proline's nitrogen lacks a hydrogen (it is part of a ring) and introduces a rigid kink, breaking the regular repeating structure of an α-helix.

column1: What is a β-turn (reverse turn)?
column3: A short loop reversing the direction of the polypeptide chain
column4: β-turns typically span four residues and are stabilized by one H-bond between residue 1 C=O and residue 4 N-H; they are common on protein surfaces.

column1: What level of protein structure involves interactions between R groups and overall 3D folding?
column4: Tertiary structure is the complete 3D shape of a single polypeptide chain, determined by R-group interactions: hydrophobic clustering, H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds.

column1: What interactions stabilize tertiary protein structure?
column3: Hydrophobic interactions, H-bonds, ionic (salt bridges), disulfide bonds, van der Waals forces
column4: Nonpolar side chains cluster in the core (hydrophobic effect); polar/charged residues on the surface form H-bonds and salt bridges with water and each other.

column1: What is a domain in protein tertiary structure?
column3: A compact, independently folding structural and functional unit within a polypeptide
column4: Domains often correspond to functional modules (e.g., DNA-binding domain, kinase domain); large proteins contain multiple domains that may fold independently.

column1: Which technique is the gold standard for determining protein 3D structure at atomic resolution?
column4: X-ray crystallography diffracts X-rays off a protein crystal and uses Fourier analysis to compute electron density maps; NMR and cryo-EM are alternatives.

column1: What is the motif (supersecondary structure) called when two α-helices are connected by a short loop?
column4: HTH is a common DNA-binding motif; one helix makes base contacts while the other stabilizes the structure. It is a supersecondary structural element, not a full domain.

column1: What is the isoelectric point (pI) of an amino acid?
column3: The pH at which the amino acid carries no net charge
column4: At the pI, the amino acid is in its zwitterionic form and does not migrate in an electric field; the pI is the average of the two flanking pKa values.

column1: How is the pI of a simple (non-ionizable side chain) amino acid calculated?
column3: pI = (pKa1 + pKa2) / 2, where pKa1 = carboxyl, pKa2 = amino
column4: For alanine (pKa1 ≈ 2.3, pKa2 ≈ 9.7): pI = (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0. This is the midpoint between the two ionization steps.

column1: How is the pI of an acidic amino acid (e.g., aspartate) calculated?
column3: pI = (pKa of α-COOH + pKa of side-chain COOH) / 2
column4: For Asp (pKa1 ≈ 2.1, pKaR ≈ 3.9): pI = (2.1 + 3.9)/2 ≈ 3.0. The pI is below 7 because both relevant pKa values involve acid groups.

column1: How is the pI of a basic amino acid (e.g., lysine) calculated?
column3: pI = (pKa of α-NH3+ + pKa of side-chain NH3+) / 2
column4: For Lys (pKa2 ≈ 9.0, pKaR ≈ 10.5): pI = (9.0 + 10.5)/2 ≈ 9.7. The pI is above 7 because both relevant pKa values involve basic groups.

column1: At a pH above its pI, what charge does an amino acid carry?
column4: Above the pI, excess OH- deprotonates ionizable groups, giving the molecule a net negative charge; it would migrate toward the anode in electrophoresis.

column1: At a pH below its pI, what charge does an amino acid carry?
column4: Below the pI, excess H+ protonates ionizable groups, giving the molecule a net positive charge; it would migrate toward the cathode in electrophoresis.

column1: What technique separates proteins based on their isoelectric points?
column4: A pH gradient is established in a gel; proteins migrate until they reach the pH equal to their pI, where they carry no net charge and stop moving.

column1: What term describes the overall 3D shape of a protein determined by all non-covalent and covalent interactions?
column4: A protein's conformation is its specific 3D arrangement of atoms. Conformational stability refers to how well a protein maintains its native conformation under physiological conditions.

column1: Which type of covalent bond contributes most to conformational stability by cross-linking polypeptide chains?
column4: Disulfide bonds form between cysteine residues and are the primary covalent cross-links stabilizing tertiary structure; they are especially important in extracellular proteins.

column1: Which level of protein structure is primarily stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amino groups?
column4: Alpha-helices and beta-sheets are secondary structures maintained by backbone H-bonds, independent of side-chain identity.

column1: What is the thermodynamic driving force for a protein adopting its native conformation?
column4: The native state is the lowest free-energy conformation; folding is driven by maximizing favorable interactions and minimizing the system's Gibbs free energy.

column1: What type of interactions between charged amino acid side chains (e.g., Lys and Glu) contribute to protein conformational stability?
column4: Salt bridges form between oppositely charged residues; they can stabilize tertiary structure but are sensitive to pH changes that alter ionization state.

column1: Which secondary structure has all peptide bonds in the same plane and uses phi/psi dihedral angles within allowed Ramachandran regions?
column4: Backbone phi (N-Cα) and psi (Cα-C) angles define secondary structure; allowed regions in the Ramachandran plot correspond to alpha-helices, beta-sheets, and other conformations.

column1: What is the approximate number of amino acids per turn in an alpha-helix?
column4: Each turn of an alpha-helix spans ~3.6 residues with a rise of ~1.5 Å per residue and a pitch of ~5.4 Å, a commonly tested MCAT value.

column1: Which proline property uniquely disrupts alpha-helices?
column3: Rigid cyclic side chain (no NH hydrogen)
column4: Proline's nitrogen is incorporated into its ring, eliminating the backbone NH needed for helix hydrogen bonding, and its rigidity introduces a kink that breaks the helix.

column1: What distinguishes parallel from antiparallel beta-sheets in terms of hydrogen bond geometry?
column3: Antiparallel has stronger, more linear H-bonds
column4: In antiparallel sheets, H-bonds are perpendicular to the strands and more linear (stronger); parallel sheets have less optimal, slightly bent H-bonds.

column1: What is the primary driving force for burying nonpolar amino acid side chains in the protein interior?
column4: Nonpolar residues are driven to the protein core to minimize unfavorable interactions with water, releasing ordered water molecules and increasing entropy of the solvent.

column1: Which amino acid property determines whether it is found on the protein surface or buried in the hydrophobic core?
column3: Polarity of the side chain (R group)
column4: Polar and charged residues favor the aqueous surface; nonpolar (hydrophobic) residues are preferentially buried in the core away from water.

column1: Name three hydrophobic amino acids commonly found in the protein interior.
column4: These nonpolar aliphatic and aromatic residues lack functional groups that would favorably interact with water and are therefore sequestered in the hydrophobic core.

column1: What type of non-covalent interaction stabilizes aromatic side chains stacked near each other in a protein core?
column4: Aromatic residues (Phe, Tyr, Trp) can engage in pi-stacking interactions, contributing to hydrophobic burial and van der Waals stabilization.

column1: How do hydrophobic interactions contribute energetically to protein folding — primarily enthalpic or entropic?
column4: The hydrophobic effect is driven by the gain in entropy when ordered water molecules surrounding nonpolar groups are released upon burial, rather than by direct enthalpic attraction between nonpolar groups.

column1: Which amino acids are considered amphipathic and can appear at the protein surface-core interface?
column4: Amphipathic residues have both polar and nonpolar character; Trp and Tyr have hydroxyl or indole groups that can H-bond, while their ring systems pack hydrophobically.

column1: What happens to hydrophobic interactions in a protein when the solution temperature is raised significantly above physiological?
column4: Elevated temperature increases thermal motion, breaking hydrophobic packing and other stabilizing interactions, leading to unfolding; this is one basis for heat denaturation.

column1: What is the term for the ordered water shell surrounding charged or polar residues on a protein surface?
column4: Water molecules form an ordered solvation layer around polar and charged protein surface residues; this layer is maintained by hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions.

column1: What happens to entropy when hydrophobic residues become exposed to water?
column4: Exposed nonpolar surfaces force surrounding water into an ordered, low-entropy cage (clathrate-like) structure; burial of these residues releases this ordered water, increasing total entropy.

column1: What is the thermodynamic sign of entropy change (ΔS) for the solvent when a protein folds and buries hydrophobic residues?
column4: Folding releases ordered water from hydrophobic surfaces, increasing solvent entropy; this favorable ΔS_solvent is a major thermodynamic driving force of protein folding.

column1: What term describes the phenomenon where nonpolar solutes cluster together in water to minimize the disruption of the hydrogen-bond network?
column4: The hydrophobic effect is fundamentally an entropic phenomenon: clustering of nonpolar molecules minimizes the surface area that disrupts the water H-bond network.

column1: How does the solvation layer around charged residues differ from that around hydrophobic residues?
column3: Charged: ordered H-bonds (enthalpic); hydrophobic: ordered cage (entropic penalty)
column4: Polar/charged solvation is stabilized enthalpically via H-bonds with water, while hydrophobic solvation imposes an entropic cost by creating ordered water cages.

column1: What is the term for the free energy cost of ordering water around an exposed hydrophobic surface?
column4: This penalty drives hydrophobic burial; proteins minimize it by folding to sequester nonpolar residues, a key thermodynamic basis of the hydrophobic effect in protein folding.

column1: What level of protein structure refers to the association of two or more polypeptide chains?
column4: Quaternary structure describes the arrangement and interactions of individual polypeptide subunits (protomers) in a multi-subunit protein complex.

column1: What is the name for each individual polypeptide chain in a quaternary protein complex?
column4: Each polypeptide in a multi-subunit protein is a subunit; the arrangement and number of subunits defines the quaternary structure (e.g., homodimer, heterotetramer).

column1: Hemoglobin is a classic example of which type of quaternary structure?
column4: Hemoglobin consists of two alpha and two beta subunits; its quaternary structure is essential for cooperative oxygen binding and the Bohr effect.

column1: What non-covalent forces primarily hold subunits together in quaternary structures?
column4: Subunit interfaces are typically stabilized by hydrophobic burial, hydrogen bonds, and salt bridges; disulfide bonds can also contribute in some proteins.

column1: What is cooperative binding in the context of quaternary structure, and which protein exemplifies it?
column3: Binding at one subunit increases affinity in others; hemoglobin
column4: Cooperative binding (allostery) occurs when ligand binding to one subunit induces conformational changes that alter affinity in adjacent subunits, as seen with O2 binding to hemoglobin.

column1: Distinguish between a homodimer and a heterodimer.
column3: Homodimer: two identical subunits; heterodimer: two different subunits
column4: Quaternary nomenclature specifies subunit identity; homo- = same, hetero- = different. Many regulatory proteins form heterodimers to expand functional diversity.

column1: What term describes a protein that loses quaternary structure but retains subunit tertiary structure?
column4: Some denaturants or conditions disrupt subunit interfaces without unfolding individual chains; the result is free, folded monomers — distinct from full denaturation.

column1: What is an example of a quaternary structure stabilized by a disulfide bond between subunits?
column4: Antibodies have inter-chain disulfide bonds linking heavy and light chains, providing covalent stabilization of quaternary structure in an extracellular environment.

column1: Define denaturation of a protein.
column3: Loss of native 3D structure without breaking peptide bonds
column4: Denaturation disrupts non-covalent interactions (and sometimes disulfide bonds), unfolding the protein and abolishing its function, while the primary sequence remains intact.

column1: Name four common protein denaturants.
column4: Heat disrupts non-covalent interactions; extreme pH alters ionization; urea/guanidinium disrupt H-bonds and hydrophobic interactions; SDS denatures via hydrophobic competition.

column1: What is meant by protein renaturation (refolding)?
column3: Restoration of native structure after denaturation
column4: Some denatured proteins can spontaneously refold to their native conformation upon removal of the denaturant, demonstrating that sequence encodes structure (Anfinsen's experiment).

column1: What did Anfinsen's ribonuclease experiment demonstrate about protein folding?
column4: Anfinsen showed that denatured RNase A refolds spontaneously and regains activity, proving that the amino acid sequence alone contains all information needed for correct folding.

column1: What is the role of molecular chaperones in protein folding?
column3: Prevent misfolding and aggregation; assist correct folding
column4: Chaperones (e.g., Hsp70, GroEL/GroES) bind to exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or stress-unfolded proteins to prevent aggregation and provide a protected environment for folding.

column1: How does urea denature proteins at the molecular level?
column3: Disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions
column4: Urea competes with intramolecular H-bonds and interacts with nonpolar residues, destabilizing the native fold and exposing the hydrophobic core to solvent.

column1: What is the difference between denaturing by heat versus reducing agents (e.g., beta-mercaptoethanol)?
column3: Heat breaks non-covalent bonds; reducing agents cleave disulfide bonds
column4: Beta-mercaptoethanol (BME) and DTT reduce disulfide bonds specifically; combined with SDS, both covalent (S-S) and non-covalent interactions are disrupted for full denaturation (as in SDS-PAGE).

column1: What thermodynamic principle explains why some proteins are irreversibly denatured by heat?
column3: Aggregation of exposed hydrophobic regions (kinetic trap)
column4: Upon heating, exposed hydrophobic surfaces from multiple unfolded proteins aggregate, forming insoluble precipitates; re-cooling cannot reverse the intermolecular associations — an irreversible kinetic trap.

column1: Which class of proteins are characterized by retaining function under extreme denaturing conditions (e.g., high temperature)?
column4: Thermophilic proteins have increased hydrophobic cores, more salt bridges, and optimized packing that confer greater conformational stability at high temperatures.

column1: What term describes a protein's ability to associate noncovalently with another molecule (ligand)?
column4: Protein binding is a reversible, noncovalent interaction central to signal transduction, transport, and immune recognition. Affinity (Kd) quantifies binding strength.

column1: What is the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) a measure of?
column3: Binding affinity between protein and ligand
column4: A lower Kd indicates higher affinity; at Kd concentration, 50% of binding sites are occupied. Kd has units of concentration (mol/L).

column1: What type of protein interactions (forces) stabilize most protein-ligand binding?
column3: Noncovalent interactions (H-bonds, van der Waals, ionic, hydrophobic)
column4: Protein-ligand binding is generally reversible because it relies on multiple weak noncovalent forces rather than covalent bonds.

column1: What phenomenon occurs when ligand binding at one subunit alters affinity at another subunit?
column4: Hemoglobin is the classic example: O2 binding to one subunit increases affinity in remaining subunits (positive cooperativity), producing a sigmoidal O2-dissociation curve.

column1: What shape is the oxygen-dissociation curve of hemoglobin, and why?
column4: Cooperativity causes a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve rather than a hyperbolic one. Myoglobin, which lacks cooperativity, shows a hyperbolic curve.

column1: What is the Hill coefficient (n) used to quantify?
column4: n > 1 = positive cooperativity; n = 1 = no cooperativity (hyperbolic); n < 1 = negative cooperativity. Hemoglobin has n ≈ 2.8.

column1: What structural feature allows allosteric proteins to switch between high- and low-affinity conformations?
column4: In the MWC (concerted) model, all subunits switch simultaneously between T (tense, low affinity) and R (relaxed, high affinity) states.

column1: How does 2,3-BPG affect hemoglobin's oxygen affinity?
column4: 2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin, stabilizing the T state and facilitating O2 release to tissues. Important at high altitude and in fetal vs. adult hemoglobin differences.

column1: Which fetal hemoglobin chain replacement reduces 2,3-BPG binding and increases O2 affinity?
column4: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF, α2γ2) binds 2,3-BPG less avidly than adult HbA (α2β2), giving HbF higher O2 affinity — enabling O2 transfer from maternal to fetal blood.

column1: What class of proteins circulates in blood and binds specific antigens to neutralize or tag pathogens?
column4: Antibodies are Y-shaped glycoproteins produced by B cells/plasma cells. They recognize antigens via their variable regions and mediate immune clearance.

column1: What are the two types of chains that make up an antibody monomer?
column4: Each antibody monomer has two identical heavy (H) chains and two identical light (L) chains linked by disulfide bonds, forming the characteristic Y shape.

column1: Which region of an antibody binds the antigen?
column4: Each arm of the Y (Fab fragment) contains hypervariable complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) that form the antigen-binding site. The Fc region mediates effector functions.

column1: What are the five classes of immunoglobulins in humans?
column4: Mnemonic: GAMED. IgG is most abundant in serum; IgA in secretions; IgM is first produced in primary response; IgE mediates allergic reactions.

column1: Which immunoglobulin class is the first to be produced during a primary immune response?
column4: IgM exists as a pentamer in serum, making it highly effective at agglutination and complement activation. It is replaced by IgG after class switching.

column1: What process generates antibody diversity at the DNA level?
column4: Somatic recombination of Variable, Diversity, and Joining gene segments in developing B cells generates enormous antibody diversity before antigen exposure.

column1: What process increases antibody affinity after initial antigen exposure?
column4: During the germinal center reaction, point mutations accumulate in antibody variable regions; B cells with higher-affinity receptors are selected, refining antibody quality.

column1: Which complement of protein structures on T cells recognizes antigen presented by MHC molecules?
column4: TCRs are antigen-binding proteins (not antibodies) on T cells. Unlike antibodies, TCRs only recognize peptide antigens displayed on MHC molecules.

column1: What is the role of MHC class I molecules in the immune system?
column3: Present intracellular peptides to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
column4: MHC I is expressed on all nucleated cells and displays peptides derived from cytoplasmic proteins (including viral). Recognized by CD8+ T cells, triggering killing of infected cells.

column1: What is the role of MHC class II molecules in the immune system?
column3: Present extracellular peptides to CD4+ helper T cells
column4: MHC II is expressed on antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells). It presents peptides from phagocytosed extracellular pathogens.

column1: What type of proteins generate force and movement within cells using ATP hydrolysis?
column4: Motor proteins (myosin, kinesin, dynein) convert chemical energy from ATP into mechanical work, enabling muscle contraction and intracellular transport.

column1: Which motor protein walks toward the plus end of microtubules?
column4: Kinesin transports cargo (vesicles, organelles) toward the cell periphery (anterograde transport) along microtubules. Dynein moves toward the minus end (retrograde).

column1: Which motor protein walks toward the minus end of microtubules?
column4: Dynein moves cargo toward the cell center (retrograde transport) and is also responsible for the movement of cilia and flagella.

column1: What is the power stroke in muscle contraction powered by?
column4: Myosin-II uses ATP hydrolysis to cock its head and then releases Pi to execute the power stroke, pulling actin filaments. ADP is subsequently released.

column1: In what state is myosin when rigor mortis occurs?
column3: Strongly bound to actin (rigor state), no ATP
column4: After death, ATP production ceases. Myosin remains tightly bound to actin without ATP to release it, causing muscle stiffness (rigor mortis).

column1: What protein complex at the Z-disc anchors thin filaments in a sarcomere?
column4: Alpha-actinin cross-links actin (thin filaments) at the Z-disc, defining the boundaries of each sarcomere. This is distinct from titin, which spans from Z to M line.

column1: Which regulatory protein blocks myosin-binding sites on actin at rest?
column4: Tropomyosin lies along actin filaments and sterically blocks the myosin-binding sites. Upon Ca2+ binding to troponin C, tropomyosin shifts to expose these sites.

column1: What triggers tropomyosin to move and expose myosin-binding sites on actin?
column4: The troponin complex (TnT, TnI, TnC) senses Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Ca2+ binding to TnC relieves TnI inhibition and shifts tropomyosin.

column1: Which troponin subunit binds calcium to initiate muscle contraction?
column4: TnC is the Ca2+-sensing subunit. It is structurally similar to calmodulin. TnI is the inhibitory subunit; TnT anchors the complex to tropomyosin.

column1: What is the directionality of actin filament growth, and which end grows faster?
column4: Actin polymerizes preferentially at the plus (barbed) end and depolymerizes at the minus (pointed) end. This treadmilling is essential for cell motility and motor protein function.

column1: What chemical property defines all lipids?
column4: Lipids are defined not by a common functional group but by their hydrophobicity. They are soluble in organic solvents such as ether and chloroform.
