column1: Which four major classes of lipids are tested on the MCAT?
column4: Waxes, sphingolipids, fat-soluble vitamins, and prostaglandins are also lipids but these four categories form the structural backbone of MCAT lipid content.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::description-types MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What distinguishes a saturated fatty acid from an unsaturated fatty acid?
column3: Saturated: no C=C double bonds; unsaturated: one or more C=C
column4: Saturated fats have all single C–C bonds; unsaturated fats contain at least one double bond, which introduces a kink and lowers melting point.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::description-types MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What configuration are most naturally occurring double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids?
column4: Cis double bonds create a bend in the fatty acid chain, disrupting packing and lowering the melting point relative to the trans isomer.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::description-types MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What term describes a fatty acid with exactly one double bond?
column4: Oleic acid (18:1) is the classic example. 'Poly-unsaturated' applies to two or more double bonds (e.g., linoleic acid, 18:2).
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::description-types MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the primary site of fat storage in the human body?
column4: Adipocytes store triacylglycerols in large lipid droplets. Fat provides ~9 kcal/g, more than double the energy density of carbohydrates or proteins.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::storage MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How many kcal of energy does 1 gram of fat provide?
column4: Compared with 4 kcal/g for carbohydrates and proteins, the high energy density of fat reflects the highly reduced state of carbon in fatty acid chains.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::storage MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What enzyme releases fatty acids from adipose triacylglycerols during fasting?
column4: HSL is activated by glucagon and epinephrine (via cAMP/PKA) and inhibited by insulin; it hydrolyzes stored triacylglycerols to free fatty acids and glycerol.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::storage MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What metabolic process converts excess glucose and amino acids into fat for storage?
column4: Acetyl-CoA generated from excess nutrients is converted to fatty acids primarily in the liver and then stored as triacylglycerols in adipose tissue.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::storage MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: In which cellular compartment does fatty acid synthesis occur?
column4: Beta-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, but fatty acid synthesis is cytoplasmic and uses NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::storage MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is a triacylglycerol (triglyceride)?
column3: Glycerol esterified with three fatty acids
column4: Each hydroxyl of glycerol forms an ester bond with the carboxyl group of a fatty acid. Triacylglycerols are the main form of dietary and stored fat.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::triacyl-glycerols MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of bond links each fatty acid to the glycerol backbone in a triacylglycerol?
column4: The reaction is a condensation (dehydration) reaction between the –OH of glycerol and the –COOH of each fatty acid, releasing water.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::triacyl-glycerols MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What products result from complete hydrolysis of a triacylglycerol?
column4: Pancreatic lipase cleaves ester bonds; the products are absorbed by intestinal epithelium, reassembled, and packaged into chylomicrons.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::triacyl-glycerols MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does the degree of saturation of fatty acids affect triacylglycerol melting point?
column4: Saturated fatty acids pack tightly due to linear chains; unsaturated (cis) fatty acids have kinks that disrupt packing, lowering the melting point (liquid oils).
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::triacyl-glycerols MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which lipoprotein primarily transports dietary triacylglycerols from the intestine?
column4: Chylomicrons are assembled in intestinal epithelial cells, enter the lymph, then blood, and deliver triglycerides to peripheral tissues via lipoprotein lipase.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::triacyl-glycerols MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is saponification?
column3: Base hydrolysis of an ester (fat) to yield soap (fatty acid salt) + glycerol
column4: Strong base (NaOH or KOH) cleaves ester bonds in triacylglycerols; the fatty acid carboxylate salts produced are soaps (amphipathic molecules).
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::free-fatty-acids-saponification MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What are the products of saponification of a triacylglycerol with NaOH?
column4: The carboxylate anion of the fatty acid (RCOONa) is the soap molecule; its amphipathic nature allows emulsification of fats.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::free-fatty-acids-saponification MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Why does saponification go to completion (irreversible) under basic conditions?
column3: The carboxylate product is resonance-stabilized and does not re-esterify
column4: Under acidic conditions ester hydrolysis is reversible, but the carboxylate anion formed under basic conditions is a poor nucleophile toward re-esterification.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::free-fatty-acids-saponification MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What property of soap allows it to remove grease from skin?
column3: Amphipathic structure: nonpolar tail + polar carboxylate head
column4: The nonpolar tails surround grease (hydrophobic core) while the polar heads face water, forming micelles that keep fat suspended.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::free-fatty-acids-saponification MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the saponification number of a fat?
column3: mg of KOH needed to saponify 1 g of fat
column4: A higher saponification number indicates shorter-chain fatty acids (more moles of ester per gram). Used to characterize fats and oils analytically.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::free-fatty-acids-saponification MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the primary structural role of lipids in cells?
column3: Form the phospholipid bilayer of cell membranes
column4: The amphipathic nature of phospholipids drives bilayer self-assembly, creating a selectively permeable barrier around all cells and organelles.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::structural MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the general structure of a structural phospholipid?
column3: Glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate group + polar head group
column4: The two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic; the phosphate and head group are hydrophilic, making phospholipids amphipathic membrane builders.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::structural MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does cholesterol affect membrane fluidity at physiological temperature?
column3: Stabilizes fluidity: decreases fluidity at high T; increases fluidity at low T
column4: Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipid tails. At high temperatures it restricts movement (reduces fluidity); at low temperatures it prevents tight packing (prevents solidification).
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::structural MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of membrane motion do phospholipids NOT readily undergo?
column4: Lateral diffusion within one leaflet is rapid, but flip-flop requires a flippase enzyme because moving the hydrophilic head through the hydrophobic core is energetically costly.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::structural MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which fatty acid tail characteristic increases membrane fluidity?
column3: More double bonds (unsaturation) in the fatty acid chains
column4: Cis double bonds introduce kinks that prevent tight packing of fatty acid tails, increasing membrane fluidity. This is why cold-adapted organisms have more unsaturated membrane lipids.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::structural MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is a phospholipid?
column3: Glycerophospholipid: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + polar head
column4: Phospholipids are the major structural lipids of biological membranes. The phosphate ester head group gives them their amphipathic character.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Name the most abundant phospholipid head groups found in mammalian membranes.
column4: Phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) is the most abundant. Phosphatidylserine is concentrated in the inner leaflet and flips outward as an apoptosis signal.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is lecithin?
column4: Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) is the most abundant phospholipid in mammalian cell membranes and is also the main phospholipid in pulmonary surfactant.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the significance of phosphatidylserine's location in the plasma membrane?
column3: Inner leaflet; flips to outer leaflet as apoptosis signal
column4: Flippases maintain phosphatidylserine on the cytoplasmic face; when cells undergo apoptosis, scramblases expose it on the outer leaflet, signaling macrophages to engulf the cell.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What enzyme cleaves a fatty acid from position sn-2 of a phospholipid to produce arachidonic acid?
column4: Arachidonic acid released by PLA2 is the precursor for eicosanoids (prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes). This is the first committed step in eicosanoid synthesis.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::phospholipids-and-phosphatids MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the backbone of a sphingolipid?
column4: Sphingosine is an 18-carbon amino alcohol. A fatty acid is linked via an amide bond to its amino group, forming ceramide — the core of all sphingolipids.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::sphingolipids-bc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is ceramide?
column3: Sphingosine + fatty acid (amide bond) — the core sphingolipid
column4: Ceramide is the structural backbone of all sphingolipids. Addition of phosphocholine gives sphingomyelin; addition of sugars gives cerebrosides and gangliosides.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::sphingolipids-bc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is sphingomyelin and where is it found?
column3: Ceramide + phosphocholine; abundant in myelin sheaths
column4: Sphingomyelin is the only sphingolipid with a phosphate head group. It is especially enriched in the myelin sheath of neurons and in lipid rafts.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::sphingolipids-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What are gangliosides?
column4: Gangliosides are complex glycosphingolipids found on neuronal cell surfaces. Defects in ganglioside degradation cause lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Tay-Sachs).
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::sphingolipids-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What enzyme is deficient in Tay-Sachs disease?
column4: Hexosaminidase A normally cleaves a terminal N-acetylgalactosamine from GM2 ganglioside. Its absence leads to GM2 accumulation in lysosomes, destroying neurons.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::sphingolipids-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What type of bond links the fatty acid to sphingosine in ceramide?
column4: The amino group of sphingosine reacts with the carboxyl of a fatty acid to form an amide bond. This distinguishes sphingolipids from glycerophospholipids, which use ester bonds.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::sphingolipids-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is a wax chemically?
column3: Ester of a long-chain fatty acid with a long-chain fatty alcohol
column4: Both the acid and alcohol components are long-chain (typically C14–C36), making waxes very hydrophobic and solid at room temperature.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::waxes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What biological function do waxes primarily serve?
column3: Waterproof protective coating (skin, feathers, leaves, insect cuticle)
column4: Waxes are highly saturated and pack tightly, creating water-impermeable barriers that prevent desiccation and protect surfaces.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::waxes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does the ester bond in a wax differ from that in a triacylglycerol?
column3: Wax ester: fatty acid + fatty alcohol; TAG ester: fatty acid + glycerol
column4: Both are carboxylic acid esters, but waxes use a fatty alcohol instead of glycerol as the alcohol component, resulting in a single ester linkage per molecule.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::waxes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Name a common example of a biological wax.
column4: Beeswax is myricyl palmitate — a C30 alcohol esterified with palmitic acid (C16). Earwax (cerumen) is another mammalian example.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::waxes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which lipids serve as second messengers in signal transduction?
column4: Phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 into DAG (activates PKC) and IP3 (releases Ca2+ from ER). Both are lipid-derived second messengers.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::signals-cofactors MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What lipid second messenger activates protein kinase C (PKC)?
column4: DAG remains in the membrane after PIP2 cleavage and recruits PKC to the membrane where it becomes activated, often requiring Ca2+ as a cofactor.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::signals-cofactors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What lipid cofactor is required for the coagulation cascade?
column4: When platelets are activated, phosphatidylserine flips to the outer leaflet, providing a negatively charged surface that assembles clotting factor complexes (e.g., prothrombinase).
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::signals-cofactors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the lipid anchor that tethers some proteins to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane?
column4: GPI-anchored proteins (e.g., decay-accelerating factor, alkaline phosphatase) are attached to the outer leaflet via a glycan bridge to phosphatidylinositol in the membrane.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::signals-cofactors MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which fat-soluble vitamin is necessary for normal blood clotting?
column4: Vitamin K is a cofactor for gamma-carboxylase, which carboxylates glutamate residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, enabling them to bind calcium.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::fat-soluble-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Name the four fat-soluble vitamins.
column4: Mnemonic: ADEK or 'fat DEKA.' These vitamins require dietary fat and bile for absorption and are stored in fat and liver (risk of toxicity with excess).
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::fat-soluble-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the role of vitamin A in vision?
column3: 11-cis-retinal is the chromophore in rhodopsin (photoreceptor pigment)
column4: Light converts 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, triggering a conformational change in opsin that initiates the visual signal cascade.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::fat-soluble-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the active hormonal form of vitamin D?
column4: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is hydroxylated first in the liver (25-OH) then in the kidney (1-OH) to form calcitriol, which promotes intestinal Ca2+ absorption.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::fat-soluble-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults?
column4: Without adequate vitamin D/calcitriol, intestinal calcium absorption falls, leading to poor bone mineralization. PTH rises to compensate, further demineralizing bone.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::fat-soluble-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the antioxidant fat-soluble vitamin that protects cell membranes?
column4: Vitamin E scavenges reactive oxygen species within lipid bilayers, preventing lipid peroxidation. Deficiency can cause hemolytic anemia and peripheral neuropathy.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::fat-soluble-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which fat-soluble vitamin, in excess, is most acutely toxic?
column4: Excess vitamin A (hypervitaminosis A) causes headache, liver damage, and teratogenicity. Vitamins D and K can also be toxic in excess, but vitamin A toxicity is classically tested.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::fat-soluble-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the basic four-ring steroid nucleus called?
column4: All steroids share this fused ring system: three six-membered rings (A, B, C) and one five-membered ring (D). Functional groups and side chains distinguish individual steroids.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::steroids MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What steroid is the precursor to all steroid hormones?
column4: Cholesterol is converted to pregnenolone (the first committed step) by the desmolase enzyme in the mitochondria of steroidogenic cells.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::steroids MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Name the five classes of steroid hormones.
column4: These are produced by the adrenal cortex (first three) and gonads (all five). Vitamin D and bile salts are also steroid derivatives.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::steroids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How do steroid hormones exert their effects on target cells?
column3: Diffuse into cell; bind intracellular receptor; complex enters nucleus to alter transcription
column4: Steroids are lipophilic and cross the plasma membrane freely. The hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, typically increasing or decreasing gene expression.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::steroids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the function of bile salts?
column3: Emulsify dietary fats in the small intestine to aid digestion and absorption
column4: Bile salts are cholesterol derivatives synthesized in the liver. Their amphipathic structure allows them to form micelles around fat droplets, increasing lipase access.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::steroids MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does cholesterol differ structurally from other steroids?
column3: Retains an 8-carbon side chain at C-17 and a hydroxyl at C-3
column4: Steroid hormones are derived by modifying/removing cholesterol's side chain and adding/altering oxygenated functional groups. The intact side chain characterizes cholesterol itself.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::steroids MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What are prostaglandins derived from?
column4: Arachidonic acid, released from membrane phospholipids by PLA2, is converted to prostaglandins by cyclooxygenase (COX). Prostaglandins are eicosanoids.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::prostaglandins-bc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What enzyme converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins?
column4: COX has two activities: cyclooxygenase (adds two O2 to arachidonic acid) and peroxidase. NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen) inhibit COX to reduce prostaglandin synthesis.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::prostaglandins-bc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does aspirin inhibit COX differently from ibuprofen?
column3: Aspirin: irreversible acetylation of COX; ibuprofen: reversible competitive inhibition
column4: Aspirin covalently acetylates Ser530 in COX-1/COX-2, permanently blocking the active site. Ibuprofen binds reversibly. This explains aspirin's lasting antiplatelet effect.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::prostaglandins-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What are the major physiological effects of prostaglandins?
column3: Inflammation, pain sensitization, fever, vasodilation/constriction, uterine contraction
column4: Prostaglandins act as local (paracrine/autocrine) mediators. Different prostaglandin subtypes (PGE2, PGI2, TXA2) have distinct and sometimes opposing vascular effects.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::prostaglandins-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What class of signaling molecules includes prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes?
column4: All eicosanoids are 20-carbon lipid mediators derived from arachidonic acid (or other 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acids). They act locally and are rapidly inactivated.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::prostaglandins-bc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Why are prostaglandins NOT considered classical hormones?
column3: They act locally (paracrine/autocrine), not via blood transport to distant targets
column4: Classical hormones are released into the bloodstream to act on distant target organs. Prostaglandins are synthesized and act near their site of production with very short half-lives.
column8: concept::CP::5D::lipids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::lipids::prostaglandins-bc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the general molecular formula for a monosaccharide?
column4: Carbohydrates are defined by this empirical formula, where n ≥ 3. The ratio of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen is 1:2:1.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carbohydrates MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carbohydrates::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What functional groups define an aldose monosaccharide?
column4: Aldoses carry a terminal aldehyde (C1) plus hydroxyl groups on remaining carbons. Glucose is the classic aldose.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carbohydrates MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carbohydrates::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What functional groups define a ketose monosaccharide?
column4: Ketoses have a ketone at C2 (usually) plus hydroxyl groups. Fructose is the most prominent biological ketose.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carbohydrates MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carbohydrates::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the minimum carbon number for a monosaccharide, and what is it called?
column4: Glyceraldehyde (aldotriose) and dihydroxyacetone (ketotriose) are the simplest monosaccharides and important metabolic intermediates.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carbohydrates MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carbohydrates::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which property of monosaccharides allows them to reduce Fehling's or Benedict's reagent?
column4: Reducing sugars oxidize the Cu²⁺ to Cu⁺ (brick-red precipitate). All monosaccharides are reducing sugars.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carbohydrates MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carbohydrates::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What structural feature makes all monosaccharides with n ≥ 2 carbons (except dihydroxyacetone) chiral?
column4: A chiral carbon has four different substituents. Glyceraldehyde (3C aldose) has one chiral center; glucose has four.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carbohydrates MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carbohydrates::description MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How many stereoisomers does a monosaccharide with n chiral centers have?
column4: Glucose has 4 chiral centers → 2^4 = 16 stereoisomers (8 pairs of enantiomers). This applies to open-chain forms.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carbohydrates MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carbohydrates::description MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What suffix denotes an aldose sugar in IUPAC-based carbohydrate nomenclature?
column4: All monosaccharides end in -ose. Prefix 'ald-' or 'aldo-' specifies an aldehyde carbon; prefix 'keto-' or 'ul-' specifies a ketone.

column1: Name the 6-carbon aldose that is the primary fuel for cellular respiration.
column4: D-Glucose (dextrose) is the most abundant monosaccharide and the central molecule of glycolysis and many metabolic pathways.

column1: What is the common name for the 6-carbon ketose that is a component of sucrose?
column4: D-Fructose (levulose) has its ketone at C2. It is sweeter than glucose and found in fruits and table sugar (sucrose).

column1: Classify galactose by carbon number and carbonyl type.
column4: Galactose is a C4 epimer of glucose. It differs only in the orientation of the -OH at C4.

column1: What is the term for a 5-carbon monosaccharide?
column4: Ribose and deoxyribose are the biologically critical pentoses, forming the backbone of RNA and DNA respectively.

column1: What monosaccharide is classified as a 2-deoxyaldopentose?
column4: Deoxyribose lacks an -OH at C2 (replaced by -H), which gives DNA its greater chemical stability compared to RNA.

column1: What distinguishes an aldopentose from a ketopentose in naming?
column3: Aldopentose has C1 aldehyde; ketopentose has C2 ketone
column4: Ribose is an aldopentose; ribulose is a ketopentose. Both have 5 carbons but differ in carbonyl position.

column1: In carbohydrate nomenclature, what does the prefix D- or L- indicate?
column3: Absolute configuration of the highest-numbered chiral carbon
column4: D/L designation is based on comparison to D-glyceraldehyde. Most naturally occurring sugars are D-configuration.

column1: What is the reference compound for assigning D/L configuration to carbohydrates?
column4: D-Glyceraldehyde has the -OH on the right in Fischer projection. D-sugars have the same configuration at the highest-numbered chiral carbon.

column1: In a Fischer projection of a D-sugar, where is the -OH group at the highest-numbered chiral carbon?
column4: If the -OH at the reference chiral carbon points right in the Fischer projection, the sugar is D. Left = L-configuration.

column1: How many chiral centers does D-glucose have in its open-chain form?
column4: Glucose carbons C2, C3, C4, and C5 are all chiral. C1 (aldehyde) and C6 (CH2OH) are not chiral in the open chain.

column1: What term describes two stereoisomers that differ in configuration at ALL chiral centers?
column4: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. Diastereomers differ at SOME but not all chiral centers (e.g., epimers).

column1: What is the R/S configuration at C1 of beta-D-glucopyranose?
column4: In beta-D-glucopyranose, the anomeric -OH is equatorial and above the ring plane; by CIP rules this C1 is R. Alpha-D-glucopyranose C1 is S.

column1: What type of ring does glucose preferentially form in aqueous solution?
column4: Glucose cyclizes via intramolecular hemiacetal formation between C1 (aldehyde) and C5 (-OH), creating a stable 6-membered ring called glucopyranose.

column1: What bond forms when glucose cyclizes to a pyranose?
column4: The C1 aldehyde reacts with the C5 hydroxyl to form a cyclic hemiacetal. C1 becomes the anomeric carbon with a new -OH group.

column1: What is the most stable ring conformation of beta-D-glucopyranose?
column4: In the 4C1 chair, all bulky -OH groups and the -CH2OH group are equatorial, minimizing steric strain. This makes glucose exceptionally stable.

column1: In a Haworth projection of D-glucose, which groups are written below the ring plane?
column3: Groups on the right in Fischer projection (typically -OH groups)
column4: Fischer 'right' → Haworth 'below'; Fischer 'left' → Haworth 'above'. The CH2OH at C6 is above the ring for D-sugars.

column1: What is a furanose ring, and which hexose commonly forms one?
column4: Fructose cyclizes between C2 (ketone) and C5 (-OH) to form a 5-membered furanose ring. Ribose also commonly forms a furanose.

column1: What percentage of glucose in aqueous solution exists in the open-chain (aldehyde) form?
column4: Glucose exists predominantly as pyranose ring forms (~99%). The small open-chain fraction is what reacts with oxidizing reagents and proteins (glycation).

column1: In the 4C1 chair of beta-D-glucopyranose, what is the orientation of the C1 anomeric -OH?
column4: Beta anomer: anomeric -OH is equatorial (trans to C5 substituent). Alpha anomer: anomeric -OH is axial. Equatorial is lower energy.

column1: What are epimers?
column3: Diastereomers differing in configuration at exactly one chiral center
column4: Glucose and galactose are C4 epimers; glucose and mannose are C2 epimers. Epimers are a subset of diastereomers.

column1: At which carbon do alpha and beta anomers of glucose differ in configuration?
column4: Anomers are epimers that differ only at the anomeric carbon (C1 for aldoses, C2 for ketoses), created during ring formation.

column1: In alpha-D-glucopyranose, where is the anomeric -OH relative to the ring (Haworth)?
column4: Alpha: anomeric -OH is on the same side as the ring oxygen substituent (below in Haworth for D-sugars). Beta: anomeric -OH is above.

column1: What process allows alpha and beta anomers of glucose to interconvert in solution?
column4: Mutarotation proceeds through the open-chain aldehyde intermediate. The optical rotation of a fresh glucose solution changes until equilibrium (~36% alpha, ~64% beta) is reached.

column1: What is the C4 epimer of glucose?
column4: Galactose differs from glucose only in the configuration of the -OH at C4. This difference matters in galactosemia, where galactose cannot be metabolized.

column1: What enzyme converts galactose to glucose-1-phosphate in the Leloir pathway?
column4: This enzyme interconverts UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, enabling galactose to enter glycolysis. Deficiency causes galactosemia.

column1: At equilibrium in water, what approximate ratio of alpha to beta exists for D-glucose?
column4: Beta-D-glucopyranose is favored at equilibrium because its anomeric -OH is equatorial in the 4C1 chair, giving lower steric energy.

column1: What type of bond connects two monosaccharides in a glycoside?
column4: A glycosidic bond forms when the anomeric -OH of one sugar reacts with an -OH of another molecule, releasing water. It is an acetal (not hemiacetal).

column1: What conditions hydrolyze a glycosidic bond?
column3: Acidic aqueous conditions or specific glycosidase enzymes
column4: Glycosidic bonds are acetals, stable to base but hydrolyzed by dilute acid or enzymatically. Each glycosidase is specific to alpha or beta linkages.

column1: Why does a glycoside NOT mutarotate or reduce Fehling's reagent?
column3: Anomeric carbon is locked in acetal form (no free carbonyl)
column4: Once the glycosidic bond forms, C1 is an acetal rather than a hemiacetal, so it cannot open to expose the aldehyde. Reducing ability requires a free carbonyl.

column1: What enzyme hydrolyzes the alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds in starch?
column4: Salivary and pancreatic alpha-amylases cleave internal alpha-1,4 bonds in amylose and amylopectin, producing maltose and dextrins.

column1: What enzyme in lysosomes hydrolyzes beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds in glycogen, and what disease results from its deficiency?
column4: Pompe disease is a lysosomal storage disorder. Absence of GAA causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation, particularly in muscle and heart.

column1: What is the product of complete acid hydrolysis of a disaccharide?
column4: Acid hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic acetal bond by adding water across C-O. For example, sucrose yields glucose + fructose.

column1: What is keto-enol tautomerism in monosaccharides?
column3: Interconversion between carbonyl (keto/aldo) form and enediol form
column4: Under basic conditions, monosaccharides form an enediol intermediate at C1-C2. This allows interconversion of aldoses and ketoses (epimerization).

column1: What is the enediol intermediate in monosaccharide tautomerism?
column3: A diol with a C=C double bond (cis-enediol)
column4: The enediol has -OH groups on adjacent doubly bonded carbons. It forms when base removes an alpha-hydrogen, enabling tautomeric interconversion.

column1: Under what conditions do monosaccharides undergo keto-enol tautomerism?
column4: Bases abstract the alpha-hydrogen adjacent to the carbonyl, forming an enolate/enediol. Acid conditions favor the carbonyl tautomer.

column1: What is the Lobry de Bruyn–Van Ekenstein rearrangement?
column3: Base-catalyzed interconversion of glucose, fructose, and mannose via enediol
column4: All three hexoses share a common C1-C2 enediol intermediate under basic conditions, explaining their interconversion. Relevant to the phosphoglucose isomerase mechanism.

column1: How does phosphoglucose isomerase convert glucose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate?
column4: This glycolysis step uses an enediol mechanism (analogous to keto-enol tautomerism) to interconvert an aldose phosphate and a ketose phosphate.

column1: What two monosaccharides compose sucrose, and what type of glycosidic bond joins them?
column4: Sucrose is joined at both anomeric carbons (C1 of glucose, C2 of fructose), making it a NON-reducing sugar — neither anomeric -OH is free.

column1: What two monosaccharides compose lactose, and what linkage joins them?
column4: Lactose (milk sugar) has free anomeric -OH on glucose, making it a reducing sugar. Lactase cleaves this bond; lactase deficiency causes lactose intolerance.

column1: What two monosaccharides compose maltose, and what linkage joins them?
column4: Maltose is a reducing sugar (free C1-OH on the second glucose). It is produced by amylase digestion of starch and is found in malted grains.

column1: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar?
column3: Both anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic bond
column4: Since neither free anomeric -OH exists, sucrose cannot open to expose a carbonyl group and cannot reduce Cu²⁺ in Benedict's/Fehling's test.

column1: What is trehalose, and why is it a non-reducing sugar?
column3: Glucose-alpha-1,1-alpha-glucose disaccharide; both anomeric carbons bonded
column4: Like sucrose, trehalose links two anomeric carbons, leaving no free reducing end. It serves as an energy storage and stress-protectant sugar in insects and fungi.

column1: What enzyme cleaves the beta-1,4-glycosidic bond in lactose?
column4: Lactase is expressed in the brush border of the small intestine. Its deficiency (lactase non-persistence) is the most common cause of lactose intolerance.

column1: What is the main storage polysaccharide in plants?
column4: Amylose is an unbranched alpha-1,4-linked polymer; amylopectin adds alpha-1,6 branches every 24-30 glucose units. Both are digested by amylase.

column1: What type of glycosidic linkage is found in cellulose?
column4: Beta-1,4 linkages cause cellulose chains to adopt a linear, hydrogen-bonded structure ideal for structural rigidity. Humans lack the cellulase enzyme to digest it.

column1: What structural feature makes glycogen more highly branched than amylopectin?
column3: Alpha-1,6 branch points every 8-12 residues (vs. 24-30 in amylopectin)
column4: More branch points in glycogen allow simultaneous release of glucose from many ends by glycogen phosphorylase, enabling rapid glucose mobilization.

column1: What enzyme cleaves alpha-1,6 branch points in glycogen degradation?
column4: Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds; the debranching enzyme then cleaves the alpha-1,6 branch point, releasing free glucose.

column1: Which polysaccharide is a structural component of the exoskeleton of arthropods?
column4: Chitin is a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine linked by beta-1,4 bonds. It is the second most abundant polysaccharide in nature after cellulose.

column1: What monosaccharide is the repeating unit of cellulose?
column4: Adjacent glucose units in cellulose are rotated 180° relative to each other due to the beta-1,4 linkage, creating a flat, ribbon-like, highly crystalline structure.

column1: What is the repeating disaccharide unit of hyaluronic acid?
column4: Hyaluronic acid is a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) in connective tissue and synovial fluid. Its high negative charge attracts water, giving it lubricating properties.

column1: What functional group defines an aldehyde?
column3: Carbonyl (C=O) at terminal carbon with one H
column4: Aldehydes have the general structure R-CHO, where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen. This terminal position distinguishes them from ketones.

column1: What functional group defines a ketone?
column3: Carbonyl (C=O) flanked by two carbon groups
column4: Ketones have the structure R-CO-R', where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two organic (non-hydrogen) substituents. Acetone (dimethyl ketone) is the simplest example.

column1: What is the general molecular formula suffix indicating the presence of an aldehyde group in IUPAC nomenclature?
column4: The parent chain is numbered so the aldehyde carbon receives the lowest possible number (always C-1). Example: propanal (3-carbon aldehyde).

column1: Which hybridization state is the carbonyl carbon in aldehydes and ketones?
column4: The sp2 carbonyl carbon forms a planar trigonal geometry (120° bond angles) with a pi bond to oxygen. This geometry is critical for understanding nucleophilic attack.

column1: Why is the carbonyl carbon electrophilic?
column3: Oxygen withdraws electron density via the C=O dipole
column4: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, creating a partial positive charge (δ+) on the carbonyl carbon, making it susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

column1: Which suffix is used for ketones in IUPAC nomenclature?
column4: The position of the carbonyl is indicated by a number (e.g., pentan-2-one). The parent chain must be the longest chain containing the carbonyl group.

column1: What is the IUPAC name for CH3CHO?
column4: The parent chain is ethane (2 carbons); the aldehyde suffix -al replaces the final -e. Common name is acetaldehyde.

column1: What is the common name for propan-2-one?
column4: Acetone (dimethyl ketone) is the simplest ketone and a common solvent. Its IUPAC name is propan-2-one.

column1: When numbering a chain containing both an aldehyde and another functional group, which group receives priority for lowest locant?
column4: Aldehydes rank above ketones, alcohols, and amines in IUPAC priority, so the aldehyde carbon is always C-1. This determines the numbering direction of the chain.

column1: What prefix is used when the CHO group cannot be included in the parent chain?
column3: formyl- (or oxo- for C=O in general)
column4: When the aldehyde carbon is a substituent rather than part of the principal chain, 'formyl-' is used. This is a less common MCAT scenario but appears in complex ring systems.

column1: Do aldehydes or ketones have higher boiling points compared to equivalent-MW alkanes?
column4: The polar C=O bond creates dipole-dipole interactions absent in alkanes, raising the boiling point significantly. However, they lack O-H bonds so cannot hydrogen-bond with each other.

column1: Can aldehydes and ketones hydrogen-bond with water?
column4: The carbonyl oxygen accepts H-bonds from water's O-H groups, making small aldehydes/ketones water-soluble. They cannot donate H-bonds because they lack O-H or N-H bonds.

column1: Why do aldehydes and ketones have lower boiling points than alcohols of similar molecular weight?
column3: Alcohols can donate and accept H-bonds; carbonyls only accept
column4: Alcohols engage in stronger, more extensive hydrogen bonding (both donor and acceptor) than carbonyl compounds, which can only accept. This raises alcohol boiling points relative to comparable aldehydes/ketones.

column1: How does carbon chain length affect the water solubility of aldehydes and ketones?
column3: Solubility decreases as chain length increases
column4: Short-chain aldehydes/ketones (≤4 carbons) are miscible with water. Longer chains increase hydrophobic character, reducing solubility despite the polar carbonyl group.

column1: Which has a higher boiling point: an aldehyde or a ketone of the same molecular formula?
column4: Ketones have greater London dispersion forces due to the additional alkyl group, and their dipole moments tend to be slightly larger than aldehydes of the same molecular weight, marginally raising the boiling point.

column1: What is the most characteristic reaction type of the carbonyl group in aldehydes and ketones?
column4: The electrophilic carbonyl carbon undergoes attack by nucleophiles, with the pi bond breaking and the oxygen retaining both electrons as an alkoxide. This is distinct from acyl substitution seen in carboxylic acid derivatives.

column1: Which is more reactive toward nucleophilic addition: aldehydes or ketones?
column4: Aldehydes have less steric hindrance (one H vs. two alkyl groups) and less electron donation to the carbonyl, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic and accessible. This is a high-yield MCAT distinction.

column1: What reagent converts an aldehyde or ketone to an alcohol?
column4: NaBH4 (mild, selective) and LiAlH4 (strong) both deliver hydride (H-) to the carbonyl carbon. Aldehydes yield 1° alcohols; ketones yield 2° alcohols.

column1: What product forms when an aldehyde is treated with Tollens' reagent?
column4: Tollens' reagent (Ag(NH3)2+) oxidizes aldehydes to carboxylates while reducing Ag+ to Ag0 (silver mirror). Ketones do not react — this is a key distinguishing test.

column1: What product results from Wittig reaction of an aldehyde or ketone?
column4: The Wittig reagent (phosphonium ylide) replaces the C=O double bond with a C=C double bond. This is a carbon-carbon bond-forming reaction used to create alkenes with defined geometry.

column1: What is the first step of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl group?
column3: Nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon
column4: The nucleophile (Nu-) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, breaking the C=O pi bond. Electrons shift to oxygen, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.

column1: What geometry does the carbonyl carbon adopt after nucleophilic addition?
column4: The carbonyl carbon converts from planar sp2 to tetrahedral sp3 after nucleophilic attack. This geometry change is key to understanding addition-elimination mechanisms at carbonyls.

column1: Under what pH conditions is nucleophilic addition to carbonyls generally fastest?
column3: Neutral to mildly basic (depends on nucleophile)
column4: Acid catalysis protonates the carbonyl oxygen, increasing electrophilicity; base conditions deprotonate to generate better nucleophiles. The optimal pH depends on the specific reaction and nucleophile pKa.

column1: What intermediate forms when a primary amine attacks a carbonyl group before losing water?
column4: The amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon forming a tetrahedral carbinolamine (R2C(OH)(NHR')). Dehydration then yields an imine. This two-step process is acid-catalyzed.

column1: Which nucleophiles can add to carbonyls without requiring a leaving group step?
column4: Simple addition nucleophiles (H-, RLi, RMgX, CN-) add and protonate to give stable alcohol products. No leaving group departs, distinguishing addition from addition-elimination.

column1: What is a hemiacetal?
column3: Product of one alcohol adding to an aldehyde carbonyl
column4: A hemiacetal (R-CH(OH)(OR')) forms when one equivalent of alcohol adds to an aldehyde. It contains both an OH and an OR group on the same carbon. It is in equilibrium with the open-chain form.

column1: What is an acetal?
column3: Product of two alcohols adding to an aldehyde (loss of water)
column4: Acetals (R-CH(OR')2) form from hemiacetals by acid-catalyzed reaction with a second alcohol and loss of water. They are stable under basic conditions but hydrolyze under acid — used as protecting groups.

column1: Under what conditions are acetals stable and under what conditions do they hydrolyze?
column3: Stable in base/neutral; hydrolyze in acid
column4: Acetals are resistant to nucleophiles and base but readily hydrolyze under acidic aqueous conditions back to the aldehyde/ketone. This makes them excellent carbonyl protecting groups in synthesis.

column1: What type of catalyst is required for acetal formation from a hemiacetal?
column4: Acid protonates the hemiacetal OH, converting it to a good leaving group (water). The resulting oxocarbenium ion is then attacked by a second alcohol to form the acetal.

column1: What is the equivalent of an acetal when formed from a ketone instead of an aldehyde?
column4: Ketals have two OR groups on the same carbon derived from a ketone carbonyl. The terms acetal/ketal are sometimes used interchangeably for the product class R2C(OR')2 in modern IUPAC.

column1: What is an imine (Schiff base)?
column3: C=N bond formed by condensation of primary amine with carbonyl
column4: Imines (R2C=NR') result from reaction of a primary amine with an aldehyde or ketone, losing water. They are important in biochemistry (e.g., Schiff bases in pyridoxal phosphate reactions).

column1: What type of amine reacts with a carbonyl to form an enamine?
column4: Secondary amines (R2NH) cannot form imines (no N-H to remain after double bond forms). Instead, they form enamines — compounds with C=C adjacent to N — by loss of an alpha proton.

column1: What is the structural difference between an imine and an enamine?
column3: Imine: C=N; enamine: C=C-N (nitrogen on adjacent carbon)
column4: Imines have the nitrogen directly doubly bonded to the former carbonyl carbon. Enamines shift the double bond to the alpha position (C=C) with the nitrogen on the beta carbon.

column1: At what pH is imine formation fastest?
column4: Acid protonates the carbonyl to increase electrophilicity, facilitating amine attack. Too much acid protonates the amine (reducing its nucleophilicity), so a mildly acidic optimum exists.

column1: What biochemical role do imines (Schiff bases) play in amino acid metabolism?
column4: PLP (vitamin B6) forms a Schiff base with amino acids via its aldehyde group and the amino group of the substrate. Imine hydrolysis/formation is central to transamination.

column1: What does NaBH4 do to an aldehyde or ketone?
column3: Reduces carbonyl to alcohol by delivering hydride (H-)
column4: NaBH4 is a mild hydride source that selectively reduces aldehydes and ketones. Aldehydes yield primary alcohols; ketones yield secondary alcohols. It does not reduce esters or carboxylic acids.

column1: Which hydride reagent is stronger: NaBH4 or LiAlH4?
column4: LiAlH4 (LAH) is a much stronger reducing agent that reduces nearly all carbonyl-containing functional groups including esters, carboxylic acids, and amides. NaBH4 only reduces aldehydes and ketones.

column1: What solvent is required for LiAlH4 reductions, and why?
column3: Anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether); reacts violently with water/protic solvents
column4: LiAlH4 reacts exothermically with protic solvents (water, alcohols), destroying the reagent and posing safety hazards. Anhydrous ethereal solvents are essential; aqueous workup is done carefully at the end.

column1: What product forms when a ketone is reduced with LiAlH4 followed by aqueous workup?
column4: Hydride delivery to the ketone carbonyl carbon gives an alkoxide, which is protonated during aqueous workup to yield a secondary alcohol (two R groups on the carbinol carbon).

column1: Which face of a prochiral ketone does hydride preferentially attack in a rigid ring system?
column4: In cyclohexanone, hydride (NaBH4) attacks axially from the equatorial direction, typically giving the more stable equatorial alcohol as the major product, illustrating steric control of stereochemistry.

column1: What is a cyanohydrin?
column3: Product of HCN addition to an aldehyde or ketone
column4: Cyanohydrins (R2C(OH)CN) form when cyanide ion (CN-) adds to a carbonyl group, followed by protonation. The product has a hydroxyl group and a nitrile on the same carbon.

column1: What base conditions favor cyanohydrin formation?
column3: Slightly basic (to generate CN- from HCN)
column4: HCN itself is a weak acid; a small amount of base deprotonates HCN to yield CN-, the actual nucleophile. Strongly basic conditions can reverse the reaction; strongly acidic conditions protonate CN-, preventing addition.

column1: How can a cyanohydrin be converted to an alpha-hydroxy acid?
column3: Hydrolyze the nitrile group with H3O+/H2O or base
column4: The nitrile (C≡N) of a cyanohydrin is hydrolyzed under acidic or basic aqueous conditions to a carboxylic acid, yielding an alpha-hydroxy acid. This is a classic carbon chain elongation strategy.

column1: Why do ketones form cyanohydrins less readily than aldehydes?
column3: Greater steric hindrance around the ketone carbonyl
column4: Two alkyl groups on the ketone carbonyl create more steric crowding for CN- attack compared to an aldehyde (one alkyl, one H). Additionally, alkyl groups donate electrons, making the carbonyl less electrophilic.

column1: What reagent oxidizes aldehydes but NOT ketones?
column4: Aldehydes are readily oxidized to carboxylic acids; ketones cannot be oxidized under mild conditions without C-C bond cleavage. Tollens' (silver mirror) and Fehling's/Benedict's (Cu2+ reduction) are classic aldehyde-specific tests.

column1: What is the product when an aldehyde is oxidized under mild aqueous conditions?
column4: Oxidation of RCHO gives RCOOH. Common mild oxidants: Tollens', Fehling's, KMnO4(dilute), or even O2/air. No carbon skeleton rearrangement occurs.

column1: What does Benedict's test detect, and what indicates a positive result?
column3: Reducing sugars (and aldehydes); brick-red Cu2O precipitate
column4: Benedict's reagent contains Cu2+ in alkaline solution. Aldehydes (and reducing sugars with free aldehyde/hemiacetal) reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ (Cu2O), forming a red-orange precipitate.

column1: What strong oxidant can oxidize ketones, and what products result?
column3: Hot KMnO4 or HNO3; cleavage products (smaller carboxylic acids)
column4: Ketones resist mild oxidation but are cleaved by vigorous oxidants on either side of the carbonyl, giving two carboxylic acid fragments. This is rarely used preparatively but appears in MCAT as a distinction.

column1: What are alpha (α) carbons in the context of carbonyl compounds?
column3: Carbon atoms directly adjacent to the carbonyl carbon
column4: Alpha hydrogens on the α-carbon are acidic (pKa ~20 for ketone α-H) due to stabilization of the resulting carbanion by the adjacent carbonyl group.

column1: What is an enolate ion?
column3: Conjugate base formed by deprotonation of an α-carbon
column4: Removing an α-H from a carbonyl compound generates an enolate — a resonance-stabilized carbanion. The negative charge is delocalized between the α-carbon and the carbonyl oxygen.

column1: Why are α-hydrogens of carbonyl compounds more acidic than typical C-H bonds?
column3: Enolate anion is stabilized by resonance with C=O
column4: Deprotonation at the α-carbon yields an enolate whose negative charge is delocalized onto the more electronegative oxygen, stabilizing the carbanion. Typical alkane C-H pKa ~50; ketone α-H pKa ~20.

column1: What is the role of LDA (lithium diisopropylamide) in enolate chemistry?
column3: Strong, hindered base that quantitatively and kinetically deprotonates α-H
column4: LDA (pKa ~36) is a strong, non-nucleophilic base that completely deprotonates ketones at the α-position at low temperature, giving the kinetic enolate. It is too bulky to add to the carbonyl.

column1: What is the keto-enol tautomerism equilibrium, and which form predominates for most simple ketones?
column3: Keto and enol forms interconvert; keto form predominates (~99%)
column4: Most simple ketones exist >99% in the keto form because C=O is stronger than C=C. However, enol content increases with conjugation (e.g., beta-keto esters) or aromatization driving force.

column1: What structural feature dramatically increases the enol content of a carbonyl compound?
column4: In 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds (e.g., acetylacetone), the enol form is stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding and conjugation with the second carbonyl, raising enol content to ~80%.

column1: How does keto-enol tautomerism lead to α-racemization?
column3: Enolization produces sp2 α-carbon, which can reprotonate from either face
column4: When a chiral center at the α-carbon undergoes enolization, the planar enol/enolate intermediate loses its stereochemistry. Reprotonation from either face gives a racemic mixture at that center.

column1: What catalysts facilitate keto-enol tautomerism?
column4: Acid catalysis involves protonation of the carbonyl oxygen followed by deprotonation at α-carbon. Base catalysis involves direct deprotonation at the α-carbon by hydroxide to form the enolate.

column1: What is the aldol condensation?
column3: Self-condensation of carbonyl compounds via α-carbon forming a β-hydroxy carbonyl
column4: An enolate from one carbonyl compound attacks the carbonyl of a second, forming a β-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone (aldol product). Heating dehydrates the aldol to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl.

column1: What is the retro-aldol reaction?
column3: Reverse of the aldol: cleavage of β-hydroxy carbonyl into two carbonyl fragments
column4: Retro-aldol cleaves a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound at the C-C bond between the α and β carbons, regenerating an enolate and a carbonyl compound. It is important in biochemistry (e.g., aldolase in glycolysis).

column1: What is the product of dehydration of the aldol addition product?
column4: Loss of water from the β-hydroxy carbonyl (β-OH and α-H) gives a conjugated C=C-C=O system. This is the condensation product — more stable due to conjugation.

column1: What enzyme in glycolysis performs a retro-aldol reaction?
column4: Aldolase cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate via a retro-aldol mechanism. In class I aldolases, a Schiff base intermediate forms with a lysine residue.

column1: What are the conditions for a crossed (mixed) aldol condensation to be synthetically useful?
column3: One reactant has no α-H (cannot form enolate)
column4: If one carbonyl compound lacks α-hydrogens (e.g., benzaldehyde, formaldehyde), it can only serve as the electrophile. This avoids statistical mixtures and gives a single crossed product.

column1: What is the kinetic enolate?
column3: Enolate formed faster (less substituted α-carbon; strong, hindered base, low T)
column4: Kinetic enolate forms at the less hindered α-carbon (less substituted, statistically accessible) under conditions of rapid, irreversible deprotonation (LDA, -78°C). It may not be the more stable enolate.

column1: What is the thermodynamic enolate?
column3: More stable enolate (more substituted α-carbon; weak base, equilibrating conditions)
column4: Thermodynamic enolate forms at the more substituted α-carbon and is the more stable regioisomer. It is favored under conditions of reversible deprotonation (weak base, room temperature, protic solvent).

column1: Which enolate does LDA at -78°C preferentially form for 2-methylcyclohexanone?
column4: LDA is a strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base that deprotonates the less hindered, less substituted α-carbon rapidly and irreversibly. This gives the kinetic enolate product.

column1: What conditions favor the thermodynamic enolate?
column3: Weak base (e.g., KOtBu or NaOEt), protic solvent, room temperature
column4: Thermodynamic control allows reversible proton transfer until the most stable (more substituted) enolate accumulates. Higher temperature and equilibrating conditions also favor the thermodynamic product.

column1: Why does the thermodynamic enolate favor the more substituted position?
column3: More substituted enolate is more stable due to hyperconjugation/alkyl stabilization
column4: Alkyl substituents at the α-carbon stabilize the developing negative charge through hyperconjugation, making the more substituted enolate lower in energy and thermodynamically preferred.

column1: Which carbonyl compound is more reactive toward nucleophilic addition: formaldehyde or acetaldehyde?
column4: Formaldehyde has two H substituents and no alkyl groups to provide steric hindrance or electron donation, making its carbonyl carbon maximally electrophilic and accessible.

column1: How does electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) on the carbonyl affect its reactivity toward nucleophiles?
column3: EWG increases reactivity (increases electrophilicity of carbonyl carbon)
column4: EWGs withdraw electrons from the carbonyl carbon, amplifying its partial positive charge (δ+) and making it a better electrophile. Example: trifluoroacetaldehyde is far more reactive than acetaldehyde.

column1: Why are carboxylic acid derivatives (esters, amides) less reactive toward nucleophilic addition-elimination than ketones?
column3: Lone pair donation from heteroatom stabilizes C=O (resonance)
column4: In esters and amides, the OR or NR2 lone pairs donate into the carbonyl, reducing electrophilicity. Aldehydes and ketones lack such resonance stabilization, making them more reactive toward addition.

column1: What determines whether nucleophilic addition stops at the tetrahedral intermediate or proceeds to substitution?
column3: Presence or absence of a leaving group on the carbonyl carbon
column4: If the tetrahedral intermediate has a good leaving group (e.g., OR in esters), elimination regenerates the C=O (substitution). Aldehydes/ketones have no leaving group, so addition products are stable.

column1: How does increasing steric bulk of substituents affect carbonyl reactivity?
column3: Steric hindrance decreases reactivity toward nucleophilic addition
column4: Bulky groups around the carbonyl carbon physically block nucleophile approach to the electrophilic carbon, slowing addition. This is why di-tert-butyl ketone is essentially unreactive toward most nucleophiles.

column1: Which ketone is more reactive: acetone or pinacolone (3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one)?
column4: Pinacolone has a bulky tert-butyl group adjacent to the carbonyl, severely hindering nucleophilic attack. Acetone has only methyl groups, offering much less steric protection.

column1: How does conjugation (e.g., in an enone) affect carbonyl reactivity at the carbonyl carbon?
column4: In alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyls, resonance extends the electrophilicity to the beta-carbon. Hard nucleophiles prefer 1,2-addition to C=O; soft nucleophiles prefer 1,4-conjugate addition (Michael addition).

column1: What is the approximate pKa of α-hydrogens in a simple ketone?
column4: The α-H of a ketone (pKa ~20) is much more acidic than a typical C-H bond (pKa ~50) because the resulting enolate is resonance-stabilized by the adjacent C=O group.

column1: Which α-H is more acidic: that adjacent to a ketone or adjacent to an ester?
column3: Ketone α-H (slightly more acidic; pKa ~20 vs ~25 for ester)
column4: The ester carbonyl is partially deactivated by lone pair donation from the OR oxygen, making the enolate of an ester slightly less stable than a ketone enolate. Beta-keto esters (~11) are most acidic.

column1: Why is the pKa of alpha-H in a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound (e.g., acetylacetone) ~9-11?
column3: Enolate is doubly stabilized by resonance with two carbonyl groups
column4: The carbanion between two C=O groups is stabilized by two resonance structures, each delocalizing charge onto an electronegative oxygen. This raises acidity dramatically, approaching that of a phenol.

column1: What is a carbanion, and why is the alpha carbanion of a carbonyl especially stable?
column3: Carbon bearing a negative charge; stabilized by adjacent C=O resonance (enolate)
column4: Carbanions are generally high-energy, unstable species. The alpha-carbanion of a carbonyl is unusually stable because the negative charge delocalizes onto the more electronegative oxygen through pi conjugation, forming an enolate.

column1: What functional group defines an alcohol?
column3: Hydroxyl group (-OH) bonded to sp3 carbon
column4: Alcohols have the general formula R-OH where the oxygen is attached to a carbon that is not part of a carbonyl. This distinguishes them from carboxylic acids and phenols.

column1: What hybridization does the oxygen adopt in an alcohol?
column4: The oxygen in an alcohol has two lone pairs and two bonding pairs, giving it tetrahedral electron geometry (sp3 hybridization), similar to water.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How are alcohols classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary?
column3: By number of carbons attached to the carbon bearing -OH
column4: Primary (1°): one alkyl group on the C-OH carbon; secondary (2°): two; tertiary (3°): three. Classification affects reactivity in oxidation and substitution.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which class of alcohol cannot be oxidized by common oxidizing agents (e.g., PCC, Jones)?
column4: Tertiary alcohols have no alpha hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so they cannot be oxidized without breaking C-C bonds. Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidized readily.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the general IUPAC suffix for alcohols?
column4: The -ol suffix replaces the terminal -e of the parent alkane. The position of the -OH group is given the lowest possible locant.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: In IUPAC nomenclature, what is the priority rule for numbering the carbon chain in an alcohol?
column4: The chain is numbered from the end nearest the hydroxyl group. This supersedes the rule for double bonds in most cases on the MCAT.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the IUPAC name for CH3CH2OH?
column4: Two-carbon chain (eth-) with an -ol suffix. Ethanol is the alcohol in beverages and is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetaldehyde.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What prefix or descriptor is used when -OH is a substituent rather than the principal functional group?
column4: When a higher-priority group (e.g., carboxylic acid) is present, -OH is named as a substituent using the prefix hydroxy-.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does glycerol's IUPAC name reflect its three hydroxyl groups?
column4: The suffix -triol indicates three -OH groups. Glycerol is the backbone of triglycerides and phospholipids.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Why do alcohols have much higher boiling points than alkanes of similar molecular weight?
column4: The O-H bond is highly polar, enabling hydrogen bonds (O...H-O). These require significant energy to break, raising the boiling point substantially compared to nonpolar alkanes.

column1: What is the approximate pKa of a simple aliphatic alcohol?
column4: Alcohols are weak acids (pKa ~16-18). Water has pKa ~15.7, making alcohols slightly weaker acids than water. Phenol (pKa ~10) is much more acidic.

column1: How does electron-withdrawing substitution affect alcohol acidity?
column4: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the alkoxide anion (conjugate base) by inductive withdrawal of electron density, making the alcohol more willing to donate its proton.

column1: Which is more acidic: ethanol or trifluoroethanol (CF3CH2OH)?
column4: The three fluorine atoms are strongly electron-withdrawing via induction, stabilizing the alkoxide conjugate base and lowering the pKa to ~12.4 vs ~16 for ethanol.

column1: Why does branching in an alcohol decrease acidity compared to a less-branched isomer?
column3: Alkyl groups are electron-donating, destabilizing the alkoxide
column4: More alkyl groups push electron density onto the oxygen of the alkoxide, making it less stable (higher energy) and thus making the alcohol less acidic. Tertiary alcohols are least acidic.

column1: What type of hydrogen bonding can alcohols engage in with water?
column3: Both donor and acceptor hydrogen bonds
column4: The -OH can donate its hydrogen to water (donor) and the oxygen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from water (acceptor), explaining why small alcohols are miscible with water.

column1: What is the product of reacting a primary alcohol with PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate)?
column4: PCC is a mild oxidizing agent that oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes but does not further oxidize to carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::oxidation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the product of oxidizing a primary alcohol with Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4) or KMnO4?
column4: Strong oxidizing agents (Jones, KMnO4, K2Cr2O7/H+) oxidize primary alcohols all the way to carboxylic acids, passing through the aldehyde stage.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::oxidation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the product of oxidizing a secondary alcohol?
column4: Secondary alcohols (R2CHOH) are oxidized to ketones (R2C=O) by PCC, Jones, KMnO4, or other standard oxidants. Further oxidation would require C-C bond cleavage.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::oxidation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which oxidation state change occurs at carbon when a primary alcohol is oxidized to an aldehyde?
column3: Carbon goes from -1 to +1 (net oxidation of +2)
column4: In a primary alcohol (RCH2OH) the carbon is at oxidation state -1; in an aldehyde (RCHO) it is +1. Loss of two hydrogen atoms (as hydride equivalents) is the formal oxidation.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::oxidation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What biological enzyme class catalyzes the oxidation of alcohols in metabolism?
column4: Alcohol dehydrogenase uses NAD+ as cofactor to oxidize ethanol to acetaldehyde, transferring a hydride to NAD+ to form NADH. This is the first step in ethanol metabolism.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::oxidation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the Swern oxidation used for?
column3: Oxidize primary alcohols to aldehydes (mild, anhydrous conditions)
column4: Swern oxidation uses oxalyl chloride and DMSO, followed by triethylamine. It is preferred for acid- or base-sensitive substrates because it avoids aqueous chromium reagents.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::oxidation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Under what conditions does an alcohol undergo an SN1 reaction?
column3: Secondary or tertiary alcohol with strong acid (H2SO4, HBr, HCl), carbocation intermediate
column4: Protonation of -OH makes water a leaving group. The carbocation intermediate then reacts with the nucleophile. Tertiary > secondary in SN1 rate due to carbocation stability.

column1: Why must the -OH group be protonated or converted to a better leaving group before SN2 on an alcohol?
column3: OH- is a poor leaving group; water (H2O) is a good leaving group
column4: The hydroxide ion is a strong base and poor leaving group (pKa of H2O ~15.7). Protonation converts it to water, a weak base and excellent leaving group.

column1: What is the stereochemical outcome of SN2 substitution at an alcohol carbon?
column4: The nucleophile attacks from the back face of the carbon bearing the leaving group, inverting the stereocenter. This is a hallmark of SN2 mechanisms.

column1: Which reagent converts an alcohol to an alkyl halide via SN2 with inversion, using a sulfonate intermediate?
column3: Tosyl chloride (TsCl) or mesyl chloride (MsCl), then nucleophilic halide
column4: The alcohol is first tosylated or mesylated (good leaving group installed), then SN2 displacement by halide (e.g., LiBr) gives the alkyl halide with inversion.

column1: What rearrangement can occur during SN1 reactions of secondary alcohols?
column4: After protonation and loss of water, a secondary carbocation can rearrange to a more stable tertiary carbocation via 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shift before nucleophile attacks.

column1: What reaction converts an alcohol to an alkyl halide using thionyl chloride (SOCl2)?
column3: Nucleophilic substitution giving alkyl chloride + SO2 + HCl
column4: SOCl2 reacts with the -OH to form a chlorosulfite intermediate, which undergoes internal ion pair SN2 (retention with pyridine) or SN1. Reaction is driven by loss of SO2 gas.

column1: What is the purpose of protecting an alcohol during a multi-step synthesis?
column3: Prevent -OH from reacting with other reagents in subsequent steps
column4: A protecting group masks the alcohol's reactivity while other functional groups are manipulated. The protecting group must be easily removed (deprotected) after the needed transformation.

column1: What common protecting group is used for alcohols, and what reagent installs it?
column4: Reaction of an alcohol with dihydropyran (DHP) under acid catalysis forms a tetrahydropyranyl (THP) ether. Removal uses dilute aqueous acid.

column1: What reagent is used to install a TMS (trimethylsilyl) ether protecting group on an alcohol?
column4: TMS ethers (R-O-Si(CH3)3) are common silyl protecting groups. They are removed by fluoride ion (e.g., TBAF) or mild aqueous acid, exploiting the strong Si-F bond as driving force.

column1: What condition removes a TMS ether protecting group?
column3: Fluoride ion (TBAF) or dilute aqueous acid
column4: The Si-F bond (~135 kcal/mol) is very strong, driving fluoride-mediated deprotection. Mild acid hydrolysis also works. This selectivity allows deprotection in the presence of other functional groups.

column1: What is a benzyl (Bn) ether protecting group, and how is it removed?
column4: Benzyl ethers are stable to many conditions but cleaved by catalytic hydrogenation. This orthogonal removal makes them useful when other protecting groups (e.g., TMS) need to remain intact.

column1: What is an acetate ester used as in alcohol protection, and how is it removed?
column3: Alcohol + acetic anhydride; removed by base (saponification)
column4: Acetylation (Ac2O, pyridine) forms an ester that protects the alcohol. Mild base (K2CO3/MeOH) selectively cleaves the ester without harming other groups.

column1: What is a mesylate (OMs)?
column4: Mesylates are formed by reacting an alcohol with methanesulfonyl chloride (MsCl) and a base (Et3N). The mesylate is an excellent leaving group for SN2 and elimination reactions.

column1: What is a tosylate (OTs)?
column4: Tosylates are formed with tosyl chloride (TsCl) and pyridine. The sulfonyl group withdraws electron density, making the oxygen an excellent leaving group comparable to a halide.

column1: What base is typically used when preparing a tosylate from an alcohol and TsCl?
column3: Pyridine (acts as base and nucleophilic catalyst)
column4: Pyridine neutralizes the HCl generated in the reaction and can activate TsCl as an acylpyridinium intermediate. The reaction proceeds at room temperature.

column1: What is the stereochemical outcome at the alcohol carbon when it is converted to a mesylate or tosylate?
column4: Mesylation/tosylation replaces -OH with -OMs/-OTs at the same carbon with retention because the C-O bond is NOT broken during ester formation; the O-H bond is broken instead.

column1: Why are mesylates and tosylates better substrates for SN2 than the parent alcohol?
column3: The sulfonate is a much better leaving group than -OH or -O-
column4: The leaving group ability tracks with the stability of the departing anion. Mesylate and tosylate anions are stabilized by resonance delocalization onto the sulfonyl oxygens, making them excellent leaving groups.

column1: What overall two-step sequence converts (R)-2-butanol to (S)-2-bromobutane with inversion?
column4: Mesylation retains configuration at C2. SN2 by bromide inverts the mesylate carbon. Net result: two stereospecific steps convert R alcohol to S bromide cleanly.

column1: What are the important reactions of alcohols on the MCAT? (Name four)
column4: Alcohols are versatile: they oxidize to aldehydes/ketones/acids, dehydrate to alkenes with acid, undergo nucleophilic substitution after activation, and form esters with acids or acid chlorides.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::important-reactions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What reagent and conditions cause an alcohol to undergo dehydration to an alkene?
column4: Protonation of -OH forms water as a leaving group; subsequent E1 (or E2 with good geometry) gives the alkene. Follows Zaitsev's rule — most substituted alkene is major product.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::important-reactions MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the product of a Fischer esterification reaction involving an alcohol?
