column4: Fischer esterification is acid-catalyzed condensation of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol. It is reversible; excess alcohol or removal of water drives it to completion.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::important-reactions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the product when an alcohol reacts with a strong base such as NaH?
column4: NaH is a strong, non-nucleophilic base that deprotonates the alcohol O-H bond, forming the sodium alkoxide and releasing hydrogen gas. Alkoxides are used in Williamson ether synthesis.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::important-reactions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is Williamson ether synthesis?
column3: SN2 of an alkoxide with a primary alkyl halide to form an ether
column4: R-O-Na + R'-X → R-O-R' + NaX. The alkoxide (strong nucleophile/base) must react with a primary halide to avoid E2 competition. Gives asymmetric ethers.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::important-reactions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the product when an alcohol reacts with an acid chloride (RCOCl) and pyridine?
column4: Acid chlorides are more reactive than carboxylic acids toward esterification. Pyridine acts as a base to neutralize HCl and prevent acid-catalyzed side reactions.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::important-reactions MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Which alcohol oxidation product (aldehyde vs. ketone) is more susceptible to further oxidation, and why?
column3: Aldehyde; it has an abstractable C-H on the carbonyl carbon
column4: Aldehydes (RCHO) can be oxidized to carboxylic acids because the carbonyl carbon still bears a hydrogen. Ketones lack this hydrogen and resist further oxidation without C-C cleavage.
column8: concept::CP::5D::alcohols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::alcohols::important-reactions MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What functional group defines a carboxylic acid?
column4: The carboxyl group is a carbonyl (C=O) directly attached to a hydroxyl (–OH). Both oxygen atoms are bonded to the same carbon.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the hybridization of the carboxyl carbon in a carboxylic acid?
column4: The carboxyl carbon forms a double bond with oxygen, requiring sp2 hybridization and a planar geometry around that carbon.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What makes carboxylic acids more acidic than alcohols?
column3: Resonance stabilization of the carboxylate anion
column4: After losing H+, the negative charge is delocalized over both oxygens via resonance, greatly stabilizing the conjugate base compared to an alkoxide.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the typical pKa range for simple carboxylic acids?
column4: Most aliphatic carboxylic acids have pKa ~4–5 (acetic acid pKa 4.76). Electron-withdrawing substituents lower the pKa further.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How does an electron-withdrawing group alpha to a carboxylic acid affect its pKa?
column4: EWGs stabilize the carboxylate anion by inductive withdrawal of electron density, making the acid stronger (e.g., chloroacetic acid pKa 2.86 vs. acetic acid 4.76).
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::description MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the IUPAC suffix for a carboxylic acid?
column4: The parent chain is named by replacing the terminal '-e' of the alkane with '-oic acid' (e.g., propane → propanoic acid). The carboxyl carbon is always C-1.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the common name for ethanoic acid?
column4: Many simple carboxylic acids retain trivial names on the MCAT: formic (methanoic), acetic (ethanoic), propionic (propanoic), butyric (butanoic).
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the common name for methanoic acid?
column4: Formic acid (HCOOH) is the simplest carboxylic acid, found in ant venom. It is also called methanoic acid by IUPAC.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: How are dicarboxylic acids named by IUPAC?
column3: '-dioic acid' suffix on the parent chain
column4: Example: HOOC–COOH is ethanedioic acid (oxalic acid). Both carboxyl carbons are counted in the chain.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What prefix is used when a –COOH group is attached to a ring?
column4: When the ring carbon is not counted (e.g., cyclohexanecarboxylic acid), the suffix '-carboxylic acid' is appended to the ring name.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::nomenclature MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Why do carboxylic acids have unusually high boiling points compared to similar-MW compounds?
column4: Carboxylic acids form stable cyclic dimers through two O–H···O=C hydrogen bonds, effectively doubling molecular mass and raising the boiling point significantly.

column1: Are short-chain carboxylic acids (C1–C4) soluble in water?
column4: Short-chain acids form hydrogen bonds with water. Solubility decreases as the nonpolar alkyl chain lengthens beyond C4–C5.

column1: How does the boiling point of acetic acid compare to 1-propanol (similar MW)?
column4: Acetic acid dimerizes via two hydrogen bonds, giving it an effectively higher intermolecular force than the single H-bond of an alcohol.

column1: What happens to the water solubility of carboxylic acids as chain length increases?
column4: The hydrophobic alkyl portion dominates over the hydrophilic –COOH for longer chains; fatty acids (C12+) are essentially insoluble in water.

column1: How does introducing a double bond into a fatty acid affect its melting point?
column4: cis double bonds introduce kinks that prevent tight packing; unsaturated fatty acids are liquid at room temperature while saturated ones are solid.

column1: What is the product when a carboxylic acid reacts with a strong base (e.g., NaOH)?
column4: Acid-base neutralization: RCOOH + NaOH → RCOONa + H2O. Carboxylate salts are water-soluble ionic compounds.

column1: What type of reaction converts a carboxylic acid to an ester?
column4: RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O under acidic conditions; the reaction is reversible and equilibrium-driven.

column1: What reagent converts a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride?
column4: SOCl2 + RCOOH → RCOCl + SO2 + HCl. Acid chlorides are the most reactive acyl derivatives.

column1: What is the product of reacting a carboxylic acid with ammonia followed by heating?
column4: RCOOH + NH3 → RCOONH4 (salt); heating dehydrates to RCONH2. Amides are less reactive than acids.

column1: What nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon in acyl substitution reactions of carboxylic acids?
column4: In nucleophilic acyl substitution, the –OH of the carboxyl is the leaving group after tetrahedral intermediate collapse; this is the general mechanism for ester and amide formation.

column1: What is the mechanism for carboxylic acid reactions with nucleophiles?
column4: Attack on the electrophilic carbonyl carbon forms a tetrahedral intermediate, then collapse expels the leaving group (–OH), regenerating the carbonyl.

column1: Which carbon of a carboxylic acid is electrophilic?
column4: The carbonyl carbon bears a partial positive charge due to the electron-withdrawing effect of two oxygens, making it susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

column1: How does acid catalysis facilitate esterification?
column3: Protonates carbonyl oxygen, activating it toward nucleophilic attack
column4: Protonation of C=O makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic, allowing the weak nucleophile (alcohol) to attack; the mechanism proceeds through a protonated tetrahedral intermediate.

column1: What is the role of the tetrahedral intermediate in nucleophilic acyl substitution?
column3: Transient intermediate before leaving group expulsion
column4: After nucleophile addition, a tetrahedral sp3 carbon forms transiently; collapse by expelling the leaving group restores the carbonyl and completes substitution.

column1: Why are carboxylic acids less reactive toward nucleophiles than aldehydes/ketones?
column3: –OH is a poor leaving group; resonance donates electron density to carbonyl
column4: In carboxylic acids, the lone pair on the –OH oxygen donates into the carbonyl, reducing electrophilicity. Aldehydes/ketones lack this effect and have no leaving group pathway.

column1: What is a lactam?
column4: Lactams are formed by intramolecular reaction of an amino group with a carboxylic acid; beta-lactams (4-membered rings) are the core of penicillin antibiotics.

column1: What is a lactone?
column4: Lactones form by intramolecular esterification; five- and six-membered lactones (gamma and delta) are especially stable due to ring strain considerations.

column1: How is a carboxylic acid anhydride formed?
column4: RCOOH + HOOCR' → RCOOCOR' + H2O. Anhydrides are highly reactive acylating agents; acetic anhydride is a common reagent.

column1: What is the reactivity order of carboxylic acid derivatives toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
column4: Reactivity decreases as the leaving group becomes worse (Cl– > RCOO– > RO– > NH2–) and resonance donation to the carbonyl increases.

column1: What ring size makes lactones and lactams most stable?
column4: Five- and six-membered rings have minimal ring strain; four-membered beta-lactams are strained but reactive (important in antibiotics like penicillin).

column1: What reagent reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol?
column4: LiAlH4 is a powerful hydride reducing agent that reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols (–CH2OH). NaBH4 is NOT strong enough to reduce carboxylic acids.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::reduction MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: Can NaBH4 reduce carboxylic acids?
column4: NaBH4 is a mild reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones but cannot reduce carboxylic acids or esters. LiAlH4 is required.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::reduction MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is the product of LiAlH4 reduction of a carboxylic acid?
column4: RCOOH + LiAlH4 → RCH2OH after aqueous workup. The carboxyl carbon (oxidation state +3) is reduced to an alcohol carbon (oxidation state –1).
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::reduction MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What reagent selectively reduces a carboxylic acid to an aldehyde?
column4: DIBAL-H at low temperature stops reduction at the aldehyde stage; at room temperature or with excess, it reduces to the primary alcohol.
column8: concept::CP::5D::carboxylic_acids MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::carboxylic-acids::reduction MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC

column1: What is decarboxylation?
column3: Loss of CO2 from a carboxylic acid
column4: Decarboxylation converts –COOH to –H plus CO2 gas. It occurs most readily with beta-keto acids and malonic acid derivatives.

column1: What structural feature makes a compound susceptible to decarboxylation?
column4: A carbonyl group two carbons from the carboxylic acid allows a six-membered cyclic transition state for concerted CO2 loss and enol formation.

column1: What is the mechanism of beta-keto acid decarboxylation?
column3: Six-membered cyclic transition state; concerted CO2 loss and proton transfer
column4: The carbonyl oxygen and –COOH participate in a pericyclic-like six-membered TS; the product is an enol that tautomerizes to the ketone.

column1: What is the malonic ester synthesis used to make?
column4: Malonic ester synthesis alkylates diethyl malonate, then hydrolyzes and decarboxylates to give a monosubstituted acetic acid product.

column1: Why do amino acids undergo decarboxylation to form biogenic amines?
column4: Amino acid decarboxylases (PLP-dependent) remove the alpha-carboxyl group; e.g., histidine → histamine, DOPA → dopamine — important in neurotransmitter synthesis.

column1: What position is the 'alpha' carbon in a carboxylic acid?
column3: Carbon directly adjacent to the carboxyl group (C-2)
column4: Greek letter nomenclature: alpha = C-2 (next to –COOH), beta = C-3, etc. The alpha carbon is central to enolization and substitution reactions.

column1: What makes alpha hydrogens of carboxylic acids acidic?
column3: Adjacent carboxyl group stabilizes the alpha carbanion (enolate)
column4: The carbonyl withdraws electron density; loss of an alpha H gives a resonance-stabilized enolate. pKa of alpha-H in carboxylic acids is ~20–25.

column1: What is Hell-Volhard-Zelinskii (HVZ) reaction?
column3: Alpha-halogenation of carboxylic acids with X2/PBr3 (or PCl3)
column4: PBr3 converts the acid to an acid bromide in situ; alpha-bromination occurs at the more reactive acid bromide; hydrolysis regenerates the alpha-halo acid.

column1: What is the product of the HVZ reaction on propanoic acid with Br2/PBr3?
column4: Bromination occurs selectively at the alpha carbon (C-2) via the acid bromide intermediate; after hydrolysis, an alpha-bromo carboxylic acid is obtained.

column1: Why cannot carboxylic acids be directly halogenated at the alpha position with Br2 alone (unlike ketones)?
column3: Carboxylic acids require PBr3/PCl3 to first form reactive acid halide intermediate
column4: Direct enolization of carboxylic acids is slow because the acidic medium disfavors enolate formation; the acid halide intermediate formed with PBr3 enolizes more readily.

column1: What nucleophile can attack an alpha halo acid to give an alpha amino acid (Strecker-related)?
column4: SN2 displacement of the alpha halogen by NH3 gives an alpha-amino acid; this is a key step in alpha-amino acid synthesis from alpha-halo acids.

column1: What functional group defines an acid anhydride?
column3: Two acyl groups linked by an oxygen (R-CO-O-CO-R')
column4: Anhydrides are formed by formal loss of water from two carboxylic acids. They are highly reactive acid derivatives.

column1: What functional group is present in an amide?
column4: Amides include primary (NH2), secondary (NHR), and tertiary (NR2) variants. The N lone pair donates into the carbonyl, making amides the least reactive acid derivative.

column1: What functional group defines an ester?
column3: Carbonyl bonded to an alkoxy group (R-CO-OR')
column4: Esters are derived from carboxylic acids reacting with alcohols. They are common in fats, oils, and many fragrances.

column1: Which acid derivative contains the linkage -CO-O-CO-?
column4: The anhydride linkage joins two carbonyl groups through a bridging oxygen. Acetic anhydride is a classic example.

column1: How do lactones differ from open-chain esters?
column4: The hydroxyl and carboxyl groups are within the same molecule, forming a ring upon intramolecular esterification.

column1: What suffix is used for esters in IUPAC nomenclature?
column4: The alcohol-derived portion is named as the alkyl group (e.g., methyl), and the acid portion drops -ic acid for -ate (e.g., methyl acetate).

column1: What suffix is used for amides in IUPAC nomenclature?
column4: The parent acid name drops -oic acid (or -ic acid) and gains -amide (e.g., ethanamide for acetamide).

column1: What suffix denotes an acid anhydride?
column4: Symmetric: acetic anhydride; mixed: acetic propionic anhydride. Both parent acid names are listed before the word 'anhydride'.

column1: How are N-substituents designated in amide nomenclature?
column4: For example, N-methylacetamide indicates a methyl group on the nitrogen of acetamide. Multiple N-substituents use N,N-.

column1: What is the IUPAC name for CH3COOC2H5?
column4: The ethyl comes from ethanol; ethanoate (acetate) is the acyl portion from acetic acid.

column1: Compared to carboxylic acids, what is the general trend in boiling points of esters?
column3: Esters have lower boiling points than corresponding carboxylic acids
column4: Esters cannot hydrogen bond to each other (no O-H), only via dipole-dipole interactions, so they boil at lower temperatures than acids of similar molecular weight.

column1: Can amides form hydrogen bonds with water?
column3: Yes — both as H-bond donors and acceptors
column4: Primary and secondary amides have N-H groups that donate H-bonds; the carbonyl oxygen accepts H-bonds. This makes primary amides relatively high boiling.

column1: Why do amides have unusually high boiling points relative to other acid derivatives of similar MW?
column3: Strong intermolecular H-bonding via N-H and C=O
column4: Primary amides can form two H-bonds per molecule. This extensive H-bonding network raises the boiling point significantly.

column1: Are esters generally soluble in water?
column3: Small esters are water-soluble; large esters are not
column4: Esters can accept H-bonds from water via their carbonyl oxygen, so short-chain esters dissolve. Larger hydrophobic R groups reduce solubility.

column1: Why do tertiary amides have lower boiling points than primary amides of similar MW?
column3: Tertiary amides lack N-H bonds, so no H-bond donation
column4: Without N-H, intermolecular H-bonding is weaker, lowering the boiling point compared to primary or secondary amides.

column1: What reaction produces an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol?
column4: Concentrated H2SO4 or HCl catalyzes the reversible condensation; water is the byproduct. Removing water drives equilibrium toward ester.

column1: What is saponification?
column3: Base-catalyzed (irreversible) hydrolysis of an ester to carboxylate and alcohol
column4: NaOH converts an ester to a carboxylate salt plus alcohol. It is irreversible because the carboxylate is resonance-stabilized and a poor electrophile.

column1: What reaction converts an amide to a carboxylic acid under acidic aqueous conditions?
column4: Prolonged heating with aqueous HCl or H2SO4 cleaves the amide bond, yielding the carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.

column1: What product forms when an anhydride reacts with an alcohol?
column3: An ester and a carboxylic acid
column4: One acyl group is transferred to the alcohol oxygen; the other portion becomes the free carboxylic acid. This is nucleophilic acyl substitution.

column1: What product results from reacting an anhydride with ammonia (or a primary amine)?
column3: An amide and a carboxylate (ammonium salt)
column4: The amine acts as a nucleophile, attacking one carbonyl of the anhydride; the other carboxylate is released as the byproduct.

column1: What is the general mechanism for nucleophilic acyl substitution?
column3: Nucleophile attacks carbonyl → tetrahedral intermediate → leaving group departs
column4: Unlike SN2, the carbonyl carbon is sp2. A tetrahedral (sp3) intermediate forms, then collapses as the leaving group is expelled.

column1: What is the tetrahedral intermediate in nucleophilic acyl substitution?
column3: An sp3 carbon bearing the incoming nucleophile, oxygen (from C=O), and the leaving group
column4: The carbonyl C=O becomes C-O⁻ as the nucleophile bonds. Collapse restores the carbonyl and expels the leaving group.

column1: In nucleophilic acyl substitution, what makes a good leaving group on the acyl carbon?
column4: The weaker the base (lower pKa of conjugate acid), the better the leaving group. Cl⁻ (pKa ~−7) is excellent; NH2⁻ (pKa ~35) is very poor.

column1: Under acidic conditions, how is nucleophilic acyl substitution activated for esters?
column3: Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen increases electrophilicity of carbonyl carbon
column4: H⁺ on O makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic, facilitating nucleophilic attack. The mechanism involves a protonated tetrahedral intermediate.

column1: What is transesterification?
column3: Exchange of the alkoxy group of an ester with another alcohol
column4: R-COOR' + R''OH ⇌ R-COOR'' + R'OH. Catalyzed by acid or base; used industrially to make biodiesel from triglycerides and methanol.

column1: Is transesterification reversible?
column3: Yes — it is an equilibrium reaction
column4: Excess of the incoming alcohol or removal of the product alcohol can drive the reaction toward the desired product.

column1: What catalyst is typically used for base-catalyzed transesterification?
column4: The alkoxide is a stronger nucleophile than alcohol; it attacks the ester carbonyl to give a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to exchange groups.

column1: In biodiesel production, what type of reaction converts triglycerides to fatty acid methyl esters?
column4: Three transesterification reactions replace the glycerol backbone esters with methyl esters, releasing glycerol as the byproduct.

column1: How does Le Chatelier's principle apply to transesterification?
column3: Excess alcohol or removal of product alcohol shifts equilibrium toward product ester
column4: Because both ester and alcohol exist on both sides, driving off one product or flooding with one reactant shifts the equilibrium.

column1: What are the products of acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of an amide?
column4: Aqueous H+ protonates the amine leaving group. The ammonium ion is the final amine product under acidic conditions.

column1: What are the products of base-catalyzed hydrolysis of an amide?
column4: OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl; the amine (not ammonium) is released because the basic conditions keep it deprotonated.

column1: Why is amide hydrolysis slower than ester hydrolysis?
column3: Nitrogen lone pair donates into carbonyl, reducing electrophilicity
column4: The nitrogen resonance (partial double bond character of C-N) makes the carbonyl less electrophilic, slowing nucleophilic attack.

column1: What conditions are required for complete amide hydrolysis?
column3: Prolonged heating with concentrated acid or base
column4: Unlike esters, amides require harsh conditions (reflux with 6M HCl or NaOH) due to the stabilizing N lone pair donation.

column1: Why is base-catalyzed hydrolysis of an amide effectively irreversible?
column3: Carboxylate ion is a poor electrophile; amine will not re-attack
column4: The negatively charged carboxylate repels nucleophiles. The driving force is formation of the stable carboxylate anion.

column1: In nucleophilic acyl substitution, which factor determines overall reactivity of acid derivatives?
column3: Electrophilicity of carbonyl carbon and leaving group ability
column4: A more electrophilic carbonyl and a better leaving group (weaker conjugate base) both increase reaction rate.

column1: What is the general order of reactivity of acid derivatives toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
column3: Anhydride > ester > amide (acid chloride most reactive overall)
column4: Acid chlorides > anhydrides > esters > amides. Leaving group ability (Cl⁻ > RCOO⁻ > RO⁻ > NH2⁻) parallels reactivity.

column1: Why can more reactive acid derivatives convert less reactive ones, but not vice versa?
column3: Reactions proceed toward the more stable (less reactive) product
column4: An acid chloride reacts with an alcohol to give an ester, but an ester does not spontaneously convert back to an acid chloride under the same conditions.

column1: In what direction do interconversions among acid derivatives typically proceed?
column3: Higher reactivity → lower reactivity (downhill in reactivity)
column4: Just as water flows downhill, acid derivative interconversions are thermodynamically driven toward the less reactive (more stable) product.

column1: What does it mean for an acid derivative to be 'activated' for nucleophilic substitution?
column3: Its carbonyl carbon is more electrophilic and its leaving group is more stable
column4: Activation lowers the energy of the transition state. Anhydrides and acid chlorides are 'activated' relative to amides.

column1: Which acid derivative is the most reactive toward nucleophilic substitution?
column4: Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group (conjugate acid HCl, pKa ~−7), and the electron-withdrawing Cl increases carbonyl electrophilicity.

column1: Which acid derivative is the least reactive toward nucleophilic substitution?
column4: NH2⁻ is a very poor leaving group (pKa of NH3 ~35), and the N lone pair donates electron density into the carbonyl, reducing electrophilicity.

column1: Place acid derivatives in order of decreasing reactivity: ester, amide, anhydride, acid chloride.
column4: This ranking reflects both leaving group ability and carbonyl electrophilicity. Acid chlorides are used to synthesize all others.

column1: Why is an anhydride more reactive than an ester?
column3: RCOO⁻ is a better leaving group than RO⁻
column4: The carboxylate (pKa ~5) is more stable (weaker base) than an alkoxide (pKa ~16), making it a superior leaving group.

column1: Why is an ester more reactive than an amide toward nucleophilic substitution?
column3: RO⁻ is a better leaving group than NH2⁻; N lone pair donation reduces electrophilicity more than O lone pair
column4: Nitrogen's lone pair is more available for resonance donation than oxygen's (lower electronegativity), making the amide carbonyl less electrophilic.

column1: How does increasing steric bulk near the carbonyl carbon affect nucleophilic acyl substitution?
column3: Bulky groups slow the reaction by hindering nucleophile approach
column4: The transition state for nucleophilic attack requires approaching the planar carbonyl. Steric crowding raises the activation energy.

column1: Does steric bulk in the leaving group affect reactivity of acid derivatives?
column3: Yes — bulkier leaving groups can slow departure from the tetrahedral intermediate
column4: Steric strain in the tetrahedral intermediate can disfavor product formation. However, leaving group electronic stability is usually more important.

column1: Why do tertiary esters hydrolyze more slowly than primary esters?
column3: Bulky alkyl groups on the oxygen hinder nucleophilic attack at the carbonyl
column4: A tert-butyl ester has three methyl groups near the reaction site, sterically blocking approach of water or other nucleophiles.

column1: How do steric effects influence regioselectivity when a nucleophile attacks an asymmetric anhydride?
column3: Attack at the less hindered (less bulky) carbonyl is preferred
column4: The nucleophile approaches the less sterically crowded acyl carbon more easily, giving the less hindered acyl product predominantly.

column1: How do electron-withdrawing groups on the acyl carbon affect reactivity in nucleophilic acyl substitution?
column3: Electron-withdrawing groups increase electrophilicity → increase reactivity
column4: EWGs remove electron density from the carbonyl carbon, making it more susceptible to nucleophilic attack and raising the reaction rate.

column1: How does lone pair donation from nitrogen into the carbonyl affect amide reactivity?
column4: The partial C=N double bond character from resonance lowers the positive character of the carbonyl carbon, slowing nucleophilic attack.

column1: Which is a better resonance donor into a carbonyl: nitrogen or oxygen?
column3: Nitrogen (less electronegative, lone pair more available)
column4: Oxygen's lone pairs are held tighter due to higher electronegativity, so it donates less effectively than nitrogen into the adjacent carbonyl.

column1: How does an electron-withdrawing group on the leaving group (e.g., halogen on alcohol) affect ester reactivity?
column3: Makes leaving group more stable → increases reactivity
column4: EWGs stabilize the negative charge on the departing alkoxide, lowering its basicity and making it a better leaving group.

column1: Why does trifluoroethyl ester hydrolyze faster than ethyl ester?
column3: CF3 group stabilizes the trifluoroethoxide leaving group (EWG lowers pKa)
column4: Trifluoroethanol (pKa ~12.4) is more acidic than ethanol (pKa ~16), so trifluoroethoxide is a better leaving group.

column1: What is a beta-lactam?
column4: The four-membered ring has ~90° bond angles, creating significant angle strain. Beta-lactams are the pharmacophore of penicillin and cephalosporin antibiotics.

column1: Why are beta-lactams highly reactive toward ring-opening?
column3: Ring strain from the four-membered ring increases carbonyl electrophilicity
column4: Angle strain destabilizes the beta-lactam ring. Nucleophilic attack relieves ring strain, making beta-lactams far more reactive than acyclic amides.

column1: How do beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit bacteria?
column3: They acylate the active-site serine of transpeptidase (penicillin-binding protein)
column4: The reactive beta-lactam ring opens and forms a covalent bond with the bacterial enzyme's serine, irreversibly inhibiting cell wall synthesis.

column1: What type of ring strain is present in beta-lactams that is absent in five- or six-membered lactams?
column4: Four-membered rings force bond angles far from the ideal 120° for sp2 carbons. Five- and six-membered lactams (gamma- and delta-lactams) are much more stable.

column1: How does ring strain in beta-lactams affect the resonance donation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl?
column3: Ring geometry prevents optimal orbital overlap, reducing nitrogen resonance donation
column4: In a planar amide, the N lone pair aligns with the carbonyl pi system. The strained four-membered ring distorts this alignment, making the carbonyl more electrophilic.

column1: What class of organic compound is a phenol?
column4: Phenols have a benzene ring directly bonded to an -OH group. The aromatic ring stabilizes the phenoxide anion, making phenols more acidic than aliphatic alcohols.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is hydroquinone?
column4: Hydroquinone has two -OH groups at the 1 and 4 positions of benzene. It is the fully reduced form of benzoquinone and acts as a 2-electron donor in redox reactions.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the oxidized form of hydroquinone?
column4: Hydroquinone loses 2 electrons and 2 protons to form benzoquinone. This reversible 2e–/2H+ redox couple is a key feature of biological electron carriers.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How many electrons are transferred in the hydroquinone/quinone redox reaction?
column4: The hydroquinone-to-quinone conversion is a 2-electron, 2-proton oxidation. This distinguishes quinone-based carriers from one-electron carriers like cytochromes (iron-based).
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is ubiquinone (coenzyme Q)?
column3: Lipid-soluble benzoquinone electron carrier in the inner mitochondrial membrane
column4: Ubiquinone (CoQ) shuttles electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III in the electron transport chain. Its long isoprenoid tail anchors it in the lipid bilayer.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the fully reduced form of ubiquinone called?
column4: Ubiquinol is the hydroquinone form of coenzyme Q, carrying 2 electrons and 2 protons. It donates electrons to Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex).
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Why are phenols more acidic than aliphatic alcohols?
column3: Resonance stabilization of the phenoxide anion by the aromatic ring
column4: The negative charge on phenoxide is delocalized into the benzene ring via resonance, lowering the pKa (~10) compared to aliphatic alcohols (~16-18).
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the semiquinone radical?
column3: One-electron intermediate between quinone and hydroquinone
column4: Semiquinone (Q•–) is a radical anion formed when a quinone accepts only one electron. It is a reactive intermediate in the Q cycle of Complex III.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which complexes in the electron transport chain directly reduce ubiquinone to ubiquinol?
column4: NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (Complex I) and succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (Complex II) both donate electrons to CoQ, converting it to CoQH2.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What property of ubiquinone allows it to diffuse freely within the inner mitochondrial membrane?
column4: The isoprenoid side chain (10 isoprene units in CoQ10) makes ubiquinone highly lipophilic, enabling lateral diffusion within the lipid bilayer to shuttle electrons between complexes.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the pKa range of a typical phenol?
column4: Phenol itself has a pKa of ~10. Electron-withdrawing substituents (e.g., nitro groups) lower pKa further; electron-donating groups raise it. This is much lower than aliphatic alcohols (~16).
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: In the hydroquinone/quinone redox couple, what happens to the two protons during oxidation?
column4: The oxidation of hydroquinone to benzoquinone involves loss of 2H+ and 2e–. In biological systems this proton release contributes to the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which vitamin is structurally related to ubiquinone and functions in blood clotting?
column4: Vitamin K contains a naphthoquinone ring system and undergoes the same 2e– hydroquinone/quinone redox cycling. It acts as a cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What distinguishes a quinone from a phenol structurally?
column3: Quinone has two C=O groups; phenol has one -OH on an aromatic ring
column4: Quinones are cyclic diketones (not aromatic), while phenols are aromatic with -OH groups. The hydroquinone-to-quinone conversion therefore involves loss of aromaticity in the product.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: Which electron transport chain complex oxidizes ubiquinol back to ubiquinone?
column4: Complex III accepts electrons from CoQH2, passes them through the Q cycle involving cytochrome b and cytochrome c1, and ultimately reduces cytochrome c. The semiquinone intermediate is key.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: How does an electron-withdrawing group on a phenol ring affect its acidity?
column4: Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., -NO2, -CN) stabilize the phenoxide anion further by additional resonance or induction, making the phenol more willing to donate its proton.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What is the standard reduction potential (E°') of the ubiquinone/ubiquinol couple approximately?
column4: The CoQ/CoQH2 couple has E°' near +0.045 V, placing it between the NADH/NAD+ couple (–0.32 V) and cytochrome c (+ 0.23 V), consistent with electron flow direction in the ETC.
column8: concept::CP::5D::phenols MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5D::phenols::oxidation-and-reduction-e-g-hydroquinones-ubiquinones-biological-2e-redox-centers MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::OC MCAT::discipline::BC

column1: What type of compound is pyridine?
column3: Six-membered aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen
column4: Pyridine's nitrogen lone pair is in the plane of the ring (part of sigma system), not contributing to aromaticity, leaving the pi system intact. It is a weak base (pKa ~5.2 of conjugate acid).

column1: What is the aromatic heterocycle that forms the core of the purine ring system?
column4: Purines (adenine, guanine) contain a pyrimidine ring fused to an imidazole ring, giving a bicyclic 9-atom system with 4 nitrogens total.

column1: Which nucleobases are purines?
column4: Purines have the fused bicyclic structure; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) are monocyclic. Remember: Pure As Gold (Purines: Adenine, Guanine).

column1: Which nucleobases are pyrimidines?
column4: Pyrimidines are six-membered rings with two nitrogens at positions 1 and 3. Thymine is found in DNA; uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

column1: What makes imidazole aromatic?
column3: Five-membered ring with 6 pi electrons; N-H nitrogen donates lone pair
column4: The N-H nitrogen donates its lone pair into the pi system, while the imine nitrogen's lone pair is in the plane. This fulfills Huckel's rule (4n+2, n=1).

column1: What is the pKa of the imidazole side chain of histidine, and why is it biologically significant?
column3: ~6.0; can be protonated/deprotonated at physiological pH
column4: The pKa near 7 means histidine's imidazole ring acts as a proton shuttle in enzyme active sites (e.g., serine proteases, carbonic anhydrase).

column1: What heterocyclic ring system forms the core structure of heme?
column3: Porphyrin (four pyrrole rings linked by methine bridges)
column4: Porphyrins are macrocyclic aromatic systems. In heme, iron is coordinated at the center; the aromatic delocalization across all four pyrrole units stabilizes the structure.

column1: What is the aromatic heterocycle in tryptophan's side chain?
column4: Indole is a bicyclic compound: a benzene ring fused to a pyrrole ring. Tryptophan is the only amino acid with an indole side chain and absorbs UV light at 280 nm.

column1: In pyrimidine, at which positions are the nitrogen atoms located?
column4: Pyrimidine is a six-membered ring with nitrogens at positions 1 and 3 (para-like arrangement). Both nitrogens are pyridine-type (lone pairs in the plane, not contributing to aromaticity).

column1: What distinguishes a pyrrole-type nitrogen from a pyridine-type nitrogen in terms of lone pair contribution to aromaticity?
column3: Pyrrole-type donates lone pair to pi system; pyridine-type does not
column4: Pyrrole N-H nitrogen is sp3-hybridized and donates its lone pair for aromaticity. Pyridine nitrogen is sp2-hybridized; its lone pair is in a sigma orbital and is available for protonation/H-bonding.

column1: Why is pyrrole a much weaker base than pyridine?
column3: Pyrrole's lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic pi system
column4: Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair contributes to aromaticity; protonating it would destroy aromaticity. Pyridine's lone pair is not part of the pi system and is freely available for protonation.

column1: What heterocyclic compound is the precursor to NAD+ and NADH?
column4: Niacin (vitamin B3) is converted to nicotinamide, which forms the nicotinamide ring of NAD+/NADP+. The pyridinium nitrogen accepts a hydride at C4 during reduction to NADH.

column1: What is the total number of pi electrons in the purine ring system, and does it satisfy Huckel's rule?
column4: The fused bicyclic purine system maintains aromaticity across both rings with 10 pi electrons, satisfying Huckel's rule. This stability underlies the role of purines in storing genetic information.

column1: Which heterocyclic ring is found in FAD and riboflavin?
column4: The isoalloxazine ring system of FAD accepts two electrons and two protons at N1 and N5 positions during reduction to FADH2. This tricyclic system is the functional unit of riboflavin (vitamin B2).

column1: Which enzyme class transfers functional groups between molecules?
column4: Transferases move groups such as phosphate, methyl, or amino groups from a donor to an acceptor substrate.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::classification-by-reaction-type MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which enzyme class catalyzes the removal of groups to form double bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation?
column4: Lyases add or remove groups across double bonds; examples include decarboxylases and aldolases.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::classification-by-reaction-type MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which enzyme class forms new bonds using ATP hydrolysis?
column4: Ligases couple bond formation to ATP cleavage; examples include DNA ligase and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::classification-by-reaction-type MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name for the catalytically inactive precursor of an enzyme?
column4: Zymogens require proteolytic cleavage for activation; examples include trypsinogen → trypsin and pepsinogen → pepsin.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::mechanism MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of bond is broken during serine protease catalysis in the acyl-enzyme intermediate?
column4: Serine proteases use a catalytic triad (Ser, His, Asp) to nucleophilically attack the peptide bond, forming an acyl-enzyme intermediate.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::mechanism MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the three residues that make up the catalytic triad of serine proteases?
column4: The triad acts as a charge relay: Asp positions His, which deprotonates Ser, making Ser a strong nucleophile to attack the substrate.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::mechanism MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which catalytic mechanism involves an enzyme temporarily donating or accepting a proton to stabilize the transition state?
column4: General acid-base catalysis uses enzyme side chains as transient proton donors/acceptors, lowering activation energy without changing equilibrium.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::mechanism MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What mechanism do enzymes use when they form a transient covalent bond with the substrate during catalysis?
column4: Covalent catalysis forms a covalent enzyme-substrate intermediate; serine proteases and transaminases are classic examples.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::mechanism MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes the specific molecule or molecules an enzyme acts upon?
column4: Enzymes bind substrates at the active site and convert them to products; enzyme specificity determines which substrates are accepted.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::substrates-and-enzyme-specificity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of specificity describes an enzyme that acts on only one specific substrate?
column4: An enzyme with absolute specificity recognizes a single substrate; urease (urea only) is a classic example.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::substrates-and-enzyme-specificity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of enzyme specificity allows activity on substrates sharing only a particular bond type?
column4: Bond-specific enzymes recognize a functional group or bond regardless of the rest of the molecule; lipases hydrolyzing ester bonds are an example.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::substrates-and-enzyme-specificity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of specificity describes an enzyme that acts on only one enantiomer of a substrate?
column4: Most enzymes are stereospecific; L-amino acid oxidase acts on L-amino acids but not D-amino acids due to the chiral active site.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::substrates-and-enzyme-specificity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and catalysis occurs?
column4: The active site is a three-dimensional cleft or pocket with specific amino acid residues that bind the substrate and stabilize the transition state.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::active-site-model MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What model proposes that the enzyme active site is rigid and complementary in shape to the substrate?
column4: Emil Fischer's lock-and-key model treats the enzyme as a rigid lock and the substrate as a matching key; largely superseded by induced fit.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::active-site-model MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What interactions stabilize substrate binding at the active site?
column3: Non-covalent interactions (H-bonds, ionic, van der Waals, hydrophobic)
column4: Substrate binding relies on multiple weak non-covalent forces that together provide specificity and sufficient affinity.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::active-site-model MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes amino acid residues in the active site that directly participate in bond-breaking/forming?
column4: Catalytic residues differ from binding residues; mutation of a catalytic residue abolishes activity while mutation of binding residues reduces affinity.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::active-site-model MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What model proposes that substrate binding induces a conformational change in the enzyme active site?
column4: Daniel Koshland's induced-fit model explains how the enzyme molds around the substrate, improving complementarity and catalytic efficiency.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::induced-fit-model MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does the induced-fit model differ from the lock-and-key model?
column3: Enzyme changes conformation upon substrate binding (vs. rigid lock-and-key)
column4: In induced fit, the active site is flexible and adjusts shape after substrate binding, enabling better transition-state stabilization than a rigid active site.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::induced-fit-model MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which enzyme is the classic example used to illustrate induced-fit binding?
column4: Hexokinase undergoes a large conformational change that closes around glucose, excluding water and preventing futile ATP hydrolysis.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::induced-fit-model MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structural change in hexokinase upon glucose binding supports the induced-fit model?
column4: Two lobes of hexokinase close around glucose, repositioning catalytic groups and excluding water from the active site.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::induced-fit-model MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a cofactor?
column3: Non-protein molecule required for enzyme activity
column4: Cofactors can be inorganic ions (e.g., Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺) or organic molecules (coenzymes); they assist catalysis or stabilize enzyme structure.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cofactors-coenzymes-and-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a coenzyme?
column4: Coenzymes are organic, non-protein molecules that transiently carry chemical groups; NAD⁺ and FAD are classic coenzymes derived from B vitamins.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cofactors-coenzymes-and-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: From which vitamin is NAD⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) derived?
column4: NAD⁺ accepts hydride ions (H⁻) in oxidation reactions; its niacin-derived nicotinamide ring is the redox-active component.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cofactors-coenzymes-and-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: From which vitamin is FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) derived?
column4: FAD accepts two electrons and two protons; its isoalloxazine ring (from riboflavin) is the redox-active part used in oxidative metabolism.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cofactors-coenzymes-and-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes an enzyme tightly bound to its cofactor, forming the complete active enzyme?
column4: Holoenzyme = apoenzyme (protein part) + cofactor. The apoenzyme alone is catalytically inactive.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cofactors-coenzymes-and-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which vitamin serves as a coenzyme precursor for coenzyme A (CoA)?
column4: Coenzyme A, derived from B5, carries acyl groups (e.g., acetyl-CoA) in metabolic reactions including the TCA cycle.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cofactors-coenzymes-and-vitamins MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the maximum reaction rate of an enzyme called?
column4: Vmax is reached when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate; it is proportional to total enzyme concentration.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::kinetics MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does the Michaelis constant (Km) represent?
column3: Substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity (½ Vmax)
column4: Km reflects enzyme-substrate affinity: a low Km means high affinity (enzyme saturated at low [S]); a high Km means low affinity.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::kinetics MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does increasing enzyme concentration affect Vmax?
column4: Vmax = kcat × [E]total; doubling enzyme concentration doubles Vmax because more active sites are available.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::kinetics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does kcat (turnover number) represent?
column3: Number of substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second
column4: kcat = Vmax / [E]total; it is a measure of catalytic efficiency when enzyme is fully saturated.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::kinetics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is catalytic efficiency and how is it expressed?
column4: kcat/Km measures how efficiently an enzyme works at low [S]; the diffusion limit (~10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹) is the upper bound for a 'perfect' enzyme.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::kinetics MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does enzymes do to the activation energy of a reaction?
column4: Enzymes stabilize the transition state, reducing the energy barrier without changing the overall free energy change (ΔG) of the reaction.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::general-catalysis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Do enzymes change the equilibrium constant of a reaction?
column4: Enzymes speed up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium position (Keq) is unchanged; only the rate changes.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::general-catalysis MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the term for the unstable, high-energy species that forms at the peak of the reaction energy diagram?
column4: Enzymes work by binding and stabilizing the transition state, which lowers activation energy and increases reaction rate.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::general-catalysis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which type of energy change (ΔG) is associated with a spontaneous reaction?
column4: Enzymes do not change ΔG; a reaction is spontaneous if ΔG < 0 regardless of whether an enzyme is present.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::general-catalysis MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the Michaelis-Menten equation?
column4: This equation relates reaction velocity (v) to substrate concentration [S]; it describes a hyperbolic curve with v approaching Vmax asymptotically.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::michaelis-menten MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What graph linearizes Michaelis-Menten kinetics to determine Km and Vmax?
column4: Plotting 1/v vs 1/[S] gives a straight line; y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::michaelis-menten MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, what does the y-intercept equal?
column4: The y-axis intercept of 1/v vs 1/[S] equals 1/Vmax; a higher y-intercept indicates a lower Vmax.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::michaelis-menten MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, what does the x-intercept equal?
column4: The x-intercept is −1/Km; a more negative x-intercept (farther from zero) indicates a lower Km (higher affinity).
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::michaelis-menten MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What assumption underlies Michaelis-Menten kinetics regarding product concentration?
column4: Michaelis-Menten kinetics applies under initial-rate conditions where [P] is negligible and back-reaction is ignored.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::michaelis-menten MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What kinetic behavior distinguishes cooperative enzymes from Michaelis-Menten enzymes?
column4: Cooperative enzymes show sigmoidal kinetics because binding of one substrate molecule increases affinity for subsequent substrate molecules.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cooperativity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the Hill coefficient (n) used to describe?
column4: n > 1 = positive cooperativity; n < 1 = negative cooperativity; n = 1 = no cooperativity (Michaelis-Menten).
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cooperativity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which protein is the classic model of positive cooperativity?
column4: Hemoglobin has a Hill coefficient of ~2.8; binding of O₂ to one subunit increases affinity of remaining subunits for O₂.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cooperativity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is negative cooperativity?
column3: Binding of one substrate decreases affinity at remaining sites
column4: Negative cooperativity (Hill n < 1) is rare but means each successive substrate molecule binds less tightly, broadening the response range.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::cooperativity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does a decrease in pH generally affect enzyme activity?
column3: Alters ionization of active-site residues, usually decreasing activity
column4: Each enzyme has an optimal pH; deviations protonate or deprotonate catalytic residues, reducing binding or catalytic efficiency.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::effects-of-local-conditions-on-enzyme-activity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the optimal pH of pepsin?
column4: Pepsin is a gastric protease that functions in the highly acidic stomach environment; it is denatured at neutral or basic pH.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::effects-of-local-conditions-on-enzyme-activity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What happens to enzyme activity when temperature exceeds the optimum?
column4: High temperatures disrupt non-covalent interactions that maintain active-site geometry, causing irreversible loss of activity.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::effects-of-local-conditions-on-enzyme-activity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the Q10 rule for enzyme kinetics?
column3: Reaction rate ~doubles for every 10°C rise (below optimum)
column4: Q10 ≈ 2 for most enzymes; this applies only below the denaturation temperature where enzyme structure is preserved.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::effects-of-local-conditions-on-enzyme-activity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does high ionic strength (salt concentration) affect enzyme activity?
column3: Can disrupt ionic interactions; may activate or inhibit depending on enzyme
column4: Salt can shield charged residues, altering substrate binding or enzyme conformation; effects are enzyme-specific and can be used to precipitate proteins.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::effects-of-local-conditions-on-enzyme-activity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is competitive inhibition?
column3: Inhibitor binds active site, competes with substrate
column4: Competitive inhibitors are structurally similar to the substrate; inhibition is reversible and overcome by increasing [S].
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::inhibition MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does competitive inhibition affect Km and Vmax?
column4: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, competitive inhibition rotates lines to the same y-intercept (same Vmax) but different x-intercept (higher Km).
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::inhibition MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is uncompetitive inhibition?
column3: Inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex
column4: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind the ES complex at a site distinct from the active site, decreasing both apparent Vmax and apparent Km proportionally.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::inhibition MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does noncompetitive inhibition affect Km and Vmax?
column4: Noncompetitive inhibitors bind enzyme or ES complex with equal affinity at an allosteric site; they cannot be overcome by increasing substrate.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::inhibition MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of inhibition cannot be overcome by increasing substrate concentration?
column4: Because these inhibitors do not compete with substrate for the active site, excess substrate cannot displace them and Vmax is reduced.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::inhibition MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which irreversible inhibitor mechanism involves covalent modification of the active site?
column4: Suicide inhibitors (e.g., aspirin acetylating COX, DFMO inhibiting ornithine decarboxylase) covalently modify the enzyme, permanently abolishing activity.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::inhibition MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two main classes of regulatory enzymes?
column3: Allosteric enzymes and covalently modified enzymes
column4: Allosteric enzymes are regulated by non-covalent binding of effectors; covalently modified enzymes are regulated by chemical modification (e.g., phosphorylation).
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::regulatory-enzymes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a feedback inhibitor in metabolic pathways?
column3: End product that inhibits an early enzyme in its own biosynthetic pathway
column4: Feedback (product) inhibition prevents overproduction; the end product allosterically inhibits the first committed step enzyme.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::regulatory-enzymes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the committed step in a metabolic pathway?
column3: First irreversible step unique to that pathway
column4: The committed step is typically the target of feedback inhibition and regulatory control; it is often catalyzed by a regulatory enzyme.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::regulatory-enzymes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is an allosteric enzyme?
column3: Enzyme regulated by effector binding at a site other than the active site
column4: Allosteric effectors (activators or inhibitors) cause conformational changes that alter enzyme activity; allosteric enzymes often show cooperative kinetics.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::allosteric MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two main models describing allosteric enzyme conformational states?
column4: MWC: all subunits switch simultaneously between T (tense/inactive) and R (relaxed/active) states. KNF: subunits change conformation sequentially upon ligand binding.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::allosteric MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: In the MWC model, which state has higher affinity for substrate?
column4: In the Monod-Wyman-Changeux model, the R state binds substrate and activators more tightly; the T state predominates without substrate.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::allosteric MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What effect does an allosteric activator have on the sigmoidal kinetic curve of an allosteric enzyme?
column3: Shifts curve left (lower [S] needed for half-maximal activity)
column4: Activators stabilize the R state, increasing affinity for substrate and shifting the S₀.₅ (equivalent of Km) to lower concentrations.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::allosteric MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the most common covalent modification used to regulate enzyme activity?
column4: Protein kinases add phosphate groups (from ATP) to Ser, Thr, or Tyr residues; phosphatases remove them. This reversibly activates or inhibits enzymes.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::covalently-modified MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What enzyme removes phosphate groups from proteins?
column4: Phosphatases hydrolyze phosphate esters, reversing the effect of kinases; they often have opposing effects on enzyme activity compared to kinases.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::covalently-modified MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is an example of a covalently modified enzyme activated by phosphorylation?
column4: Phosphorylase b (inactive) is converted to phosphorylase a (active) by phosphorylation, triggering glycogen breakdown in response to glucagon/epinephrine.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::covalently-modified MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What covalent modification activates trypsinogen to form trypsin?
column4: Enteropeptidase cleaves trypsinogen, removing the N-terminal hexapeptide to expose the active site; trypsin then activates other zymogens autocatalytically.
column8: concept::CP::5E::enzymes MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::enzymes::covalently-modified MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::BC MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does the first law of thermodynamics state?
column3: Energy is conserved; it cannot be created or destroyed
column4: In biological systems, energy is converted between forms (chemical, thermal, mechanical) but the total energy of the universe remains constant.

column1: What does the second law of thermodynamics state about entropy?
column3: Entropy of the universe always increases in a spontaneous process
column4: Biological organisms locally decrease entropy but do so at the cost of increasing entropy elsewhere (e.g., releasing heat), obeying the second law.

column1: Define enthalpy (H) in thermodynamic terms.
column3: Total heat content of a system at constant pressure
column4: ΔH = heat released or absorbed during a reaction at constant pressure; exothermic reactions have negative ΔH.

column1: What is an exergonic reaction?
column3: A reaction that releases free energy (ΔG < 0)
column4: Exergonic reactions are thermodynamically spontaneous and can do work on surroundings; metabolism couples exergonic reactions to drive endergonic ones.

column1: What is the relationship between spontaneity and ΔG?
column4: A negative ΔG means the reaction proceeds spontaneously as written; ΔG = 0 at equilibrium; ΔG > 0 is non-spontaneous in the forward direction.

column1: Which thermodynamic quantity determines whether a reaction is spontaneous at constant T and P?
column4: ΔG = ΔH – TΔS; only when ΔG < 0 is a reaction spontaneous under constant temperature and pressure conditions relevant to biology.

column1: What is the equation for Gibbs free energy change?
column4: At higher temperatures, the entropy term (TΔS) becomes more significant; reactions that are entropy-driven become more spontaneous as T increases.

column1: What is the standard Gibbs free energy change (ΔG°)?
column3: ΔG measured at standard conditions (1 M, 1 atm, 25°C, pH 0)
column4: For biochemistry, ΔG°' denotes standard free energy at pH 7; this distinguishes biological standard state from the chemical standard state.

column1: What is the relationship between ΔG° and the equilibrium constant Keq?
column4: A large Keq (products favored) gives a large negative ΔG°; at equilibrium ΔG = 0, not ΔG° = 0.

column1: What does a Keq greater than 1 indicate about ΔG°?
column4: Because ΔG° = –RT ln Keq, if Keq > 1 then ln Keq > 0, making ΔG° negative, indicating the standard reaction is exergonic.

column1: What is the value of RT at 37°C (310 K) used in MCAT approximations?
column4: R = 8.314 J/mol·K; at 310 K, RT ≈ 2577 J/mol ≈ 2.58 kJ/mol. Used to estimate ΔG° from Keq without a calculator.

column1: If Keq = 1, what is ΔG°?
column4: ln(1) = 0, so ΔG° = –RT(0) = 0; products and reactants are equally favored under standard conditions.

column1: What is the equation relating actual ΔG to ΔG° and the reaction quotient Q?
column4: When Q < Keq, ln Q is negative and ΔG < ΔG°, driving the reaction forward; at equilibrium Q = Keq and ΔG = 0.

column1: At equilibrium, what is the value of ΔG?
column4: At equilibrium there is no net driving force; the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and the system does no net work.

column1: How does increasing reactant concentration affect ΔG for a reaction?
column3: Makes ΔG more negative (drives reaction forward)
column4: Higher reactant concentration lowers Q below Keq, so ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q becomes more negative, increasing spontaneity.

column1: How does increasing product concentration affect the spontaneity of a reaction?
column3: Makes ΔG less negative (less spontaneous forward)
column4: Accumulating products raises Q toward Keq, reducing the driving force; at Q = Keq the reaction reaches equilibrium (ΔG = 0).

column1: Le Chatelier's principle: what happens when a product is continuously removed from a reaction?
column3: Equilibrium shifts to the right (more product formed)
column4: Removal of product keeps Q < Keq, maintaining a negative ΔG; cells exploit this (e.g., ATP hydrolysis products removed) to drive reactions.

column1: How do cells maintain metabolic reactions far from equilibrium?
column3: By continuously supplying reactants and removing products
column4: Metabolic pathways are open systems; steady-state concentrations differ from equilibrium, keeping ΔG negative throughout the pathway.

column1: What is the approximate ΔG°' of ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi?
column4: This large negative standard free energy makes ATP an effective energy currency; actual ΔG in cells is even more negative (~–50 kJ/mol) due to low [ADP] and [Pi].

column1: What are the three phosphate groups of ATP called?
column4: The γ-phosphate is the terminal phosphate hydrolyzed in most ATP-utilizing reactions; the α-phosphate is attached to ribose.

column1: What nucleoside is the backbone of ATP?
column4: ATP = adenosine triphosphate; the ribose sugar distinguishes it from the deoxyribose-containing dATP used in DNA synthesis.

column1: What type of bond links the phosphate groups in ATP?
column4: Hydrolysis of the phosphoanhydride bonds (β–γ or α–β) releases energy; the bond between ribose and α-phosphate is a phosphoester bond.

column1: Why do phosphoanhydride bonds release large amounts of energy upon hydrolysis?
column3: Relief of electrostatic repulsion and resonance stabilization of products
column4: Negative phosphate charges repel each other in ATP; after hydrolysis, Pi and ADP are individually better resonance-stabilized, lowering product energy.

column1: What is substrate-level phosphorylation?
column3: Direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate to ADP to form ATP
column4: Occurs in glycolysis (phosphoglycerate kinase, pyruvate kinase) and the TCA cycle (succinyl-CoA synthetase); does not require oxygen or a membrane.

column1: What is oxidative phosphorylation?
column3: ATP synthesis driven by the electron transport chain and proton gradient
column4: The proton-motive force generated across the inner mitochondrial membrane powers ATP synthase (complex V) to phosphorylate ADP.

column1: What is the actual ΔG of ATP hydrolysis inside a living cell (approximate)?
column4: Cellular [ADP] and [Pi] are low and [ATP] is high relative to standard conditions; using ΔG = ΔG°' + RT ln Q yields a more negative value than –30.5 kJ/mol.

column1: Why is the actual cellular ΔG of ATP hydrolysis more negative than ΔG°'?
column3: Low [ADP] and [Pi], high [ATP] in the cell
column4: Q = [ADP][Pi]/[ATP] is much less than 1 under cellular conditions, making RT ln Q negative and ΔG more negative than ΔG°'.

column1: What does it mean that ATP hydrolysis has ΔG << 0?
column3: The reaction is highly exergonic and thermodynamically favorable
column4: A large negative ΔG provides the driving force to power endergonic biological processes when ATP hydrolysis is coupled to them.

column1: Name the two products of ATP hydrolysis (most common reaction).
column4: Some reactions hydrolyze ATP to AMP + pyrophosphate (PPi); subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase makes those reactions essentially irreversible.

column1: Why is hydrolysis of ATP to AMP + PPi (pyrophosphate) especially favorable?
column3: Rapid hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase pulls the reaction forward
column4: Pyrophosphatase cleaves PPi → 2 Pi (also exergonic), so the net release of two phosphoanhydride bonds drives the coupled reaction irreversibly.

column1: What is a phosphoryl group transfer in biochemistry?
column3: Transfer of the γ-phosphate of ATP to an acceptor molecule
column4: ATP donates its terminal phosphate to substrates, activating them (e.g., glucose→glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase), coupling exergonic ATP hydrolysis to the reaction.

column1: Which enzyme catalyzes the first committed step of glycolysis using ATP group transfer?
column4: This phosphorylation traps glucose inside the cell and initiates glycolysis; it is an irreversible step due to the negative ΔG.

column1: What is an acyl-phosphate intermediate and which glycolytic enzyme forms one?
column3: A high-energy mixed anhydride; phosphoglycerate kinase substrate (1,3-bisphosphoglycerate)
column4: 1,3-BPG is an acyl-phosphate; its hydrolysis is highly exergonic, driving substrate-level phosphorylation of ADP to ATP by phosphoglycerate kinase.

column1: What is aminoacyl-AMP an example of in ATP group transfer?
column3: An activated amino acid intermediate used in tRNA charging
column4: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase uses ATP → AMP + PPi to form aminoacyl-AMP; the amino acid is then transferred to tRNA, linking amino acid to the correct tRNA.

column1: What is the difference between a kinase and a phosphatase?
column3: Kinase adds phosphate (from ATP); phosphatase removes phosphate (hydrolysis)
column4: Kinases are ATP-dependent and produce ADP; phosphatases use water and release Pi. Both are critical regulatory enzymes in signal transduction and metabolism.
