column1: What is oxidation in biological systems defined as?
column3: Loss of electrons (or loss of hydrogen atoms)
column4: Biological oxidation often involves removal of hydrogen (H+ + e–); oxidation of metabolic fuels releases electrons captured by NAD+ and FAD.

column1: What is reduction in biological systems defined as?
column3: Gain of electrons (or gain of hydrogen atoms)
column4: NADH and FADH2 are reduced electron carriers; they donate electrons to the electron transport chain, which ultimately reduces O2 to H2O.

column1: What is a redox reaction?
column3: A reaction in which one species is oxidized and another is reduced simultaneously
column4: Oxidation and reduction always occur together; the reducing agent (reductant) loses electrons; the oxidizing agent (oxidant) gains them.

column1: What is standard reduction potential (E°)?
column3: The tendency of a molecule to gain electrons under standard conditions (relative to H2)
column4: More positive E° = stronger oxidizing agent; electrons flow spontaneously from lower E° (reductant) to higher E° (oxidant).

column1: How is ΔG°' related to ΔE°' in a redox reaction?
column4: n = moles of electrons transferred; F = Faraday's constant (96,485 C/mol); a positive ΔE°' gives a negative ΔG°' (spontaneous).

column1: What is the standard reduction potential of O2/H2O at pH 7?
column4: The high positive E°' of O2 makes it the ultimate electron acceptor in aerobic respiration; electrons flow downhill to O2, releasing energy.

column1: In a standard half-reaction table, which species appears on the left side?
column4: Format: Oxidized form + ne– → Reduced form; E°' values are given for the reduction direction; reverse the sign for oxidation.

column1: How do you calculate ΔE°' for a full redox reaction from half-reactions?
column4: Subtract the E°' of the half-reaction being reversed (oxidation) from the E°' of the reduction half-reaction; a positive ΔE°' indicates spontaneity.

column1: What is the standard reduction potential of NAD+/NADH at pH 7?
column4: The negative E°' of NAD+/NADH means NADH is a good electron donor; electrons flow from NADH (–0.32 V) to O2 (+0.82 V), releasing energy.

column1: What is the standard reduction potential of FAD/FADH2 at pH 7?
column4: FADH2 has a slightly higher (less negative) E°' than NADH, so it enters the electron transport chain at a later complex, generating fewer ATP equivalents.

column1: What is a soluble electron carrier?
column3: A mobile molecule that shuttles electrons between enzyme complexes (e.g., NAD+, NADP+, CoQ, cytochrome c)
column4: Unlike membrane-embedded complexes, soluble carriers diffuse freely; coenzyme Q diffuses within the lipid bilayer; cytochrome c is in the intermembrane space.

column1: What is NAD+ and what is its reduced form?
column3: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide; reduced form is NADH
column4: NAD+ accepts 2 electrons and 1 H+ to become NADH; it is the primary electron carrier in catabolic pathways (glycolysis, TCA cycle).

column1: What is the difference between NAD+ and NADP+?
column3: NADP+ has an extra phosphate on the 2' ribose of AMP
column4: NADPH is used primarily in anabolic (biosynthetic) reactions and antioxidant defense (glutathione reduction); NADH is used in catabolic energy production.

column1: What is coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) and what is its role?
column3: A lipid-soluble electron carrier in the inner mitochondrial membrane
column4: CoQ accepts electrons from complexes I and II and transfers them to complex III; its lipid-soluble nature allows diffusion in the membrane.

column1: What is the role of cytochrome c in the electron transport chain?
column3: Soluble carrier that transfers electrons from complex III to complex IV
column4: Cytochrome c is a small heme-containing protein in the intermembrane space; it carries one electron at a time via its iron center (Fe3+/Fe2+).

column1: How many electrons does NAD+ accept per molecule?
column4: NAD+ accepts a hydride ion (H–, equivalent to 2e– + H+) from a substrate; the other hydrogen appears as a proton (H+) in solution.

column1: What are flavoproteins?
column3: Proteins that contain a flavin cofactor (FMN or FAD) as a prosthetic group
column4: Flavoproteins can accept 1 or 2 electrons, making them versatile in electron transfer; examples include succinate dehydrogenase (complex II) and NADH dehydrogenase (complex I).

column1: What are the two flavin cofactors found in flavoproteins?
column3: FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide)
column4: Both contain riboflavin (vitamin B2); FAD is FMN with an additional AMP moiety; both can cycle between oxidized and reduced forms.

column1: Which vitamin is the precursor to both FMN and FAD?
column4: Riboflavin deficiency impairs flavoprotein function, affecting energy metabolism, fatty acid oxidation, and the electron transport chain.

column1: Why are flavoproteins able to participate in both 1-electron and 2-electron transfers?
column3: Their flavin ring can form a stable semiquinone radical intermediate
column4: The semiquinone (one-electron reduced form) is stable enough to allow single-electron transfers to iron-sulfur clusters or cytochromes, unlike NAD+ which only accepts 2 electrons.

column1: Which complex of the electron transport chain contains FAD as a prosthetic group and what substrate does it oxidize?
column3: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase); oxidizes succinate to fumarate
column4: FADH2 formed in complex II feeds electrons directly into CoQ at a lower energy level than NADH, yielding ~1.5 ATP instead of ~2.5 ATP.

column1: What is the oxidized form of FAD and what is its fully reduced form?
column4: FAD accepts 2 electrons and 2 protons to become FADH2; the semiquinone FADH· is the one-electron intermediate between FAD and FADH2.

column1: Which electron transport chain complex contains FMN as a cofactor?
column4: FMN in complex I accepts electrons from NADH; electrons then pass through iron-sulfur clusters to CoQ, and four protons are pumped across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

column1: What is a thermodynamic system?
column3: The portion of the universe under study
column4: The system is distinguished from its surroundings; together they make up the universe. Everything outside the system is the surroundings.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What is a state function?
column3: A property dependent only on current state, not path
column4: Examples include U (internal energy), H (enthalpy), S (entropy), G (Gibbs free energy), T, P, and V. Work and heat are NOT state functions.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: Which of the following is NOT a state function: enthalpy, work, entropy, temperature?
column4: Work (and heat) depend on the path taken between states; state functions such as H, S, and T depend only on the initial and final states.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What defines an open thermodynamic system?
column3: Exchanges both energy and matter with surroundings
column4: A closed system exchanges only energy; an isolated system exchanges neither. Biological cells are open systems.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What defines an isolated thermodynamic system?
column3: No exchange of energy or matter with surroundings
column4: A perfectly insulated, sealed container approximates an isolated system. The universe as a whole is considered isolated.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: Because state functions are path-independent, the change in a state function depends on what?
column3: Only the initial and final states
column4: This allows calculation of ΔH or ΔG for a process without knowing the mechanism, enabling use of Hess's Law.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: Why is heat (q) not a state function?
column3: It depends on the path taken, not just initial and final states
column4: The same change in internal energy can be achieved by different combinations of heat and work, so q alone is path-dependent.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: Name two examples of extensive state functions.
column4: Extensive properties scale with the amount of substance; intensive state functions (T, P) do not. On the MCAT, U and H are the most commonly tested extensive state functions.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What does the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics state?
column3: If A=B and B=C in temperature, then A=C
column4: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This law establishes temperature as a meaningful, measurable property.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What physical concept does the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics define?
column4: The Zeroth Law provides the logical foundation for thermometry — it guarantees that temperature is a consistent, transitive property used to compare thermal states.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What condition exists between two objects in thermal equilibrium?
column3: They are at the same temperature
column4: Thermal equilibrium means there is no net heat flow between the objects. The Zeroth Law uses this to justify temperature measurement with a thermometer.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: Why is the Zeroth Law numbered 'zeroth' rather than 'first'?
column3: It was recognized after the First Law but is more fundamental
column4: Scientists realized this law is logically prior to (more foundational than) the First and Second Laws, so it was inserted before them with the label 'zeroth.'
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: At absolute zero (0 K), what is the theoretical kinetic energy of particles?
column4: Absolute zero is defined as the temperature at which molecular motion ceases; it cannot be reached in practice. 0 K = -273.15 °C.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What is the relationship between the Celsius and Kelvin temperature scales?
column4: The Kelvin scale is an absolute scale with no negative values; it is required for gas law and thermodynamic calculations on the MCAT.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: Which direction does heat flow spontaneously according to the Zeroth Law framework?
column3: From higher temperature to lower temperature
column4: Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold until thermal equilibrium is reached. This underpins the Second Law's directionality as well.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: State the First Law of Thermodynamics in equation form.
column4: ΔU is the change in internal energy, q is heat added to the system, and w is work done ON the system. Sign conventions: q > 0 means heat in; w > 0 means work done on system (IUPAC convention).
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What does the First Law of Thermodynamics state conceptually?
column3: Energy is conserved; it cannot be created or destroyed
column4: The total energy of an isolated system is constant. Any energy lost by the system is gained by the surroundings, and vice versa.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: In IUPAC sign convention, what sign does q have when a system releases heat?
column4: Heat leaving the system is exothermic; the system loses energy, so q is negative. An endothermic process absorbs heat, so q is positive.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What is work (w) in thermodynamics for a gas?
column3: w = -PΔV (work done BY system) or w = PΔV (work done ON system)
column4: Under IUPAC convention, w = -PextΔV; a gas expanding does negative work (loses energy). On the MCAT, be clear which sign convention a question uses.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: For a process at constant volume with no non-expansion work, what does ΔU equal?
column4: With ΔV = 0, no PV work is done, so all energy change comes from heat. This is why bomb calorimetry (constant volume) measures ΔU directly.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: How is enthalpy (H) related to internal energy (U)?
column4: At constant pressure, ΔH = ΔU + PΔV = q_p (heat at constant pressure). Enthalpy is the relevant energy function for most biological and chemical processes.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process, what is ΔU?
column4: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. At constant T, ΔU = 0, so q = -w; all heat absorbed is converted to work.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: For an adiabatic process, what is true about q, and what does the First Law reduce to?
column4: An adiabatic process has no heat exchange with surroundings. All internal energy change comes from work; expanding adiabatically cools the gas.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What does Hess's Law follow from regarding state functions?
column4: Because ΔH depends only on initial and final states, reaction enthalpies can be summed algebraically regardless of the route taken. This is a direct consequence of the First Law.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: On a PV diagram, what does the area under a curve represent?
column3: Work done by (or on) the gas
column4: Work = ∫P dV. The area under the P-V curve equals the magnitude of work; the sign depends on direction (expansion = work done by system, compression = work done on system).
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: On a PV diagram, what does a horizontal line (isobaric process) look like, and how is work calculated?
column4: At constant pressure, work is simply P times the change in volume. The area under this horizontal line equals PΔV.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: On a PV diagram, what does a vertical line represent?
column4: With ΔV = 0, no PV work is done — the area under a vertical line is zero. All energy change is as heat (ΔU = q).
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: For a cyclic process on a PV diagram, what does the enclosed area represent?
column4: If the cycle is clockwise, the system does net positive work (e.g., a heat engine). Counterclockwise indicates net work done ON the system (e.g., refrigerator).
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: On a PV diagram, what is the sign of work when a gas expands (volume increases)?
column3: Positive work done BY the system (negative in IUPAC: w < 0)
column4: Expansion moves right on the PV diagram; the system pushes against surroundings, doing positive work on surroundings. Under IUPAC, this is w = -PΔV < 0 for the system.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What is an isothermal process on a PV diagram, and what curve does it follow?
column3: Constant T; follows a hyperbola (PV = nRT = constant)
column4: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, P and V are inversely proportional, tracing a hyperbola. The area under this curve still equals work done.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: For a cyclic process on a PV diagram, what is ΔU for the complete cycle?
column4: Because internal energy is a state function and the system returns to its initial state, ΔU = 0 over a full cycle. Therefore q_net = -w_net (heat absorbed equals work done by system).
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: On a PV diagram, how does the work done by an ideal gas differ between a reversible and irreversible isothermal expansion?
column3: Reversible expansion does more work (larger area under curve)
column4: A reversible process involves infinitesimal steps at near-equilibrium, maximizing work output. An irreversible expansion against a constant external pressure yields a smaller rectangular area, hence less work.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What is the work done during an adiabatic process on a PV diagram compared to an isothermal process between the same initial and final volumes?
column3: Adiabatic process has a steeper curve and does less work
column4: The adiabatic curve falls faster (steeper slope) because temperature drops during expansion; thus the area under the adiabatic curve is smaller than the isothermal curve over the same ΔV.
column5: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions ― Thermochemistry, Thermodynamics

column1: What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics state about entropy in an isolated system?
column3: Entropy of an isolated system always increases (or stays constant)
column4: The Second Law states that spontaneous processes increase the total entropy of the universe (ΔS_universe ≥ 0). This sets the direction of spontaneous change.

column1: What is the mathematical condition for a spontaneous process according to the Second Law?
column4: For a spontaneous process, the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) must increase. At equilibrium, ΔS_universe = 0.

column1: What is the SI unit of entropy?
column4: Entropy has units of energy divided by temperature. Molar entropy is reported in J/(mol·K).

column1: How is the entropy change of the surroundings related to heat flow at constant temperature?
column4: At constant temperature, heat lost by the system is gained by surroundings: ΔS_surr = –q_sys/T. This links calorimetry to entropy calculations.

column1: What is the Boltzmann entropy equation?
column4: k_B is Boltzmann's constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K) and W is the number of microstates. More microstates = higher entropy.

column1: Which thermodynamic quantity predicts spontaneity at constant T and P by combining enthalpy and entropy?
column4: ΔG = ΔH – TΔS. A negative ΔG indicates a spontaneous process, linking the Second Law to practical chemistry.

column1: What does entropy measure in thermodynamics?
column3: Degree of disorder or number of microstates
column4: Entropy quantifies the dispersal of energy or matter. A higher number of accessible microstates corresponds to greater entropy.

column1: Does dissolving NaCl in water increase or decrease entropy?
column4: Dissolving disperses ions throughout the solvent, greatly increasing the number of accessible microstates (positional disorder).

column1: Which process is associated with an increase in entropy: mixing two ideal gases or separating them?
column4: Mixing increases the number of accessible positions for each gas molecule, raising the number of microstates and thus entropy.

column1: Why does increasing temperature increase entropy?
column3: More energy microstates become thermally accessible
column4: Higher temperature distributes energy over more microstates (translational, rotational, vibrational), increasing S.

column1: Which has higher entropy: a perfectly ordered crystal at 0 K or a gas at room temperature?
column4: The Third Law states that a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0. A gas has far more translational microstates, giving much higher entropy.

column1: What term describes the entropy change due to energy dispersal among many molecules?
column4: Entropy increases when energy is spread over more degrees of freedom. Both positional and thermal dispersal contribute to total entropy.

column1: Which state of matter has the highest entropy: gas, liquid, or crystal?
column4: Gas molecules have the greatest freedom of motion and number of accessible microstates, giving the highest entropy.

column1: Rank the following from lowest to highest entropy: gas, liquid, crystalline solid.
column4: Crystals have highly ordered structures (low microstates); liquids have more freedom; gases have the most, so entropy increases in this order.

column1: What sign does ΔS typically have when a gas condenses to a liquid?
column4: Condensation decreases the number of accessible microstates as molecules go from a highly disordered gas to a more ordered liquid.

column1: A reaction produces more moles of gas than it consumes. What is the expected sign of ΔS?
column4: More moles of gas mean more translational degrees of freedom and microstates, increasing entropy. Counting moles of gas is a quick MCAT predictor of ΔS sign.

column1: Which has higher standard molar entropy: diamond or graphite? Why?
column4: Graphite's layered structure allows more vibrational modes than diamond's rigid 3-D network, giving graphite higher S°.

column1: What is calorimetry?
column3: Measurement of heat exchanged during a physical or chemical process
column4: A calorimeter measures q by tracking temperature changes, using q = mcΔT or q = CΔT (where C is heat capacity of the calorimeter).

column1: Define specific heat capacity.
column3: Heat required to raise 1 g of substance by 1°C (or 1 K)
column4: q = mcΔT, where m is mass and c is specific heat. Water's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C), the highest of common liquids.

column1: What is the specific heat of water?
column4: Water's unusually high specific heat (due to hydrogen bonding) makes it an excellent biological heat buffer and a standard in calorimetry.

column1: What is the difference between heat capacity and specific heat?
column3: Heat capacity is for a whole object; specific heat is per gram
column4: Heat capacity C = mc (J/°C for the entire sample). Specific heat c is an intensive property (J/g·°C) independent of sample size.

column1: In a coffee-cup calorimeter at constant pressure, what thermodynamic quantity does q_rxn equal?
column4: At constant pressure, q_p = ΔH. Coffee-cup calorimeters are open to the atmosphere, so P is constant.

column1: A bomb calorimeter measures heat at constant what?
column4: Bomb calorimeters are sealed rigid vessels, so volume is constant and q_v = ΔU (internal energy), not ΔH directly.

column1: What is the primary mechanism of heat transfer in metals?
column4: Metals have free electrons that transfer kinetic energy rapidly through the lattice, making conduction the dominant heat-transfer mode.

column1: Which mode of heat transfer requires a medium (fluid) to transfer heat by bulk movement?
column4: Convection transfers heat via the physical movement of fluid (liquid or gas). It requires mass flow and cannot occur in a vacuum.

column1: Which mode of heat transfer can occur through a vacuum?
column4: Radiation transfers heat via electromagnetic waves (infrared) and requires no medium. It is how the Sun heats Earth.

column1: What law describes radiative heat transfer, relating power emitted to the fourth power of temperature?
column4: ε is emissivity, σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴), and T is absolute temperature.

column1: Which type of heat transfer is responsible for a warm room heating a cold object across open air without a breeze?
column4: Radiation from warm surfaces heats cooler objects directly via infrared EM waves; still air also allows gentle convection currents.

column1: Fourier's Law of conduction states that heat flow rate is proportional to what?
column4: Q/t = kAΔT/L, where k is thermal conductivity, A is area, and L is thickness. Greater ΔT or larger area → faster conduction.

column1: Define an exothermic reaction.
column3: A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings
column4: Exothermic reactions have ΔH < 0. The products are at lower energy than the reactants, and heat flows out of the system.

column1: Define an endothermic reaction.
column3: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings
column4: Endothermic reactions have ΔH > 0. The surroundings cool as heat flows into the system to raise product energy.

column1: When a cold pack activates, is the dissolution process endothermic or exothermic?
column4: Ammonium nitrate dissolving in water absorbs heat from surroundings, making the pack feel cold. ΔH_soln > 0.

column1: A reaction is exothermic and increases entropy. What is the sign of ΔG?
column4: ΔG = ΔH – TΔS; if ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, then ΔG < 0 at all temperatures, guaranteeing spontaneity.

column1: Which type of reaction (endothermic or exothermic) is favored at low temperature when ΔS < 0?
column4: When ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0, ΔG = ΔH – TΔS is negative only at low T (the –TΔS term is small), so the reaction is spontaneous only at low T.

column1: Define enthalpy (H).
column3: H = U + PV (total heat content at constant pressure)
column4: Enthalpy combines internal energy U with the pressure-volume work term PV. At constant P, ΔH = q_p, the heat exchanged.

column1: What is the standard enthalpy of formation (ΔH°_f)?
column3: ΔH for forming 1 mol of a compound from its elements in standard states
column4: By definition, ΔH°_f for any element in its most stable form at 25°C, 1 atm is zero.

column1: What are the standard conditions for thermodynamic measurements?
column4: Standard state does NOT mean 0°C. It is 25°C and 1 atm; concentrations of 1 M are also standard for solutions.

column1: How is the standard enthalpy of reaction calculated from standard heats of formation?
column4: This is an application of Hess's Law. Multiply each ΔH°_f by the stoichiometric coefficient before summing.

column1: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of O₂(g)?
column4: All elements in their most stable standard state (O₂ is the stable form of oxygen) have ΔH°_f = 0 by definition.

column1: What is the relationship between ΔH°_rxn and bond energies (approximate)?
column3: ΔH°_rxn ≈ Σ BE(bonds broken) – Σ BE(bonds formed)
column4: Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic); forming bonds releases energy (exothermic). This gives an estimate of ΔH using average bond energies.

column1: State Hess's Law of Heat Summation.
column3: ΔH for a reaction equals the sum of ΔH values of any series of steps that add up to the overall reaction
column4: Because enthalpy is a state function, ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not the pathway taken.

column1: If a reaction is reversed, what happens to its ΔH?
column3: The sign of ΔH changes (ΔH becomes –ΔH)
column4: Reversing a reaction reverses the direction of heat flow. This is a direct consequence of Hess's Law and enthalpy being a state function.

column1: If a reaction is multiplied by a factor n, what happens to ΔH?
column4: Enthalpy is extensive — doubling the moles of reactants doubles the heat released or absorbed.

column1: Why can Hess's Law be used to calculate ΔH for reactions that are difficult to measure directly?
column3: Enthalpy is a state function; path is irrelevant
column4: Since ΔH depends only on initial and final states, measurable reactions can be combined algebraically to find ΔH of an unmeasurable reaction.

column1: Using Hess's Law, if Reaction 1 + Reaction 2 = Reaction 3, what is ΔH_3?
column4: Hess's Law allows direct addition of enthalpies when reactions are added. Manipulate (reverse/scale) steps so they sum to the target reaction.

column1: What is bond dissociation energy (BDE)?
column3: Energy required to homolytically break one mole of a bond in the gas phase
column4: BDE is always positive (endothermic) because breaking bonds requires energy input. It is an average for a given bond type across molecules.

column1: Are bond dissociation energies endothermic or exothermic?
column4: Energy must be supplied to overcome the attractive forces holding atoms together; bond breaking always absorbs energy.

column1: How does bond order affect bond dissociation energy?
column4: Triple bonds (e.g., N≡N, 945 kJ/mol) are stronger and harder to break than double bonds, which are stronger than single bonds.

column1: How does bond length relate to bond dissociation energy?
column4: Shorter bonds result from stronger electron-nucleus attraction; more energy is needed to separate the atoms, so BDE is higher.

column1: Using BDE, when is ΔH_rxn estimated to be negative (exothermic)?
column3: When energy released forming bonds > energy absorbed breaking bonds
column4: ΔH ≈ Σ BE(broken) – Σ BE(formed). If bonds formed are stronger/more numerous, the reaction releases net energy (ΔH < 0).

column1: Why are BDE-based ΔH estimates less accurate than Hess's Law calculations using ΔH°_f?
column3: BDE values are average bond energies, not bond-specific
column4: Bond energies vary with molecular context (e.g., C–H in CH₄ vs. CHCl₃). Using averages introduces error compared to precise calorimetric ΔH°_f data.

column1: What does the symbol G represent in thermodynamics?
column4: G is the thermodynamic potential that predicts whether a process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure, the conditions relevant to most biological systems.

column1: What is the equation relating Gibbs free energy to enthalpy and entropy?
column4: H is enthalpy, T is absolute temperature in Kelvin, and S is entropy. This relationship is central to predicting spontaneity on the MCAT.

column1: What are the SI units of Gibbs free energy?
column4: Free energy is an energy quantity; kJ/mol is the most common unit seen in MCAT problems involving ΔG values.

column1: What is the equation for standard Gibbs free energy change in terms of enthalpy and entropy?
column4: Standard state conditions are 298 K and 1 atm. This formula lets you calculate whether a reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
column8: concept::CP::5E::formation MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::formation::free-energy-g-gc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: How is ΔG related to the reaction quotient Q and standard free energy ΔG°?
column4: R is the gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K). This equation shows how free energy changes as a reaction proceeds away from standard conditions.
column8: concept::CP::5E::formation MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::formation::free-energy-g-gc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: What is the relationship between ΔG° and the equilibrium constant K?
column4: A large K (products favored) gives a large negative ΔG°, confirming spontaneity under standard conditions. Memorize this key equation.
column8: concept::CP::5E::formation MCAT::section::CP MCAT::5E::formation::free-energy-g-gc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::GC

column1: If ΔG° is negative, what does that indicate about K?
column4: Negative ΔG° means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions, which corresponds to an equilibrium constant greater than 1.

column1: What sign of ΔG indicates a spontaneous (thermodynamically favorable) process?
column4: A process with ΔG < 0 releases free energy and proceeds spontaneously in the forward direction at constant T and P.

column1: What sign of ΔG indicates a nonspontaneous process?
column4: A positive ΔG means the process requires an input of free energy to proceed; the reverse reaction would be spontaneous instead.

column1: Under what enthalpy/entropy conditions is a reaction always spontaneous regardless of temperature?
column4: Exothermic and entropy-increasing reactions have ΔG = ΔH - TΔS that is always negative, so they are spontaneous at all temperatures.

column1: Under what enthalpy/entropy conditions is a reaction always nonspontaneous regardless of temperature?
column4: Endothermic and entropy-decreasing reactions always have ΔG > 0, making them nonspontaneous at every temperature.

column1: For a reaction that is exothermic (ΔH < 0) and entropy-decreasing (ΔS < 0), at what temperatures is it spontaneous?
column4: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS: at low T the -TΔS term is small, so the negative ΔH dominates, giving ΔG < 0. At high T the positive entropy term dominates.

column1: For a reaction that is endothermic (ΔH > 0) and entropy-increasing (ΔS > 0), at what temperatures is it spontaneous?
column4: At high T, the +TΔS term becomes large, making -TΔS very negative and driving ΔG below zero despite the positive ΔH.

column1: Does a negative ΔG guarantee a fast reaction?
column4: Thermodynamics predicts spontaneity (feasibility), not rate. A reaction can be thermodynamically favorable but kinetically slow due to a high activation energy.

column1: If ΔG° = 0, what is the value of K?
column4: From ΔG° = -RT ln K: if ΔG° = 0, then ln K = 0, so K = 1, meaning reactants and products are present in equal amounts at equilibrium.

column1: What is the coefficient of thermal expansion?
column3: Fractional change in volume per degree of temperature change
column4: α = (1/V)(dV/dT) at constant pressure. It quantifies how much a material expands when heated, important for understanding thermal stress and fluid behavior.

column1: What are the SI units of the coefficient of thermal expansion?
column4: Because it is a fractional change in volume divided by a temperature change, the units are reciprocal temperature (K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹).

column1: Which state of matter generally has the largest coefficient of thermal expansion?
column4: Gases expand dramatically with temperature (described by PV = nRT), giving them much larger expansion coefficients than liquids or solids.

column1: What is the linear coefficient of thermal expansion (α_L)?
column3: Fractional change in length per degree of temperature
column4: ΔL/L₀ = α_L ΔT. For isotropic solids, the volumetric coefficient α_V ≈ 3α_L, a useful approximation on the MCAT.

column1: Water has an anomalous thermal expansion behavior near what temperature?
column4: Water is densest at 4°C; cooling below this causes it to expand rather than contract. This anomaly is critical for aquatic ecosystems surviving winter.

column1: How does the volumetric expansion coefficient relate to the linear expansion coefficient for an isotropic solid?
column4: Volume scales as the cube of length; differentiating gives a factor of 3 for small expansions, so volumetric expansion is approximately three times linear expansion.

column1: What is heat of fusion (enthalpy of fusion)?
column3: Heat absorbed to melt 1 mol of solid at its melting point
column4: ΔH_fus is the energy needed to break intermolecular forces during the solid-to-liquid transition at constant temperature and pressure.

column1: What is heat of vaporization (enthalpy of vaporization)?
column3: Heat absorbed to vaporize 1 mol of liquid at its boiling point
column4: ΔH_vap is always larger than ΔH_fus for the same substance because vaporization requires complete separation of molecules, not just partial loosening.

column1: What is the heat of vaporization of water?
column4: Water's unusually high ΔH_vap is due to extensive hydrogen bonding. Memorize ~2260 J/g for quick MCAT calculations involving evaporative cooling.

column1: For a given substance, how does heat of vaporization compare to heat of fusion?
column3: Heat of vaporization is much larger
column4: Melting only partially disrupts intermolecular forces; vaporization requires complete separation, so ΔH_vap >> ΔH_fus (e.g., water: 40.7 vs. 6.01 kJ/mol).

column1: What is Hess's Law application for heat of condensation vs. heat of vaporization?
column4: Condensation is the reverse of vaporization; by Hess's Law the enthalpy change is equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.

column1: What is the heat of fusion of water?
column4: This relatively modest value compared to ΔH_vap reflects that melting only loosens hydrogen bonds rather than breaking them entirely.

column1: Why does sweating cool the body?
column3: Evaporation absorbs the large heat of vaporization from skin
column4: Water's high ΔH_vap (~2260 J/g) means that evaporating a small amount of sweat removes substantial heat energy from body surfaces.

column1: What is sublimation enthalpy in terms of fusion and vaporization enthalpies?
column4: Sublimation (solid→gas) is the sum of melting and vaporization steps. By Hess's Law the enthalpies are additive since enthalpy is a state function.

column1: What are the three regions on a phase diagram?
column4: Each region represents conditions of temperature and pressure where that phase is the stable form. Boundaries between regions are phase transition lines.

column1: What is the triple point on a phase diagram?
column3: Temperature and pressure where all three phases coexist
column4: At the triple point, solid, liquid, and gas are in equilibrium simultaneously. For water, this occurs at 0.01°C and 611.7 Pa.

column1: What is the critical point on a phase diagram?
column3: Temperature and pressure above which liquid and gas are indistinguishable
column4: Above the critical temperature, no amount of pressure can liquefy a gas. Beyond the critical point exists a supercritical fluid.

column1: What happens to the boiling point of a liquid as external pressure increases?
column4: Higher pressure requires the liquid to reach a higher vapor pressure to boil, which happens at a higher temperature. This is the principle behind pressure cookers.

column1: On a phase diagram, what does the slope of the solid-liquid boundary indicate for water?
column3: Negative slope (melting point decreases with pressure)
column4: Water is anomalous: ice is less dense than liquid water, so applying pressure favors the denser liquid phase, lowering the melting point. Most substances have a positive slope.

column1: What is a supercritical fluid?
column3: A phase above both critical temperature and critical pressure
column4: Supercritical fluids have properties of both liquids and gases — high density like a liquid but low viscosity like a gas. CO₂ supercritical fluid is used in decaffeination.

column1: On a phase diagram, what does the liquid-gas boundary represent?
column3: Vapor pressure curve (boiling points at each pressure)
column4: Each point on this line is the boiling point at that external pressure. The line ends at the critical point, beyond which the two phases merge.

column1: Why does most substances' solid-liquid phase boundary have a positive slope on a phase diagram?
column3: Solid is denser than liquid, so pressure favors solid
column4: For most substances, applying pressure at the melting point shifts equilibrium toward the denser solid phase, raising the melting temperature. Water is the key exception.

column1: What phase transition occurs when moving from the solid region to the gas region without crossing the liquid region on a phase diagram?
column4: At pressures below the triple point, there is no liquid phase; a solid heated under these conditions converts directly to vapor. Dry ice (CO₂) sublimes at atmospheric pressure.

column1: What is the reaction rate?
column3: Change in concentration of reactant or product per unit time
column4: Rate is expressed as -Δ[reactant]/Δt or +Δ[product]/Δt; negative sign for reactants because they decrease.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What are the standard units of reaction rate?
column4: Rate measures molarity change per second; on the MCAT any equivalent unit (mM/min) is valid but M/s is most common.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How is the rate of disappearance of a reactant related to the rate of appearance of a product for the reaction 2A → B?
column3: Rate of disappearance of A = 2 × rate of appearance of B
column4: Stoichiometric coefficients create the ratio; rate = -1/2 · d[A]/dt = d[B]/dt.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What does it mean if a reaction rate increases as reactant concentration increases?
column3: Rate depends on (is proportional to) reactant concentration
column4: Not all reactions show this; zero-order reactions have rates independent of concentration.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Which factor does NOT directly appear in the rate law for a simple reaction: temperature, concentration, or stoichiometry?
column3: Temperature (it is absorbed into the rate constant k)
column4: Temperature affects k, not the concentration terms of the rate law; stoichiometric coefficients also do not dictate rate-law exponents.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does doubling the concentration of a first-order reactant affect the reaction rate?
column4: For first-order dependence, rate ∝ [A]^1, so doubling [A] doubles the rate.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does doubling the concentration of a second-order reactant affect the reaction rate?
column4: Rate ∝ [A]^2; (2)^2 = 4. This is a classic MCAT calculation question type.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does changing the concentration of a zero-order reactant affect the reaction rate?
column4: Rate = k for a zero-order reaction; concentration does not appear in the rate law.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If tripling [B] increases the rate by a factor of 9, what is the order with respect to B?
column4: 3^n = 9 → n = 2. Use the ratio method: (rate2/rate1) = ([B]2/[B]1)^n.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If quadrupling [A] increases the rate by a factor of 8, what is the order with respect to A?
column4: 4^n = 8 → 2^(2n) = 2^3 → n = 3/2. Fractional orders are uncommon but testable.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the rate law (rate equation) of a reaction?
column4: Exponents m and n are determined experimentally; they are NOT necessarily the stoichiometric coefficients.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What does the rate constant k represent?
column3: Proportionality constant relating rate to concentrations
column4: k is specific to a reaction at a given temperature; larger k means faster reaction at the same concentrations.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What are the units of k for a first-order reaction?
column4: Rate (M/s) = k · [A] (M) → k = M/s ÷ M = s⁻¹.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What are the units of k for a second-order reaction?
column4: Rate (M/s) = k · [A]^2 (M^2) → k = M/s ÷ M^2 = M⁻¹s⁻¹.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What are the units of k for a zero-order reaction?
column4: Rate = k for zero order, so k has units of M/s directly.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Can the rate constant k be determined from stoichiometry alone?
column3: No; k must be determined experimentally
column4: Rate laws and k values require experimental data; stoichiometry only reveals overall mole ratios.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the overall reaction order?
column3: Sum of all exponents in the rate law
column4: For rate = k[A]^2[B]^1, overall order = 2 + 1 = 3 (third order).
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What defines a first-order reaction?
column3: Rate is proportional to concentration raised to the first power
column4: Rate = k[A]; half-life for first-order reactions is constant: t₁/₂ = ln2/k ≈ 0.693/k.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the half-life expression for a first-order reaction?
column4: Derived from the integrated first-order rate law; the half-life is constant regardless of initial concentration.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: For a zero-order reaction, how does half-life depend on initial concentration?
column4: Unlike first order, zero-order half-life is NOT constant; it shrinks as the reaction proceeds.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: For a second-order reaction, how does half-life depend on initial concentration?
column4: As reactant is consumed, each successive half-life is longer—opposite trend to zero order.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the rate-determining step?
column3: The slowest step in a multi-step reaction mechanism
column4: The overall reaction rate equals the rate of the slowest step; intermediates formed before this step appear in the rate law.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does the rate-determining step relate to the overall rate law?
column3: Overall rate law reflects the elementary steps up to and including the rate-determining step
column4: If the slow step is A + B → intermediate, the rate = k[A][B], regardless of later fast steps.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If a fast equilibrium precedes the rate-determining step, how are intermediates handled in the rate law?
column3: Substitute the intermediate using the equilibrium expression
column4: Express [intermediate] in terms of original reactants via Keq = [int]/([A][B]), then substitute into the rate law.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Generally, how does increasing temperature affect reaction rate?
column4: Higher temperature → more molecules exceed activation energy → more successful collisions per unit time.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Approximately, how much does a 10°C rise in temperature increase the reaction rate?
column4: This is an empirical rule of thumb, not exact; the Arrhenius equation gives the precise relationship.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Why does increasing temperature increase reaction rate beyond simply increasing collision frequency?
column3: Greater fraction of molecules have energy ≥ Ea
column4: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shifts; even modest temperature rises dramatically increase the high-energy tail.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Which variable in the Arrhenius equation is most strongly influenced by temperature?
column4: This term changes exponentially with T, making temperature the dominant rate determinant for most reactions.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the activation energy (Ea)?
column3: Minimum energy required for reactants to undergo a reaction
column4: Ea is the energy barrier between reactants and the transition state; units are kJ/mol or kcal/mol.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does a catalyst affect activation energy?
column4: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea, increasing rate without being consumed.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Does activation energy affect the overall ΔH of a reaction?
column3: No; Ea affects rate, not thermodynamics
column4: ΔH depends on energies of reactants vs. products; Ea is the kinetic barrier and is independent of ΔH.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the relationship between Ea (forward) and Ea (reverse) for an exothermic reaction?
column4: For exothermic reactions, products are lower in energy; the reverse reaction must climb a larger energy hill.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How is Ea related to Ea(reverse) and ΔH for a reaction?
column3: Ea(forward) = Ea(reverse) + ΔH (for exothermic: ΔH negative)
column4: Rearranges to ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse); read directly from a reaction energy diagram.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the activated complex (transition state)?
column3: Highest-energy, unstable species at the peak of the energy profile
column4: The transition state cannot be isolated; it exists momentarily as bonds are simultaneously breaking and forming.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does the transition state differ from a reaction intermediate?
column3: Transition state is a maximum on the energy diagram; intermediate is a minimum
column4: Intermediates have finite lifetimes and can sometimes be detected; transition states are instantaneous.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Can the activated complex be isolated in a laboratory?
column3: No; it is too unstable and exists only at the energy maximum
column4: Its fleeting existence distinguishes it from intermediates, which occupy local minima and may be isolable.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: For a two-step mechanism with two transition states, how many energy maxima appear on the energy profile?
column4: Each transition state corresponds to a peak; the intermediate between them appears as a valley (local minimum).
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: On a reaction energy profile, what does the peak represent?
column4: The height of the peak above the reactants equals Ea; the height above products equals Ea(reverse).
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: On a reaction energy profile, how is ΔH read?
column3: Energy difference between products and reactants (right minus left baseline)
column4: Negative ΔH = exothermic (products lower); positive ΔH = endothermic (products higher).
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: On an energy profile for a two-step reaction, which peak corresponds to the rate-determining step?
column4: The taller peak has the greater activation energy, making that elementary step slower and rate-determining.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If a catalyst is added, how does the energy profile change?
column3: Both peaks (Ea forward and reverse) are lowered; ΔH is unchanged
column4: Catalysts lower the activation energy but do not alter the thermodynamic stability of reactants or products.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: On an energy diagram, what does a local minimum between two peaks represent?
column4: Intermediates sit in energy wells between transition states; they are formed and then consumed during the reaction.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the Arrhenius equation?
column4: A = frequency (pre-exponential) factor; R = 8.314 J/mol·K; T in Kelvin. Larger Ea or lower T → smaller k.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: In the Arrhenius equation, what does the pre-exponential factor A represent?
column3: Collision frequency and proper orientation factor
column4: A accounts for how often molecules collide AND whether they are oriented correctly; it is approximately constant for a given reaction.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the linearized (logarithmic) form of the Arrhenius equation?
column4: Plotting ln k vs. 1/T gives a straight line with slope = −Ea/R, allowing graphical determination of Ea.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Using the two-temperature Arrhenius formula, how is Ea calculated?
column4: Derived by subtracting two ln k expressions; allows Ea calculation from two rate constants at two temperatures.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If the slope of a ln k vs. 1/T plot is −8000 K, what is Ea?
column4: Slope = −Ea/R → Ea = −slope × R = 8000 × 8.314 J/mol·K ≈ 66,500 J/mol ≈ 66.5 kJ/mol.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is kinetic control of a reaction?
column3: The product formed fastest (lowest Ea) predominates
column4: Kinetic products accumulate under mild conditions (low T, short time) when reversibility is limited.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is thermodynamic control of a reaction?
column3: The most stable (lowest energy) product predominates
column4: Thermodynamic products predominate at higher temperatures or longer reaction times allowing equilibration.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Under what conditions does thermodynamic control typically prevail?
column3: High temperature, long reaction time, reversible conditions
column4: Sufficient energy and time allow molecules to surmount barriers and equilibrate toward the most stable product.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If the kinetic product is LESS stable than the thermodynamic product, what happens at equilibrium?
column3: The thermodynamic (more stable) product accumulates at equilibrium
column4: Given enough time/energy, reversible reactions favor the thermodynamic product even if it forms more slowly.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: In 1,2- vs. 1,4-addition to a conjugated diene, which product is the kinetic product?
column4: The 1,4-addition product is more stable (thermodynamic), but 1,2 forms first at low temperature — classic kinetic vs. thermodynamic example.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is a catalyst?
column3: A substance that increases reaction rate without being consumed
column4: Catalysts lower Ea, providing an alternative reaction pathway; they are regenerated at the end of the reaction.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Does a catalyst shift the equilibrium position of a reaction?
column3: No; it only speeds up the approach to equilibrium
column4: A catalyst lowers Ea equally for forward and reverse reactions, so Keq is unchanged.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the difference between a homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst?
column3: Homogeneous: same phase as reactants; heterogeneous: different phase
column4: Heterogeneous catalysts (e.g., Pt metal for H₂ reactions) act at surfaces; homogeneous catalysts are dissolved in the reaction mixture.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How do enzymes function as biological catalysts?
column3: They lower Ea by stabilizing the transition state in an active site
column4: Enzyme–substrate specificity (lock-and-key or induced-fit) positions reactants for optimal bond forming/breaking.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is a negative catalyst (inhibitor)?
column3: A substance that slows a reaction by raising the effective energy barrier or blocking active sites
column4: Not truly a catalyst; inhibitors can be competitive (block active site) or noncompetitive, reducing reaction rate.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is a reversible reaction?
column3: A reaction that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions
column4: Indicated by a double arrow (⇌); at equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What condition defines chemical equilibrium?
column3: Rate of forward reaction equals rate of reverse reaction
column4: Concentrations remain constant (not necessarily equal) at equilibrium; the system is dynamic, not static.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the difference between a system at equilibrium and a system that has stopped reacting?
column3: At equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue but at equal rates
column4: Equilibrium is dynamic: molecules still react, but there is no net change in concentration.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If Keq >> 1, what does that indicate about the equilibrium position?
column3: Products are strongly favored at equilibrium
column4: Large Keq → products predominate; small Keq (<1) → reactants predominate at equilibrium.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Can a reaction reach equilibrium if it is irreversible?
column3: No; irreversible reactions go to completion
column4: Irreversible reactions have Keq so large that essentially all reactants convert to products; no back-reaction is measurable.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the Law of Mass Action?
column3: At equilibrium, the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations (each raised to their stoichiometric powers) is constant
column4: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Keq = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). This ratio equals Keq at a given temperature.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: For the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, write the equilibrium expression.
column4: Products over reactants, each raised to their stoichiometric coefficients; pure solids/liquids are omitted.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Why are pure solids and pure liquids excluded from the equilibrium expression?
column3: Their concentrations (activities) are defined as 1 and remain constant
column4: Only species whose concentrations change during reaction affect the equilibrium expression.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does the equilibrium expression change when a reaction is reversed?
column3: The new Keq is the reciprocal of the original Keq
column4: If forward Keq = K, then reverse Keq = 1/K; reversing a reaction inverts the expression.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If reaction (1) is multiplied by n, how does Keq change?
column4: Multiplying stoichiometric coefficients raises each concentration term to a higher power, which equals raising K to the power n.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the equilibrium constant (Keq)?
column3: The ratio of product to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, each raised to their stoichiometric coefficients
column4: Keq is dimensionless in formal thermodynamics (uses activities), though concentrations are used as an approximation.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is Kp and how does it differ from Kc?
column3: Kp uses partial pressures; Kc uses molar concentrations
column4: Related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = moles gaseous products − moles gaseous reactants.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the reaction quotient Q?
column3: Same ratio as Keq but calculated with non-equilibrium concentrations
column4: If Q < K, reaction proceeds forward; if Q > K, reaction proceeds reverse; if Q = K, system is at equilibrium.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If two reactions are added, how are their equilibrium constants combined?
column4: Hess's law analog for equilibrium: K_total = K₁ × K₂; used to find K for a reaction derived from steps.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: State Le Châtelier's Principle.
column3: A system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any imposed stress
column4: Stresses include changes in concentration, pressure/volume, and temperature; the system partially counteracts the change.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If a reactant is added to a system at equilibrium, which direction does the reaction shift?
column4: Adding reactant increases Q below K; the system shifts right to restore equilibrium.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: For a reaction with more moles of gas on the product side, how does decreasing volume (increasing pressure) affect equilibrium?
column3: Shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas (reactants)
column4: Higher pressure favors fewer gas molecules; Le Châtelier's says the system shifts to reduce pressure.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does adding an inert gas at constant volume affect a gas-phase equilibrium?
column4: Partial pressures of reactants and products are unchanged, so Q = K is maintained; the reaction does not shift.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does increasing temperature affect an exothermic equilibrium reaction?
column3: Shifts toward reactants (reverse direction), decreasing Keq
column4: Heat is a product for exothermic reactions; adding heat favors the reverse reaction and lowers K.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: Does adding a catalyst shift the equilibrium position of a reaction?
column3: No; equilibrium position and Keq are unchanged
column4: A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but at the same position.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the relationship between ΔG° and the equilibrium constant Keq?
column4: R = 8.314 J/mol·K, T in Kelvin. Negative ΔG° → Keq > 1 (products favored); positive ΔG° → Keq < 1.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If ΔG° = 0, what is Keq?
column4: ΔG° = −RT ln Keq = 0 → ln Keq = 0 → Keq = e^0 = 1; neither products nor reactants are favored at standard state.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does ΔG° relate to whether a reaction is spontaneous?
column4: ΔG° predicts spontaneity only at standard state; ΔG (not ΔG°) predicts spontaneity at any conditions.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If Keq increases with rising temperature, what is the sign of ΔH°?
column4: Van't Hoff equation: d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/RT². Positive ΔH° means K increases with T; endothermic reactions are favored by heat.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is the van't Hoff equation used for?
column3: Predicting how Keq changes with temperature
column4: ln(K₂/K₁) = −ΔH°/R · (1/T₂ − 1/T₁); analogous in form to the two-point Arrhenius equation.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What does Ea represent in the context of reaction kinetics?
column3: Activation energy: minimum energy needed for a successful collision
column4: Ea determines the sensitivity of rate to temperature; higher Ea → rate increases more steeply with temperature.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How is Ea determined graphically using the Arrhenius equation?
column3: Ea = −slope × R from a plot of ln k vs. 1/T
column4: Linearized Arrhenius: ln k = −Ea/R · (1/T) + ln A; the slope of ln k vs. 1/T equals −Ea/R.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: If reaction A has Ea = 50 kJ/mol and reaction B has Ea = 100 kJ/mol, which is more sensitive to temperature change?
column4: The exponential term e^(−Ea/RT) changes more steeply with T when Ea is larger; high-Ea reactions are more temperature-sensitive.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What happens to the rate constant k as Ea approaches zero?
column3: k approaches A (the pre-exponential factor); rate is determined by collision frequency only
column4: e^(−0/RT) = 1, so k = A; every collision leads to reaction when there is no energy barrier.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What does Te represent in reaction kinetics?
column3: Temperature at which the equilibrium constant is measured or the transition temperature between kinetic and thermodynamic control
column4: On the MCAT, Te often refers to the temperature variable in Arrhenius/equilibrium calculations; context determines exact meaning.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does temperature (Te) affect the value of Keq for an endothermic reaction?
column3: Increasing Te increases Keq (shifts equilibrium toward products)
column4: Van't Hoff: for endothermic ΔH° > 0, raising T increases ln K and therefore K itself.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: How does temperature (Te) affect the value of Keq for an exothermic reaction?
column3: Increasing Te decreases Keq (shifts equilibrium toward reactants)
column4: For exothermic ΔH° < 0, higher T decreases K; heat is a product so adding temperature pushes equilibrium left.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: At what temperature would a non-spontaneous reaction (ΔH° > 0, ΔS° > 0) become spontaneous?
column4: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° < 0 when T > ΔH°/ΔS°; at that crossover temperature the reaction shifts from non-spontaneous to spontaneous.
column5: Rate Processes in Chemical Reactions ― Kinetics and Equilibrium

column1: What is sensation?
column3: Detection of physical stimuli by sensory receptors
column4: Sensation is the process by which sensory receptors and the nervous system receive and represent stimulus energies from the environment. It precedes perception.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is transduction in sensory processing?
column3: Conversion of stimulus energy into neural signals
column4: Transduction is the step in which sensory receptor cells convert the physical or chemical stimulus (light, pressure, sound, etc.) into electrical impulses that the brain can interpret.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the process that occurs after transduction to send a signal to the brain?
column4: After transduction, the generated action potential travels along afferent sensory neurons to the appropriate region of the brain for processing.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which term describes the conversion of a perceived sensation into a meaningful experience?
column4: Perception is the brain's interpretation and organization of sensory information. Sensation provides the raw data; perception gives it meaning.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the difference between sensation and perception?
column4: Sensation is the bottom-up, receptor-level detection of stimuli. Perception is the top-down, cognitive interpretation of those signals, influenced by experience and expectation.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the absolute threshold?
column3: Minimum stimulus intensity detectable 50% of the time
column4: The absolute threshold is the smallest amount of stimulation needed for a person to detect a stimulus half of the time it is presented. It reflects the sensitivity of the sensory system.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::threshold MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the difference threshold (just noticeable difference, JND)?
column3: Smallest detectable difference between two stimuli
column4: The JND is the minimum change in stimulus intensity that a person can detect 50% of the time. It is related to Weber's Law.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::threshold MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the terminal threshold in sensory processing?
column3: Intensity at which a stimulus causes pain or is no longer perceived as the same sense
column4: Beyond the terminal threshold, a stimulus may become painful or be perceived differently (e.g., very loud sound causes pain rather than hearing). It marks the upper limit of perception.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::threshold MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the subliminal threshold?
column3: Stimulus intensity below the absolute threshold
column4: A subliminal stimulus is one that is too weak to be consciously detected yet may still influence behavior or cognition without awareness.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::threshold MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does signal-to-noise ratio relate to absolute threshold?
column3: Higher noise raises the absolute threshold
column4: When background noise (internal or external) is high, a stronger signal is needed to reach the absolute threshold, illustrating that thresholds are not fixed values but depend on context.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::threshold MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does Weber's Law state?
column3: JND is a constant fraction of the original stimulus
column4: Weber's Law: ΔI/I = k, where ΔI is the JND, I is the baseline intensity, and k is the Weber fraction (a constant specific to each sense). It explains why we notice a 1 lb change in 10 lbs more than 1 lb in 100 lbs.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::weber-s-law-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the Weber fraction?
column3: The constant ratio of JND to original stimulus intensity
column4: Expressed as k = ΔI/I, the Weber fraction differs for each sensory modality. Smaller k means more sensitivity (e.g., vision has a smaller k than weight perception).
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::weber-s-law-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which sense has the smallest Weber fraction (highest sensitivity to change)?
column4: Human vision is exquisitely sensitive; the Weber fraction for brightness is approximately 0.02. Weight discrimination has a larger fraction (~0.02–0.05), and loudness is around 0.04.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::weber-s-law-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: If a person can just notice a 5 g difference in a 100 g weight, what is their Weber fraction for weight?
column4: k = ΔI/I = 5/100 = 0.05. Weber's Law predicts they would need to detect a 10 g difference in a 200 g weight to reach the same JND.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::weber-s-law-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Weber's Law applies most accurately at what stimulus intensities?
column4: Weber's Law breaks down at very low (near absolute threshold) and very high (near terminal threshold) stimulus intensities; it holds best for moderate ranges.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::weber-s-law-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does signal detection theory (SDT) explain?
column3: How we detect signals amid noise, influenced by bias
column4: SDT holds that detecting a stimulus is not just about sensory sensitivity but also about the observer's decision criterion (bias), which is shaped by costs, benefits, and expectations.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::signal-detection-theory-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: In SDT, what are the four possible outcomes?
column3: Hit, miss, false alarm, correct rejection
column4: Hit = signal present, detected; Miss = signal present, not detected; False alarm = no signal, but reported; Correct rejection = no signal, correctly not reported. These form a 2x2 matrix.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::signal-detection-theory-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is d-prime (d') in signal detection theory?
column3: Measure of sensitivity (ability to discriminate signal from noise)
column4: d' reflects how well an observer distinguishes a true signal from background noise, independent of response bias. Higher d' = better sensitivity.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::signal-detection-theory-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is response criterion (beta) in SDT?
column3: The observer's decision threshold for reporting a signal
column4: A liberal criterion (low beta) leads to more hits but also more false alarms. A conservative criterion (high beta) reduces false alarms but increases misses.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::signal-detection-theory-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: In SDT, a radiologist who reads every ambiguous scan as positive has what type of criterion?
column4: A liberal criterion means the observer is willing to say 'yes, signal present' even with minimal evidence, maximizing hits but also increasing false alarms.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::signal-detection-theory-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is sensory adaptation?
column3: Decreased sensitivity to a constant, unchanging stimulus
column4: When a stimulus is constant and continuous, receptor firing rates decline over time, reducing perceived intensity. Example: not noticing your shirt after wearing it for a few minutes.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-adaptation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which sensory system shows the LEAST adaptation?
column4: Pain receptors adapt minimally, which is biologically protective. In contrast, olfactory and tactile receptors adapt rapidly to constant stimuli.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-adaptation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the adaptive value of sensory adaptation?
column4: By filtering out constant background stimuli, sensory adaptation frees cognitive resources to detect novel or changing signals that may signal danger or new information.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-adaptation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is dark adaptation, and approximately how long does full rod dark adaptation take?
column3: Rods regain sensitivity in the dark; ~20-30 minutes
column4: After exposure to bright light, rhodopsin in rods is bleached. Full regeneration (dark adaptation) takes 20–30 minutes, enabling vision in dim conditions.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-adaptation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the difference between sensory adaptation and habituation?
column3: Adaptation = receptor level; habituation = neural/cognitive level
column4: Sensory adaptation occurs at the receptor itself (reduced firing). Habituation is a learned decrease in response at a higher neural level, not dependent on receptor fatigue.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-adaptation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is psychophysics?
column3: Study of relationship between physical stimuli and perception
column4: Psychophysics quantifies how changes in physical stimulus properties (intensity, frequency) relate to changes in subjective sensory experience. Weber and Fechner were pioneers.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::psychophysics MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is Fechner's Law?
column4: Fechner extended Weber's Law, proposing that perceived sensation grows as the logarithm of the stimulus intensity. This means equal ratio increases in stimulus produce equal perceived steps.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::psychophysics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is Stevens' Power Law?
column4: Stevens proposed that the relationship between sensation and stimulus is a power function, not logarithmic. The exponent n varies by modality (n<1 for brightness, n>1 for electric shock).
