column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::psychophysics MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does an exponent (n) greater than 1 in Stevens' Power Law indicate?
column3: Stimulus is amplified perceptually (e.g., pain, electric shock)
column4: When n > 1, doubling the physical stimulus more than doubles perceived intensity. This holds for pain and electric shock, which may be an adaptive safety response.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::psychophysics MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the method of limits in psychophysics?
column3: Gradually increasing/decreasing stimulus until threshold is detected
column4: An experimenter systematically raises or lowers stimulus intensity until the participant reports detection (ascending) or loss of detection (descending) to measure threshold.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::psychophysics MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are sensory receptors?
column3: Specialized cells that detect specific stimuli and initiate transduction
column4: Sensory receptors are located at the first stage of sensory processing and convert specific physical or chemical energy into electrical signals. Different receptors are tuned to different stimuli.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What property describes a sensory receptor's preference for one type of stimulus?
column4: Each receptor type has an adequate stimulus — the type of energy it is most sensitive to (e.g., photoreceptors for light, mechanoreceptors for pressure). This is the basis of sensory coding.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the generator potential in sensory receptors?
column3: Graded potential produced by receptor in response to a stimulus
column4: The generator (receptor) potential is a graded, non-propagating depolarization. If large enough, it triggers an action potential in the sensory neuron. Its magnitude reflects stimulus intensity.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the law of specific nerve energies?
column3: Each sensory nerve produces only one type of sensation regardless of how it is stimulated
column4: Proposed by Muller: stimulating the optic nerve always produces visual sensations even if done mechanically. The brain interprets input based on the pathway, not the type of stimulus.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the receptive field of a sensory receptor?
column3: Area of the body/environment that, when stimulated, activates that receptor
column4: Receptive fields vary in size; smaller fields (e.g., fingertips) allow finer spatial discrimination than larger fields (e.g., back skin). Two-point discrimination depends on receptive field size.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the general route of a sensory pathway from receptor to cortex?
column3: Receptor → afferent neuron → spinal cord/brainstem → thalamus → primary sensory cortex
column4: Most sensory information is relayed through the thalamus (the 'gateway to the cortex') before reaching the appropriate primary sensory cortex. Olfaction is a notable exception, bypassing the thalamus.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-pathways MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which sensory modality bypasses the thalamus on its way to the cortex?
column4: Olfactory signals travel from the olfactory bulb directly to the olfactory cortex (piriform cortex) and limbic system, bypassing the thalamic relay. All other senses pass through the thalamus.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-pathways MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the role of the thalamus in sensory pathways?
column3: Relay station; routes sensory signals to appropriate cortical area
column4: The thalamus receives sensory input (except olfaction), filters it, and directs it to the correct primary sensory cortex. It also plays a role in attention and arousal.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-pathways MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Where does somatosensory information from the body cross the midline?
column3: Spinal cord (for pain/temperature) or medulla (for touch/proprioception)
column4: The spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature) decussates in the spinal cord at the level of entry. The dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway (touch, proprioception) crosses in the medulla.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-pathways MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Where is the primary somatosensory cortex located?
column3: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
column4: The postcentral gyrus contains the somatosensory cortex, organized somatotopically (homunculus). Areas with greater tactile sensitivity (hands, lips) have disproportionately large cortical representation.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-pathways MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What does the sensory homunculus represent?
column3: Cortical map of the body, sized by sensory receptor density
column4: Body parts with more sensory receptors (e.g., hands, tongue, lips) occupy larger areas on the somatosensory cortex. This distorted 'map' is the sensory homunculus.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::sensory-pathways MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are mechanoreceptors?
column3: Receptors that detect mechanical stimuli (pressure, vibration, touch, stretch)
column4: Mechanoreceptors include Meissner's corpuscles (light touch), Pacinian corpuscles (vibration), Merkel's discs (sustained pressure), and Ruffini endings (skin stretch).
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are nociceptors?
column3: Receptors that detect painful or damaging stimuli
column4: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that respond to potentially tissue-damaging stimuli (mechanical, thermal, or chemical). They show very little adaptation, which is protective.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of receptor detects temperature?
column4: Thermoreceptors detect warm and cold temperatures. Cold receptors are more numerous and are activated by temperatures below ~35°C; warm receptors respond to temperatures above ~30°C.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are photoreceptors, and where are they located?
column3: Light-detecting receptors; located in the retina
column4: Rods (dim light, peripheral vision, no color) and cones (bright light, color, central/foveal vision) are the two photoreceptors of the eye.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are chemoreceptors?
column3: Receptors that detect chemical stimuli (taste, smell, blood gases)
column4: Chemoreceptors include taste (gustatory) receptors, olfactory receptors, and internal receptors that monitor blood O2, CO2, and pH. They transduce chemical energy into neural signals.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are proprioceptors, and where are they found?
column3: Receptors detecting body position/movement; in muscles, joints, tendons
column4: Proprioceptors include muscle spindles (muscle stretch), Golgi tendon organs (muscle tension), and joint receptors. They provide the sense of limb position and movement (kinesthesia).
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which receptor type detects rapid vibration (e.g., 200-300 Hz) and is located deep in the skin?
column4: Pacinian corpuscles are encapsulated mechanoreceptors found in deep skin layers, joints, and viscera. They adapt very rapidly and are best tuned to high-frequency vibration (~250 Hz).
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which mechanoreceptor is responsible for fine spatial discrimination and two-point touch, located near skin surface?
column4: Merkel's discs are slowly adapting, small-receptive-field mechanoreceptors in the superficial dermis. They are crucial for shape and texture discrimination and reading Braille.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are hair cells in the auditory and vestibular systems classified as?
column4: Hair cells in the cochlea (hearing) and vestibular system (balance) are specialized mechanoreceptors that detect movement of stereocilia caused by fluid waves or head movement.
column8: concept::PS::6A::sensory_processing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::sensory-processing::types-of-sensory-receptors MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the transparent outer covering of the eye that performs most of the eye's refraction?
column4: The cornea contributes about two-thirds of the eye's total refractive power. Unlike the lens, its curvature is fixed and cannot accommodate.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the colored portion of the eye that controls pupil size?
column4: The iris contains smooth muscle (dilator and sphincter pupillae) that adjusts pupil diameter in response to light intensity and autonomic input.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structure of the eye changes shape to fine-tune focus on near vs. far objects?
column4: The ciliary muscles alter lens curvature (accommodation). Contraction of ciliary muscles rounds the lens for near vision; relaxation flattens it for far vision.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eye?
column4: The retina contains photoreceptors (rods and cones), bipolar cells, and ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What fluid fills the anterior chamber of the eye between the cornea and lens?
column4: Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body and drained via the canal of Schlemm. Impaired drainage leads to glaucoma (elevated intraocular pressure).
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the gel-like substance that fills the posterior chamber of the eye (between lens and retina)?
column4: Vitreous humor is a transparent, gel-like substance that maintains the eye's spherical shape. Unlike aqueous humor, it is not continuously replenished.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the region of the retina where the optic nerve exits and no photoreceptors are present?
column4: Because there are no rods or cones at the optic disc, this area produces no visual signal. The brain fills in this gap using surrounding visual information.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the area of the retina with the highest density of cones, responsible for sharp central vision?
column4: The fovea is located at the center of the macula and contains only cones. It provides maximum visual acuity and color discrimination.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which autonomic division mediates pupil constriction (miosis)?
column4: The parasympathetic fibers of CN III (oculomotor) innervate the sphincter pupillae. Parasympathetic activation in bright light constricts the pupil.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which layer of the eye is pigmented and lies between the retina and sclera, supplying blood to the outer retina?
column4: The choroid is highly vascular and absorbs excess light to prevent internal reflection. It is part of the uveal tract along with the iris and ciliary body.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which photoreceptors are responsible for color vision and function best in bright light?
column4: Cones are concentrated in the fovea and contain one of three opsins (S, M, L) sensitive to short, medium, or long wavelengths (blue, green, red).
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which photoreceptors are responsible for dim-light (scotopic) vision and are more numerous in the peripheral retina?
column4: Rods contain rhodopsin and are exquisitely sensitive to light but do not distinguish color. They vastly outnumber cones (~120 million vs ~6 million).
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What photopigment is found in rods?
column4: Rhodopsin consists of opsin protein + retinal (a vitamin A derivative). Light isomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, initiating the phototransduction cascade.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What ion channel closes in photoreceptors when light activates the phototransduction cascade?
column4: In the dark, cGMP keeps Na+ channels open (dark current). Light activates phosphodiesterase, which hydrolyzes cGMP, closing channels and hyperpolarizing the photoreceptor.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the term for the process by which photoreceptors become less sensitive after prolonged exposure to bright light?
column4: During light adaptation, rhodopsin bleaches and the visual system becomes less sensitive. Dark adaptation (recovery of sensitivity in dim light) takes ~20-30 minutes for full rod recovery.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of cells transmit signals from photoreceptors to retinal ganglion cells?
column4: The direct pathway in the retina is: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → retinal ganglion cells. Horizontal and amacrine cells modulate this pathway laterally.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the phenomenon where stimulation of the center of a ganglion cell's receptive field has the OPPOSITE effect of stimulating its surround?
column4: ON-center cells are excited by light in the center and inhibited by light in the surround. This mechanism, mediated by horizontal cells, enhances edge detection and contrast.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes the gradual increase in visual sensitivity that occurs when moving from a bright environment to a dark one?
column4: Cone adaptation occurs rapidly (~5-10 min); full rod adaptation requires ~20-30 minutes and is limited by the regeneration of rhodopsin from vitamin A.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which wavelength of light is detected by L-cones (long-wavelength cones)?
column4: The three cone types peak at ~420 nm (S/blue), ~530 nm (M/green), and ~560 nm (L/red). Color perception arises from the ratio of activation across cone types (opponent-process theory).
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of color blindness results from absence or defect of L-cones?
column4: Protanopia is the most common form of red-green color blindness, inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. Deuteranopia involves M-cones; tritanopia (rare) involves S-cones.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-processing MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: After leaving the retina, where do optic nerve fibers from each eye first converge?
column4: At the optic chiasm, fibers from the nasal (medial) half of each retina cross to the opposite side; fibers from the temporal (lateral) half remain ipsilateral.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which visual field is processed by the LEFT cerebral hemisphere?
column4: Light from the right visual field strikes the nasal retina of the right eye and the temporal retina of the left eye; both project (after crossing at the chiasm) to the left hemisphere.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the major thalamic relay nucleus for visual information?
column4: The LGN of the thalamus receives input from retinal ganglion cells and sends projections to primary visual cortex (V1) via the optic radiations.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the primary visual cortex also called, and where is it located?
column4: V1 is located in the banks of the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe. It is also called striate cortex due to the stripe of Gennari (a prominent myelin band).
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: A lesion at the optic chiasm (e.g., pituitary tumor) classically produces which visual field deficit?
column4: The crossing nasal fibers (representing the temporal visual fields) are damaged. Each eye loses its temporal (outer) visual field, a pattern called 'tunnel vision.'
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: A complete lesion of the right optic tract produces which visual field defect?
column4: After the chiasm, the right optic tract carries information from the left visual field of both eyes. A complete lesion eliminates the entire left visual field.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the pathway from V1 that projects dorsally toward the parietal lobe, involved in spatial processing ('where')?
column4: The dorsal stream projects from V1 → V2 → V5/MT → parietal cortex. It processes motion, depth, and spatial location. Damage can cause visual neglect or optic ataxia.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the pathway from V1 that projects ventrally toward the temporal lobe, involved in object recognition ('what')?
column4: The ventral stream projects from V1 → V2 → V4 → inferotemporal cortex. It is involved in object recognition and form perception. Damage can cause visual agnosia.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cortical area in the ventral stream is critical for face recognition?
column4: The FFA is in the fusiform gyrus of the temporal lobe. Damage causes prosopagnosia (inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact basic vision).
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::visual-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is parallel processing in the context of visual perception?
column3: Simultaneous processing of different visual attributes by separate brain pathways
column4: The visual system processes color, motion, form, and depth concurrently in different cortical areas rather than sequentially, allowing rapid integration of a complete scene.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::parallel-processing-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which two major visual processing streams exemplify parallel processing in the brain?
column4: These streams operate simultaneously: the dorsal stream analyzes spatial location and motion; the ventral stream analyzes object identity and color, illustrating true parallel processing.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::parallel-processing-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which visual attribute is preferentially processed by area V4 in the ventral stream?
column4: V4 is a color-selective region in the ventral occipital/temporal cortex. Damage to V4 causes cerebral achromatopsia — the inability to perceive color despite intact retinal function.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::parallel-processing-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which visual attribute is preferentially processed by area V5/MT in the dorsal stream?
column4: Area V5 (also called MT, middle temporal area) is specialized for motion detection and direction selectivity. Damage causes akinetopsia — the inability to perceive visual motion.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::parallel-processing-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the advantage of parallel processing in vision over strictly serial processing?
column3: Faster, more efficient integration of multiple features simultaneously
column4: Parallel processing allows the brain to analyze color, motion, depth, and form at the same time, enabling rapid scene understanding without bottlenecks from sequential analysis.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::parallel-processing-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which layers of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) carry information related to fine detail and color (parvocellular)?
column4: Parvocellular (P) layers receive input from midget retinal ganglion cells and project to V1 blobs/interblobs. They carry high spatial frequency and color info to the ventral stream.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::parallel-processing-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which layers of the LGN carry information about motion and contrast (magnocellular)?
column4: Magnocellular (M) layers receive input from parasol retinal ganglion cells and are sensitive to low spatial frequency, motion, and luminance contrast. They feed primarily into the dorsal stream.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::parallel-processing-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is feature detection in the context of visual neuroscience?
column3: Neural response to specific stimulus properties (e.g., edges, orientation, movement)
column4: Feature detectors are neurons that respond selectively to particular visual attributes. Hubel and Wiesel discovered orientation-selective cells in V1 using bar stimuli in cats.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::feature-detection-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Who first described feature detector cells in the visual cortex?
column4: Hubel and Wiesel (Nobel Prize 1981) discovered simple, complex, and hypercomplex (end-stopped) cells in cat V1 that responded selectively to bar orientation, motion direction, and edge length.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::feature-detection-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of V1 cell responds to a bar of light at a specific orientation in a fixed retinal location?
column4: Simple cells have distinct ON and OFF subregions in their receptive fields; they respond best to a bar or edge at a particular orientation and spatial position.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::feature-detection-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of V1 cell responds to a bar of a specific orientation regardless of its exact position within the receptive field?
column4: Complex cells sum inputs from many simple cells, giving them position invariance within their receptive field. Many are also selective for direction of motion.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::feature-detection-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What psychological phenomenon supports feature detection: briefly viewing one type of motion causes stationary objects to appear to move in the opposite direction?
column4: After prolonged exposure to downward motion, stationary objects appear to move upward. This adaptation effect reflects fatigue of directionally selective motion detectors in V5/MT.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::feature-detection-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is a 'grandmother cell' hypothesis in feature detection?
column3: Single neuron encoding a specific complex object or person
column4: The grandmother cell hypothesis posits that one neuron recognizes one object (e.g., your grandmother's face). Modern neuroscience favors distributed population coding over strict single-cell coding.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::feature-detection-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes the progressive specialization of neurons from V1 to inferotemporal cortex for increasingly complex visual features?
column4: Early visual areas (V1) detect simple features (edges); higher areas detect increasingly complex patterns (shapes, objects, faces), with neurons becoming more selective and invariant at each stage.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::feature-detection-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the near point of accommodation?
column3: Closest distance at which the eye can maintain clear focus
column4: The near point increases with age (presbyopia) as the lens becomes less flexible. In young adults it is ~10 cm; by age 45-50 it recedes to arm's length or beyond.
column8: concept::PS::6A::vision MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::vision::structure-and-function-of-the-eye MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the outer, funnel-shaped portion of the ear that collects sound waves?
column4: The pinna directs sound into the external auditory canal toward the tympanic membrane. Its asymmetric shape aids in localizing sounds vertically.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What membrane separates the outer ear from the middle ear?
column4: Sound waves cause the tympanic membrane to vibrate, transmitting mechanical energy to the ossicles of the middle ear.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Name the three ossicles of the middle ear in order from lateral to medial.
column4: The ossicles form a lever system that amplifies and transmits vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the oval window of the cochlea.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structure connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalizes pressure?
column4: The Eustachian tube allows air pressure equalization across the tympanic membrane; its dysfunction causes the sensation of 'blocked' ears during altitude changes.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What membrane does the stapes footplate push against to transmit vibrations into the inner ear?
column4: The oval window is a membrane-covered opening between the middle and inner ear; stapes movement creates pressure waves in the cochlear fluid (perilymph).
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two fluid-filled compartments of the cochlea called, and what fluid fills each?
column3: Scala vestibuli and scala tympani — perilymph; scala media — endolymph
column4: Perilymph (high Na+) fills scala vestibuli and tympani; endolymph (high K+) fills scala media (cochlear duct). The unique ionic composition of endolymph is critical for hair cell depolarization.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the function of the round window in the cochlea?
column3: Relieves pressure after oval window displacement
column4: Because fluid is incompressible, when the stapes pushes the oval window inward, the round window membrane bulges outward to accommodate the pressure wave.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the sensory organ within the cochlea that contains hair cells?
column4: The Organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane within the scala media and is the actual transducer converting mechanical vibration to electrical signals.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What property of the basilar membrane determines which region responds maximally to a given sound frequency?
column3: Width and stiffness vary along its length (tonotopy)
column4: The base of the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff (responds to high frequencies); the apex is wide and floppy (responds to low frequencies). This forms a tonotopic map.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which end of the basilar membrane responds to high-frequency sounds?
column4: Tonotopic organization: high frequencies resonate at the base, low frequencies at the apex. This principle underlies frequency discrimination (pitch perception).
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::structure-and-function-of-the-ear MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What cranial nerve carries auditory signals from the cochlea to the brain?
column4: CN VIII has two divisions: the cochlear branch (hearing) and the vestibular branch (balance). Damage causes sensorineural hearing loss or vertigo, respectively.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: After leaving the cochlea via CN VIII, what is the first brainstem nucleus where auditory signals synapse?
column4: The cochlear nuclei are the first obligatory relay in the auditory pathway. From here, signals travel bilaterally — this bilateral projection is clinically important.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What brainstem structure is involved in sound localization by comparing timing differences between the two ears?
column4: The superior olive receives input from both cochlear nuclei and detects interaural time differences (ITD) and interaural level differences (ILD), critical for horizontal sound localization.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What midbrain structure is a major relay for auditory information and coordinates auditory reflexes (e.g., orienting to a sound)?
column4: The inferior colliculus integrates ascending and descending auditory signals and plays a role in reflexive responses to sudden sounds (startle reflex involves superior colliculus for visual, inferior for auditory).
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What thalamic nucleus relays auditory information to the cortex?
column4: The MGN of the thalamus projects to the primary auditory cortex (A1) in the temporal lobe. Compare to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) for vision.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: In which lobe and gyrus is the primary auditory cortex (A1) located?
column3: Temporal lobe, superior temporal gyrus (Heschl's gyrus)
column4: A1 (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) maintains tonotopic organization. Wernicke's area for language comprehension is adjacent in the left hemisphere.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of hearing loss results from damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve?
column4: Sensorineural loss cannot be corrected by amplifying sound transmitted through bone; it contrasts with conductive hearing loss (outer/middle ear problem), which the Rinne and Weber tests help distinguish.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of hearing loss results from damage to the outer or middle ear structures that conduct sound?
column4: Examples include cerumen impaction, otitis media, or ossicle damage. Bone conduction bypasses the problem, so hearing is better with bone conduction than air conduction in conductive loss.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::auditory-processing-e-g-auditory-pathways-in-the-brain MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the primary ion that flows into hair cells through mechanically gated channels to cause depolarization?
column4: Endolymph is uniquely high in K+. When stereocilia deflect toward the tallest cilia, K+ flows in down its electrochemical gradient, depolarizing the hair cell — the opposite of most neurons where K+ flows out.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::sensory-reception-by-hair-cells MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structures on hair cells open mechanically gated ion channels when deflected?
column4: Tip links are protein filaments connecting adjacent stereocilia. When the bundle deflects toward the tallest stereocilium, tip links pull open mechanically gated K+ channels, initiating transduction.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::sensory-reception-by-hair-cells MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What happens to hair cell ion channels when stereocilia deflect away from the tallest stereocilium?
column4: Deflection toward tall stereocilia opens channels (depolarization); deflection away closes channels (hyperpolarization). This bidirectional modulation allows encoding of sound wave compression and rarefaction.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::sensory-reception-by-hair-cells MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What neurotransmitter do inner hair cells release onto afferent auditory nerve fibers?
column4: Depolarization of inner hair cells causes Ca2+-dependent exocytosis of glutamate at ribbon synapses, which excites the afferent fibers of the cochlear branch of CN VIII.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::sensory-reception-by-hair-cells MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the two types of hair cells in the cochlea, and which type is primarily responsible for sound transduction to the brain?
column3: Inner hair cells (transduction) and outer hair cells (amplification)
column4: Inner hair cells (~3,500) send the majority of afferent signals to CN VIII. Outer hair cells (~12,000) act as mechanical amplifiers via electromotility (prestin protein), sharpening frequency tuning.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::sensory-reception-by-hair-cells MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What motor protein in outer hair cells enables electromotility to amplify basilar membrane vibrations?
column4: Prestin changes shape in response to membrane voltage, causing outer hair cells to shorten or elongate and actively amplify basilar membrane motion, boosting sensitivity by ~40 dB.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::sensory-reception-by-hair-cells MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the name of the membrane against which hair cell stereocilia are embedded (or make contact) in the cochlea?
column4: The tectorial membrane lies above the Organ of Corti. When the basilar membrane vibrates, a shearing motion between the tectorial and basilar membranes deflects the stereocilia of the hair cells.
column8: concept::PS::6A::hearing MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::hearing::sensory-reception-by-hair-cells MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of receptors are responsible for somatosensation?
column4: Somatosensation encompasses touch, temperature, and pain, each served by distinct receptor types in the skin and deeper tissues.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::somatosensation-e-g-pain-perception MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is nociception?
column3: Detection of painful or tissue-damaging stimuli
column4: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that respond to noxious stimuli; their activation triggers the perception of pain.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::somatosensation-e-g-pain-perception MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which spinal tract carries pain and temperature signals to the brain?
column4: The anterolateral (spinothalamic) pathway crosses the midline near the level of entry and ascends to the thalamus, carrying pain, temperature, and crude touch.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::somatosensation-e-g-pain-perception MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the gate control theory of pain?
column3: Non-painful input can close 'gates' to painful signals in the spinal cord
column4: Melzack and Wall proposed that large-diameter mechanoreceptor fibers can inhibit transmission of pain signals from small-diameter fibers at the dorsal horn.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::somatosensation-e-g-pain-perception MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is referred pain?
column3: Pain felt at a site distant from the actual injury
column4: For example, cardiac ischemia is often felt as left arm or jaw pain because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal neurons.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::somatosensation-e-g-pain-perception MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which fiber type (A-delta vs. C) carries fast, sharp pain?
column4: A-delta fibers are thinly myelinated and conduct rapidly, producing the sharp first pain; unmyelinated C fibers carry slow, burning, or aching pain.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::somatosensation-e-g-pain-perception MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What neurotransmitter is released by C fibers and is associated with chronic pain transmission?
column4: Substance P is a neuropeptide released at synapses in the dorsal horn; it facilitates pain transmission and contributes to central sensitization.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::somatosensation-e-g-pain-perception MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the structures that contain taste receptor cells?
column4: Taste buds are located primarily on papillae of the tongue and contain chemoreceptor cells that detect dissolved chemicals in saliva.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::taste-e-g-taste-buds-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Name the five basic tastes detectable by human taste buds.
column4: Each taste quality is detected by specific receptor proteins or ion channels on taste receptor cells; umami corresponds to glutamate detection.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::taste-e-g-taste-buds-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of receptor detects bitter and sweet tastes?
column4: Sweet and umami are detected by T1R family GPCRs; bitter by T2R family GPCRs. GPCR activation leads to second-messenger cascades and depolarization of taste cells.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::taste-e-g-taste-buds-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cranial nerves carry taste information from the tongue to the brain?
column4: CN VII (chorda tympani branch) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; CN IX carries taste from the posterior one-third.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::taste-e-g-taste-buds-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How is salty taste transduced at the receptor level?
column3: Na+ flows directly through ion channels, depolarizing the cell
column4: Salt taste (NaCl) is detected by amiloride-sensitive sodium channels on taste receptor cells — a direct ionotropic mechanism, unlike sweet or bitter.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::taste-e-g-taste-buds-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the primary cortical region for taste perception?
column4: Taste information travels from the nucleus of the solitary tract (brainstem) to the thalamus and then to the primary gustatory cortex in the insula.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::taste-e-g-taste-buds-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of receptors are olfactory receptors?
column4: Olfactory receptor neurons express GPCRs on their cilia; odorant binding triggers cAMP production, opening ion channels and depolarizing the cell.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::smell MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Where are olfactory receptor neurons located?
column4: The olfactory epithelium lines the roof of the nasal cavity; olfactory neurons project axons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::smell MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the first synapse in the olfactory pathway?
column4: Axons from olfactory receptor neurons synapse in glomeruli within the olfactory bulb; each glomerulus receives input from neurons expressing the same receptor type.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::smell MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How does the olfactory pathway differ from other sensory pathways regarding thalamic relay?
column3: Olfaction bypasses the thalamus (projects directly to cortex)
column4: Olfactory signals travel from the olfactory bulb directly to the piriform cortex and amygdala without first relaying through the thalamus — unique among senses.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::smell MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Approximately how many distinct olfactory receptor genes does the human genome contain?
column4: Humans have about 400 functional odorant receptor genes (out of ~800 total, many pseudogenes), allowing discrimination of a vast number of odor combinations.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::smell MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What cellular mechanism underlies olfactory adaptation (decreased response to a continuous odor)?
column4: Prolonged odorant exposure causes receptor phosphorylation and decreased cAMP, reducing ion channel opening and diminishing the perceived intensity of the odor.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::smell MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of cells are olfactory receptor cells?
column4: Olfactory receptor neurons are true bipolar neurons: one dendrite projects to the epithelial surface, and one axon projects to the olfactory bulb.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-cells-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What second messenger is central to olfactory signal transduction?
column4: Odorant binding activates Golf (a Gs-type protein), stimulating adenylyl cyclase to produce cAMP, which opens cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, allowing Ca2+ and Na+ influx.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-cells-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the combinatorial coding principle in olfaction?
column3: Each odor activates a unique combination of receptor types
column4: With ~400 receptor types, unique combinations allow discrimination of millions of odors; the pattern across activated receptors encodes odor identity.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-cells-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which protein family do olfactory receptors belong to?
column4: All olfactory receptors are GPCRs with seven membrane-spanning domains; they are the largest gene family in the mammalian genome.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-cells-chemoreceptors-that-detect-specific-chemicals MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are pheromones?
column3: Chemical signals that communicate information between individuals of the same species
column4: Pheromones influence behavior or physiology of conspecifics (e.g., mating, territorial marking); they are detected by chemoreceptors, often in the vomeronasal organ.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::pheromones-bio MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which organ is primarily responsible for detecting pheromones in many non-human mammals?
column4: The VNO contains pheromone-sensing neurons that project to the accessory olfactory bulb; its role in humans is largely vestigial.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::pheromones-bio MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What class of receptors do vomeronasal organ neurons express for pheromone detection?
column4: These vomeronasal receptor families are distinct from the main olfactory receptor family and are specialized for pheromone detection in non-human mammals.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::pheromones-bio MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: How do pheromones differ from conventional odorants in their mode of action?
column3: Pheromones trigger stereotyped behavioral/physiological responses, not just perception
column4: Unlike general odorants that produce conscious smell, pheromones activate innate circuits (via VNO → hypothalamus) to drive fixed behavioral or hormonal responses.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::pheromones-bio MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the evidence that humans may respond to chemical social signals similar to pheromones?
column3: MHC-related mate preference and menstrual synchrony studies
column4: Studies show humans prefer odors of individuals with dissimilar MHC alleles, and some report menstrual synchrony in cohabiting women, suggesting rudimentary pheromone-like signaling.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::pheromones-bio MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Where does the olfactory pathway first synapse after leaving the olfactory epithelium?
column4: Olfactory nerve (CN I) axons pass through the cribriform plate and synapse on mitral cells in olfactory bulb glomeruli.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-pathways-in-the-brain-bio MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which brain structure receives direct projections from the olfactory bulb and is involved in emotional responses to smell?
column4: The olfactory system projects directly to the amygdala (part of the limbic system), explaining the strong emotional and memory associations with odors.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-pathways-in-the-brain-bio MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Name the primary olfactory cortex region that receives direct input from the olfactory bulb.
column4: The piriform cortex is the largest component of the primary olfactory cortex; it contributes to odor identification and projects to the orbitofrontal cortex for conscious odor perception.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-pathways-in-the-brain-bio MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What role does the orbitofrontal cortex play in olfaction?
column3: Conscious odor perception and odor-flavor integration
column4: The orbitofrontal cortex (secondary olfactory cortex) integrates olfactory and gustatory inputs, contributing to flavor perception and the rewarding aspects of food smell.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-pathways-in-the-brain-bio MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Why can olfactory stimuli evoke vivid autobiographical memories more readily than other senses?
column3: Olfactory bulb projects directly to hippocampus and amygdala
column4: Direct connections to the hippocampus (memory) and amygdala (emotion) without thalamic relay allow smells to trigger emotionally laden memories — the 'Proust phenomenon.'
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-pathways-in-the-brain-bio MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cranial nerve carries olfactory information?
column4: CN I consists of the bundled axons of olfactory receptor neurons; they are among the shortest cranial nerves, passing through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::olfactory-pathways-in-the-brain-bio MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the kinesthetic sense?
column3: Awareness of body position and movement of limbs
column4: Kinesthesia relies on proprioceptors (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint receptors) to provide information about limb position and movement to the CNS.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::kinesthetic-sense-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which receptors in muscles provide information about muscle stretch for kinesthesia?
column4: Muscle spindles detect changes in muscle length and rate of stretch; they send signals via Ia afferent fibers, contributing to proprioception and the stretch reflex.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::kinesthetic-sense-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the role of Golgi tendon organs in the kinesthetic sense?
column3: Detect tension/force in tendons; inhibit muscle contraction when excessive
column4: Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) signal muscle tension via Ib afferents; they mediate autogenic inhibition to protect muscles and tendons from damage.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::kinesthetic-sense-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which spinal tract carries proprioceptive information to the cerebellum?
column4: The spinocerebellar tracts (dorsal and ventral) relay proprioceptive signals from muscle spindles and GTOs ipsilaterally to the cerebellum for coordination.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::kinesthetic-sense-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cortical region processes kinesthetic (proprioceptive) information?
column4: Proprioceptive signals travel via the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway to the thalamus and then to the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) in the postcentral gyrus.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::kinesthetic-sense-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What distinguishes kinesthesia from proprioception?
column3: Kinesthesia = sense of movement; proprioception = sense of position (broader term)
column4: Proprioception encompasses both the static sense of limb position and the dynamic sense of movement (kinesthesia); some use the terms interchangeably, but kinesthesia specifically refers to motion detection.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::kinesthetic-sense-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the vestibular sense?
column3: Sense of balance, head position, and linear/rotational acceleration
column4: The vestibular system, located in the inner ear, detects gravity and head movement, contributing to balance and coordination of eye movements.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::vestibular-sense MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Where are the sensory structures of the vestibular system located?
column3: Inner ear (vestibular labyrinth: semicircular canals, utricle, saccule)
column4: The three semicircular canals detect rotational acceleration; the utricle and saccule (otolith organs) detect linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::vestibular-sense MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structures detect rotational (angular) acceleration of the head?
column4: Each of the three semicircular canals is oriented in a different plane; movement deflects the cupula, bending hair cell stereocilia in the ampulla and signaling rotation.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::vestibular-sense MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are otoliths, and what do they detect?
column3: Calcium carbonate crystals that detect linear acceleration and gravity
column4: Otoliths (otoconia) are dense crystals resting on hair cells in the utricle and saccule; inertia causes them to lag during linear motion, bending hair cells to signal linear acceleration or head tilt.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::vestibular-sense MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which cranial nerve transmits vestibular signals to the brain?
column4: The vestibular branch of CN VIII carries signals from the semicircular canals and otolith organs to the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::vestibular-sense MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)?
column3: Reflex that stabilizes gaze during head movement by moving eyes opposite to head
column4: The VOR uses vestibular input to drive compensatory eye movements, keeping the visual image stable on the retina; its pathway involves vestibular nuclei and oculomotor nuclei.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::vestibular-sense MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What condition results from displaced otoliths in the semicircular canals?
column4: BPPV occurs when otoconia detach and enter a semicircular canal, causing aberrant signals of rotation with head position changes, producing brief but intense vertigo.
column8: concept::PS::6A::other_senses MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::other-senses::vestibular-sense MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is bottom-up processing in perception?
column3: Stimulus-driven; starts with raw sensory data
column4: Bottom-up processing builds perception from basic sensory features upward to a whole percept, with no prior knowledge guiding the initial analysis. Also called data-driven processing.

column1: What is top-down processing in perception?
column4: Top-down processing uses prior knowledge, context, and expectations to interpret incoming sensory data. It can fill in gaps or override ambiguous stimuli.

column1: Which type of processing is primarily responsible for recognizing a familiar face in a crowd?
column4: Recognizing a familiar face relies heavily on stored mental templates and expectations, hallmarks of top-down (concept-driven) processing.

column1: Which type of processing dominates when a person encounters a completely novel, unambiguous stimulus?
column4: Without prior knowledge to apply, the perceptual system must rely entirely on the raw sensory features of the stimulus, making bottom-up processing dominant.

column1: What term describes the interactive model in which both bottom-up and top-down processing work simultaneously?
column4: Most real-world perception involves both systems operating in parallel and influencing each other, rather than strictly sequential stages.

column1: The word-superiority effect (letters recognized faster in words than alone) illustrates which type of processing?
column4: Context provided by the word form guides recognition of individual letters, demonstrating that higher-level knowledge speeds lower-level feature detection.

column1: What is perceptual constancy?
column3: Perceiving objects as stable despite changing stimuli
column4: Size, shape, brightness, and color constancy allow us to recognize that an object is unchanged even as retinal image size, angle, or illumination varies.

column1: What is size constancy?
column3: Perceiving an object's true size despite distance changes
column4: As an object moves farther away its retinal image shrinks, but the brain uses distance cues to compute the object's actual size as unchanged.

column1: Name two monocular depth cues available to a single eye.
column3: Linear perspective and relative size (any two monocular cues)
column4: Monocular cues include linear perspective, interposition, texture gradient, relative size, motion parallax, and aerial perspective — all usable with one eye.

column1: What binocular depth cue relies on the difference between the two retinal images?
column4: Because the eyes are horizontally separated, each receives a slightly different image; the brain uses this difference to compute depth. Greater disparity = closer object.

column1: What is the depth cue called convergence?
column3: Eyes turning inward as objects approach
column4: Convergence is a binocular, proprioceptive cue: as an object nears, the extraocular muscles rotate the eyes inward, and the brain uses the degree of rotation as a distance signal.

column1: What is the phi phenomenon?
column3: Illusion of motion from sequential static images
column4: Rapidly presenting still images in sequence creates apparent motion (e.g., film). This stroboscopic effect is a classic example of illusory motion perception.

column1: Which monocular depth cue describes how objects partially blocking others appear closer?
column4: When one object occludes part of another, the occluding object is perceived as nearer. This is a powerful pictorial (monocular) depth cue.

column1: What is the Moon illusion an example of?
column4: The moon appears larger near the horizon than overhead; current explanations involve apparent-distance cues making the horizon moon seem farther, triggering size-constancy scaling upward.

column1: What is the Gestalt principle of figure-ground?
column3: Distinguishing an object (figure) from its background (ground)
column4: The visual system automatically segregates the perceptual field into a prominent figure and a receding background, a fundamental step in form perception.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the Gestalt principle of proximity state?
column3: Objects close together are grouped as a unit
column4: Proximity is one of the simplest grouping rules: elements near each other tend to be perceived as belonging to the same group or pattern.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the Gestalt principle of similarity state?
column4: Elements sharing features (color, shape, size) are perceptually grouped. This overrides proximity if similarity is stronger than nearness.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the Gestalt principle of closure state?
column3: Incomplete figures are perceived as whole
column4: The brain fills in gaps to complete a familiar form, reflecting top-down influence on perceptual organization. Example: a circle with a small gap is still seen as a circle.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the Gestalt principle of continuity (good continuation) state?
column3: Elements are grouped along smooth, continuous paths
column4: We perceive lines and curves as continuing in their established direction rather than making abrupt turns, minimizing interruptions in a contour.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the Gestalt principle of common fate state?
column3: Elements moving together are grouped together
column4: Objects that move in the same direction and speed are perceived as a unit, which is especially important for motion perception and detecting biological motion.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What overarching Gestalt law states that people organize stimuli into the simplest, most regular form?
column4: Pragnanz ('precision' in German) is the master Gestalt principle; proximity, similarity, closure, and continuity are all special cases of seeking the simplest perceptual interpretation.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the Gestalt principle of symmetry?
column3: Symmetric regions are grouped as figures
column4: Symmetric elements tend to be perceived as belonging together and as the figure rather than the ground, aiding object recognition even with ambiguous stimuli.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: How do Gestalt principles relate to top-down vs. bottom-up processing?
column4: Gestalt grouping principles operate early and automatically (bottom-up), though context (top-down) can modulate figure-ground assignment and other groupings.
column8: concept::PS::6A::perception MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6A::perception::gestalt-principles MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is selective attention?
column3: Focusing on one stimulus while ignoring others
column4: Selective attention allows the brain to prioritize relevant sensory input; it is foundational to conscious perception and is heavily tested on the MCAT.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which classic paradigm demonstrated selective attention by asking subjects to repeat one ear's message while ignoring the other?
column4: Colin Cherry's dichotic listening task showed that people could follow one auditory stream but retained little content from the unattended channel.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the 'cocktail party effect'?
column3: Detecting your own name in an unattended channel
column4: Even when attention is focused elsewhere, personally salient stimuli (like your name) can break through, illustrating that unattended information is partially processed.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: According to Broadbent's filter model, where does selective attention filter unattended information?
column3: Early — before semantic processing (at sensory stage)
column4: Broadbent proposed an early-selection bottleneck that filters by physical features before meaning is analyzed.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What did Treisman's attenuation model propose about unattended messages?
column3: They are weakened (attenuated), not fully blocked
column4: Unlike Broadbent's all-or-none filter, Treisman argued unattended channels are processed at reduced strength, explaining why salient words still reach awareness.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the late-selection model of attention?
column3: Filtering occurs after full semantic analysis of all inputs
column4: Deutsch & Deutsch proposed that all stimuli reach perceptual processing; selection happens at the response/memory stage based on relevance.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: In visual selective attention, what does the spotlight metaphor describe?
column3: A movable zone of enhanced processing in the visual field
column4: Like a spotlight, visual attention can shift to different spatial locations, boosting processing within the attended region.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is inattentional blindness?
column3: Failure to notice an unexpected stimulus when attention is engaged elsewhere
column4: Simons & Chabris' gorilla study is the classic demonstration; it shows selective attention limits awareness of unattended objects.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is change blindness?
column3: Failure to detect changes in a visual scene across interruptions
column4: Change blindness occurs because attention must be directed to a location for changes there to be noticed; related to selective attention limits.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which brain structure is most associated with directing top-down selective attention?
column4: The frontoparietal network, especially the dorsal attention network, controls voluntary (top-down) allocation of selective attention.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What distinguishes top-down from bottom-up selective attention?
column3: Top-down is goal-driven; bottom-up is stimulus-driven
column4: Top-down attention is voluntary (e.g., searching for a friend); bottom-up is automatic capture by salient stimuli (e.g., a loud noise).
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What term describes the automatic capture of attention by a biologically or emotionally salient stimulus?
column4: Stimuli like sudden movement or threat-related faces reflexively grab attention, bypassing voluntary control.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::selective-attention MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is divided attention?
column3: Distributing attention across two or more simultaneous tasks
