column4: Divided attention is the cognitive capacity to process multiple inputs or tasks at once; it differs from selective attention, which filters to one source.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the general effect of task difficulty on divided attention performance?
column3: Performance decreases as task difficulty increases
column4: When tasks demand more resources, competition for limited attentional capacity degrades performance on one or both tasks.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: According to resource theories (e.g., Kahneman), what limits divided attention?
column3: A single pool of limited cognitive resources (capacity)
column4: Kahneman's capacity model holds that a general, flexible resource pool is shared across tasks; exceeding capacity causes performance decrements.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the multiple-resource theory of divided attention?
column3: Different tasks draw from separate resource pools (e.g., verbal vs. spatial)
column4: Wickens proposed that tasks using different modalities or codes (auditory vs. visual, spatial vs. verbal) interfere less than tasks sharing the same resource pool.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Why is talking on a cell phone while driving more dangerous than talking to a passenger?
column3: Cell phone conversation demands more cognitive resources; passenger adjusts to road conditions
column4: The passenger moderates conversation during demanding driving; the remote caller cannot, imposing continuous divided attention costs.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What happens to divided attention performance with extensive practice on a task?
column3: One task becomes automatized, freeing resources for the other
column4: Automaticity reduces the resource demand of a practiced task, allowing effective dual-task performance (e.g., experienced drivers can converse more easily).
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is automaticity in the context of attention?
column3: Processing that occurs without conscious attentional resources
column4: Highly practiced tasks (like skilled typing) run automatically, leaving attentional capacity for other concurrent tasks.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which dual-task paradigm measures divided attention by having subjects respond to stimuli in two separate tasks simultaneously?
column4: The PRP effect shows slowed response to the second stimulus when it follows the first closely, revealing a processing bottleneck during divided attention.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the psychological refractory period (PRP)?
column3: The delay in responding to a second stimulus while processing a first
column4: When two stimuli occur in rapid succession, response to S2 is slowed, indicating a central bottleneck limits parallel processing.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: How does similarity of tasks affect divided attention performance?
column3: More similar tasks produce greater interference
column4: Tasks sharing the same modality or cognitive codes (e.g., two verbal tasks) compete for the same resources and interfere more than dissimilar tasks.
column8: concept::PS::6B::attention MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::attention::divided-attention MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the information-processing model of cognition?
column3: Mind as computer: input, processing, output
column4: The information-processing model compares the mind to a computer, with sensory input encoded, stored, and retrieved. It emphasizes attention, working memory, and long-term storage stages.

column1: In the information-processing model, what is the role of attention?
column3: Selective filter that determines what enters working memory
column4: Attention acts as a bottleneck; only attended stimuli are encoded into working memory, explaining why we miss unattended information (inattentional blindness).

column1: What are the three main stages of the information-processing model in order?
column4: Information must first be encoded (input), then stored (retained), and finally retrieved (output). Failure at any stage produces memory errors.

column1: What is the capacity limit of working memory according to Miller's Law?
column4: George Miller's 1956 paper established that working memory holds approximately 7 chunks of information, which can be expanded by chunking smaller units into larger meaningful groups.

column1: Which information-processing concept refers to grouping individual items into larger meaningful units to expand memory capacity?
column4: Chunking reduces the number of units held in working memory; for example, remembering '149217761865' as three dates (1492, 1776, 1865) uses only 3 chunks instead of 12 digits.

column1: What is the difference between bottom-up and top-down processing in the information-processing model?
column4: Bottom-up processing builds perception from raw sensory data; top-down processing uses prior knowledge and schemas to interpret incoming information, explaining how context influences perception.

column1: What milestone marks the beginning of Piaget's sensorimotor stage?
column4: The sensorimotor stage spans birth to ~2 years; infants learn through sensory experiences and motor actions. The key achievement is object permanence, typically gained around 8-12 months.

column1: What is object permanence, and in which Piagetian stage does it develop?
column3: Understanding objects exist when out of sight; sensorimotor stage
column4: Before object permanence (before ~8 months), infants act as if hidden objects cease to exist. Its development signals a major cognitive milestone in the sensorimotor stage.

column1: What is the hallmark limitation of Piaget's preoperational stage?
column4: Children aged 2-7 cannot adopt others' viewpoints, as shown by the three-mountain task. They also lack conservation and use animism and magical thinking.

column1: What is conservation, and in which Piagetian stage does it develop?
column3: Understanding quantity stays the same despite appearance changes; concrete operational
column4: Conservation (e.g., same amount of liquid in tall vs. wide glass) develops around age 7. Its absence in preoperational children is shown by the classic Piagetian liquid task.

column1: Which Piagetian stage is characterized by abstract and hypothetical reasoning?
column4: Formal operational thinkers can reason about hypothetical scenarios, use deductive logic, and think systematically about possibilities — skills that emerge around age 12.

column1: What term describes a Piagetian child's belief that inanimate objects have feelings or intentions?
column4: Animism is characteristic of the preoperational stage; children attribute life-like qualities to toys, clouds, and other objects. It reflects egocentric, magical thinking.

column1: What is the process by which a child incorporates new information into existing schemas?
column4: In assimilation, new experiences are fit into current cognitive frameworks without changing them. Contrast with accommodation, where schemas are modified to fit new information.

column1: What Piagetian term describes modifying an existing schema to accommodate new information that does not fit?
column4: Accommodation produces cognitive growth; the tension between existing schemas and new discrepant information drives the process of equilibration in Piaget's theory.

column1: In which Piagetian stage does decentration and reversibility first appear?
column4: Decentration (focusing on multiple attributes) and reversibility (mentally undoing actions) allow conservation and logical operations on concrete objects during this stage.

column1: What does cognitive development research suggest happens to processing speed in late adulthood?
column4: Processing speed declines with age, contributing to slower reaction times and longer decision latencies. It is one of the first cognitive abilities to show age-related decline.

column1: Which type of memory is most resistant to decline in late adulthood?
column4: Crystallized knowledge — vocabulary, facts, and procedural skills — tends to remain stable or even improve with age, while episodic and working memory show greater decline.

column1: What term describes the age-related cognitive decline in processing speed and working memory capacity?
column4: Cognitive aging is a normal process distinct from dementia; it primarily affects fluid intelligence (novel problem-solving, speed) while crystallized intelligence is spared.

column1: Which neurodegenerative condition is the most common cause of dementia in late adulthood?
column4: Alzheimer's is characterized by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, leading to progressive memory loss, language problems, and executive dysfunction — beyond normal aging.

column1: What cognitive ability typically shows the steepest decline in late adulthood: recall or recognition?
column4: Recall (free retrieval without cues) declines more sharply than recognition (identifying previously seen items with cues), because recall demands more effortful retrieval processes.

column1: What is the term for older adults' relative sparing of implicit memory and procedural skills compared to explicit memory?
column4: Implicit memory (e.g., how to ride a bike) is mediated by the cerebellum and basal ganglia, which are less affected early in aging than the hippocampus-dependent explicit memory.

column1: How does culture influence cognitive development according to Vygotsky?
column3: Through social interaction, language, and cultural tools
column4: Vygotsky emphasized that children develop higher cognitive functions by internalizing culturally mediated interactions — especially language — within their Zone of Proximal Development.

column1: What is Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)?
column3: Gap between what a child can do alone vs. with guidance
column4: The ZPD represents the range of tasks a child can complete with skilled support (scaffolding) but not independently. Cultural transmission happens within this zone.

column1: What is 'scaffolding' in the context of cognitive development?
column3: Temporary support provided by a more skilled person within the ZPD
column4: Scaffolding — a concept derived from Vygotsky — involves adjusting support to match the learner's current level, gradually withdrawing it as competence grows.

column1: How do cross-cultural studies challenge Piaget's theory of cognitive development?
column3: Stages are not universal in timing; culture affects developmental rate
column4: Research shows that the age at which conservation and formal operations appear varies across cultures, suggesting that cultural context and experience, not just biology, shape cognitive milestones.

column1: What is the Whorfian (Sapir-Whorf) hypothesis as it relates to culture and cognition?
column3: Language shapes thought and perception (linguistic relativity)
column4: The strong version argues language determines thought; the weaker (widely accepted) version says language influences cognition. MCAT may test this as a cultural factor in cognitive processes.

column1: What concept describes how cultural values shape which cognitive skills are emphasized and practiced?
column4: For example, collectivist cultures may emphasize holistic/contextual thinking, while individualist cultures emphasize analytic thinking — leading to measurable differences in cognitive tasks.

column1: What is heritability, as it applies to cognitive development?
column3: Proportion of population variance in a trait due to genetic differences
column4: Heritability estimates for intelligence range from ~0.5 in childhood to ~0.8 in adulthood. Importantly, heritability says nothing about the absolute contribution of genes to any individual.

column1: What does twin research suggest about the genetic contribution to intelligence?
column3: Identical twins show higher IQ concordance than fraternal twins
column4: Monozygotic twins raised apart still show greater IQ similarity than dizygotic twins, supporting a substantial heritable component to intelligence — roughly 50-80% of variance.

column1: What is the Flynn Effect?
column3: Average IQ scores have risen ~3 points per decade over generations
column4: Because genes cannot change this fast, the Flynn Effect demonstrates that environmental factors (nutrition, education, reduced toxin exposure) substantially influence cognitive development.

column1: How does early childhood deprivation (e.g., neglect, malnutrition) affect cognitive development?
column3: Impairs cognitive development; reduces IQ and academic achievement
column4: Environmental enrichment or deprivation during sensitive periods has lasting effects on brain development and cognition, highlighting gene-environment interaction (GxE).

column1: What is a gene-environment interaction (GxE) in the context of cognitive development?
column3: Genetic effects on cognition depend on environmental context (and vice versa)
column4: For example, the negative effect of low SES on cognitive development may be larger in children with certain genetic variants, illustrating that nature and nurture interact rather than act independently.

column1: What is the concept of reaction range in cognitive development?
column3: Genotype sets limits; environment determines actual cognitive outcome within those limits
column4: Each genotype has a range of possible phenotypic outcomes; enriched environments push expression toward the upper end of the reaction range, while deprived environments push toward the lower end.

column1: Which brain structure is most critical for the formation of new explicit (declarative) memories?
column4: The hippocampus consolidates short-term to long-term explicit memories. Bilateral hippocampal damage (e.g., patient H.M.) causes anterograde amnesia — inability to form new explicit memories.

column1: Which neurotransmitter is most closely associated with attention and arousal in the context of cognition?
column4: Norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus modulates alertness and attention; acetylcholine from the basal forebrain is critical for learning and memory. Both are depleted in Alzheimer's disease.

column1: What effect does the neurotransmitter dopamine have on working memory and executive function?
column3: Inverted-U relationship: optimal dopamine = best performance
column4: Too little or too much dopamine in the prefrontal cortex impairs working memory. This explains why stimulants at therapeutic doses improve, but high doses impair, executive function.

column1: What role does the prefrontal cortex play in cognition?
column3: Executive functions: planning, decision-making, working memory, impulse control
column4: The prefrontal cortex is the last brain region to fully myelinate (mid-20s), which explains why adolescents show poorer impulse control and long-term planning than adults.

column1: How does traumatic brain injury (TBI) to the frontal lobe typically affect cognition?
column3: Impairs executive function, personality, and impulse control
column4: The classic case is Phineas Gage; frontal lobe damage disrupts planning, decision-making, and social behavior while often sparing language and basic motor skills.

column1: What is an algorithm in problem-solving?
column3: Step-by-step procedure that guarantees a correct solution
column4: Algorithms are exhaustive and always produce the correct answer if followed correctly (e.g., long division), but may be time-consuming compared to heuristics.

column1: What is a heuristic in problem-solving?
column3: Mental shortcut that is efficient but not guaranteed to be correct
column4: Heuristics (e.g., trial-and-error, means-end analysis) are faster than algorithms but can lead to errors. The MCAT tests this distinction and specific heuristic biases.

column1: What is insight problem-solving?
column3: Sudden 'aha' realization of a solution after impasse
column4: Insight involves a restructuring of the problem representation; it is associated with gamma-wave activity in the right temporal lobe and cannot be achieved by step-by-step search.

column1: What is means-end analysis in problem-solving?
column3: Reducing the difference between current state and goal state step by step
column4: Means-end analysis is a general-purpose heuristic: identify the largest obstacle to the goal, find an action to reduce it, and repeat. It is a form of subgoal decomposition.

column1: What is analogical reasoning as a type of problem-solving?
column3: Applying a solution from a similar past problem to a new problem
column4: Analogical transfer uses stored problem schemas; experts use it more efficiently than novices because they have richer, well-organized knowledge structures to draw upon.

column1: What is a mental set in problem-solving?
column3: Tendency to use previously successful strategies even when inappropriate
column4: Mental set is a barrier to problem-solving; the Einstellung effect is the classic demonstration where a learned water-jar strategy prevents people from finding a simpler solution.

column1: What is functional fixedness in problem-solving?
column3: Inability to see an object's uses beyond its conventional function
column4: Functional fixedness prevents creative solutions (e.g., Duncker's candle problem). Seeing a box only as a container, not a platform, illustrates this cognitive bias.

column1: What is confirmation bias in the context of problem-solving?
column3: Tendency to seek information that confirms existing beliefs
column4: Confirmation bias leads problem-solvers to ignore disconfirming evidence and prematurely close on a solution, as shown in Wason's 2-4-6 task.

column1: What is the difference between a well-defined and an ill-defined problem?
column3: Well-defined: clear start, goal, rules; ill-defined: ambiguous goal or path
column4: Solving a math equation is well-defined; writing a research proposal is ill-defined. Ill-defined problems are harder because they require greater problem representation work.

column1: What cognitive phenomenon occurs when the solution to a problem eludes you, but comes to you later after a break (incubation)?
column4: During incubation, unconscious processing continues and mental sets dissipate. Returning to the problem fresh often leads to insight. Part of the creative problem-solving sequence.

column1: What is the availability heuristic?
column3: Judging probability by how easily examples come to mind
column4: People overestimate the frequency of dramatic events (plane crashes, shark attacks) because vivid examples are easily retrieved from memory — a systematic reasoning bias.

column1: What is the representativeness heuristic?
column3: Judging probability by how well something matches a prototype
column4: People neglect base rates and focus on similarity to a category prototype (e.g., assuming a quiet, bookish person is a librarian rather than a farmer, despite farmer being far more common).

column1: What is overconfidence bias?
column3: Tendency to overestimate the accuracy of one's own knowledge or judgments
column4: Overconfidence is pervasive; people rate their knowledge as more certain than warranted. It contributes to errors in diagnosis, forecasting, and decision-making.

column1: What is belief perseverance?
column3: Maintaining beliefs even after contradicting evidence is presented
column4: Belief perseverance occurs because people generate reasons why the disconfirming evidence is wrong. It explains why misinformation is so hard to correct once established.

column1: What is anchoring bias?
column3: Over-reliance on the first piece of information encountered when making decisions
column4: The initial anchor disproportionately influences subsequent estimates; e.g., seeing a high suggested price makes any lower price seem like a good deal, even if it is not.

column1: What is the framing effect in decision-making?
column3: Decisions differ based on how options are presented (gain vs. loss framing)
column4: People prefer 'saves 90 lives' over 'results in 10 deaths' even though they are equivalent. Loss aversion (Kahneman & Tversky) amplifies framing effects.

column1: What is base-rate neglect?
column3: Ignoring statistical prevalence of a category when making probability judgments
column4: The classic error is the conjunction fallacy (Linda problem); people rate 'bank teller and feminist' as more probable than 'bank teller' because she seems more representative, ignoring base rates.

column1: What are the two main approaches to problem-solving described in cognitive psychology?
column4: Trial-and-error involves random attempts until success; systematic approaches include algorithms and structured heuristics. Experts tend toward systematic approaches using domain schemas.

column1: What is working backward as a problem-solving approach?
column3: Starting from the goal state and working toward the initial state
column4: Working backward is effective for problems where the goal is clear (e.g., proofs, mazes). It avoids exploring irrelevant paths that start from the initial state.

column1: What distinguishes expert problem-solvers from novices in terms of cognitive approach?
column3: Experts use schemas/forward reasoning; novices use backward/weak methods
column4: Experts recognize problem types and apply stored solution patterns (forward chaining from the problem), while novices rely on general heuristics like means-end analysis.

column1: What does the term 'general intelligence' (g factor) refer to?
column3: A single underlying cognitive ability that influences performance across domains
column4: Proposed by Spearman, the g factor is extracted by factor analysis of many cognitive tests. It correlates with academic achievement, job performance, and brain efficiency metrics.

column1: What is Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences?
column3: 8 distinct intelligences (linguistic, logical-math, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic)
column4: Gardner proposed that intelligence is not unitary; each type is relatively independent. This theory is widely used in education but has limited empirical support from psychometric testing.

column1: What does Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory of intelligence include?
column4: Sternberg proposed that traditional IQ tests capture only analytical intelligence, missing creative (novel thinking) and practical (real-world adaptation) components of intelligent behavior.

column1: What is the distinction between fluid and crystallized intelligence?
column3: Fluid: novel problem-solving ability; crystallized: accumulated knowledge
column4: Proposed by Cattell; fluid intelligence (Gf) peaks in young adulthood and declines with age; crystallized intelligence (Gc) accumulates with experience and remains stable or grows into late adulthood.

column1: What is emotional intelligence (EQ)?
column3: Ability to perceive, understand, manage, and use emotions effectively
column4: Proposed by Salovey and Mayer; popularized by Goleman. EQ predicts interpersonal success and leadership effectiveness, and is relatively independent of g.

column1: What method does psychometrics use to identify the structure of intelligence (e.g., g factor)?
column4: Factor analysis identifies clusters of correlated test scores and extracts latent variables (factors). Spearman used it to support a single g; Thurstone found seven primary mental abilities instead.

column1: What does twin-adoption research reveal about the heritability of IQ?
column3: Heritability is substantial (~50-80%); increases with age
column4: MZ twins raised apart have IQ correlations of ~0.75; adopted children's IQs correlate more with biological than adoptive parents by adulthood — showing genes dominate over shared environment over time.

column1: What environmental factor is one of the strongest predictors of IQ score differences between groups?
column4: Low SES is associated with reduced cognitive stimulation, malnutrition, toxin exposure, and stress — all of which depress intellectual development. SES differences explain much of observed group IQ gaps.

column1: What is the concept of 'stereotype threat' as it relates to intelligence testing?
column3: Awareness of a negative stereotype impairs test performance
column4: Steele & Aronson showed Black students underperformed on verbal tests when race was made salient, but not otherwise — demonstrating that social context influences measured intelligence.

column1: What does adoption into a higher-SES home do to children's IQ scores?
column3: Raises IQ scores above biological family baseline
column4: Studies of French adoptions (Schiff et al.) showed children adopted into affluent families showed IQ gains of ~12-15 points compared to siblings raised by biological low-SES families.

column1: What does the term 'shared environment' mean in behavioral genetics research on intelligence?
column3: Environmental factors shared by siblings in the same home (family-level influences)
column4: Shared environment has a larger effect on IQ in childhood but diminishes in adulthood when individuals create their own environments (gene-environment correlation/active niche-picking).

column1: How does lead (Pb) exposure in early childhood affect cognitive development?
column3: Lowers IQ; impairs attention, working memory, and executive function
column4: Lead is a neurotoxin that damages developing neural circuits. Even low blood lead levels are associated with measurable IQ deficits, making it a critical environmental factor in intellectual development.

column1: How is intellectual disability (ID) defined in terms of IQ score?
column3: IQ below ~70 with adaptive functioning deficits, onset before age 18
column4: ID is defined by both cognitive testing (IQ < ~70, more than 2 SD below mean) and impairments in adaptive behavior (communication, self-care, social skills), present during the developmental period.

column1: What is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability?
column4: Fragile X is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, leading to absent FMRP protein, which is essential for synaptic development.

column1: What chromosomal abnormality causes Down syndrome, and how does it affect cognition?
column4: Extra chromosome 21 leads to intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, and increased risk of early-onset Alzheimer's disease (amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21).

column1: What is giftedness typically defined as in terms of IQ score?
column3: IQ of 130 or above (2 SD above the mean)
column4: Gifted individuals show advanced cognitive abilities. Longitudinal studies (Terman) show giftedness predicts but does not guarantee professional achievement; motivation and opportunity also matter.

column1: What is the normal distribution of IQ scores, including mean and standard deviation?
column4: IQ tests are standardized so ~68% of scores fall between 85-115 (±1 SD), and ~95% fall between 70-130 (±2 SD). This bell-curve distribution is intentionally constructed, not discovered empirically.

column1: What is savant syndrome in the context of intellectual ability?
column3: Coexistence of severe cognitive disability with one extraordinary specific skill
column4: Savants show profound abilities in narrow domains (e.g., calendar calculation, musical memory) despite overall intellectual disability. It challenges unitary views of intelligence and supports modularity.

column1: What prenatal exposure is one of the leading preventable causes of intellectual disability?
column3: Fetal alcohol syndrome (alcohol exposure in utero)
column4: Alcohol is a teratogen that disrupts neural migration and synaptogenesis. FAS is associated with characteristic facial features, growth restriction, and intellectual disability.

column1: What stage of cognitive development is associated with the appearance of hypothetico-deductive reasoning?
column4: Hypothetico-deductive reasoning — generating and testing hypotheses systematically — is the signature achievement of the formal operational stage, typically emerging around age 12.

column1: What does the term 'schema' mean in Piaget's theory?
column3: Mental framework for organizing and interpreting information
column4: Schemas are cognitive structures that develop through assimilation and accommodation. They represent categories (dog), events (eating at a restaurant), or procedures (how to ride a bike).

column1: What is the primary criticism of Piaget's theory regarding the timing of developmental stages?
column3: Piaget underestimated children's abilities; stages appear earlier with simpler tasks
column4: Researchers like Bower and Baillargeon showed infants demonstrate object permanence earlier than Piaget claimed. Simplified tasks reveal competence that Piaget's complex tasks obscured.

column1: What does Vygotsky emphasize that Piaget de-emphasizes in cognitive development?
column3: The role of social interaction and language in driving cognitive development
column4: Vygotsky argued that thought is largely internalized social speech and that cognitive development is fundamentally social; Piaget emphasized solitary exploration of the physical environment.

column1: What is the term for the general process by which cognitive abilities develop through interaction with the environment?
column4: Cognitive development encompasses how perception, memory, language, reasoning, and problem-solving change across the lifespan. Both Piaget's and Vygotsky's theories are key MCAT frameworks.

column1: What is consciousness?
column4: Consciousness encompasses both wakefulness and subjective experience. The MCAT treats it as a psychological construct with biological underpinnings.

column1: What term describes a state of reduced consciousness in which one is not fully aware of surroundings?
column4: Altered states include sleep, hypnosis, meditation, and drug-induced states — all reduce or shift normal waking awareness.

column1: Which state of consciousness is associated with focused, goal-directed thought and full environmental awareness?
column4: Normal waking consciousness is characterized by beta waves on EEG and engagement with the external world.

column1: What is preconscious information?
column3: Information not in awareness but retrievable
column4: Preconscious material (e.g., a forgotten phone number you can recall when prompted) contrasts with unconscious material, which is inaccessible to awareness.

column1: Which Freudian level of consciousness contains repressed wishes and instinctual drives that are inaccessible to awareness?
column4: Freud's topographic model: conscious → preconscious → unconscious. The unconscious drives behavior without awareness.

column1: What EEG wave pattern characterizes normal waking alertness?
column4: Beta waves are fast, low-amplitude waves seen during active thinking and alertness. Alpha waves (8-12 Hz) appear during relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed.

column1: Which neurotransmitter system is primarily responsible for promoting wakefulness and alertness?
column4: The locus coeruleus releases norepinephrine broadly to promote arousal. Acetylcholine, histamine, and orexin also support wakefulness.

column1: Which hypothalamic neuropeptide is critical for maintaining stable wakefulness and is deficient in narcolepsy?
column4: Orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus stabilize the sleep-wake switch. Loss of orexin-producing neurons causes narcolepsy with cataplexy.

column1: Which brain structure is considered the primary regulator of arousal and consciousness?
column4: The RAS (ascending reticular activating system) in the brainstem filters sensory input and modulates cortical arousal; damage causes coma.

column1: What EEG pattern is associated with relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed?
column4: Alpha waves replace beta waves when a person closes their eyes and relaxes but remains awake. They are often used as a baseline in EEG studies.

column1: How many stages of NREM sleep are there (current AASM classification)?
column4: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine classifies NREM into N1, N2, and N3 (slow-wave sleep). The older system had 4 NREM stages; consolidate stages 3 and 4 into N3.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::stages-of-sleep MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which sleep stage is characterized by sleep spindles and K-complexes on EEG?
column4: Sleep spindles are bursts of 12-15 Hz activity; K-complexes are large biphasic waves. Both appear in N2 and are thought to protect sleep from external stimuli.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::stages-of-sleep MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which sleep stage is characterized by delta waves (slow-wave sleep) and is most restorative?
column4: N3 features high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves (<4 Hz). Growth hormone is secreted during N3; it is the hardest stage to awaken from.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::stages-of-sleep MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What EEG pattern characterizes REM sleep?
column4: REM EEG resembles wakefulness, so REM is called 'paradoxical sleep.' The defining features are rapid eye movements, muscle atonia, and vivid dreaming.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::stages-of-sleep MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which neurotransmitter is responsible for the muscle atonia seen during REM sleep?
column4: Glycinergic and GABAergic neurons in the brainstem hyperpolarize spinal motor neurons during REM, preventing dream-enactment. Loss of this atonia causes REM sleep behavior disorder.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::stages-of-sleep MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the approximate duration of one complete sleep cycle?
column4: Each cycle moves through N1→N2→N3→N2→REM. Across a night's sleep, later cycles have proportionally more REM and less N3.

column1: How does the proportion of REM sleep change across successive sleep cycles in a single night?
column3: REM periods lengthen in later cycles
column4: Early cycles contain more N3 (slow-wave) sleep; REM periods grow progressively longer in the third through fifth cycles of the night.

column1: How does sleep architecture change with normal aging?
column3: N3 (slow-wave sleep) decreases; sleep becomes more fragmented
column4: Older adults spend less time in deep N3 sleep, experience more nighttime awakenings, and may show advances in sleep timing (earlier bedtime/wake time).

column1: Which hormone suppresses N3 sleep and increases REM when administered exogenously?
column4: Alcohol initially increases N3 in the first half of the night but suppresses REM. In the second half a 'REM rebound' occurs as blood alcohol falls.

column1: What is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)?
column3: Master circadian clock in the hypothalamus
column4: The SCN receives photic input from retinal ganglion cells and synchronizes peripheral clocks throughout the body to the 24-hour light-dark cycle.

column1: Which hormone is secreted by the pineal gland to signal darkness and promote sleep?
column4: Melatonin secretion rises ~2 hours before habitual sleep onset. Light (especially blue light) suppresses melatonin via the retinohypothalamic tract to the SCN.

column1: What is the approximate period of the endogenous human circadian clock in the absence of external cues?
column4: Without zeitgebers (time cues), the human free-running period is slightly longer than 24 hours; light is the dominant zeitgeber that entrains the clock daily.

column1: Which photoreceptors in the retina project to the SCN and entrain circadian rhythms?
column4: ipRGCs contain melanopsin and respond to blue light (~480 nm). They relay photic information to the SCN even in people who are rod/cone-blind.

column1: What is a zeitgeber?
column3: External time cue that entrains circadian rhythms
column4: From German for 'time giver.' Light is the primary zeitgeber; others include meal timing, exercise, and social schedules.

column1: Which theory of dreaming proposes that dreams result from the brain's attempt to interpret random neural signals during REM?
column4: Proposed by Hobson and McCarley. Random brainstem activation is synthesized into narrative by the cortex, producing the bizarre but meaningful quality of dreams.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::dreaming MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: According to Freud, what are the two levels of dream content?
column4: Manifest content = what the dreamer recalls; latent content = the hidden unconscious wish or meaning. Dream work (condensation, displacement) converts latent to manifest.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::dreaming MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: During which sleep stage do most vivid, narrative dreams occur?
column4: REM dreams are story-like, emotional, and often bizarre. NREM dreams do occur but tend to be shorter, more thought-like, and less vivid.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::dreaming MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What phenomenon occurs after REM deprivation, where the brain spends more time in REM on subsequent nights?
column4: After REM deprivation (selective awakening at REM onset), the brain compensates with increased REM density and duration on recovery nights.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::dreaming MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which theory proposes that dreaming consolidates memories and processes emotional experiences?
column4: This view holds that REM sleep replays and consolidates hippocampal memories, and emotional events are processed, explaining why dreams often reflect recent experiences.
column8: concept::PS::6B::consciousness MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::consciousness::dreaming MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is insomnia?
column3: Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep for ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months
column4: Chronic insomnia disorder requires daytime impairment plus the sleep difficulty. It is the most common sleep-wake disorder and is often treated with CBT-I.

column1: What is narcolepsy?
column3: Excessive daytime sleepiness with sudden sleep attacks
column4: Narcolepsy results from loss of orexin neurons. Cardinal features: sleep attacks, cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion), sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations.

column1: What is cataplexy?
column3: Sudden bilateral muscle weakness triggered by strong emotion
column4: Cataplexy is pathognomonic for Type 1 narcolepsy. It is caused by intrusion of REM atonia into wakefulness, triggered by laughter, surprise, or excitement.

column1: What is sleep apnea?
column3: Repeated cessation of breathing during sleep
column4: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) results from upper airway collapse; central sleep apnea results from failure of CNS respiratory drive. Both fragment sleep and cause hypoxia.

column1: What is REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)?
column3: Acting out dreams due to loss of REM muscle atonia
column4: In RBD, the normal atonia of REM is absent, so patients move, shout, or strike out. RBD strongly predicts future Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia.

column1: Which sleep-wake disorder involves repeated episodes of stopping breathing during sleep and is most commonly treated with CPAP?
column4: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) splints the airway open. OSA is associated with obesity, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease.

column1: What is hypnosis?
column3: State of focused attention and heightened suggestibility
column4: During hypnosis, subjects show increased responsiveness to suggestions and reduced peripheral awareness. It is NOT sleep — EEG shows waking patterns.

column1: Which theory proposes that hypnosis creates a 'hidden observer' — a split in consciousness?
column4: Hilgard's neodissociation theory holds that hypnosis divides consciousness so one part responds to the hypnotist while another (the hidden observer) monitors reality.

column1: What is the sociocognitive (role) theory of hypnosis?
column3: Hypnotic behavior reflects social compliance, not altered consciousness
column4: This theory argues that hypnotized subjects are highly motivated to play the expected role. It contrasts with dissociation theory, which posits a genuine altered state.

column1: What EEG pattern is associated with mindfulness meditation?
column4: Meditation increases alpha (relaxed attention) and theta (deep relaxation/creativity) activity. Long-term meditators also show increased gamma coherence.

column1: What physiological change characterizes the relaxation response induced by meditation?
column3: Decreased sympathetic arousal (heart rate, cortisol, respiration)
column4: The relaxation response is the physiological opposite of the fight-or-flight response — reduced HR, BP, and stress hormones, and increased parasympathetic tone.

column1: Which class of drugs mimics acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors and is found in tobacco?
column4: Nicotine binds nicotinic ACh receptors, releasing dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. It is both a stimulant and a reinforcing drug that creates dependence.

column1: What is the mechanism of action of opioids (e.g., morphine, heroin)?
column3: Agonists at mu (and kappa/delta) opioid receptors
column4: Opioids bind G-protein-coupled opioid receptors, decreasing cAMP, hyperpolarizing neurons, and reducing pain. They also activate mesolimbic dopamine pathways, producing euphoria.

column1: Which neurotransmitter system do benzodiazepines enhance?
column3: GABA (increase Cl- influx at GABA-A receptors)
column4: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening. They produce sedation, anxiolysis, and muscle relaxation.

column1: What is the mechanism of action of LSD and other classical hallucinogens?
column4: LSD binds 5-HT2A receptors in prefrontal cortex, altering sensory perception and cognition. Despite profound effects, classical hallucinogens do not cause physical dependence.

column1: How do stimulants such as cocaine and amphetamines increase synaptic dopamine?
column3: Block dopamine reuptake transporter (cocaine) or reverse transporter (amphetamines)
column4: Cocaine blocks DAT; amphetamines reverse DAT and also promote vesicular release. Both flood the synapse with dopamine, producing euphoria via the nucleus accumbens.

column1: What is the primary mechanism of alcohol's CNS depressant effects?
column3: Enhances GABA-A and inhibits NMDA glutamate receptors
column4: Alcohol potentiates inhibitory GABA (via GABA-A) and antagonizes excitatory glutamate (via NMDA), causing sedation. Withdrawal involves rebound excitation (seizures).

column1: What distinguishes a depressant drug from a stimulant drug in terms of CNS effect?
column3: Depressants decrease CNS activity; stimulants increase CNS activity
column4: Depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines) slow neural activity; stimulants (cocaine, amphetamine, caffeine) increase arousal and activity via monoamine elevation.

column1: Which drug is a dissociative anesthetic that blocks NMDA glutamate receptors?
column4: NMDA antagonists produce analgesia, dissociation, and hallucinations. Ketamine is used clinically as an anesthetic and rapidly-acting antidepressant (esketamine).

column1: What brain structure is the center of the reward pathway that mediates drug reinforcement?
column4: The nucleus accumbens receives dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area (VTA). Surge of dopamine here is the common mechanism of all addictive drugs.

column1: Name the two main structures of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway.
column4: VTA dopamine neurons project to the nucleus accumbens (and prefrontal cortex, forming the mesocortical pathway). Together they constitute the brain's reward circuit.

column1: What is the difference between physical dependence and addiction?
column3: Physical dependence = tolerance + withdrawal; addiction = compulsive use despite harm
column4: Physical dependence can occur with non-addictive drugs (e.g., beta-blockers). Addiction (substance use disorder) requires compulsive drug-seeking and loss of control over use.

column1: What is tolerance in the context of drug use?
column3: Reduced effect with repeated use; higher dose needed for same effect
column4: Tolerance results from receptor downregulation, decreased sensitivity, or increased metabolism. It develops quickly with opioids and benzodiazepines.

column1: What dopamine-related change in the reward pathway underlies the transition from drug use to addiction?
column3: Decreased baseline dopamine and blunted reward response (reward deficiency)
column4: Chronic drug use downregulates D2 receptors in the nucleus accumbens, reducing sensitivity to natural rewards. This drives compulsive drug-seeking to restore dopamine levels.

column1: Which brain region is critical for the motivational aspects of addiction (craving and relapse)?
column3: Prefrontal cortex (also amygdala for cue-triggered craving)
column4: Impaired prefrontal inhibitory control over the limbic system contributes to impulsivity and relapse. Drug-associated cues activate the amygdala, triggering craving.

column1: What is conditioned place preference and what does it demonstrate?
column3: Association of environmental cues with drug reward; demonstrates classical conditioning of reward
column4: Animals spend more time in an environment paired with drug administration. This Pavlovian conditioning model shows how cues become powerful triggers for craving in addiction.

column1: What is withdrawal syndrome?
column3: Physiological symptoms opposite to drug's acute effects upon cessation
column4: Withdrawal reflects homeostatic rebound. Opioid withdrawal causes hyperalgesia, diarrhea, and anxiety; alcohol withdrawal can cause life-threatening seizures and delirium tremens.

column1: What is encoding in the context of memory?
column3: Converting information into a storable memory trace
column4: Encoding is the first stage of memory formation; without successful encoding, information cannot be stored or retrieved later.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::encoding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which level of encoding produces the deepest, most durable memory traces?
column4: Craik and Lockhart's levels-of-processing model holds that processing meaning leads to stronger memory traces than processing sound or appearance.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::encoding MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What term describes encoding that occurs without conscious effort or intention?
column4: Automatic processing handles things like frequency, time, and well-learned spatial information; contrasts with effortful processing that requires deliberate attention.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::encoding MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What term describes encoding that requires deliberate mental effort?
column4: Effortful processing underlies learning new facts or skills and is improved by strategies like rehearsal and elaboration.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::encoding MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which encoding type focuses on the sound of words?
column4: Acoustic encoding is associated with short-term memory; it is shallower than semantic encoding per levels-of-processing theory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::encoding MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which encoding type focuses on the physical appearance or visual features of information?
column4: Structural encoding is the shallowest level and produces the weakest long-term memory traces compared to acoustic or semantic encoding.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::encoding MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the process by which sensory information is first transformed into a neural code the brain can process?
column4: Sensory receptors convert physical stimuli into electrical signals, which are then encoded into memory representations during perception.

column1: What is chunking in memory encoding?
column4: Chunking increases working memory capacity by reducing the number of independent items to remember (e.g., remembering a phone number as three chunks).

column1: What is the phonological loop in Baddeley's working memory model?
column4: The phonological loop uses articulatory rehearsal to maintain spoken or written material; it is distinct from the visuospatial sketchpad.

column1: What does the central executive do in Baddeley's working memory model?
column3: Directs attention and coordinates subsidiary systems
column4: The central executive is the supervisory component; it allocates resources to the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer.

column1: What encoding phenomenon explains why items at the beginning of a list are best remembered?
column4: Early items receive more rehearsal and are transferred to long-term memory, leading to better recall; part of the serial position effect.

column1: What encoding phenomenon explains why items at the end of a list are best remembered immediately?
column4: Recent items are still in working memory at time of recall; the recency effect disappears after a delay, unlike the primacy effect.

column1: What mnemonic strategy links items to specific locations along a familiar route?
column4: By mentally placing items at landmarks along a well-known path, retrieval involves mentally 'walking' the route; very effective for ordered lists.

column1: What is elaborative rehearsal?
column3: Linking new information to existing knowledge
column4: Elaborative rehearsal produces deeper encoding than maintenance rehearsal (simple repetition) by creating more retrieval cues.

column1: What term describes memory improvement when learning is distributed over time rather than massed?
column4: The spacing effect is one of the most robust findings in memory research; spaced repetition exploits it for long-term retention.

column1: What is the self-reference effect in memory encoding?
column3: Better memory for information related to oneself
column4: Encoding information with respect to one's own traits or experiences adds semantic depth and personal relevance, boosting retention.

column1: What is the generation effect in memory?
column3: Better memory for self-generated vs. read information
column4: Actively generating an answer (fill-in-the-blank) leads to stronger encoding than passively reading the answer; related to testing effect.

column1: What is the testing effect (retrieval practice effect)?
column3: Repeated retrieval strengthens long-term memory more than re-reading
column4: Actively recalling information restructures memory traces; the MCAT itself is an example of retrieval practice benefiting test-takers.

column1: What is the capacity (in chunks) of short-term (working) memory?
column4: George Miller's classic study found people can hold about 5-9 chunks in working memory at once; modern estimates lean closer to 4.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::storage MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What are the three main stages of memory storage?
column4: Atkinson-Shiffrin's multi-store model describes information flowing from sensory registers through short-term into long-term memory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::storage MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is consolidation in memory storage?
column3: Stabilizing a memory trace into long-term storage
column4: Consolidation occurs at synaptic (hours) and systems (sleep-dependent) levels; disruption before consolidation causes amnesia.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::storage MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What brain structure is critical for transferring information from short-term to long-term memory?
column4: Patients with bilateral hippocampal damage (e.g., H.M.) cannot form new declarative long-term memories (anterograde amnesia) but retain procedural memory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::storage MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What type of long-term memory is impaired in anterograde amnesia but spared in procedural memory?
column4: Declarative memory includes episodic and semantic memory; it requires hippocampal involvement, unlike procedural (implicit) memory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::storage MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which sleep stage is most associated with memory consolidation of declarative memories?
column4: During slow-wave sleep, hippocampal replay transfers memories to neocortex; REM sleep is more associated with procedural/emotional memory consolidation.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::storage MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What type of memory stores brief sensory impressions (< 1 second for vision)?
column4: Iconic memory is the visual sensory store; echoic memory is the auditory equivalent and lasts slightly longer (~3–4 seconds).

column1: What is the difference between episodic and semantic long-term memory?
column3: Episodic = personal events; semantic = general facts
column4: Episodic memory is autobiographical ('I ate pizza last night'); semantic memory is factual knowledge independent of personal experience.

column1: What is implicit (nondeclarative) memory?
column3: Unconscious memory for skills and conditioned responses
column4: Implicit memory includes procedural skills, priming, and classical conditioning; it does not require hippocampal formation.

column1: What brain structure is most important for procedural (skill) memory?
column4: The basal ganglia underlie habit learning and motor sequence memory; the cerebellum is key for motor skills and conditioned reflexes.

column1: What is the approximate duration of echoic (auditory sensory) memory?
column4: Echoic memory lasts longer than iconic memory (~0.5 s), allowing ongoing speech to be held briefly for phonological processing.

column1: What is prospective memory?
column4: Prospective memory (e.g., remembering to take medication) is distinct from retrospective memory; it declines with age and cognitive load.

column1: What is a semantic network?
column3: Mental organization of concepts by meaning and relationship
column4: Concepts are nodes; associations are links. Activating one concept spreads activation to related concepts, aiding recall.

column1: What is spreading activation in memory?
column3: Activation of one concept activates related concepts
column4: Proposed by Collins and Loftus; explains priming — hearing 'doctor' speeds recognition of 'nurse' because both are linked in the semantic network.

column1: What memory phenomenon is best explained by spreading activation theory?
column4: In semantic priming, a prime word (e.g., 'bread') speeds recognition of a semantically related target (e.g., 'butter') because activation has already spread.

column1: What determines the strength of links in a semantic network?
column4: Concepts activated together repeatedly develop stronger links; cultural associations and prior knowledge shape network structure.

column1: How do prototype and exemplar models differ in semantic network organization?
column3: Prototype = average; exemplar = stored specific instances
column4: Prototype theory holds we compare new items to a mental average; exemplar theory holds we compare to stored individual examples we have encountered.

column1: What is retrieval in memory?
column3: Accessing and bringing stored information into consciousness
column4: Retrieval is the final stage of memory; even stored memories can fail to be retrieved if retrieval cues are unavailable.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) phenomenon?
column3: Knowing a word exists but being unable to retrieve it fully
column4: TOT states suggest partial activation in semantic networks; they are more common for rare words and increase with age.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is context-dependent memory?
column3: Better recall when retrieval context matches encoding context
column4: Godden and Baddeley showed divers recalled more words underwater if they learned them underwater; environmental cues reinstate encoding context.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is state-dependent memory?
column3: Better recall when internal state at retrieval matches encoding state
column4: Alcohol, drugs, or emotional states during learning serve as internal cues; recall improves when the same state is reinstated.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the encoding specificity principle?
column3: Memory is best when retrieval cues match encoding conditions
column4: Tulving's principle: any stimulus present at encoding can become a retrieval cue; explains context- and state-dependent memory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is free recall?
column4: Free recall is the most demanding retrieval task; it shows primacy and recency effects in the serial position curve.

column1: What is recognition memory?
column3: Identifying previously encountered items from choices
column4: Recognition (e.g., multiple choice) is easier than recall because the test item itself serves as a retrieval cue; relies on familiarity and recollection.

column1: What is the savings score in relearning?
column3: Reduction in trials or time to relearn previously learned material
column4: Even when recall and recognition fail, relearning is faster than original learning, revealing residual (implicit) memory; introduced by Ebbinghaus.

column1: Which memory measure is most sensitive to what has been learned — recall, recognition, or relearning?
column4: Relearning detects memory even when recall and recognition both fail, making it the most sensitive measure of retained information.

column1: What is cued recall?
column3: Retrieval prompted by a hint or partial cue
column4: Cued recall (e.g., fill-in-the-blank with a first letter) is easier than free recall but harder than recognition, reflecting intermediate cue quality.

column1: What is a retrieval cue?
column3: Any stimulus that helps access a stored memory
column4: Retrieval cues can be external (smell, location) or internal (mood, physiological state); effective cues match the context at encoding.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval-cues MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is priming as a retrieval cue?
column3: Prior exposure increases accessibility of related information
column4: Priming is an implicit memory phenomenon; it works without conscious awareness and can last days to weeks.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval-cues MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the principle of transfer-appropriate processing state?
column3: Memory is best when retrieval mode matches encoding mode
column4: If information was encoded phonologically, a phonological cue retrieves it better; extends encoding specificity to processing type.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval-cues MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What type of retrieval cue is activated by the smell of a childhood food triggering a vivid memory?
column4: Olfactory cues are particularly powerful because the olfactory bulb projects directly to the hippocampus and amygdala, linking smell to emotional memory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval-cues MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is mood-congruent memory?
column3: Tendency to recall memories that match current mood
column4: Being in a sad mood biases retrieval toward sad memories; distinct from state-dependent memory, which requires the mood to match both encoding and retrieval.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::retrieval-cues MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What role does the amygdala play in retrieving emotional memories?
column3: Enhances consolidation and retrieval of emotionally arousing memories
column4: The amygdala modulates hippocampal consolidation via norepinephrine; emotionally charged events are remembered more vividly (flashbulb memory phenomenon).

column1: What is a flashbulb memory?
column3: Vivid, detailed memory for the context of a shocking/emotional event
column4: Flashbulb memories feel accurate but are not necessarily more accurate than ordinary memories; the amygdala-norepinephrine system underlies their vividness.

column1: Which neurotransmitter system mediates the amygdala's enhancement of emotional memory consolidation?
column4: Beta-adrenergic receptors in the amygdala are activated during stress; beta-blockers (propranolol) can blunt emotional memory enhancement.

column1: What is the relationship between arousal level and memory performance (Yerkes-Dodson)?
column3: Moderate arousal optimizes memory; very low or very high impairs it
column4: The inverted-U relationship applies to memory encoding and retrieval; extreme stress (cortisol) impairs hippocampal function.

column1: How does chronic high cortisol affect the hippocampus?
column4: Sustained glucocorticoid exposure reduces hippocampal neurogenesis and dendritic branching, contributing to stress-related memory deficits and PTSD.

column1: What is the mood-dependent memory phenomenon distinct from mood-congruent memory?
column3: Recall is best when mood matches mood during encoding
column4: Mood-dependent memory is a state-dependent effect; mood-congruent memory is a bias toward content matching current mood regardless of encoding mood.

column1: What retrieval strategy involves mentally recreating the context of the original learning event?
column4: Used in cognitive interviews with eyewitnesses; mentally reinstating the environment, emotions, and thoughts present at encoding improves recall.

column1: What is the cognitive interview technique used to enhance eyewitness recall?
column3: Mental context reinstatement + multiple retrieval attempts
column4: Cognitive interviews also ask witnesses to report everything, recall in different orders, and change perspectives to maximize retrieval.

column1: How does sleep aid memory retrieval?
column3: Consolidates memories during slow-wave and REM sleep
column4: Sleep-dependent consolidation strengthens memory traces and integrates new information with existing schemas, improving later retrieval.

column1: What is the spacing effect's impact on retrieval?
column3: Spaced practice produces more durable, retrievable memories
column4: Repeated retrieval spaced over time strengthens and elaborates memory traces more than massed practice, enhancing long-term retrieval.

column1: What is forgetting?
column3: Failure to retrieve previously stored information
column4: Forgetting can result from decay, interference, retrieval failure, or motivated forgetting; it is a normal and adaptive memory process.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::forgetting MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What did Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve show?
column3: Most forgetting occurs rapidly after learning, then slows
column4: Ebbinghaus documented exponential forgetting of nonsense syllables; relearning (savings) still occurred, demonstrating residual memory traces.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::forgetting MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is motivated forgetting (repression)?
column4: Freud's concept; empirical evidence is contested, but directed forgetting studies show intentional suppression can reduce memory accessibility.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::forgetting MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is absentmindedness in the context of forgetting?
column3: Encoding failure due to inattention at time of learning
column4: Many everyday 'forgetting' instances are actually encoding failures; not attending at encoding leaves no trace to retrieve.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::forgetting MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is transience in memory?
column3: Gradual weakening of memories over time
column4: Transience follows the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve; it is distinct from interference and represents passive decay of unused traces.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::forgetting MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which type of forgetting is more attributable to retrieval failure than trace decay?
column4: Interference from other memories blocks retrieval; the information may still exist in storage but cannot be accessed due to competing traces.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::forgetting MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: How does normal aging affect working memory?
column4: Age-related declines in working memory are due to reduced prefrontal cortex function and slower processing; episodic memory also declines, but semantic memory is relatively spared.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::aging-and-memory MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which type of memory is relatively preserved in normal aging?
column4: Older adults retain vocabulary and general knowledge well; skill-based procedural memory also remains largely intact compared to episodic memory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::aging-and-memory MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is source memory, and how does aging affect it?
column3: Memory for the origin of information; declines with age
column4: Older adults may remember a fact but forget where or when they learned it; source monitoring failures underlie increased susceptibility to misinformation.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::aging-and-memory MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What explains the increased tip-of-the-tongue states in older adults?
column3: Reduced retrieval efficiency due to weaker spreading activation
column4: Aging reduces connectivity in semantic networks, making partial activation more common and full retrieval less reliable, especially for names.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::aging-and-memory MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in relation to aging and dementia?
column3: Memory decline beyond normal aging but not meeting dementia criteria
column4: MCI is a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease; characterized by episodic memory deficits that do not impair daily functioning.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::aging-and-memory MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What memory system is earliest and most severely affected in Alzheimer's disease?
column4: Alzheimer's first destroys hippocampal and entorhinal cortex function, impairing encoding of new episodic memories while remote memories and procedural memory are initially spared.

column1: What pathological hallmarks are found in Alzheimer's disease brain tissue?
column4: Beta-amyloid plaques accumulate extracellularly; hyperphosphorylated tau forms intracellular neurofibrillary tangles that disrupt neuronal function.

column1: What nutritional deficiency causes Korsakoff's syndrome?
column4: Korsakoff's syndrome typically follows Wernicke's encephalopathy in chronic alcoholics; thiamine deficiency damages the mammillary bodies and thalamus.

column1: What is confabulation, and in which disorder is it characteristic?
column3: Fabricating memories without intent to deceive; Korsakoff's syndrome
column4: Patients with Korsakoff's syndrome unconsciously fill memory gaps with fabricated information; confabulation results from frontal lobe and diencephalic damage.

column1: What type of amnesia is associated with Korsakoff's syndrome?
column3: Anterograde amnesia with some retrograde amnesia
column4: Korsakoff's patients cannot form new declarative memories (anterograde) and lose some older memories (retrograde); procedural memory is relatively intact.

column1: What brain regions are most damaged in Korsakoff's syndrome?
column4: These diencephalic structures are part of the Papez circuit for memory; their damage explains the severe declarative memory impairment in Korsakoff's.

column1: What is memory decay?
column3: Fading of memory traces over time due to disuse
column4: Decay theory proposes unused neural pathways weaken; most supported for sensory and working memory, less so for long-term memory.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::decay MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What did Peterson and Peterson's (1959) study demonstrate about short-term memory decay?
column3: STM decays rapidly (~18–30 seconds) without rehearsal
column4: Participants who performed a distractor task (counting backward) forgot trigrams within 18–30 seconds, showing rapid STM decay without rehearsal.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::decay MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the main argument against pure decay theory of forgetting?
column3: Interference from other information, not just time, causes forgetting
column4: If decay were the sole cause, recall after a delay filled with activity should be worse than rest; interference better explains long-term forgetting.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::decay MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is proactive interference?
column3: Old memories interfere with learning/recalling new information
column4: Pro-active = forward-acting; knowing Spanish makes learning Italian harder because old (Spanish) memories intrude on new (Italian) retrieval.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::interference MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is retroactive interference?
column3: New memories interfere with recall of old information
column4: Retro-active = backward-acting; learning Italian after Spanish makes recalling Spanish harder because new learning disrupts old traces.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::interference MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which type of interference explains why learning new material before sleeping preserves the old material better?
column3: Retroactive interference is minimized during sleep
column4: Sleep reduces new competing learning, so retroactive interference is less; Jenkins and Dallenbach showed sleep preserves memory better than waking activity.
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::interference MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the fan effect in interference?
column3: More associations to a concept slow retrieval of each one
column4: As more facts are associated with a concept node, activation is 'spread thinner,' increasing reaction time to retrieve any single fact (Anderson, 1974).
column8: concept::PS::6B::memory MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::memory::interference MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is memory construction?
column3: Memories are rebuilt/reconstructed at retrieval, not played back
column4: Bartlett showed memory is not a recording; people use schemas, expectations, and new information to reconstruct what 'must have' happened.

column1: What is the misinformation effect in memory?
column3: Post-event information distorts the original memory
column4: Loftus's studies showed that misleading questions (e.g., 'How fast were the cars going when they smashed?') alter eyewitness recall, demonstrating memory malleability.

column1: What is source monitoring?
column3: Attributing a memory to its correct origin
column4: Source monitoring failure leads to cryptomnesia (thinking someone else's idea is your own) and false memories when the source is misattributed.

column1: What is cryptomnesia?
column3: Mistaking a previously encountered idea as one's own original thought
column4: A source monitoring error; the person recalls the idea but forgets its external origin, leading to unintentional plagiarism.

column1: What did Elizabeth Loftus's lost-in-the-mall study demonstrate?
column3: False memories of entire events can be implanted
column4: Roughly 25% of participants came to 'remember' a fabricated childhood event (being lost in a mall), showing how suggestion creates false memories.

column1: What is the DRM (Deese-Roediger-McDermott) paradigm used to study?
column3: False memory / illusory memory for non-presented words
column4: Participants hear semantically related word lists and often falsely recognize a critical non-presented lure; demonstrates associative memory construction.

column1: What cellular/molecular change underlies long-term memory formation?
column4: Repeated co-activation of pre- and post-synaptic neurons strengthens synapses via AMPA receptor insertion and dendritic spine growth (Hebbian plasticity).

column1: What is Hebb's rule for synaptic strengthening?
column3: Neurons that fire together wire together
column4: Simultaneous pre- and postsynaptic activity potentiates the synapse; LTP is the cellular mechanism implementing Hebb's rule.

column1: Which glutamate receptor acts as a coincidence detector critical for LTP induction?
column4: NMDA receptors require both glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization to open; they allow calcium influx that triggers downstream LTP signaling.

column1: What protein synthesis requirement distinguishes long-term from short-term memory?
column3: Long-term memory requires new protein synthesis (gene expression)
column4: Blocking protein synthesis prevents late-phase LTP and long-term memory consolidation; short-term memory uses existing proteins and signaling cascades.

column1: What structural synaptic change accompanies long-term memory formation?
column3: Growth of new dendritic spines and synapse remodeling
column4: Sustained LTP leads to morphological changes: increased spine density, larger post-synaptic densities, and even formation of new synapses.

column1: What is long-term depression (LTD) and its role in memory?
column3: Weakening of synapses after low-frequency stimulation; enables forgetting/selectivity
column4: LTD decreases AMPA receptor number and is thought to underlie erasure of memories and the pruning of irrelevant synaptic connections.

column1: What is neural plasticity?
column3: Brain's ability to change structure/function with experience
column4: Neural plasticity (neuroplasticity) refers to the nervous system's capacity to reorganize synaptic connections in response to learning, injury, or environmental input.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which type of neural plasticity involves the formation of entirely new neurons?
column4: Neurogenesis is the birth of new neurons, most prominently documented in the hippocampus and olfactory bulb in adults, and is considered a form of structural plasticity.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes the strengthening of a synapse that results from repeated co-activation of pre- and postsynaptic neurons?
