column4: Hebb's rule: 'Neurons that fire together, wire together.' Repeated co-activation increases synaptic strength and is the cellular basis of associative learning.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is synaptic pruning?
column3: Elimination of weak or unused synaptic connections
column4: Synaptic pruning occurs most extensively during early childhood and adolescence, refining neural circuits by removing connections that are infrequently used.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the critical (sensitive) period in neural plasticity?
column3: Time window when the brain is maximally responsive to specific environmental stimuli
column4: Classic example: ocular dominance columns form during a critical period; monocular deprivation during this window causes permanent vision loss in the deprived eye.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of neural plasticity is demonstrated when one brain region takes over functions of a damaged region?
column4: In blind individuals, the visual cortex can be recruited for tactile or auditory processing — an example of cross-modal plasticity driven by reorganization.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What molecular change at the synapse underlies most forms of synaptic plasticity?
column3: Changes in number or phosphorylation state of AMPA receptors
column4: Insertion of additional AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane increases synaptic strength; removal decreases it. NMDA receptor activation drives these changes.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is homeostatic plasticity?
column3: Synaptic scaling to maintain stable neuronal firing rates
column4: When a neuron is chronically over- or under-active, homeostatic plasticity adjusts overall synaptic strength up or down to keep activity within a functional range.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::neural-plasticity MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the definition of learning in psychology?
column3: Relatively permanent change in behavior due to experience
column4: Learning is distinguished from temporary changes (fatigue, habituation) by its relative permanence and from innate behavior by its experiential basis.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of memory stores facts and events that can be consciously recalled?
column4: Explicit memory has two subtypes: episodic (personal events) and semantic (general facts). It depends heavily on the hippocampus for encoding.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What brain structure is most critical for encoding new explicit (declarative) memories?
column4: Bilateral hippocampal damage (as in patient H.M.) prevents formation of new declarative memories (anterograde amnesia) while leaving procedural memory intact.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What type of memory includes skills, habits, and conditioned responses that are not consciously recalled?
column4: Implicit memory subtypes include procedural memory (motor skills), priming, and classically conditioned responses. It is largely independent of the hippocampus.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What brain structure is most associated with procedural (skill) memory?
column4: The basal ganglia underlie habit learning and sequence learning; the cerebellum is critical for motor skill acquisition and timing of conditioned responses.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What are the three stages of memory processing in order?
column4: Information must first be encoded (attended to and processed), then consolidated into stable storage, and later retrieved. Failure at any stage produces forgetting.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the capacity and duration of working memory?
column4: Miller's Law describes working memory capacity as 7 ± 2 chunks. Without rehearsal, information decays within about 20–30 seconds (demonstrated by Brown-Peterson task).
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the spacing effect in learning?
column3: Distributed practice yields better long-term retention than massed practice
column4: Spaced repetition outperforms cramming because retrieval practice and time-distributed encoding strengthen memory consolidation.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What term describes the phenomenon where previously learned information interferes with recall of new information?
column4: Proactive interference = old information interferes with new. Retroactive interference = new information interferes with old. Both reduce recall accuracy.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the difference between anterograde and retrograde amnesia?
column3: Anterograde: inability to form new memories; Retrograde: loss of memories before injury
column4: Anterograde amnesia typically follows hippocampal damage (e.g., H.M.); retrograde amnesia can involve varying time gradients depending on injury severity.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is state-dependent memory?
column3: Better recall when retrieval context matches encoding context (internal state)
column4: Information learned under a specific internal state (e.g., intoxicated, emotional) is recalled more easily in a similar state — an example of encoding specificity.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::memory-and-learning MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is long-term potentiation (LTP)?
column3: Long-lasting increase in synaptic strength following high-frequency stimulation
column4: LTP is the primary cellular/molecular model of learning and memory; it was first described in the hippocampus and requires NMDA receptor activation.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which receptor type must be activated to INDUCE LTP?
column4: NMDA receptors are voltage-gated AND ligand-gated (require both glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization to remove Mg²⁺ block), making them coincidence detectors.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What ion primarily enters through the NMDA receptor during LTP induction?
column4: Ca²⁺ influx through unblocked NMDA receptors triggers downstream kinase signaling (notably CaMKII) that drives AMPA receptor insertion and LTP expression.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: Which receptor mediates the EXPRESSION (maintained strength) of LTP at the postsynaptic membrane?
column4: After LTP induction, additional AMPA receptors are inserted into the postsynaptic density, increasing the response to subsequent glutamate release — this is early LTP expression.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What distinguishes early LTP from late LTP?
column3: Late LTP requires new protein synthesis (gene transcription); early LTP does not
column4: Early LTP (~1–3 h) involves post-translational modifications and AMPA receptor trafficking. Late LTP (>3 h) requires CREB-mediated transcription and structural synaptic changes.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the role of CaMKII in LTP?
column3: Ca²⁺/calmodulin-activated kinase that phosphorylates AMPA receptors and drives their insertion
column4: CaMKII (calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II) is a key molecular switch; its autophosphorylation keeps it active even after Ca²⁺ levels return to baseline, sustaining LTP.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is long-term depression (LTD) and how does it contrast with LTP?
column3: LTD: long-lasting decrease in synaptic strength from low-frequency stimulation
column4: LTD and LTP are bidirectional forms of synaptic plasticity. LTD is induced by modest Ca²⁺ rises (low-frequency stimulation), activating phosphatases rather than kinases.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What is the Mg²⁺ block of the NMDA receptor and when is it removed?
column3: Mg²⁺ plugs channel at rest; removed by postsynaptic depolarization
column4: At resting membrane potential, Mg²⁺ occludes the NMDA channel. Sufficient AMPA-mediated depolarization expels the Mg²⁺ block, allowing Ca²⁺ entry — this is the coincidence detection mechanism.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: What structural change occurs at dendritic spines during late LTP?
column3: Spine enlargement and formation of new dendritic spines
column4: Late LTP is associated with physical remodeling: existing spines enlarge (increasing postsynaptic density) and new spines form, providing a structural substrate for persistent memory storage.
column8: concept::PS::6B::and_learning MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6B::and-learning::long-term-potentiation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::BIO

column1: According to learning theory of language development, how do children acquire language?
column4: B.F. Skinner proposed that children learn language through reinforcement of correct utterances and imitation of adults. This view is criticized because children produce novel sentences they have never heard.

column1: Who proposed the nativist theory of language development?
column4: Chomsky argued that humans are born with an innate language acquisition device (LAD) that allows rapid grammar learning, explaining why all children acquire language similarly regardless of culture.

column1: What is the Language Acquisition Device (LAD)?
column3: Innate mental module that facilitates grammar learning
column4: Chomsky's LAD is a hypothetical brain mechanism that provides children with an inborn blueprint for universal grammar, enabling fast and uniform language acquisition across cultures.

column1: What is Universal Grammar in Chomsky's nativist theory?
column3: Shared grammatical rules underlying all human languages
column4: Universal Grammar refers to structural properties common to every human language; nativists argue these rules are innately specified, explaining why children master complex grammar so rapidly.

column1: Which theory of language development holds that both biology and social interaction are required?
column4: Interactionist theorists (e.g., Vygotsky, Bruner) argue that innate capacity is necessary but not sufficient; rich social interaction and a language acquisition support system (LASS) are also required.

column1: What is the critical period for language acquisition?
column4: Lenneberg proposed that language is most easily acquired during a biologically determined critical period; individuals deprived of language input during this window (e.g., Genie case) show permanent deficits.

column1: Which case study is most often cited as evidence for the critical period of language acquisition?
column4: Genie was isolated from language until puberty; despite later instruction she never achieved full grammatical competence, supporting the idea of a critical period for syntax acquisition.

column1: What is the Language Acquisition Support System (LASS)?
column3: Social scaffolding provided by caregivers that aids language learning
column4: Bruner's LASS complements Chomsky's LAD: caregivers use child-directed speech (motherese), joint attention, and routines to support language development, emphasizing interactionist processes.

column1: What key criticism distinguishes nativist theory from learning theory of language?
column3: Children produce novel grammatical sentences never heard before
column4: Nativists argue that productivity and creativity of language (generating novel sentences) cannot be explained by imitation alone, supporting an innate grammatical component rather than pure reinforcement.

column1: What is the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis?
column3: Language shapes or determines thought (linguistic relativity/determinism)
column4: The strong version (linguistic determinism) claims language determines thought; the weak version (linguistic relativity) claims language influences thought. The weak version has more empirical support on the MCAT.

column1: What is the difference between linguistic determinism and linguistic relativity?
column3: Determinism: language determines thought; relativity: language influences thought
column4: Linguistic determinism (strong Sapir-Whorf) is largely discredited; linguistic relativity (weak form) is supported by studies on color perception, spatial reasoning, and number concepts across cultures.

column1: Which study on color terms supports linguistic relativity?
column3: Languages with more color terms lead to faster color discrimination
column4: Research (e.g., Berlin & Kay; Winawer et al. on Russian blue terms) shows that having distinct color vocabulary speeds discrimination of those colors, suggesting language influences perceptual categories.

column1: What does the concept of 'framing' illustrate about language and cognition?
column3: Word choice influences judgment and decision-making
column4: Framing effects (Tversky & Kahneman) show that describing the same outcome as '90% survival' vs '10% mortality' changes choices, demonstrating how language shapes cognitive evaluation.

column1: How does bilingualism relate to cognitive flexibility?
column3: Bilinguals show enhanced executive function and attentional control
column4: Managing two languages requires constant inhibition of the non-target language, which exercises the executive control network and is associated with better task-switching and attentional flexibility.

column1: What is the phoneme?
column3: Smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning
column4: Phonemes are the basic sound units of language (e.g., /p/ vs /b/ in 'pat' vs 'bat'). English has approximately 44 phonemes. Distinguishing phonemes is a key early step in language perception.

column1: What is a morpheme?
column3: Smallest unit of language that carries meaning
column4: Morphemes include free morphemes (standalone words like 'dog') and bound morphemes (prefixes/suffixes like '-ed' or 'un-'). Morpheme knowledge is distinct from phonological processing.

column1: What is the relationship between thought and language according to Vygotsky?
column3: Language drives the development of higher-order thought
column4: Vygotsky argued that inner speech (internalized language) is the primary tool for organizing thought; language begins as social communication and is progressively internalized to guide cognition.

column1: What brain area is primarily responsible for speech production?
column4: Broca's area (Brodmann areas 44/45) in the left hemisphere controls the motor planning of speech. Damage causes Broca's aphasia: non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension.

column1: What brain area is primarily responsible for language comprehension?
column3: Wernicke's area (left posterior superior temporal gyrus)
column4: Wernicke's area processes spoken language meaning. Damage causes Wernicke's aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech (word salad) with severely impaired comprehension.

column1: What is the arcuate fasciculus?
column3: White matter tract connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas
column4: The arcuate fasciculus links the frontal speech production area to the temporal comprehension area. Damage to it causes conduction aphasia: intact comprehension and production but inability to repeat words.

column1: What type of aphasia results from damage to Broca's area?
column4: Broca's aphasia is characterized by telegraphic, halting speech and frustration, while reading and comprehension remain relatively intact; patients know what they want to say but cannot produce it fluently.

column1: What type of aphasia results from damage to Wernicke's area?
column3: Fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension (receptive aphasia)
column4: Wernicke's aphasia produces fluent but nonsensical speech filled with paraphasias (word substitutions) and neologisms; patients are unaware of their errors due to poor self-monitoring.

column1: What type of aphasia results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus?
column4: Conduction aphasia: speech is fluent, comprehension is intact, but repetition is severely impaired; patients can understand and spontaneously speak but cannot repeat phrases accurately.

column1: In which hemisphere is language typically lateralized?
column4: Language lateralization to the left hemisphere is seen in the vast majority of people; left-handers show more variability (~70% still left-lateralized). The MCAT expects you to know left-hemisphere dominance.

column1: What is global aphasia?
column3: Severe impairment of both speech production and comprehension
column4: Global aphasia results from large left-hemisphere lesions affecting both Broca's and Wernicke's areas; it is the most severe form, leaving patients with minimal communicative ability.

column1: What role does the angular gyrus play in language?
column3: Integrates written words with auditory language; involved in reading
column4: The angular gyrus (left parietal lobe) bridges visual word-form recognition and phonological processing. Damage causes alexia (reading difficulty) and agraphia (writing difficulty) without other aphasias.

column1: What distinguishes Broca's aphasia from Wernicke's aphasia in terms of speech fluency?
column3: Broca's = non-fluent; Wernicke's = fluent but meaningless
column4: A high-yield MCAT distinction: Broca's patients struggle to produce speech but understand well; Wernicke's patients speak easily but produce word salad and cannot understand spoken language.

column1: What is a paraphasia, as seen in Wernicke's aphasia?
column3: Unintended word or sound substitution in speech
column4: Semantic paraphasias substitute meaning-related words (e.g., 'chair' for 'table'); phonemic paraphasias substitute sounds (e.g., 'trable' for 'table'). Both are hallmarks of Wernicke's aphasia.

column1: What are the three components of emotion?
column4: Emotions involve a subjective thought/appraisal (cognitive), bodily arousal (physiological), and an outward expression or action tendency (behavioral). All three components interact to produce the full emotional experience.

column1: Which component of emotion involves subjective appraisal or interpretation of a situation?
column4: The cognitive component refers to how we think about or evaluate an event; this appraisal shapes which emotion is felt. Cognitive appraisal theories (e.g., Lazarus) emphasize its central role.

column1: Which component of emotion encompasses changes in heart rate, respiration, and hormone release?
column4: These autonomic and endocrine changes prepare the body for action. The physiological component is often mediated by the autonomic nervous system and the HPA axis.

column1: Which component of emotion includes facial expressions and approach/avoidance behaviors?
column4: The behavioral component is the observable action tendency of an emotion — smiling when happy, fleeing when afraid. Facial expressions are a key cross-cultural behavioral signal.

column1: What is the relationship between the cognitive and physiological components of emotion according to appraisal theories?
column3: Cognitive appraisal precedes and shapes physiological response
column4: Appraisal theorists (e.g., Lazarus) argue that the meaning we assign to an event determines which physiological pattern is triggered. This contrasts with James-Lange theory where physiology comes first.

column1: Which component of emotion is most directly measured by polygraph (lie-detector) tests?
column4: Polygraphs record skin conductance, heart rate, and respiration — all physiological markers. The test assumes deception produces detectable autonomic arousal, though its accuracy is disputed.

column1: Name the six universal emotions identified by Paul Ekman.
column3: Fear, anger, happiness, disgust, sadness, surprise
column4: Ekman's cross-cultural research showed these six emotions have consistent facial expressions across cultures, suggesting a biological basis. The MCAT list also includes joy — treat fear/anger/happiness/surprise/joy/disgust/sadness as the testable set.

column1: Who conducted the foundational cross-cultural research establishing universal emotions?
column4: Ekman studied isolated tribes in Papua New Guinea and found that facial expressions for basic emotions were reliably recognized, supporting universality and an evolutionary basis for emotion.

column1: What does the universality of basic emotions suggest about their origin?
column4: Because the same facial expressions appear across unrelated cultures, universal emotions are thought to be innate products of natural selection, not purely learned social constructs.

column1: Which universal emotion is thought to have evolved primarily to protect against ingestion of harmful substances?
column4: Disgust triggers withdrawal, nausea, and rejection behaviors that prevented ancestors from consuming pathogens or toxins. It has since expanded to moral and social domains.

column1: How does surprise differ from the other universal emotions in its valence?
column3: Surprise is valence-neutral (can be positive or negative)
column4: Unlike fear (negative) or happiness (positive), surprise itself has no inherent positive or negative valence — its hedonic quality depends on the subsequent appraisal of the surprising event.

column1: What distinguishes joy from happiness as listed among universal emotions?
column3: Joy is often more intense/transient; happiness is a longer-lasting mood state
column4: On the MCAT, both appear in the universal-emotions list. Joy tends to refer to a peak positive feeling, whereas happiness describes a broader, sustained positive state. The key MCAT fact is that both are on the list.

column1: What is the adaptive role of fear as an emotion?
column3: Motivates avoidance of danger / activates fight-or-flight
column4: Fear prepares the organism to escape or confront threats by triggering sympathetic arousal, enhanced attention, and avoidance behavior — increasing survival likelihood.

column1: How do emotions serve an adaptive communicative function?
column3: Facial expressions signal emotional states to others
column4: Displaying emotions (e.g., anger to deter aggression, fear to warn of danger) coordinates group behavior and enhances survival. This social-signaling function is a core adaptive benefit.

column1: How does the emotion of disgust contribute to biological fitness?
column4: By generating a strong aversion response, disgust reduces exposure to disease vectors and poisonous food, directly increasing reproductive success — a classic adaptive function.

column1: What adaptive function does anger serve?
column3: Motivates approach to remove obstacles / defend resources
column4: Anger mobilizes energy and motivation to overcome barriers or injustices. It can be socially adaptive by signaling dominance and deterring competitors.

column1: How do positive emotions contribute to adaptation according to Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory?
column3: They broaden attention and build lasting psychological resources
column4: Positive emotions (joy, curiosity) widen the scope of attention and cognition, fostering creativity and social bonds — resources that confer long-term adaptive advantages beyond the immediate situation.

column1: According to evolutionary perspectives, why do emotions often feel automatic and difficult to suppress?
column3: Rapid emotional responses evolved for quick, survival-critical reactions
column4: Subcortical emotion circuits (e.g., amygdala) operate faster than prefrontal deliberation. Speed was adaptive in ancestral environments where delays in responding to threats could be fatal.

column1: What does the James-Lange theory of emotion propose?
column3: Physiological arousal precedes and causes the subjective emotional feeling
column4: James and Lange independently argued: we see a bear → body trembles → we feel afraid. Emotion is the perception of bodily change, not its cause.

column1: In the James-Lange theory, what is the correct sequence of events?
column4: This bottom-up model holds that different emotions arise from distinct patterns of peripheral arousal. The subjective feeling is a readout of bodily state.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::james-lange-theory MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What prediction does James-Lange theory make about people with spinal cord injuries affecting body feedback?
column3: They should experience reduced emotional intensity
column4: If emotion depends on perceiving bodily changes, cutting off that feedback (as in high spinal injuries) should blunt emotion. Some evidence supports this, though patients still report emotions, limiting the theory.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::james-lange-theory MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the main criticism of the James-Lange theory?
column3: Different emotions share similar physiological arousal patterns
column4: Cannon argued that the visceral changes are too slow and too similar across emotions to be the source of distinct feelings — the body alone cannot differentiate fear from anger.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::james-lange-theory MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the facial feedback hypothesis share with the James-Lange theory?
column3: Both claim peripheral body states influence subjective emotion
column4: The facial feedback hypothesis (forcing a smile can induce mild positive affect) is a modern descendant of James-Lange logic — proprioceptive signals from muscles feed back to shape emotional experience.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::james-lange-theory MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the Cannon-Bard theory of emotion propose?
column3: Physiological arousal and subjective feeling occur simultaneously and independently
column4: Cannon and Bard argued the thalamus relays signals to both the cortex (feeling) and the body (arousal) at the same time — not sequentially. The two components are parallel, not causal.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::cannon-bard-theory MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: In Cannon-Bard theory, which brain structure was proposed as the key relay for emotional signals?
column4: Cannon proposed the thalamus simultaneously sends signals to the cortex (producing conscious feeling) and to the hypothalamus/body (producing arousal). This was a major revision from a purely peripheral account.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::cannon-bard-theory MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What was Cannon's main evidence against the James-Lange theory?
column3: Visceral responses are too slow and non-specific to generate distinct emotions
column4: Cannon noted that: (1) the same visceral changes occur in different emotions, (2) internal organs are relatively insensitive, and (3) artificially inducing arousal does not always produce emotion.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::cannon-bard-theory MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: According to Cannon-Bard theory, can an emotional experience occur without complete peripheral feedback?
column3: Yes — feeling and arousal are independent parallel processes
column4: Because the theory decouples subjective feeling from peripheral arousal (both originate from the thalamus simultaneously), disrupting peripheral signals does not eliminate the emotional experience.
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::cannon-bard-theory MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: How does Cannon-Bard theory differ from James-Lange theory regarding the timing of arousal and feeling?
column3: Cannon-Bard: simultaneous; James-Lange: arousal precedes feeling
column4: This is a critical comparison point. James-Lange is sequential (body first, then feeling); Cannon-Bard is parallel (both at the same time, neither causing the other).
column8: concept::PS::6C::emotion MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::emotion::cannon-bard-theory MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does the Schachter-Singer (two-factor) theory of emotion propose?
column3: Emotion = physiological arousal + cognitive label explaining the arousal
column4: Schachter and Singer argued that undifferentiated arousal is cognitively interpreted using contextual cues. The same arousal state can become different emotions depending on the available explanation.

column1: What was the key experimental manipulation in Schachter and Singer's 1962 study?
column3: Injecting epinephrine (adrenaline) and manipulating available explanations
column4: Participants given epinephrine but no explanation attributed arousal to the confederate's behavior (euphoria or anger), demonstrating that cognitive labeling of ambiguous arousal determines the emotion felt.

column1: In Schachter-Singer theory, what happens when a person has a clear explanation for their arousal?
column3: They do not need to seek an external label — no emotion mislabeling
column4: If participants were told the injection would cause arousal, they did not adopt the confederate's emotional state. Unexplained arousal drives the search for a cognitive label.

column1: What phenomenon does Schachter-Singer theory explain via misattribution of arousal?
column3: Excitation transfer — arousal from one source intensifies a later emotion
column4: Zillmann's excitation-transfer paradigm showed residual physiological arousal from exercise can intensify anger or attraction when people misattribute the arousal to a new stimulus.

column1: How does Schachter-Singer theory differ from Cannon-Bard regarding the role of cognition?
column3: Schachter-Singer assigns cognition a causal role; Cannon-Bard does not
column4: In Cannon-Bard, feeling and arousal are parallel and automatic. In Schachter-Singer, the cognitive label actively determines which emotion is felt from an undifferentiated arousal state.

column1: What is the 'suspension bridge study' and which emotion theory does it illustrate?
column3: Dutton & Aron (1974) — misattribution of arousal; supports Schachter-Singer
column4: Men crossing a scary bridge showed more attraction to a female interviewer than men on a stable bridge — arousal from fear was misattributed as romantic attraction, consistent with two-factor theory.

column1: What brain region is most central to the biological processing of fear?
column4: The amygdala detects threat-related stimuli, coordinates fear responses, and forms fear memories. Bilateral amygdala damage (Urbach-Wiethe disease) produces deficits in recognizing fearful faces.

column1: What is the role of the prefrontal cortex in emotion perception?
column3: Regulates and appraises emotional responses from the amygdala
column4: The prefrontal cortex (especially ventromedial PFC) modulates amygdala activity through top-down inhibition, allowing deliberate regulation of emotional reactions.

column1: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with mood regulation and is targeted by SSRIs?
column4: Serotonergic pathways (especially from the raphe nuclei) regulate mood, appetite, and sleep. SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin and are first-line treatments for depression and anxiety.

column1: What role do mirror neurons play in perceiving others' emotions?
column3: They activate when observing others' emotional expressions, enabling empathy
column4: Mirror neurons fire both when performing an action/emotion and when observing it in others. They are proposed to underlie empathy and emotional contagion.

column1: Which hormone is released during stress and can impair accurate emotion perception at high levels?
column4: Elevated cortisol (from HPA axis activation) can bias attention toward threatening stimuli and impair prefrontal regulation of the amygdala, distorting emotion perception.

column1: What biological difference is associated with left vs. right prefrontal cortex activity in emotion?
column3: Left PFC: approach/positive affect; Right PFC: withdrawal/negative affect
column4: EEG studies (Davidson) show greater left prefrontal activation correlates with positive emotions and approach motivation, while right activation correlates with negative emotions and withdrawal.

column1: Which brain region is most important for generating and experiencing emotions?
column4: The limbic system integrates emotional memory and response generation. The amygdala is central to fear; the hippocampus links emotion to context and memory.

column1: What is the role of the hypothalamus in emotion?
column3: Coordinates physiological responses to emotion (autonomic/endocrine output)
column4: The hypothalamus translates emotional signals from the limbic system into bodily responses via the ANS and HPA axis — controlling heart rate, stress hormones, and visceral changes.

column1: What happens to emotional experience when the amygdala is damaged bilaterally?
column3: Impaired fear recognition and reduced fear conditioning
column4: Patients with bilateral amygdala lesions (e.g., Urbach-Wiethe) cannot recognize fearful faces and fail to acquire conditioned fear responses, demonstrating its essential role in fear processing.

column1: What role does the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) play in emotion?
column3: Integrates emotional and cognitive processing; monitors conflict and pain affect
column4: The ACC bridges the limbic system and prefrontal cortex, involved in the affective component of pain and in regulating emotional responses to cognitive demands.

column1: Which brain region links emotional memory to context, and is critical for fear extinction?
column4: The hippocampus provides contextual information to the amygdala. During fear extinction, the hippocampus and ventromedial PFC signal safety context, suppressing amygdala-driven fear responses.

column1: What is the insula's role in emotional experience?
column3: Mediates interoception and subjective feeling states (especially disgust)
column4: The insular cortex processes signals from internal body organs (interoception) and is especially active during disgust and the conscious 'feeling' of emotions. It is part of the visceral-emotional loop.

column1: What structures are classically included in the limbic system?
column3: Amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus, thalamus, cingulate gyrus
column4: The limbic system (Papez circuit) was originally defined as the 'emotional brain.' Key structures: amygdala (fear/emotion), hippocampus (memory), hypothalamus (drives), cingulate gyrus (attention/conflict).

column1: What is the primary function of the amygdala within the limbic system?
column3: Processing and learning fear and threat-related emotions
column4: The amygdala rapidly evaluates stimuli for threat, triggers fight-or-flight, and consolidates emotional memories via interactions with the hippocampus and hypothalamus.

column1: What is the Papez circuit and its relevance to emotion?
column3: A circuit (hippocampus→hypothalamus→thalamus→cingulate cortex) proposed as the neural basis of emotion
column4: James Papez (1937) proposed this circuit as the substrate for emotional experience. It predates modern limbic system concepts and remains historically important for MCAT contexts.

column1: How does the limbic system interact with the prefrontal cortex during emotion regulation?
column3: PFC exerts top-down inhibitory control over limbic (especially amygdala) activity
column4: When we consciously regulate emotions (reappraisal, suppression), the ventromedial and dorsolateral PFC suppress amygdala reactivity. Dysfunction in this loop underlies anxiety and mood disorders.

column1: Which limbic structure is most implicated in emotional memory consolidation?
column4: The amygdala enhances memory consolidation for emotionally arousing events by modulating hippocampal activity. This is why emotionally charged memories are often vivid and long-lasting.

column1: What does the Kluver-Bucy syndrome reveal about the limbic system and emotion?
column3: Bilateral temporal lobe (amygdala) damage causes emotional blunting, hypersexuality, and hyperorality
column4: Kluver-Bucy syndrome results from bilateral amygdala/temporal lobe ablation. Animals/humans show loss of fear, inappropriate sexual behavior, and compulsive oral exploration — demonstrating the amygdala's role in emotional evaluation.

column1: Which division of the autonomic nervous system is activated during an emotional fear response?
column4: Fear triggers the sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' response: increased heart rate, dilated pupils, bronchodilation, and epinephrine release from the adrenal medulla.

column1: What is the role of the parasympathetic nervous system in emotion?
column3: Promotes rest-and-digest; restores baseline after emotional arousal
column4: After a stressor resolves, the parasympathetic system (via vagus nerve) decreases heart rate and promotes digestion. High resting vagal tone is associated with better emotional regulation.

column1: Which neurotransmitter does the sympathetic nervous system primarily release at end organs during emotional arousal?
column4: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto target organs (heart, blood vessels, glands). The adrenal medulla releases both epinephrine and norepinephrine directly into blood.

column1: What is the autonomic nervous system component of the emotion anger compared to fear?
column3: Both activate the sympathetic system, but anger involves more cardiac output increase; fear more peripheral vasoconstriction
column4: Research suggests anger and fear have subtly different autonomic profiles — anger tends to increase heart rate via cardiac output; fear via vasoconstriction. This distinction was used by Ax (1953) to challenge James-Lange.

column1: What is the vagal tone and why is it relevant to emotion regulation?
column3: High vagal tone (strong parasympathetic resting state) correlates with better emotion regulation
column4: Vagal tone reflects the influence of the vagus nerve on heart rate variability. High vagal tone is associated with greater flexibility in shifting between emotional states and better self-regulation.

column1: How does the ANS mediate the 'freeze' response seen in extreme fear?
column3: Parasympathetic dominance (dorsal vagal complex) causes immobility and reduced heart rate
column4: In extreme danger, some organisms show tonic immobility ('playing dead'). Polyvagal theory (Porges) attributes this to an evolutionarily older dorsal vagal parasympathetic circuit, distinct from the social-engagement system.

column1: What is skin conductance response (SCR) and what does it measure?
column3: A change in skin electrical conductance due to sweat gland activity; measures sympathetic arousal
column4: SCR (also called galvanic skin response) reflects eccrine sweat gland activation by the sympathetic nervous system. It is a sensitive physiological marker of emotional arousal used in psychophysiology research.

column1: What cardiovascular changes are physiological markers of emotional arousal?
column3: Increased heart rate and blood pressure
column4: Sympathetic activation during emotional arousal causes the heart to beat faster and with more force, raising both heart rate and arterial blood pressure — easily measured as emotion signatures.

column1: What is the significance of cortisol levels as a physiological marker of emotion?
column3: Elevated cortisol indicates HPA axis activation and chronic stress/negative emotion
column4: Cortisol (released from adrenal cortex via CRH→ACTH→cortisol axis) peaks 20-30 minutes after a stressor. Chronically elevated cortisol signals ongoing stress and negative emotional states.

column1: What does pupil dilation indicate as a physiological marker of emotion?
column3: Sympathetic arousal and increased cognitive/emotional engagement
column4: Pupil dilation (mydriasis) results from sympathetic activation of the dilator pupillae muscle. It occurs during fear, interest, and cognitive effort, and can be measured as an index of arousal.

column1: What is the difference between the physiological markers of fear and disgust?
column3: Fear: sympathetic arousal (↑HR, ↑SCR); disgust: parasympathetic elements (nausea, reduced HR)
column4: Disgust has a distinct autonomic profile from fear — it can produce bradycardia and nausea via parasympathetic activation, whereas fear is predominantly sympathetically driven. This supports distinct biological signatures per emotion.

column1: What does facial electromyography (EMG) measure in emotion research?
column3: Electrical activity of facial muscles indicating emotional expressions
column4: Facial EMG detects subtle muscle contractions invisible to the eye — e.g., zygomaticus major (smiling), corrugator supercilii (frowning). It provides a covert physiological signature of emotional valence.

column1: What is the startle reflex and how is it used as a physiological marker of emotion?
column3: An automatic blink/muscle response to sudden stimuli; potentiated by negative emotion (fear potentiated startle)
column4: The startle response is larger (fear-potentiated) when subjects are in a negative/fearful state, reflecting amygdala sensitization of the startle circuit. It is used as an objective measure of emotional state in research.

column1: Define stress in the context of psychology.
column3: A response to perceived demands exceeding resources
column4: Stress is defined as the perception that environmental demands tax or exceed one's ability to cope; it is inherently subjective.

column1: Who developed the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) model of stress?
column4: Selye identified a three-stage biological response to prolonged stress: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion.
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::the-nature-of-stress MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Name the three stages of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome.
column4: Alarm = fight-or-flight activation; resistance = body adapts; exhaustion = resources depleted and disease/breakdown risk rises.
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::the-nature-of-stress MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the alarm stage of GAS characterized by?
column3: Activation of the sympathetic nervous system (fight-or-flight)
column4: During the alarm stage, cortisol and catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) are released to mobilize the body.
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::the-nature-of-stress MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What physiological system is primarily active during the resistance stage of GAS?
column4: Sustained stress keeps cortisol elevated via the HPA axis, allowing the body to cope temporarily but depleting reserves over time.
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::the-nature-of-stress MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which stage of GAS is associated with immunosuppression and increased disease vulnerability?
column4: Prolonged cortisol elevation in the exhaustion stage suppresses immune function and can lead to ulcers, cardiovascular disease, and breakdown of homeostasis.
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::the-nature-of-stress MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Define eustress.
column4: Eustress (e.g., excitement before a competition) is associated with positive arousal and can enhance performance, unlike distress.
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::the-nature-of-stress MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is primary appraisal in the context of stress?
column3: Initial judgment of whether an event is threatening, harmful, or irrelevant
column4: Lazarus & Folkman's transactional model: primary appraisal evaluates the significance of a stressor (threat, loss, challenge, or benign).
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::appraisal MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is secondary appraisal?
column3: Evaluation of one's ability to cope with the stressor
column4: Secondary appraisal asks 'What can I do?' — assessing available coping resources; if resources seem adequate, stress is reduced.
column8: concept::PS::6C::stress MCAT::section::PS MCAT::6C::stress::appraisal MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Who developed the transactional model of stress and coping?
column4: Their 1984 model emphasizes that stress is a transaction between person and environment, mediated by cognitive appraisal.
