column1: From which embryonic layer does the nervous system develop?
column4: Neural tube closes around week 4; failure causes neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly); folic acid is protective.
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::prenatal-development MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What are the three stages of prenatal development in order?
column4: Germinal (0–2 weeks, implantation), embryonic (weeks 3–8, organ formation), fetal (week 9–birth, growth and maturation).
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::prenatal-development MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is a teratogen?
column3: Agent that causes birth defects by disrupting prenatal development
column4: Examples: alcohol (fetal alcohol syndrome), thalidomide, rubella, radiation. Teratogens are most harmful during the embryonic period (organogenesis).
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::prenatal-development MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the most critical period for organ development in prenatal life?
column4: Organogenesis occurs during this window; teratogen exposure here has the greatest potential to cause structural birth defects.
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::prenatal-development MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the rooting reflex, and when does it normally disappear?
column3: Turning head/mouth toward cheek touch; disappears around 4 months
column4: Rooting helps neonates find the nipple; its disappearance is replaced by voluntary feeding behavior as cortical control develops.
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::motor-development MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What is the typical sequence of gross motor milestones in the first year of life?
column3: Head control → sitting → crawling → standing → walking (around 12 months)
column4: Motor development proceeds cephalocaudal (head-to-toe) and proximodistal (center-to-extremities).
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::motor-development MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does 'cephalocaudal development' mean?
column3: Development proceeds from head downward toward feet
column4: Infants gain head/neck control before trunk control, which precedes leg control; mirrors the direction of fetal neural maturation.
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::motor-development MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What does 'proximodistal development' mean?
column3: Development proceeds from body center outward to extremities
column4: Children control trunk/shoulder movements before hands/fingers; seen in both prenatal and postnatal motor development.
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::motor-development MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: At what age do most children develop a mature pincer grasp (thumb-index finger)?
column4: Fine motor skill requiring coordinated cortical control; precedes ability to hold and manipulate small objects purposefully.
column8: concept::PS::7A::behavior MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::behavior::motor-development MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What are the primary physical changes associated with puberty in males?
column3: Testicular enlargement, pubic/body hair, deepening voice, growth spurt, spermarche
column4: Driven by rising testosterone; testicular enlargement is typically the first sign; spermarche (first ejaculation) around age 13.

column1: What are the primary physical changes of puberty in females?
column3: Breast development, pubic hair, growth spurt, menarche
column4: Driven by rising estrogens; breast budding (thelarche) is typically the first sign; menarche (first menstruation) occurs relatively late.

column1: What is Piaget's stage of cognitive development in adolescence?
column4: Adolescents gain ability for abstract, hypothetical-deductive reasoning; allows scientific thinking and consideration of possibilities.

column1: What is the imaginary audience in adolescent psychology?
column3: Adolescent belief that others are constantly watching and judging them
column4: Elkind's concept of adolescent egocentrism; contributes to self-consciousness and identity development during this period.

column1: What is Erikson's psychosocial stage of adolescence, and what is its central conflict?
column4: Adolescents explore social roles and form a coherent identity; failure leads to role confusion and an unclear sense of self.

column1: What brain region undergoes significant pruning and myelination during adolescence, contributing to risk-taking behavior?
column3: Prefrontal cortex (last to fully mature, around mid-20s)
column4: The PFC governs impulse control and planning; its delayed maturation relative to the limbic system explains adolescent risk-taking.

column1: Which major psychological domain does personality theory fall under on the MCAT?
column3: Psychological, Social, and Biological Foundations of Behavior
column4: Personality is tested in Category 7A (Individual influences on behavior), emphasizing how stable traits and dispositions shape behavior.

column1: Which four major theoretical perspectives of personality are most emphasized on the MCAT?
column4: Biological and behaviorist perspectives are also tested; knowing the defining assumptions of each is essential for MCAT questions.

column1: What does a 'nomothetic' approach to personality focus on?
column3: Universal laws and general traits across people
column4: Nomothetic approaches (e.g., trait theories) seek generalizable patterns, whereas idiographic approaches focus on the unique individual.

column1: What does an 'idiographic' approach to personality focus on?
column3: Unique traits and patterns of the individual
column4: Humanistic and some psychoanalytic methods are more idiographic, exploring the individual's subjective experience.

column1: Which personality theory emphasizes unconscious processes and early childhood experiences as determinants of personality?
column4: Freud's psychoanalytic theory holds that much of personality is shaped by unconscious conflicts rooted in early development.

column1: What are the three components of Freud's structural model of the mind?
column4: The id operates on the pleasure principle, the superego on morality, and the ego mediates between the two on the reality principle.

column1: Which component of Freud's structural model operates entirely on the pleasure principle?
column4: The id is the primitive, unconscious reservoir of drives that demands immediate gratification without regard for reality or morality.

column1: What are Freud's five psychosexual stages of development in order?
column4: Fixation at any stage due to unresolved conflict is thought to produce characteristic adult personality traits.

column1: During which Freudian psychosexual stage does the Oedipus/Electra complex occur?
column4: The phallic stage (ages 3-6) involves identification with the same-sex parent as a resolution to the complex, shaping gender identity and morality.

column1: What defense mechanism involves attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to others?
column4: For example, a person who is angry at a friend may instead believe the friend is angry at them — a classic projection defense.

column1: Which defense mechanism involves reverting to behaviors characteristic of an earlier developmental stage under stress?
column4: An adult who throws a temper tantrum under extreme stress is exhibiting regression to an earlier, more infantile mode of coping.

column1: What Jungian concept refers to the unconscious shared across all humans?
column4: Jung proposed that the collective unconscious contains archetypes — universal symbols and themes common to all cultures.

column1: What is the central assumption of the humanistic perspective of personality?
column3: People are inherently good and driven toward self-actualization
column4: Humanistic theorists like Maslow and Rogers emphasize free will, subjective experience, and the innate drive for growth.

column1: Who developed the concept of self-actualization as the pinnacle of human motivation?
column4: Maslow's hierarchy of needs places self-actualization at the top; only after lower needs are met can one pursue full personal potential.

column1: What concept central to Carl Rogers's personality theory refers to the person one believes oneself to be?
column4: Rogers emphasized that a healthy personality develops when the self-concept aligns with actual experience; incongruence leads to distress.

column1: What does Rogers mean by 'unconditional positive regard'?
column3: Acceptance and support regardless of what the person says or does
column4: Rogers believed unconditional positive regard from others fosters a healthy, congruent self-concept and facilitates personal growth.

column1: What is the 'conditions of worth' concept in Rogers's humanistic theory?
column3: Standards others impose that one must meet to receive positive regard
column4: When people internalize others' conditions of worth, their self-concept becomes distorted and incongruent with true experience.

column1: What is the difference between the 'real self' and the 'ideal self' in Rogerian theory?
column3: Real self = who you actually are; ideal self = who you want to be
column4: Large discrepancy between real and ideal self produces anxiety and psychological distress; congruence promotes well-being.

column1: What is the basic premise of the trait perspective of personality?
column3: Personality consists of stable, enduring traits that predict behavior
column4: Trait theorists identify and measure specific dimensions (e.g., the Big Five) that are consistent across situations and time.
column8: concept::PS::7A::personality MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::personality::trait-perspective MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Name the five dimensions of the Big Five (OCEAN) personality model.
column4: OCEAN is the dominant trait model; each dimension is a continuum and is considered largely stable across adulthood.
column8: concept::PS::7A::personality MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::personality::trait-perspective MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which Big Five trait is most strongly associated with academic and job performance?
column4: Conscientiousness reflects discipline, organization, and goal-directedness — consistently the best trait predictor of performance outcomes.
column8: concept::PS::7A::personality MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::personality::trait-perspective MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Who proposed the 16 Personality Factor (16PF) model?
column4: Cattell used factor analysis to reduce hundreds of trait descriptors to 16 source traits underlying personality.
column8: concept::PS::7A::personality MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::personality::trait-perspective MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Which trait theorist proposed that personality is organized into three superordinate dimensions: Extraversion, Neuroticism, and Psychoticism?
column4: Eysenck's PEN model linked his three dimensions to biological arousal systems, bridging trait and biological perspectives.
column8: concept::PS::7A::personality MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::personality::trait-perspective MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What statistical technique do trait theorists commonly use to identify personality dimensions?
column4: Factor analysis groups correlated variables (trait ratings) into underlying factors, revealing the dimensional structure of personality.
column8: concept::PS::7A::personality MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::personality::trait-perspective MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: Who is the primary theorist associated with the social cognitive perspective of personality?
column4: Bandura's social cognitive theory emphasizes observational learning, self-efficacy, and the reciprocal interaction between person, behavior, and environment.

column1: What does 'self-efficacy' mean in Bandura's social cognitive theory?
column3: Belief in one's own ability to succeed in specific situations
column4: High self-efficacy increases persistence and performance; it is domain-specific, not a global personality trait.

column1: What is 'reciprocal determinism' in Bandura's social cognitive theory?
column3: Bidirectional interaction among person, behavior, and environment
column4: Unlike purely behaviorist views, reciprocal determinism holds that the person is both shaped by and shapes the environment.

column1: What is 'locus of control' in personality psychology?
column3: Belief about whether outcomes are controlled internally or externally
column4: Internal locus = belief in personal control; external locus = belief that luck, fate, or others control outcomes. Julian Rotter developed the concept.

column1: What personality variable did Walter Mischel propose to replace global traits in predicting behavior?
column4: Mischel's CAPS model argues behavior is best predicted by how individuals encode, expect, and respond to particular situational features.

column1: What is an 'expectancy' in social cognitive personality theory?
column3: A person's belief about what outcomes will follow from a behavior
column4: Expectancies (learned from experience) guide whether a person will initiate a behavior in a given situation.

column1: What is the central claim of the biological perspective of personality?
column3: Personality traits have a heritable, neurobiological basis
column4: Twin and adoption studies show roughly 40-60% heritability for major personality traits, supporting a biological foundation.

column1: Which neurotransmitter system is most associated with extraversion in biological personality theories?
column4: Extraverts show greater dopaminergic activity in reward circuits; they seek stimulation to maintain an optimal arousal level.

column1: According to Eysenck's biological theory, why are introverts more reserved?
column3: They have higher baseline cortical arousal and seek less stimulation
column4: Eysenck proposed introverts' ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) is more reactive, so they avoid overstimulation.

column1: Which neurotransmitter is associated with neuroticism and negative emotionality in biological personality models?
column4: Low serotonergic activity is linked to anxiety, negative affect, and emotional instability — core features of high neuroticism.

column1: What evidence most directly supports heritability of personality traits?
column3: Identical (MZ) twins reared apart show similar personalities
column4: High concordance in MZ twins raised in different environments isolates genetic contributions from shared environment.

column1: What is the basic assumption of the behaviorist perspective on personality?
column3: Personality is a pattern of learned behaviors shaped by reinforcement and punishment
column4: Behaviorists like Skinner reject internal mental constructs; personality differences reflect different reinforcement histories.

column1: Which behaviorist is most associated with operant conditioning as a basis for personality?
column4: Skinner argued that what we call personality is simply a set of behavioral tendencies shaped and maintained by contingencies of reinforcement.

column1: How does classical conditioning contribute to personality in the behaviorist view?
column3: Conditioned emotional responses become stable emotional tendencies
column4: For example, phobias and anxious dispositions can be classically conditioned and generalized, forming lasting personality-like patterns.

column1: What criticism is most commonly leveled at the behaviorist perspective of personality?
column3: It ignores internal mental processes (cognition, emotion, unconscious)
column4: Pure behaviorism cannot easily account for individual differences in perception, expectation, or self-concept that influence behavior.

column1: In the behaviorist view, what accounts for individual differences in personality?
column4: Two people exposed to the same situation may respond differently because of differing past conditioning, not innate traits or cognitions.

column1: What is the core argument of the situational approach to explaining behavior?
column3: Behavior is primarily determined by situational factors, not internal traits
column4: Situationists like Mischel argue that people's behavior varies greatly across situations, challenging the predictive power of stable traits.

column1: What is the 'person-situation debate' in personality psychology?
column3: Debate over whether traits or situations better predict behavior
column4: Trait theorists argue for cross-situational consistency; situationists argue context is the stronger determinant of specific behaviors.

column1: What is the 'fundamental attribution error'?
column3: Overestimating dispositional causes and underestimating situational causes
column4: People tend to attribute others' behavior to personality traits while underweighting the powerful role of the situation.

column1: What did Mischel's 1968 review conclude about the predictability of behavior from traits?
column4: This finding challenged trait theory and sparked the person-situation debate; later work showed aggregated behavior is more predictable.

column1: What is the 'interactionist' resolution to the person-situation debate?
column3: Behavior results from the interaction of traits and situations
column4: Modern personality psychology adopts an interactionist view: stable traits manifest differently depending on situational context and affordances.

column1: What does 'behavioral aggregation' demonstrate about trait predictability?
column3: Averaging behavior across many situations reveals stable trait-behavior correlations
column4: Single behaviors are situation-dependent, but aggregated behaviors correlate reliably with traits, supporting the validity of trait measures.

column1: What is a psychological disorder?
column3: Clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion, or behavior
column4: A psychological disorder involves patterns that reflect dysfunction in psychological, biological, or developmental processes and cause significant distress or impairment.

column1: What are the three core criteria used to define a psychological disorder?
column4: A behavior must be atypical (deviant), cause personal distress, and impair daily functioning to be considered a disorder; no single criterion is sufficient alone.

column1: What does the term 'psychological dysfunction' refer to in defining disorders?
column3: Breakdown in cognitive, emotional, or behavioral functioning
column4: Dysfunction means the individual's ability to perform everyday activities is compromised, distinguishing disorder from mere eccentricity.

column1: Which criterion distinguishes a harmful dysfunction from cultural nonconformity?
column4: Jerome Wakefield's harmful dysfunction definition requires both an internal mechanism failure and that the failure causes harm, preventing labeling of mere social deviance as disorder.

column1: What is the 'four Ds' framework for identifying psychological disorders?
column4: The four Ds provide a practical checklist; 'danger' (risk of harm to self or others) is sometimes added to the classic three-D model.

column1: What does the biomedical model of psychological disorders attribute illness to?
column4: The biomedical model treats mental disorders as diseases with physical causes, analogous to medical illnesses, emphasizing pharmacological treatment.

column1: What does the biopsychosocial model add to the biomedical model?
column4: Engel's biopsychosocial model integrates biological, psychological (thoughts, emotions), and social (culture, relationships, stress) contributors to illness.

column1: Who proposed the biopsychosocial model of health and illness?
column4: Engel argued that the purely biomedical model was reductionist and proposed integrating psychological and social dimensions into medical understanding.

column1: Which approach to mental disorders best accounts for the role of stress and social support in recovery?
column4: By including social and psychological factors, the biopsychosocial model can explain why the same biological vulnerability leads to disorder in some environments but not others.

column1: What is a key limitation of the biomedical model when applied to psychological disorders?
column4: The biomedical model cannot fully explain conditions like PTSD or culture-bound syndromes, where social and cognitive factors are primary drivers.

column1: What manual is used to classify psychological disorders in the United States?
column3: DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed.)
column4: The DSM-5, published by the American Psychiatric Association, provides diagnostic criteria, prevalence data, and coding for mental disorders.

column1: What international system classifies all diseases, including mental disorders?
column4: The WHO's ICD is used globally; ICD-11 is the current version and includes mental and behavioral disorder classifications compatible with DSM-5.

column1: What major structural change was made in DSM-5 compared to DSM-IV?
column4: DSM-IV used five axes; DSM-5 collapsed Axes I, II, and III into a single diagnosis list, simplifying documentation and removing the stigma of separate personality/medical axes.

column1: What is a culture-bound syndrome?
column3: A disorder recognized only within a specific cultural context
column4: Examples include taijin kyofusho (Japan) and ataque de nervios (Latin America); they illustrate that cultural norms shape what is classified as pathological.

column1: What is the primary criticism of categorical (DSM) classification of mental disorders?
column3: Disorders exist on a continuum, not discrete categories
column4: Critics argue the dimensional approach better captures symptom severity and overlap between disorders, which the DSM-5 partly addresses with specifiers and severity ratings.

column1: Approximately what percentage of U.S. adults experience a diagnosable mental disorder in a given year?
column4: The National Comorbidity Survey Replication found roughly 26% of Americans meet criteria for a DSM disorder annually, with anxiety disorders being most common.

column1: Which category of psychological disorder has the highest lifetime prevalence in the U.S.?
column4: Anxiety disorders (including phobias, GAD, panic disorder) are the most prevalent class, affecting roughly 28% of people over a lifetime.

column1: What does comorbidity mean in the context of psychological disorders?
column3: Co-occurrence of two or more disorders in the same individual
column4: Comorbidity is common (e.g., depression + anxiety); it complicates diagnosis and treatment and often indicates shared underlying vulnerabilities.

column1: Which sex has higher rates of internalizing disorders (depression, anxiety)?
column4: Women are diagnosed with depression and anxiety disorders approximately twice as often as men; hormonal, social, and reporting-bias factors all contribute.

column1: Which sex has higher rates of externalizing disorders (conduct disorder, antisocial personality)?
column4: Externalizing disorders involve outward-directed behaviors; men show higher rates, possibly due to biological and socialization differences.

column1: Name the major DSM-5 categories of psychological disorders (list at least five).
column3: Anxiety, depressive, bipolar, schizophrenia spectrum, OCD, trauma-related, somatic, dissociative, personality
column4: DSM-5 reorganized disorders into 20 chapters; knowing the major categories helps locate specific diagnoses on the MCAT.

column1: What distinguishes a neurodevelopmental disorder from other DSM-5 categories?
column4: Neurodevelopmental disorders (ADHD, autism spectrum, intellectual disability) manifest early and affect personal, social, and academic functioning.

column1: What is the distinction between psychotic and neurotic disorders?
column3: Psychotic: loss of reality contact; neurotic: distress without reality loss
column4: Although DSM-5 dropped the neurosis/psychosis dichotomy, the conceptual distinction remains useful: psychotic disorders involve hallucinations/delusions while neurotic disorders do not.

column1: Which DSM-5 disorder category includes both feeding and eating disorders?
column4: This category includes anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder, recognized for their significant medical and psychological morbidity.

column1: What is generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)?
column3: Excessive, uncontrollable worry about multiple topics for ≥6 months
column4: GAD involves chronic, pervasive worry accompanied by symptoms like fatigue, muscle tension, irritability, and sleep disturbance.

column1: What neurotransmitter system is most implicated in anxiety disorders?
column4: Reduced GABAergic inhibition increases neuronal excitability; SSRIs and benzodiazepines (enhance GABA) are first-line pharmacological treatments for anxiety.

column1: What distinguishes a panic attack from panic disorder?
column3: Panic disorder requires recurrent attacks + persistent worry about future attacks
column4: Isolated panic attacks can occur in anyone; panic disorder is diagnosed only when attacks are recurrent and accompanied by behavioral changes (e.g., agoraphobia).

column1: What is agoraphobia?
column3: Fear/avoidance of situations where escape would be difficult during a panic attack
column4: Agoraphobia often co-occurs with panic disorder; situations avoided include crowds, public transportation, and open spaces.

column1: What cognitive distortion is most characteristic of social anxiety disorder?
column3: Fear of negative evaluation by others
column4: Individuals with social anxiety disorder believe others are scrutinizing and judging them harshly, leading to avoidance of social/performance situations.

column1: What are the two core symptoms of OCD?
column4: Obsessions cause anxiety; compulsions are performed to neutralize that anxiety temporarily, reinforcing the cycle through negative reinforcement.

column1: What learning principle explains why compulsions are maintained in OCD?
column4: Performing a compulsion reduces distress short-term, reinforcing the behavior; this is an operant conditioning mechanism.

column1: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with OCD, and what medication class targets it?
column4: OCD responds to serotonin reuptake inhibitors at higher doses than depression requires, implicating serotonergic dysregulation in the cortico-striato-thalamic circuit.

column1: Which brain circuit is hyperactive in OCD?
column4: Neuroimaging shows hyperactivity in the orbitofrontal cortex and caudate nucleus; this circuit normally gates repetitive behaviors.

column1: What DSM-5 change moved OCD out of the anxiety disorders chapter?
column3: OCD received its own chapter: 'Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders'
column4: DSM-5 recognized OCD's distinct features and grouped it with body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, and trichotillomania in a separate chapter.

column1: What is PTSD?
column3: Disorder following traumatic event: intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions, hyperarousal
column4: PTSD requires exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, followed by four symptom clusters persisting >1 month.

column1: What is acute stress disorder?
column3: PTSD-like symptoms lasting 3 days to 1 month after trauma
column4: Acute stress disorder is a precursor diagnosis; if symptoms persist beyond a month, the diagnosis changes to PTSD.

column1: Which neurotransmitter system is dysregulated in PTSD, producing hyperarousal?
column4: PTSD involves elevated noradrenergic activity; prazosin (alpha-1 blocker) reduces nightmares, and propranolol has been studied for blocking traumatic memory consolidation.

column1: What is the HPA axis finding in PTSD compared to depression?
column3: PTSD: low cortisol; depression: high cortisol
column4: PTSD is associated with hypocortisolism (possibly due to enhanced cortisol feedback), while major depression typically shows hypercortisolism and dexamethasone non-suppression.

column1: What distinguishes adjustment disorder from PTSD?
column3: Adjustment disorder: any stressor, milder reaction; PTSD: severe trauma, specific symptom clusters
column4: Adjustment disorder is a maladaptive response to an identifiable stressor (not necessarily traumatic) without the full PTSD symptom profile.

column1: What is somatic symptom disorder?
column3: One or more physical symptoms with excessive health-related thoughts/feelings/behaviors
column4: Formerly called somatization disorder; the DSM-5 diagnosis focuses on excessive psychological response to symptoms rather than whether symptoms are medically explained.

column1: What is illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis)?
column3: Preoccupation with having a serious illness despite minimal or no symptoms
column4: DSM-5 replaced 'hypochondriasis' with illness anxiety disorder; the individual interprets normal sensations as signs of serious disease.

column1: What is conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)?
column3: Neurological symptoms (paralysis, blindness) with no neurological cause
column4: Conversion disorder involves incompatibility between symptoms and known neurological disease; it was historically linked to psychological conflict.

column1: What is la belle indifférence in conversion disorder?
column3: Lack of concern about neurological symptoms
column4: Patients with conversion disorder sometimes show surprising indifference to serious-seeming deficits; however, this sign is not reliable for diagnosis.

column1: What is factitious disorder?
column3: Deliberately faking illness to assume sick role (without external incentives)
column4: Factitious disorder differs from malingering: the motivation is the sick role itself (attention, care), not external gains like money or avoiding work.

column1: What distinguishes bipolar I from bipolar II disorder?
column3: Bipolar I: full manic episode; bipolar II: hypomania + major depression only
column4: A manic episode in bipolar I lasts ≥7 days and may require hospitalization; hypomanic episodes in bipolar II last ≥4 days and are less severe.

column1: What is the minimum duration of a manic episode for a bipolar I diagnosis?
column3: 7 days (or any duration if hospitalization required)
column4: The 7-day criterion distinguishes mania from hypomania (≥4 days); hospitalization or psychotic features override the duration requirement.

column1: What first-line mood stabilizer is used in bipolar disorder?
column4: Lithium reduces manic and depressive episodes and lowers suicide risk; it has a narrow therapeutic index requiring serum level monitoring.

column1: What is cyclothymic disorder?
column3: Chronic mood fluctuations (hypomania + mild depression) for ≥2 years, not meeting full criteria
column4: Cyclothymia is a milder, chronic form of bipolar disorder; individuals never meet criteria for a full hypomanic or major depressive episode.

column1: Which neurotransmitter imbalance is most associated with the manic phase of bipolar disorder?
column4: Mania is thought to involve hyperdopaminergic and hypernorepi-nephrinergic states; antipsychotics (dopamine blockers) are used acutely for mania.

column1: What are the two core symptoms of major depressive disorder (MDD)?
column3: Depressed mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia)
column4: At least one of these two must be present, along with four additional symptoms, for ≥2 weeks to diagnose MDD.

column1: What neurotransmitter deficiencies are classically associated with depression?
column4: The monoamine hypothesis of depression proposes deficiency of these neurotransmitters; SSRIs, SNRIs, and NDRIs increase their availability.

column1: What is dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder)?
column3: Depressed mood most days for ≥2 years without meeting MDD criteria
column4: Persistent depressive disorder is a chronic, milder depression; individuals may experience 'double depression' if an MDD episode is superimposed.

column1: What is the learned helplessness model of depression?
column3: Depression results from perceived inability to control outcomes after repeated uncontrollable stress
column4: Seligman's model: exposure to inescapable aversive events leads to passive resignation; applies to human depression via attributional style.

column1: What is seasonal affective disorder (SAD), and which direction is most common?
column3: Recurrent depression tied to season; most common: fall/winter onset
column4: SAD is a specifier in DSM-5; winter SAD involves reduced light exposure, implicating circadian rhythm disruption and serotonin changes; light therapy is first-line.

column1: What are the positive symptoms of schizophrenia?
column4: Positive symptoms represent added abnormal experiences; they respond better to antipsychotic medications than negative symptoms.

column1: What are the negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
column3: Flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality
column4: Negative symptoms reflect diminished normal function; they are associated with poorer prognosis and are less responsive to typical antipsychotics.

column1: What is the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia?
column3: Excess dopamine activity (especially D2 receptors) causes positive symptoms
column4: Evidence includes: antipsychotics block D2 receptors; dopamine agonists (amphetamines) can induce psychosis; mesolimbic pathway is implicated.

column1: What minimum duration of symptoms is required for a schizophrenia diagnosis?
column4: The 6-month criterion distinguishes schizophrenia from schizophreniform disorder (1–6 months) and brief psychotic disorder (<1 month).

column1: What is the difference between schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder?
column3: Schizoaffective: psychotic symptoms co-occur with a mood episode for most of illness
column4: In schizoaffective disorder, a major mood episode (depressive or manic) is present for a substantial portion of the psychotic illness, unlike schizophrenia.

column1: What is dissociative amnesia?
column3: Inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually after trauma
column4: Dissociative amnesia is often related to stressful events; a rare severe form includes dissociative fugue (purposeful travel + identity confusion).

column1: What is depersonalization/derealization disorder?
column3: Persistent feelings of detachment from one's self (depersonalization) or surroundings (derealization)
column4: Individuals feel like an outside observer of their thoughts/body; reality testing remains intact, distinguishing it from psychosis.

column1: What is dissociative identity disorder (DID)?
column3: Presence of two or more distinct personality states with amnesia between them
column4: DID is associated with severe early childhood trauma; distinct identities may differ in behavior, voice, and even physiological measures.

column1: What mechanism underlies dissociative disorders?
column3: Compartmentalization of memories/identity to cope with trauma
column4: Dissociation is a defense mechanism that segregates overwhelming experiences from conscious awareness, disrupting memory and identity integration.

column1: How does dissociative amnesia differ from organic (neurological) amnesia?
column3: Dissociative: psychogenic, typically retrograde for personal info; organic: neurological cause, often anterograde
column4: Organic amnesia usually stems from brain lesions (hippocampal damage); dissociative amnesia has no structural lesion and often remits when stress resolves.

column1: What are the three DSM-5 clusters of personality disorders?
column3: Cluster A (odd/eccentric), Cluster B (dramatic/emotional), Cluster C (anxious/fearful)
column4: Cluster A: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal. Cluster B: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C: avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive.

column1: Which personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of disregard and violation of others' rights?
column4: ASPD requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 and persistent antisocial behavior in adulthood; associated with low fear response and reduced empathy.

column1: What is the core feature of borderline personality disorder (BPD)?
column3: Instability in relationships, self-image, emotions, and marked impulsivity
column4: BPD involves fear of abandonment, identity disturbance, self-harm, and intense, unstable relationships; DBT (dialectical behavior therapy) is the evidence-based treatment.

column1: Which personality disorder is most associated with psychopathy/sociopathy?
column4: Psychopathy (Hare's construct) overlaps substantially with ASPD but emphasizes affective features (callousness, lack of remorse) more than behavioral rule-breaking.

column1: What distinguishes schizotypal from schizoid personality disorder?
column3: Schizotypal: magical thinking, odd speech, ideas of reference; schizoid: emotional detachment only
column4: Schizotypal is on the schizophrenia spectrum (Cluster A) with cognitive-perceptual distortions; schizoid lacks distorted thinking but lacks desire for relationships.

column1: What dopamine pathway abnormality is most associated with positive symptoms of schizophrenia?
column4: Excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway (VTA → limbic structures) produces hallucinations and delusions; antipsychotics block D2 receptors here.

column1: Which brain structure shows reduced volume in schizophrenia?
column4: Neuroimaging reveals enlarged lateral ventricles and reduced prefrontal and hippocampal volume in schizophrenia, consistent with neurodevelopmental origin.

column1: Which neurotransmitter hypothesis extends the dopamine model of schizophrenia to explain negative symptoms?
column4: NMDA receptor hypofunction in prefrontal interneurons may disinhibit dopamine release in mesolimbic areas and impair prefrontal function causing negative symptoms.

column1: What monoamine neurotransmitter deficiency is the classic hypothesis for depression?
column4: The monoamine deficiency hypothesis led to development of SSRIs, SNRIs, and MAOIs; however, the full picture involves neuroplasticity and HPA axis dysregulation.

column1: Which brain structure shows reduced volume in major depression?
column4: Chronic stress and elevated cortisol suppress hippocampal neurogenesis, leading to volume loss; antidepressants promote BDNF and hippocampal neurogenesis.

column1: What is the role of the HPA axis in depression?
column3: Hypercortisolism from HPA hyperactivation; impaired negative feedback
column4: Elevated CRH and cortisol suppress neurogenesis and impair immune and cognitive function; the dexamethasone suppression test was historically used to detect this.

column1: What brain-derived factor is reduced in depression and increased by antidepressants?
column4: BDNF supports neuronal survival and plasticity; decreased BDNF in the hippocampus contributes to volume loss; antidepressants and exercise increase BDNF.

column1: What is the mechanism of action of SSRIs?
column3: Block serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT), increasing synaptic serotonin
column4: SSRIs are first-line for depression and anxiety; therapeutic effects take 2–4 weeks, likely due to downstream receptor adaptations and neuroplasticity rather than immediate serotonin increase.

column1: What are the two hallmark pathological features of Alzheimer's disease?
column4: Beta-amyloid peptides aggregate extracellularly; hyperphosphorylated tau forms intracellular tangles disrupting microtubule transport and causing neuronal death.

column1: Which neurotransmitter is most deficient in Alzheimer's disease?
column4: The basal nucleus of Meynert (cholinergic neurons) degenerates in Alzheimer's; AChE inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) are used to increase ACh and slow decline.

column1: Which gene variant is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease?
column4: APOE ε4 increases amyloid accumulation and reduces clearance; one copy increases risk ~3-fold, two copies ~12-fold. APOE ε2 is protective.

column1: What is the amyloid cascade hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease?
column3: Accumulation of beta-amyloid triggers tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and neuronal death
column4: The APP gene on chromosome 21 produces amyloid precursor protein; cleavage by beta- and gamma-secretase produces toxic Aβ42 peptides that aggregate.

column1: What is the earliest affected memory system in Alzheimer's disease?
column4: The hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, critical for episodic memory encoding, are affected earliest; procedural memory is relatively preserved until later stages.

column1: What are the cardinal motor features of Parkinson's disease?
column4: The mnemonic TRAP (Tremor, Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability) captures the four classic motor signs of Parkinson's disease.

column1: Which brain region degenerates in Parkinson's disease?
column4: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra reduces striatal dopamine, impairing the basal ganglia's ability to facilitate smooth voluntary movement.

column1: What protein aggregates form Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease?
column4: Misfolded alpha-synuclein accumulates in Lewy bodies (intraneuronal inclusions) in the substantia nigra and other brain regions in Parkinson's disease.

column1: What is the standard pharmacological treatment for Parkinson's disease motor symptoms?
column4: Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine; carbidopa inhibits peripheral decarboxylation, reducing side effects and increasing CNS availability.

column1: What basal ganglia pathway imbalance underlies Parkinson's disease symptoms?
column3: Underactive direct pathway, overactive indirect pathway → excess inhibition of thalamus
column4: Dopamine normally facilitates direct (movement-promoting) and inhibits indirect (movement-suppressing) pathways; dopamine loss shifts balance toward inhibition, reducing movement.

column1: What is the potential of stem cell therapy for neurodegenerative diseases?
column3: Replace lost neurons or provide trophic support to surviving neurons
column4: Stem cells (embryonic, iPSC, or neural progenitors) could theoretically repopulate damaged circuits; Parkinson's disease is a lead candidate due to discrete dopaminergic cell loss.

column1: What type of stem cells are most ethically accepted for neural regeneration research?
column4: iPSCs are generated by reprogramming adult somatic cells (e.g., skin fibroblasts) to pluripotency, avoiding the ethical concerns of embryonic stem cells.

column1: What is a major challenge of stem cell-based neural replacement therapy?
column3: Ensuring correct integration, differentiation, and avoiding tumorigenesis
column4: Transplanted cells must differentiate into the correct neuron type, form appropriate synaptic connections, and not form teratomas; immune rejection is also a concern.

column1: Which disease has seen the most clinical progress in stem cell-based neural therapy?
column4: Clinical trials transplanting fetal dopaminergic neurons into the striatum showed proof-of-concept; iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons are the current focus of trials.

column1: What is the therapeutic rationale for using stem cells in Alzheimer's disease vs. Parkinson's disease?
column3: Alzheimer's: widespread degeneration makes circuit replacement harder; Parkinson's: focal dopamine loss is more tractable
column4: The relatively discrete cell loss in Parkinson's (substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons) makes it more amenable to cell replacement than the diffuse pathology of Alzheimer's.

column1: What are the two main divisions of the central nervous system (CNS)?
column4: The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord; all other neural tissue (nerves, ganglia) belongs to the peripheral nervous system (PNS).

column1: Which glial cell type forms myelin in the CNS?
column4: Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons in the CNS; Schwann cells perform the equivalent function in the PNS. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons.

column1: What is the function of the blood-brain barrier (BBB)?
column3: Restricts passage of substances into brain
column4: Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells, supported by astrocyte end-feet, limit entry of pathogens and many drugs while allowing glucose and O2 to pass.

column1: Which brain structure serves as the primary relay station for sensory information to the cortex?
column4: Almost all sensory signals (except olfaction) synapse in the thalamus before being routed to appropriate cortical areas.

column1: What is the role of the reticular activating system (RAS) in the CNS?
column3: Regulates arousal, alertness, and sleep-wake cycles
column4: The RAS is a network in the brainstem that modulates consciousness and attention; damage causes coma.

column1: Which CNS structure controls homeostatic functions such as body temperature, hunger, and thirst?
column4: The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems, regulating the pituitary gland and maintaining internal homeostasis.

column1: What type of glial cell is the primary immune cell of the CNS?
column4: Microglia are resident macrophages of the CNS; they survey for pathogens and cellular debris and are activated during neuroinflammation.

column1: Which descending spinal tract carries voluntary motor commands from the primary motor cortex to lower motor neurons?
column4: Most corticospinal fibers decussate at the medullary pyramids, so the left cortex controls the right body side. Damage above the decussation causes contralateral deficits.

column1: What is motivation in psychology?
column3: Internal state that drives goal-directed behavior
column4: Motivation energizes and directs behavior toward goals; it can be intrinsic (from within) or extrinsic (from external rewards).

column1: Which type of motivation arises from internal enjoyment rather than external reward?
column4: Intrinsic motivation is driven by personal satisfaction or interest; it tends to produce more sustained engagement than extrinsic motivation.

column1: Which type of motivation is driven by external rewards or punishments?
column4: Extrinsic motivation includes pay, grades, or praise; over-reliance can undermine intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect).

column1: What is the overjustification effect in motivation?
column4: When people receive external rewards for an already intrinsically enjoyable task, their internal motivation for that task decreases.

column1: What term describes the degree of effort and persistence a person directs toward a goal?
column4: Intensity and direction are two key dimensions of motivation; high intensity means more energy devoted to goal pursuit.

column1: What is self-efficacy and how does it influence motivation?
column3: Belief in ability to succeed; higher self-efficacy increases motivation
column4: Bandura's concept: individuals with high self-efficacy set more challenging goals and persist longer when facing obstacles.

column1: What is an instinct in the context of motivation?
column3: Innate, fixed pattern of behavior in response to stimuli
column4: Instincts are unlearned, species-specific behaviors (e.g., suckling in newborns); instinct theory proposes these drive motivation.

column1: Which early motivation theory proposed that behavior is driven by innate biological instincts?
column4: William McDougall popularized instinct theory; it fell out of favor because cataloguing human instincts proved circular and unfalsifiable.

column1: Why was instinct theory largely abandoned as an explanation of human motivation?
column3: Circular reasoning; too many proposed instincts
column4: Labeling any behavior an 'instinct' without independent evidence is circular; the theory also failed to explain learned or culturally variable behaviors.

column1: What distinguishes a fixed action pattern from a simple reflex?
column3: Fixed action pattern is a complete, stereotyped behavioral sequence; reflex is a single automatic response
column4: Fixed action patterns are triggered by sign stimuli (releasers) and run to completion even if the stimulus is removed, unlike simple reflexes.

column1: What is the Yerkes-Dodson law?
column3: Performance is optimal at moderate arousal levels
column4: The inverted-U relationship: too little or too much arousal impairs performance; optimal arousal varies by task complexity.

column1: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, what arousal level is best for simple tasks?
column4: Simple, well-learned tasks benefit from higher arousal, while complex tasks requiring fine discrimination need lower arousal for peak performance.

column1: What is the arousal theory of motivation?
column3: People are motivated to maintain an optimal level of arousal
column4: Individuals seek stimulation when under-aroused and reduce stimulation when over-aroused; this optimal level varies across individuals (sensation seeking).
column8: concept::PS::7A::motivation MCAT::section::PS MCAT::7A::motivation::arousal MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY

column1: What personality trait describes individuals who chronically seek high arousal?
column4: Zuckerman's sensation-seeking trait; high sensation seekers tolerate more risk and novelty to maintain their preferred arousal level.
