column4: Taste aversion can occur with a single pairing, even hours after exposure, and preferentially links tastes (not lights/sounds) with nausea — showing biological constraints on classical conditioning.

column1: Who conducted the foundational research on taste aversion learning?
column4: Garcia showed that rats avoided saccharin water after radiation-induced nausea, even with long delays. This 'Garcia effect' challenged the equipotentiality premise of early behaviorism.

column1: What does 'preparedness' mean in the context of associative learning?
column3: Species are biologically predisposed to learn certain associations more readily than others
column4: Seligman's concept: phobias commonly develop to evolutionary threats (snakes, heights, spiders) far more easily than to modern dangers (guns, cars), reflecting prepared learning.

column1: Why does instinctive drift challenge a purely behavioral account of operant conditioning?
column3: It shows innate biological behaviors override reinforcement history
column4: The Brelands' observations showed that reinforcement alone cannot indefinitely maintain a trained behavior if it conflicts with the animal's instinctive behavioral repertoire, supporting the role of biology in learning.

column1: What is observational learning?
column3: Learning by watching others' behavior and outcomes
column4: Also called social learning or vicarious learning; coined by Albert Bandura. No direct reinforcement is required for the observer.

column1: Who is most associated with the theory of observational learning and modeling?
column4: Bandura's Bobo doll experiments demonstrated that children imitate aggressive behavior after watching a model, even without direct reinforcement.

column1: What term describes the person whose behavior is observed and imitated during observational learning?
column4: Models can be live (in person), symbolic (TV, books), or verbal (instructions). The observer does not need to personally perform the behavior to learn it.

column1: Name the four steps in Bandura's model of observational learning.
column4: Mnemonic: ARRM. The observer must attend to the model, retain the information, be able to reproduce the behavior, and be motivated to do so.

column1: What is vicarious reinforcement?
column3: Increased imitation after observing a model being rewarded
column4: Seeing a model rewarded for a behavior increases the likelihood the observer will imitate it, even though the observer received no direct reward.

column1: What is vicarious punishment?
column3: Decreased imitation after observing a model being punished
column4: The observer learns to avoid the behavior by watching the model suffer consequences, without experiencing punishment directly.

column1: Which characteristic of a model most increases the likelihood of imitation?
column3: High status, similarity to observer, or perceived competence
column4: Observers are more likely to imitate models who are similar to themselves, have high prestige, or appear competent — key factors in social learning theory.

column1: What distinguishes modeling from simple imitation?
column3: Modeling involves abstract rule extraction, not just copying specific acts
column4: Through modeling, observers extract general principles and apply them to new situations; imitation is direct, specific copying of observed behavior.

column1: What famous experiment demonstrated modeling of aggression in children?
column4: Bandura (1961) showed children imitated aggressive behavior toward an inflatable doll after watching an adult model do so, even without reinforcement.

column1: Which brain region is critically involved in the biological basis of observational learning?
column4: The prefrontal cortex supports working memory and executive function needed to encode, retain, and plan reproduction of observed behaviors.

column1: What neurotransmitter system is most associated with the motivational component of observational learning?
column4: Dopamine underpins reward and motivation; it drives the observer's desire to reproduce behaviors observed to be rewarded.

column1: Which memory system stores the behavioral sequences acquired through observational learning?
column4: Motor sequences learned by watching others are stored as procedural memories, though declarative (explicit) memory also plays a role in encoding the observed event.

column1: How does arousal level affect observational learning?
column3: Moderate arousal optimizes attention and encoding; very high or low arousal impairs it
column4: Consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law, optimal arousal is needed for the attentional step of observational learning to be effective.

column1: What role does the cerebellum play in observational learning?
column3: Coordinates motor reproduction of observed actions
column4: The cerebellum is involved in motor learning and timing; it helps translate mentally retained action sequences into smooth physical reproduction.

column1: Which lobe of the brain is most associated with visual processing required for observational learning?
column4: Initial visual processing of the model's actions occurs in the occipital lobe before information is relayed to parietal and frontal regions for encoding and planning.

column1: How does stress physiology (cortisol) affect observational learning?
column3: Chronic high cortisol impairs hippocampal memory consolidation
column4: Sustained stress elevates cortisol, which damages hippocampal neurons and impairs formation of the declarative memories needed to retain observed behaviors.

column1: What are mirror neurons?
column3: Neurons that fire both when performing and observing an action
column4: Discovered in macaque monkeys by Rizzolatti et al.; they activate during action execution and when watching another perform the same action, providing a neural basis for imitation.

column1: In which brain region were mirror neurons first discovered?
column4: Giacomo Rizzolatti's lab found mirror neurons in the ventral premotor cortex of macaques in the 1990s while studying motor planning.

column1: What human brain region is considered the homolog of the macaque mirror neuron area?
column4: The human inferior frontal gyrus (including Broca's area) and inferior parietal lobule show mirror-neuron-like activity on fMRI during action observation and execution.

column1: What cognitive function are mirror neurons hypothesized to support?
column3: Understanding others' intentions and actions (theory of mind/empathy)
column4: Mirror neurons are proposed to allow us to simulate others' actions internally, enabling imitation, empathy, and understanding of goal-directed behavior.

column1: What is the 'broken mirror' hypothesis?
column3: Autism spectrum disorder may involve mirror neuron dysfunction
column4: Some researchers propose that impaired mirror neuron activity underlies social deficits in ASD; however, this hypothesis remains controversial and not fully established.

column1: Do mirror neurons respond to all observed movements or only goal-directed ones?
column4: Mirror neurons in macaques fire selectively for purposeful actions (e.g., grasping food) but not random hand movements, suggesting they encode the intent behind an action.

column1: Mirror neurons are thought to provide the neural basis for which type of learning?
column4: Because mirror neurons activate when observing and performing actions, they are considered a plausible neural substrate for learning by watching others.

column1: What is vicarious emotion?
column3: Feeling an emotion by observing someone else experience it
column4: Also called empathic emotion; you feel fear, joy, or pain by watching another person undergo those experiences, without direct exposure to the stimulus.

column1: Which brain structure is central to processing vicarious fear?
column4: The amygdala activates when observing others in fearful situations, mirroring the response to direct threat and supporting empathic fear and vicarious conditioning.

column1: What is the anterior insula's role in vicarious emotions?
column4: The anterior insula activates both when experiencing pain/disgust and when watching others experience them, linking bodily states with empathic responses.

column1: Which prefrontal area is involved in regulating vicarious emotional responses?
column4: The mPFC helps distinguish self from other during empathic processing and modulates the intensity of vicarious emotions through top-down regulation.

column1: What is the anterior cingulate cortex's (ACC) role in vicarious pain?
column3: Activates during observed and experienced pain (affective component)
column4: The ACC encodes the unpleasant affective aspect of pain; neuroimaging shows it activates when we see someone else in pain, forming a key node in the empathy network.

column1: What neuroimaging technique most commonly demonstrates vicarious emotion neural correlates?
column4: fMRI measures blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals to show which brain regions activate during observation of others' emotional experiences.

column1: What distinguishes vicarious emotion from emotional contagion?
column3: Vicarious emotion preserves self-other distinction; emotional contagion does not
column4: In vicarious emotion, the observer knows they are reacting to another's state; emotional contagion involves automatic 'catching' of another's emotion without clear self-other boundary.

column1: How does observational learning explain the development of phobias?
column3: Watching someone react fearfully to a stimulus can condition vicarious fear
column4: A child who sees a parent panic around dogs may develop a dog phobia through observational fear conditioning, without ever being bitten.

column1: How does Bandura's social learning theory apply to the development of aggressive behavior in children?
column3: Children imitate aggression modeled by parents, peers, or media
column4: Bobo doll research showed that exposure to aggressive models increases children's aggressive behavior; this applies to real-world violence and media effects.

column1: How is observational learning used in behavioral therapy (e.g., modeling therapy)?
column3: Clients watch a model interact fearlessly with feared stimuli to reduce phobia
column4: Participant modeling (watching then doing with the therapist) is highly effective for specific phobias; it works via vicarious extinction of the fear response.

column1: What is self-efficacy, and how does observational learning affect it?
column3: Belief in one's ability to perform a behavior; boosted by watching similar others succeed
column4: Bandura identified vicarious experience (seeing peers succeed) as a major source of self-efficacy. Observing a similar model succeed raises the observer's own confidence.

column1: How does observational learning contribute to gender-role socialization?
column3: Children imitate same-sex models, adopting gender-typed behaviors
column4: Bandura's gender-role findings show children preferentially imitate same-gender models, learning culturally defined gender norms through social observation.

column1: What is the role of observational learning in the transmission of cultural norms?
column3: Individuals learn acceptable behaviors by observing and imitating community members
column4: Cultural practices, rituals, and social norms are passed across generations largely via observational learning rather than explicit instruction.

column1: What is 'abstract modeling' and how does it differ from behavioral modeling?
column3: Abstract modeling extracts general rules; behavioral modeling copies specific acts
column4: In abstract modeling, observers infer underlying principles (e.g., grammatical rules, moral standards) from multiple examples and apply them in novel contexts.

column1: Which concept explains why people avoid behaviors they have only seen punished, even without personal experience?
column4: Watching a model receive punishment is sufficient for an observer to suppress that behavior — a core application of observational learning in social and legal contexts.

column1: What does the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) describe?
column3: Two routes of persuasion: central and peripheral
column4: ELM proposes that attitude change occurs via a central (high elaboration) or peripheral (low elaboration) route depending on motivation and ability to process a message.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Which ELM route involves careful, critical evaluation of message arguments?
column4: The central route requires cognitive effort and results in more durable, resistant attitude change when the argument is strong.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Which ELM route relies on heuristics and superficial cues rather than argument quality?
column4: Peripheral processing uses cues like speaker attractiveness or credibility shortcuts; resulting attitudes are less stable and more susceptible to counter-persuasion.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What two factors determine which ELM route a person uses?
column3: Motivation and ability to process the message
column4: If a person lacks motivation (low personal relevance) or ability (distraction, low expertise), they default to the peripheral route.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: In ELM, attitude change via the central route is characterized as what relative to the peripheral route?
column3: More durable and resistant to change
column4: Deep cognitive elaboration creates stronger, more stable attitudes that better predict behavior over time.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: According to ELM, what happens to persuasion when argument quality is high and elaboration is high?
column3: Strong attitude change via central route
column4: High-quality arguments under high elaboration produce the most enduring attitude shifts; weak arguments under high elaboration actually boomerang, reducing persuasion.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: In ELM, an attractive spokesperson increases persuasion primarily through which route?
column4: Physical attractiveness is a peripheral cue — it signals liking without engaging argument evaluation.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What term describes the degree to which a person thinks about a persuasive message in ELM?
column4: Higher elaboration means deeper processing of argument content; ELM is named for this construct.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Who proposed the Elaboration Likelihood Model of persuasion?
column4: Richard Petty and John Cacioppo introduced ELM in the 1980s as a dual-process model of attitude change.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is the central concept of Social Cognitive Theory (SCT)?
column3: Behavior, cognition, and environment interact reciprocally (reciprocal determinism)
column4: Bandura's SCT holds that personal factors, behavior, and the environment continuously influence each other in a triadic reciprocal relationship.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Who developed Social Cognitive Theory?
column4: Bandura expanded social learning theory into SCT, emphasizing cognitive processes like self-efficacy and observational learning.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Define self-efficacy as used in Social Cognitive Theory.
column3: Belief in one's ability to perform a specific behavior
column4: High self-efficacy increases motivation and persistence; it is the most important SCT construct for predicting behavior change on the MCAT.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is observational learning (modeling) in SCT?
column3: Learning by watching others' behavior and its consequences
column4: Bandura's Bobo doll experiments demonstrated that children imitate aggressive behavior observed in models, even without direct reinforcement.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Name the four processes required for observational learning in SCT.
column4: A learner must notice (attention), remember (retention), be physically able to replicate (reproduction), and want to perform (motivation) the modeled behavior.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: In SCT, what is the term for the expected outcomes a person anticipates from a behavior?
column4: Distinct from self-efficacy (can I do it?), outcome expectations address the anticipated consequences (what will happen if I do it?).
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: How does vicarious reinforcement influence behavior in SCT?
column3: Observing others being rewarded increases likelihood of imitating that behavior
column4: Vicarious reinforcement is a core mechanism in SCT: rewards (or punishments) to a model alter an observer's motivation to replicate the behavior.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Which SCT construct refers to a person's global confidence in organizing and executing courses of action?
column4: Self-efficacy is behavior-specific, not a general trait — someone can have high self-efficacy for surgery but low self-efficacy for public speaking.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: In SCT, what distinguishes the concept of reciprocal determinism from simple stimulus-response behaviorism?
column3: Reciprocal determinism includes cognitive and environmental factors acting bidirectionally
column4: Unlike behaviorism's unidirectional S→R, SCT's reciprocal determinism posits that behavior also shapes the environment and personal cognitions, and vice versa.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is cognitive dissonance, and how does it drive attitude change?
column3: Discomfort from inconsistent cognitions motivates attitude or behavior change
column4: Festinger's theory: when behavior and attitude conflict, people alter one to reduce mental discomfort — a key mechanism for behavior-driven attitude change.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is the 'foot-in-the-door' technique?
column3: Getting compliance with a small request first to increase agreement with a larger request later
column4: Behavior change (agreeing to small request) shifts self-perception, making the person more likely to comply with larger subsequent requests.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What message characteristic is described by the term 'fear appeal'?
column3: A persuasive message that emphasizes negative consequences to motivate attitude change
column4: Fear appeals are most effective when paired with high self-efficacy messages; very high fear without efficacy information can cause reactance or denial.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Which source characteristic most strongly increases persuasiveness of a message?
column4: A highly credible source is more persuasive; on the MCAT, source credibility encompasses both perceived expertise and trustworthiness.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What target characteristic makes a person more susceptible to peripheral route persuasion?
column3: Low need for cognition or low personal relevance
column4: Individuals with low need for cognition (prefer simple over complex thinking) rely on peripheral cues rather than argument quality.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What social factor describes changing attitudes due to group norms and desire to conform?
column4: Normative influence drives attitude change to gain acceptance; informational influence changes attitudes because others are seen as knowledgeable.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is the sleeper effect in attitude change?
column3: A persuasive message from a low-credibility source becomes more effective over time as source is forgotten
column4: Initially discounted, the message content is remembered while the discounting cue (low-credibility source) fades, increasing persuasion after a delay.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is psychological reactance, and when does it occur?
column3: Resistance to persuasion when perceived freedom is threatened
column4: Brehm's reactance theory: if people feel coerced to change an attitude, they often move in the opposite direction to reassert autonomy.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What does the two-sided message approach involve in persuasion?
column3: Presenting both supporting and opposing arguments before refuting the opposition
column4: Two-sided messages (with refutation) are more persuasive than one-sided messages for audiences already aware of counterarguments; they also inoculate against later counter-persuasion.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is the Theory of Planned Behavior's key predictor of actual behavior?
column4: Ajzen's model holds that intention (shaped by attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control) is the most proximal determinant of behavior.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: In the Theory of Planned Behavior, what does 'subjective norm' refer to?
column3: Perceived social pressure to perform or not perform a behavior
column4: Subjective norms reflect beliefs about what important others think one should do, influencing behavioral intention.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is the 'door-in-the-face' technique?
column3: Making a large request first; after refusal, making the desired smaller request
column4: The contrast and reciprocal concession effects make the smaller request seem reasonable after the large request is declined.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is the primacy effect in persuasion?
column3: Information presented first has the greatest influence on attitude
column4: Primacy effect favors the first argument; recency effect (last argument remembered best) occurs when there is a delay before judgment. MCAT often tests this distinction.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What attitude change strategy involves inducing someone to argue against their own beliefs?
column4: Counterattitudinal advocacy creates cognitive dissonance, which motivates attitude change toward the position argued; used in role-playing interventions.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Category 8A of the MCAT focuses on which psychological construct?
column4: Category 8A covers self-concept, self-esteem, identity development, and related topics critical to understanding individual psychology.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Which MCAT content category addresses attitudes and beliefs affecting social interaction?
column4: Category 8B covers topics like prejudice, discrimination, stereotypes, and attribution, all of which shape how people interact socially.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: Which MCAT content category covers social interactions, including actions and processes such as cooperation, conflict, and communication?
column4: Category 8C includes social influence, group dynamics, and communication processes relevant to clinical and social contexts.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is the Transtheoretical Model's (Stages of Change) first stage?
column4: In precontemplation, the individual is not considering behavior change within the next 6 months; they may be unaware of the problem or resistant.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: List the five stages of the Transtheoretical Model of behavior change in order.
column4: Each stage represents readiness to change; relapse is possible, making the model cyclical rather than strictly linear.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What is inoculation theory in the context of attitude change?
column3: Exposing people to weak counter-arguments to make attitudes more resistant to future persuasion
column4: Like a vaccine, small doses of opposition help people develop counter-arguments, strengthening the original attitude against stronger future attacks.
column5: Theories of Attitude and Behavior Change

column1: What term describes an individual's subjective sense of who they are, encompassing roles, values, and group memberships?
column4: Self-concept is the cognitive representation of oneself and includes various identities such as racial, gender, and class identities that shape how a person sees themselves.

column1: What type of identity refers to a person's membership in a racial or ethnic group, often shaped by culture, ancestry, and shared history?
column4: Racial and ethnic identity is a key component of self-concept; it influences social experiences and can be a source of pride or stigma depending on societal context.

column1: What type of identity reflects an individual's internal sense of being male, female, both, neither, or another gender?
column4: Gender identity is distinct from biological sex and sexual orientation; it is largely considered a stable internal sense of one's own gender, though it can be fluid.

column1: What term describes the identity dimension related to an individual's enduring emotional, romantic, or sexual attraction to others?
column4: Sexual orientation identity (e.g., heterosexual, homosexual, bisexual) is distinct from sexual behavior; it is part of the broader self-concept and influenced by social and biological factors.

column1: What type of identity refers to how individuals define themselves in relation to their economic position in society?
column4: Class identity encompasses perceptions of one's socioeconomic status (SES) and can affect access to resources, health outcomes, and social interactions.

column1: What term describes an individual's internalized sense of their own age-related roles and characteristics?
column4: Age identity can differ from chronological age; people may identify as younger or older than their actual age, and age norms shape expected behaviors at different life stages.

column1: What concept describes the overlapping and interdependent nature of multiple social identities (e.g., race, gender, class) and their combined effect on experience?
column4: Coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw, intersectionality explains that identities do not operate in isolation — combinations of race, gender, and class create unique patterns of privilege or discrimination.

column1: According to social identity theory, what motivates individuals to favor their own group (in-group) over other groups (out-groups)?
column3: Desire for positive self-esteem / positive social identity
column4: Tajfel and Turner's social identity theory posits that people categorize themselves into groups and enhance self-esteem by viewing their in-group favorably relative to out-groups.

column1: What process describes how individuals internalize and integrate their racial or ethnic identity over time, often following stages of exploration and commitment?
column4: Models such as Cross's Black Identity Development model describe stages from pre-encounter (little awareness) to internalization (secure, positive racial identity) relevant to minority groups.

column1: What psychological term describes the stress experienced by individuals whose sexual orientation identity conflicts with societal or family expectations?
column4: Minority stress theory (Meyer) holds that stigma, prejudice, and discrimination create chronic stressors for LGBTQ+ individuals that contribute to elevated rates of mental health problems.

column1: What term refers to the process by which individuals attribute different characteristics or roles to people based on their age group?
column4: Ageism involves prejudice or discrimination based on age; it can negatively affect older adults' self-concept and health outcomes through stereotype threat and social marginalization.

column1: What is the distinction between gender identity and gender expression?
column3: Identity is internal sense; expression is outward presentation
column4: Gender identity is one's private experience of their own gender, while gender expression refers to how that identity is communicated externally through clothing, behavior, and appearance — the two need not align.

column1: What concept describes the phenomenon where awareness of a negative stereotype about one's group impairs performance on tasks related to that stereotype?
column4: Stereotype threat (Steele & Aronson) can affect individuals across racial, gender, age, and class identities; the anxiety of confirming a negative group stereotype undermines actual performance.

column1: What term distinguishes an individual's self-identified class position from their objective socioeconomic status as measured by income, education, and occupation?
column3: Subjective class identity vs. objective SES
column4: People often misidentify their class; many middle- and working-class individuals in the US identify as 'middle class.' This discrepancy affects political attitudes, health behaviors, and social comparisons.

column1: What psychological defense mechanism involves individuals from a stigmatized group distancing themselves from their own group to avoid negative stereotypes?
column4: Disidentification occurs when a person detaches self-esteem from performance in a domain stereotyped as weak for their group (e.g., women disidentifying with math ability) to protect overall self-concept.

column1: What term describes the internalization of society's negative attitudes about one's own marginalized identity group?
column4: Internalized oppression occurs when members of stigmatized groups (e.g., racial minorities, LGBTQ+ individuals) accept and apply societal prejudices to themselves, harming self-concept and mental health.

column1: In Erikson's psychosocial stages, which stage is primarily associated with the formation of a coherent personal identity?
column4: During this stage, adolescents explore different roles and integrate aspects of gender, ethnic, and social identities into a stable self-concept; failure leads to role confusion and identity diffusion.

column1: According to Erikson, what is the central crisis of adolescence (Stage 5)?
column4: Erikson's fifth psychosocial stage occurs during adolescence; successful resolution produces a coherent sense of self.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term did Erikson use for the period of exploration before identity commitment?
column4: A moratorium allows adolescents to try out roles and ideologies without committing permanently, facilitating identity formation.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: James Marcia described four identity statuses. Name the status characterized by commitment without exploration.
column4: Foreclosed individuals adopt an identity (often parental) without exploring alternatives; common in authoritarian family structures.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: In Marcia's framework, which identity status involves neither exploration nor commitment?
column4: Diffusion is the least mature status; individuals show little concern about identity and no active exploration.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: Which of Kohlberg's levels of moral development corresponds to reasoning based on social contracts and universal principles?
column4: Post-conventional morality (Stages 5-6) emphasizes abstract principles over rules or social approval; it defines one's moral identity.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: According to Freud's psychosexual theory, during which stage does the Oedipus/Electra complex occur and gender identity begins solidifying?
column4: Resolution of the Oedipus/Electra complex via identification with the same-sex parent is a key mechanism for gender identity formation in Freudian theory.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What does Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner) propose as the basis of one's social identity?
column4: People derive part of their self-concept from belonging to groups (ingroup), often boosting self-esteem through favorable intergroup comparisons.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: Kohlberg's Stage 3 moral reasoning is characterized by what primary motivation?
column4: Stage 3 (conventional) involves conforming to social norms and seeking approval from others, linking moral reasoning to social identity.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: In Marcia's identity status model, which status involves active exploration with no commitment yet made?
column4: Moratorium individuals are in crisis, actively exploring options; this status often precedes identity achievement.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the term for Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg — arguing his theory was biased toward whose moral reasoning?
column4: Gilligan argued Kohlberg's justice-based model undervalued care-based moral reasoning more common in women, influencing gender identity research.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::theories-of-identity-development-e-g-gender-moral-psychosexual-social MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What social process involves learning the norms, values, and roles of one's society, shaping identity?
column4: Socialization is the lifelong process through which individuals acquire culture and form their social identity via family, peers, media, and institutions.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: Which social factor most strongly predicts identity formation in early childhood?
column4: Parents are the primary agents of socialization; their values, attachment styles, and expectations heavily shape a child's early identity.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the term for the process by which individuals adopt the identity, values, and behaviors of a dominant group?
column4: Assimilation involves minority group members taking on the cultural identity of the majority group, often at the cost of their original identity.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: How does socioeconomic status (SES) influence identity formation?
column3: Shapes access to resources, roles, and opportunities
column4: Low SES limits educational and occupational options, constraining identity exploration; high SES broadens opportunity and role experimentation.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What concept describes the stress and identity conflict experienced by individuals navigating two cultural identities?
column4: Acculturative stress arises when immigrants or minorities must reconcile their heritage identity with a new dominant culture's demands.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: Which social institution acts as a secondary agent of socialization and strongly influences peer-based identity?
column4: Schools expose children to peer groups, authority structures, and achievement norms outside the family, broadening identity development.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes the identity threat that occurs when one's social group is negatively stereotyped?
column4: Stereotype threat can cause individuals to internalize negative group labels, undermining performance and identity coherence in affected domains.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What social factor during adolescence often supersedes parental influence in identity formation?
column4: Peer influence peaks in adolescence; peers provide comparison standards, norms, and belonging that shape values, style, and self-concept.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-social-factors-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the 'looking-glass self' concept and who proposed it?
column3: Self-concept formed from others' perceived judgments; Charles Cooley
column4: Cooley's looking-glass self has three elements: imagining how we appear to others, imagining their judgment, and developing self-feeling (pride or shame) based on that judgment.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What process involves observing and copying another person's behavior to shape one's own identity?
column4: Bandura's social learning theory emphasizes imitation of role models; children imitate parents and peers, internalizing behaviors into their self-concept.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is role-taking in the context of identity development?
column3: Mentally adopting another's perspective to understand social expectations
column4: G.H. Mead described role-taking as essential to developing the 'self'; by imagining others' viewpoints, individuals learn how to behave in social roles.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: According to Mead, what is the 'generalized other'?
column3: The collective attitudes and expectations of society as a whole
column4: Mead proposed that mature identity requires internalizing the generalized other — not just specific individuals, but broader societal norms.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: In Mead's theory, what are the 'I' and 'Me' components of the self?
column4: The 'I' is the impulsive, creative aspect; the 'Me' is the internalized social standards one uses to regulate behavior — together they form the complete self.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the term for copying behaviors of high-status or admired individuals to shape identity?
column4: Identification goes beyond mere imitation — the individual fully internalizes the model's values and traits as part of their own identity (e.g., Freudian identification with same-sex parent).
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What three elements make up Cooley's looking-glass self?
column3: Perception of appearance to others, perception of their judgment, emotional response (pride/shame)
column4: All three steps are required; the emotional response — pride or shame — is the mechanism by which others' perceived judgments alter the self-concept.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: In Bandura's model, what cognitive factor allows an individual to regulate identity-relevant behavior without direct imitation?
column4: Self-efficacy — belief in one's capability — mediates whether observed behaviors are adopted; high self-efficacy supports identity exploration and commitment.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-individuals-e-g-imitation-looking-glass-self-role-taking MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is a reference group?
column3: A group used as a standard for self-evaluation and identity comparison
column4: Reference groups can be membership groups (groups one belongs to) or aspirational groups (groups one wishes to join); both shape self-concept and behavior norms.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-groups-e-g-reference-group MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the difference between a normative and a comparative reference group?
column3: Normative sets standards of conduct; comparative provides benchmarks for self-assessment
column4: Normative reference groups supply norms (rules to follow); comparative reference groups supply comparison points (e.g., 'Am I successful compared to my peers?').
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-groups-e-g-reference-group MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes the tendency to conform one's identity and behavior to the expectations of a group one aspires to join?
column4: Anticipatory socialization occurs when individuals begin adopting the values and norms of a reference group before actually joining it.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-groups-e-g-reference-group MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is an ingroup vs. an outgroup in social identity theory?
column3: Ingroup = group one belongs to; outgroup = group one does not belong to
column4: Ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation arise from the need to maintain positive social identity; these dynamics shape intergroup behavior and self-concept.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-groups-e-g-reference-group MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What psychological phenomenon occurs when individuals lose their personal identity within a group and follow group norms?
column4: Deindividuation can reduce personal accountability and shift identity from individual to group-defined, sometimes leading to antisocial behavior.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-groups-e-g-reference-group MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: How does group cohesion affect individual identity?
column3: High cohesion strengthens group identity, may suppress individuality
column4: In highly cohesive groups, members' self-concepts merge with group identity; this can produce conformity pressure and groupthink.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-groups-e-g-reference-group MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is social comparison theory, and who proposed it?
column3: People evaluate themselves by comparing to others; Leon Festinger
column4: Festinger (1954) proposed that in the absence of objective standards, individuals use social comparisons — upward (to those better off) or downward (to those worse off) — to assess their abilities and opinions.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-groups-e-g-reference-group MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the primary agent of socialization responsible for transmitting culture and basic identity in childhood?
column4: The family transmits language, values, religious beliefs, and social roles first; it is considered the most influential socializing agent in early development.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes a culture that emphasizes individual goals and autonomy over group harmony?
column4: In individualistic cultures (e.g., U.S., Western Europe), identity is defined by personal achievement and uniqueness; contrasts with collectivistic cultures where group membership defines self.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is enculturation?
column3: The process of learning one's own culture's norms and values
column4: Enculturation occurs throughout life via family, language, religion, and media; it shapes the cultural component of personal identity.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the difference between enculturation and acculturation?
column3: Enculturation = learning one's native culture; acculturation = adapting to a new/different culture
column4: Enculturation is the primary socialization into one's birth culture; acculturation occurs when individuals encounter and adapt to a second culture.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: Which socialization agent is particularly influential in transmitting gender roles and societal norms in adolescence?
column4: Media portrayals of gender, race, and success provide powerful cultural scripts that adolescents internalize as part of their social identity.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is resocialization, and in what setting does it most dramatically occur?
column3: Replacing old identity with new norms; total institutions (e.g., prisons, military)
column4: Erving Goffman described total institutions as environments that strip prior identity and systematically rebuild a new one through rigid schedules and rituals.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What concept from symbolic interactionism holds that the self is constructed through social interaction and shared cultural symbols?
column4: Symbolic interactionists argue that meaning — including the meaning of 'self' — arises from social interaction using shared cultural symbols like language.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: Name the four Berry acculturation strategies.
column4: Integration (biculturalism) is associated with best psychological outcomes; marginalization (rejecting both cultures) is associated with the worst identity outcomes.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is gender socialization?
column3: Learning culturally appropriate gender roles through social interaction
column4: Gender socialization begins at birth via toys, clothing, and language; family, peers, and media reinforce gendered behaviors that become part of gender identity.
column8: concept::PS::8A::formation_of_identity MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8A::formation-of-identity::influence-of-culture-and-socialization-on-identity-formation MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the fundamental attribution error (FAE)?
column4: When judging others' behavior, people tend to attribute it to stable personality traits while ignoring situational pressures. Classic demo: assuming a nervous speaker is an anxious person, ignoring their stage-fright context.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: Which type of attribution assigns behavior to internal, stable traits of a person?
column4: Dispositional attributions link behavior to character, ability, or personality. Contrasted with situational attributions that point to external circumstances.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: Which type of attribution assigns behavior to external circumstances or context?
column4: Situational attributions recognize that environment, social pressure, or chance can drive behavior rather than the person's character.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the actor-observer bias in attribution?
column3: Actors attribute own behavior situationally; observers attribute it dispositionally
column4: When we are the actor we notice situational constraints, but as observers of others we default to character explanations — an extension of the FAE that applies to self vs. other asymmetry.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the self-serving bias in attribution?
column3: Taking credit for successes (internal), blaming failures on situation (external)
column4: People protect self-esteem by attributing good outcomes to ability/effort and bad outcomes to bad luck or difficult circumstances. It is the opposite of how we judge others.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: How do individualist cultures differ from collectivist cultures in attribution tendency?
column3: Individualist: more dispositional; collectivist: more situational
column4: Western individualist cultures emphasize personal agency, increasing FAE. East Asian collectivist cultures attend more to context and relationships, reducing dispositional bias.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What are the three dimensions of Weiner's attribution model?
column4: Weiner's model is used to explain achievement outcomes. For example, failing due to low ability = internal, stable, uncontrollable — predicts helplessness; failing due to lack of effort = internal, unstable, controllable — predicts motivation to try harder.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the correspondence bias, and how does it relate to the FAE?
column3: Tendency to infer stable traits from single observed behaviors; essentially synonymous with FAE
column4: Correspondence bias emphasizes the inferential leap from one behavior to a broad, enduring disposition — observers 'correspond' the act directly to character even when situational factors are salient.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the just-world hypothesis in the context of attribution?
column3: Belief that people get what they deserve; blaming victims
column4: Believing the world is fair leads people to make dispositional attributions for victims' misfortune (e.g., 'she must have done something wrong'), preserving the illusion of a just world.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What psychological concept describes judging others more harshly when we see their flaws reflected in ourselves?
column4: When individuals are unaware of their own negative traits, they may project those traits onto others and judge them harshly — linking self-perception to perception of others.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is social projection in the context of self-perception and perceiving others?
column3: Assuming others share our own attitudes, traits, or behaviors
column4: People tend to see their own characteristics as common and normal, projecting their internal states onto others — 'false consensus effect' is a related concept.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the false consensus effect?
column3: Overestimating how many others share our own beliefs or behaviors
column4: Because our social circle tends to agree with us, we generalize that agreement to the broader population. It biases perception of others based on our own self-view.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: How does high self-esteem influence perceptions of others' abilities?
column3: High self-esteem individuals tend to rate others more positively
column4: Secure self-concept reduces threat from others' competence, so high-self-esteem individuals show less derogation of outgroups and perceive others more charitably.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the spotlight effect, and how does it relate to self-perception affecting social judgment?
column3: Overestimating how much others notice and evaluate us
column4: Because we are acutely aware of our own appearance/actions, we assume others attend to us as much as we attend to ourselves — a self-perception distortion that shapes social interaction.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What attribution style do individuals with depressive self-perceptions tend to apply to others' failures?
column3: Internal, stable, global attributions (similar to their own negative self-attribution)
column4: Depressive attributional style involves seeing bad events as caused by permanent, pervasive internal factors. This lens can also color how depressed individuals interpret others' setbacks.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the false uniqueness effect, and how does it contrast with false consensus?
column3: Underestimating how many others share our positive abilities or virtues
column4: While false consensus applies to common opinions/behaviors, false uniqueness applies to special skills — people see their talents as rarer than they are, bolstering self-image.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What environmental perception principle states that we infer others' dispositions from the situation they are placed in, even when the situation was assigned?
column3: Correspondent inference / FAE with situational priming
column4: Even knowing someone was assigned a role (e.g., quiz-show host), observers still attribute superior knowledge to that person — demonstrating how perceived environment shapes dispositional inference.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is priming in the context of social perception of others?
column3: Prior environmental stimuli activate related mental schemas, biasing judgments of others
column4: Exposure to hostile words primes an aggressive schema; subsequently ambiguous behavior by another person is more likely to be interpreted as hostile — environment shapes person perception.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the halo effect in person perception?
column3: One positive trait leads to overall positive evaluation of a person
column4: Environmental or contextual cues (e.g., attractive appearance, prestigious setting) trigger a global positive impression that colors perception of unrelated traits like competence or honesty.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: How does the physical environment (e.g., crowded vs. spacious) influence attributions about others' behavior?
column3: Crowding/stress cues increase situational attributions for negative behavior
column4: Observers who know someone is in an aversive environment (noise, crowding) are more likely to attribute that person's irritability to the situation rather than their character.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the concept of behavioral confirmation (self-fulfilling prophecy) in social perception?
column3: Perceiver expectations shape interactions, eliciting behavior that confirms the expectation
column4: If a perceiver believes someone is unfriendly (due to environmental stereotype), they act coldly, causing the target to respond coldly — environment-based expectation alters actual behavior.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is thin-slicing in person perception?
column3: Accurate judgments of others made from very brief environmental/behavioral samples
column4: Research shows short clips (seconds) predict outcomes like teacher effectiveness. The environment provides rapid cues that the perceiver integrates into impressions with surprising accuracy.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is the contrast effect in social perception, and how does prior environmental context cause it?
column3: Judging a target as more/less extreme due to prior contrasting stimuli
column4: After seeing very attractive faces, an average face is rated less attractive. Prior environmental exposure sets an anchor that distorts subsequent person judgments via contrast.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is construal level theory's prediction about psychological distance and dispositional attribution?
column3: Greater psychological distance increases dispositional (abstract) attributions
column4: When events feel distant (far future, different place), we think more abstractly and attribute behavior to stable traits. Close, concrete situations promote situational attributions.
column5: Attributing Behavior to Persons or Situations

column1: What is prejudice?
column3: Negative attitude toward a group member
column4: Prejudice is an unjustified or incorrect attitude (usually negative) toward an individual based solely on their group membership. It has affective, cognitive, and behavioral components.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::processes-that-contribute-to-prejudice MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What social process involves placing individuals into categories and attributing group traits to them?
column4: Social categorization is the cognitive tendency to sort people into in-groups and out-groups, which is a foundational process leading to stereotyping and prejudice.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::processes-that-contribute-to-prejudice MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes the tendency to favor one's own group over out-groups?
column4: In-group bias leads people to evaluate in-group members more positively and allocate more resources to them, a key mechanism in the development of prejudice.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::processes-that-contribute-to-prejudice MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What process involves learning prejudiced attitudes through observation of others?
column4: Children and adults acquire prejudiced attitudes by observing prejudice expressed by parents, peers, and media, consistent with Bandura's social learning theory.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::processes-that-contribute-to-prejudice MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What phenomenon occurs when competition over scarce resources increases hostility between groups?
column4: Sherif's Robbers Cave experiment demonstrated that intergroup competition for limited resources generates prejudice and hostility, which cooperation can reduce.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::processes-that-contribute-to-prejudice MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: Which theory holds that prejudice results from using out-groups as targets for frustration?
column4: When people cannot vent frustration at its true cause, they displace aggression onto a weaker out-group, fueling prejudice and discrimination.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::processes-that-contribute-to-prejudice MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What contact condition, identified by Allport, is necessary for intergroup contact to reduce prejudice?
column4: Allport's contact hypothesis states that prejudice decreases when groups interact on equal footing, with common goals, institutional support, and cooperative rather than competitive aims.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::processes-that-contribute-to-prejudice MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is social prestige in sociological terms?
column3: Honor or esteem granted by society to a social position
column4: Max Weber distinguished prestige (status honor) from wealth (class) and power, forming his three-component model of social stratification.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::power-prestige-and-class-soc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: According to Weber, what are the three components of social stratification?
column4: Weber's tripartite model separates economic class, social honor/prestige, and political power as distinct but interrelated dimensions of inequality.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::power-prestige-and-class-soc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What sociological term describes the overall rank of an individual combining wealth, prestige, and power?
column4: SES integrates income, occupational prestige, and education to measure one's position in the social hierarchy; low SES correlates with numerous health disparities.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::power-prestige-and-class-soc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is meant by 'power' in Weber's model of stratification?
column3: Ability to achieve goals despite resistance of others
column4: Power refers to the capacity to impose one's will in social relations; it can derive from economic, political, or other forms of social authority.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::power-prestige-and-class-soc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes a situation in which an individual's ranks on different status dimensions are inconsistent?
column4: A person with high education but low income exemplifies status inconsistency; this can cause stress and motivate advocacy for social change.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::power-prestige-and-class-soc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What type of prestige is ascribed to an occupation based on its social importance and required education?
column4: Surveys consistently rank physicians, lawyers, and scientists near the top of occupational prestige scales, reflecting the MCAT-relevant link between education, income, and social standing.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::power-prestige-and-class-soc MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What emotion is most consistently linked to the development and maintenance of prejudice toward out-groups?
column4: Intergroup fear and disgust are strongly predictive of prejudice; the amygdala mediates threat-based evaluations of out-group faces, reflecting the biological basis of emotional prejudice.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-emotion-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What emotional state, arising from perceived group inequity, can fuel prejudice toward higher-status groups?
column4: Envy toward higher-status out-groups can manifest as hostile prejudice, whereas pity toward lower-status groups involves paternalistic prejudice, per the stereotype content model.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-emotion-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What model links stereotyped warmth and competence to distinct emotional prejudices?
column4: Groups seen as high-competence/low-warmth elicit envy; low-competence/high-warmth elicit pity; low-competence/low-warmth elicit contempt; high-competence/high-warmth elicit admiration.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-emotion-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes the emotional discomfort felt during interracial interactions that can reinforce avoidance and prejudice?
column4: Intergroup anxiety leads people to avoid contact with out-group members, thereby preventing the corrective experiences that could reduce prejudice.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-emotion-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the affective component of prejudice?
column3: Emotional feeling (e.g., dislike, fear, contempt) toward a group
column4: Prejudice has three components: affective (feelings), cognitive (beliefs/stereotypes), and behavioral (discrimination). The affective component drives much of its persistence.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-emotion-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What cognitive shortcut involves applying group-level beliefs to individual group members?
column4: Stereotyping is the cognitive component of prejudice. It involves overgeneralizing traits of a group to each of its members, saving cognitive effort but causing bias.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-cognition-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes the tendency to see out-group members as more similar to each other than in-group members?
column4: 'They all look alike' reflects out-group homogeneity; we perceive greater variability within our own group, which facilitates stereotyping of out-groups.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-cognition-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What cognitive bias involves seeking and interpreting information in ways that confirm existing stereotypes?
column4: People notice and remember stereotype-consistent information and discount inconsistent evidence, making prejudiced beliefs resistant to change.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-cognition-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What phenomenon occurs when a minority group member inadvertently confirms a negative group stereotype, causing anxiety that impairs performance?
column4: Claude Steele's research showed that invoking a negative stereotype (e.g., 'women are worse at math') before a test reduces performance for in-group members, demonstrating the cognitive-emotional impact of prejudice.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-cognition-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What cognitive error leads people to attribute a single positive out-group member's behavior to an exception rather than updating the stereotype?
column4: When an out-group member disconfirms a stereotype, people often 'subtype' them as an exceptional individual rather than revising the broader stereotype.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-cognition-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is illusory correlation in the context of prejudice?
column3: Perceiving a relationship between minority group membership and rare negative behaviors
column4: Because both minority group members and unusual behaviors are rare (and thus salient), people overestimate their co-occurrence, creating biased associations.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::the-role-of-cognition-in-prejudice-psy MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is a stereotype?
column3: Oversimplified generalized belief about a social group
column4: Stereotypes are the cognitive component of prejudice. They can be positive or negative but are problematic when rigidly applied to individuals regardless of actual traits.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stereotypes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What type of stereotype threat occurs when a person is aware of a negative stereotype but fears confirming it?
column4: Stereotype threat was documented by Steele and Aronson (1995) with African-American students on GRE-like tests; reducing salience of the stereotype improved performance.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stereotypes MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes the automatic activation of a stereotype upon perceiving a group member?
column4: Implicit Association Tests (IAT) measure automatic stereotype activation; these operate below conscious awareness and can conflict with explicitly held egalitarian beliefs.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stereotypes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the 'kernel of truth' hypothesis regarding stereotypes?
column3: Stereotypes may contain a small basis in real group differences
column4: Some stereotypes arise from actual (often statistically small) group differences, but they are exaggerated and misapplied, making the 'kernel of truth' a weak defense of stereotyping.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stereotypes MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is benevolent sexism as it relates to stereotypes?
column3: Positive but paternalistic stereotypes that limit women's roles
column4: Unlike hostile sexism, benevolent sexism portrays women as pure, warm, and in need of male protection. Both forms reinforce gender hierarchy and are measured by the Ambivalent Sexism Inventory.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stereotypes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is the self-fulfilling prophecy in the context of stereotypes?
column3: A belief that causes behavior confirming the belief
column4: When teachers expect less of certain students, they interact with them differently, leading to lower performance that 'confirms' the initial stereotype — Rosenthal's Pygmalion effect.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stereotypes MCAT::difficulty::hard synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is stigma in sociology?
column3: Deeply discrediting attribute that reduces a person to a spoiled identity
column4: Goffman (1963) defined stigma as a mark that disqualifies a person from full social acceptance, creating a discrepancy between actual and virtual social identity.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stigma-soc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What are Goffman's three types of stigma?
column3: Abominations of the body, tribal stigma, blemishes of character
column4: Goffman classified stigma into physical deformities, group-based stigma (race, ethnicity, religion), and character flaws (mental illness, addiction, imprisonment).
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stigma-soc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is a 'discreditable' stigma according to Goffman?
column3: A hidden stigma not immediately apparent to others
column4: Unlike a 'discredited' stigma that is already known, a discreditable stigma (e.g., a hidden illness) requires information management — the person can choose whether to disclose or 'pass.'
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stigma-soc MCAT::difficulty::medium synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What term describes an unearned negative label applied to those with mental illness that reduces treatment-seeking?
column4: Structural and social stigma against mental illness leads to discrimination, self-stigma, and reduced likelihood of seeking care — a major public health concern tested on the MCAT.
column8: concept::PS::8B::prejudice_and_bias MCAT::section::PS MCAT::8B::prejudice-and-bias::stigma-soc MCAT::difficulty::easy synapse::demo-content MCAT::discipline::PSY MCAT::discipline::SOC

column1: What is courtesy stigma (stigma by association)?
column3: Stigma extended to those associated with a stigmatized person
